en: Table of Contents for the Sections and Subjects of the *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā*:
General Definition of Varṇasphoṭa; The Category of Sphoṭa.
The conceptual nature of bases, suffixes, and so forth;
an investigation into the denotative capacity of substituends and other elements; and the definition of linguistic power (*śakti*).
The varieties of linguistic usage; the Nyāya school's position; the establishment of expressive power (śakti) in corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa).
The failure to define causality:
the Naiyāyika position and the author’s own position.
The definition of correctness;
the statement from the *Vākyapadīya*; and an investigation into the formation of case-endings (*sub*) in vernacular words.
The threefold nature of power,
the definition and etymology of *lakṣaṇā*,
and the respective views on those matters.
The twofold nature of the definition; the twofold nature of the definition by way of another method; and the definition of fitness.
The author of the *Prakāśa* states that there are two types of pure [superimposition]:
"the ox is a Vāhīka."
In this regard, there is the view of the Navyas,
the view of the Kuvalayānanda, and the view of the Mīmāṃsakas.
The explanation of the phonemes is concluded;
the investigation into the function of words has been treated in detail in the *Jippaṇī*.
An investigation into the meaning of verbal roots: the view of the Guru and the view of Maṇḍanamiśra.
The view of the ancient Naiyāyikas; an investigation into the view of the moderns regarding the meaning of the verbal root; the refutation of the view of the modern Mīmāṃsakas.
The definition of intransitivity and transitivity;
an investigation into the general meaning of particles; and the refutation of the Naiyāyika position.
The detailed exposition of the meaning of particles according to the grammarians' view, including an investigation into the meaning of the negative particle *nañ*, is contained in the commentary.
The Navya-mata [is presented] as an investigation into the meaning of the particle *eva*;
the investigation into the meaning of the particle *eva* is found in the *ṭippaṇī*.
In this regard, the detailed examination of the views of the modern Naiyāyikas is intended for the purpose of enumeration in the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*).
An investigation into the meaning of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*); its detailed exposition is in the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*), while the view of the Naiyāyikas is in the root text (*mūla*).

An investigation into the meaning of the term "anabhihite" [is presented], as well as the demonstration that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) denotes both the effort and the fruit [of the action], and the refutation of the view that words such as "tat" possess multiple meanings, as discussed in the *Ṭippaṇī*.
The Mīmāṃsaka position, its justification in the commentary,
and an investigation into the meaning of the mantra "aruṇyā piṅgākṣyā" [are presented].
The justification for that is in the commentary;
[it includes] an investigation into the meaning of the mantra "aruṇayā piṅgākṣyā," and the justification for that is in the commentary.
The justification for that is in the commentary;
this follows the maxim "the cause of that is in the commentary," and one should not speak untruth.
The details thereof are in the *Ṭippaṇī*; in the root text is the view of Bhaṭṭa,
while in the *Ṭippaṇī* is the manifold nature of the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*).

In the main text (mūla), there is an investigation of the Navya-mata school; in the commentary (ṭippaṇī), there is an examination of the meaning of the rule *supa ātmanaḥ* and an analysis of the meanings of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) such as present time and so forth.
The manner of its inclusion, the definitions,
the view of the Neo-Naiyāyikas, and the view of the Ultra-Neo-Naiyāyikas.
In the *Ṭippaṇī*, there is an investigation into the nature of the *takranyāya* (the maxim of the curd), the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as prescribed by injunctions and other rules,
and the definition of its instigating character (*pravartakatva*).
An Examination of the Jyotiṣṭoma Sacrifice;
A Refutation of the Mīmāṃsaka View; A Reconciliation with the Bhagavadgītā.
An investigation into the authority of explanatory passages (arthavāda),
an investigation into the meaning of verbal suffixes such as the present participle (san), and an investigation into the meaning of primary nominal suffixes (kṛt).
The refutation of the views of the Neo-Naiyāyikas;
an investigation into the denotation of action according to the *Ṭippaṇī*; and an elaboration on the meaning of the suffix *tumun* according to the *Ṭippaṇī*.
In the *Ṭippaṇī*, there is an elaboration on the meaning of the suffix *-tumun*:
the view of the Naiyāyikas and the view of the modern Naiyāyikas.
The investigation of the meaning of the name Harimata,
with its detailed exposition in the commentary (ṭippaṇī).
In the root text, there is the definition of "being an indicator" (*upalakṣaṇatva*);
in the commentary, there is an investigation of the maxim "that which has not apprehended the qualifier" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇā*) and the theory of the "crooked power" (*kubjaśaktivāda*).
In the *Ṭippaṇī*, its essential nature, the presentation of Bhaṭṭa’s view,
and the investigations according to the perspectives of various teachers [are discussed].
In the *ṭippaṇī*, there is an examination of the authority of the *svarūpa-sūtra*, a citation of the words of the author of the *bhāṣya*,
and an analysis of gender according to the perspective of the grammarians (*śābdika*).
An investigation into whether number constitutes the meaning of a nominal stem;
an extraction of the meanings of nouns in the commentary;
and an inquiry into the difference or non-difference between an imitation and its object of imitation.
An examination of the views of the Neo-Naiyāyikas regarding past objects such as fire,
and an investigation into the meaning of the expression "He says, 'Gauḥ'."
An investigation into the meaning of the Vedic injunction "One should sacrifice with the udbhid," an exposition of the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine,
and the fact that the repetition of words is sometimes not a defect.
In the *Ṭippaṇī*: the status of even a word as the object of verbal cognition;
an investigation into the apprehension of power (*śakti*) in all names; and the justification for the apprehension of power in the case of the *apūrva*.
An investigation into the denotative capacity of words such as "hare-marked" (the moon),
an investigation into the meaning of case-suffixes,
and the meaning of the nominative case.
In the *Ṭippaṇī*, there is an investigation into the meaning of the vocative case;
the meaning of the accusative as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*); and a refinement of the concept of the object (*karman*) in the *Ṭippaṇī*.
The twofold nature of action, the delineation of its two types of objects,
and examples thereof.
Refutation of the Naiyāyika view;
the Mīmāṃsaka view; and the determination of the meaning of the accusative case-ending as a secondary word.
The meaning of the third case in *kāraka* is the sense of the agent; the meaning of the third case in *upapada* is the sense of the subordinate word.
The meaning of the dative case as denoting the agent is the opinion of Śūlapāṇi; it is a more recent view.

The manner of verbal cognition regarding various examples; the exposition of the fourth case ending used with a governing word (*upapada-caturthī*); and an investigation of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*).
In the *Ṭippaṇī*, there is an examination of various views,
an analysis of the compound in the rule "janikartuḥ," and an explanation of the ablative case used for a *upapada*.
The explanation of the meaning of the genitive case is in the commentary; its detailed exposition and the investigation of the meaning of the locative case follow.
The determination of whether number is intended to be expressed;
following the discussion of number, the explanation of when the subject and the predicate are intended to be expressed or not;
and the semantic power of compounds.
In the *Ṭippaṇī*, its specific detail—
the investigation into the category of difference (*bhedapadārtha*)— is the opinion of the author of the *Pradīpa*.
The Mīmāṃsaka view in the commentary;
the discussion on *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) in the commentary;
and the analysis of the compound *niṣādasthapati* in the commentary.
The definition of *jahatsvārtha*,
the doctrine of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), and the definition of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*).
If a compound is meaningless, how is the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) established?
In the *ṭippaṇī*, the meaning of the word "sāhitya" is discussed,
followed by the presentation of the views of the Alaṅkārikas regarding the subject of the non-consideration of the predicate.
An investigation into the meaning of the word *puṣpavantau*; a presentation of Harikārikā;
an investigation into [the rule concerning] *aruṇayā* and so forth.
The Mīmāṃsaka view—
that the composition of the meaning of the word *durupapāda* as stated in the Bhāṣya is difficult to justify— is that *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) occurs only in a compound (*vṛtti*).

Even in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, there is *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning); the purpose of *ekaśeṣa* is not redundant; in *ekaśeṣa*, there is merely the notion of association (*sāhitya*).
In the absence of an understanding of literary genres, there is the technical usage [of the term *tantra*];
in the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*), there is an investigation of Harikārikā; and in the commentary, there is an analysis of the meaning of the sentence beginning with "kapiñjalān."
The presentation of the Mīmāṃsaka view:
the meanings of afflicted *avyayībhāva* compounds,
and the meanings of such *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
The referents of such bahuvrīhi compounds, the referents of such dvandva compounds and the like,
and the referents of suffixes such as *kyac* which have *sub*-ending bases as their primitives.
The view of the Mīmāṃsakas is that the meaning of suffixes such as *kyaṅ* and others, which have nominal stems (*subanta*) as their base, is the meaning of the abstract (bhāva) suffixes.
Kaiyaṭa’s observation,
the etymology of the word *kākatālīya*, and an inquiry into the meaning of the suffix *cv-* (the cvi-suffix).
An exposition of *sphoṭa*: the *padasphoṭa* and *vākyasphoṭa*,
and the presentation of one's own philosophical position.
In the *Ṭippaṇī*, the justification for that [view] is given:
the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) is the indivisible word-sentence-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍapadavākyasphoṭa*).
The definition of the universal *sphoṭa* and the conclusion of the work; thus ends the table of contents for the *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā*.

Having bowed to Sāmba, this *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā* is composed—indeed, written—by the learned Nāgeśabhaṭṭa. (In the *Laghumañjūṣā* and other works, he says "having bowed to Sāmba," meaning Sāmbasadāśiva. || 1 ||

Now follows the determination of the universal *sphoṭa* of phonemes (*varṇa*). In this regard, the established doctrine is that there are eight *sphoṭas*: the phoneme-*sphoṭa*, the word-*sphoṭa*, the sentence-*sphoṭa*, and the indivisible word-*sphoṭa* and sentence-*sphoṭa*. These five are *vyakti-sphoṭas* (individual *sphoṭas*). Their status as *vyakti-sphoṭas* is because they are expressive [of meaning] either as unconditioned by a universal (*jāti*) or as conditioned by it; however, in the case of the base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), the word (*pada*), and so forth, they are expressive only in their own form. We shall explain how this is so further on. There are three *jāti-sphoṭas* (universal *sphoṭas*)—distinguished as phoneme, word, and sentence—making eight in total.

In this context, "sphoṭa" means that from which the meaning bursts forth clearly; that is to say, it is the signifier (*vācaka*). Thus, the meaning of terms such as *varṇasphoṭa* and so on is that phonemes (*varṇa*) and the like are the signifiers. [Note: The word "kha" does not exist here; the remainder is that by the word "phoneme" (*varṇa*), both stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) are to be understood.]

In that regard, regarding examples such as *rāmaḥ* and *bhavati*, the position of the *varṇasphoṭa* (phoneme-sphoṭa) is as follows: first, the expressive units (*vācakāḥ*) are the collections of phonemes delimited by their respective sequences (*ānupūrvī*), which constitute the portions of base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) heard in the words and sentences currently being employed; however, it is not the substituends (*ādeśinaḥ*) remembered through those [substitutes] that are expressive. The phrase "delimited by their respective sequences" is included to exclude the lack of distinction between forms such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*.

The body of the dispute is whether or not the phonemes (*varṇa*) contained within a word being employed are expressive (*vācaka*). Here, the affirmative position (*vidhikoṭi*) belongs to the opponents, while the negative position (*niṣedhakoṭi*) is ours. It might be argued as follows: since the substitutes (*ādeśa*), such as *ti* and so on, which are inherent in the actual usage (*prayoga*), are numerous, it would result in the postulation of an infinite number of delimiters for expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*); therefore, they are not expressive. Rather, it is the original bases (*sthānin*), such as *l* and so on, which are recalled by those substitutes that are truly expressive; for in their case, there is only a single delimiter of expressive power, namely the universal (*jāti*) consisting of the property of being *l* (*latva*).

Nor should it be argued that there is an additional reading "abhūt talla" in this context, and that understanding could arise even from "bhū talla"; for even you would have to maintain that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "bhavati" is a necessary cause for such understanding—just as required to prevent understanding from "bhū --- ti"—and thus there is no fault. [Response: No, because understanding would not arise for those who are ignorant of the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix).

Nor can comprehension arise from an error regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) residing solely in the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), because it is impossible to establish an error concerning a power that is constituted by both the word and its meaning; furthermore, there is no evidence for such an error. Moreover, since the bases (*sthānin*) are infinite—due to the infinite variety of suffixes such as *kaṭac*, *aṇ*, and others according to different grammatical systems, as well as the infinite variety of *su*, *si*, and so on in forms like "rāmaḥ"—the resulting necessity of postulating an infinite number of delimiters for the expressive power remains as it was. Nor is it the case that only one [suffix] among them possesses the power, as there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) to determine which one it is.

Nor should it be argued that words whose substituends (*sthānin*) are taught by Pāṇini’s grammar possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) merely as auxiliary parts of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*); for this would lead to the undesirable consequence that even those who have studied other [Vedic] branches, yet do not know this [grammar], would lack understanding. As for the objection that, in cases such as "rāmaḥ," where suffixes like *su*, *si*, and *ru* are substitutes, there would be an obstruction to comprehension for one who has studied the entire grammar—due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*)—that is not so.

For there is no fault in the non-sequential occurrence of the remembered and the rememberer, as if they were two distinct mental impressions (*smāraka* and *kalipā*). This is because a cognition is possible through that very [word] which has been remembered by the same set of conditions that awakened its latent impression. However, where there are many such conditions, it is understood by all of them; thus, there is no fault.

Furthermore, since linguistic usage—the crown jewel among the factors that determine word-potency (*śakti*)—establishes potency only with respect to those words actually heard, the apprehension of potency does not apply to the substituends (*sthānin*), as expressed by the rule "not in the case of substituends."

Furthermore, regarding the hypothesis that substitutes (ādeśins) are remembrancers (*smāraka*), that which is for us the delimitor of denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) must, in your view, be the delimitor of remembrance-capacity (*smārakatāvacchedaka*), because if anything in any form were a remembrancer, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And thus, by the maxim "that which is the cause of that [is its cause]," it is more appropriate that they [the substitutes] possess the status of being delimiters of denotative capacity. Moreover, in cases such as *papāca*, there would result the predicament of many [elements] being delimiters of remembrance-capacity.

Furthermore, if the substituenda (*sthānins*) were the denoters, then in the case of *tiṅ* suffixes, there would be denotation of the action (*kṛti*), while in the case of *śatṛ* and other suffixes, there would be denotation of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

The systematic arrangement accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas would not be established. Nor can it be argued that, based on the grammatical rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), suffixes such as *śānac* [and others] denote the agent because they possess the property of being *śānac*, etc.; for that rule does not apply to their prescription. The phrase "etc. includes the production of case-endings (*sub*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *śānac* being unavailable in the sense of the object (*karman*).

Nor can it be argued that because a relation [of identity] is impossible between a name and its referent due to their difference, one must maintain that in cases such as ‘Caitraḥ pacamānaḥ’ (‘Caitra, while cooking’), the agent is the denotation of the *la*-suffix in order to avoid the fault of non-relation (*ananvaya*); for this would result in a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) with the rule “*laḥ karmaṇi*” (Pāṇini 3.4.69). Nor is it the case that even if the property of being a *la*-suffix (*latva*) is the delimiting factor of denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), the occurrence of the *la*-suffix produced by substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *tiP* alone brings about the cognition of the action (*kṛti*); for [the action] is brought about by the *la*-suffix as recalled by the *śatṛ* and other affixes.

Or else, it must be stated that the cognition of that [meaning] arises from the [substitute] being uttered in its own form (*svarūpa*). For one who asserts this, must it be accepted in cases such as the suffix *śatṛ* that the expressive power (*vācakatva*) belongs to the substitutes (*ādeśa*), or to the original bases (*sthānin*)? Not the first, because it would result in the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*)—that is, an inconsistent application of two contradictory properties to the same thing. Nor the second, because it would result in a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*). Nor is there any inconsistency with the grammatical rule (Pāṇini 3.4.69), "The *l*-suffixes [denote] the object," if the expressive power belongs only to the substitutes; for, in reality, the power residing in the *tiṅ* and other suffixes is attributed to the letter *l*, which is postulated for the sake of brevity in the instruction, and thus the rule is justified.

In this regard, the following should be understood: according to this view, the function (*vṛtti*) conducive to the comprehension of meaning resides in the collection of phonemes (*varṇasamūha*) as a whole, not in each individual one. If it were otherwise, since each [phoneme] would possess meaning, they would qualify as nominal stems (*prātipadika*), leading to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the production of case-endings (*sub*). Consequently, in forms such as *dhanam* and *vanam*, there would result the undesirable application of rules such as the elision of the final *n* (*nalopa*).

Furthermore, if each [letter] were individually possessed of power (*śaktimattva*), it would follow that the meaning is understood from each individual letter. Moreover, it would follow that the utterance of the second and subsequent letters would be purposeless. Nor can it be argued that each letter merely produces the recollection (*smaraṇa*) of the meaning, while the final letter produces it clearly—as there is no obstacle to accepting a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) even in the case of memory, just as in the case of perception—because the recollection of the meaning after every single letter contradicts experience and is cumbersome (*gurutva*).

Nor can it be asked how there can be a collective function (*samudāyavṛttitva*) for those [sounds] that do not function individually; for this is established just as in the case of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth. For this very reason, in the section beginning with "The phonemes possess meaning" (*arthavanto varṇāḥ*), regarding the rule *hayavaraṭ* (MbhS 5), it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Since meanings are observed for single phonemes belonging to roots, stems (*prātipadika*), and suffixes, stems consisting of a single phoneme possess meaning—as in *ābhyām*, *ebhiḥ*, *eṣu*. (The sequence of the Bhāṣya on that point is: "Stems consisting of a single phoneme possess meaning—as in *ābhyām*, *ābhiḥ*, *eṣu*").

This is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *arthavat* (Pāṇini 1.2.45) in the passage: "The base (*prakṛti*) occurs in the sense of the base; the suffix (*pratyaya*) occurs in the sense of the suffix. Regarding this, some partial theorists (*ekadeśin*) maintain that only the final phoneme (*caramavarṇa*) possesses the expressive power (*śakti*). The impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme act as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for the final phoneme in generating the cognition of the meaning. Thus, the cognition of the meaning does not arise from that [final phoneme] alone, nor does the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) apply to each individual phoneme. This is the general definition of the *varṇasphoṭa*; the reading "here is the general definition" (*atra sāmānyanirūpaṇam*) is appropriate.
Now, the definition of *śakti* (denotative power).

Here, in order to exclude the possibility that space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities—which are presented to the mind upon hearing words like "pot" (*ghaṭa*)—become objects of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that in verbal cognition, the cause is a presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the apprehension of a linguistic relation (*vṛttigraha*). This is the underlying intention: since words reside in space through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), according to the rule that "the knowledge of one related thing causes the recollection of the other related thing," space would also be presented by the word "pot," and consequently, space would also appear in the verbal cognition.

And that [unrestricted relation] is not desired; therefore, one must accept the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) that "with respect to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) concerning a particular object, the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the *vṛtti* residing in that word. Thus, because space (*ākāśa*) is not presented through a *vṛtti*, it does not appear in verbal cognition. Furthermore, *vṛtti* is threefold: *śakti* (denotative power), *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function), and *vyañjanā* (suggestive function). The nature of *vṛtti* is the state of being a relation between a word and its meaning that is conducive to the mental presentation of the word-meaning, which is the cause of verbal cognition.

The phrase "conducive to the presentation of the word-meaning" (*padārthopastityanukūla*) is included in order to exclude the intention (*tātparya*), which consists of a convention regarding the word as the object of cognition by virtue of its being a cause of awakening [the meaning], from being a *vṛtti* (linguistic function). Furthermore, it should be understood that this [function] is directly useful for verbal comprehension (*śābda*), not by means of the presentation of the word-meaning.

If it is asked what the category of *śakti* (potency) is therein, the ancient Naiyāyikas hold that *śakti* consists of the will of God (*īśvarecchā*). According to their view, even in the case of a modern convention (*ādhunika-saṅketa*), there is indeed *śakti*, because the will of God exists there as well, based on [the scriptural injunction]: "On the eleventh day, the father shall give a name. However, those who know the tradition maintain that there is no *śakti* in a modern convention. Gadādharabhaṭṭācārya, however, holds that *śakti* is merely desire (*icchāmātra*) and not specifically the will of God; thus, in his view, there is indeed *śakti* even in a modern convention.

In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, however, *śakti* (potency) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). It is that which regulates the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between the word and its meaning. That potency resides in the meaning by means of the relation called "qualificative connection" (*vaiśiṣṭya*), and it resides in the word by means of the relation of "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*). The ancient grammarians, on the other hand, state that potency is the capacity to produce cognition. Thus it has been said by Dīkṣita in the *Bhūṣaṇa*:
"Just as there is an beginningless fitness of the sense organs toward their respective objects..."
"The relation of words with their objects is beginningless, as is their fitness (yogyatā).

Just as the sense organs—the eyes and so forth—possess an innate fitness toward their respective objects, such as the visual forms of jars and the like, which consists in their being the causes of the cognition of those objects, in the same way, for words too, fitness is precisely their being the cause of the cognition of the object; that itself is what is meant by 'power' (śakti)."

According to the view of Nāgeśa, however, it will become clear immediately hereafter that *śakti* (denotative power) is simply the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*). Alternatively, *śakti* is the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) characterized by the form "this meaning is to be understood from this word," or "may this word convey this meaning. Although its relation—defined as the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*)—subsists both in the word and in the meaning, nevertheless, within that [will], the word is the signifier (*vācaka*) because it is the object [of the will] insofar as it possesses the capacity to generate understanding, or because it is the determiner of the producedness [in the understanding] which has understanding as its specific nature.

Since it is the object of the cognition of awakening (*bodha*), the object must be stated in relation to that [cognition]. Therefore, the word (*pada*) is not the denoted, nor is the meaning (*artha*) the denoter. 3kha. By this, [the objection] is refuted because there is no fault; for, due to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the Lord’s will (*īśvarecchā*), it is not the case that it constitutes "power" (*śakti*) therein. This is because we accept that power resides in each respective word by means of a specific relationship—namely, a unique objecthood (*viṣayatā*) qualified by its respective object. Furthermore, this [power] resides only in correct words (*sādhuśabda*), not in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) and the like, because there is no conventional usage of "possessing power" regarding them, and because it would otherwise entail the [undesirable] consequence of those [corrupt forms] being considered correct.

But surely, since it is accepted that even from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) meaning is understood through a misconception of expressive power (*śakti-bhrama*), it follows that [corrupt forms] must also have existence (*sanmātra*) as their object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the Lord’s intention has only existence as its object. Furthermore, because they too necessarily possess the status of being objects, they would incur the status of being expressive (*śakta*). Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the destruction of the Lord’s intention having only existence as its object. Likewise, by the aforementioned reasoning, even words like *gaṅgā* used in a secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*) would incur the status of being denoters of the bank (*tīra*) and so forth. 1. *sanmātraviṣayake* (kha); 2. *bhagavatsaṃkete* (not present in kha); 3. *uktayukteḥ* (kha).

It should not be argued that Miśra’s statement—that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because words such as corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) were not uttered by the Blessed One with the intention of conveying meaning, nor was their status as being uttered by the Blessed One due to such an intention—correct; for this would result in [the definition] applying to figurative expressions (*lākṣaṇika*) in the context of the Veda. Furthermore, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of modern conventional terms like "Maitra," since word-forms such as "Devadatta" were not uttered by the Blessed One.

If it is argued that one cannot say that all words have been uttered by [the Lord] simply because they are called "names" (*nāmapada*), since even corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are uttered by Him—as evidenced by the rule *nāpabhraṃśitavai*—we reply: no.

Power (*śakti*) consists precisely in the possession of the Lord’s will, related through the relation of being the qualificandum as determined by the mode of being the cognition of that word. Since this [will] must necessarily be postulated as a relation because the recollection of the word-meaning would otherwise be inexplicable, it is postulated only for correct Sanskrit (*sādhu-saṃskṛta*), and not for corrupt forms, secondary meanings (*lakṣaṇika*), and so forth, because these are accounted for through superimposition (*āropa*) and because they can be explained by other modes of operation (*vṛtti*).

Furthermore, according to the view that inherence (*samavāya*) is one, this is the implication: for logicians who maintain the oneness of inherence, since the inherence of touch and the inherence of color are identical, the existence of a relation would necessarily entail the existence of its relata; consequently, there would be the cognition "the air possesses color. Thus, in the perception "the air possesses color," the existence of the inherence relation having color as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is required, and not merely inherence in general. This applies likewise to the case of air.

Even though inherence exists, there is no fault because the inherence that has "color" as its counter-correlative does not exist [in the case of taste]. However, in the view of those who maintain the manifoldness of inherence, there is not even a trace of a fault.

Even though both the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) and the state of being the substratum (*anuyogitva*) may reside in one and the same entity, such as color (*rūpa*), there exists only a relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between them, and not a relation of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*); thus, air and the like do not possess color. Similarly, although the objective-locusness (*viśeṣyatā*)—which is the object of the cognition produced by words such as "Gaṅgā" and is qualified by the mode (*prakāratā*) of being the object of that cognition—possesses both the state of being the counter-correlate of God’s will (*īśvarecchā*) and the state of being the substratum of the riverbank (*tīra*), there is no relation of the delimited and the delimiter between those two; therefore, the riverbank and the like are not the denotata (*vācyatva*) of words such as "Gaṅgā."

Alternatively, even though the bank (*tīra*) and other such objects possess the status of being the object of a cognition produced by words such as "Ganges," it is accepted that God’s will has that [bank] as its qualificandum-part (*viṣayatva*) precisely through the universal property of being the object-status of a cognition produced by the word "Ganges" (*gaṅgādipadajanyabodhaviṣayatvatva*), and not through the property of being the object-status of a cognition produced by the word "Ganges" itself (*gaṅgādipadajanyabodhaviṣayatvatva*). This is because there is no evidence for the latter. Even if that [latter property] is not admitted, there is no contradiction with its [God's will's] having everything as its object, because [the former property] is pervaded by the status of being an object (*viṣayatvavyāpya*). [Otherwise,] there would be a contradiction.

And this being the case, there is no inconsistency regarding the cognition having everything as its object on the grounds that it does not apprehend the state of being produced by words such as "Ganges" with respect to the cognitive aspect (*bodhāṃśa*); for even if that [state of being produced by the word] is not apprehended as a constituent of the delimitor of the qualifier-nature (*prakāratā*) as determined by the qualificand-nature (*viśeṣyatā*) of the riverbank and so forth, we accept that the cognition has everything as its object because it apprehends that [state] independently within the cognitive aspect. And thus, [the definition of a word is] the possession of God’s will, related through a qualificand-nature (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a qualifier-nature delimited by the property of being the object-nature of a cognition produced by that word.

[The view that] there is the possession of such a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) as determined by the will of God [is held]; or else, [the reading "of the possession of qualificandhood" (viśeṣyatāvattvasya) is followed by the text: "Or rather, its apprehension is caused by its being a *śakti* itself; for according to the theory of an additional *śakti*, it is apprehended precisely as such," which appears in the present manuscript as an unconnected interpolation]. Or, since [the word] is accepted as denoting only the flow [of water] etc., as defined by the Sanskrit language, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is there a logical reason (*yukti*) that favors one side over the other as a means of definitive determination (*vinigamanā*). There is no lack of such a determining factor, because a means of determination exists in the form of its being well-known and its acceptance by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) throughout all regions. Furthermore, even if the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) were the power (*śakti*), there would be no contingency of providing understanding to those who do not know God—namely the Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists, and others—since it is only in its capacity as a convention (*saṃketa*) that it serves as a factor for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

For this very reason, even from a corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*), there is comprehension of the meaning because a convention exists; for it must be stated that even the convention of God is such [i.e., a cause of comprehension] only when it has been grasped, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of comprehension for those who have not mastered the language. And since the grasping of that [divine convention] occurs through the linguistic usage of people like us, it is necessary that the convention consisting of the instruction of people like us alone be the expressive power (*śakti*); what is the use of postulating a divine convention? This cannot be argued, because, in the absence of a decisive criterion (*avinigama*), there would be multiple conventions belonging to various individuals residing in a single word denoting a single object.

Rather than postulating a power (*śakti*) for that many [words], it is more appropriate to postulate a single convention (*saṃketa*) of the Lord (*īśvara*) with respect to one [word]. Furthermore, in the worldly activity of creation and so forth, it is the activity of the Blessed One alone [that is primary]; therefore, corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) do not possess the status of being correct (*sādhutva*). And since knowledge of that [correct form] is a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), no understanding arises from expressions such as *grāma grāma*.
They say that even for words used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*), the status of being a reality exists because a power (*śakti*) is present in some cases.

Since there is no evidence for the *pariśeṣa* (method of elimination) due to the absence of a decisive factor (*vinigamanā*) between cognition and effort, and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to attribute this to all [linguistic items], the *śakti* (denotative power) is simply another relation between the word and its meaning. Furthermore, by the reasoning previously stated, that power resides only in the refined (*saṃskṛta*) form, being determined by the continuous stream [of usage] and so forth; thus, corrupt forms, metaphorical expressions, and the like do not possess denotative power.

Furthermore, because Sanskrit is one and the same in all regions, whereas spoken languages differ from region to region, there can be no expressive power (śakti) residing in those [vernaculars], both out of respect [for the status of Sanskrit] and because it would result in their being mere synonyms for Sanskrit. Nor can it be argued that the problem of the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding knowledge and so forth remains even when assuming an additional property (*dharma*), for such an assumption would be rendered useless; moreover, due to the contradiction with what must be accepted as foundational (*upajīvya-virodha*), those assumed properties are not admitted.

As for the claim that *sādhutva* (grammatical correctness) is simply the state of being endowed with expressive power (*śaktatva*) in the form of being designated by God’s convention and so forth—that is not correct. This is because the conventional usage of the term *sādhu* occurs even when one lacks knowledge of such designation and the like. Furthermore, in the case of a compound (*samāsa*) or similar forms which are *sādhu* words, if a convention and so forth were present, that very convention would constitute their expressive power, resulting in the undesirable consequence that they would possess [only] that [conventional] power. Moreover, since there is no expressive power residing in the aggregate of stem and suffix as a whole, it would follow that such an aggregate would lack *sādhutva*.

If one were to take each individual power [of the letters], then just as the form *bādhate* would be correct, the form *bādhati* would also result in being correct; furthermore, this would lead to an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to particles (*nipāta*), which are merely indicators (*dyotaka*). If it is argued that "indication" (*dyotana*) is simply a power residing in a collection (*saṃdānika*), then since there is no distinction between the *ṭ* following *pra* and the *ṭ* following *jita*, there would be no basis for determining which is the expressive element, resulting in the status of being a denoter (*śakta*). Moreover, "residing in a collection" (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*) means residing in multiple substrates simultaneously. If one were to assume such a collective power, there would be no certainty regarding the doubling of *aṭ* and so forth due to the lack of a limiting factor.

By this, the view that "it is the state of possessing a function" (*vṛttimattva*) and so forth is refuted, because it does not extend to compounds (*samāsa*) and the like. Nor is it a specific universal (*jāti*), because that would result in the fallacy of confusion (*saṅkara*) with [the universals] *katva* and so on. Rather, it is the state of being produced by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

It has also been stated that knowledge of that [correct form] is a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), because comprehension occurs even for those who do not possess such knowledge. However, the certain cognition of ungrammaticality (*asādhutva-niścaya*) acts as an obstacle. For this very reason, there is no comprehension even from a correct word when its ungrammaticality is ascertained. Nor does it follow that comprehension would not arise from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) because they lack expressive power (*aśaktatva*) and are ungrammatical; for in the case of one who is linguistically proficient (*vyutpanna*), comprehension arises from the recollection of the corresponding correct form, whereas in the case of one who is not proficient (*avyutpanna*), comprehension arises precisely from a misconception regarding their expressive power.

And those who are proficient (*vyutpanna*) are of two kinds: those possessing specific knowledge of the refined forms (*saṃskṛta*) of the respective denoters, and those lacking that. Among them, for the former, the recollection of the correct word (*sādhu*) is indeed clear. For the latter, it should be inferred that understanding arises either through the recollection of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*)—which serves as an indicator of its meaning—or through the recollection of the correct word itself. Nor is there any point in the reading "in the apprehension of power" (*śaktigrahe*), which is found in manuscript *kha*; for that is utterly irrelevant to the present context.

If the capacity (*śakti*) is not apprehended, how can there be an error regarding it? [The answer is: because subsequent errors are possible based on preceding errors. Furthermore, even if one accepts an additional capacity, is it accepted that all words possess it in relation to all meanings, or that some words possess it only in relation to specific meanings? For instance, the Āryas employ the word *yava* for long-awned barley and understand it as such, whereas the Mlecchas employ that very same word for the *priyaṅgu* plant and understand it as such; thus, there would be no such restriction.

For it cannot be said that a lamp, while possessing the power to illuminate visible forms, also illuminates taste; [this is not so] because, in some cases, a word [expresses its meaning] even through convention (*saṃketa*).

Because there is no absence of a defect in its capacity to cause comprehension (*bodhakatva*), and thus there is no fault in the view that for *mlecchas* (barbarians), comprehension arises solely from convention (*saṃketa*). Nor should it be argued that since the cognition of convention is the cause in some cases and the cognition of *śakti* (inherent power) in others, there would be a lack of uniformity (*vyabhicāra*) such that even one [of these two] could not be the reality; and furthermore, that because of the complexity (*gaurava*) of the latter, simplicity (*lāghava*) dictates that the cause is simply the cognition of convention. For, in the absence of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*), the existence of an additional category of entity is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatva*), and therefore the complexity resulting from that is not a defect; this is so because [the alternative view] involves the inclusion of factors such as "immediately following" (*avyavahitottaratva*).

This is because there is no deviation [in the usage], and because even among the Mlecchas, comprehension occurs solely through a misconception regarding the expressive power (*śakti*). However, the modern grammarians (*navīna-vaiyākaraṇas*) maintain that there is no establishment of a separate entity [for *śakti*] due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*); for since it is possible for cognition itself to possess the nature of *śakti*—given that it is the first to be presented as a qualifier of desire (*icchā*)—there is no evidence for postulating a separate entity. Furthermore: "Desire would be produced by cognition; action (*kṛti*) would be produced by desire; effort (*ceṣṭā*) would be produced by action; and the fruit (*phala*) would be produced by effort."
Thus, by virtue of this sequential demonstration, the primacy of *jñāna* (cognition) is established.

Furthermore, since a distinct category (*padārtha*) would have to be differentiated according to its various substrates and objects, the postulation of an infinite number of categories would result in the fallacy of excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Otherwise, the undesirable consequence of every word producing cognition of all things would be unavoidable. Moreover, it would lead to the absurd linguistic usage: "The word 'cloth' possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward a jar qualified by jar-ness. Nor can it be argued that the power qualified by being directed toward a jar qualified by jar-ness does not reside in the word 'cloth', for a qualified entity is not something distinct [from its constituents].
For this very reason, in the view of the Navya-Naiyāyikas, the plurality of inherence (*samavāya*) is established.

By this [it is shown that] the state of being expressive of that [inherence] consists in possessing a property that serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka-dharma*) for the capacity to generate a verbal cognition having that [inherence] as its object; and that property, like the power (*śakti*) conducive to burning and so forth in fire and other things, is indeed a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*).

For instance: because there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the causality of grass, fire-sticks, and jewels with respect to that which is delimited by the universal "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*); and because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to posit three distinct causal relations by accepting a triad of specific universals (*vaijātya*) residing in fire as the delimiters of the effect-ness; and just as a single power (*śakti*) exceeding the individual [causes] is accepted as the delimiter of the causality of fire in the case of grass and so forth, so too here, since a single object is understood through various synonyms, there would be a deviation in their being causes with respect to that understanding of the object as delimited by its own nature.

Because it would be cumbersome to include the specific qualification of each respective cause by way of the relation of "immediately preceding," and because the reading "a single cognition of that meaning distinct from all other modes" is missing [in some versions], there is established a potency (*śakti*)—which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the causality of the cognition of that meaning—as something distinct from all individual modes (*paryāya*), since it would otherwise be cumbersome to include the specific qualification of each respective cause.

However, this distinction remains: the capacity conducive to burning and so forth is useful only when it exists in its own right (*svarūpasatī*), whereas for that which does not so exist, it is useful only when known (*jñātā*). Thus, since the linguistic convention of denoting something is based solely on the capacity residing in the cognition of that thing, the objection regarding past or future words and the like is refuted; yet even this view of the Mīmāṃsakas is rejected.

Furthermore, since even a word with a secondary (lakṣaṇika) meaning generates verbal cognition, it would follow that one must postulate such a property [of being a cause of cognition] for that word as well, which would result in its being endowed with primary denotative power (*śakti*). Nor can it be argued that a word with a secondary meaning is not a producer of experience; rather, in a sentence containing a word with a secondary meaning, it is only the word that denotes another object within that sentence which produces the experience of the secondary (indicated) meaning—just as it produces the experience of its own primary meaning—and therefore there is no fault. For if that were so, then in the case of a word such as "ghoṣa" (the bank), [the same logic would apply].

Because it would follow that [the sentence] would possess denotative power (*vācakatā*) by virtue of possessing a power delimited by the capacity to produce an experience of objects such as the bank of the Gaṅgā; and because there would be the consequence that a sentence not composed of words possessing power would lack the capacity to produce an experience. Furthermore, [there would be the consequence that] there would be no capacity to produce an experience for a sentence not consisting of words endowed with power. Nor should it be argued that the denoted meaning (lakṣyārtha) does not enter into verbal cognition (śābdabodha), but rather that there is merely a lack of apprehension of its non-connection with the meanings of the co-occurring words once it has been remembered; for if this were the case, it would follow that such a situation occurs everywhere, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of verbal cognition. Furthermore, it would result in the impossibility of the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) "I am cognizing [the object] through verbal means" being colored by the denoted meaning. This is because the required causal efficacy is already established by the fact that, specifically, for the cognition of a particular meaning as connected with the meaning of a particular word, the knowledge of that specific word—possessing expectancy for that specific word—is the necessary cause.

Furthermore, there is no evidence for the claim that the cognition of a word not denoting that [object]—as opposed to the cognition of some word denoting it—is a cause with respect to the verbal cognition delimited by having that as its object, provided that the word's expressive power (*śakti*) is taken into account. Therefore, even the metaphorical [word] must indeed be recited. Moreover, if the cause were the possession of a single power by the fire-drill (*araṇi*), the upper wood (*uttarāraṇi*), and so forth, then when there is contact with the fire-drill, and when there is a blowing sound (*pūtkāra*), but in the absence of friction (*manthana*), it would follow that fire would arise as delimited by the universal *vahni-tva* (fire-ness).

If one accepts three such universals (*jāti*) and posits three respective causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), there is no fault, because it is accepted that the blowing (*phūtkāra*) acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) specifically for the production of the effect when delimited by the universal "grass-ness" (*tṛṇatva*). Similarly, in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of understanding [the meaning] from the word "kumbha" even when its expressive power (*śakti*) has not been grasped, provided that the expressive power of the word "ghaṭa" has been grasped.

If, however, it is argued that the causality [of word-cognition] consists in the cognition of each respective word as possessing its specific capacity (*śaktimat*), then there would result an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations. To avoid such deviation (*vyabhicāra*), one would have to specify the causality of the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) with respect to the object possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth that arises immediately after hearing the word "jar," and the causality of the word "kalaśa" with respect to the object possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth that arises immediately after hearing the word "kalaśa. This would take the form of incorporating the condition of "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*). Furthermore, effort [to establish such relations] is indispensable; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

Nor, then, can it be maintained that the knowledge of God alone is such [the basis for linguistic usage], because since the single knowledge of the Blessed Lord has everything as its object, the determination of word-meanings would be impossible. Furthermore, the refutation offered by the aforementioned method is not tenable from a logical standpoint; for popular usage (*prasiddhi*) is not restricted [to a specific region], and because [words] are accepted through figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*) by all learned people across all regions, there would be no possibility of establishing a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for those Sanskrit forms restricted to specific regions, as they would not be accepted by the learned people of all regions.

Furthermore, if *śakti* (potency) were a form of knowledge (*jñāna*), its causality would have to be stated as being by way of a knowledge characterized by the specific mode of "being a signifier" (*bodhakatva-viśeṣa-prakāraka-jñānatvena*). However, since it is simpler (*lāghava*) to posit its causality simply as "knowledge of being a signifier" (*bodhakatva-jñānatvena*), and because common people experience comprehension immediately after grasping that words such as "cow" (*gavādi-pada*) produce verbal cognition of an object—even though they lack the grasp of such a [specific] knowledge regarding those words—it follows that potency is precisely the capacity to generate a cognition whose object is that [signified meaning]. 1 kha.

Nor should it be argued that because the capacity to generate the cognition of an object-meaning is inexplicable without a relation to that object, one must therefore postulate convention (*saṃketa*) itself as that [relation], since such a capacity is already established; for even in the case of a staff (*daṇḍa*), there is the additional reading "gha," which has been disregarded as it is unfavorable to the present context and its syllables are indistinct.

Nor is there a deviation from this causal principle in the case of modern names such as "Devadatta," where [the word] is a communicator only through the knowledge of its convention (*saṃketa*); for there is no fault, since even the capacity to generate that verbal cognition is apprehended therein as a qualifier. Nor should it be argued that the knowledge of that [convention] independently is necessary; otherwise, for one who knows "this is not a generator of that cognition" or "this person has understood this meaning from this word," that cognition would arise. This is because, in those cases, the capacity to generate that cognition is not apprehended due to sublation (*bādha*).

Otherwise, for one who knows the error—that "this is not silver"—the same logic would lead to the undesirable consequence that the person cognizing the error would also be mistaken regarding the appearance of silver-ness in the object before them. Others, however, maintain that there is no fault, because even in cases where cognition arises from the knowledge of a convention, one must postulate a mental cognition of the generative capacity (*janakatva*) of that [conventional] knowledge, in accordance with the parsimony (*lāghava*) of the causal relationship.

Furthermore, being a producer does not consist merely in being a prior entity while being non-redundant (*ananyathāsiddha*). Redundancy (*anyathāsiddhatva*) consists in the fact that when the effect can be accounted for by a prior entity whose presence is necessarily postulated, the [other] thing is merely a concomitant of that. Therefore, the color of a staff, a donkey, and so forth, do not possess the status of a cause. However, there is no purpose in including the factor of "necessity" (*niyatattva*), because things such as donkeys—which would otherwise need to be excluded—are already ruled out by their very nature of being redundant.

It should not be argued that its positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are the means of apprehension [of its causal status], and that because there is no apprehension of positive and negative concomitance when there is knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), there is no apprehension of its being a cause; for if that [causal capacity], which is composed of multiple entities, were the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), it would involve complexity (*gaurava*). This is because, even for you, that [capacity] enters [the definition] by way of being a specific desire (*icchā-viśeṣa*), so the complexity is equal. Furthermore, this is because we accept that "being a producer" (*janakatva*) is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), and because "power" (*śaktitva*) itself is the delimiting factor of causality.

Furthermore, there is an additional reading stating that "the reality (tattva) consists of an indivisible limiting adjunct (akhaṇḍopādhi). Moreover, since *śakti* (potency) is simply the cognition [of meaning] through the relation of being the generator (*janakatā*) residing in the same locus as the word-ness (*śabdatva*), that which possesses this potency by means of the aforementioned relation is called "possessing potency" (*śakta*), and that which is the object of the cognition delimited by the aforementioned relation is called "the potentialed" (*śakya*). And because it must be postulated that this [potency], which has various word-meanings as its objects, is distinct for every individual word, the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) is quite evident.

Since it is necessary that [causality] be distinct due to the difference between the delimiters of the causal capacities (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), causality is, by parsimony (*lāghava*), simply the nature of the property that serves as the delimiter of the causal capacity. Nor does this imply an impossibility of the relationship between the delimited and the delimiter when there is non-difference; for even if that relationship is impossible in terms of a single form, there is no defect in accepting that it is delimited as "causality" (*kāraṇatātvena*) while its delimiter is its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Even in the view that accepts a distinct entity called "causality" (*kāraṇatā*), there is no loss for us, because we maintain that the very cognition of a property as being the delimitor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-dharma*) is itself the cognition of *śakti*.
Thus, since such a generative capacity exists even in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), they too possess the capacity to convey meaning through *śakti*.

As for the claim that understanding arises either from the recollection of a correct form (*sādhu*) or from an error regarding its expressive power (*śakti*), that is not so; for we observe that understanding occurs even among those who are proficient [in a language] without the recollection of a correct form. Furthermore, this is evident from the linguistic usage of the proficient, who say, "This meaning was not understood through these Sanskrit forms you mentioned, but rather through the vernacular (*bhāṣā*) spoken here."

Furthermore, since the Lord’s will—which is composed of various words and word-meanings—is apprehended as residing in words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), the occurrence of error in cases such as the word "gargarī" (a large water-jar) is impossible; for there exists the perception of a specific feature, namely its having a different phonetic sequence (*ānupūrvī*), and thus there is an absence of the perception of a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). For this very reason, the Naiyāyikas maintain in various places that there can be no error regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) constituted by those respective word-meanings.

Since the form of an additional entity has already been apprehended, by the very reasoning stated previously, it is untenable to maintain that there is an error regarding the power (*śakti*) [of the word] as being one in cases such as the word *gagarī*. [Kha]: If, however, it is argued that—just as in the case of "gāvī" or "baḍava"—one can establish the existence of power based on the error that the understanding of the person being prompted arises from the recollection of the correct word "go," and that the cognition of the object "jar" arises from the word "gāvī" itself; and if it is further claimed that this applies to all other such cases as well—even so... [the following text follows].

Furthermore, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the vernacular language (*bhāṣā*) as well, because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) [to the contrary]. Nor is there a multiplicity of vernaculars; for, like Sanskrit, the Mahārāṣṭrī vernacular is uniform across all regions, and thus it is impossible to avoid attributing expressive power to it. By this, the argument that expressive power cannot reside in a single [language] due to the lack of a decisive criterion among various vernaculars is refuted; for the same applies to Sanskrit as well.

Because there is no definitive criterion (*vinigamanā*) among the various regional languages [to determine which one is primary]. Nor is being accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) in all regions a definitive criterion; for if it were so, it would follow that the word *duścyavana* would acquire denotative power (*śakti*) in the sense of Indra, and words such as *aneḍamūka* would acquire power in the sense of a mute or a deaf person, simply because they are not employed by the learned in those senses. For this very reason, the author of the *Prakāśa* cited words such as *duścyavana* when discussing the fault of being "unemployed" (*aprayuktatva*).

Nor can it be assumed that the [grammatical] treatises (kośa) are authoritative in this regard, for it is possible to argue that the authors of those treatises included such readings due to a delusion regarding their expressive power (*śakti*). Furthermore, if a denotative word were merely suggestive (*vyañjaka*), it would follow—by virtue of the examples of Prakrit and other languages cited by the Alaṅkārikas—that expressive power (*śakti*) must be established even there. Moreover, the unhesitating conviction of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) inhabitants of various regions regarding the expressive power of their respective languages cannot be considered an error unless there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), and such an error is impossible.

Furthermore, since it is established by parsimony that *janakatva* (the capacity to produce a cognition) alone constitutes *śakti* (expressive power), and since this [capacity] exists even in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), it is difficult to deny that these too possess expressive power. This is because you yourself accept that understanding arises from corrupt forms, and because the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and other factors that apprehend expressive power are identical in both cases. By this, the view that "expressive power is the capacity to convey meaning residing exclusively in correct words (*sādhuśabda*)" is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that there is no occurrence of understanding from those [corrupt forms] because of the certainty of their being incorrect (*asādhutva*), since such certainty acts as an obstacle to that understanding; for even when that certainty exists, understanding still arises from Prakrit and other corrupt forms for those who do not know Sanskrit, proving that such certainty does not act as an obstacle. Furthermore, it cannot be claimed that in those cases the understanding is purely mental, for if that were so, the same would apply elsewhere, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of destroying the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda-prāmāṇya*). Thus it is established that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*); they simply lack correctness (*sādhutva*).

Now, what is this "correctness" (*sādhutva*) that is absent in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*)? Nor can it be "being produced by grammar," for if every mere sound were considered correct simply because it could be produced by grammar—even in cases of imitation—this would result in the collapse of the distinction between the correct and the incorrect. Nor can it be defined as: "a word is correct in a particular sense if it has been derived by grammar for that sense. For the determination of such derivation occurs sometimes through the explicit observation of grammar, and sometimes through inference from the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), lexicons, and so forth.

And its inclusion [in the grammatical system] is by virtue of the rule *bāhulaka* (diversity) and so forth. For instance, the word *puṣpavant* is correct only when it conveys a meaning consisting of both [sun and moon] as delimited by their coexistence (*sāhitya*), but not when it conveys the meaning of only one of them. Or, for example, the word *dāra* is correct only when ending in the plural number, but not when ending in the singular. Or, for example, the verbal root *vac* is correct in the forms *ti* and *tas*, but not in *anti*. If it is argued that this must be stated because derivative words (*lākṣaṇika*) lack etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) in their respective meanings, and thus correctness (*sādhutva*) would not apply to them in those meanings—[we reply: no.

They say that there is no contradiction because, through the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and other means, it is inferred that even in those specific senses, such words are derivable by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, it is accepted that modern metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) usages are indeed *asādhūni* (ungrammatical).

Others, however, argue that since "metaphor" (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in conveying a meaning grasped as being related to the primary sense (*śakya*), and since the cognition of the sublation of the primary sense is a cause for the understanding produced by metaphor, the primary sense must necessarily be understood first in cases of metaphor; thus, by taking that primary sense into account, grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is established.

For this very reason, in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), even though the word *gaṅgā* refers to the bank (*tīra*), the feminine suffix and so forth are justified; for the grammatical operation conditioned by femininity and the like proceeds precisely because it is more immediate (*antaraṅga*), since the application of the rule occurs by taking the meaning that is first presented and is thus more proximate, as they say.

If it is asked, "What is the utility of such grammatical correctness (sādhutva)?"—it should be replied that its utility lies in either being a cause for verbal cognition (śābda-bodha) when it is known, or in being an obstacle to it when its absence is ascertained; for these [objections] have already been refuted previously. Furthermore, it is useful for generating merit, as taught in such passages as: "A single word, correctly understood and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty in heaven and in this world; one should employ only correct words."

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that merit (*dharma*) arises from the employment of correct words (*sādhu-śabda*), preceded by the knowledge of the specific derivations (*vyutpatti*) taught by grammar for those respective meanings. Thus, it follows that correctness (*sādhutva*) is the state of being derivable by grammar for a particular meaning, which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the production of merit. This very point is expressed by the term "fitness for prosperity" (*abhyudaya-yogyatā*).

Alternatively, *sādhutva* (grammatical correctness) is a specific universal (*jāti*) residing in words that is manifested by grammar, which serves as the delimitor of the capacity to produce merit. For this very reason, statements found here and there in the *Bhāṣya* and other works—such as "Grammar is that which makes known correctness through the sentence obtained via presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), namely: 'That which is fully established here [in grammar] is correct'"—become consistent. This would not be consistent if correctness were merely the state of being expounded by grammar, because such a property could not possibly be something cognizable by the scripture itself.

And thus, it is established that merit (*dharma*) results from the employment of correct words known as correct through the knowledge gained from proficiency in grammar; otherwise, the purpose of teaching correctness via the treatise would be clearly redundant. With this very intention, the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other texts—namely, "When the comprehension of meaning is equal [whether] by means of words and corrupt words, there is a restriction regarding merit (*dharma*) by means of the treatise" (Pāṇini’s *Vārttika* 4.3.48)—is consistent.

Nor is there any confusion [of categories] due to the presence of both labiality (*oṣṭhya*) and non-labiality (*anoṣṭhya*), because such overlap is not a defect when it pertains to a genus residing in a quality (*guṇagatajāti*). To explain: when a person such as Devadatta has previously heard non-labial phonemes, and later hears labial phonemes obstructed by a wall or other barrier, the inference that arises is only possible if one accepts a genus that is common to both labials and non-labials and serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*). It is not possible, however, if one accepts multiple distinct genera each pervaded by those respective qualities, because the inferential apparatus would be deficient—the genus residing solely in labials having been previously unperceived. (Note: Variant *kha* reads "the genus unique to labials.")

In reality, let there be a confusion of universals (jāti-saṅkara) everywhere, just as there is a confusion of limiting adjuncts (upādhi-saṅkara), since no logical ground for its being a defect has been stated. Or rather, let it be simply an indivisible limiting adjunct (akhaṇḍopādhi). Some, however, hold that whatever word has been used for a certain meaning since beginningless time is correct (sādhu) in that sense. Nor is this [correctness] coextensive with the technical designation "correct" (sādhutva); rather, it is a restriction for the sake of linguistic usage, such that in some cases a specific name is applied to the named object.
But the relationship [between word and meaning] is indeed eternal, just as in the case of "cow" and other words, it is so in the case of "Dittha" and others.

Regarding this and other points, on leaf 1 of the Bhāṣya and other works on Pāṇini 4.1.162 concerning the technical term *gotra*, it is stated: "When the designation *gotra* applies to descendants beginning with the grandson (*pautra*), it should be stated that the designation *gotra* applies to that descendant beginning with the grandson for whom one intends to express the status of being a descendant. For [otherwise], Garga might be considered a grandson in relation to someone, and Kuśika might likewise be so; this must not happen. Should this then be stated? No, it need not be stated."

The commentary on that [sūtra] states: "Of those that are capable [of forming a compound], it is understood that the offspring of the first among those capable [of forming a compound] is [denoted by the suffix], beginning with the grandson. Since these [technical names] are also beginningless, there is no fault. However, according to the view that technical names (*sañjñā*) are created by one's own will, modern technical names would simply fall outside the category of correct (*sādhu*) and incorrect (*asādhu*) forms. And there is no exclusion from the category of the incorrect [for them]. (Note: The phrase "na cāsādhubahirbhāvaḥ" is absent in manuscript *kha*.)

How so? Because when a specific word is employed for its respective meaning, the very fact of its being uttered otherwise—due to a deficiency in linguistic capacity (*śaktivaikalya*) and so forth—is the definition of *asādhutva* (grammatical incorrectness). For this very reason, all learned persons (*śiṣṭas*) in every land do not consider it a transgression (*pratyavāya*) to employ modern conventional names during sacrifices and other rites. Otherwise, since prohibitions such as "one should employ only what is correct (*sādhu*), not what is incorrect (*asādhu*)" exist, the occurrence of that [transgression] would be unavoidable.

This is precisely the derivation for names such as *kūcī*, *maṃcī*, *appi*, and *koṃḍā*, which are formed according to regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*). And this has been indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Māṇḍūkya-sūtra* 2, "ṛlṛk," they say.

If it is argued that, since colloquial words (*bhāṣāśabda*) thus possess meaning, they would be nominal stems (*prātipadika*); and upon the production of case-endings (*sub*), they would consequently result in being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) because they are derivable through grammar—[we reply: no; for the application of the science of grammar (*śāstra*) concerns words employed for the purpose of conveying meaning according to common usage (*loka*). It is precisely on this basis that statements such as "it does not occur because it is not denoted" (*anabhidhānāt*) and so forth are made. This is clear from the Vārttika and Bhāṣya on the sūtras beginning with "The relationship between word and meaning being established" (P. 1.1.1) and "In accordance with common usage when meaning is employed" (P. 1.1.2).

For the learned do not employ vernacular words (*bhāṣāśabda*) in the form of a combination of stem and suffix, as they would in the case of words like *vacanti*. Furthermore, if *su*-suffixes were produced from such vernacular words, it would result in the destruction of their very status as vernacular speech; such is the direction of the argument.

Thus, it is established that *śakti* (denotative power) is simply the capacity to generate a cognition regarding a specific meaning residing in a specific word. And how, this being the case, there is no elimination of *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function) and so forth, we shall explain immediately thereafter—so they say.

Indeed, since no cognition is observed to arise for one who has not grasped the word’s expressive power (*śakti*), it must be stated that the prior apprehension of that power is a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) for cognition. If it is asked how that apprehension occurs there, [the answer is: first, its apprehension arises from the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of experienced elders—the one who employs the word (*prayojaka*) and the one who is prompted by it (*prayojya*); subsequently, it also arises from lexicons (*kośa*), grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa*), the statements of authoritative persons (*āpta-vākya*), and so forth; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

And this power (*śakti*) is threefold: *rūḍhi* (conventional), *yoga* (etymological), and *yogarūḍhi* (both conventional and etymological). Among these, when a word possesses the capacity to convey a meaning based solely upon its collective form (*samudāya*), that capacity, as determined by that specific meaning, is *rūḍhi*. This capacity to convey the meaning based on the collective form consists in the fact that the individual constituent parts (*avayava*) do not separately present their own respective meanings—as, for example, in the case of words like *maṇi-nūpura*. When the very constituent parts of a word convey a particular meaning, that capacity, as determined by that meaning, is *yoga*-power—as, for example, in the case of words like *pācaka*.

In the case of words such as *aśvagandhā*, there is conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) defined by the cognition of a specific medicinal herb; however, in the cognition of a horse-stable and the like through its connection with horses, there is merely etymological derivation (*yoga*). This very [type of word] is called "etymologically derived-conventional" (*yaugikarūḍha*). By this, the Naiyāyika position—which maintains that a word is fourfold based on the fourfold nature of linguistic power (*śakti*), namely: etymologically derived (*yaugika*), conventional (*rūḍha*), etymologically derived-conventional (*yaugarūḍha*), and etymologically derived-conventional (*yaugikarūḍha*)—is refuted.

Yoga-ruḍhi (etymological-conventional) is that [type of word] where there is a denotative capacity residing in the whole [word], which is determined by an object associated with meanings understood from parts that do not constitute that [whole]. An example is the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus") and others. In that case:

This is because the capacity to convey a meaning qualified by "lotus-ness" (padmatva), which is connected to the meanings of its constituent parts—namely, the state of being produced in mud and the state of being an agent—is accepted as residing in the whole [the word *paṅkaja*]. Otherwise, the regular presentation of that meaning from the word *paṅkaja* would not occur. Nor should it be argued: "Let there simply be a secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) for the suffix *-ḍa*, which is a constituent part of that word, with respect to the object qualified by lotus-ness; since even opponents accept two simultaneous functions in cases such as 'In the Gaṅgā, there are fish and noise,' what is the use of a power (*śakti*) in the whole? This cannot be said, because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) among the constituents [to determine which one alone should bear the function].

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the meaning of the case-ending following the word *paṅkaja* could not be construed with the object qualified by "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*). For suffixes convey their own meaning as being connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), rather than conveying it as residing in a merely proximate object; this will be elaborated upon later when it is explained that suffixes convey their own meaning as being connected with the meaning of the entire complex base (*prapañca-prakṛti*), and not as residing in a proximate object.

Furthermore, if the letters *ka*, *kha*, and so on—whose powers are established in monosyllabic lexicons (*ekākṣarakośa*)—can be accounted for through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, then the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) of words such as *vaka* (heron) and *nakha* (nail) would also be dissolved. If it is argued that in those cases the collective power exists because students acquire an unhesitating conviction regarding its power, then the same applies here as well. Nor is it the case that at one time there is the mere agency of producing mud by virtue of etymological power (*yogaśakti*), while at another time there is the mere quality of being a lotus by virtue of collective power.

It should not be argued that there is a cognition of only [the object] *bodha* from the word *bodhāpatti*, just as there is a cognition of only a specific medicinal herb or only a stable for horses from the words *aśvagandhā* and so forth; for we accept that the power (*śakti*)—which is established by the force of the result—is determined specifically with respect to a qualified cognition, and thus it is impossible for a cognition of the connection with each individual referent to arise [from such a word].

As for the claim that "because conventional meaning (rūḍhi) acts as an impediment, there is no cognition of the purely etymological meaning," its underlying intention is this: the knowledge of the conventional meaning stands in opposition to the cognition of the etymological connection—specifically, the cognition that takes as its qualificandum something not delimited by "lotus-ness" (padmatva) but rather produced from the word *paṅkaja* through the power of its constituent parts (*avayavaśakti*).
