In your view, since "cloth-ness" (paṭatva) is not introduced as a qualifier (prakāra) with respect to the potency (śakti), and because there is an absence of identical qualificative structure (samānaprakārakatva) between the sublated and the sublator, you must necessarily admit that the potency resides in that which is delimited by cloth-ness; if this is what you say, then why do you resort to "closing one's eyes like an elephant" (gajanimīlikā) regarding words such as "ether" (ākāśa) as well, on the basis of the same logic?

In that case as well, although the word "space" (*ākāśa*) is capable of denoting that which possesses sound, when there is a definitive sublation in the form "it does not possess the capacity to be the substratum of sound," the sky is not perceived as the substratum of sound from the word "space. Therefore, let it be understood that the primary denotative power of the word "space" lies precisely in its being the substratum of sound.

And thus—‘[The opponent might argue: “Let there be no denotative power (śakti) of the word ‘cloth’ even with respect to that which is delimited by cloth-ness (paṭatva), because the apprehension of power occurs only with respect to the substratum (dharmin) as characterized (upalakṣita) by cloth-ness and so on, but not with respect to that which is qualified (viśiṣṭa) by the universal (jāti) of cloth-ness; for [the cognition] is a cause of the experience having a cloth as its object precisely through that form, namely cloth-ness. However, let the power reside only in individuals characterized by cloth-ness and so on. Oh, what a variety of rules this is, according to the author of the Dīdhiti, who says: “[It resides] only in individuals characterized by cloth-ness and so on, as in the case of the expression] ‘there is a lamp in the house’! (Note: The phrase *gehe rajanī* is likely a corruption or a specific idiom intended to illustrate the point; it literally means "there is a lamp in the house," where "lamp" (*rajanī*) is used as a metaphorical term for light or illumination.)

A name that possesses a convention (*saṃketa*) with respect to multiple things existing through a single relation, by virtue of their being qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are properties (*dharma*), is "conditional" (*aupādhikī*). For example: *bhūta*, *yūta*, and so forth. For such a term is capable [of denoting its object] only by taking as its basis an inclusive limiting adjunct (*anugatopādhi*), such as "possessing specific qualities that function in conscious beings" or "being a carrier of news. However, [properties] such as "having sound as its substratum" are not inclusive limiting adjuncts because they do not reside in both [the two categories of the definition], due to their being indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*); therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to technical terms (*pāribhāṣika*) such as "ether" (*gagana*).

If it is argued that, in this case, even the word "jar" (ghaṭa) would not be *naimittika* (based on a specific cause), but rather the universal "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva-jāti*) would be *aupādhika* (conditional) because it resides in a particular conjunction of parts, we reply: this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Furthermore, if the word "jar" is considered to have its denotative power (*śakti*) based on the possession of a distinct class-character (*vaijātya*) through a transitive relation consisting in being the substratum of its own substratum, then it is indeed *naimittika*; thus, there is no contradiction with common usage. So he says.

The venerable Bhartṛhari states: "That which has a particular name for a particular meaning, possessing a modern convention, is precisely what is technical (pāribhāṣika) in that context. And thus, it is established that a word possesses technicality with respect to a particular meaning if its specific sequence of phonemes (ānupūrvī) is the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of a specific objectivity belonging to a non-eternal convention whose content is the state of being the object of some produced cognition having that meaning as its qualificandum.

For example, names such as Caitra, which are conventionally assigned by fathers and others to their sons; or, for instance, terms such as *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject of an inference), which are conventionally assigned by the authors of treatises to the absence of proof (*siddhyabhāva*) and so forth.

A name is *naimittika* (denotative) with respect to that object for which it possesses a power delimited by a genus (*jāti*). Thus, *naimittikatva* (denotative status) with respect to a particular object is defined as having such a sequence [of phonemes] whose delimitor of the relatum of the power residing in itself has as its qualificandum a particular object delimited by a genus; this is what is intended. For example: the name "cow" (*go*) applies to a cow, and the name "gavaya," etc., applies to a gavaya. A name is *aupādhika* (conditional) with respect to an object for which it possesses a power delimited by a particular attribute (*upādhi*).

And thus, it follows that [the definition] consists in possessing such a sequence as is the delimitor of the denotative function (*nirūpakatā*) of a stem (*prakṛti*) qualified by a complex property (*sakhaṇḍadharma*) having such-and-such a meaning as its qualificandum (*viśeṣyaka*). For example, *ākāśa*, *paśu*, and so forth.

[Objection: But since even a modern convention possesses the status of *śakti* (inherent power), it would follow that conventional words such as "Caitra" are *naimittika* (occasioned), and it would further follow that words such as "river" (*nadī*) and "vṛddhi" are *aupādhika* (conditional). If this consequence is accepted, then a classification [of words] on that basis is impossible, because only mutually contradictory properties can serve as the delimitors of a classification. [Reply: This is not so; for while convention is indeed *śakti*, a modern convention lacks the status of *śakti*. To explain: convention is held to be of two kinds—innate (*ājānika*) and modern (*ādhunika*). Among these, the innate is eternal, and that which is [eternal] is designated as *śakti*.
But that which is occasional is modern, created by contemporary authors and others.

In that context—meaning between those two—a *nitya-saṃketa* (eternal convention) is *ājānika*. That which has no birth (*januḥ*) or origin (*utpattiḥ*) is *ajani*; *ājānika* is simply *ajanika* with the suffix *ikaṇ* added in the sense of the base itself; thus the word *ājānika* is etymological (*yaugika*). Others, however, say that *ājātika* means "pervading time" (*kālatva-vyāpaka*), and thus they claim the word *ājānika* is technical (*pāribhāṣika*). That is not correct; for when an etymological meaning is possible, it is improper to assume a technical definition.

Nor should it be argued that since eternality (*nityatva*)—defined as being a non-counterpositive of destruction while being a counterpositive of prior non-existence—is obtainable only through its etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*), how can it be considered etymological when it is intended to convey that very meaning? This is because a thing that has not arisen, distinct from prior non-existence, is necessarily a non-counterpositive of destruction; or alternatively, because the word "eternal" (*nitya*) itself signifies that which has not arisen. Nor is there tautology due to those two terms having the same referent, because the term "beginningless" (*anādika*) refers to that which is conveyed by the word "unborn" (*ajānika*).

Therefore, although the word *yat* in the phrase "that which is power" (*yā śaktiḥ*) refers to an eternal convention (*nityasaṃketa*), there is no tautology, because the statement "it is called power" (*śaktir ity abhidhīyate*) explains that it is the object denoted by the word *śakti*.

For this very reason, there is no tautology even in such cases as "the brother's wife is *prajāvatī*," "the husband's brothers are *śyālas*," or "he who gives away a daughter, having honored and adorned her, is a *kūkuda*. *Kādācitkatva* (occurrence at certain times) means being the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva*). An *ādhinika* is one denoted by the word *ādhinika*. To the question "Who is that? he says: "By the authors of the scriptures and others. By the word "others" (*ādi*), barbarians (*mleccha*) and so forth are included. For example, there is a convention (*saṃketa*) for the word "river" (*nadī*) regarding a woman who has performed the *ikāra* [initiatory rite], for the word "vṛddhi" regarding things like *ārā*, and for the word "barley" (*yava*) regarding the two *raṅgas*.

Furthermore, there is no evidence that words such as *Caitra*, which are designated by fathers and others through convention, possess an eternal convention (*nityasaṃketa*); for it would follow that they were used previously by preceding speakers on the twelfth day [of birth], since it has been stated that such usage is restricted to those specific individuals. Although words such as Persian (*pārasīka*) and others are no different from words like *Caitra* in their possession of convention, they are not employed in religious rites (*dharmakarma*), because the Veda prohibits them there, stating: "One should speak with correct words (*sādhu*), not with incorrect ones; one should not speak corruptly, nor should one speak like a barbarian (*mleccha*)."

*mlecchitavai* means "by those designated solely by barbarians"; however, they say that words such as *khara* and so forth are designated even by Āryas in cases of haste and the like, just as they are by barbarians.

The grammarians (Śābdikas) also accept a third function, namely *vyañjanā* (suggestion). Thus it was stated by Nāgeśa: "Suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*), awakened by the knowledge of the particularities of the speaker and other factors and by intuition (*pratibhā*), which produces a cognition independent of the apprehension of the obstruction of the primary meaning; its object is both well-known and unknown meanings, whether related or unrelated to the primary meaning. For this very reason, the status of particles (*nipātas*) as indicators (*dyotakas*) and the fact that the *sphoṭa* is what is manifested (*vyaṅgya*) have been asserted by Hari and others.

Furthermore, "suggestiveness" (*dyotakatva*) consists, in some cases, in the manifestation of the power (*śakti*) of a word with which it is uttered in proximity; thus, its acceptance is necessary even for the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). And this [suggestiveness] exists everywhere—in words, their meanings, whole words, parts of words, phonemes, compositions, gestures, and so forth—because such experience occurs in every instance. While the knowledge of the specific qualities of the speaker and other factors is an auxiliary cause for the cognition of particular suggested meanings, it is not required in all cases; this is explained in detail elsewhere (Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntalaghumañjūṣā, p. 133). For the Grammarians, that [suggestion], being of three kinds, is indeed nothing but memory (*smṛti*), like [the perception of] accents and the like.
The triad consisting of denotation (abhidhā), indication (lakṣaṇā), and suggestion (vyakti) is considered [the threefold function of words].

"Though there is a difference in their characteristics, in reality the various functions are but one"—so say the grammarians, for they fear the burden of complexity that would arise from their being distinct. (Kovidananda, p. 1, verse 42)
(Kauvidānanda, p. 26, verse 16):

Just as a single sound becomes threefold through the distinctions of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*), so too does *śakti* alone—the function of a word—become threefold through the distinctions of denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and suggestion (*vyañjanā*). The commentary on that [verse] states: "There is complexity in accepting a distinction between the functions. On this point, the Grammarians maintain: "The function of a word is *śakti* alone; and it is designated as *śakti* or *lakṣaṇā* based on whether it is well-known or not; as for *vyañjanā*, it is included within that [same *śakti*] because its operation is prolonged" (Triveṇikā, pp. 36–37).

Thus, having inferred the view of the Grammarians—that grammarians do not accept the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*)—Āśādharabhaṭṭa refuted it in his *Kovidānanda* and *Triveṇikā*. His intention was likely this: that in the most ancient foundational treatises (*ākaragrantha*), such as the *Mahābhāṣya*, no specific discussion regarding the subject of suggestion is found anywhere. Furthermore, in works such as the *Tārkikarakṣā*, it is stated: "And the function (*vṛtti*) consists of either denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*)" (*Manoramā-śabda-ṭippaṇa*, p. 25, l. [fragment]).

Thus it is written [in the *Laghuśabdenduśekhara*] as "itself" (*eva*), and not as "one of the various forms" (*anyatamarūpā*) with the intention of implying *vyañjanā*. This is done while keeping in mind the doubt that the referent of the secondary meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), such as a schoolboy (*māṇavaka*), lacks a fixed presence and therefore cannot be the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consisting of the word "lion" (*siṃha*). [As stated in the *Laghuśabdenduśekhara*, p. 516; *Pīyūṣasūtra*: "Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) preceded by the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) occurs only in the case of a word (*pada*)."

Thus it was stated by the author of the Śekhara; however, no doubt or resolution regarding the case of *vyañjanā* (suggestion) was raised there. Had *vyañjanā* been accepted, then even in that context, since the state of being restricted would be absent, the presentation of those two [doubt and resolution] would necessarily have had to be made.
Although those who place their faith in the doctrine of *sphoṭa* must certainly accept *vyañjanā*, otherwise [the doctrine] of all Grammarians would be undermined.

The state of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatā*) would not be established at all. For this very reason, Nāgeśabhaṭṭa, having demonstrated the nature of *vyañjanā*, stated: "For this very reason, the fact that particles (*nipāta*) are indicators (*dyotaka*) and that the *sphoṭa* is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) has been asserted by Harivṛṣabha and others. Furthermore, since 'indicativeness' (*dyotakatva*) consists in the manifestation of the power (*śakti*) residing in a word uttered in proximity [to it], its acceptance is necessary even for the Grammarians" (*Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntalaghumañjūṣā*, p. ...).

133) Thus, even so, among the logicians (*tārkika*), the effort of the grammarians (*śābdika*) to support *vyañjanā* would have as its sole result the mere rejection of the logical view, because otherwise—given the rejection of *lakṣaṇā*—it would be improper to assume a secondary function (*vṛtti*) that is not the least [inferior], because it would involve the complexity (*gaurava*) of assuming two delimiters for two functions, and because, when there is an intention (*tātparya*), there is no *lakṣaṇā*, according to the *Bhāṣya*: "All words denote all meanings. (Paraśurāma Laṭakana)

Furthermore, how could all the reasons demonstrated by Nāgeśa, such as *lakṣaṇāni* (Pṛ. 62) and so forth, not contradict the theory of *vyañjanā*? Whatever meaning is manifested (*vyaṅgya*) by *vyañjanā*, all of that will be made manifest through the power of what is otherwise unestablished (*aprasiddha-śakti*).

In the view of the Alamkārikas—who maintain that faith in the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) should be maintained—it is only by those possessed of aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) that the suggested meaning is apprehended. Such a meaning will be understood by the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) through an "unestablished power" (*aprasiddha-śakti*); what is the use of *vyañjanā*? Regarding this, it was stated by Nāgeśa: "Power (*śakti*) is twofold: established (*prasiddhā*) and unestablished (*aprasiddhā*). Being knowable by those of dull intellect is 'establishedness'; being knowable by the hearts of the aesthetically sensitive alone is 'unestablishedness'."

"In that regard, what is incongruous about the fact that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as *gaṅgā* is well-known with respect to the river-current and the like, yet unknown with respect to the bank (*tīra*) and the like? If you object: 'If you maintain that all words denote all objects, then why would there not be a cognition of a cloth from the word "jar"?'—we reply: No; for it has been stated that [cognition occurs] when there is an intention (*tātparya*). Understand, therefore, that it is due to the absence of such intention. Furthermore, this intention is obtained by people like us from the tradition of the Lord, the deities, the great sages, and the elders of the world; thus, everything is perfectly established. (Paramalaghumañjūṣā, Laghunyāsa, p. 63)

And thus, just as in the case of *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function), the desired meaning is obtained through a non-established [conventional] power (*śakti*) alone due to the force of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), so too in the case of *vyañjanā* (suggestive function), the desired meaning will be obtained through a non-established power alone, aided by the particularities of the speaker and other factors; what then is the need for *vyañjanā*? If grammarians accept *vyañjanā* in the form of "illuminator-ness" (*dyotakatā*)—because they accept that particles like *hari* and others are "illuminators" (*dyotaka*) and because they accept that the *sphoṭa* is the "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*)—then [the same applies to] prefixes (*prādi*)...

If that [function] is accepted by the Naiyāyikas as well because they accept [prefixes like *pra-*, etc. as being indicative (*dyotaka*), then it would have to be accepted by them too because they accept *pra-* and so on as being indicative; yet it is not accepted by them. If their nature as suggestors (*vyañjakatva*) is something different, then let that of the Grammarians also be something else. What is the point of the excessive burden of accepting a distinction based on a difference in definition? Thus, it appears that the Grammarians have no regard for suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

The *Paramalaghumañjūṣā* is not a work by Nāgeśa. The sequence of exposition employed for a particular doctrine within the *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā* is not observed in the *Paramalaghumañjūṣā*. Furthermore, a displacement of topics is seen here and there; the vigor with which the rejection of *lakṣaṇā* (secondary signification) is treated in the *Paramalaghumañjūṣā* is not found in that [work].

Thus, since many such differences in interpretation are observed between the two grammatical systems (*grantha*), how can it be determined that the Grammarians do not accept *vyañjanā* (suggestion) on that basis? This is indeed a point of contention among the learned. Nevertheless, the arguments of Āśādhara Bhaṭṭa cannot be disregarded by those possessed of discernment. The secret underlying this matter should be reflected upon by the tigers among linguists who are free from envy and have applied their minds to it. Now, the investigation into the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*).
Since the meaning of the verbal root is the foundation of all words, it is now defined.

On this point, the Prābhākaras [among the Mīmāṃsakas]—namely Maṇḍana Miśra—hold that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the result (*phala*) alone, whereas the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is the favorable operation (*anukūlavyāpāra*). Temporal properties such as "presentness," which are the meanings of *laṭ* and other suffixes, are construed with the operation, because they are conveyed by the same word (*ekapadopāttatvāt*). Thus, the result functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) with respect to the operation that is the meaning of the verbal suffix. Other Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that the meaning of the verbal root is the mere operation, while the result is the meaning of the accusative case (*dvitīyārtha*).

The Neo-Mīmāṃsakas maintain that both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). A single power (*ekāśakti*) resides in each part [of the meaning]. In this context, the relation between the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*) constitutes the semantic connection (*saṃsarga*). The resulting cognition has the operation as its primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyaka*), and within that [cognition], the case-factors other than the object (*karman*) are construed; furthermore, when the object-case-factor is mentioned alongside the agent-word (*kartṛpada*), it is construed with the result. The Naiyāyikas, however, hold that both the result and the operation constitute the meaning of the verbal root, while the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is effort (*kṛti*). They further maintain that the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) has the meaning of the nominative-terminated word (*prathamāntārtha*) as its primary qualificand.

On this point, the ancient grammarians [hold as follows]: Regarding the rule *phalavyāpārayordhātuḥ* (the root denotes both the result and the operation), because there are two [terms], the root possesses distinct powers (*śakti*) relative to the result and relative to the operation. For this very reason, there is the co-referential connection (*anvaya*) of an object such as *stoka-* with the result by way of identity, while an object such as a village (*grāma-*) connects with the operation by way of difference. If one were to accept a single power residing in the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa*), then since the word-meaning would be a single unitary entity, it would follow that objects such as the *karman* could not connect with the result.

Nāgeśabhaṭṭa, however, maintains that the denotative power (*śakti*) of verbal roots resides both in the operation qualified by the result and in the result qualified by the operation; otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of a cognition in which either the operation is the subject and the result the predicate, or the result is the subject and the operation the predicate, because the separate presentation (*pṛthagupasthiti*) required for the relation of subject and predicate exists in both cases.

[Objection: "The cause for the cognition of an operation delimited by a result is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a verbal root (*dhātu*) occurring in co-utterance with an agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*); thus, there is no risk of the unwanted consequence of such a cognition arising in all cases. [Reply: The meaning of the verbal root is the result alone; *bhāvanā*, however, is certainly not its denotation (*vācya*), because the linguistic cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding it is subject to dispute. It is only in the case of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) that it is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

To the question "What does he do?"—which implies the inquiry as to what kind of effort is involved—the answer "He cooks" (*apacati*) is justified even through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the verbal root denoting cooking has that [effort] as its object. Furthermore, when the question "What does he do? refers exclusively to the action (*karman*), an answer referring exclusively to the act of cooking is likewise justified. Even the paraphrase "He performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) is justified, just like the paraphrase "He performs [the action of] non-linguistic objecthood. Therefore, this [paraphrase] is not a proof for the fact that *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is the expressed meaning of the verbal suffix.

[Fn kha: The reading is "Caitra is the qualifier of cooking by means of the relation of being produced by an effort residing in itself. Cooking is the qualifier of Caitra by means of the relation of possessing an effort that produces it. And thus, it is the very effort included within the relation that is explained [by the verbal suffix]. Otherwise, since both objecthood and substratum-hood would also be explained by the second case-ending and the verbal suffix respectively, it would follow that these two are also denotable meanings (vācyatā). Furthermore, in a cognition where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the qualificandum, the cause is precisely the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case.

Otherwise, there would be excessive complexity (gaurava), as one would have to postulate two causal relations—namely, that "the presentation of the suffix *tiP* and so on is the cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the verbal root," and "the presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case is the cause for a cognition of the meaning of *tiP* and so on"—as well as the postulation of the denotative power (*śakti*) of the verb-ending itself.

Because the cause of the occurrence of a word-meaning (nāmārtha) qualified by a relation distinct from identity (abhedātirikta-saṃsarga), which is introduced by a verb-ending (ākhyāta), an indeclinable (nipāta), or a case-ending (sub), is [the requirement for] the presence of such [a relation], there is no undesired consequence (āpatti) such as "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*). However, they say that the meaning of the verb-ending (ākhyātārtha) consists only of number and time, and that the connection with the *kāraka*s occurs only with the fruit (phala) which is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha); thus, "Cooking by means of husks" (*kāṇṭhaiḥ pākaḥ*) is indeed accepted. That is not correct; for if the root *kṛ* also had only effort (*yatna*) as its meaning, it would follow that it is not an *akarman* (intransitive) root, just like the root *yat*.

Furthermore, because the action would not reside in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*), sacrifices and the like could not have an agent who is simultaneously the object (*karmakartṛ*). Moreover, even if the root *kṛ* (to do/make) were to mean "origination," it would result in its being intransitive, just as in the case of the verb "to originate" (*utpadyate*). Furthermore, if roots signified only the fruit [of the action], the distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs would be abolished. Finally, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the village possesses going" (*grāmo gamanavān*).

Furthermore, even when an activity conducive to cooking has begun, there would be no occurrence of the expression "cooking is taking place" during the stage when the result has not yet arisen; conversely, there would be the unwarranted occurrence of the expression "mutual movement" (like "the mutual conjunction of the village and Caitra"). Moreover, when the result exists but the activity has ceased, there would be no occurrence of the expression "cooking has occurred. [Fn kha: The phrase "'vyāpra .... anāpattiśca'" does not appear.]

Furthermore, there is an over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of a verb (*ākhyāta*) as established in the *Nirukta*—namely, "a verb has being (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning"—in cases such as *pacati*, because the fruit of the verbal root’s meaning (*dhātvartha-phala*) alone is accepted as the action (*kriyā*) that constitutes the verbal root’s meaning.

If, however, one accepts [that fruit] as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), then in cases such as *caitraḥ pacati*, the nominal meaning would not be construed with the verbal root’s meaning through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), according to the reasoning already stated. This is the direction of the argument. [The additional reading is absent.]

As for the view of those who follow Maṇḍanamiśra: the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the result (*phala*) alone, while the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*). Transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in the denotation of a result that resides in a locus different from the operation denoted by the suffix; intransitivity (*akarmakatva*) consists in the denotation of a result that resides in the same locus as that operation. Furthermore, the state of being an object (*karmatva*) is simply the state of being the substratum (*āśraya*) of the meaning of the verbal root, which resides in a locus different from the operation denoted by the suffix.

Even in expressions such as *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he brings about a pot"), the pot and so forth possess the status of an object (*karman*) by virtue of being the locus of the arising that is non-co-referential with the operation denoted by the suffix *ṇic*. Even when the causative meaning is internalized (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), there is no fault, because the suffix itself indicates the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇijartha*). Agency (*kartṛtva*) consists precisely in being the locus of the operation denoted by the suffix. For this very reason, while the pot is an object in *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*, it is indeed the agent in *ghaṭo bhavati*.

Even though the *ṇic* suffix has the function of denoting the activity of an instigator (*prayojaka*), in forms such as *bhavati*, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes only the activity of the agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, time also acquires the property of being connected with the activity expressed by the verbal suffix that denotes it; this is another favorable point. It is also favorable that [this connection] is obtained even in the case of *jānāti*. In *jānāti*, the connection occurs only with the activity of the meaning of the suffix—namely, the contact between the mind and the sense organ (*manas-saṃyoga*) which is the generator of knowledge—and not with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Furthermore, because the *ghañ* and other suffixes prescribed for abstract action (*bhāva*) denote activity, there is no undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) such as "the village possesses going" (*grāmo gamanavān*).

In expressions such as "the cooking of rice" (*odanasya pākaḥ*), the case-endings denoting kārakas arise precisely because they are construed with the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) which is the meaning of the suffix *ghañ*. Furthermore, since agentive and objective *kṛt* suffixes denote both the *kāraka* and the *bhāvanā*, there is no inconsistency in the construction of kārakas even in cases such as "the cooker of rice" (*odanasya paktā*).

If it is argued that, in this case, the root *jñā* (to know) would consequently fail to be transitive because a function (*vyāpāra*) residing in a different locus from the cognition—which is the meaning of the verbal root—is precluded in the case of Devadatta and others, we say: no. This is because the required "residing in a different locus" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) exists in the function precisely in the form of residing in a locus other than that of the cognition, by way of the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*), which is the delimitor of the result. Otherwise, since all functions would reside in the same locus as the result through relations such as temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*), there would be a great deal of confusion regarding the definition of transitivity.

Nor does it follow that if an operation (*vyāpāra*) were the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*), then—given that it expresses an action (*kriyā*)—its status as a root, defined by its being listed in the *gaṇa* (the list of roots), would be untenable. For in this context, "action-ness" (*kriyātva*) is not the state of being an operation; rather, it is the state of not being a substratum for the productivity (*janakatā*) determined by the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), while simultaneously not being connected with gender, number, and so forth. Therefore, there is no fault. Or else, that [action-ness] is simply the state of being the meaning of a root. Nor is there a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*), because the previously mentioned status of being a root is not what is meant here; for since action-ness lacks unity, it cannot be a universal (*anugama*). Rather, it is a specific technical designation (*sañjñāviśeṣa*). And since the words that serve as designata are themselves generic terms (*jātiśabda*), that [action-ness] is indeed a specific universal.

Alternatively, it is simply the state of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) by virtue of its connection with a specific technical convention (*saṅketa*); and the rule *bhūvādi* serves as its indicator. Nor does the view that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has action (*vyāpāra*) as its meaning contradict Yāska’s statement that "the verb (*ākhyāta*) is primarily action," for in that context the word *ākhyāta* refers to the verbal root itself, based on the etymological derivation: "that by which the meaning, which is the primary element in all cases, is expressed."

Because in that context, only the *prakṛtis* (bases) are enumerated in the rule "Nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles" (*nāmākhyātopasarganipātāḥ*), and because it is stated later in that same work that "according to Śākaṭāyana and the convention of the etymologists (*nairukta*), nouns are born from verbs" (*nāmānyākhyātajāni*). [Note: In the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), the word *ākhyāta* sometimes refers to the verbal root (*dhātu*) and sometimes to a form ending in a personal suffix (*tiṅanta*), depending on the power of its etymological derivation.]

For it cannot be maintained that a name (nāman) is produced from a verbal suffix (ākhyātapratyaya), but rather that it is produced from a root (dhātu); this must be stated because the term "verb" (ākhyāta) refers exclusively to that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix. This is because Yāska, having introduced the topic with "This is the definition of noun and verb," stated: "The verb has action as its primary meaning. According to your view, there would be the consequence of under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the definition of a root, since it would fail to apply to roots that serve as the base for *kṛt*-suffixes. For this very reason, there are four meanings of the verb: state (*bhāva*), tense (*kāla*), grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and number (*saṅkhyā*).

In this regard, the commentary on that [sūtra], "the state of being (bhāva) is the primary meaning," is consistent. Furthermore, the statement that the *kāraka* (participant in action) is the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) is based merely on its being implied by that [meaning]. For this very reason, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "Devadatta cooks" is logically established. Moreover, in the rule concerning nouns, verbs, and prefixes (*nāmākhyātopasarga*), it is appropriate to understand that the term "verb" (*ākhyāta*) refers only to that which ends in a suffix whose base is a verbal root (*dhātu*), due to its association with the noun (*nāman*) which likewise ends in a suffix whose base is a verbal root.

For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *prarśasāyāṃ rūpap* (Pāṇini 5.3.66), having raised the objection that forms such as *apacatirūpam*, *pacatorūpam*, and *pacantirūpam* would be unestablished, it is stated: "A verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, whereas a noun (*nāman*) has substance as its primary meaning; for when asked about the action, one answers with a verbal suffix—'What is Devadatta doing?'—'He is cooking. When asked about the substance, one answers with a nominal suffix—'Which Devadatta?'—'The one who is a cook. This statement is thus consistent. Furthermore, prepositions (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*) are mentioned separately because they are merely indicative (*dyotaka*) and because they do not occur in syntactic coordination with an action.

The view that "nouns are derived from verbs" (*nāmānyākhyātajāni*) refers to the verbal root (*dhātu*) only by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as there is no other recourse. In cases such as *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"), the rice and so forth are construed with the operation (*vyāpāra*) itself through the relation of being the generator of a result residing in itself. Some claim that this very [view] also upholds the general rule that the meaning of the suffix is primary; however, that is not correct. For in cases such as *pacati*, *pakṣyati*, and *pakvavān*, rather than postulating a separate power (*śakti*) for multiple suffixes to convey the blowing of air (*phūtkāra*) and so forth, it is more appropriate to postulate the power for the single verbal root alone.

Furthermore, if the suffix were the meaning of the term *pratyaya* [in the sense of "the meaning of the affix"], then even in cases such as "he goes" (*gacchati*), one would have to state that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the root *pac* is the cause for the cognition of that [action], in order to prevent the cognition of it; thus, it is more appropriate that the action belongs to *pac* alone. Moreover, in roots such as *as* (to be), existence (*sattā*) itself is the operation (*vyāpāra*), and pervasion (*vyāpti*)—in the form of a delimiting relation (*avacchedakatā*)—is the result (*phala*). For this very reason, it is clear in the Bhāṣya and other works that in expressions such as "he exists for a month" (*māsam asti*), the time-period like the month functions as the object (*karman*). Consequently, in that case, there is great complexity in abandoning the established verbal root-meaning regarding the aspect of existence and postulating an unestablished suffix-meaning.

Furthermore, in the case of the sentence "caitreṇa supyate" (it is slept by Caitra), since there is no meaning other than time for the suffix in a verb expressing a state (*bhāvārtha-lakāra*), Caitra would not attain the status of an agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, the definition of a verb as "that which has action as its primary meaning" (*kriyāpradhāna*) would suffer from the fault of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*). Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence that sentences such as "guruḥ śiṣyābhyāṃ pācayati" (the teacher causes the two students to cook) would not be accounted for; for in that case, while the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is established as the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the operation of the one being prompted (*prayojya-vyāpāra*) must be expressed as the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

Furthermore, since number would only be construed with that which is construed with the operation expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha-vyāpāra) as its own denotatum, there would be no occurrence of the dual ending for "two disciples" (*śiṣyābhyām*), nor would there be the occurrence of the singular ending in "he causes [them] to cook" (*pācayati*). Moreover, because the agent (the teacher) is not denoted, the nominative case would not occur there; yet it would occur after the word "disciple" (*śiṣya*). Finally, because the operation expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) with respect to the operation prompted by the meaning of the verbal suffix, its status as the primary element (*prādhānya*) would not be established.

Furthermore, the fruit (*phala*) is not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*); rather, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) that is conducive to the [instigated's] activity. In this context, the fruit is construed as being conducive to the primary activity. The meanings of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are tense, number, and the activity of the instigator; there is no repetition of the cognition, as in the case of [the word] "two" (*dvau*), because [the activity of the instigator] is the predominant factor. Moreover, by the force of the sūtraic restatement beginning with "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the substratum is implied solely through the activity of the instigator. And [the rule] beginning with "anabhihite" (Pāṇini 2.3.1) applies to cases where [the agent or object] is not already expressed, whether by implication through power (*śakti*) or otherwise.

It should not be argued that there is no fault because this is precisely the intended meaning; for such a conclusion cannot be obtained from the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26). Since everything is consistent without difficulty according to our own view, there is no need for a strained interpretation. This is the general direction. As for what the ancient Naiyāyikas maintain—that the root (*dhātu*) has power (*śakti*) only in its mere operation (*vyāpāra*), while the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the object-case suffix (*karmapratyaya*), because postulating the power of many roots in the fruit would be more cumbersome than postulating it in relation to the object-suffix—[that is rejected].

Furthermore, on the view that the verbal root (*dhātu*) conveys the result (*phala*), since there can be no direct syntactic connection between the meaning of the noun (*nāmartha*) and the meaning of the root through the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā-sambandha*), one must accept that the status of being the substratum of the result is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Consequently, one must admit that the object (*karman*) appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*), which necessitates the postulation of an additional appearance of its relation; thus, this view is cumbersome (*gaurava*). On the other hand, if the result itself is the meaning of the suffix, then the relation is simply "being the substratum of that [result]," which is parsimonious (*lāghava*).

Since the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the verb ‘*gam*’ is the cause for the manifestation of conjunction as the result, and the co-occurrence with ‘*tyaji*’ is the cause for the manifestation of disjunction, the two expressions ‘he goes to the village’ (*grāmaṃ gacchati*) and ‘he abandons [it]’ (*tyajati*) do not have the function of signifying disjunction and conjunction respectively.

Nor should it be argued that this results in no distinction between "leaving" (*tyāga*) and "going" (*gamana*), since both produce the same conjunction and disjunction; for there is no fault, as we accept that in such usages where the verb is not co-occurrent with the word "action" (*karman*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for an operation delimited by disjunction and so forth, based on beginningless linguistic convention. Transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting an operation whose locus is distinct from the fruit of the meaning of the suffix coreferential with itself. And "objectness" (*karmatva*) is simply the state of being a fruit understood by a suffix construed with the meaning of the verbal root.
And the state of being intransitive is precisely the absence of that [object]; it consists simply in the presence of a specific quality produced by such a result in the object.

The state of being an object (*karmasthatva*) belongs to the action; thus, in cases such as *kriyate* ("is done"), the suffix *yaṅ* and others are established for the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*). In the case of verbal roots that have objects, "being transitive" (*sakarmakatva*) consists precisely in the fact that [the action] is construed with [the object] by way of being its objective (*viṣayitva*). For this very reason, suffixes denoting the object occur after roots such as *karoti* ("does") and *jānāti* ("knows"). However, the root *yat* ("to strive") is not transitive, because the effort presented by it does not construe with [the object] as its objective, but rather only as its intended goal (*uddeśyatva*); therefore, there is no fault.

For this very reason, there is the usage "he strives for eating" (*bhojanāya yatate*) even when one is not currently eating. Furthermore, the capacity of a verb such as *gam* (to go) to convey its own meaning as connected with a result depends upon its inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Due to the absence of that [inherent nature], verbs such as *spandi* (to throb) are treated as intransitive (*akarmaka*). That is not so; because the second and fourth cases are prescribed for the object of verbs whose meaning is "going" and the like—according to the rule: "The second and fourth cases are used for the object of a verb meaning 'to go,' provided it refers to an action of movement and not a path" (*gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyā-caturthyau ceṣṭāyām anadhvani*, Pāṇini 2.3.12)—as well as by the Vārttika: "When the suffix *lyap* is elided, [the case ending is used] for the object" (*lyablope karmaṇi*).

[2|4|31] It is more appropriate to postulate that the root itself possesses power (śakti) with respect to the result, rather than postulating powers for multiple *sup*-s and *tiṅ*-s based on the prescription of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) by the rule "after a root denoting motion, the fifth case is used for the goal" (Vārttika 2|3|36), or based on the prescription of the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) by the rule "the seventh case is used for the object of a verb meaning 'to seek'" (Vārttika 2|3|36), or rather than postulating that the co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) of specific roots is the cause for the cognition of specific results.

For me, however, there is only one causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*): that the presentation of the result produced by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the cause for the cognition of the locus (*āśraya*) generated by the conditions prescribed by *karma* (the object). This is because, in accordance with the usage of the "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*) such as *grāmo gamyate svayameva*, it is necessary that the result (*phala*) also be denoted by the verbal root; and because in cases such as *grāmam adhyāste*, the locus is already established as the meaning of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). Furthermore, [if my view were not accepted], this would result in the contingency of the accusative case having multiple meanings.

Furthermore, when there is the delusion that roots such as *tyaji* and *gami* are synonyms just like *yā* and *gami*, the assumption—that the co-occurrence with a specific verbal root acts as a regulator for the cognition of a specific result—is untenable, because from expressions such as "he abandons" (*tyajati*) and "he goes" (*gacchati*), a cognition no different [in content] arises than from "he goes" (*yāti*) and "he moves" (*gacchati*). Nor can it be argued that the causal complex consisting of the knowledge of the sentence "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*) possesses the status of an inhibitor toward inference and other cognitions having the same object...

Since the semantic representation (*upasthiti*) generated by the verbal root—which has as its qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) the operation (*vyāpāra*) qualified by a mode (*prakāratā*) residing in the fruit (*phala*)—must be included [in the definition of the action], there is no deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether that representation is included by virtue of possessing such a qualificandumness, or by virtue of possessing a mode-ness toward the fruit qualified by a qualificandumness toward the operation. Consequently, this results in an increase in the causal obstruction (*pratibandhakatā*) of the complex of conditions and a heaviness of the delimitors (*avacchedaka-gaurava*).

It should not be argued that, in my view, the inclusion of the presentation of a result not produced by the second case (accusative) within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) merely occupies the place of the presentation of that [result] produced by it as established in your own system, and thus there is no complexity (*gaurava*). For, in cases such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), where one has either a misconception regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal root in the sense of an operation delimited by a result and of the second case in the sense of the locus (*āśrayatva*), or who grasps [the meaning] as being figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), such an inference does not arise from the verbal causal complex. Consequently, in accordance with that fact, you too must necessarily accept such a relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*).

Furthermore, in cases such as "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajate*) or "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to" (*viṣṇur yaṣṭavyaḥ*), since the accusative case ending (and others) prescribed for the dative sense conveys a relation solely as the *uddeśya* (the intended recipient), the root *yaj* would likewise result in being intransitive, just like the root *yat*. Moreover, since Viṣṇu would not be the object of the verbal root's meaning, there would be no occasion for the application of suffixes such as the *laṭ* (present tense) or *tavya* (gerundive) with respect to him as an object. If it is argued that Viṣṇu is the object of the sacrifice by virtue of being the content of the *uddeśyatā* (intendedness), then eating (*bhojana*) would also be the object of the meaning of *yat* in the same way, and thus *yat* would also result in being transitive.

Furthermore, in this way, in the expression "it is done for the sake of eating" (*bhojanāya kriyate*), the word *bhojana* would have to be [the object], because *kṛñ* (to do/make) would then incur the status of being intransitive, just like the verb *yat* (to strive). Nor can it be said that "transitivity" consists merely in being different from intransitivity; for in that case, one could not include the distinction between *kṛñ*, *jñā* (to know), and so on, based on actual usage, because even transitive verbs would incur the impossibility [of being transitive] when they are intransitive in another sense. By the same logic, "intransitivity" must also be defined as simply being different from transitivity, since any other kind of intransitivity is difficult to define.

Furthermore, due to the resulting fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) would fail to convey their intended meaning. Moreover, the previously mentioned definition of a transitive verb—where the object is distinct from the meaning of the suffix—and the definition of an object (*karman*) are both under-extended (*avyāpta*) to causative transitive verbs such as *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he causes the pot to come into being") and *edhayati* ("he makes grow"), as well as to their respective objects. This is because, in those cases, the result is obtainable from the verbal root itself through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and thus it cannot be the meaning of the suffix due to the principle that what is already obtained elsewhere should not be the meaning of a word, as well as due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Therefore, the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to a result (*phala*). As for the connection of the substratum (*āśraya*), which is the referent of the second case (*dvitīyā*), it occurs with respect to the result—which is a single part [of the whole denoted by the root]—due to grammatical rules such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2) and due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). By this, the objection that the expression ‘movement is not an operation’ would be logically untenable is refuted; for there is no linguistic convention for connecting a negation with a specific part of an operation when that part is the result. [Note: The negation refers to the qualificand of the cognition produced by the word with which it is co-occurrent.]

[The reading "evānvayānutpatteḥ" is an addition. Or let it be so—the potency (śakti) of the fruit and the operation is indeed distinct. In that regard, the aspect of the fruit is generally a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the operation, and "being produced" (*janyatva*) is generally the relation (*saṃsarga*). However, in some cases, "being the object" (*viṣayatva*) is the relation; for example, as in the case of the occurrence of verbs such as *paśyati* ("he sees") in reference to a perception preceded by that [operation]. Other relations should likewise be inferred according to the circumstances.

And being a result (*phalatva*) consists in having a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) determined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of that verbal root, when it is co-occurrent with an agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*). This is because even others accept the mutual coreferential relation (*parasparānvaya*) between effort (*kṛti*) and being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), even though both are presented by a single word. However, when co-occurrent with an objective suffix (*karmapratyaya*), there is also [the status of] the qualificand. In that case, due to its internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*), the result first becomes a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*) and only then relates to another meaning.

For this very reason, we maintain that "going is not motion" (*gamanaṃ na spandaḥ*), because it is a rule of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that a word's own meaning (*svārtha*) is construed with that which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by the word uttered in its proximity. All case-factors (*kāraka*) other than the object (*karman*) are construed with the operation (*vyāpāra*), either directly or through mediation; however, the object is construed with the result (*phala*). Nor does this contradict the rule that case-factors must be construed with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself is the productive urge. Or, let it be that even for that [object], the construction occurs with the operation itself by way of the result. And the operation consists of [actions such as] blowing and so forth. In this context, the term "action" (*kriyā*) possesses a conventional (*sāṃketikī*) denotative power (*śakti*).
Whatever is designated as something to be accomplished (sādhya), whether it be already established or not yet established,
is called "action" (kriyā) because it possesses a nature that relies upon a temporal sequence.

A collection of parts that arise in succession is designated as "action" (kriyā) when its non-difference is conceptually constructed by the intellect through those parts which serve as its subordinate qualities.

Thus, from the passage in the *Harikārikā* explaining the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.1), the meaning of the second verse is as follows: a collection (*saṃghāta*) of these operations, which arise in succession, is—by its very nature—composed of constituent parts that appear as subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) in their respective forms; this collection, having its internal distinctions constructed by a unifying cognition (*ekatvabuddhi*) consisting of synthesis (*saṅkalana*), is "made" and thus designated in linguistic usage.

In expressions such as ‘pacati’ (he cooks) and ‘pakṣyati’ (he will cook), the action is unaccomplished; whereas in expressions such as ‘apākṣīt’ (he cooked), the action—whether already accomplished or being denoted as something yet to be accomplished—is what is intended. The term ‘āśritā’ (dependent) serves to demonstrate its nature as a process. The meaning of ‘kriyā’ is that which is produced—that is, produced sequentially through the successive arising of its constituent parts.

In this context, *siddhatva* (the state of being accomplished) is that specific generic quality (*vaijātya*) which delimits the fitness for syntactic connection (*anvaya-yogyatā*) by way of being either the object to be denoted (*uddeśyatva*) or the limit (*avadhitva*). It is this very quality that constitutes the form [of *siddhatva*]. Furthermore, it is precisely this that delimits the capacity to give rise to an expectancy for another action (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣotthāpakatāvacchedaka*). *Sādhyatva* (the state of being in the process of accomplishment), on the other hand, is that specific generic quality which delimits the fitness for connection with *kārakas* (factors of action) and so forth, while being co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the property of having constituent parts arranged in a temporal sequence (*pūrvāparībhūtavayavatva*). In this regard, *siddhatva* is conveyed by the suffix *ghañ* in expressions such as "pākaḥ" (cooking), whereas *sādhyatva* is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) in all cases.

As for the claim that "sādhyatva" (the state of being the object to be accomplished) consists in non-connection with the denotatum (*uddeśyatva*) and so forth, or non-connection with the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, or non-connection as a means of proof (*sādhanatva*), or possessing a nature that excludes the arousal of expectancy for another action—that does not appear in the cognition [of the sentence]. This is because the statement "it is expressed as the object to be accomplished" (*sādhyatvenābhidhīyate*) indicates a cognition having that [state] as its qualifier. Furthermore, when asked why there is non-connection with the inferential mark and so forth, one must necessarily accept a specific distinctness (*vaijātya*) as the regulating factor for that.

As for the claim that what appears is the state of being produced (*utpādyamānatva*), and therefore an action does not connect as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) because in common worldly usage only that which has already been produced is seen to be an instrument—that is incorrect. For [otherwise] there would be no occurrence of such expressions as "enmity was created by the cooking while it was being produced," nor the occurrence of "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"; furthermore, in cases such as "if one bows to Kṛṣṇa, one shall attain happiness," "having eaten, one is satisfied," and "having bowed to the proud woman, he becomes soft," there is an connection of something unestablished as a means (*sādhana*).

For me, however, there is no fault, because that specific generality (*vaijātya*) is absent from the fruit-component (*phalāṃśa*) therein; or rather, that generality resides only in the activity (*vyāpāra*). That very activity is called *bhāvanā*. Nor should it be argued that there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) due to the absence of a requirement for another action (*kriyāntara*) from the verbal root (*dhātu*), because such a requirement arises from the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the words *yat* and *cet*. Even in the case of *bhūtvā*, that [requirement] exists due to the co-occurrence of the suffix *ktvā* being prescribed in connection with a verbal root.

In expressions such as *pacati bhavati*, although there is no mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between *pacati* and [the other verb], since *bhavati* and so forth require a subject (*kartṛ*) and the like, there is no fault because the connection occurs through the expectancy of one or the other by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*). In that context, the universal property (*jāti*) "action-ness" (*kriyātva*), which is common to all [actions], is the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). The universal property "verbal root-ness" (*dhātutva*), common to all [roots], is the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). The result, such as "softening" (*viklitti*), is denoted in its respective form. Furthermore, *pacitva* (the state of being the root *pac*) and so forth are the delimiters of the expressive power. As for the cognition in those respective forms, it is accounted for by the fact that the specific co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of those [words] serves as the cause for such a cognition; this is the view.

The moderns (*navyās*), however, maintain that the operation (*vyāpāra*) such as blowing is to be denoted by its respective specific form—such as "blowing-ness" (*phūtkāratva*) or "under-heating-ness" (*adhaḥ-santāpanatva*)—precisely because cognition is experienced in that very way, and because it is impossible to state another single, common property (*anugata-eka-dharma*) shared by all such instances. Nor can it be said that the operation is "conducive to softening" (*viklitty-anukūlatva*) and so forth; for if the operation of the instrument were also included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then by the rule governing a single designation (*eka-sañjñā-adhikāra*), wood and other instruments would incur the status of being the agent (*kartṛ*). Since that [agenthood] has already been expressed, there would follow the undesired consequence of using the nominative case (*prathamā*) in sentences such as *kāṣṭhair devadattaḥ pacati* ("Devadatta cooks with wood").

Nor should it be argued that the notion of being a cause (kāraṇasañjñā) will sublate the notion of being an agent (kartṛsañjñā) because it has no scope [elsewhere], for the nature of motion (gati) will be explained later. Nor should it be argued that a specific universal (jāti-viśeṣa) is established as the delimitor of the denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka) of a word for action, etc., on the grounds that "water-ness" (jalatva) is likewise established as the delimitor of the denotability of the word "water," as seen in the *Līlāvatyupāya*; for there is no experience of cognition in that form, and it is precisely the cognition in those respective forms that is restated.

Likewise, since the necessity of a causal relation must be maintained, if one were to postulate yet another causal relation by means of the property being postulated, it would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Otherwise, there would be the consequence of postulating a single property residing in horses, salt, and so forth, as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the denotative capacity (*śakyatā*) of words such as "saindhava. If it is argued that the cognition of those [objects] is established by experience through horse-ness (*aśvatva*) and so on alone, this is equally true in the present case.

For this very reason, the universal *vibhutva* (all-pervasiveness) is not established as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*), because the cognition [of all-pervasiveness] arises from [the object] being characterized by the possession of the dimension of supreme greatness (*paramamahatparimāṇavatva*) alone—or, according to another reading, from its being conjoined with all substances (*sarvadravyasaṃyogitva*). For this same reason, when it is said, "Devadatta cooks," there is no doubt such as, "Does Devadatta possess volitional effort (*kṛti*) or not? and so forth.

Nor is there a multiplicity of meanings, for that is accepted; moreover, since there exists a unifying factor—such as "being present in the intellect" (*buddhisthatva*)—which serves as the delimiting condition of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), just as in the case of the word *tad* (that). In this regard, whenever a particular thing is present in the intellect, that very thing is denoted, and at that time, its substratum is the agent. For this very reason, the expression "the pieces of wood cook" (*kāṣṭhāni pacanti*) is justified. And when one does not intend to express the operation of those [pieces of wood] as being the meaning of the root *dhav* (to cook), one says "they cook with the pieces of wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacanti*).

And the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is precisely [the property] such as "having cooked" (*pacitva*) and so forth. It is not correct, however, to hold that "verbal root-ness" (*dhātutva*) is the delimitor of the expressive power, because understanding occurs even for one who does not know what "verbal root-ness" is.

By this, the objection raised by the Neo-Mīmāṃsakas—that even in the absence of blowing or similar actions, the expression ‘Caitra cooks’ would inappropriately apply to rice being cooked by a fire ignited by a flame produced through some other action residing in Caitra—and that if each respective operation were denotable in its own specific form, the conflicting views among disputants as to whether it is the sacrifice (*yāga*), desire (*icchā*), or knowledge (*jñāna*) would be untenable—is refuted. For in the case of one who has already acquired the power [to cook] through blowing, the expression ‘he cooks’ certainly does not occur when he fans the fire with a fan at the time of igniting it.

The conflicting views among theorists are also justified solely by their respective adherence to such understandings. Furthermore, they argue that there is no risk of the undesirable consequence of using expressions like *apākṣīt* ("he cooked") when another operation is currently underway, merely because the act of blowing (*phūtkāra*) has passed; for it will be demonstrated later that pastness (*bhūtatva*) and other such properties are construed with the entire complex [of operations].

Others, however, maintain that the denotative capacity (*śaktatā*) of the root *pac* is delimited by the property of being an operation (*vyāpāra*) distinct from an effort (*kṛti*), whereas since effort is perceived as being present in all verbal roots, the property of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*)—which is common to them all—is the delimitant of the denotative capacity in that case.

If it is argued that, in this case, roots such as *as* (to be) would fail to qualify as verbal roots (*dhātu*) because they denote mere existence and the like, and thus lack the capacity to express an action consisting of an operation (*vyāpāra*), we say no; for even there, the meaning is precisely the operation conducive to existence and so forth. Furthermore, because the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and its fruit reside in the same locus, [the operation] is not perceived as clearly as it is in cases such as *gacchati* (he goes). Nor does this imply that, when asked "What is he doing?", the word *asti* (he is) would serve as an answer just as *pacati* (he cooks) does.

This is because, when referring to someone whose destruction is imminent, the answer "he exists" to the question "what is he doing? is universally accepted; whereas in other cases, since existence is determined through stability, the question "what is he doing? is restricted in scope to specific actions such as cooking, and thus "he exists" is not an appropriate answer. Furthermore, the root *as* (to exist) also signifies an activity conducive to maintaining one's own nature, and "maintaining" refers to a connection with a subsequent time; therefore, there is no inconsistency in expressions such as "the self exists."

Even the operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to origination is present in expressions such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being"). Furthermore, transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting a result that resides in a locus different from the operation, while intransitivity (*akarmakatva*) consists in denoting a result that resides in the same locus as the operation. They say that this is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya*: that even in cases such as *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"), verbs like *as* (to sit) and others possess transitivity when they signify an operation in the form of existence (*sattā*) conducive to pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the sense of a delimiting relation (*avacchedakatā*).

Others, however, maintain that in verbs such as *asti* ("is"), the meaning is exclusively the operation (*vyāpāra*), not the result (*phala*). And that [operation] consists precisely of existence (*sattā*) and so forth, because it alone appears as being pervaded by the specific universals (*vaijātya*) mentioned previously. For this very reason, in expressions such as "Being sees" (*paśyati bhavaḥ*), where the causal instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, the result is indeed of the nature of objectivity (*viṣayatā*).

Action-ness (*kriyātva*) has been accepted [as the definition]. Therefore, agency (*kartṛtva*) resides in its locus. However, in cases such as "he sees existence" (*bhavaṃ paśyati*), object-ness (*viṣayatva*) does not possess the nature of an operation; thus, its locus does not have agency, both because of the absence of an operation and because the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) would be sublated. Action-ness consists precisely in being the object of the verbal cognition produced by that verb, while not being the locus of the property of being a determinant of suitability residing in the meaning of that verb. And since this [action-ness] does not apply to object-ness in cases such as "he sees existence," there is no fault.

They say that being intransitive (*akarmaka*) consists in denoting only the operation (*vyāpāra*), whereas being transitive (*sakarmaka*) consists in denoting both the result (*phala*) and the operation. If it is objected: "In that case, [verbs such as] *jīvati* (he lives) and *nṛtyati* (he dances) would incur the status of being transitive, because there exists a result consisting of the maintenance of life or the movement of limbs, and because [the operation] has a locus distinct from [that] result"—we reply: No. There is no fault, because being transitive is defined as the denotation of an operation whose locus is distinct from the result, qualified by the absence of non-intentionality, provided that [the verb] does not denote the locus of the result. For these [verbs], such as *jīvati*, do indeed denote the locus of the result, namely life or the limbs.

The phrase "qualified by the absence of the intention to denote" (*vivakṣāvirahaviśiṣṭa*) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases where the object (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed. [Note: According to variant *kha*, the first view alone is correct. For in the final view, in examples such as ‘*uttiṣṭhati*’ (he rises), the meaning would have to be the action of rising itself, namely contact with a higher location. In that case, since contact with a higher location exists [at the time of the present tense], the usage ‘*utthitaḥ*’ (he has risen) would be impossible. In my view, however, because the activity conducive to that [contact] is past, such usage occurs even while [the contact] is present; this is the essential point.]

Others, however, say: "Intransitivity is the absence of denoting a result that resides in the locus of the operation (*vyāpāra*). This [absence] occurs in some cases due to a lack of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and in others due to the absence of the result-component. Thus, in the case of *asti* and so forth, the meaning is merely existence and the like; in 'he stands up' (*uttiṣṭhati*) and so forth, both [components] are present, so there is no fault. [This is an additional reading.]

The meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) is an operation conducive to the softening (*viklitti*) [of food]. As for the claim that the meaning of *pac* is merely contact with heat (*tejaḥ-saṃyoga*), that is incorrect; for if it were so, the usage ‘he cooks’ (*pacati*) would be impossible in the case of a person who, while lacking the effort conducive to contact with fire, is performing the act of sitting down as a means conducive to the softening of the food.

In relation to the sphere of the cognitive faculty (*jñadhātu*), cognition is the result (*phala*) by virtue of its objective relation (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), while the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*). Alternatively, the result is either the destruction of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*) or the objective relation itself. Even that which has perished possesses the status of having a result because it ascends into the intellect (*buddhi*). [Note: This applies even in cases such as "he makes a jar. However, if one accepts the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), there is no suspicion of any fault; furthermore, in instances such as "he knows himself," a distinction between selves must be postulated: one is delimited by the body, while the other is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

In that case, the agent (*kartṛ*) is that which is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while the object (*karman*) is that which is delimited by the body; thus, there is no violation of the requirement that the fruit and the operation must reside in different loci. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *karmavat* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.87). [Objection: But how can a single entity possess distinct properties merely through a difference in words, as in "the self kills itself" (*hanty ātmānam ātmā*) or "the self is killed by the self" (*ātmanā hanyata ātmā*)? To this, the question is asked: "Who, then, is the one who kills the self, and who is the one killed by the self?"

It has been said: "There are two selves: the bodily self (*śarīrātman*) and the inner self (*antarātman*). The inner self performs that action by which the bodily self experiences pleasure and pain; the bodily self performs that action by which the inner self experiences pleasure and pain.
[The word] *jan* signifies mere origination, or the operation coreferential with it.

In the case of "perishes" (*naśyati*), the meaning is an operation consisting in the convergence of the causal complex for destruction, accompanied by the counter-positive, which is favorable to destruction.

The root *pat* is inherently transitive (*sakarmaka*). For this very reason, the example "one fallen into hell" (*narakapatitaḥ*) fits correctly under the rule *dvitīyāśrita-* (Pāṇini 2.1.24). Its intransitivity (*akarmakatva*), however, should be understood as referring to its being restricted to the mere sense of the action (*vyāpāra-mātra*).

The meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is an operation conducive to that [result] which resides in a different substratum from the arising [of the result]; for if its meaning were merely effort (*yatna*), it would result in being intransitive (*akarmaka*). Now, one might object: "A verbal root is transitive when the requirement for an object (*karma-ākāṅkṣā*) is invariably present upon its utterance. Thus, there is no fault even if *kṛ* has merely effort as its meaning—just like the root *yat* (to strive)—because although the effort denoted by *kṛ* lacks a requirement for an action (*kriyā-ākāṅkṣā*) since the word 'object' (*karman*) and so forth is not present, it is nonetheless reasonable for that effort to require an object, just as that which is presented by the accusative case-suffix (*dvitīyā*) requires such an action."

Furthermore, if one wishes to preclude the status of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) for verbs whose objects are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita-karman*), then the qualification of "being characterized by the absence of non-intention" (*avivakṣābhāva-vaiśiṣṭya*) must also be included [in the definition]. In this way, it is logically established that a single [verb] can be both transitive and intransitive depending on the difference in meaning. That which has a requirement for an object (*karmākāṅkṣā*) qualified by the absence of non-intention with respect to a particular meaning is transitive in that meaning.

If it is argued that this is because only that which has been understood (*nugata*) possesses the characteristic [of being an object], we say no; for there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of verbs such as *gacchati* ("he goes"), since they lack an expectancy for an object (*karmākāṅkṣā*). This is because the expectancies "where? and "what? present here are equivalent to the expectancies "where? and "what? found in verbs such as *yatate* ("he exerts himself") and *bhavati* ("it comes into being"). Furthermore, one must understand that the verb *kṛ* (to do/make) functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nor is it correct to define transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) as "being one of the various types of transitive roots," because a single root is designated as either transitive or intransitive depending on the difference in its meaning. This is the general direction of the argument.
Thus concludes the investigation into the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātu*).
Now follows the investigation into the general meaning of particles (*nipāta*).

If it is objected: "In that case, the transitivity of such expressions as *anubhūyate sukham* ('pleasure is experienced') and *sākṣāt kriyate guruḥ* ('the teacher is directly perceived') would not be possible; for although the results consisting of experience and direct perception are the meanings of the particles, they do not constitute the meanings of the verbal roots," we reply: No, there is no fault, because particles function as indicators (*dyotaka*).

As for the claim that in cases such as *prajayati*, "eminent victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*) is not denoted by the prefix (*upasarga*), because—since it is not the meaning of the verbal root—it could not be construed with the agenthood (*kṛti*) which is the meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*); nor is victory the meaning of the root, while eminence is the meaning of the prefix *pra*—[this is incorrect]. [Note: A supplementary reading in manuscript *kha* states: "The grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that 'the meanings of nouns and roots do not directly connect through a relation of difference without mediating the meaning of a case-suffix' applies to instances other than prefixes."]

This must be stated: for if this were so, there would be no cognition of the form of "going" (*gamana*) in the case of the word *pratiṣṭhate*; because if the verbal root (*dhātu*) meant the cessation of motion and the prefix (*pra*) meant negation, the resulting cognition would necessarily be merely that "the absence of going does not exist. Yet such an experience of cognition does not occur. Nor is the qualified victory (*viśiṣṭo jayaḥ*) the meaning of the verbal root, because otherwise, just as with any other distinct meaning, the cognition of this very meaning would arise even without the prefix.

Furthermore, since there is no distinct entity called "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) apart from its constituents, the verbal root (*dhātu*) must be said to possess its power (*śakti*) toward each [meaning] individually in both cases. Thus, when the power of the root is already established for "victory" (*jaya*), the prefix (*upasarga*) serves merely as a delimitator of that power; its true nature is simply to function as a qualifier within the delimitor of the power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, the power resides in the root *ji* preceded by *pra*, signifying "excellent victory. It cannot be argued that the power resides in the root *ji* preceded by *pra*, because that would entail the postulation of a power not previously established and would result in the impossibility of connecting the meaning with the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

And being a *dyotaka* (indicator) consists precisely in delimiting the expressive power (*śakti*) [of a word]. Alternatively, there is *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in those respective meanings, while the prefixes (*upasarga*) serve to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*). This alone constitutes being a *dyotaka*. As for the cognition [of that meaning] in cases such as *vyatisete*, it arises from the recollection of what has been elided; however, for one who does not know the elision, no such cognition occurs at all. Or else, according to the principle that "what remains expresses the meaning of what is elided," the *lakṣaṇā* regarding that meaning belongs to the suffix (*pratyaya*) itself.
