Furthermore, if the prefix (*upasarga*) were to possess that meaning [of the action], the verbal root (*dhātu*) would be intransitive; consequently, in expressions such as *anubhūyate sukham* ("pleasure is experienced"), the *L*-suffix (the passive marker) would not occur in the objective case (*karman*), because "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists precisely in denoting an operation whose locus is distinct from the result inherent in its own meaning. Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since some degree of non-co-location with the result exists everywhere. By this, the view that the prefix possesses a qualified meaning is also refuted, because even a qualified form is not a verbal root; and if it were a verbal root, there would be the undesirable consequence of irregularities regarding the application of *aṭ* and other augments.

Therefore, prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely illuminators (*dyotaka*), whereas particles such as *ca* and others are indeed denoters (*vācaka*). In expressions such as *sākṣātkriyate*, it is the word *sākṣāt* itself that denotes the respective results—such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—by means of the relation of objectness (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the operation conducive to the production of that [result]. For this very reason, the entry in the lexicon, "sākṣāt means direct perception and similar," is consistent.

Furthermore, since it is established in common worldly usage that the word *namaḥ* has the sense of salutation (*namaskāra*), and since transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting an operation that has a result distinct from the locus of the meaning of either the verb itself or its associated particle, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) likewise consists precisely in being the substratum of such a result. And thus, the use of the *L*-suffix (the verbal ending) in the sense of the object is also justified.

Nor should it be argued that the direct syntactic connection of the meaning of a word such as *pada* with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is improper—on the grounds that, in order to prevent the cognition of a relation of objecthood (*karmatva*) in cases such as ‘*odanaḥ pacati*’ (‘The rice cooks’), a condition must be established whereby a verbal cognition having a nominal stem meaning as its qualifier is caused by the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by an affix (*pratyaya*), provided that the relation is other than identity (*abheda*)—because [in our view] the qualification ‘other than a particle (*nipāta*)’ is added [to the definition]. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that one could ask ‘What kind of conjunction is it? just as one might ask ‘What kind of *ca* is it? [since *ca* is a particle].

It should not be argued that, just as in the case of "the conjunction (*samuccaya*) is to be seen as beautiful," there would also follow the implication of "it is also beautiful" [in the case of *ca*]; for since particles (*nipāta*) present their own meaning only as a qualifier of another, there is no possibility of its being connected with a further qualifier. Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "the pot and [the cloth]" (*ghaṭaśca*), there would be a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) without the genitive case, because two nominal stem meanings cannot be related through difference without mediating the meaning of a case-ending.

Otherwise, one would have to admit a similar connection even from "the king man" (*rājā puruṣaḥ*) as one does from "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). This is not so, because we qualify [the rule] by excluding particles (*nipātātiriktatva*).

Furthermore, because particles such as *ca* (and) denote a collection (*samuccita*), the genitive case is not based on a distinction [between the parts]. There is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) precisely through non-distinction, as in "the jar is collected" (*samuccito ghaṭaḥ*). By its very nature, that which is presented by *ca* and other particles has the status of denoting a non-substantial entity (*asattva-vācakatva*). Nor is there any complexity in postulating a power (*śakti*) for the substratum-portion (*dharmyaṃśa*) within the collection, since this is supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatvāt*). Likewise, because the collection is a single unit, qualifiers such as "beautiful" do not apply to it.

By this, the objection that in expressions such as "the jar and [so on]," there would be the consequence of non-difference (abhedānvaya) because the meaning of the nominal stem is not restricted by contradictory case-endings—since one might say "of the jar and the conjunction"—is refuted; for it is accepted that the word "jar" possesses a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) with respect to the counter-correlate of the jar, and thus only non-difference is admitted.

Furthermore, regarding the verse "na cāśarairusrairivodīcyānuddhariṣyan rasāniva" (Raghuvamśa 4.66), the meaning is not that he will extract the northerners—who are like juices—with arrows that are like rays of light. In that case, even if the sense of the word *iva* were to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*), there would be a lack of purpose for the third case ending following the word *usra*, because the rays themselves are not the instruments. Moreover, due to the presence of the word *iva*, the third case ending does not occur, and thus the status of being an instrument cannot be attributed to the "similar" object.

However, it cannot be said that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) following *usrapada* is able to convey instrumentality as residing in something similar (*sadṛśagata*), because that is not the meaning of the base word (*aprakṛtyarthatvāt*). Nor can it be argued that there is no fault if [the suffix] is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), because that [instrumentality] is already understood from the third case ending following the word *iva*. Furthermore, there is no consequence of hearing [the suffix], since it is elided (*luka*) due to its being an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Nor is [the word *usra*] non-indeclinable because it denotes a substance (*sattva*), for its status as a non-substance—defined by the absence of connection with gender (*liṅga*)—remains intact; furthermore, indeclinability is accepted even for words denoting substances when they appear at the beginning of a *ca*-compound, by virtue of their placement there. In the case of *usraih*, the word is construed with its own correlate through the relation of similarity (*sādṛśya*). As for the instrumental case-ending, it is established by grammatical authority (*jñāpaka-siddha*) that the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) must share the same case-ending.

Furthermore, if [the particle] were merely indicative (*dyotaka*), there would be no established rule that in a *nañ*-compound and the like, the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is the primary one, because the preceding member would then be devoid of meaning. Moreover, according to the Naiyāyikas, case-endings (*vibhakti*) would not arise after indeclinables (*nipāta*), since they lack meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) and thus lack the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). That is not so; for it would follow that even prepositions (*upasarga*) would become denoters (*vācaka*). Meaningfulness, too, is established only by taking into account the meaning indicated (*dyotya*).

Now, meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) consists in being a word that is the object of the knowledge produced by its own cognition, and not in being a signifier through either the relation of primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member [of a compound] is also relative only to the meaning that is manifested.

But if this were so, then in forms such as *rāmaḥ*, the case-ending would apply even after the segment *rā*; nor can it be argued that it does not apply because it lacks the capacity to denote number, for then it would not apply to particles (*nipāta*) either, and because the default singular number (*autsargikaikavacana*) would be unavoidable here as well. Nor can it be argued that this is like the maxim of "doubling a single vowel" (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*), as stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.1): "In *nij*, there are four single-vowel (*ekāc*) elements: *ij*, *ni*, *i* [and *j*]."

In that regard, if there were reduplication of the syllable *ij*, *ni*, or *i*, the resulting form would be unestablished; furthermore, in forms such as *nenijuḥ* and *nenijati*, because of the intervention of the letter *j*, the suffix *jus* and others would not apply, resulting in a grammatical fault. Having stated this, [the author] says: "But it is established because that [reduplicated] aggregate is a single vowel (*ekāc*), since the rule [of reduplication] is not abandoned."

This is its meaning: because the whole [compound] consists of a single vowel (*ekāctvāt*), that is, due to the state of having one vowel, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) will take place; for in this way, the grammatical treatise remains unimpaired. Furthermore, later on—having raised the objection that if it were a *bahuvrīhi* designation, reduplication would apply to that which lacks a vowel—the matter was resolved by resorting to the view of "inclusion of the quality" (*tadguṇasaṃvijñānapakṣa*). Thus, it should be understood that the principle underlying reduplication has as its sole intent this fourfold state of being a single vowel.

As for the objection that if words such as *jyā* were used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*), no direct experience (*anubhava*) would arise from them—since that which is figurative does not produce experience—that is not so; for a word produces experience precisely by virtue of its capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*). For this very reason, according to the view of the opponent, experience arises even from corrupt forms of speech (*apabhraṃśa*).

In reality, since there is no cognition of the form "it was experienced" (*anubhūtam*) regarding inferential and verbal cognitions, the property of being an experience (*anubhavatva*) is indeed pervaded by the property of being perception (*pratyakṣatva*); thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, it is impossible even to assert that verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) does not arise from words used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*). Moreover, if one accepts figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a verbal root, then since the final phoneme of a word such as *ghaṭa* can denote its respective meaning through figurative indication—given that single-syllable lexicons (*ekākṣaranighaṇṭu*) assign those meanings to it—the consequence would follow that words like *ghaṭa* themselves would lack expressive power (*avācaka*).

Nor can the assumption of a power for those [prefixes] be justified on the grounds that they possess a knowledge of the power of the aggregate (samudāya-śakti) due to the resulting cognition—even while being ignorant of the power of the individual parts—because such a status is indispensable; for even one who is ignorant of the power of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is obstructed [from understanding the meaning] if they lack the apprehension of the prefix (*upasarga*).

Nor should it be argued that even when the meaning of a prefix is grasped through its expressive power (*śakti*), no cognition arises because there is a lack of *ākāṅkṣā*—defined as the causality of the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a verbal root with respect to a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) via the relation of mode-ness (*prakāratā*). This is because such causality belongs only to the verbal cognition of a person who possesses the grasp of that specific causality. Furthermore, it is appropriate to postulate that the presentation generated by a particle (*nipāta*) is also a cause for a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of the verbal suffix, in order to account for forms such as *vyatise*.

Even in the grammatical (vaiyākaraṇa) system, there is no fault, because the cognition having the meaning of the verbal root as its qualificandum—related through the relation of modehood (prakāratā)—is caused by the presentation [of the object] generated by a particle (nipāta). Furthermore, other linguistic rules (vyutpatti) concern objects other than particles; thus, there are no other faults either.

Or let it be that the meaning of the first member (*prādyartha*) is a distinguished substratum (*prakṛṣṭo dharmī*); since there is co-referentiality (*anvaya*) precisely through non-difference (*abheda*) with that, there is no fault. Nor does the status of being denotative lead to the undesirable consequence of their isolated usage; for according to the *Bhāṣya*, "A base (*prakṛti*) should not be used alone, nor should an affix (*pratyaya*) be used alone," just as the use of a base alone or an affix alone is not permitted, likewise the use of particles (*nipāta*) alone is also not permitted.

The intended meaning here is as follows: in the world, words are employed for the purpose of conveying meaning. Just as in common usage there is no comprehension of meaning from a base (*prakṛti*) alone or an affix (*pratyaya*) alone, likewise there is no comprehension from a particle (*nipāta*) alone, because it lacks expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). This is because, like a base and an affix, it requires resolution through syntactic connection. Furthermore, since qualities such as excellence—which are to be conveyed by that particle—cannot be related to anything unless there is a correlate, the isolated employment [of a particle] is impossible.

Even though [the particle *nañ*] does not primarily denote a collection (*samuccaya*) and so forth, its usage occurs only in a state of constant dependence, because the cognition remains incomplete without the specific presentation of those [meanings]. Furthermore, since it is universally established that the verbal cognition of negation (*abhāva-śābdabodha*) arises when only "not" (*na*) is uttered, it is impossible for it to be merely indicative (*dyotaka*) in the absence of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with another word. For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *nañ* [Pāṇini 2.2.6], the demonstration of the meaning "there is no negation" was made regarding the expression "not not" (*na na*). And here, the verb "is" (*asti*) is to be supplied at the beginning.

Furthermore, if [particles] were merely dyotakas (indicators), one would have to postulate a function (*vṛtti*) for other words therein, and one would also have to postulate a dyotaka-power in particles such as *ca* and so forth; thus, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*). For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsaka statement that "the negative particle (*nañ*) has an indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)" is consistent. Therefore, if it is argued that being a denoter (*vācakatva*) alone is logical, we say no; for it is improper to postulate a power (*śakti*) for what can be obtained through other means. As for positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), they serve to apprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya*) and do not establish [the existence of] another [power].

In reality, however, for one who has grasped the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of particles (*nipāta*), understanding arises even when their secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) is unknown; therefore, the causal relationship between the knowledge of that power and the resulting cognition is necessary. Likewise, for those who do not know that power, understanding arises through the knowledge of the indicative function alone; thus, the causal relationship between that [indicative function] and the cognition is also necessary. This is the essential conclusion: that particles possess both the status of being indicators (*dyotakatva*) and the status of being denotable (*śakyatva*).

The Naiyāyika claim that particles (*nipātas*) are denotative (*vācaka*) while prefixes (*upasargas*) are indicative (*dyotaka*)—this "half-old-woman" approach (*ardhajaratīya*) must certainly be rejected. [Note: After "must certainly be rejected," some manuscripts include the following additional passage: "Nor should it be argued that if particles were denotative, expressions such as 'there is indeed' (*ivāsti*) would have to be like 'there is similarity' (*sādṛśyamasti*), because we accept their capacity to convey meaning only through the employment of words such as the correlate (*pratiyogin*) or the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)."]

Since the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) favor the universal (*sāmānya*)—whether that universal consists of the nature of being a particle (*nipāta*) defined by its relation to expressive power (*śakti*), or as an impartite attribute (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), or as a genus (*jāti*)—it is logical that either dyotakatva (suggestiveness) or śaktatā (expressive power) serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). [Following the word "yuktatvāt," the text implies: because suggestiveness or denotative power relative to those respective meanings resides in those respective particles, the status of being a delimiting factor belongs to the unique property residing in each of them.

There is no evidence that a non-specific property (*asāmānyadharma*) serves as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by virtue of necessity; furthermore, understanding occurs even for one who does not know [the word] to be a particle (*nipāta*). Moreover, there is no reason accepted by both parties to prove either its being a *dyotaka* (indicator), its being a *vācaka* (denoter), or its being a non-denoter, based on a common delimitation. — This is the additional reading. In some cases, however, prefixes (*upasarga*) are also denoters (*vācaka*); for example, in "pratiṣṭhate" and the like, the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes the cessation of motion, whereas the word "pra" denotes motion. As stated by Bhartṛhari:
"Or it may be the designator of particulars, or even their indicator, because they are possible"— this is the second position. (Vākyapadīya 2.160)

Roots and prefixes together express the meaning; however, since the prefix merely provides a specific capacity, the prefixes act as auxiliaries in the expression of that meaning. As it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"Or, [the prefix] is employed as an auxiliary for the root to impart its specific capacity."
[Verse 2.190] Thus ends the third position.

Upon examining which of these three positions is the most excellent, it is appropriate that the prefixes (*upasarga*) possess only the function of indicating (*dyotaka*). In the case of "he sets out" (*pratiṣṭhate*), because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the meaning of "going" belongs to the root *sthā* itself, while the prefix *pra-* merely indicates that meaning. As it has been said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"And since going and so forth are not perceived by means of the [actions] standing and so forth alone,
in that case, based on the two kinds of inference, standing and so forth are said to possess the property of that [going]. [Vākya-kāṇḍa 2.161]

The meaning is this: by common usage, the root *sthā* denotes the cessation of motion; therefore, by that [root] alone, motion is not established. However, on the grounds that "roots have multiple meanings," its status as a denoter of motion is also determined through inference. The prefix (*upasarga*), however, merely serves to illuminate that [meaning].

Establishing through inference that verbal roots (*dhātu*) possess multiple meanings and that prefixes (*upasarga*) are indicative (*dyotaka*), he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). The method of inference is as follows: "A verbal root has multiple meanings, because it is a verbal root; like the root *yaj*, which is accepted by both disputants as having multiple meanings. "The word *pra* is indicative, because it is the word *pra*; like the observed word *pra* in examples such as *prapacati*. In this way, one should understand that there are three positions regarding the primary particles (*nipāta*) as well. As stated by Hari: "Some particles are indicative; others express distinct meanings."
"Or perhaps they might be like words (*āgama*), which, when combined, express a meaning. [Vākya-p.

2.164] Here too, the position that they are *dyotaka* (manifesters) alone is logical, because particles (*ca*-etc. are never used in isolation. If they were *vācaka* (denoters), then, like the word "cow" (*go*) and others, they would be used even in isolation. Therefore, the inference is established: "Particles such as *ca* are not denoters, because they are not used in isolation, just like suffixes (*pratyaya*). This has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"Particles such as *ca* are not employed alone when they possess the status of a word (*pada*);
likewise, even though a suffix possesses denotative power, it is not employed in isolation.
[Vākyapadīya 2.166]
And thus, it is the view of Hari that particles such as *pra* and *ca* possess only the function of indication (*dyotakatva*).
This same position is favored by Nāgeśabhaṭṭa as well, since he repeatedly supports it in his *Mañjūṣā*.

However, ancient grammarians such as Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita and others maintain that all particles, as delimited by the property of being particles (*nipātatva*), possess both the functions of indication and denotation (*vācakatva*).

The Naiyāyika position—that particles such as *pra* and so forth possess an indicative (*dyotaka*) function, whereas particles such as *ca* and so forth possess only a denotative (*vācaka*) function—is not tenable, as there is no reason for such a disparity. For this very reason, having established the theory of indication, the theory of denotation is also supported in works such as the *Bhūṣaṇa* by such statements as: "The denotative power of particles is established through positive and negative concomitance" (*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, Nipātana section, p. 380).

The venerable author of the Bhāṣya maintains that particles (*nipāta*) other than prefixes (*upasarga*) are both expressive (*vācaka*) and indicative (*dyotaka*). Indeed, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *avyayaṃ vibhakti* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), having raised the objection regarding the absence of an indeclinable compound in examples such as *sumadrāḥ*, *sumagadhāḥ*, and *saputraḥ*, he states that since an *avyayībhāva* is characterized by the predominance of the first member, there is no such predominance of the first member here. He then says: "Alternatively, these are not indicated as the meanings of compounds; rather, these are indicated as the meanings of indeclinables."

He stated: "That indeclinable (*avyaya*) which occurs in these senses is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Kaiyaṭa further explained that because the indeclinable is explicitly mentioned [in the rule] and is thus more internal (*antaraṅga*), its very own case-endings and so forth serve as its qualifiers. In that context, when it is intended to express prosperity and the rest as delimited by the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), then the indeclinable becomes the signifier of prosperity and the rest, and they (prosperity, etc. thereby become its referents.

In the case of *sumadra*, however, it has been explained that the word *madra* alone expresses the meaning qualified by prosperity (*samṛddhi*), while the prefix *su-* merely indicates prosperity and is not its denoter; thus, according to this commentary by Kaiyaṭa on the Bhāṣya, it is clear that for indeclinables (*nipāta*) both functions appear, whereas for prefixes (*upasarga*) there is only the function of indication (*dyotakatva*).

This is clear from the commentary on the sūtra *gati-gatau* (Pāṇini 8.1.70). The commentary there states: "'But surely, first the verbal root is joined with a prefix, and afterwards with an inflectional suffix (*sādhana*). This is not sound... and so forth. Furthermore, in the phrase *atha śabdānuśāsanam* (Mahābhāṣya, Introduction), the word *anuśāsana* itself indicates that; it is understood that even the author of the Bhāṣya accepts only the view that [the prefix] is a *dyotaka* (indicator).

In the *Paspaśā*, regarding the rule "the particles *ad-* and *pari* are meaningless" [Pāṇini 1.4.93] and in the rule for the negative particle *nañ* [Pāṇini 2.2.6], this is likewise established by their own inherent force; so, enough of this.

Thus ends the investigation into the general meaning of particles (*nipāta*). [The underlying intention here is as follows: Regarding the meaning of particles, three positions are observed in the treatises. Since meanings such as "experience" (*anubhava*) cannot be understood from verbal roots (*dhātu*) alone, they are understood through their connection with prefixes (*upasarga*); thus, prefixes merely indicate specific meanings. For example, in the word *anubhavati*, the word *anu* indicates the sense of "experience. As stated by Hari: "In some cases, possible distinctions that are not shown by the [roots] alone..."
In connection with a prefix such as *pra*, *parā*, and so forth, [the meaning] is manifested.

[Vākya-paddhati 2.286] Now, the investigation of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Following this context, the meaning of the specific indeclinable *nañ* is examined. It might be argued as follows: the meaning of *nañ* is not non-existence (*abhāva*). For, it is established by all that non-existence appears only as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) defined by its counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). Consequently, in cases such as ‘*aghaṭaḥ*’ (non-pot), if the cognition were ‘different from a pot,’ the predominance of the second member (*uttarapada-prādhānya*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound would be violated. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the grammatical operations applicable to pronouns (*sarvanāma-kārya*)—as seen in examples like ‘*atisarvāya*’—would fail to apply in cases such as ‘*añprasah*.’

If it is argued that the qualifier-nature of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) in the case of absence is universally established and therefore secondary (*gauṇa*), because "being secondary" consists in being an object of presentation as a qualifier of another word-meaning—[we reply: no; for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is either the locus of superimposition (*āropa*) or the superimposition itself, while "locus-ness" is the relation (*saṃsarga*). And since that [relation] is a qualifier, the cognition is "the jar is the locus of superimposition."

And thus, in cases such as *asaḥ* ("non-existent"), since the referent of the word *tat* (*tad-padārtha*) functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is no fault regarding its being figurative (*gauṇatva*). Furthermore, this [rule] applies only to the domain of compounds; however, in the domain of non-compounds, the meaning is simply "absence" (*abhāva*). That [absence] is of two kinds: difference (*bheda*) and absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*). Among these, the latter [absolute absence] is connected only with the verbal action (*kriyā*), because the presentation of the verbal process (*bhāvanā*) is the cause for a cognition in which the object of cognition has the absolute absence denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*) as its qualificand.

For this very reason, the determination of person (*puruṣa*) in cases such as "I am not" (*ahaṃ nāsmi*) and "the jar does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*), as well as the restriction of number (*vacana*) in cases such as "the two jars do not exist" (*ghaṭo na staḥ*) and "the jars do not exist" (*ghaṭā na santi*), is logically justified because of the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *yuṣmad* and other pronouns. Furthermore, that [restriction] would not occur in the case of the syntactic connection "the absence of the jar exists" (*ghaṭābhāvo'sti*).

Nor should it be argued that the determination of person and number is established for "the jar does not exist" and so forth, on the grounds that the cognition produced is "the jar possesses the absence of being a substratum of existence" (*sattāśrayatvābhāvavān ghaṭaḥ*); for this would render impossible the cognition of the absence of the jar as established by the universal experience of all people.

In my view, however, since the absence of the existence of the jar—which has the jar as its agent—is non-different from the absence of the jar due to the identity of their co-occurrent properties (*samanaiyatyabhāva*), that [absence] is established; furthermore, there is no risk of a breakdown in syntactic connection (*anvayabhaṅga*) because the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) connects with that which is connected to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Moreover, according to the reasoning to be stated later, if the meaning of the verbal suffix were a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), such a cognition would be impossible.

Nor is there any non-occurrence [of the cognition] because of the absence of a cognition of non-existence conjoined with a locus; for in cases such as "there is no jar here," the understanding is not that "the jar, which is the counter-positive of the non-existence in this locus, is a substratum of existence. This is because, according to the consensus of grammar, grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) pertains only to the connection of words with a verb (*kriyā*), and thus [if they were connected otherwise], there would be the consequence of these words being ungrammatical (*asādhutā*). If, however, those [words] were connected only to "existence" (*sattā*), the resulting cognition would be merely that "the jar is the counter-positive of some non-existence residing in something," and not specifically that of the non-existence of the jar.

Nor is there any fault, for since it is accepted that there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the negative particle (*nañ*)—which is co-occurrent with those [words]—in the absence of the existence of the action, this is merely some triviality; because, in the case of a jar which is the counter-positive of the absence of existence in this place, there exists the certainty of the absence of existence in this [jar], and thus there is no impossibility of the connection of the substratum of existence (*satāśrayatva*) therein.

Furthermore, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the action (*kriyā*) presented by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) with a distinct entity as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), because such a cognition does not arise from expressions such as "he does not cook, he goes. For this very reason, it should also be understood that the negative particle (*nañ*) occurring in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word ending in a verbal suffix has exclusively the sense of an absence (*abhāva*). It is precisely on this basis that they state that the *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) is stronger than the *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation).

And it is not the case that, when the non-compounded negative (*nañ*) is construed with the verbal noun (*ktin*), as in the passage "He performs the *ye yajāmahe* in sacrifices, but not in the *anuyāja*s," there is only an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—even in the absence of a compound due to its being optional—and not a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), because of parsimony (*lāghava*). For if that were so, since a prohibition presupposes a prior application (*prāpti*), and since such an application here cannot arise from any source other than scripture, it would have to be stated by the scriptural injunction itself in the words "in sacrifices. And thus, because it would be both enjoined and prohibited by scripture, the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) would follow.

Nor should it be argued that the established Mīmāṃsā doctrine—that "negation possesses greater force because it uproots injunction, whereas injunction also possesses force as its substratum"—would be undermined; for we admit that in a non-compound (asamāsa), the negative particle (*nañ*) denoting negation itself connects with the verbal action (*kriyā*). By the term "negation" (*pratiṣedha*), absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is meant.

For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *suḍanapuṃsakasya* (P. 1.1.43)—which states that the term *napuṃsakasya* means "not [of] the neuter"—is consistent with the statement: "The neuter has no syntactic connection (*sāmarthya*); with what then? With the verb *bhavati*. Furthermore, in compounds such as *asandehāḥ* ("free from doubt") and *avivādaḥ* ("free from dispute"), the word *asamāse* ("in a non-compound") was stated because the negative particle *nañ*, which carries the sense of negation, also connects with the verbal action (*bhāva*). Nor does there arise here the contingency of these being obligatory *avyayībhāva* compounds; for the two *Bhāṣya* passages—"in a non-rapid [utterance], *asaṃhitam*" and "*asandehāḥ*, the purpose"—indicate that both [the *nañ* of negation and the *nañ* of privation] apply even in the absence of a [positive] referent (*arthābhāve*).

And thus, where there is a connection between the counter-positive (pratiyogin) presented by a word and the locus (anuyogin) through the relation of container and contained (ādhārādheyabhāva), there is the cognition of its absolute absence (atyantābhāva). This is as in "There is no jar on the ground," and likewise in "The jar does not exist," because the locus, which is the meaning of the verb, is connected as the contained within existence (sattā).

It should be understood that by the force of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) qualified precisely by the subsistence in that [locus] in which the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogipratyaya*) occurs. Consequently, the cognition "there is no jar on the ground" does not arise by taking up a non-existence residing in some arbitrary [other] locus.

By this, it is explained that in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground," depending on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), the non-existence of the jar may sometimes reside in the ground and so forth, and at other times in the jar itself.

The claim that "the absence of existence on the ground" is what is cognized is refuted, because there is a rule that the negative particle (*nañ*), which signifies absolute non-existence, must invariably connect with its counter-positive action, and because there is a rule that factors of action (*kārakas*) invariably connect with an action.

Furthermore, since an *avyayībhāva* compound is eternal (*nitya*), it would follow that a sentence (as a distinct syntactic unit) would be impossible. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would be no experience of a single qualificand (*ekaviśeṣyakatva*) in cognitions such as "There is smell in earth, but not in water," for we accept this consequence; such an experience simply does not occur. However, where the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is capable of being construed as non-different from the substratum (*anuyogin*), there the meaning is either a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) or a specific kind of negation (*kadvān*). As in examples such as "A pot is not a cloth."

In expressions such as "This belongs to Maitra, not to Caitra," however, the meaning of the genitive case is the possessor (*svatvavat*), since that too is a *śeṣa* (subsidiary element). And thus, the cognition is: "This [object] possesses a property of ownership related to Maitra, which is distinct from the property of ownership related to Caitra."

By this, the claim that the negative particle (*nañ*) expressing negation cannot be construed with the verbal suffix *ktin*—on the grounds that it conveys the absence of ownership (*svatvābhāva*) here—is refuted. Furthermore, the property of having a counter-correlate delimited by the delimitor of the relation of occurrence (*anvayitāvacchedakāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva*) is obtained here through the force of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), because one does not employ expressions such as "there is no pot" or "the blue pot is not a pot" in a place where there is a blue pot; whereas one does employ expressions such as "there is no blue pot" or "the yellow pot is not a blue pot" in a place where there is a yellow pot.

However, in cases such as "there is no genus in a genus" (*jātau jātirnāsti*), although the existence (*sattā*)—qualified by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) residing in a genus and having a genus as its agent—is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), how can there be a cognition of its absence? Nevertheless, since there is no fault because existence is established in its constituent parts (*khaṇḍaśaḥ prasiddhi*), and because the cognition of the existence of a category as existing in its own nature (*svarūpasat*) is required, this has been explained at length elsewhere.

In expressions such as "there is no jar" (*na ghaṭo'sti*), the understanding is that "there is something other than a jar," because the negative particle (*nañ*) occurring immediately before a noun—provided it is distinct from a particle (*nipāta*)—generally conveys an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). To prevent such an understanding in cases like "Indeed, this arrow is certainly not to be discharged at him" (*na khalu na khali bāṇaḥ sannipātyo'yamasmin* [Abhijñānaśākuntala 2.6]), the phrase "distinct from a particle" is included. With this very intention, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* stated through the negative particle in the verse "No woman abandoned her husband" (*sajaṃ na kācid vijahau*) that there was a lack of manifestation (*asphuraṇatva*).

It should be noted that even a contradictory meaning can be conveyed, as in the statement, "Some abandoned their broken [vessels]. Furthermore, they say that the nature of the absence of others (anyābhāvatva) and absolute non-existence (atyantābhāvatva) are indivisible adjuncts (akhaṇḍopādhi).

As for the claim that even in cases such as "The jar does not exist," the cognition occurs precisely through the superimposition (āropa) of existence having the jar as its agent, and so forth; and likewise, in the case of "The yellow conch does not exist," the cognition is the superimposition of existence having the yellow conch as its agent. Nor can it be argued: "How can there be a superimposition when a qualified existence is unestablished? For the individual word-meanings are well-established. And the lack of establishment regarding their combination is irrelevant.

Or, let there be a distinct, produced (āhārya) apprehension; however, since the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the cause of the cognition of absence, it is more cumbersome to include the condition of being non-produced (*anāhāryatva*) [as a requirement for that cause]. Therefore, even on the view that the causality of the cognition of the counter-positive consists simply in its being a cognition whose mode is the delimiting property of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāraka-jñāna*), from a produced cognition [of the counter-positive], only a produced cognition of the qualifiedness of the qualification (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-bodha*) arises.

And thus, since the cognition of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is possible, there is no logical inconsistency. Furthermore, the claim that there is no such thing as "induced" (āhārya) verbal comprehension is simply not credible. According to this view, one adopts the cognition of absence—such as "the jar does not exist"—as the basis for the linguistic convention that the cognition has the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*). And the obstruction of the cognition of the counter-positive and so forth can be easily reconciled. That is not correct; for there is no evidence to deny what is established by experience.

Furthermore, in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), there is no regulating principle (*niyāmaka*) in your view as to whether there is a connection with the action (*kriyā*) or a connection with the locus (*ityanvaya*). In my view, however, a regulation is possible: if the word has the sense of being superimposed (*āropitatva*), there is a connection with the substance (*dravya*); if it has the sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), there is a connection with the action. Otherwise, following the cognition "the jar does not exist," there would be no obstruction to the cognition that the jar exists. Nor can it be argued that such a cognition arises later and thus constitutes an obstruction, because there is invariably no evidence for its occurrence.

Nor can it be argued that the cognition of being superimposed (*āropitatvajñāna*) itself functions in this way, for this is necessary for you as well; otherwise, the distinction between the occasional cognition of absolute non-existence and the occasional cognition of difference would not be established.

It should not be said, "In my view, there is no fault because the first [cognition of absolute non-existence] occurs when there is a superimposition of relation (*saṃsarga*), while the latter [cognition of difference] occurs when there is a superimposition of identity (*tādātmya*)," since it is possible for that which restricts the superimposition of relation and so forth to be precisely what brings about the cognition of absolute non-existence and the like.

Nor should it be argued that, because the superimposition of the counter-positive is a cause for the cognition of absence in accordance with the requirement that excellence (*guṇa*) is a cause for valid cognition (*pramā*), it must therefore be a cause in all cases; for there is no evidence that valid cognition is produced by excellence, and the property of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) is not a subsumer of causal efficacy (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).

Or, let it be granted that superimposition (*āropa*) is the cause; nevertheless, the cognition of that [superimposition] from the word is not established by experience, because the cognition of non-existence (*abhāva*) alone is established by the experience of everyone—this is the traditional view (*sampradāya*). In reality, however, where there is no co-utterance with the negative particle (*nañ*), and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) are construed in the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), there is invariably a cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) following the cognition of that superimposed [entity]. Elsewhere, there is a cognition of difference (*bheda*); such is the settled rule.
And thus, others maintain that the negative particle is accounted for everywhere by a single power (*śakti*) alone—this is an additional reading.

The Navyas, however, maintain that even in a compound, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is indeed difference (*bheda*); nevertheless, it functions as a qualifier, and the resulting cognition is precisely "the jar is the counter-correlate of the difference. Consequently, the grammatical operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma-kārya*), the predominance of the meaning of the second member in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, and the regulation of person in cases such as "you are not" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*) and "I am not" (*anahaṃ bhavāmi*) are all accounted for. Even in instances such as "the removal of demons, [addition of] words, brevity, and absence of doubt" (*rakṣohāgamaladhvasandehāḥ*), the cognition is simply "doubt is the counter-correlate of non-existence. Thus, the rule regarding the singular number in expressions like "more than one" (*anekam*) is also logically justified.

As for the claim that "patantyaneke" is correct by means of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from a group of similar items), and that this is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya*, that is not so; for it contradicts experience. Furthermore, when one says "bring a jar," it would follow that bringing jars is not required [if the term were interpreted as a singular collective], and it would instead result in the bringing of any jar whatsoever that serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of some difference.

Others, however, maintain that the cognition is simply "different from a jar. In cases such as "you are not" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*), since the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*), the word *yuṣmad* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean something other than that [the referent of the pronoun]. Because there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of *yuṣmad* as a distinct form, the determination of person is established, as is the application of the rules for pronouns (*sarvanāma-kārya*). This is proven by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule, "There is elision of the *su* [case-ending] of *etad* and *tad*, except when followed by *ak* or in a compound with *nañ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.132); furthermore, this is because the distinct entity is the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound.

Regarding the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24), the singular number is used because the word *sup*, which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), ends in the singular; or else, it is used with the intention of referring to the genus (*jāti*). As for the expression *sevyate 'nekayā* ("is served by many"), the singular number is likewise employed here due to the requirement of concord with the qualificand *yoṣayā* ("by a woman") and because of the requirement that the act of serving be construed with each individual [woman]. For this very reason, they say that in expressions such as *patanty aneke* ("many fall"), the plural number is also used. However, that is not correct, because it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the rule *tasya bhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.119); this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Thus concludes the investigation into the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Now follows the investigation of the meaning of the particle *eva*.
This is the intended sense:
"Non-connection, as well as connection with another, and absolute non-connection..."
The particle *eva* excludes the property in three ways.

Thus, according to the direction stated by the learned, there are three meanings of the particle *eva*. To explain: where the particle *eva* is conjoined with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it negates the non-connection—that is, the lack of relation—of that qualifier. For example, in the statement "The conch is white indeed" (*śaṅkhaḥ pāṇḍura eva*), the particle *eva*, being conjoined with the qualifier "white," excludes the non-connection of whiteness from the subject, the conch; thus, the whiteness of the conch is restricted. And by that [restriction], with respect to the delimitation of "conch-ness" (*śaṅkhatva*)...

The absence of the absence of the inherence of whiteness (*pāṇḍuratva-samavāya-abhāva-abhāva*) is what is cognized. The resulting cognition is: "The conch possesses the absence of the absence of the relation to whiteness" (*pāṇḍuratva-sambandha-abhāva-abhāva-vān śaṅkhaḥ*).

However, where the particle *eva* (only) resides in the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), it excludes the connection of the property serving as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with anything other than that qualificandum. For example, in the expression "Pārtha alone is the archer" (*pārtha eva dhanurdharaḥ*), by excluding the connection of the state of being an archer with anyone other than Pārtha, it restricts the state of being an archer to Pārtha.

In this very context, the meaning is the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). The word "other" (*anya*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) residing in difference (*bheda*); "connection" (*yoga*) means relation; "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) means non-existence (*abhāva*). The word *pārtha* (Arjuna) is construed with "difference" by way of the relation of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogikatva*). That [difference] is construed with "relation" by way of the relation of subsistence (*vṛttitva*) in that which is the locus of that [difference]. And that relation is construed with the referent of the word "non-existence" by way of the relation of having that as its counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitākatva*). That [non-existence] is construed with "being an archer" (*dhanurdharatva*), and that [archerness] is construed with *pārtha*.
And thus, the cognition is: "The archer Pārtha is one who possesses the absence of a relation that has as its counter-correlative a difference whose counter-correlative is Pārtha."

Where, however, the particle *eva* is connected with the verb (*kriyā*), there it negates absolute non-connection—that is, total lack of relation—at all times. The resulting meaning is that it indicates a connection of that action with some particular locus. For example: "The lotus is indeed blue. Here, blueness is not restricted to every lotus, nor is the absence of blueness restricted to what is not a lotus; rather, it indicates the connection of blueness with some lotus whatsoever.

In this context, by the particle *eva*, the pervasion of "being a lotus" (*sarojatva*) is negated with respect to the absence of "being a blue lotus. Thus, the absence of "being a blue lotus" is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of that absence which resides in the lotus; in other words, it is "the state of being a blue lotus residing in the lotus," because an absence has the nature of its own counter-positive. The term *eva* possesses the function of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and the function of [excluding] connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Of these, when it is connected with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it functions as the former; when connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it functions as the latter.

Nor should it be said that [the rule] is incorrect because, in cases such as "smell is in earth alone," the second [word] is understood even though it is connected to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and in cases such as "cognition indeed grasps the object," the first [word] is understood even though it is connected to the action (*kriyā*) which is the universal qualificand (*sarvaviśeṣya*); for there is no fault, since the word expressing the qualifier has the sense of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), while the word expressing the qualificand has the sense of the subject of reference (*uddeśya*).

The status of being the subject (*uddeśyatva*) and the status of being the predicate (*vidheyatva*) are indeed distinct types of objectivity (*viṣayatā*), and not merely of the nature of the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) and the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*), nor are they co-extensive with them. For this very reason, there is the cognition of the verbal root-meaning as the action being the predicate in that context.

This is the general rule: in expressions such as "the face should be similar to the moon," even the particle *eva*, when co-occurring with the moon which is the predicate and functions as a qualifier, conveys the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Therefore, the governing factor for such a cognition is simply the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*). For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2), having kept in mind the restriction that "the second case ending occurs only when there is an object" (*karmaṇy eva dvitīyā*), it is stated that "this is a restriction relative to non-common [factors]."

Many scholars maintain that, having in mind the exclusion of connection with anything else (anyayogavyavaccheda), it was stated that "the restriction of the suffix depends on the non-contextual meaning."

In this context, "non-connection" (*ayoga*) means the absence of a relation; the negation of that [is *ayogavyavaccheda*]. Similarly, the absence of a relation is "exclusion of non-connection. Regarding the statement "the conch is white indeed," some hold that the cognition is: "the conch possesses the absence of non-connection with whiteness. This is not correct; for since the conch is presented as a qualifier of something else, it would be impossible for it to connect with "whiteness" if it were distinct from it. Therefore, the cognition is: "the conch possesses the absence of identity with non-whiteness. And its connection [with the predicate] occurs through the delimitation of "conch-ness" (*śaṅkhatva*), and not otherwise.

In a case where the very relation by which that which is co-uttered (samabhivyāhṛta) is construed with another, that very relation appears there as the meaning of the particle *eva*. Due to the force of co-utterance, in examples such as "in the conch, whiteness alone [exists]," the cognition is that existence resides in the locus of the conch, having as its agent something characterized by the absence of identity with anything other than whiteness.

Alternatively, the cognition is that "there is a non-existence whose agent is the absence of connection with paleness, and which has that [conch] as its locus. In that case, there generally appears, in that which is delimited by conch-ness (*śaṅkhatva*), the absence of the absence of a relation delimited by paleness and so forth. However, where such a cognition does not arise, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) even through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For example, in cases such as "the lotus is indeed blue. For instance, here:

In the case of the expression "existence has as its agent a lotus-ness that is co-referential with the absence of connection to a blue abode," the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs precisely through co-reference with lotus-ness, and not by way of the delimiting property (*avacchedakāvacchedena*), because that would lead to contradiction. It is well known that in such cases, when [the verb] is used in conjunction with the verbal suffix (*ktin*), there is an understanding of the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).

Alternatively, the cognition is: "The coming into being is the exclusion of non-connection, having as its agent a lotus non-different from blue, through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) which is co-referential with lotus-ness."

As for the claim that in every instance where the suffix *kṛt* is connected [to a verb], an absolute exclusion of non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) is perceived—that is not so. For in cases such as "knowledge certainly grasps an object" (*jñānam arthaṃ gṛhṇāty eva*) or "space is indeed possessed of supreme magnitude" (*ākāśaṃ paramamahattvavad bhavaty eva*), there is the perception of a mere exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). In cases such as "Pārtha alone is the archer" (*pārtha eva dhanurdharaḥ*), there is the perception of an exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), namely, that the archer is non-different from one who lacks identity with anyone other than Pārtha.

For this very reason, it is not the case that [the sentence] "Pārtha and Ākāśa alone are archers" results in the undesirable consequence of "Pārtha alone is an archer," because the exclusion of connection with others (anyayogavyavaccheda) is construed with the referent of the other word (Ākāśa), and because there is no cognition of the exclusion of connection with others as qualifying Pārtha by means of the delimitor of the referent of the co-occurring term (pārtha).

As for those who claim the cognition is "The archer is Pārtha, being one who lacks identity with anyone other than Pārtha," it should be understood that, due to the diversity of linguistic convention (vyutpatti), the referent of the word "Pārtha" is construed in two ways; thus, the [exclusion of connection with others] is necessary to preclude the possibility that "Pārtha and Ākāśa alone are [archers]."

In this case, the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), in that which is other (*anyasmin*), and in that which possesses it (*tadvati*). By this, if it is argued that there is an exclusion delimited by "connection with another" (*anyayogatvāvacchinna-vyavaccheda*), how can there be such a power? For, since a connection consisting of identity with another (*anyatādātmya-rūpa-yoga*) exists [in the case of non-substances], it is unestablished [that such a connection is absent]. Furthermore, because the exclusion whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is a relation with another exists in non-substances (*adravya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that a non-substance could be called "like Arjuna" (*pārtha iva adravyam*).

If [it is argued that] there is an exclusion delimited by "being a relation with another" (*anyasaṃyogatva*) and "being inherence" (*samavāyatva*), then the objection—that there would be the non-occurrence of the perceived exclusion of identity with anyone other than Pārtha in cases such as "Pārtha alone is the archer"—is refuted. For in that case, the connection of Pārtha and so forth occurs with "otherness" (*anyatva*), which is one part of the meaning of the word "another" (*anya*), just as in expressions like "different from a pot," due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). It is for this very reason that there is also mutual connection among those things presented by a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Regarding this, the modern Naiyāyikas maintain that there is direct denotative power (*śakti*) in the case of exclusion by non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), while in other cases there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This should be understood likewise for exclusion by non-connection. Thus, from the statement "odor exists only in earth," it follows that odor is excluded from what is other than earth and is resident in earth. For this very reason, one does not say "ether exists only in earth," because [ether] is not resident therein.

When a certain relation is understood through the co-utterance of particular words, then upon the co-utterance of the particle *eva*, there is the cognition of the exclusion of that very relation from others; thus, there is no over-extension whatsoever. Since no meaning exists without the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), there can be no syntactic connection [without it]; this is due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*).

Some, however, hold that the cognition is: "smell occurs in that which possesses the absence of identity with non-earth. Precisely by the force of the meaning of the particle *eva*, there arises a cognition of its occurrence [in the subject] as delimited by the delimitor of the co-referential term; thus, the expression "color exists in earth alone" (*pṛthivyām eva rūpam*) is not employed. They say that after the word *eva*, the locative case-ending is elided, while the locative in "in earth" (*pṛthivyām*) serves for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvārtha*), intended to indicate that the word *eva* itself ends in the locative. In reality, since that [word *eva*] also has the nature of earth, its status as a locus (*ādhāratva*) should also be understood.

In such cases as "This wealth belongs to Caitra alone" and "This brother is Maitra's alone," there is the cognition of the exclusion of ownership by anyone other than Caitra, and the exclusion of brotherhood by anyone other than Maitra. By this, the view that in all instances the meaning is merely the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is refuted; for even in the case of property owned by both [brothers], since the non-connection with Caitra’s ownership exists [in the case of the other brother], and the non-connection with Maitra’s brotherhood exists [in the case of the other brother], such usage would result [even where it is not intended].

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "existence [resides] in earth alone" (*pṛthivyām eva sattā*), because existence possesses the absence of the absence of connection with earth. It should also be considered whether the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is indeed the function (*śakti*) [of the particle *eva*]. Now, if this were so, since in expressions such as "perform the going" (*gamanaṃ kuru*) the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is naturally understood, and since in cases like "the jar [arises] from the staff alone" (*daṇḍādeva ghaṭaḥ*) there is an understanding of the exclusion of non-connection even without metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it would follow that such correct usage would become incorrect.

Now, one might object: since the exclusion of connection with anything other than that which is associated with the word to which the particle *eva* is attached is understood as residing in that very thing, then in the case of "there is smell in earth, [but] not in others," it would be so; however, in cases such as "the touch in water is cold indeed," the meaning would have to be that the touch, which excludes identity with anything other than cold, resides in water.

If it is argued that, in this way, there would also be the possibility of the expression "coldness alone [resides] in touch in a substance," we say no. There is no fault, because in cases where the particle *eva* is used in conjunction with a case-ending of an adjective intended to convey propriety (*sādhutva*), the exclusion of connection with anything other than its own associated substantive occurs through differentiation, and this serves as the primary factor for the connection with the meaning of the other word. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "cold touch is that which resides in water and is devoid of being the locus of cold touch."

Alternatively, there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) consisting in the exclusion of non-coldness (*śītānyatva-vyavaccheda*), delimited by the property of touch as it occurs in water. In the sentence "This Yajñadatta is seen by Caitra alone," what is cognized with respect to Yajñadatta is the exclusion of a relation—namely, being the object of a seeing whose agent is someone other than Caitra—due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti-vaicitrya*); it is not, however, the exclusion of the occurrence of the seeing in someone other than Caitra.

For if it were so, then even when both [Caitra and another] are looking at him, such a connection would undesirably apply, since Caitra’s seeing would still have occurrence in someone other than him (the other person).

Alternatively, in such a case, there is the cognition that [the action] does not reside in anything other than that which is endowed with a function connected to a factor other than itself, due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. It should be understood that in the expression *anyayoga* (exclusion of connection with another), where "connection" (*yoga*) relates by way of a distinction, it takes the form of difference; whereas where it relates without distinction, it is non-difference. Furthermore, when exclusion of connection with another applies to the denotative power (*śakti*), it should be seen as identity (*tādātmya*) alone.

In expressions such as "Pot-ness exists only in earth" (*ghaṭatvaṃ pṛthivīvṛttyeva*), the particle *eva* (only) possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the exclusion of existence in anything other than earth. This is because, within a compound, the subordinate member—the referent of the word "earth"—cannot be construed with anything else [directly]. However, the cognition that "existence in earth is excluded from connection with others" could also arise from the statement "Substance-ness exists in earth" (*dravyatvaṃ pṛthivivṛtti*). In the case of "Existence resides only in that which possesses a genus" (*jātimatyeva sattā*), the cognition is that existence does not reside in anything other than that which possesses a genus.

If, however, by means of inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*), it is understood that "existence" (*sattā*) is also the exclusion of anything other than that which possesses a genus (*jātimadanyāvṛtti*), or if "existence" also has the property of residing in something other than that which possesses a genus through inherence in a single substrate, then—by supplying the word "inheres" (*samavaiti*)—the exclusion of being related to a locus other than that which possesses a genus must be seen as occurring in the case of non-inherence (*asamavāya*). The meaning of the locative case is "substratum-ness" (*ādhāratva*) as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Alternatively, the cognition is: "Existence is the substratum of that which is devoid of identity with anything other than that which possesses a genus."

In this context, based on the statement "In this house, only Maitra will cook; the seasoning, however, shall be yours" (*Abhidhānaciṃtāmaṇi*, 3rd Kāṇḍa, verse 63), the specific substance that produces sourness—which in common parlance is denoted by the word *kaṭhī*—is called *temana* (seasoning/sauce) when it serves as a food item. In such examples as "temanam," there arises, through the particularity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), the cognition that the action delimited by the nature of being a future activity whose locus is this house and whose object is the *temana* is not to have any agent other than Maitra. This occurs due to the diversity of grammatical derivation.

In such cases as "form indeed exists on the earth," the understanding—due to the diversity of grammatical derivation—is: "the act of existing has form as its agent and possesses the exclusion of non-connection with the act of existing whose locus is the earth. Alternatively, the understanding is: "the act of existing has form as its agent and excludes non-connection [with itself] while having the earth as its locus."

Regarding the injunction "one should approach one's own wife during her season," the understanding—due to the diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*)—is: "The act of approaching, characterized by the exclusion of non-engagement in approaching one's own wife as delimited by the period of her season, is a means to the desired end consisting in the absence of transgression. That the desired end takes the form of the absence of transgression is understood through its syntactic unity with such scriptural statements as, "But he who [approaches] his wife who has bathed after her menses... Therefore, even when one approaches her during a single season, there is an inclination to do so again in subsequent seasons for the sake of avoiding transgression.

And thus, the absence of approaching her (the wife) during her fertile period—which is qualified solely by that time—is established as a cause of sin, residing in the wife through the relation of being its object (*karmatā*). Alternatively, the cognition is that such an act of approaching is the object of the injunction.

Only the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is possible. However, the claim that the cognition of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) occurs either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or by way of reversal is not withstands critical examination, because particles (*nipāta*) possess multiple meanings. Nor should it be argued that this leads to the fault of redundancy in cases such as "The conch is white indeed, not non-white," or "Your face is equal only to your own face, not to anything else," for there is no such defect; the meaning is "A conch that is non-white does not exist," "No other archer exists," or "The face possesses an absence of similarity relative to any other thing. Thus, there is no fault.

Nor is the charge of tautology still applicable here, because the cognition of that meaning has already arisen through inference or suggestion (*vyañjanā*) upon the exclusion of identity with other things such as "pale" and so forth; for rhetoricians have stated that there is no tautology even when a meaning obtained through the function of implication (*ārthī vṛtti*) is subsequently expressed by a word.

Others maintain that this is an explanation of the meaning of the particle *eva* (only) in order to exclude its sense of "abundance" and the like, since in expressions such as "he eats only salt," it is observed to carry such meanings.

In this manner, if the particle *eva* were to possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), there would be the burden of postulating various types of unestablished linguistic conventions (*vyutpatti*) across numerous instances; therefore, the position that it is merely indicative (*dyotakatā*) is superior.

In that case, one should infer that the word co-occurring with *eva* has a metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇā*) in some cases toward that which excludes connection with anything other than itself (*svānyayogavyavacchedavat*), in some cases toward the exclusion of connection with others (*svānyayogavyavaccheda*), in some cases toward the exclusion of non-connection with itself (*svāyogavyavaccheda*), in some cases toward its own meaning as qualified by such exclusion, in some cases toward that which possesses the exclusion of non-connection with itself, and in some cases toward that which lacks a relation to anything else of the same class as that which is qualified by a property not conjoined with *eva*. Thus it should be understood.

In such cases as "This Yajñadatta is seen by Caitra alone," there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the act of seeing as qualified by the exclusion of others than Caitra and qualified by other causal factors (*kāraka*s); the word "other" (*itarat*) serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Alternatively, there is a secondary signification of the word "Caitra" as that which lacks identity with anything other than Caitra. Or, in cases such as "One should certainly approach one's wife during her season," there is a secondary signification of the verb "to go" (*gam*) as referring to an agent whose action of approaching his own wife during the prescribed period is characterized by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Such instances are to be inferred accordingly. As for the avoidance of tautology in expressions like "not by another," it is exactly as explained previously.

And thus, when used in conjunction with the particle *eva*, it has the sense of *parisaṅkhyā*. [Note: *Parisaṅkhyā* is a rule whose fruit is the exclusion of one thing when both are simultaneously applicable;

that is to say: "An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when there is absolute non-attainment; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when there is partial attainment; and when there is attainment both here and elsewhere, it is called *parisaṅkhyā*. Thus it is said.]

This is the meaning: an injunction (*vidhi*) applies where there is absolute non-attainment [of a result]. When the fact that something serves as a means for another is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the injunction that prescribes it for that purpose is an *apūrva-vidhi* (injunction of what was previously unknown). For example, in the case of "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the fact that the sacrifice has heaven as its fruit is not established by any other means of valid cognition, but rather by this very statement; therefore, this is an *apūrva-vidhi*.

Regarding "niyama": that injunction which restricts a matter already applicable in one alternative is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). For example: "One threshes the rice grains" (*vrīhīn avahanti*). In the absence of this statement, the act of dehusking for the purpose of producing rice would be applicable both by means of scratching with the fingernails and by means of threshing; since both cannot occur simultaneously, at the time when scratching with the fingernails is applicable, threshing would not be applicable. Thus, threshing would have only an optional application (*pākṣikī prāptiḥ*).

And when that procedure exists, once the restrictive rule (*niyama*) arises that "dehusking must be accomplished by threshing alone," the splitting [of grains] is excluded; for it is accepted that the production of the *apūrva* occurs only when dehusking is performed by threshing alone—this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

Regarding the attainment of both [alternatives] here and elsewhere: when there is a simultaneous attainment of both, an injunction that results in the exclusion of the other is a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive) injunction. For example: "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten. By this sentence, eating is not enjoined, because it is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*); nor is this a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), because there is simultaneous attainment. It is not a restrictive injunction, because of the simultaneous attainment.

And likewise, when there is a simultaneous possibility of eating both the five five-nailed animals and other five-nailed animals, the rule "the hunger must be appeased by the eating of the five five-nailed animals" serves as a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). Thus, the eating of other five-nailed animals is excluded; this is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*). Furthermore, a restrictive injunction consists in the cognition of the absence of the co-occurring items, with respect to what is in excess of that which has been mentioned.

For example, in the expression "Pārtha alone is the archer," there is an absence of archery in anyone other than Pārtha. And this is not the sentence-meaning constituted by the particle *eva* itself, but rather it is implied (*ārtha*), because of the stated rule. However, the verbal (*śābda*) [exclusion] occurs in cases such as "Your face is equal only to your own face, not to any other," where, due to the futility of restating what is already established, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding eating as being that act of eating which lacks the status of having five-clawed animals other than the five [permitted] as its object.
The resulting cognition is: "The five-clawed animals, numbering five, are those that have become the objects of such an act of eating."

In this context, as in the case of "those with red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣāḥ*) and so forth, through the distinction between what is already established and what is to be attained, one should understand that the status of being enjoined (*vidheyatā*) belongs to the absence of the state of being the object of eating for those five-clawed animals other than the five [permitted]. Therein, the cognition of the absence of the state of being the object of eating in regard to the five-clawed animals other than the five is implied (*ārthī*). This too is indeed an implied exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*).

As for the claim that there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *pañca* (five) for "that which exceeds five," and in the word *bhakṣya* (eatable) for "that which lacks the state of being edible"—thereby producing the cognition "those other than the five lack the status of being the object of eating"—that is not correct. This is because the aforementioned method [of indication in both words] alone is more logical than indicating both words simultaneously. Furthermore, it would contradict the texts of Prakāśa and others, who cite the verse "What should be resorted to by men? The vicinity of the faultless celestial river" as an example of verbal exclusion (*paryudāsa*). For according to your view, the cognition would be "that which is other than the vicinity of the celestial river lacks the status of being resorted to," and thus the exclusion would be verbal (*śābda*).

Furthermore, regarding the question "What is to be practiced?", there is no possibility of it being an answer, because it lacks the general sense of a question. Nor is there figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even in the interrogative sentence itself, as there is no sublation (*bādha*) or other such grounds for it. For this very reason, the authors of the *Prakāśa* have cited the example of "exclusion by the word" (*śabdapari-saṅkhyā*): "What is the firm ornament here? Fame, not a jewel.

Moreover, it is clear that rules such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* [Pāṇini 2.3.2] are intended as restrictive (*niyamārtha*), meaning "in the case of the object, only the second case suffix is used. In the *Bhāṣya*, the meaning there is that in the case of the object, no case suffix other than the second occurs.

And thus, if the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) were to convey the object (*karman*), then because they would not convey grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), it would be difficult to avoid the undesirable consequence that second case endings and so forth would arise meaninglessly from parts of compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), namely from the word *rāja* (king) and others; furthermore, these grammatical rules would fail to function as indicators of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words.

Nor is there a restrictive rule such as "the second case-affix is used for the object," because there is no evidence for its application in cases of repetition (*āvṛtti*). If one were to establish an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and then apply that rule to meanings other than the object—even when the object is present—the occurrence of a meaningless second case-affix after words like *rājan* (king) and others would be unavoidable, since there is no provision for its use in the sense of the object. For me, however, there is no fault; for by the meaning "the second case-affix is used for an object that lacks the property of being understood by a case-affix other than the second," the [use of the second case] does not apply to a meaningless word.

By this, the restrictive rule "from indeclinables, all seven case-endings [occur]" is refuted. Even under the alternative view that "the second case occurs only when there is an object," there is no fault whatsoever in the meaning of the sentence: "the second case occurs when the object lacks the capacity to convey a meaning other than [that of] an object."

The three defects—the abandonment of its own primary meaning (*svārthahāni*), the assumption of another’s meaning (*parārthakalpanā*), and the occurrence of sublation (*prāptabādha*)—which are traditionally attributed to the word itself when it functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), can likewise be easily established by me as residing in the word. This is because there is the abandonment of the primary meaning already established for that word elsewhere, and the assumption of a word-meaning not previously established; thus, two defects reside in the word, while the sublation occurs through the sentence whose meaning is being inferred. Let the wise discern this. Thus ends the investigation into the meaning of the particle *eva*. Now begins the investigation into the meaning of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).

Now, since the verbal roots (*dhātu*), their inherent meanings (*prakṛti*), and the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are well-established, their specific meanings are being determined. [Note: This section on the investigation of the meaning of *tiṅ* is commenced for the purpose of defining the meaning of the *l*-substitutes, i.e., the *tiṅ*s.

According to the *Bhāṣya*—"A word conveys its meaning only when it is uttered, not when it is unuttered"—and because such is the experience in the world, this chapter begins to define the meaning of the *tiṅ*s.
