Furthermore, the application of the prescriptive rules such as "the *laṭ* suffix occurs in the present tense" and the rules that apprehend the expressive power (*śakti*) such as "the *laṭ* suffix denotes the object," proceeds by superimposing the meaning of the substitutes onto the original bases (*sthānin*).]

In this context, the specific number, specific time, and specific agent are the meanings of the *l*-substitutes (*lādeśa*) alone. For verbal roots (*dhātu*), the meanings are the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). The meanings of the *tiṅ*-suffixes are the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), the number (*saṅkhyā*), and the time (*kāla*). Among these, number is a qualifier of the agent when the suffix denotes the agent, but it is a qualifier of the object when the suffix denotes the object. Time, however, is a qualifier of the operation, which is the meaning of the root. Between the result and the operation, the result is the qualifier and the operation is the primary element.

The secret here is this: according to the *Nirukta*’s principle that “a verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning,” and from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra “*bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*” which indicates that action is predominant, in every instance—whether it be an active voice (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*) or a passive voice (*karma-ākhyāta*)—the cognition has the operation (*vyāpāra*) as its principal qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For this very reason, the statement “the operation is primary with respect to the fruit (*phala*), but the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-artha*) is a qualifier” becomes logically consistent.

Thus, the ancient grammarians hold that in the sentence "Caitra goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati caitraḥ*), there is an action occurring at the present time, which is conducive to a conjunction residing in an object non-different from the village, and whose agent is Caitra as delimited by singularity. In the sentence "The village is being gone to by Caitra" (*grāmo gamyate caitreṇa*), however, there is an action occurring at the present time, residing in an agent non-different from Caitra, which is conducive to a conjunction residing in an object non-different from the village as delimited by singularity.

The moderns, however, maintain that in a verb expressing the agent (kartṛ-ākhyāta), the cognition has the operation as the primary qualificand, whereas in a verb expressing the object (karma-ākhyāta), the cognition has the result as the primary qualificand. As for the indication of the primacy of the operation in passages such as "the operation is primary with respect to the result," that is intended specifically with reference to the agent-verb.

Alternatively, in that context, there is a division of both primary and secondary word-meanings (*pada*). A primary meaning is that which has as its purport the co-occurrence with a verbal suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*); a secondary meaning, however, is that which has as its purport the co-occurrence with an object suffix (*karma-pratyaya*). Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* is consistent.

The time [categories] such as the present are expressed by the *laṭ* and other suffixes; they are also denoted [by them]. This is because both positions have been stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other works, and because they are supported by reasoning. To explain: the meaning "present" belongs to the verbal roots themselves, while the *laṭ* suffix merely indicates it.

Nor should it be argued that there is complexity (*gaurava*) due to the multiplicity of the delimiters of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) when postulating a capacity for many verbal roots (*dhātu*) therein; for time is accepted as being nothing other than a continuum of operations (*vyāpārasantāna*), and that [continuum] is the meaning of the verbal root. Furthermore, there is no evidence that time is distinct from the continuum of operations. Thus, the meaning of the rule *vartamāne laṭ* ("the suffix *laṭ* occurs when [an action] is present") is that the suffixes *laṭ* and so forth are used when that [time] is indicated. Therefore, the suffix *laṭ* is indeed merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

Likewise, the present tense suffix *laṭ* is also denotative [of time], because the rule "the *laṭ* occurs in the present" (*vartamāne laṭ*) prescribes *laṭ* for the present time, and because a continuum of activity lacks the nature of being time itself. Thus it has been said by Bhartṛhari:
"Time serves to distinguish actions, while number is the differentiator of everything.
By this, it is clearly stated that time is the delimiter of action; for it is not possible for something to be its own delimiter. Therefore, *laṭ* is indeed denotative.

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) resides in effort (*kṛti*), because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) when the universal property of effort-ness (*kṛtitva-jāti*) serves as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*). In cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the operation (*vyāpāra*). Furthermore, the delimitor of denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is simply the property of being a *la*-suffix (*latva*), which is common to all such suffixes. They argue that if properties such as *tip*-ness were taken as the delimiters of denotative power, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Herein lies the distinction: they say that by virtue of being a *la*-suffix, there is denotative power for effort, while by virtue of being a middle-voice suffix (*ātmanepada*), there is denotative power for the fruit (*phala*). This is because, according to the rule that only a property that is neither too narrow nor too broad can serve as a delimiter, the property of being a middle-voice suffix (*ātmanepadatva*) satisfies this requirement.

Thus concludes the essential portion of the investigation into the meaning of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). In this context, the meaning of verbal suffixes prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) is the substratum (*āśraya*). That [substratum] is, in the case of the agent, the locus of the operation (*vyāpāra*), and in the case of the object, the locus of the result (*phala*). Furthermore, "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) that serves as the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Nor does there arise an infinity of delimiting factors due to the diversity of the relations of that [substratum-ness], such as its being the relatum of inherence or its being the counter-correlative of a relation; for, just like inherence (*samavāya*), there is no fault even if it is a single entity.

It should be understood that the nature of being a substratum (*āśrayatātattva*) is something distinct that serves as the unifier (*anugamaka*) of all instances of being a substratum. Nor should it be argued: "Since the substratum is already obtained by the word ending in the nominative case, it is not proper to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for it there, because the meaning of a word is precisely that which cannot be obtained otherwise. This is because, in expressions such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), although Caitra is obtained [as the agent] by way of his specific property of being Caitra (*caitratva*), he is not obtained as the substratum of the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is the meaning of the verbal root *pac*.

As for the Naiyāyikas: [they argue that] effort (*kṛti*) and its locus (*āśraya*) need not be denoted [by the suffix], because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to assign a primary denotative power (*śakti*) to them as being the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. Rather, when the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-lakāra*) occurs, it denotes effort. Nor is this effort already obtained by the verbal root alone; for in the analysis "he cooks" (*pacati*) as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), effort and the like are explained as distinct [from the action], and thus they cannot be the meaning of the root.

Nor does the verbal root, when co-occurring with suffixes such as *ghañ*, have its power (*śakti*) restricted solely to the result (*phala*), because that would lead to the erroneous cognition "the village possesses going" (*grāmo gamanavān*). Furthermore, in cases such as "cooking by means of wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ*), the connection of the factors of action (*kāraka*) would be impossible for you, since in your view there is a rule that the factors of action must connect with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, the power of the verbal root resides in an activity (*vyāpāra*) distinct from effort (*yatna*).

Now, in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), since effort (*kṛti*) is precluded and since the root *kṛ* (to do) signifies action in general, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is simply an operation conducive to the meaning of the verbal root. For this very reason, there is the common usage: "the sprout was produced by means of a seed, etc. Furthermore, the analysis (*vivaraṇa*) of "he cooks" (*pacati*) is seen as "he brings about cooking" (*pākaṃ bhāvayati*), using the verb *bhāvayati*, which signifies action in general; and the analysis "the chariot performs going" (*gamanaṃ karoti*) is also observed. Moreover, even by the term "agent" (*kartṛ*), only the substratum of the operation is denoted.

The view that [the object] is the substratum of the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārthāśraya*)—as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas (an additional reading in manuscript *kha*)—is not tenable, because a fault would arise in the case of forms such as *āmanta* and *kṛti*. Furthermore, in expressions like *kṛtiḥ*, there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) of the root *kṛñ* in the sense of "action" (*kṛti*). Since the act of buying rice and so forth does not possess the property of being conducive to cooking, and since the relation is precisely the qualifier of conduciveness, the fault consisting in the use of the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*) does not apply. (An additional reading in manuscript *kha*: "there is no fault").

In cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the experience of effort (*yatna*) arises from the inference of that effort which is the cause of specific actions like cooking, which are invariably concomitant with effort. Furthermore, the cognition of the presentness of the effort is accounted for simply by accepting an inference of presentness regarding that which is delimited by the nature of effort, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). However, the claim that such a cognition of presentness is verbal in nature (*śābdatva*) remains indeed a matter of dispute.

If it is argued that the connection with [the properties of] presentness and so forth belongs only to the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), and that the gloss ‘pacati’ (he cooks) = ‘pākayatnavān’ (one who possesses the effort of cooking) is merely an explanation of the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), we say no; for compared to the property of being an activity (*vyāpāratva*), the property of being an effort (*yatnatva*)—being a universal (*jāti*)—is the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

The same applies to the root *kṛ* (to do). Even when Caitra trembles due to a wind-disease (*vātaroga*)—that is, even while he possesses the operation consisting of contact with a dissimilar wind conducive to trembling—the cognition arises: "I am not performing the trembling; rather, my body is trembling due to a wind-disease. Therefore, it is more appropriate that the meaning of *kṛ* is indeed effort (*yatna*). Furthermore, this is supported by the linguistic usage of "done" (*kṛta*) and "not done" (*akṛta*) regarding a cloth and a sprout respectively. In expressions such as "the sprout was produced by the seed," the term *kṛ* is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote a favorable operation. The explanatory gloss (*vivaraṇa*) "he brings about" (*bhāvayati*) likewise intends the sense of effort.

Nor does it follow that if *kṛñ* has the meaning of "effort," it would be intransitive like *yatati*, because of the inherent nature of verbal power (*śabda-śakti-svabhāva*). Alternatively, the meaning of *kṛñ* is an effort conducive to production (*utpatti-anukūlā kṛtiḥ*), whereas the meaning of *yatati* is simply effort; thus there is no fault. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the commentary explaining *utpādayati* as "he performs production" (*utpattiṃ karoti*) would be inconsistent because production lacks another production; for in that case, we accept a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the mere operation (*vyāpāra-mātra*).

Nor should it be argued that because the property of being an effort (*yatnatva*) is common to the effort involved in verbal activity (*ākhyāta-vācya-nivṛtti*), the effort that is the source of life (*jīvanayoni-yatna*), and so forth, it is impossible for it to be the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); for there is no such fault, since we accept that the very genus of "activity" (*pravṛttitva-jāti*), which is delimited by being produced by the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna-janya-avacchedaka-pravṛttitva*), is the basis for the application of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pravṛtti-nimitta*). For this very reason, even though God’s creative action (*īśvarakṛti*) is the generator of all that is produced, expressions such as "God cooks" (*īśvaraḥ pacati*) or "God eats" (*īśvaro bhuṅkte*) do not occur.

However, in expressions such as "The Lord speaks this Veda," the usage is not natural (svārasika), unlike in "Caitra cooks. Nor is there a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the operation (vyāpāra) in cases like "he does" (karoti); therefore, effort (yatna) alone is the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta).

For this very reason, there is a natural linguistic usage such as, "Caitra alone cooks; the insentient wood and so forth do not. However, the expression "the woods cook" is not a natural usage in the same way that "Caitra cooks" is. Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence of a twofold cognition of effort (yatna) in cases such as "he acts," for this is justifiable in the same manner as [the cognition of] "two" and so on. Furthermore, in expressions such as "the chariot goes," there is a secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the activity conducive to the action.

Furthermore, the action (vyāpāra) is construed [with the root] by virtue of both its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the result and its being conducive (*anukūlatva*) to it, due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). Consequently, the expression "he goes" (*gacchati*) is not applied to one who possesses an activity such as pushing that is conducive to the movement of another person. Alternatively, since there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), this is because the relation [in question] is precisely a specific kind of conduciveness.

If, however, it is argued that in cases such as ‘he sleeps’ (*nidrāti*), there is no established [intrinsic] activity conducive to sleep—consisting of the mind’s contact with the *mūlādhāra* nerve—and that likewise there is no such experience in cases like ‘the chariot goes’ (*ratho gacchati*), then in instances such as ‘he knows’, ‘he goes’, ‘he exerts effort’, ‘he hates’, ‘he acts’, and ‘he sleeps’, there must be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the locus (*āśrayatva*).

Now, one might object: let the meaning of the verbal root itself be construed with the referent of the nominative case through the relation of being the locus; what is the need for figurative indication? Furthermore, on the view that there is figurative indication, there is the burden of having to accept the manifestation of an additional relation, namely the state of being the locus, in cases such as ‘he knows’.

And one should not argue that in cases such as "the rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), the possibility of such a cognition is precluded because it is an unestablished linguistic principle (*avyutpatti*) that the meaning of a noun can be directly construed with the meaning of a verbal root through a relation of objecthood (*karmatā*); for even if a cognition where the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the qualifier and the action is the qualificand is unestablished, there is no evidence that a cognition where the action is the qualifier and the meaning of the nominal stem is the qualificand is likewise unestablished. To this we say: no.

In cases such as "the pot acts" (*ghaṭaḥ karoti*), the understanding that "the pot is the object of the act of acting" (*kṛtikarmībhūto ghaṭaḥ*) must be prevented; for it is unestablished by grammatical tradition (*avyutpanna*) that there can be a verbal cognition where the meaning of a noun functions as the qualifier of an action. As for the complexity of positing a relation [between the action and the noun], it does not constitute a fault, because it is supported by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*).

Or, let it be so; nevertheless, in such cases, the connection with "presentness" and so forth belongs exclusively to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and not to the substratum (*āśrayatva*) and so on. For if the substratum—whether as a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) or as a distinct entity (*atirikta*)—were to exist in its relation [to the object] even when cognition and the like were absent, there would result the undesirable consequence of using expressions such as "he knows" (*jānāti*). However, if the connection with presentness and so forth were to apply to the substratum as qualified by cognition and the like, then that connection would necessarily apply to the qualifier (cognition) as well; therefore, it is more appropriate to accept that [the connection] belongs to the meaning of the root itself.

Nor does the view that effort (*yatna*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) contradict the grammatical rule "laḥ kartari" (Pāṇini 3.4.67), because the denotation of the action (*kṛti*) itself serves as the qualifier for the meaning of the nominative case-ending; thus, since the agent qualified by the action is understood through its connection with the action, there is no contradiction regarding the suffix *la* being the indicator of that [agent]. This is because in the rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the meaning of the locative case is simply "indicativeness" (*bodhakatā*), and not "denotative capacity" (*vācakatā*), for the latter is precluded due to the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a linguistic power (*śakti*) for a qualified substratum.

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—characterized by the denotation of a single substratum by two distinct forms—in cases such as "Caitra cooks," for no such experience occurs; rather, what is perceived as coreferentiality is simply the denotation of an object connected to its own [respective] referent, without the inclusion of identity (*tādātmya*).

Or, let there be such grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); however, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the effort (*yatna*) alone. For this very reason, there is no inconsistency in rules such as "when *yuṣmad* is a coreferential word" (Pāṇini 1.4.105). And for this same reason, when the question "What is he doing? is answered with "He cooks," even in the absence of a word like "Devadatta," there is no doubt regarding the number of the agent who is present to the mind; for there is no fault in the number being construed with the substratum (*dharmin*) presented through secondary indication.

In expressions such as ‘pacati’ (he cooks), the temporal relation pertains only to the effort (*kṛti*), and not to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). This is because even when there is no effort—as in the case of a flower where the process of cooking, consisting of contact with fire and so forth dependent on that effort, is nonetheless present—the usage ‘this does not cook’ occurs; furthermore, when ‘this cooks’ is said, the doubt as to whether or not this person possesses the effort for cooking at this moment is removed. In cases such as ‘jānāti’ (he knows), the temporal relation necessarily pertains to the meaning of the verbal root itself.

The same applies to cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*); for even when the effort has ceased while the cooking continues, the cognition "this person does not cook" never arises, precisely because one perceives the very act of "cooking.

Furthermore, in this way, there is no need to postulate various cause-and-effect relationships (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) regarding the connection with time. Others maintain that the removal of the doubt—"Does he now possess the effort to cook, or not?"—is accounted for by accepting an inference of presentness (*vartamānatva*) within the scope of "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*), based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

In expressions such as "perishes" (*naśyati*), origination (*utpatti*) is also the meaning of the verbal root, or else it is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); therefore, the temporal relation (*kālānvaya*) pertains to that [origination] alone. Consequently, even though destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is eternal, the expression "it perishes at all times" is not employed.

Alternatively, since the very absence of origination (*utpatti*) constitutes the category of destruction (*nāśa*), there is a connection with that [absence] when its constituent part, namely origination, occurs. Furthermore, regarding rules such as "the third case ending is used when the agent (*kartṛ*) is not expressed," the meaning is "when the action (*kṛti*) is not expressed. Some maintain that "action" (*kṛti*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [properties] such as being a substratum (*āśrayatva*), and thus the rule means "when the property of the agent is not expressed. That is not correct; for if the general verbal suffix (*lākāra*) itself were endowed with the power (*śakti*) to denote agency, then the third case ending would undesirably follow even in examples such as *pacyate taṇḍulaś caitreṇa* ("the rice is cooked by Caitra").

In response to the question "What is being done by Devadatta?", the answer "It is cooked" (pacyate) [indicates the action]; and in cases such as "The rice is being cooked" (pacyate taṇḍulaḥ), where the agent-word is not explicitly mentioned, there is the vibration (spanda) that produces the result.

Furthermore, since the doubt as to whether [an action] is produced by a present effort (*kṛti*) does not arise, and because the sentence "caitreṇa pacyate" (it is cooked by Caitra) is glossed as "caitreṇa pakvaḥ kriyate" (that which was cooked is being made by Caitra), it is necessary that the verbal suffix alone possesses the capacity to denote agency (*kartṛtva*). Nor is the meaning [of the rule Pāṇini 2.3.18] that the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is not intended to be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of agency, whereas the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) occurs when the meaning of the nominal stem is intended to be the qualificand of objecthood (*karmatva*), and so forth.

Therefore, one should not argue that there is no fault because the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) in the Sūtra has already served its purpose; for in a case where Caitra and Maitra are both the agents of cooking, if the intended connection were "Maitra is the agent of the cooking whose agent is Caitra," it would follow that such expressions as "Maitra cooks by means of Caitra" (*caitreṇa pacati maitraḥ*) or "Maitra has cooked by means of Caitra" (*caitreṇa pakvavān maitraḥ*) would also be possible.

The meaning of the sūtra is that the third case suffix occurs after a word denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) when that word functions as a qualifier for an action that has not itself become a qualifier [of another], provided there is an intention to express the agenthood as a qualifier whose primary referent is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). In examples such as *caitreṇa pācayati maitraḥ* ("Caitra causes Maitra to cook"), the third case is established by qualifying the cooking—which is itself qualified by the agenthood expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—with the agency of Caitra and others; thus, the phrase "not becoming a qualifier of anything other than its own substratum" (*āśrayātiriktāviśeṣaṇatāpanna*) is included.

And that [the agent] is a qualifier of the substratum of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Furthermore, its being distinct from the substratum is quite clear. It might be argued that, with the intention of providing a cognition where the effort (*kṛti*) is the qualificandum, the qualification "not being a qualifier of the substratum" was set aside and replaced by "not being a qualifier of anything other than the substratum," in order to exclude such usages as *caitreṇa pacati* ("Caitra cooks by means of [himself]"). However, this must not be said, because such a meaning cannot be obtained from the actual words of the Sūtra. Moreover, just as there is an apprehension of the *tip*-suffix as denoting the substratum in *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), in the usage *caitreṇa pācayati maitraḥ* ("Maitra causes Caitra to cook by means of him[self]"), it would follow that the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) would be grammatically incorrect.

Therefore, the meaning of the rule beginning with "anabhihite" (when not already expressed) is "when number has not been expressed. Nor can it be argued that in cases such as "the jar was seen by Caitra" (*caitreṇa dṛṣṭo ghaṭaḥ*) or "Caitra saw the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ dṛṣṭavān caitraḥ*), since number is understood even without a finite verb (*tiṅ*), and since the presence of number can be accounted for by the nominal suffixes (*sup*) whose expressive power is already established, the finite verbs do not denote number.

And thus, one might argue that in cases such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), there would also be the undesirable consequence of a third-case ending (*tṛtīyā*). However, this need not be said, because in examples like "Caitra and Maitra go" (*caitro maitraśca gacchataḥ*), the cognition of duality and so forth occurs even without a *sup*-suffix denoting duality. Nor can it be asked: "How is there a cognition of duality when the delimiting property of the substratum (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is singularity? For it is possible to have a cognition of duality delimited by two instances of singularity. Nor should it be suggested that the singular number of the *sup*-suffix itself has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for duality and so forth; for since a *sup*-suffix conveys a number residing in the meaning of its stem (*prakṛtyartha*), this would lead to the absurdity of cognizing two Caitras and two Maitras.

If it is objected: "But how can there be a fault there on the grounds that number is not denoted?", we say: no; for in that case, the distinction is possible precisely through the denotation or non-denotation of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). The meaning of the rule (Pāṇini 2.3.18) is that when one of these two is not denoted, the third suffix (*tṛtīyā*) is used. However, according to the view that in the *lākāra* (verbal endings) the effort (*kṛti*) is not the expressed meaning, the non-denotation of effort itself constitutes the non-denotation of the agent.

Nor should it be argued that the distinction between what is expressed and what is unexpressed depends solely on whether number is denoted or not denoted; for since there is no obstacle to the number being construed as common to both the agent and the object when it is not so denoted, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of a second case ending (dvitīyā) occurring even when the agent is marked by a verbal suffix (lakāra) and the object is likewise intended. This objection is invalid because we accept a rule that number must necessarily be construed with the qualificand of the productive operation (bhāvanā), provided that both are conveyed by a single word (ekapadopātta). Thus, there is no fault.

The connection of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is with that which is denoted by the word ending in the nominative case and serving as a qualifier for something else, precisely because such is the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*). By the term *bhāvanā*, that which is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—excluding number and tense—is understood. By this, forms such as *jānāti* ("he knows") are included. In the examples "A man kills like Nārāyaṇa" and "The face is seen like the moon," the phrase "qualifier of something else" (*itaraviśeṣaṇībhūta*) is used to exclude the connection of number (*saṅkhyā*) with Nārāyaṇa and the moon.

In reality, since there is no understanding from such statements as "the pot is eternal" (*ghaṭo nityaḥ*), because [the verbal suffix] presents itself as a qualifier of something else, and because it acts as an obstacle to verbal cognition alone, there is no deficiency even if that [verbal suffix] is not specifically included here. Thus, the causal relationship is established as follows: the presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta-pada*) is the cause for the cognition of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-artha*) other than [properties such as] being a time or being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

And thus, in the case of "he does not cook" (*na pacati*), there is no fault even if the agent—which is otherwise unconnected with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—is connected with it; for in that instance, it is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) that is connected with the productive operation. In the case of "it is slept by Caitra" (*caitreṇa supyate*), because the cognition is that "the sleep resides in Caitra," the term "ending in the first case" (*prathamānta*) is included to exclude [number] from the sleep, which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For this very reason, in that case, when the verbal suffix denotes a state (*bhāva-lakāra*), number remains unconnected because there is no presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the first case. For this very reason, the singular number alone is the default rule (*autsargika*) there.

Furthermore, even for you, where should the agent be denoted, and where should the object be denoted? Since there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) regarding this, you must state that something such as the verbal suffix (*śap*) or the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) serves as the regulator. And so, for me as well, when it is asked where number is to be construed, or where the effort (*kṛti*) alone is to be denoted and where the result (*phala*) is also denoted, that very same factor [the verbal suffix, etc. is the regulator; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. In the sentence "The rice is cooked by Maitra," the understanding is: "The rice possesses the result produced by the cooking, which is the object of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) residing in Maitra."

The meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) consists of both the effort (*kṛti*) and the result (*phala*). In this context, the effort is the qualifier and the result is the qualificand; "residing in" (*niṣṭhatva*) is the meaning of the instrumental case, or rather, it is the relation (*saṃsarga*); or the instrumental case may signify number alone. By the term *bhāvanā*, that which is the meaning of the verbal suffix—excluding number and tense—is expressed. For this very reason, there is no disruption of the coreferential connection (*anvaya*) of number with the qualificand of the *bhāvanā*. In the sentence "the village is reached by means of a chariot" (*rathena gamyate grāmaḥ*), the cognition is: "that which possesses a result produced by an operation conducive to reaching, residing in the chariot."

In this context, the state of being the locus (*niṣṭhatva*) is the meaning of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*). Its connection is with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), namely, "going. Nor is the result (*phala*) connected to "going" through that relation, because it is unestablished in linguistic theory (*avyutpatti*) that there can be a distinct connection between the meaning of a nominal stem and the meaning of a verbal root.

Alternatively, by that relation, the chariot connects only with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) which is the meaning of the verb ending. Nor should the result itself be the relation; for what is the point of postulating a specific denotative power (*śakti*) for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) there, given that it is experienced as appearing as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*)?

Nor can it be argued that since the operation delimited by the result is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), that [result] is obtained by the root itself; for it is impossible for the relationship between qualifier and qualified to be reversed, and thus the result produced by the action would not be obtained. This is because a word brings to mind only that which is qualified by the form in which the word's expressive power (*śakti*) resides. Therefore, the operation alone is the meaning of the verbal root, while the result and the effort (*kṛti*) are the meanings of the middle voice affix (*ātmanepada*).

Now, if the action (*kṛti*) itself were the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in that context, would the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) presented by the suffix—which has the action as its object—be construed with the fruit (*phala*), or would the action, qualified by the *bhāvanā*, be construed with the fruit? Not the first, because it would contradict the cognition that the fruit possesses the status of an object (*karman*), defined as being that which possesses a fruit produced by the action. As for the latter, the action’s role as a qualifier of the *bhāvanā* presented by the *tiṅ*-suffix would be abandoned, since its construal elsewhere [as a qualifier] is already established; rather, it would have to be construed only with the meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*).

In accordance with expressions such as "cooked by Caitra" (*caitreṇa pakvaḥ*), there is a linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that an action denoted by the meaning of a *su*-affix must be construed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the [verbal] action; therefore, the comprehension of the relation occurs only through the second mode [of construction]. However, in cases such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the result (*phala*) is the meaning of the accusative case.

In reality, however, due to the aforementioned inconsistency, it is necessary that the effort (*kṛti*) also be the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) here. The ancients maintain that a different linguistic rule must simply be postulated for this specific instance.

Some, however, maintain that according to the arguments stated in the analysis of the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātu*), a root denotes an activity delimited by its respective fruit. Nor can it be argued that because it is ungrammatical for a fruit—presented as a qualifier of the root-meaning—to be construed with the object, the fruit denoted by the meaning of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) must be construed [with the agent]; for that [middle voice] denotes the fruit in a general form or a specific form, and thus it is a denoter of the fruit in general.

And it should not be argued that, in cases such as "the village is being gone-to" (*gamyate grāmaḥ*), the fact that the village possesses a result in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth would not necessarily be understood; for there is no fault, since we accept that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), although generally denoting a result, conveys only a result in the form of conjunction and the like, precisely through its co-occurrence with verbs such as *gam* which denote an operation delimited by conjunction and so forth. Nor does this imply an infinite number of potencies (*śakti*) on the grounds that the general result is conveyed in a specific form, because such an infinity is accepted. Alternatively, just as in the case of pronouns (*tadādi*), there is no infinity of potencies due to the unification of the delimitors of potencies (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) by virtue of their being present in the mind.

And thus, in the case of "the village is being gone to" (*gamyate grāmaḥ*), the understanding is that the village is the locus of the conjunction produced by an activity delimited by conjunction. In expressions such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the meaning of the accusative case is "inherence" (*ādheyatva*); due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), this inheres even in the result, which is the delimitor of the verbal root's meaning. However, for those who do not accept partial inherence (*ekadeśānvaya*), the meaning of the accusative in that instance is simply the result itself. They state that the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to an action delimited by conjunction, which produces a conjunction residing in the village."

In this view as well, since the twofold manifestation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) contradicts experience, the meaning of the two *ātmanepada* endings is not the result (*phala*), but rather belongs to the verbal root alone; for the result and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are distinct *śakya*s (denotable meanings). And thus, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) denotes the locus (*ādheyatva*), while the agentive suffix (*karmākhyāta*) denotes the substratum (*āśrayatva*). As for the result, however, when co-occurring with an agentive suffix, it is a qualifier of the operation which is the meaning of the verbal root. But when co-occurring with an agentive suffix denoting the object (*karmākhyāta*), [the situation is different]. [Note: The intended point here is as follows: Just as words such as *tad*, *yad*, etc.,...]

In order to avoid the consequence of polysemy—which would arise because [words like *tad*] have the capacity to denote multiple objects in the form of "pot-ness," "cloth-ness," and so on—it is accepted that words such as *tad* possess their denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to those properties, such as pot-ness and cloth-ness, which are qualified by the specific speaker through the relation of being the delimitors of their own object-spheres (*svīyaviṣayatāvacchedakatva*). By this means, they do not become polysemous.

Likewise, here too, since it is accepted that the roots *pac* and so forth possess a denotative power (*śaktatva*) defined by a denotative capacity (*śakyatā*) delimited by properties such as "the nature of blowing" (*phūtkāratva*), which are themselves characterized by a specific cognition inherent in the speaker of the root *pac* and the like, through the relation of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of their own object-sphere (*viṣayatā*).

Since having the capacity (*śaktatā*) determined by a denotative capacity (*śakyatā*) that is delimited by various non-uniform properties (*anugatanānādharmāvacchinna*) constitutes polysemy (*nānārthakatva*), and since in the present case there exists a unifying factor (*anugamaka*) in the form of a specific cognition (*buddhiviśeṣa*), there is an absence of polysemy. Therefore, it is appropriate to hold that [the word] denotes only the substantive (*viśeṣya*) by virtue of the intention (*tātparya*) conveyed through forms such as the *parasmaipada* or *ātmanepada*.

In expressions such as "it is known by Devadatta" (*devadattena jñāyate*), the meaning of the accusative suffix is the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*), while the meaning of the instrumental suffix is the state of being a locus (*ādheyatva*). In expressions such as "the pot is made" (*kriyate ghaṭaḥ*), the meaning of the accusative suffix is precisely the state of being the object of an effort (*kṛti*) by way of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*). Therefore, expressions such as "he makes space" (*ākāśaṃ karoti*) are not valid usages.

[Objection: But in this way, even if [the action] is produced, the power (*śakti*) of the agent and the object would not be established, because it is more appropriate for power to reside precisely in that which is the locus of what has been produced. [Response: If you argue that—just as with the meaning of indeclinables and particles—the suffix also brings about a cognition of a distinct relation, and thus there is no contradiction with the rule of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of the noun and the suffix; [we reply: No. Consider these examples: *caitro gantā* (Caitra is the goer), *gato grāmaḥ* (the village is gone to), *mitrā paktrī* (Mitrā is the cooker), *gataṃ puram* (the city is gone to), *bhoktā tṛpyati* (the eater is satisfied), *pakvāni bhuṅkte* (he eats the cooked things), and *paktā 'pasāryatām* (let the cooker be removed). In these cases, the suffix expresses a distinct relation.

In such cases, since we observe a restriction regarding masculine, feminine, and neuter gender, and since we accept that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) arises only through the relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) among the factors introduced in the first half of the verse, this would be untenable without the verbal root possessing the power [to denote] the substratum (*dharmin*). Furthermore, there is a contradiction: the state of being the locus of satisfaction (*tṛpti-āśrayatva*) does not apply to the effort conducive to eating, nor does the state of having "cooking-resultant softening" (*viklitti*) as its object apply to the act of eating itself.

Therefore, roots followed by *kṛt* suffixes prescribed for the agent denote the agent, while those prescribed for the object denote the object; in cases such as *caitrasya naptā* ("Caitra's grandson"), the verbal meaning (the action) is construed with the *kṛti* (volition/effort) and so forth, which serve as the delimiters of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka*).

Alternatively, in expressions such as *paktā* (the cooker), the cooking (*pāka*) and so forth are construed with the agent (*kartṛ*) and others through the relation of being the locus of an activity conducive to itself. There is no fault in this, because the third and second case endings are prescribed when agency, objecthood, and so on are not expressed; for even that which is qualified by an action is not expressed [by the suffix] in the case of *kṛt* participles.

[Objection: "Let it be that even for a *kṛt* suffix, its denotation is indeed the property (*dharma*) alone; however, let there be secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). This is because, in accordance with the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in cases such as 'the enjoyer is satisfied,' the same must hold true for cases like 'Caitra is a goer. [Reply: No; for this would result in the abolition of the primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the qualified entity. It could be argued that in all cases the denotative power resides in the property, while secondary indication applies to the qualified entity. Furthermore, the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the heard *tiṅ*-ness (*titva*) and so forth, and not *tiṅ*-ness in general as applicable to all [suffixes], because the latter is difficult to define.

Nor can it be said that being a *tiṅ* word consists in its relation to a specific convention established by Pāṇini, or that the rule "the first [is designated] by the last" (P. 1.1.71) constitutes the apprehension of that convention; for even those who do not know that [rule] possess understanding [of the meaning].

Furthermore, in this way, even in the case of words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) which denote objects like pots, since it is possible for some word to have a convention (*saṅketa*) belonging to a particular person, by the same logic, that very word would also incur the status of being the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Moreover, just as there is a convention of the word *tiṅ* belonging to Pāṇini regarding the suffixes *tiṅ* etc., since conventions of other words belonging to other persons are also possible, all those respective words would also incur the status of being the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), due to the absence of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*).

By this, the view that the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for [the suffix] *ākhyāta* and so forth consists in the form of being an *ākhyāta*-word and so on, through its relation to a specific convention, is refuted. Nor is it the property of being a *la*-suffix (*latva*), because understanding occurs even when one is ignorant of that [property]. Furthermore, if that were the denotative power, there would result a multiplicity of meanings for the suffix *sat* due to its conformity with [other suffixes such as] *śatṛ* and so forth.

Furthermore, rather than postulating both a delimitor of the capacity to cause remembrance (*smārakatāvacchedaka*) and a delimitor of the expressive capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate only the delimitor of the expressive capacity. Moreover, since in forms such as *apapāca*, many [elements] would otherwise result in being mere reminders (*smāraka*), and because the substituends (*sthānin*) are not fixed while the substitutes (*ādeśa*) are consistently applied, it is more appropriate that these [substitutes] themselves possess the denotative power (*vācakatva*). For this very reason, in forms such as *aidhām*, the agent is understood precisely through the suffix *ām*.

Nor should it be argued that, because rules such as *paralopa* (elision of the subsequent element) are prescribed in cases like *harerava* involving *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute for preceding and following vowels), there would be a dispute among grammarians regarding how much of the meaning belongs to the vocative case, how much to the action, how much of the meaning in forms like *vas* and *nas* denotes the substance (*dravya*), and how much denotes the objectness (*karmatva*) and so forth; and since the primary acquisition of meaning occurs only in the aggregate, this would lead to the postulation of a power (*śakti*) in both the word and the sentence, resulting in the undesirable consequence of a *vākya-sphoṭa* and *pada-sphoṭa*. For [the meaning] exists in each individual [element].

They argue that there is no such contingency [of the suffix being the sole denoter], because it is possible for words whose individual powers have been ascertained to convey the sentence-meaning through the presentation of their respective meanings by means of their collective occurrence as remembered from linguistic usage; however, since no power has ever been ascertained for the verbal suffix (*la*) anywhere, there is no fault.

On this point, they say: there is no obstacle to accepting that even a heavy property may be the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), just as it is accepted as the delimitor of being denoted (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatva*). Nor should it be argued that denotability-delimitingness is a specific kind of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*)—similar to causality-delimitingness—and that such a relation is only possible when a light property is available, whereas a heavy one is not; for there is no reason to maintain such a disparity between the two cases.

Furthermore, if the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) were merely those respective individual essences (*svarūpa*), then since even heavy properties (*gurudharma*) possess existence (*sattva*), what inconsistency would there be? If, however, it is something distinct, how can one postulate [the relation] for a heavy property that serves as the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*)? Moreover, rather than postulating the absence of delimitingness (*avacchedakatva*) in heavy properties, it is more reasonable to postulate the very relation belonging to the delimitingness that is postulated elsewhere, because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating a positive entity.

Furthermore, delimitorhood (*avacchedakatva*) is neither an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) nor something distinct [from the entity itself], as there is no evidence for its existence. Rather, it is simply the state of occurring in that which is neither less nor more [than the locus]. And this [state] exists even in the case of a heavy [property]. Thus, the detailed discussion regarding being a delimitant of causality (*kāraṇatā-avacchedakatva*), being a delimitant of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-avacchedakatva*), and so forth, is to be found elsewhere. Consequently, an inquiry into the lightness or heaviness of a delimitant is improper.

Furthermore, where there is no dispute regarding the cognition [of a meaning] through both light and heavy forms, it is only in that case that the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in what is delimited by the light form, while the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) applies to what is delimited by the heavy form. In the present context, however, the cognition of effort (*kṛti*) from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as "effort-ness" (*kṛtitva*) is subject to dispute. Nor does the contingency of an infinite number of denotative powers arise because of the difference among infinite efforts as the delimitors of denotability; for it is "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) alone that serves as the single delimitor of denotability.

Even if that [substratum-ness] were manifold, there is no infinity of denotative powers, because the universal "substratum-ness-ness" (*āśrayatātva*) exists as the unifying factor for the delimitors of denotability.

Furthermore, in your own position, there is an infinite plurality of powers (*śakti*): the agent-suffixes (*kartṛ-taṅ*) have "effort" (*kṛti*), while the object-suffixes (*karma-taṅ*) have either "the fruit" (*phala*) or "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*). For me, however, [the suffixes] everywhere denote only the substratum, so that [this problem] does not arise. Moreover, because there is no determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) regarding the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, even the verb *karoti* is merely an explanation (*vivaraṇa*) of a portion of the verbal root itself; and in such an explanation, the word *pāka* denotes only "softening" (*viklitti*). For this very reason, when asked whether "cooking has occurred" or "not" at a time when the result has not yet been produced, the answer "it will occur" is also seen. And when the question includes the operation (*vyāpāra*), the answer is "it is occurring."

Nor is it untenable to provide a separate explanation of the meaning of the verbal root; for just as in the case of "pacati" (he cooks), the favorability (*anukūlatva*)—which appears through the constraints of the relation between the meaning of the root and the meaning of the suffix, and which, though consisting of a non-agentive power (*akārakaśakti*), is explained by the accusative ending in "pākam" as having the form of an agentive power (*kārakaśakti*) as a qualifier—likewise, it is possible to explain even the *kṛti* (volitional effort) that constitutes the meaning of the root in such a manner.

Furthermore, since *kṛti* (the effort of volition) is a specific type of activity (*vyāpāra*) common to both [the agent and the object], it is necessary to postulate the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in cases such as *phūtkāra* (blowing), which would result in the verbal root in expressions like *karoti* (he does) becoming semantically redundant. Since it is more appropriate to postulate the power in the base itself (*prakṛti*), and because [the meaning] is obtained from the root alone, there is no possibility at all of asserting that the power resides in the suffix (*ākhyāta*).

In fact, it has been stated in the *Dhātvarthanirūpaṇa* that no verbal root whatsoever possesses the meaning of "effort" (*yatna*). As for the common usage "I am not moving" even when Devadatta is trembling due to a disease such as rheumatism, this is justified because the meaning of the verb consists in an uncommon operation (*asādhāraṇavyāpāra*) conducive to the production of motion; such an operation is absent in Devadatta, and furthermore, because "effort" (*kṛti*) is included within the scope of that operation.

The conventional expression "the sprout was not made" (*aṅkuro na kṛtaḥ*) intends merely the absence of an action conducive to its arising; or, in that context, the root *kṛ* (to do/make) functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In your own view—as in the case of expressions such as "it was made by the seed and so forth"—although the various operations are denoted in their respective forms, there is no infinite number of primary powers (*śakti*), because the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) are subsumed under the state of being present in the intellect. Even for a word whose power consists in an operation delimited by arising, the expression "he performs arising" (*utpattiṃ karoti*) and the like are accounted for through secondary indication with respect to the operation in general.

Furthermore, in your view, there is no triad of causal relations (kāryakāraṇabhāva) such that: (1) with respect to a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the agent (āśraya) denoted by the verb suffix, the cause is the mental presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case; (2) with respect to a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the number (saṅkhyā) of that [agent], the cause is the presentation of the substratum (āśraya) of that meaning; and (3) with respect to a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the time (kāla) of that meaning, the cause is the presentation generated by the verbal root (dhātu).

However, it must be said that for me, in the cognition of the meaning of the verbal suffix as something distinct from the state of being a means to accomplish what is desired at a particular time, the cause is the presentation of a word ending in the nominative case; thus, there is parsimony in the view that number and bhāvanā reside in one and the same locus. This is because, when the question "What is he doing? is asked, we observe that the mere answer "He cooks" (pacati)—even though it does not contain a word explicitly denoting the agent—removes doubt regarding the singularity of the agent. Furthermore, you yourself must admit that the number (singularity) is construed with the agent who is presented through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) in that context, since the cognition has singularity as its qualifier.

For you, too, must necessarily state the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the presence of the agent who intends that [action] and the action itself; otherwise, by not accepting it in all such cases, there would be extreme complexity due to the necessity of including the status of being expressed by each respective verbal suffix (*tattadvākyīyatva*). Furthermore, regarding the causal relation between number and the connection with *bhāvanā*, there would be even greater complexity because one would have to include as the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) everything other than time, the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), and so forth.

In your view, because the meaning is restricted such that the understanding of the action (*kṛti*) arises from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in some cases and of its locus (*āśrayatva*) in others; and the understanding of the action arises from the root (*dhātu*) in some cases and from the suffix (*pratyaya*) in others, there results a multiplicity of cumbersome causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Furthermore, since all such causal relations are necessary according to their respective linguistic conventions (*vyutpatti*), any consideration of economy or complexity (*lāghava-gaurava*) regarding them is improper.

Furthermore, in rules such as *yuṣmadyupapade* [Pāṇini 1.4.105], when "coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is mentioned, coreferentiality established by the experience of the seers (*ṛṣi*) would be untenable in your view. Nor can it be argued that coreferentiality there consists merely in denoting that which possesses the same number as the referent; for such a thing is not conventionally designated by the term "coreferentiality. Nor can it be coreferentiality through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since primary denotation (*śakti*) alone is more appropriate.

Otherwise, there would be the destruction of the specific capacity [of the suffix], since there is nowhere a cognition of mere effort (kṛti) alone. If, however, it is argued that when only "pacati" is uttered, there is a cognition of that much alone, then upon uttering that [suffix], there would arise the doubt regarding the number of the agent; for in cases such as "paktā jātaḥ," it could be claimed that even with respect to effort, the usage is intended to convey effort alone. Furthermore, it would be difficult to establish a distinction between the *tiṅ* and the *kṛt* suffixes.

Furthermore, regarding the causal relation that "the cause for the cognition of a verbal root meaning (ākhyātārtha) distinct from [the properties of] being a means to what is desired at a particular time (*kāleṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth, is the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case," there is a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Moreover, to postulate an additional causal relation would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, your proposed interpretation is inappropriate because it is unsuitable to include the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*) within the scope of the subject (*uddeśya*); rather, the correct interpretation is simply this: "The second person (*madhyama*) occurs in place of that *la*-affix which is coreferential with 'you' (*yuṣmat*) when it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth."

Furthermore, the restriction regarding the connection with number is also difficult to establish. Nor can *śap* and the like be taken as indicators of the speaker's intention (*tātparya-grāhaka*), because since the meaning of rules such as *śap* [is applied] when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix denotes the agent, it is impossible to determine that they indicate the intention for the connection with number; for even if one were to claim that the rule *anabhihite* means "when the number is not already expressed," that too is incorrect, as it would result in the undesirable application of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in examples such as *devadattaḥ paktā*.

Furthermore, regarding the rule for the *tiṅ* suffixes (*tiṅvidhi*), does the meaning "in [the sense of] singularity and so forth" refer to the singularity and so forth of the meaning of the *l*-suffix (the verbal root) which is present through the application of *ekavacana* and so forth, or does it refer to the singularity and so forth residing in that which is connected with the meaning conveyed by the *tiṅ* suffix? In the first case, what is established is not desired [by you]. In the second case, however, since that [singularity] has already been expressed by the *sup* suffix following words such as "Devadatta," the prescription of the *tiṅ* suffix there would be untenable.

Moreover, in your view, in instances such as *pacati* ("he cooks") or *jñātaḥ* ("known"), the agency (*kartṛtva*) denoted would have various forms; in my view, however, it is of one and the same form in all cases.

Furthermore, in your theory regarding the rule for the suffix *la*, there arises the contingency of multiple meanings for the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*); even in the rules for the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth, there is a lack of uniformity, as it would mean "in some cases [the agent is] the action itself (*kṛti*), and in others, the substratum (*āśrayatva*)," and so on.

Nor is it the case that the meaning of the sūtra is merely "the third [case-ending] is used for the instrument" (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*) and so forth; for one must not claim that the third case-endings and others function through *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in examples such as "it is traveled by chariot" (*rathena gamyate*), because of your own established tenet that there is no *lakṣaṇā* in the case of nominal case-endings (*sub-vibhakti*). Furthermore, this would result in the specification of the meaning being redundant, since its purpose—according to you—is to indicate that the word is ungrammatical when used in another sense, whereas in your view, grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is desired everywhere through *lakṣaṇā*. Moreover, it would follow that the grammatical rule concerning the transposition of case-endings (*vyatyaya-anuśāsana*) would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, just as in expressions such as "the bank wishes to fall" (kūlaṃ pipatiṣati), where sentience is superimposed upon the insentient, it is possible for verbal suffixes (tiṅ-ādi) to have the sense of effort (kṛti) even when sentience is superimposed upon a chariot and so forth; thus, resorting to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is redundant.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*)—having as its sole purport correctness (*sādhutva*)—does not determine the meaning. For correctness must be predicated precisely by way of a specific meaning; thus, by the force of restating a meaning already established through the experience of the seers (*ṛṣi*), it is appropriate that correctness applies only to such a meaning. For this very reason, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is said, the question "Who? Of what kind? and the answer "The scholar Ghanaśyāma" are both logically consistent. Otherwise, if the agent were not presented [by the word], the desire for specific knowledge regarding "Who? would be untenable.

Furthermore, even if this were the case, there would still be no problem regarding the agent being the expressed meaning [of the suffix]. Nor should it be argued that, because of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that two meanings expressed by words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—as in "Caitra is going" (*caitro gantā*)—are construed as non-different (*abheda*), and because a construction through difference requires the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a word with a conflicting case-ending following a single word, a construction through non-difference must be asserted; and since that non-difference construction is untenable without the agent being the expressed meaning, [the agent must be the expressed meaning]. For in cases such as "the king's son's wealth" (*rājñaḥ sutasya dhanam*), when there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*), [the relation is understood despite the case endings].

Since both types of cognition are observed, both types of causal relation are subject to deviation; therefore, it is necessary that the understanding of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) serves as the cause for such various cognitions. Consequently, there is no obstacle to the agent (*kṛti*) being construed with Caitra as its locus, just as in the case of "Caitra goes. Nor does it follow from this that the agent must be the expressed meaning (*vācya*) because of grammatical coreferentiality (*liṅga-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in an expression like "Mitrā is a cook" (*mitrā paktrī*); for even if such words denote a property (*dharma*), they can be described as being dependent on the substantive (*viśeṣya-nighna*), like the word "white," and thus do not determine the actual ontological status of the thing itself.

Furthermore, just as a coreferential qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) must share the same gender as its qualificand (viśeṣya), there is a rule that such a qualifier must also have the same number as its qualificand; therefore, it is necessary that the verb (ākhyāta) also denotes the substratum (dharmin). Otherwise, expressions such as "devadattāḥ pacati" (Devadattas cooks) would result. If you argue that this rule does not hold because of counter-examples such as "caitro maitraśca sundarau" (Caitra and Maitra are handsome), we reply that your stated rule is equally absent due to counter-examples such as "kṣud upahantuṃ śakyam" (hunger is capable of being destroyed).

Nor is there an absence of usage for the term *kṛti* (action) alone, since this applies equally to verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) as well; furthermore, because the self—the substratum of action—cannot be born, expressions such as "the cook has been born" (*pācako jātaḥ*) are indeed possible. If only *kṛti* were denoted by the suffix, there would be the undesirable consequence of using "Caitra is a goer" (*caitre gantā*), but there would also be the undesirable consequence of using "Caitra goes" (*caitre gacchati*).

Even if the meaning of a verbal suffix (ākhyāta) can only be construed with that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case, nevertheless, if one intends to construe the *kṛti* (volitional effort) with firewood (*kāṣṭha*) and so forth by way of its objecthood (*viṣayatā*), then expressions such as "Caitra cooks the firewood" (*caitre pacati kāṣṭham*) would be unavoidable. Furthermore, in cases such as "The eater is satisfied" (*bhoktā tṛpyati*), one might simply assume a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *kṛti* in the agent. Therefore, it must be stated that the very experience of non-differential construction (*abhedānvaya*) is the proof for the agent being the primary denotation (*śakti*) of verbal suffixes; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of abolishing the specific denotative power [of the suffix].

Furthermore, since non-difference (abheda) is observed in constructions such as "Devadatta cooks for a kalpa" (*pacati kalpaṃ devadattaḥ*)—which is logical according to your own position—and since there is an experience of grammatical connection (*anvaya*) in cases such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), it follows that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) also expresses the agent (*kartṛ*); otherwise, the theory of a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) [of the verb] would result in its total abolition. Thus, the fact that the verbal suffix denotes the agent is established.

As for the claim that "in the expression *nāmārthayoḥ* (of the name and the object), 'name-ness' (*nāmatva*) is not defined by the technical terminology of grammarians, but rather consists in having meaning while occurring prior to a case-ending (*sup*); and thus, since there is no case-ending after a *tiṅ*-suffix, there is no fault," that is not correct. Because a case-ending does exist after the suffix *ām*, in forms such as *pācayāmāsa*, it would follow that the action (*kṛti*) could not be construed with the agent through a relation of identity; furthermore, if the *liṭ* following *ām* were to denote the substratum (*dharmī*), then the construction of non-difference between the *ām*-ending and the *tiṅ*-ending would be impossible.

Furthermore, if this were the case, in expressions such as *chatrī* (an umbrella-bearer), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of an identity relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). If, however, the determination of the relation between meanings is based solely on the force of grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*), then what is established is not what is desired [by you]. Nor can it be argued that in words like *kalpa*, etc., there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the agent; for in cases like *pācaka* (a cook) as well, the form would be accounted for through indication alone [of the nominal suffix]. Moreover, just as in *ācāryakalpau* (two who are almost teachers), if one intended to express the duality of the agent, there would be the undesirable consequence of a dual ending in *pacati kalpam* (he cooks almost); and because if one were to employ indication at will regarding a meaning taught by grammatical rules, the word would incur the status of being ungrammatical (*asādhutā*).

Furthermore, if there were *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) regarding the agent in that case, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that one could say "he goes having cooked" (*pacati kalpaṃ gacchati*), just as one says "the cooker goes" (*pakṭā gacchati*). As for the claim that in the passive construction (*karmākhyāta*) the fruit is the meaning of the middle voice suffix (*ātmanepada*), that is not tenable; for since the meaning of the verbal root itself can be accounted for by merely reversing the relationship between qualifier and qualified, it is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for the suffix. Let the middle voice suffixes such as *yag* and others simply serve as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) in those instances.

Furthermore, in the view of the Neo-Naiyāyikas, since *kṛti* (effort) is not the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) there, the answer "it is cooked" (*pacyate*) would be untenable in response to the question "What is being done? (*kiṃ kriyate*), which lacks a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*). This is because, for you, the root *kṛñ* has the sense of effort (*yatna*). Nor can effort itself be the meaning of the verbal suffix there; for since its status as the qualificand of the root-meaning is already established, it could not be construed [as the subject]. Moreover, if one accepts the rule of expression based solely on the denotation of effort, then the third case would fail to apply to the agent (*kartṛ*). However, if effort were the meaning of the root, then what is established is not what is desired.

Furthermore, according to the older view, since the connection with time is accepted as part of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) in cases such as *karoti* ("he does"), whereas in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks") it is connected to the meaning of the suffix (*ākhyātārtha*), a disparity arises. For me, however, there is no such fault, because in all instances the connection is with the verbal root-meaning alone.

By this, the argument that your theory involves a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) composed of two words (root and suffix) because time connects to the root-meaning, while our theory is simpler because it connects to the suffix-meaning alone, is refuted; for even in your view, that [connection to the root] is necessary in order to account for the temporal connection in expressions such as *bhūtaṃ pakvaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the rice was cooked").

Furthermore, if the connection with time were applied to the *kṛti* (volitional effort), then when one sees rice being cooked after having performed an activity conducive to the kindling of wood and so forth in the kitchen, there would be no fault in saying "Devadatta cooks" even while he stands inactive; for according to my view, there is no such defect, because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—an activity consisting in staying in the kitchen characterized by its subsistence in a locus that possesses an activity conducive to the softening of the substance to be cooked—is indeed present. This is the general direction of the argument.

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an activity (*vyāpāra*) conducive to an activity delimited by a result; the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is an activity consisting of volition (*kṛti*) and so forth, and this [activity] exists solely as an activity (*vyāpāratva*). Thus, in cases such as *jānāti* ("he knows"), there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the activity consisting of volition and so forth must be denoted by the verbal suffix itself (*tiṅ*), both because of the arguments advanced by the Naiyāyikas and because of the requirement of its being the primary qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). As for the connection with time (*kāla*), it occurs either with the activity that is the meaning of the root, or with the activity that is the meaning of the verbal suffix.

Agency (*kartṛtva*) consists precisely in being the substratum of the operation that constitutes the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha-vyāpāra*), while objecthood (*karmatva*) consists in being the substratum of the result (*phala*) of that operation. The phrase "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*) means "when the agent and so forth have not been conveyed"; and this conveyance occurs either through direct denotation (*śakti*) or through implication (*ākṣepa*). [Note: In the Mīmāṃsā system, *ākṣepa* refers to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), whereby something is postulated because without it, another thing would be inexplicable.]

Just as in the case of the statement, "This Devadatta is fat, yet he does not eat during the day," eating is postulated because [his] corpulence—which would otherwise be inexplicable without eating—is incompatible with the absence of eating; and since that [eating during the day] is sublated, the conclusion rests upon eating at night. Likewise, in the present case, because the mental state (*bhāvanā*) is inexplicable without an agent, it postulates a substratum in the form of an agent. Thus, the cognition of this inexplicability is *ākṣepa* (implication), which is another name for *arthāpatti* (presumption).
The cognition produced by that is also designated by that same name as a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramiti*).

In the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), *ākṣepa* (implication) is inference (*anumāna*). For example, the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth—which generates the inference: "The mental impression (*bhāvanā*) must reside in something, because it is a quality (*guṇatva*)," or "It must have an agent, because it is an effect (*kāryatva*), like a jar"—is called *ākṣepa*. Thus, after the cognition of the *bhāvanā* through implication, the agent is understood either by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or by inference. Since the Mīmāṃsakas accept that even what is obtained through implication can be an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), its appearance in the verbal cognition produced by a verb (*ākhyāta*) is not contradictory.
Similarly, since an action (*phala*) is otherwise inexplicable without its own substratum, the substratum is implied by it.

Is it not the case that, since the presence of word-meanings (*padārtha*) produced by words through their *vṛtti* (direct denotative function) is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is impossible for what is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) to be a cause of verbal cognition? Furthermore, there would be the impossibility of that cognition being established by experience even for those devoid of the knowledge of "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) and so forth; moreover, there would be the impossibility of the number associated with the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha-saṅkhyā*) applying to the implied [agent], because it is not presented by the word through its *vṛtti*. And thus it is said: "Verbal expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is indeed satisfied by a word alone."

"It is fulfilled" means: verbal expectancy (*śābdī ākāṅkṣā*), which consists of a desire for knowledge, is fulfilled—that is, it is removed—by the word itself, through the establishment of the object by means of the presentation of the word-meanings via their respective functions (*vṛtti*). This is the intended meaning. Therefore, he says: "either by indication (*lakṣaṇayā*)," or "by indication. In that regard, [it is fulfilled] in the case of a *kṛt*-suffix by its primary denotative power (*śakti*), and in the case of a *tiṅ*-suffix either by implication (*ākṣepa*) or by indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nor could it be argued that the opposite is the case, because [the agent] is perceived as being predominant. Since it is established that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is denoted by the suffix, it is logical that the agent is implied by it in the case of a *tiṅ*-suffix; however, if the agent were obtainable through implication in the case of a *kṛt*-suffix, then—just as in the case of a *tiṅ*-suffix—it would follow that the agent is not predominant. Furthermore, because it is perceived as predominant, its status as the expressed meaning [of the suffix] is established.

Due to the impossibility of the numerical concordance and the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and because of the mention of the grammatical subject (*dharmin*) in rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* [Pāṇini 3.4.69], it is determined that there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the agent and so forth. And only by taking the indicated agent is the coreferentiality in sentences such as *devadattaḥ pacati* ("Devadatta cooks") logically established. They maintain, however, that the grammatical rule *laḥ karmaṇi* and others are indeed rules concerning the indicated meaning.

Although this too has already been refuted by the previously mentioned objections, nevertheless, some other points will also be stated. For instance: the implication [of the object] is not tenable because it contradicts the experience that "I am hearing [the word]."

Furthermore, if implication (*ākṣepa*) were the regulator for denoting [the agent], then since we observe the analysis of forms such as *pacyate* (it is cooked) as *pākaḥ kriyate* (cooking is being done), it would be necessary that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) be directly expressed (*vācyatva*). And since that [activity] is untenable without a substratum, the agent could be obtained through implication; however, if [the agent] were not denoted, the use of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) would be improper. Nor can it be argued that while there is a basis for resorting to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of an agent-suffix due to the force of its being prescribed for the agent, there is no evidence for either implication or indication in the case of an object-suffix.

It must be stated that the expectation for a substratum (*āśraya*) is satisfied by words such as "Caitra" and so forth; even so, since in your view the individual (*vyakti*) possesses primacy because it is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), it is not logical to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) based on that primacy. Otherwise, if the individual were also [directly] denoted, there would be the undesirable consequence of the abolition of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the class-form). Furthermore, if the individual were not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there would be no syntactic connection with actions such as carrying or milking.

Nor can it be argued that the substance is the qualificand because it is understood as the object to be delimited (*paricchedyatayā*), for then the agent implied in the verb (*ākhyāta*) would likewise have to be the qualificand.
Furthermore, the claim that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the primary factor is contradicted in cases such as *ajā* (goat) and *chāga* (goat), where it is not so.
