Moreover, let there be an implication (*ākṣepa*) of the agent by the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) itself; let there be no need for the productive energy to be the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*) [of the suffix]. If it is argued: "It is logical that the agent is implied by the productive energy, but the agent does not imply it [in turn], because in the case of object-suffixes (*karman-pratyaya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the productive energy not being perceived"—we say no. This is because the object (*karman*) also connects with the productive energy, and thus it too implies it. Furthermore, you yourself must accept this very principle in order to account for the implication [of the agent] in the case of object-reflexive verbs (*karmakartr-kṛt*).

For this very reason, there occurs the linguistic usage: "What is to be done is the cooking; what has been done is the cooked," and so forth, as well as "he cooked the cooked. Nor is it the case that the agent is the expressed meaning of the *kṛt* suffixes simply because of the grammatical rule "the *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67); for the rule "the *la*-suffixes [denote] the object" (3.4.69) applies to *tiṅ* suffixes as well, and it is precisely for that reason that the mention of the "agent" is carried over (*anuvartate*) into that context. Furthermore, this rule is not intended merely to establish a conventional secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), because if it were, the same consequence would apply to the rule "the *kṛt* suffixes [denote] the agent" (3.4.67).

If it is argued that, since the rules "laḥ karmaṇi ca," "tiptasjhi," and "dvayekayoḥ" function as a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā) as injunctions, the sense that "when the singularity residing in the agent is to be expressed, the singular suffix *ti* and so forth are to be employed in place of *la*" implies—by the very force of the meaning—that the status of the agent being the expressed meaning (*vācyatā*) follows from the sūtra, we say: no.

Since designations such as *jhi* and so forth reside in the substitutes (*ādeśa*), even if there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between those rules and rules such as "for two or one" (*dvayekayoḥ*), the term "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) is absent therein; consequently, it is impossible for that [designation] to function as a qualifier of singularity and so on. If it is argued that there is also syntactic unity between the rule for *la* (*lavidhi*) and the rules for suffixes (*taddhitavidhi*) and so forth, [we reply]: yes, there is, but that is syntactic unity at the level of the sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*), not syntactic unity at the level of the word (*padaikavākyatā*). This is because the rule for the substitutes operates by way of restating the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) obtained through the rule for *la*.

And likewise, at the time of understanding the meaning of its own sentence (*svavākyārtha*), since singularity and so forth are not present, how could there be a qualification by them [of the agent]? Nor should it be argued that because [the agent] is connected to the meaning of the intermediate sentence (*antaravākyārtha*), it is also qualified by singularity and so forth at the time of the unity of that single sentence (*tadekavākyatā*), for there is no evidence (*māna*) for such a repetition (*āvṛtti*).

Now, one might object: in the rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the term *laḥ* ends in the suffix *ṅas*; the genitive case is used in relation to the substitutes (*ādeśa*), meaning "that which is the substitute for *la*" is...

If it is argued that there is no fault because the meaning follows the sequence beginning with "action" (*karman*) and so forth, and the *la*-suffix is prescribed by the rule itself—"*laṭ* for the present" (Pāṇini 3.2.123)—we reply: no; for in that case, the *la*-suffix would either be meaningless or a denoter of time alone. Consequently, the agent, object, and so forth would not be the expressed meanings (*vācya*) of the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes. Furthermore, as a result, the *śānac* suffix would not occur in forms such as *āsyamāne* (in the sense of the abstract state, *bhāva*) or *gataḥ* (in the sense of the object, *karman*), where it is actually employed.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the grammatical rule *kartari kṛt* [Pāṇini 3.4.67], only the agent (*kartṛ*) is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of the suffixes *śānac* and others, whereas the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) are merely indicated (*lakṣaṇā*). For if one were to resort to indication based on mere whim by transgressing the scriptures, the result would be grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutā*). Furthermore, by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* [Pāṇini 3.2.124], since the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed as forming part of a single syntactical unit with those suffixes that prescribe the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the active voice (*parasmaipada*), the absence of such a prescriptive status would mean that, due to the lack of expressive power in the primary sense (*vṛtti*), the meaning of that [suffix] would not be specified.

Furthermore, there is no fault because the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* [Pāṇini 3.4.69] forms a single syntactical unit (*vākyaikavākyatā*) with the rule prescribing the substitutes *am* and so on; thus, by the word *luk*, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *am* suffix which is co-occurrent (*sahacarita*) with it. Even so, if it were in the nominative plural (*jas*), the connection would be with what is directly heard (*śruta*); however, if it were in the genitive, one would have to supply (*adhyāhārya*) the word "substitute. Moreover, according to the method already stated, in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* [3.4.69], the substitutes themselves are also the things to be restated (*anuvādya*). And these are prescribed by the rule *tiptasjhi* [3.4.78] under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "of *la*" (*lasya*).

And thus, since only a complete sentence possesses the capacity to justify what is to be restated (anuvādya) and serves as the cause for the cognition of the meaning of a great sentence (mahāvākya), it follows that—given its status as a single syntactical unit—the activity [of grammatical rules] regarding the specification of particular words and persons is constant; however, the current activity [of applying case-endings] is now baseless, because the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are devoid of designations such as the dual number and the like.

Furthermore, the further application [of the rule] is redundant, because the denotability of singularity and so forth is already established through the syntactic unity of rules such as *tip-tas-ḍhi* [Pāṇini 3.4.78] and *dvyekayoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.22]. Nor is the result of this [repetition] simply the establishment of the Mīmāṃsaka position by not teaching a verbal power (*śakti*) in the agent and so forth; for there would be a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*), wherein the establishment of the position depends on the further application, and the further application depends on the establishment of the position. Moreover, a further application is undesirable due to the presence of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, even if one accepts the meaning "in the case of singularity [residing] in the agent," the denotability of the agent and so forth remains difficult to avoid, since they enter [into the meaning] as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Nor can it be argued that their status as denotable is avoided because they are obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for in various instances, since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) would otherwise be inexplicable, it is more appropriate to assume secondary indication precisely with respect to the agent and so forth as qualified by singularity and the like, which would result in that [singularity] also not being denotable. Moreover, since number functions as a delimiter, it is proper that it be a qualifier alone—as in "in a single agent. And thus, the presence of a primary power (*śakti*) with respect to the substantive (*dharmin*) is unavoidable.

Furthermore, just as the capacity for the substratum (*dharmin*) is understood through the rules prescribing *śatṛ* and other suffixes—such as "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" [Pāṇini 3.4.69] and "śeṣāt" [Pāṇini 3.1.76]—by virtue of their forming a single syntactical unit with those rules, so too is it logical that this occurs through a single syntactical unit with the rules prescribing *tiṅ* suffixes, since there is no reason for such a discrepancy.

Moreover, if according to your method the absence of capacity in the substratum were established by the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), then the capacity of *tiṅ* suffixes for denoting a property (*dharma*) would also not be established, due to the lack of such an instruction. If that [capacity for properties] were established even without such an instruction, then rules such as "kartari kṛt" [Pāṇini 3.4.67] would result in being rendered useless.

Furthermore, according to the theory that the genus (jāti) is the denotatum, just as the genus is a qualifier of the substance implied by it in expressions such as "the pot" (*ghaṭam*), so too would the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) become a qualifier of the object implied by it; this would result in the failure to obtain a cognition in which the efficient force is the primary element, yet such a cognition is accepted even by you. Moreover, to postulate a separate linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) for this case would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, even if the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of Devadatta and the like with a denoted agent were to be established, then derivative terms such as *piṅgākṣī* ("tawny-eyed") would also fail to denote a substance, since their coreferentiality could be accounted for by means of a substance merely implied [by the word]. To illustrate: it is an established fact of experience that from the word *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer"), there arises the cognition "one who possesses a connection with a staff."

In this regard, according to the grammatical rule "The suffix *matup* is used in the sense of possession when it means 'this belongs to him' or 'this is in him'" (Pāṇini 5.2.94), and because the genitive case-meaning is seen to be predominant in the analysis (*vigraha*) of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the relation itself would constitute the expressive power (*śakti*). And by that which is implied by it, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established.

And so, here there arises a doubt: should the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) be introduced as a qualifier (*prakāra*) by breaking the sentence, or should it be connected with the act of buying (*krīṇāti*)? In this doubt, [the opponent argues that] it is connected with "buying"; because of that connection, it would belong to the context of buying. However, since it is not possible for an incorporeal thing to be connected with that [act], it has no connection with buying; therefore, it must be introduced into a separate context—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The established position (*siddhāntapakṣa*), however, is as follows: since it is appropriate for words to be included in a context when they relate to proximate referents, and because words such as *piṅgākṣī* denote substances, it is easy for them to relate to that [substance]; thus, by means of that [substance], they also obtain a relation with the meaning of the verb "to buy" (*krīṇāti*), and therefore they constitute part of the sentence itself. But this is untenable, because derivative words (*yaugika*) such as *piṅgākṣī*, according to the reasoning already stated, have "relation" as their primary meaning and do not denote a substance through them.

Furthermore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is also untenable. Since the relationship between the meanings of the words *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old) is likewise incorporeal (*amūrta*), it cannot serve as an instrument for the act of purchasing; thus, this [quality of] redness cannot be obtained from this sentence as an instrument for purchasing. Moreover, since there is a suspicion of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) regarding the redness itself, the very foundation of the argument is weak. Finally, because the application of the *bahuvrīhi* compound and the word *aruṇa* (red) to the injunction of a substance characterized by indication (*lākṣaṇika*) is indistinguishable, there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) to establish that the *bahuvrīhi* compound alone is the injunction of the substance and not the word *aruṇa*.

In the sentence, "He purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow," because no substance is explicitly mentioned, there would arise the undesirable consequence of nullifying the *aruṇādhikaraṇa* (the section on the red cow), which establishes that the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) must be construed only with the substance mentioned within its own sentence.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault in the view of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because even in the view of implication (*ākṣepa*), according to the theory that the word's power resides in the genus (*jāti*), although the individual (*vyakti*) is not directly presented by the primary function (*vṛtti*) of the stem, one can still maintain that it is included in the sentence because it is the object of a presentation brought about by that function; and thus, just as the meaning of the suffix is construed there, it can be said that the implied [individual] is also "contained within its own sentence. Even so, if a substance were introduced through indication, then since the word *aruṇa* (red) would also be indicative of the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), the matter would be resolved solely by the introduction of the substance belonging to that word, making the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the substance is introduced by the sentence clearly untenable.

For me, however, because the requirement for further specification is satisfied by the substance itself presented through its own power (*śakti*), there is no scope for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even in the word *aruṇa*; thus, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established. Furthermore, if this were the case, it would entail the destruction of the theory of qualified potency (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*). Nor can this be accepted on the grounds of the principle of the section on generic form (*ākṛti-adhikaraṇa*), for if the point were already established by that alone, the separate commencement of the section on the agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*) would be rendered redundant.

Furthermore, since from words such as "jar" there arises a determinate cognition of that which is qualified by "jarness," it is impossible for "jarness" to be the object of verbal cognition if it is not the object of the word's denotative function (*vṛtti*). Therefore, when the postulation of a denotative function for that portion [of the meaning] becomes necessary, the implication of the substance (*dravyākṣepa*) is logical, because the rule "that which has not grasped the qualifier [cannot grasp the qualified]" prevents the establishment of the word's denotation being restricted to that [quality] alone. Nor does it follow that, because the implied [substance] is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix-meaning and so forth not connecting with it; for there is no fault here, as the criterion in that case is simply the presence of an understanding brought about by the denotative function (*vṛtti*). This, however, is not the case in instances such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*).

If it is argued that here too, because there is the cognition "related to a staff," the relation must be the denoted meaning (*vācya*), the relation is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and the property of being a relation (*sambandhatva*) is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the delimitors of denotability; and thus, even in this case, the relation itself—standing in the place of "pot-ness"—must be the denoted meaning, we say: no.

For, out of fear of defects such as infinity (*anantya*) regarding the genus (*jāti*), concomitance (*anvaya*) is accepted by the logic of "not grasping the qualifier" (*anāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*). Even if there were a power residing in the relation (*sambandhaśakti*), since that [genus] remains in the same state, there would be no distinction from the position of the individual (*vyaktipakṣa*). Nor, even if there were a power in the relation, could there be a focus on the operation (*vyāpāra*), because this general definition of the verb (*ākhyāta*) would result in the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) to the verb expressing existence (*bhāvākhyāta*); for you yourself must accept that in cases such as *caitreṇa supyate* ("Caitra sleeps"), the meaning of the verbal root alone is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*).

Furthermore, since the answer "it is cooked" (pakvam) is seen in response to the question "what was done? (kiṃ kṛtam), and since explanations such as "one who has cooked" (pakvavān) and so forth are seen to mean "one who has performed the act of cooking" (pākaṃ kṛtavān) and so forth, and since it is observed to be distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), the efficient force (bhāvanā) must also be denoted by the suffix (kṛt). Moreover, according to your own position, that [efficient force] would result in being the primary meaning, because it is the meaning of the suffix.

If the agent and the object are obtained there [in the case of *kṛt* suffixes] through implication (*ākṣepa*), then they would likewise be so in the case of verbal endings (*tiṅ*) as well; thus, the difference between the two is difficult to justify. Nor can it be argued that the agent is denoted by the verbal ending because gender and number are seen to be coreferential with what is indicated by a *kṛt* suffix—for if that were so, the agent would have to be denoted by the verbal ending too for the sake of coreference with number, since coreference with gender and number is possible even through an implied element, as in "the pot" (*ghaṭam*), and because the designation of "kṛt" as a "great term" (*mahāsaṃjñā*) for both *kṛt* and *tiṅ* suffixes indicates their equality.

Furthermore, if the factors of action (*kāraka*) were to be construed with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix, then you would have to state that the relation in the case of the construction of factors such as "in the pot" (*sthālyām*) is their being the producer of the softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice grains residing in themselves; for me, however, the relation is simply "residing in what resides in itself" (*svavṛttivṛttitva*), and thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*). Likewise...

It is not possible to establish, by its own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*), that wood and the like function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of becoming (*bhāvanā*) through effort. However, if their connection to the act of becoming is mediated by their being the instrument—by virtue of generating the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—then the principle applies: "When the cause of that [cause] itself [is sufficient], what is the use of that [intermediate cause]? This principle is rooted in parsimony (*lāghava*). The term *taddhetunyāya* refers to the maxim of the cause of that which is itself a cause (*tasya* = the cause; *hetuḥ* = cause; *taddhetuḥ* = the cause of that; and *nyāyaḥ* = the maxim). Thus, it is the maxim of the cause of that cause.

The distilled meaning is that once a task is accomplished by a cause already established for it, to postulate an additional cause for that same cause is fruitless. For example, when simplicity dictates that the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*) alone is postulated as the cause of completion, it would be cumbersome to further postulate the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)—which produces the destruction of obstacles—as the cause.

Thus, because there is a unifying factor through the relation characterized as a *upalakṣaṇa* (an incidental indicator), defects such as infinite regress do not arise; for it is more appropriate to grasp the power (*śakti*) as residing in the related object itself, having that [relation] as its indirect indicator.

Nor can it be argued that the denotative power (śakti) resides in the relation itself; for while [the property of] being present in the intellect appears in the cognition produced by words such as *tad* (that), it does not appear in the cognition produced by words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer). Furthermore, it is established by experience that from words like *nīla* (blue), one perceives the possessor of the quality blue precisely through the universal "blueness" (*nīlatva*). Thus, the view that the power resides solely in the universal residing in the quality is logically consistent.

And so, it should be understood that the application of the principle of the *Akṛtyadhikaraṇa* occurs only where a certain thing invariably appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by a word and possesses a recurring nature (*anugatatva*); only there is the coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) maintained through that which is implied, and not elsewhere.

Regarding the position that "the capacity (*śakti*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*)," we have no fault. For when there is the cognition of an agent, an object, and so forth, the agency (*kartṛtva*) and other such properties—which are of the nature of indivisible adjuncts (*akhaṇḍopādhi*)—necessarily appear as qualifiers (*prakāra*). Since the capacity is established precisely therein, the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is accounted for by what is implied by that [capacity]; or rather, its accounting is due to the non-difference between the capacity and that which possesses the capacity (*śaktimat*), as it is clearly stated in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on *Pāṇini* 3.1.67 (*sārvadhātuke yak*) that "by the word *karman*, the capacity itself is expressed as having attained non-difference from that which possesses the capacity."

Therefore, by the arguments stated previously, even *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is indeed denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Furthermore, the general rule that "the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is primary" must be set aside on the strength of the experience of the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and others. Moreover, if this were so, there would be a contradiction with the *Nirukta* and other texts stating that "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning"; for in those contexts, it is more appropriate to connect the word "action" (*kriyā*) with the meaning of the verbal root, according to the principle that the meaning of the suffix is subordinate. Furthermore, there would result an inconsistency with rules such as Pāṇini’s *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [2.3.65], *karaṇe yajaḥ* [3.2.85], and *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* [2.3.32]. Enough of this.

Now, if the agent (*kartṛ*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), then consider the prohibition recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. For there, a doubt arises as to whether this prohibition is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) or for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). In that case, the determination that the suffix denotes the agent is reached through the cognition of the agent from the verbal suffix in the word *vaded* ("one should speak"), and because the grammatical rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) establishes that the suffix has reference to the agent. Furthermore, from that very rule, one obtains the fact that the suffix is directed toward the agent.

Since speaking is primary as the object of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*), speaking is first of all for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, the prohibition is also for the sake of the person. This is because the word "one should speak" (*vadet*), by restating the act of speaking as the counter-positive of the prohibition, conveys it precisely as being for the sake of the person; and since the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys that such speaking—namely, the speaking of untruth—is a means to an undesirable result (*aniṣṭasādhana*) by indicating its contrary nature, while no other kind of speaking of untruth is presented [by the sentence].

For this very reason, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in holding that this same [Vedic] source also serves as the basis for the Smṛti prohibition of speaking while facing north—which was studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*). Otherwise, one would incur the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) by having to postulate another, distinct human-purpose-based prohibition as its source. Thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), according to the maxim "the meaning of a word must not be obtainable through any other means," the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) alone is denoted by the verbal suffix; the agent (*kartṛ*), however, being invariably concomitant with the efficient force denoted by the suffix, is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), and therefore the suffix has no expressive power (*śakti*) regarding it.

The traditional rule (smṛti) beginning with "laḥ karmaṇi" is also intended solely to express that number [of the agent], as it forms a single syntactical unit with the rule "dvayekayoḥ. Furthermore, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks," grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of "the cow is white"; thus, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) does not denote the agent. Consequently, since the agent is not presented by direct audition (*śruti*), he does not serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*); rather, it has been determined in the *Kartradhikaraṇa* that the agent serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) based on the context (*prakaraṇa*).

If it were argued that the prohibition "one shall not speak untruth" would fail to establish its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), because there is the consequence—based on direct statement (*śruti*)—that it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); and that its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice is established through context (*prakaraṇa*), which is clearly weaker than direct statement—[we reply: No, for the aforementioned conclusion holds if the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted [by the verbal suffix]. And if that conclusion holds, then the denotation of that [agent] follows in accordance with it; thus, [the argument] is seized by the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

Furthermore, even if the agent is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), this [act of yawning] shall be a duty for the person associated with the sacrifice (*kratuyuktapuruṣadharma*) by virtue of both direct statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*). Otherwise, your own established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that the sentence concerning one who yawns (*jañjabhyamāna-vākya*) has the purpose of the sacrifice by way of being a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) through both syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)—would be destroyed. As it was said by the Bhaṭṭas:

"Even though the consumption of meat obtained from women and so forth is heard as being for the sake of the person, its prohibition is accepted as a subsidiary of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) because it relies upon the context."*

Furthermore, even if the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted [by the verbal suffix], because the action (*kriyā*) alone is primary and the agent is subordinate, the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of speaking untruth does not have the person as its purpose. And thus, when the productive urge has a requirement for its purpose (*kaimarthyākāṅkṣā*), it can be said—just as you maintain—that it serves solely the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) on account of the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, in the case of a *kṛt* suffix, since the agent is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the action serves the purpose of the sacrifice only by way of being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that agent.

Furthermore, since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is what is denoted by the verbal suffix, and according to your own view the agent is implied by it, then—given that the agent implied by the *bhāvanā* presented by the direct statement (*śruti*) is apprehended prior to the meaning presented by the context (*prakaraṇa*)—the fact that [the act] is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) would not be established. Thus it is proven that the substratum (*āśraya*), or the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*), is the expressed meaning of the agentive or objective case endings (*kartṛ-karma-ṭiṅ*). And this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "gatyarthaloṭā" (Pāṇini 8.1.51).

In this context, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which is the result—is generally a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*) that constitutes the meaning of the suffix; the agent (*kāraka*), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*), is a qualifier of the verbal root's meaning, as is tense (*kāla*); however, number (*saṅkhyā*) is a qualifier of that which is conjoined with the meaning of the verbal suffix. If it is asked where the substratum (*āśraya*) is conjoined—in the result or in the operation?—on this point they say: the affixes *taṅ*, *yak*, *ciṇ*, and so forth, indicate the conjoining of the substratum with the result, while *śap*, *śnam*, and so forth, indicate it with the operation.

In reality, context and other factors alone are the indicators [of the agent], because we observe the opposite in the case of the agent and the object. Nor does the cognition of the agent arise twice—once from the force of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) regarding the *tiṅ* suffixes and *śatṛ* etc., and again from the suffix itself—since it is accepted that *śatṛ* and the others are merely indicators (*dyotaka*).

It might be argued: "The predominance of the substratum (*āśraya*) is appropriate, because in a cognition where the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—distinct from time—is the qualifier (*prakāra*), the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case. This is not so; for, on grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), the cause of a cognition where the meaning of the verbal suffix is the qualifier is simply the mental presence generated by the verbal root (*dhātu*). As for the application of number (*saṅkhyā*), it occurs in the very substratum of the meaning of the verbal suffix, due to the scriptural rule of coreferentiality (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*). Furthermore, any additional causal relation you would have to postulate for the application of time is equivalent to what we [postulate].
However, even your two proposed relations of cause and effect are cumbersome because they consist of distinct terms, whereas mine is concise because it consists of only one.

Furthermore, since the temporal relation in expressions such as "he does" (*karoti*) and "he knows" (*jānāti*) also pertains to the meaning of the verbal root itself, that too must necessarily be included in your view, resulting in extreme prolixity.

Furthermore, your proposed causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because, in cases such as "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is construed with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Moreover, there is a deviation from the rule that number (*saṅkhyā*) is construed only with that which is construed with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), since in that very same instance, the number is construed with Caitra himself. Nor should it be argued that in instances involving the co-occurrence with particles (*nipāta*), a separate causal relation must be postulated for number and productive urge; for that would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) due to the assumption of multiple causal relations.

Furthermore, in cases such as "caitreṇa supyate" (it is slept by Caitra), there would be the undesirable consequence of having to supply a word ending in the nominative case even in the impersonal passive construction (*bhāvākhyāta*); and if one were to provide the qualification "being distinct from that which has the meaning of an action," the resulting complexity would be even greater.

Furthermore, this contradicts Yāska’s statement that "a verb has action as its primary meaning" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*), and it also contradicts the statement recorded in the Bhāṣya to the same effect: "it has action as its primary meaning. The meaning of that [Yāska's] statement is that, in relation to the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*) is primary. Nor should it be argued that primacy indeed exists in relation to the meaning of the root, because by the etymology "that which brings about" (*bhāvayati*), even the word *bhāva* denotes only the efficient force (*kṛti*); for such an argument would result in the definition being over-exclusive (*avyāpti*) with respect to those verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) whose meaning is the action itself (*bhāvārthaka*).

Furthermore, for you, the sentence "Look, the deer runs" would be impossible; however, for me, there is no fault because [the deer] is the object (*karman*) of the action of running. Nor does this contradict your own tenet that the action is primary when it serves as a qualifier of the act of seeing, because the primacy of the action is understood in relation to the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-ghaṭaka-pratyaya-artha*) through proximity, and because the supplementary statement "nouns have substance as their primary referent" (*sattva-pradhānāni nāmāni*) indicates precisely the absence of being a qualifier of the denoted meaning of a word that expresses substance (*sattva-vācaka*).

This is because [the view] is understood from the statement "action is primary" (*kriyāpradhānam*). In this context, since the representation produced by words (*śabdajanyopasthiti*) alone is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is merely a relation (*saṃsarga*). For you, however, in such a case, the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) established in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts would be undermined. Nor can there be an anvaya of the deer itself as the object in the act of seeing, because a direct anvaya by way of difference between the meaning of a nominal stem and the meaning of a verbal root is impossible without mediating through the meaning of an inflectional ending (*vibhaktyartha*). Nor can a second-case ending (*dvitīyā*) be introduced after that [deer], for even so, the aforementioned sentence would remain unestablished.

Furthermore, due to the absence of a presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case, it would follow that the word *dhāvati* cannot function as an adjective qualifying "deer.

Moreover, in the case of non-nominative coreferentiality (*aprathamā-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the suffixes *śatṛ* and others, thereby subverting the application of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Nor can it be argued that the verbal suffix applies here by the rule of alternative forms (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), because it has been established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that this rule does not apply to substitutes for *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*). Finally, one cannot claim that the nominative itself is expressly prescribed here to signify the object (*karmatva*), for no such express statement (*vacana*) is found.

Nor can there be a syntactic connection by supplying the words "and look at that deer which is running," because this would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), and because it is precisely the act of running with intensity that is intended to be presented as the object of the act of seeing.

Nor can there be an application of the qualified sentence-meaning (*viśiṣṭa-vākyārtha*) as the object (*karmatā*) in relation to the act of seeing (*darśana*), for if that were so, there would be no contradiction with linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), since such usage pertains only to the meaning of nominal stems (*nāmartha*). Furthermore, one should not argue that the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not arise because the word expressing the qualified entity is not a nominal stem (*apratipadikatva*); for even in your own view, the qualified entity is not something distinct [from its constituents]. For this very reason, even when one intends to express that a jar qualified by "blue" is the object of the act of seeing, the accusative case is established in expressions such as "I know the blue jar" (*nīlaṃ ghaṭaṃ jānāmi*).

Furthermore, [if the agent were defined as] "the effort conducive to the arising of the object of the act of cooking whose agent is Devadatta," then the sentences "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*) and "Do you cook? (*karoṣi*) would not be possible, because the action conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is unfit to be referred back by a pronoun; thus, there is no way to resolve this even through the method of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

Furthermore, regarding the meaning "the act of cooking occurs," there is no fault in the expression *pacati bhavati* ("he cooks [and] exists"), whereas there is a fault in *pacati vajrati* ("he cooks [and] strikes with a thunderbolt"). Nor should it be argued: "Since such understanding and such grasp of expressive power (*śakti*) exist for those who are proficient in those respective ways, how can there be faults? For even though understanding arises in accordance with proficiency, correctness (*sādhutva*) must still be established for such a meaning;

and since correctness is constituted by the meaning itself, it is said here that this [correctness] applies only to that meaning which is accepted by grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) who are intent on defining that specific sense, and not elsewhere.

Nor should it be argued that there is no contingency of the rule *na caivamedhām* because it is not a verbal form (*tiṅanta*), since its primary element is the root; for the *liṭ* suffix is expressive, and in the absence of any other suitable factor, the root itself becomes primary by virtue of being the inherent meaning (*svārthika*). Consequently, it is that very root which possesses primacy. [Note: In some instances, the term *ākhyāta* refers to the root. For this reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *nāmākhyātopasarganipātāḥ*, it is mentioned as the base (*prakṛti*). And for this same reason, Śākaṭāyana stated: "Nouns are derived from verbs" (*nāmānyākhyātajāni*).]

In the rule *ākhyātamākhyātena kriyāsātatye*, according to this view, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a *tiṅ*-ending word whose base is a verbal root (*ākhyātaprakṛtika*). In the statement *bhāvapradhānamākhyātam* as well, according to this view, there is a metaphorical indication for a *tiṅ*-ending word whose base is a verbal root; furthermore, in the phrase *bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*, the word *ākhyāta* should be understood as referring to the verbal root (*dhātu*).

The author of the *Śabdaratna*, however, intends by the term *ākhyāta* the inclusion of that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix. On the authority of the *Nirukta*, in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), sometimes there is the inclusion of that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix, and sometimes there is the inclusion of the verbal root (*dhātu*) by the term *ākhyāta*. Therefore, the statement of the logicians (*tārkika*) that "by the term *ākhyāta* there is the inclusion of *tiṅ*s" is indeed to be disregarded. If, however, by the term *ākhyāta* one includes forms ending in *la* (the *l*-suffixes) excluding those replaced by *kṛt* suffixes, then there is no suspicion of a fault at all; for since such forms lack suffixes denoting a substance (*sattva*), the rule "those whose primary meaning is a substance" (*sattvapradhānāni*) does not apply to them.

Furthermore, it has been determined elsewhere that because there is no decisive factor for distinction, both verbal falsehood and factual falsehood are prohibited by the statement "one should not speak untruth," which is taught as a general rule (anārabhyādhīta) and also occurs within the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Furthermore, since the authors of the *Sūtras*, *Vārttikas*, and *Bhāṣyas*—who determine what constitutes correct usage (*sādhutva*)—have stated that verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are correct only when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), one must consider this: how could the Mīmāṃsakas and others, who employ them in Vedic rituals for the sake of the meaning of "efficient force" (*bhāvanā*) while transgressing that rule, not incur sin as if using a dative case in the sense of a genitive? Or how is it that the sacrifice remains unimpaired? Nor is this grammatical instruction baseless; for its source is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating: "The Veda with its six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is to be studied and understood by a Brahmin as a duty without ulterior motive."
The great treatise of Pāṇini, which defines the correctness of words and is beneficial to all, should be accepted in its entirety; not even a single syllable should be discarded.

This is also evident from the *Parāśarīya Purāṇa*. However, because Jaimini and others lack any underlying intent (*tātparya*) regarding this matter, their statements do not determine correctness. As it has been said: "This very tradition of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*) has as its object the knowledge of correctness. Furthermore, that grammar serves to apprehend linguistic capacity (*śakti*) has been stated by the elders in such passages as: "The apprehension of capacity [is derived] from grammar, comparison," and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that if these [words] were incorrect (*asādhutva*), there would be no comprehension of their respective meanings for those speakers; for even if they are in fact incorrect, a cognition of them as such can arise through error, since the knowledge of correctness is not a necessary cause of comprehension, and the certainty of incorrectness does not constitute an obstacle to comprehension. This is the general direction of the argument.

Furthermore, if the understanding has the word ending in the nominative case as its primary qualificand (viśeṣya), then there would be the undesirable consequence that, just as "the rice is cooked" and "Caitra is a cooker" serve as answers to the questions "What kind of rice? and "What kind of Caitra?", respectively, the answers "it is being cooked" (pacyate) and "he cooks" (pacati) would likewise be appropriate.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "see, the deer runs," "he cooks," or "it exists," the action would not possess the nature of a non-substance (*asattva*) when it is construed as the agenthood, objecthood, or other [roles] of the agent; for its status as a non-substance follows either from the mere fact of being construed as a *kāraka* other than the agent or object, or from being construed as a *kāraka* that is not the locus of the action, or from the admission that objecthood and so forth do not function as qualifiers (*prakāra*).

Nor should it be argued that even so, since what is unestablished cannot be an agent of seeing, how can running be the object of seeing; for although the aggregate as a whole may be unestablished, its status as an object of perception is established because its constituent parts are established.

But even so, in cases such as *roditīva paṭhati* ("he reads as if weeping"), since there exists a relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between two actions, the status of being a locus for a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—as defined by Kaiyaṭa and others in the commentary on the rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.115)—is present; thus, the claim that it is of the nature of non-existence (*asattvarūpatā*) is undermined. Nor should it be argued that because the word *iva* is heard after a suffix, a comparison between the meanings of the verbal roots is difficult to establish; for when *iva* is heard after a finite verb ending (*tiṅanta*), the comparison between their meanings is easily established.

If it is argued that, in this case, let there be a relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between the agents alone, since such a relationship is impossible because the agent functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the action (*kriyā*), we say no; for the word *iva* when uttered in conjunction with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) lacks the capacity to signify similarity (*sādṛśya*).

As stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "There is indeed no comparison with a finite verb; rather, the word *iva* there has the sense of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)," so says Kaiyaṭa. For this very reason, even the theorists of poetics (*alaṅkārikas*) have cited verses such as "Darkness, as if it were smearing the limbs," as examples of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) alone.

Others maintain that the very nature of the non-existence (*asattva*) of an action consists in its being unfit for reference by a pronoun (*sarvanāma*). Now, one might object: even in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in the sentence "Devadatta cooks somewhat" (*pacati kalpaṃ devadattaḥ*) is difficult to establish; for although the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the substratum (*dharmin*), the cognition produced has the action as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), which contradicts the [required] identity [of the agent]. Furthermore, if it is argued that a distinct relation (*bheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns is unestablished [in grammar], we say no; because for us, the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) does not relate to Devadatta, since it is the primary qualificand of the verbal suffix.

Nor can Devadatta [be connected] with that [effort], because there is no evidence for its connection due to the absence of a case-ending denoting an agent (*kāraka*), and because the requirement for the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) regarding that portion is satisfied by its connection with the substratum (*āśraya*), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). However, since the substratum of the verbal suffix possesses a requirement for a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) through identity (*abheda*), it is more appropriate for Devadatta to connect with that very substratum. Thus, the principle "of the two nominal meanings" means that the connection between the two things qualified by the cognitions produced by the respective nouns occurs precisely through identity; it does not mean that there is a connection of identity between those two [nominal meanings] themselves, and therefore there is no fault.

If it is argued that even so, according to your view, in cases such as *pacati bhavati* ("he cooks, he is"), two *tiṅ*-affixes are obtained within a single sentence; therefore, since the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* in the rule *tiṅṅatiṅa* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) is necessary to exclude such instances, this contradicts the Bhāṣya which rejects that rule—[we reply: no, for the intention of the Bhāṣya is that although worldly (*laukika*) oneness of sentence exists, the technical definition provided by Pāṇini himself, namely "a sentence consists of one *tiṅ*," does not apply here.

And regarding "being a single syntactical unit in common worldly usage" (*laukikaikavākyatva*): Yādava stated, "A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of *sup*- and *tiṅ*-endings, or it is an action (*kriyā*) connected with its factors (*kāraka*). Here, the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, the meaning is: a collection of *sup*- and *tiṅ*-endings that expresses an action connected with its factors. By the term *suptiṅ*, both *sup* and *tiṅ* are included; through the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), all three types of collections—those ending in *sup*, those ending in *tiṅ*, and those consisting of both—are obtained. By the phrase "or an action," meaningless clusters of words are excluded.

As for the claim that, by the force of the word "or" (*vā*), the meaning (*artha*) also possesses the status of a sentence (*vākyatva*), that is not correct; for the term "sentence" (*vākya*) is not applied to the meaning, and because of the prohibition in the rule "vaco’śabdasaṃjñāyām" [Pāṇini 7.3.67], the substitution of *kutva* would not occur. This is the general direction of the argument.

Thus it is established that, in consideration of the substratum of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the primary element. And so, in the case of "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), the cognition is: "an action conducive to cooking, having Devadatta as its single agent. However, in the passive construction "The rice is cooked by Caitra" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacyate caitreṇa*), the ancient scholars maintain that the cognition has the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as its qualificand, specifically: "the present productive activity conducive to that softening (*viklitti*) which has a single Caitra as its substratum and a single rice-grain as its non-differentiated substratum."

The Navyas (modern grammarians), however, maintain that in cases such as "uncooked rice" (*apakvastanḍulaḥ*), where there is co-occurrence with a kṛt-affix denoting the object, the understanding necessarily involves a reversal of the roles of the result and the operation; therefore, even in the case of an ākhyāta (finite verb) denoting the object, the cognition has the result as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For this very reason, there is no abandonment of the rule established everywhere—that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) must be connected directly to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) as its qualificand. This relation of being connected may be either as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatayā*) or as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*).

For this very reason, when the suffix *lakāra* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), the resulting cognition does not have the fruit (*phala*) as its qualificand, because that would entail the violation of the previously stated established rule. For this same reason, there is no such usage as *putrīyati* in the sense of "he desires a son" (*iṣyate putraḥ*), because the meanings are distinct; rather, it occurs only in the sense of "he desires a son" (*putram icchati*).

A suffix denoting the object (*karman*) after a root ending in *kyac* is difficult to obtain because such roots are intransitive; this is clear from the rule *sup ātmanaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.8]. For here—regarding the examples *iṣṭaḥ putraḥ* ("the son is desired") and *iṣyate putraḥ* ("the son is being desired")—if *kyac* occurs, then since *kyac* expresses only the mere act of desiring, a suffix must necessarily arise to express the object by means of a word signifying that object.

The doubt as to how the suffix *pratyaya* can arise in the sense of the object (*karman*) from a desiderative form ending in *kyac*—such as when one intends to express the agent by saying "he desires a son" (*putrīyati*)—is raised by the words: "In this case, [the suffix] *kyac* ought to occur, as in the expressions 'the desired son' (*iṣṭaḥ putraḥ*) or 'the son is desired' (*iṣyate putraḥ*)," and so forth.

When the intention is to convey that the object (*karman*) of the fruit of the action is primary, then a full sentence alone is employed—such as "the son is desired" (*iṣṭaḥ putraḥ*) and so on—and not a form ending in *kyac*, because the latter is intransitive (*akarmaka*) and thus no suffix can arise in the sense of an object; with this intention, he offers the resolution: "First, some say: 'It should not be [so],' and so forth. Furthermore, later on: "There must be a sentence with the same meaning as that which ends in a suffix; and whatever meaning is understood here by the sentence..."

The intended meaning [of the *Bhāṣya*] is that the *vivaraṇa* (the explanatory gloss) and the *vivriyamāṇa* (that which is being explained) possess identical meanings. However, due to the diversity of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*), time (*kāla*) is construed with the entire meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Consequently, it is refuted [by this view] that if the operation (*vyāpāra*) has ceased while the softening (*viklitti*) still exists, one would have to say "it is being cooked" (*pacyate*) rather than "it was cooked" (*apāci*); likewise, it is refuted that in a state such as blowing air onto the rice when the softening has not yet begun, one would not be able to say "it is being cooked" (*pacyate*).

Regarding this, they say: when the desired result has been produced and all the operations that bring it about have ceased, there is "pastness"; when such a totality of operations delimited by the result is yet to come, there is "futureness"; and as long as the action that brings about the desired result has not reached its completion, there is "presentness"—these points we shall explain immediately below.

In the case of the *bhāvalakāra* (the passive/imperfective aspect), the verbal activity (*vyāpāra*) alone is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Since we observe that in forms ending in *kta* and the like, there is a mutual connection between two activities through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is no evidence for abandoning the general rule that the fruit resides in the activity as the qualificand. In the case of finite verb endings (*tiṅ*), they merely restate the meaning of the verbal root; however, they certainly possess the function of indicating time (*kāla*). Number (*saṅkhyā*), on the other hand, is simply not present there, because neither an agent nor an object—which would be the locus for the application of number—is perceived.

Furthermore, the meaning of the verbal root itself is inherently incapable of being conjoined with number, for if it were, expressions such as "by Maitra it is stayed" (*maitreṇa sthīyate*) or "it is slept" (*supyate*) would result in the unintended implication of plurality.

And thus, in the absence of number, the singular alone is used as the general rule (*utsarga*). Neither the middle nor the first person endings occur, because there is an absence of *yuṣmad* and so forth which would share the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Regarding the examples "uṣṭrāsikā āsyante" (camel-sittings are being sat) and "hataśāyikāḥ śapyante" (corpse-lying is being lain), they state that the plural is correct precisely because of the usage found in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "sārvadhātuke yak" [Pāṇini 3.1.67]. And in cases such as "ākāśo'sti" (space exists), the meaning is understood through a process such as: "the present activity conducive to maintaining its own nature, having as its locus a single space non-different from itself"—this is the direction of the argument.
Now, the manner of the syntactic connection (anvaya) of the meanings of the verbal suffixes, such as presentness and so forth, and their definitions are stated.

In that context, the connection of [tenses such as] the present and so forth is with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and not with the agent or the object; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using *pacati* ("he cooks") even when the action has passed, and the non-occurrence (*anāpatti*) of *apākṣīt* ("he cooked"). This is because the rules such as *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123), which mean "the suffix *laṭ* occurs after a verbal root denoting a present action," teach that the connection is indeed with the meaning of the verbal root itself. And it has already been stated that this [connection] is with the entire operation (*vyāpāra*) of the verbal root's meaning. Nor is there any contradiction in the case of one whose body is rendered inert by a rheumatic seizure (*āmavāta*).

And it has already been stated that this [activity] consists in the operation of the complete meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence of using the expression "he rises" (*uttiṣṭhati*) in the case of one whose body is rendered inert by rheumatism (*āmavāta*), simply because an effort conducive to rising exists; for although that effort is directed toward the purpose of rising, it lacks the status of being the actual cause (*prayojaka*) of the rising. For this very reason, in such a case, the only usage is: "He exerts himself for the sake of rising, but he does not rise."

In order to exclude [the application of] terms such as ‘yajati’ (he sacrifices) and ‘pacati’ (he cooks) when one undertakes efforts like purchasing a sacrificial pit or a mandala with the aim of performing a sacrifice or cooking—just as one says ‘yatate’ (he exerts himself) for the sake of a sacrifice—it must be accepted that the relation [denoted by the verbal suffix] is specifically that of being an instigator (*prayojakatā*). Likewise, in order to exclude [the application of] terms such as ‘gacchati’ (he goes), it must be accepted that the relation is specifically that of being an instigator. Thus, in order to exclude [the application of] terms such as ‘gacchati’, it must be accepted that the relation is specifically that of being an instigator.

Thus, in cases such as "he goes" (*gacchati*), there is a connection [of the agent] with the meaning of the verbal root, which consists of an action conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location. In "it perishes" (*naśyati*) as well, there is a connection with the meaning of the verbal root, which consists of the causal complex for destruction accompanied by its counter-positive. Therefore, when that complex exists, "it perishes" (*naśyati*) is appropriate; when it has passed away, "it has perished" (*naṣṭaḥ*) and so forth are justified.

However, some say that since destruction is also counted among the six modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*), like origination, it too is simply the relation to the final moment; thus, while it exists, "it perishes," and upon its cessation, "it has perished."

In the expressions ‘*naśyati*’ (is perishing), ‘*naṅkṣyati*’ (will perish), and ‘*naṣṭaḥ*’ (has perished), the present, future, and past occurrences of origination (*utpatti*), as well as counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*), are indicated by the suffixes in their respective order. Thus, the comprehension occurs in such a sequence as "the counter-positive of the non-destruction of such an origination," and so forth. For this very reason, since destruction is eternal, the modern Naiyāyikas maintain that there is no contingency of [the absurd conclusion] that "it is always perishing," "it will perish tomorrow" in the case of a cloth, or "it will perish the day after tomorrow," or "it perished yesterday" in the case of what perished on the previous day.

Non-existence (*nāśatva*) consists in being an absence that possesses origination (*utpattimat*). Thus, according to the Neo-Naiyāyikas (*tannavyatarāḥ*), the temporal relation (*kālānvaya*) occurs only with respect to "origination" (*utpatti*), which is precisely what is delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Furthermore, it is clear in other systems (*tantrāntara*) that time is nothing other than action (*kriyārūpa*); it is not an additional entity (*atirikta*), because there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*) and because such a view involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the *Vākyapadīya*, which states: "Time serves to differentiate actions, whereas number is the differentiator of everything. For it cannot be said that a thing can possess its own delimiting factor; rather, in that context, the word "time" intends only the "presentness" (*vartamānatva*) and so forth inherent in that [action].
Or, according to the view that "time is an additional category" (atirikta), [it is expressed by the suffix].

Some also hold that there is a relationship consisting of the delimitation of one person's action by another person's action. And since time is thus expressed by the verbal root (dhātu), its properties such as presentness and so forth are indicated (dyotya) by the *laṭ* and other suffixes; and "indicative function" (*dyotakatva*) consists in the capacity to impart a specific power (*śakti*). Furthermore, this [indicative function] is the delimitation of a power belonging to a word that possesses multiple powers, through the proximity of the suffix itself. But surely, let it be denoted (*vācya*) rather than indicated; for many roots have [the power to denote] that [time].

Because it would entail the fault of theoretical complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a separate denotative power (*śakti*), it is more appropriate to postulate the power for the single suffix *laṭ* alone.

Furthermore, even though the rule "the suffix *laṭ* is used in the sense of the present" (Pāṇini 3.2.123) is a specific injunction, if *laṭ* lacked denotative power there, the agent (*kartṛ*) would likewise not be denoted; rather, it would be merely indicated (*dyotya*), as there would be no distinction between the two cases.

Moreover, one would have to assert that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with *laṭ* is the cause for the cognition of an action qualified by presentness. In that case, since the principle is the same, let it simply be said that *laṭ* is the denoter (*vācaka*).

Nor can it be said that there is a distinction in expressibility between the particular and the universal. [Note: It should be understood here that according to the *takra-nyāya*, where there is a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*) between the objectivities (*viṣayatā*) of the cognitions produced by two accepted scriptures standing in the relation of sublated and sublator (*bādhya-bādhakatva*), there is a restriction (*saṅkoca*) of the objectivity of the sublated scripture upon that which is distinct from the locus of the objectivity of the sublator scripture.]

And thus—the nature of the *nyāya* (maxim) is as follows: there is a restriction (*saṅkoca*) of the universal property delimited by the collection of sentences intended for application to a single effect, by means of its being distinct from that which is delimited by the particular property delimited by the same collection of sentences. In this case, there is a restriction of the universal property "Brahmin-ness" delimited by the collection of sentences, by means of its being distinct from that which is delimited by the particular property "Kauṇḍinya-ness."

And thus, according to the *takra-koṇḍinya* maxim, the gift of curd is not more complete or superior to the gift of buttermilk intended for Kauṇḍinya; this is the general direction. If it is argued that, by the logic of *takra-koṇḍinya*, when there is sublation (*bādha*), the agenthood itself should not be expressed because the rule *saḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) would then have no scope (*niravakāśatva*), we say: no; for that rule finds its application in cases such as *māṅi luṅ* (3.3.175) and *laṭ sme* (3.2.118). Furthermore, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for multiple substitutes of *laṭ* derived from a single verbal root.
Therefore, [the agent] is merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

In this context, "presentness" (*vartamānatva*) consists in having begun but not yet completed, or alternatively, being distinct from the past and the future. "Pastness" (*bhūtatva*) is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a presently existing destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). "Futurity" (*bhaviṣyatva*) is the state of having an origination at a time that is the counter-positive of a presently existing prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). However, if prior non-existence is not accepted, it is the state of having an origination at a time that is the locus of the destruction of the time which is the locus for the employment of the word. And this [presentness] is construed with the action (*kriyā*), which is of the nature of a collection of operations (*vyāpāra*).

However, it is not tenable to claim that the grammatical connection (anvaya) occurs only with the operations of the individual parts [of the action]. For if that were the case, since the constituent parts would exist for only three moments, such a connection would be impossible therein; consequently, the very application of the term *pacati* ("he cooks") would find no objective basis. Even in the expression *pañcakṛtvaḥ pacati* ("he cooks five times"), the connection of [temporal] presentness and so forth occurs with respect to the entire collection of cooking acts—which are counted as repetitions and unified by the result, such as excessive satisfaction.

However, in cases such as *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta has begun the mat"), the use of the past tense occurs either by superimposing the form of the whole upon the part, or by superimposing the pastness residing in the part upon the whole; this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 3.2.102).

It should not be argued that such linguistic conventions as "the self does not exist," "the mountains stand," "they will stand," and "they stood" would be untenable—on the grounds that since an action has not yet begun, there is no presentness as previously defined, and consequently, neither pastness nor futurity could exist. This objection is invalid because, by taking the actions of the kings belonging to those respective times, the aforementioned presentness and so forth are possible for the existence of the self as qualified by those actions. Thus, statements such as "Nārāyaṇa alone existed" are justified.
This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on Pāṇini’s rule *vartamāne laṭ* (3.2.123).

Thus, the *liṭ* suffix [is prescribed] after verbal roots whose meaning is an action (*kriyā*) that is past (*bhūta*), non-contemporary (*anadyatana*), and beyond the perception (*parokṣa*) [of the speaker]. In the cognition produced by a sentence such as "he cooked" (*papāca*), there arises no doubt regarding its being past; therefore, just like the property of being past (*bhūtatva*), the property of being non-contemporary (*anadyatanatva*) and so forth are also objects of that cognition. Furthermore, "being beyond perception" (*parokṣatva*) consists in not being an object of either the speaker's direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) or the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced thereby. [Objection: But here, the qualification "beyond perception" (*parokṣe*) is inconsistent. For an action (*kriyā*) is a collection [of parts] denoted as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena abhidhīyamāna*), whose constituent parts are subordinate (*guṇabhūtāvayava*), and which is grasped by a single unifying cognition (*ekabuddhi*) consisting in the production of a single result from successive operations (*kramikavyāpāra*). [Response: [This is not so. Action is indeed such a collection. However, it is not perceived directly by the speaker because it is composed of parts that are themselves imperceptible. Consequently, since the speaker lacks direct perception of the action, the condition of being "beyond perception" is satisfied. Thus, the qualification is entirely appropriate.

In that regard, although the individual parts (*avayava*) are indeed directly perceived—and for this very reason, in expressions such as "see, the deer is running," the action [of running] functions as the object of the act of seeing—nevertheless, because the parts lack conjunction, the entire aggregate remains imperceptible and thus fails to function as a differentiator. As it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*:

If it is argued that this action (*kriyā*) is absolutely imperceptible and cannot be demonstrated as a concrete entity, and therefore it must be known through inference alone, we say no; for what is intended here is the invisibility (*pārokṣya*) of the means (*sādhana*) when they are endowed with the power conducive to that [action] and are engaged in its operation. Consequently, the perfective suffix *liṭ* occurs even when there is perception of the mere means not yet engaged in the action, as in "he cooked" (*papāca*).

Thus, when one is engaged in one's own activity and, due to distraction or other causes, does not personally recollect it, yet it becomes known through inference from its various effects or by the testimony of a friend and so forth, the *liṭ* (perfect tense) indeed occurs. For example: "I was indeed told much by my mother in his presence," and "Udayana spread forth a garland of rays"—these are justified by superimposing the states of being past, non-recent, and extraneous, according to the method stated in the *bhāṣya* on the rule *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 3.2.102].

The "fruit of the superimposition," however, is understood as the ease of composition and the swiftness of completion regarding this treatise. That fruit, moreover, is simply the delight of those students of that time—his own disciples—who, eager to understand this work, find its result to be the discernment of meaning and so forth. Furthermore, the superimposition of transcendence has precisely this as its fruit.

Thus, by making known that what cannot be personally realized even by oneself during the time of diligent practice can be accomplished through subtle effort, the composition of the treatise itself is suggested as being effortless. The simile of the sun serves only to nourish this point. Furthermore, the distinction of this treatise from other works, and of its author from other authors, is also suggested. They also say that since the actual capacity to protect [beings] will exist at the time of future application, there is no need for superimposition (āropa) regarding that aspect.

Some, however, claim that remoteness (*pārokṣya*) belongs only to the action (*kriyā*), and not to every action being remote; thus, they argue that [the definition] is non-exclusive because [an action] is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) in its constituent parts. Yet, it is not the case that each part lacks the nature of action (*kriyātva*), for even by that much, there would be no loss of its status as the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*); moreover, the nature of action is common to both the parts and the whole.

Furthermore, they say that if one assumes *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the word *dhātuḥ* [in Pāṇini’s rule *dhātoḥ*], there is complexity: if it indicates the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*), the relation is "being its own denotation" (*svavācyatva*); if it indicates the means (*sādhana*), the relation is "being the means denoted by itself" (*svavācyasādhanatva*). Moreover, it is precisely because [the action] resides in the constituent parts [of the agent] that Devadatta’s status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) and so forth is logically consistent.

Regarding "non-immediate time" (*anadyatanatva*): the present day (*adyatana*) is the period consisting of the latter half of the past night and the former half of the coming night; non-immediacy is simply being different from that. Thus, *luṭ* is used for the future that is not immediate, while *lṛṭ* is used for the general future, and so on—this should be understood from the force of the respective grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) and from linguistic usage.
Now, something is said regarding the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as prescribed in the context of injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth.

Among these: *vidhi* (injunction) is instigation, as in the case of a lowly servant and the like; *nimantraṇa* (invitation) is the performance of a duty, the impelling toward a necessary act such as eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony; *āmantraṇa* (request) is permission to act according to one's own will; *adhīṣṭa* (authorization) is an activity preceded by respect. The common factor of instigation (*pravartanā*) that runs through these four is the meaning of the optative suffix. The separate mention of the four in the rule concerning injunctions (*vidhyādi-sūtra*) is for the sake of clarity. The property of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*) is the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Since the portion exceeding that [the meaning of the verbal root] is characterized by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it does not constitute the denotable capacity (*śakyatva*) [of the word].

Nor is the inclusion of "commanding" (*preṣa*) and so forth in the rule *preṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca* [Pāṇini 3.3.163] redundant; for its necessity is established in order to prevent the occurrence of the *kṛtya* suffixes in cases such as "invitation" (*nimantraṇa*). The prescription of the *loṭ* suffix is for the purpose of expressing "proper time" (*prāptakāla*). Furthermore, instigation (*pravartanā*) is an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to the basic action (*prakṛti*), consisting of the speaker's intention. And that [intention] takes the form of a specific desire (*icchā*), because, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the specific universal (*vaijātya*) residing in the desire serves as the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

For this very reason, *prārthanā* (request) is mentioned separately. Although the desire of the speaker (*vaktricchā*) exists in that case, it does not invariably function as an instigator; therefore, it is necessary to include a distinct category (*vaijātya*) here. Furthermore, in common worldly usage, this desire resides in a person, whereas in the Veda, it resides solely in God (*Īśvara*), according to the Bhāṣya: "God does not command, nor do the authors of the Dharmasūtras recite [such commands]. Thus, the Veda is indeed the command of God.
And being an instigator consists precisely in being the utterer of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which convey such a meaning, provided one possesses independence (*svātantrya*).

As for the claim that the very fact of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is the verbal operation (*vyāpāra*), because it has been established that the knowledge of being a means to a desired end is the cause of all activity, it is appropriate that this alone should be the denoted meaning. Furthermore, what is desired is sometimes direct [to the agent] and sometimes indirect. For this reason, the conventional usage of saying "I bring the cow because I am impelled by my teacher" is consistent; the usage "I teach because of your prompting, not because of anything I myself desire" is intended to mean "nothing is directly desired by me."

And being an instigator (*pravartakatva*) consists precisely in being the utterer of an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or the like that causes the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), which in turn generates activity. It should not be argued that this would result in the absurdity that a foot soldier (*padāti*) commanded by a king would be an instigator [of action] simply by virtue of being the utterer of such an optative suffix; nor should it be said that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for it would contradict common usage, as one would not say, "I am not doing this because I was urged by the foot soldier, but because I was urged by the king. This objection is invalid because of the qualification "provided there is independence" (*svātantrye sati*). Even in the case of a queen who is urged by a sycophant, independence still exists.

Even when teaching children and others who have been urged by a teacher or superior through force, the desired result is simply the absence of beating caused by the anger of the teacher or superior, which would otherwise arise from that [teaching].

Although in rules such as *svaritajitaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.72], by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the word "fruit of action" (*kriyāphala*) refers only to that fruit which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), nevertheless, there is no evidence for such a restriction here. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the cognition of something being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is not the motivator, because one does not act toward what is a means to an undesired end or toward what is indifferent due to aversion, according to the maxim "action is painful. For if that were so, it would follow that one would act during a state where aversion toward the intermediate labor has ceased, or during a state where that [undesirability] is not cognized.

Nor should it be argued that there is no undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) even when there is a desire to act, because such a desire does not exist at all without the cognition that [the action] is a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatvajñāna). Thus, being a means to a desired end is precisely what is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*). And this is only as a means to [results] such as heaven; for it is only the cognition of it in that form which is the motivator. It is not, however, as "being desired," because that [desirability] is a cause by its very existence (*svarūpasat*) and thus does not depend on its being known; furthermore, in the case of actions to be accomplished through great expenditure of wealth and effort, or those whose results are in the hereafter, there is no engagement without specifically knowing [them to be means to a desired end].

In this regard, it should be understood that in order to avoid the fault of having multiple referents (*nānārthatva*), there is an inclusive intention (*anugamikecchā*) regarding the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), just as in the case of the word *tad* (‘that’). For instance, the apprehension of the denotative power (*śaktigraha*) of words like *tad* is as follows: the word *tad* is denotative of those things possessing jar-ness, cloth-ness, and so forth—which are presented [to consciousness] under the form of being objects of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*)—provided they possess the delimiter of being an object of cognition. Here, being an object of cognition serves merely as an inclusive indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of presentation; there is no denotative power in that specific aspect. Similarly here, the apprehension of the denotative power of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others is simply that they are denotative of the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*), just as [the word ‘heaven’] is denotative of heaven-ness (*svargatva*) and other such delimiters of being an object of desire (*icchāviṣayatāvacchedaka*).

Nor does, by that much alone, a cognition or a desire for that [object] enter into the initial stage [of the verbal comprehension]. Even when the word-meaning is presented, it is first made an object of cognition by means of its delimitor (avacchedaka)—such as "pot-ness" in the case of a pot—through the power of the context and so forth; likewise here, by the power of the co-occurring word "svarga," it is understood as a means to heaven and the like, but neither the cognition nor the desire itself appears in the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
