And thus, since the verbal comprehension arises under the mode of "heaven-ness" and so forth—which is the specific delimitor of the desired—the production of the motivating knowledge from an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*) is secured.

And thus, it follows that the power (*śakti*) of the injunction (*vidhi*) resides in the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*) characterized by such properties as "heaven-ness" (*svargatva*), which are themselves delimited by the objectivity of desire (*icchāviṣayatāvacchedakatva*).

Nor can it be argued that there is no power in this [state of being a means] because it is already obtained from words such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*); for even though heaven and the like are presented by the word ending in "-kāma," there is no factor there that makes known the state of being a means, and furthermore, in cases such as the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, there is not even the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of such a word. It is another matter altogether that, although the state of being a means to a desired end is known in a general sense, the specific terms are postulated later when there arises a desire to know the particular details.

However, the cognition that [an action] is followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitvajñāna*) is not what motivates activity; for otherwise, activity would never arise toward an action that must be accomplished through great effort, since even greater suffering arises in such cases. Furthermore, it is difficult to state a consistent criterion for "powerfulness," as even a small amount of suffering may become powerful due to some circumstance. Nor does this lead to the absurdity of engaging in activities such as eating food mixed with honey and poison, because a powerful aversion toward those specific objects acts as an independent inhibitor.
For this very reason, one who possesses intense aversion toward the intermediate labor does not engage in [rites] such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, whereas another indeed engages in them.

By this, the view that the knowledge of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvajñāna*) is the motivator is refuted. Furthermore, there is an absence of engagement in grasping the lunar orb and the like because they cannot be achieved through effort; this is due to aversion arising from the fact that, in the absence of a desired object, such acts produce useless labor. Moreover, since it would follow that even one incapable of acting would engage in whatever can be achieved by some effort, the motivator must be stated as being qualified by the element of "my" (*mama*).

And thus, because it cannot be made known in that way by the Veda, it is not [known] through that [Veda]. Furthermore, since its apprehension is possible even through worldly means of knowledge in the form of inference—such as "Sacrifice is achievable by my effort, because it does not possess a property incompatible with being achievable by my effort"—and because it is obtainable through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) in the form "Let sacrifice be achievable by my effort" is established precisely through the understanding of that [fact] from the world.

If the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) were the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), then in such cases as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) would not occur, because that case is prescribed only when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not already expressed. Nor can it be argued that even though the status of being a means inherent in the root-meaning of *yaj* (to sacrifice) is expressed, the instrumental case is established because the status of being a means inherent in the specific object—the Jyotiṣṭoma—is not expressed; for there is no difference between the Jyotiṣṭoma and the root-meaning of *yaj*. For this very reason, in expressions such as "Devadatta cooks," the instrumental case does not occur after the word "Devadatta" either.

If it is argued that even by those who maintain that the term *anabhihite* means "when number is not expressed," the meaning must necessarily be stated as "when neither the object nor its number is expressed"—in order to ensure consistency with all instances of the *kṛt* suffixes—otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the accusative] would apply even to [the word] *pacanīyasya* (of the one to be cooked) when used with *alpa-* (little); [we reply: no, because even though the status of being a "means" (*sādhanatva*) common to both that which possesses activity and that which lacks activity is expressed, there is no fault since the power of causality (*kāraṇatva-śakti*) and its substratum are not expressed.

[Objection: Even so, it must be understood that the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice is the means for that which is qualified by the property of being heaven (*svargatva*); yet this is not possible. Since properties such as *svargatva* are common to the heavens produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā, the *vājapeya* sacrifice, and so forth, they cannot serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the state of being produced from the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Consequently, the status of being the means for that which is qualified by *svargatva* and so on is sublated (*bādha*) in the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, because a property that is not a delimiter of the state of being produced cannot function as a qualifier in the definition of the state of being a producer (*janakatva*), due to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [Response: This is not so.

There is no fault, because the injunction (*vidhi*) conveys precisely the status of being the means for various [specific] heterogeneous results. This heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) arises from the acceptance of such a capacity on the part of the injunction. It is for this very purpose that it has been stated that the injunction possesses a power (*śakti*) regarding the status of being the means for those respective results.

Thus, since the "task-ness" (*kāryatva*)—defined as possessing a property that delimits the task—is difficult to grasp when its delimiting factor is not apprehended, the postulation of heterogeneity is made; and it should be understood that the power of the verbal root *vid* resides in that which is qualified by it.

Alternatively, the state of being heaven (*svargatva*) itself may be the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the effect; for there is no fault in something that is over-pervasive (*atiprasakta*) serving as a delimiting property. If it is objected: "In that case, since even that which is delimited by the state of being heaven would not arise from the *Agnihotra* sacrifice due to the absence of a cause in the form of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, such an outcome would follow [if it were the cause]; and even if it did arise, then—just like a donkey in relation to a jar—the *Agnihotra* and so forth would be subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), leading to the undesirable conclusion that they are not causes; likewise, color and other qualities would also arise in substances and so on. Therefore, being heaven is not an over-pervasive delimiting property," we reply: No.

There is no fault, because the property of being heaven (*svargatva*) serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) in each respective injunction by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) qualified by the *apūrva* produced by the *agnihotra* and other such rites.

In this way, even in the case of grass and the like, grass-ness (*tṛmatva*) is the cause with respect to fire-ness (*vahnitva*) by means of the relation of conjunction delimited by possession of grass; thus, there is no need to postulate a distinct universal (*vaijātya*) in that case either. For this very reason, in injunctions such as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), there is no fault even though each [substance] produces the result individually through mutual exclusion. This is because the delimiting factor for the causal efficacy of the rice (*vrīhikāryatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the relation to time delimited by the transcendental merit (*apūrva*) arising from the resolve (*saṅkalpa*) that "one must sacrifice with rice. Thus, there is no fault.

Furthermore, since the *apūrva* of the fruit arises from the *apūrva* of the ritual intention (*saṅkalpa*), it is not untenable that once [the barley] has perished, other materials such as barley are employed in a subsequent performance.

Nor does this lead to the absurd conclusion that even a donkey is a cause of a jar; for while the causal status of barley and the like is established through perception aided by positive and negative concomitance—namely, that when grass and the like are present in a collection lacking fire-sticks or gems, the jar is produced, and when they are absent, it is not produced—there is no evidence for the donkey’s causality. Rather, its status as a cause is merely "otherwise explained" (*anyathāsiddhi*) by the necessary postulation of the potter's stick and other such factors.

Likewise, there is no occurrence of color and so forth in qualities and the like; for since it is necessary that a substance be the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of its respective form, the absence of such [color] is established simply by the absence of the specific causal complex (sāmagrī).

By this, the argument of the Mīmāṃsakas is refuted: that if one does not accept a difference in nature (*vaijātya*) at the time of investigating a meaning obtainable through an injunction, then since the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and the *Agnihotra* would result in an equality of fruit, and since the *Agnihotra*—which is accomplished with less expenditure of wealth and effort—is already established, one might fail to engage in it due to aversion caused by its greater fatigue and so forth; consequently, there would arise a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) characterized by the non-performance of injunctions such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and *Aśvamedha*. For engagement is possible only for one who has a desire for the very fruit consisting of worldly status and the like.

For this very reason, Yudhiṣṭhira and others, who were conversant with all the scriptures, engaged in actions for the sake of a kingdom that yields only meager results and for the purpose of killing their own kinsmen, such as Brāhmaṇas. For this same reason, the engagement of modern people—even those who know the worthlessness of ritual action—in performing rites such as the Agnihotra, which are accomplished through great expense and effort, for the sake of worldly prestige, becomes intelligible.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are performed] for the sake of all desires," their obligatory nature means that through the very performance for a specific desire (*kāmyaprayoga*), the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) can be accomplished by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Consequently, out of a desire for parsimony in effort, one would not engage in rites such as the *Putreṣṭi*; thus, even for you, the futility of the *Putreṣṭi* and similar rites is unavoidable. Nor can this futility be avoided by claiming that for one who has established the sacred fires (*kṛtādhāna*) and is longing for a son, the performance of the *Putreṣṭi* and so on is authorized even prior to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Even so, the cessation of engagement in optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) on the new and full moon days—such as the *Māravadhū* offerings—would be unavoidable; nor is there a fixed rule based on the distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable regarding rituals that yield identical results. For this very reason it is said: "Whether one gives a thousand with the power [to give] a hundred, or a hundred with the power to give ten, or even ten with whatever power one has—if one gives according to one's capacity, all are remembered as having equal fruit."

If it is argued that [the injunction] "one should recite the *Bhārata*" is thus connected [to the result], then the same applies to my position as well. Therefore, it is read in the respective sections on vows: "One should not practice deceit regarding wealth.

Now, if it is objected that there is an inconsistency in the meaning of the prohibitive sentence "One should not eat *kalañja*," because since the eating of *kalañja* and so forth produces a desired result such as satisfaction, it is impossible to convey the non-existence of that [desirable result], we say: no; in such cases, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is "being a means to an undesirable end" (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*), and the negative particle (*nañ*) functions merely to indicate the intention toward that very meaning. Thus, there is no fault.

Alternatively, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is that the performance of the act together with [the negation] is a means to a desired end consisting in the absence of transgression (*pratyavāya*). This absence is conveyed by the negative particle (*nañ*). Furthermore, "being a means" consists in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): namely, that when this [act] exists, there is necessarily an absence of transgression, and when it is absent, there is necessarily a transgression. Thus, by implication, the transgression resulting from acts such as eating [forbidden food] is established; therefore, there is no fault.

In cases such as "one suffering from fever should not eat," however, the meaning of the injunction should be understood as being a means to a desired end consisting in the absence of an increase in suffering, and so forth.

Nor can it be argued that because permanent (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites lack a [desirable] fruit, the meaning [of the injunction] cannot be "the state of being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) in those cases; for even there, a fruit exists in the form of the avoidance of sin (*pratyavāya*). And activity toward such [rites] occurs precisely through the knowledge that they are means to a desired end, since by the force of the injunction, the sin that would otherwise accrue from their non-performance is necessarily avoided when they are performed. Nor should it be assumed that activity occurs toward something entirely fruitless simply because it is taught by the Veda; for even if something is taught by thousands of Vedas, one does not act toward it while in a state of knowing it to be fruitless. Nor—
That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits,
with the mind composed in the thought that "sacrifice must indeed be performed," is characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
This contradicts the words of the Blessed One [in Bhagavadgītā 17.11]:
"Knowledge, charity, and austerity—these threefold acts are purifiers for the wise. [Note: The reading of the Bhagavadgītā is "tapaścaiva" (and austerity as well).]
But even these actions, having abandoned attachment as well as the fruits, [should be performed].
"O Pārtha, it is my firm and supreme conviction that these [rites] must be performed. (Bhagavad Gītā 18.5–6).

This is because the Blessed Lord himself has declared their purifying nature in the eighteenth chapter. Therefore, even though the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*) was not explicitly mentioned as a result, the intention is that purification occurs when the rite is performed even while abandoning the desire for results.
"But those who constantly perform the *saṃdhyā* worship, being steadfast in their vows..."
With their sins shaken off, they go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Furthermore, because in some cases a fruit is heard of even though [the rite] is eternal.

If it is argued that this is merely a commendatory eulogy for the purpose of generating interest (*prarocanā*), and that such interest is for the sake of inciting human activity, we say no; for the desire for a fruit is satisfied by such texts as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa rites for the sake of all desires."

Furthermore, for one who knows that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) lacks authority, even engagement [with the ritual] would be untenable, just as it is for one who knows the lack of authority of a sentence such as "This cow yields much milk" regarding that very sentence. If it is argued that although there is a lack of authority regarding its having heaven and so forth as its object, it possesses authority with respect to the matter accepted—namely, its being a eulogy by way of conveying excellence (*prāśastya*)—we say no; for excellence is nowhere conceived as anything other than the capacity to produce that result. Moreover, the cognition of excellence through some other property would fail to be a motivator for action. Therefore, these [explanatory passages] possess authority only with respect to their own literal meaning.

And thus, although the desired end is understood from the injunction in such passages as "one should perform the twilight worship" (*saṃdhyām upāsīta*), the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves the purpose of a specific motivation—either by making known its intermediate form or by making known its swift production. For this very reason, the Bhaṭṭas stated in the *Sarvaśakti* section: "Just as that which is optional is taught for the sake of a fruit, so too is that which is obligatory. Therefore, they say that the meaning of an injunction is "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). That is not correct;

For in this way, since it would follow that a person could act toward one thing when it is actually the means to achieve something else they do not desire, it must be stated that the cognition of being a means to achieve what one desires (*madiṣṭasādhanatvajñāna*) is the motivator. And thus, just as [the property of] being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), this [property of] being capable [of being performed] (*śakyatā*) also cannot be said to be denotable [by the optative suffix].

Furthermore, if this were the case, there would arise the inconsistency of the following: [the objection] "Why does the causative suffix (*ṇic*) not occur in the sense of 'May your honor question me'?"—which is raised in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26)—and the subsequent resolution that "the imperative (*loṭ*) is used for instigation regarding a mere substance, whereas the causative (*ṇic*) is used for instigation regarding an action," and so forth. For no one accepts that the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is what is conveyed by the causative suffix. Therefore, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is simply the aforementioned instigation (*preraṇā*).

And thus, through the instigation by a reliable person (*āpta-pravartanā*), the fact of being something that makes known what was previously unknown (*ajñāta-jñāpyatva*) implies, as it were, its status as a means to the good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatva*); therefore, the cognition of it as a desired means (*iṣṭa-sādhanatva*) which prompts action is established. However, in some cases, due to the lack of co-utterance with terms such as "one who desires heaven" (*svarga-kāma*), that cognition is initially even mental; this is another matter. And is that instigation (*pravartanā*) expressed (*dyotya*) by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), or is it denoted (*vācya*)? Regarding the first [position], there is a logical justification: if that [instigation] were the meaning of the suffix, then injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth would be the denoters of meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and others, which already find their scope in other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).

And thus, in the case of "caitreṇa pacet" (Caitra should cook), is that which is indicated by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) the expressed meaning (*vācyā*) or not? Regarding this, in the first case [where it is the expressed meaning], there is a logical difficulty: if that [optative force] were the meaning of the suffix, then since meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth already have scope in other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*), injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like would become their expressers. And in that case, one would have to say "caitreṇa pacet," and dual endings and the like would not occur, nor would *śap* and the rest, nor would there be the fixed assignment of persons (*puruṣavyavasthā*). In the second case...

However, this argument is untenable because there is no contradiction, and because in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the plural marker *bahuvacana* is used to include all *lakāras*. Therefore, these [suffixes] do not exclude the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth; for since number requires a thing to be numbered (*saṅkhyeya*), it is necessary that they denote those [meanings]. Furthermore, because in the case of the present tense (*laṭ*) and others, there is a co-occurrence of [meanings] such as "present time" and "remoteness from the speaker's sight," the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* would otherwise be rendered without scope (*niravakāśa*).

Nor does [the rule] "māṅi luṅ" [Pāṇini 3.3.175] and others find scope among those [rules] prescribed for general time, because even there, since the denoted bhāvanā—which is the qualificand—is non-existent, it stands in need of time, and thus time is accepted as being directly expressed (vācya). For this very reason, its status as an exception to all verbal suffixes (lakāra) is logically consistent.

Nor should it be argued that "I would not invite you" is impossible because an invitation has already been stated; for one accepts that the two distinct acts of inviting, which reside in the instigator (*prayojaka*), constitute the meaning of the suffixes. In each such case, the view that [the suffix] is merely indicative (*dyotaka*) is superior, because in expressions such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), the instigation (*pravartanā*) is understood even without the suffix, and because in expressions such as *pañcabhir halaiḥ kṛṣati* ("he ploughs with five ploughs"), the instigation is seen to be the meaning of the verbal root itself.

And thus, in this context, the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is also the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because that too is conducive to the cooking (*pāka*) and so forth. Among the operations presented there, which are all conducive to the result, the operation of the instigator is construed as a qualifier by way of being the object (*viṣayitayā*), while the others are construed as the qualified (*viśeṣyatvena*) by way of being the [actual] object. Thus, in this twofold mode of relation, the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. serve to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Consequently, in such expressions as *pacet*, the understanding arises in the form: "an action conducive to cooking, which has a single locus and is the object of the instigation."

Nor should it be argued that, since the substratum of the instigation (*pravartanā*) is also the agent because it is the substratum of the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the *L* suffix would consequently apply to that agent; for prior to the production of the optative (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes, the instigation is not yet conveyed, and thus its substratum lacks the status of an agent. Consequently, the rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) does not apply with reference to it. Many scholars maintain that there is no fault here, as the two rules [Pāṇini 1.4.55 and 3.4.69] form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) through the optative suffixes and thereby enjoin the action.

Others, however, argue that since in cases such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook") the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) for the instigation (*pravartanā*) is already established, let it be the same here as well. Thus, the understanding is that the instigation has as its object an action conducive to cooking which has a single locus. Nor is there any fault in this, because under the view that the instigation is expressed by the suffix, there is no contradiction with the rule "the verb is primarily concerned with action," since this very [instigation] is understood as having the meaning of the verbal root as its qualificand.

Furthermore, they say that in cases such as the *ṇic* suffix or *san* (desiderative), the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) alone is not the qualificand; for there is no evidence for abandoning the general rule of the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), and because this would contradict experience. Moreover, in forms such as *pācayitā* ("one who causes to cook"), the predominance of the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix and so forth is indispensable. In that context, there is either an inherence (*anvaya*) of the verbal root's meaning—qualified by its factors of action (*kāraka*)—within the instigation (*pravartanā*), or an inherence of the instigation within such a verbal root-meaning; for it is impossible to determine the meaning of the verbal root without the inherence of its factors of action.

And thus, the state of being non-informative (*ajñāpyatva*) and the status of being a means to the good (*śreyassādhanatva*), which are projected by the instigation (*pravartanā*), reside specifically in the qualified [action], because it is only an action qualified by its factors (*kāraka*) that constitutes the object of the instigation. However, when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is already established [as known], the [instigation] ultimately culminates in the aspect of the subordinate element (*guṇāṃśa*), as in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). Furthermore, in the case of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others, the instigation appears in reality at the very time of its utterance, due to the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*) and because the present time is more immediate (*antaraṅga*).
The meaning of the verbal root, however, pertains only to the future time, due to the inherent nature of the word's power.

By this, the objection that the use of the form ‘pacet’ (‘one should cook’) would result during the stage when the cooking is already being performed by the person being prompted is refuted. However, there is no first-person optative suffix (*vidhiliṅ*), because for one’s own activity, the actual existence of one’s own desire (*svarūpasatyā*) alone is the cause, and thus the knowledge of that [desire] is not required. With this very point in mind, the Mīmāṃsakas state: “The first-person suffix is an inhibitor of the injunctive force.

But in cases such as ‘One should not eat *kalañja*’, where there is a co-occurrence with the negative particle (*nañ*), cessation (*nivṛtti*) is the meaning of the optative; thus all desired results are established.
This concludes the investigation into the meaning of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).
Now, the investigation of the meaning of the *san*-class suffixes (*sanādi*): Next, the meaning of the *san*-class suffixes, which have verbal roots as their base, is determined.

In examples such as *apipaṭhiṣati*, the meaning of *san* is "desire. In that context, the meaning of the root is construed through two relations—namely, being the object (*karmatva*) and having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*)—due to the peculiarity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) and the natural force of the rule: "After a root whose meaning is an object [of desire] and which has the same agent, [the suffix *saN* is added] when desire is intended" (Pāṇini 3.1.7). Furthermore, in examples such as *pāpacyate* ("he cooks repeatedly or excessively"), the *yaṅ* suffix conveys repetition or abundance residing in the meaning of the base.

In some cases, there is even the censure of crookedness (*kauṭilya*) and so forth, based on the authority of various grammatical treatises such as Pāṇini’s rules: *nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau* (3.1.23) and *lupasadaacara* (3.1.24). In expressions such as *śvā mumūrṣati*, the desiderative suffix (*san*) has the sense of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*); the understanding is that death, which is the object of apprehension, has the dog as its agent. The same applies to the expression *kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*.

In the view that the suffix (*pratyaya*) functions through the superimposition of desire (*icchāropeṇa*), the previously mentioned meaning becomes the object of subsequent mental cognition (*mānasabodha*). In that case, such co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) alone is the cause. In expressions such as *pācayati*, it should be inferred that the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is instigation (*preraṇā*), and so forth.
This concludes the investigation into the meanings of the *san*-class and other affixes. Now follows the investigation into the meanings of *kṛt* affixes.
Now, the meaning of *kṛt* suffixes based on verbal roots (*dhātu*) and their inherent nature is investigated.

In this regard, the referent (*āśraya*) of *kṛt* suffixes prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) is as follows: in the case of the agent, it is the substratum of the activity (*vyāpāra*); in the case of the object, it is the substratum of the result (*phala*). Furthermore, when used in conjunction with a *kṛt* suffix denoting the object, there is a transposition of the result and the activity. Thus, in expressions such as "the village has been gone to" (*gato grāmaḥ*), the understanding is that the village is the substratum of the contact with a subsequent location produced by the activity.

Nor should it be argued that since it is observed that in verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) the agent and object function as qualifiers of the meaning of the root, the same must be appropriate here as well; for the rule "the [verbal form] has the action as its primary meaning" (*bhāvapradhānam*) applies specifically to verbal forms, and the subsequent Nirukta statement "they have substance as their primary meaning" (*sattvapradhānāni*) indicates that those two [agent and object] function as the qualificands therein. Furthermore, the primacy of substance (*sattva*) in a noun is only with respect to the meaning of the root that constitutes its own base. Consequently, there is no contradiction even if the meaning of the case-ending—which is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*)—is predominant.

And here, by the term "noun" (*nāmapada*), that which ends in a suffix denoting a sentient being (*sattva*) is understood; for this very reason, there is no fault in cases such as *pacati kalpam* ("he cooks for a long time"). Among the kṛt-affixes expressing action (*bhāva*), those designated as *kṛtya*—namely, *tavya* and so on—as well as those with the sense of *kta* and *khala*, merely restate the meaning of the verbal root as it exists in a state yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). For this very reason, in forms such as *edhitavyam* ("it is to be increased"), there is no expectancy for another action. Therefore, the singular number alone is used for them. Because of the statement, "Nouns have substance (*sattva*) as their primary meaning," even that which is in a state of being accomplished possesses gender.

Existence (*sattva*) consists precisely in being connected with the application of a gender-mark (*liṅga*). Since no other gender-mark is possible there, and because it is a pronoun for gender (*liṅgasarvanāman*), it is necessarily neuter. For this very reason, they say that in the rule *tayoreva kṛtyakta* (Pāṇini 3.4.70), the reference by the word *tayoḥ* ("of those two") is properly understood as referring only to the "action" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*) grasped by the preceding rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

However, the state [of an action] expressed by *ghañ* and other suffixes has reached the stage of accomplishment (*siddhāvasthā*), because in cases such as ‘pākaḥ’ (cooking), one observes the requirement for another action and so forth. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, there would be no syntactic connection with a *kāraka* (participant) in expressions like ‘odanasya pākaḥ’ (the cooking of rice), since the rule for such connection is established only with respect to an action situated in the state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*); for this is due either to the governing heading ‘kārake’ or to the creation of the technical term ‘kāraka’ itself. This is not the case, because the verbal root presents the action precisely as being in the state of being to-be-accomplished.

Nor should it be argued that the syntactic connection of the *kārakas* occurs only with the action (the meaning of the verb) supplied by ellipsis, as in "the cooking of rice" (*odanasya pākaḥ*) and similar cases; for this would result in the non-occurrence of the genitive case prescribed by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" [Pāṇini 2.3.65] when joined with a *kṛt*-suffix, due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), and it would further result in the non-occurrence of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) in the form "odanapākaḥ. Nor can it be argued that the compound is formed with the "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) and that the sentence form is also established because the formation of compounds is optional; for this would fail to account for the actual experience of a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, in this way, the meaning of the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" would become redundant. If it is argued that this being the case, one could also say "kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ" (cooking by means of wood), we reply that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as "pākaḥ" (cooking), there would be a cognition of the action twice over; for the intended meaning is that a single word-meaning is presented through both its states of being a goal (*sādhyatva*) and being established (*siddhatva*). Nor can it be asked how a single word-meaning can be presented by these two contradictory states, since—on the authority of the *Bhāṣya* and other sources—it is accepted that they are presented as residing in the same substratum due to a difference in their expressive capacities. Others maintain that there is no contradiction between the two at all.

In that case, when there is a connection with the result of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), we have only "śobhanaḥ pākaḥ" ("a beautiful cooking"). Even from words such as *pāka*, it is the result alone that is presented as the objective (*sādhya*), and thus by that very fact [the genitive is not applied]. However, the genitive prescribed by "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" [Pāṇini 2.3.65] does not apply here, because, due to its association with the agent (*kartṛ*), the term "object" (*karman*) in that rule refers only to an object that is not the meaning of the root itself. This is clear from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the eighth book, under the rule "pūjanāt pūjitam" [Pāṇini 8.1.67].

However, when there is a connection with the activity (*vyāpāra*), because the suffix *ghañ* conveys even the state of being accomplished (*siddhatva*) therein, we have only "a beautiful cooking" (*śobhanaḥ pākaḥ*). But in the case of a verbal ending (*tiṅanta*), even when there is a connection with the activity—as in "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma preceded by devotion"—there is only the neuter gender. Furthermore, the nominative (*prathamā*) is used, not the accusative (*dvitīyā*), because since that [activity] lacks the status of an object (*karman*), the accusative does not apply to its qualifier.

This is because verbal roots are not the base for nominal case-endings; thus, since the meanings of case-endings—such as number and objecthood—cannot logically connect with the meaning of the root, just as they do not with the root itself...

It must be admitted that even a word ending in *ghañ* (a kṛt-suffix) denotes an action (*kriyā*). However, if one were to accept the connection of the suffix with only a portion of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), then there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of such usage as "he sees two cooks" (*pacantau paśyati*) in cases where duality and so forth are precluded for the agent of cooking, while they are not precluded for the act of cooking itself. Furthermore, if one were to propose that a cognition regarding the fact that a particular suffix following a verbal root has some other meaning is an obstacle to the comprehension of the case-meaning (*sub-artha*) as connected to the meaning presented by the root, that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

And thus, where the intention (*tātparya*) pertains only to the verbal root (the *dhātu*) in cases such as cooking, there only the accusative case is used after a word like *stoka* which expresses a qualifier of that [root]; however, where the intention pertains to the entire complex ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, there the word expressing its qualifier must indeed possess the same case-ending as it. Having stated this as the view of the modern Naiyāyikas—the opinion of the author of the *Kātantra-pariśiṣṭa*—he refutes it with the words "by this" (*etena*). By this, the statement of the modern Naiyāyikas—that "affixes such as *ghañ* and others merely ensure the grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*) of the usage when they do not convey number, present time, and so forth"—is rejected. As it has been said: [The text continues with the refutation.]
"In that context, action (*kriyā*) is based on the form of the verbal root (*dhātu*) as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*);
whereas its state of being accomplished (*siddha-bhāva*), however, is based on the *ghañ* suffix and others.
Here, "the state of being accomplished" (*siddhasya bhāvaḥ*) means "accomplishedness" (*siddhatva*). This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "sārvadhātuka" (Pāṇini 3.1.67).

Nor should it be argued that even if the state of being accomplished (*sādhyāvasthā*) were manifested [in the cognition], one would have to say "fivefold cooking" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ pākaḥ*), because suffixes such as *kṛtvasuc* are grammatically correct only when they connect with an action (*kriyā*). This objection is untenable, for we accept this very consequence based on the observation of usage such as "dvirvacane 'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59), which involves double application. Some maintain that such over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be prevented by the principle of non-utterance (*anabhidhāna*).

Others, however, say: since the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) in the rule *kṛtvasuc* (Pāṇini 5.4.17)—which prescribes the suffix *kṛtvasuc* when counting the non-repetition of an action—is otherwise redundant, by virtue of that very fact, only an action whose nature is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyasvabhāvā*) is understood there; thus, there is no fault. As for the statement "twofold usage" (*dviḥ prayogaḥ*) and so forth, they maintain that it is resolved by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *durvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.56).

Furthermore, if the state of being a goal (*sādhyatva*) were not manifested there, then suffixes such as *ktvā*, which are prescribed by the rule governing connection with a verbal root (*dhātusambandhikāra*), and suffixes such as *tumun*, which are prescribed when a verb denoting an action is the subordinate element (*upapada*), would not occur. This is because words such as "cooking for the sake of eating" (*bhoktuṃ pākaḥ*) are conventionally understood as qualified by the state of being a goal. The same applies to expressions such as "cooking after having eaten" (*bhuktvā pākaḥ*).

However, forms such as "a cook for the sake of eating" (*bhoktuṃ pācakaḥ*) or "a cook after having eaten" (*bhuktvā pācakaḥ*) do not occur; this is because, according to the maxim "qualities (subsidiary elements) exist for the sake of another," it is inappropriate for them to connect with a subordinate action, as we shall explain in the section defining the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix *-tṛ*.

Nor is it correct to say that expressions such as *yuktaṃ pacati paśya* ("see him cook properly") would not be possible; for [in those cases], due to their being *antaraṅga* (internal), only the primary status existing at the time of the presentation of the word-meanings is grasped. However, in examples such as *bhoktuṃ pācako'sti* ("there is a cook who intends to eat"), the suffix *tumun* is applied by the rule *śakadhṛṣajñāglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhāstyartheṣu tumun* (Pāṇini 3.4.65). In the case of *bhuktvā pācakaḥ*, however, there is also a connection with a verb such as "exists," due to the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For this very reason, they say that in instances like *dattena gato grāmaḥ* ("the village was gone to by Datta") or *kartṛpūrvī kaṭam* ("the mat was previously made by the agent"), there is a connection with a *kāraka* (participant in action); but that is not so.

The meaning of that [rule] is simply this: "when a primary element (*pradhāna*) and a subordinate element (*guṇa*) are in proximity, there is no grammatical connection with the subordinate"; however, when the primary element is not in proximity, there is connection even with a subordinate. Thus, they maintain that forms such as *bhoktuṃ pācakaḥ* (a cook who intends to eat), *bhuktvā gataḥ* (having eaten, he went), and *bhuktvā pācakaḥ* (having eaten, he is a cook) are indeed correct.

If it is argued that, in this case, since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) expressing a simple negation would have to connect with what is denoted by words such as "cooking" (*pāka*), there would follow the cognition "there is no cooking," because the understanding would be that existence has as its agent the absence of cooking delimited by duality—[we reply: no; for, due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), it is accepted that the negative particle expressing negation connects only with an object that denotes an action in its state of being merely to-be-accomplished (*sādhyāvasthā*).

Although the suffix *vati* in the rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.117) is also connected with an action, nevertheless it is indeed accepted [to denote the action], as in the expression *yāgavat pākaḥ* ("cooking like a sacrifice"). For this very reason, in examples such as *goṣu duhyamānāsu devadattasya gamanam* ("while the cows are being milked, Devadatta goes"), the genitive case and so forth are applied by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena* (Pāṇini 2.3.37), because the verbal root conveys the state of being in the process of accomplishment (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*). This is the general direction. Likewise, the meaning of suffixes such as *tumun* is also solely the action (*bhāva*); for the author of the Bhāṣya states regarding the rule *tumarthe* (Pāṇini 3.3.10): "The meaning of *tumun* is action."

Those who reject [the view that] *kvat* and other suffixes denote an action (*bhāva*) maintain instead that the meaning of *ktvā*, *tumun*, and so forth, is indeed an action that has not yet attained the status of a substance (*asattvabhūta*), just as in the case of words like *pāka*. This is because of the rule stating, "The *avyaya*-kṛt suffixes are used in the sense of an action. That action is strictly non-substantial, since there is no connection with gender and other such qualities in the meaning of an indeclinable, and because one does not experience any difference from the meaning of the suffix itself.

In this regard, because of the rule "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are used] when one action is for the sake of another action" (Pāṇini 3.3.10), the state of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) is also expressed by *tumun*; this state of being for the sake of that consists in the nature of being the objective (*uddeśyatva*). And that [objective] is either a relation (*saṃsarga*) or a qualifier (*prakāra*). Furthermore, the fact that the base and the upapada have a common agent is also obtained here by the force of the expression as a condition of usage; for, when two actions require a locus, it is appropriate to grasp only this [common agent] due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). And that [common agency] is either a relation or a qualifier.

In this context, the requirement that the two actions share a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*)—between the root meaning and the meaning of the *upapada*—is obtained by the force of the rule's enunciation as a condition for usage; for when there is an expectancy for a locus for both actions, it is appropriate that they belong to a single agent due to their proximity. However, the suffix *ṇvul* prescribed here [by Pāṇini 3.2.78] applies only to the agent (*kartṛ*). In that case, the meaning of the root of the *tumun* suffix serves as a qualifier with respect to the meaning of the *upapada*.

And thus, in such cases as "He goes to see Kṛṣṇa," the understanding is that the going has for its purpose a future act of seeing whose object is Kṛṣṇa. [Note: This is the summary here—In "He cooks in order to eat," the relationship between eating and the act of cooking, which consists of the nature of the produced and the producer, is indicated by the suffix *tumun*, because of the rule: "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when one action is for the sake of another action. The sense is that this "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) takes the form of the relationship between the produced and the producer.]

Just like "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) also appears as a relation between two actions due to the very nature of verbal expressive power (*śabdaśakti*). For this very reason, the expression "he cooks in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pacati*) is not employed when it intends two actions having different agents.

For those who know the truth, however, the *tādarthya* (purposefulness) consisting of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) and being the determinant of that reference (*nirūpakatva*), which is also expressed by the suffix *-tumun*, appears as a relation (*saṃsarga*). And this [purposefulness] is the state of being the object of a desire dependent upon a [primary] desire for that [action]. Since the word "in the future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is understood in the rule "the suffixes *-tumun* and *-ṇvul* [are used when the action is in the future]," futurity is also expressed by that [suffix]. Thus, the cognition is: "cooking performed by the agent of eating, having as its object of reference a future act of eating.

Furthermore, the suffix *-tumun* does not denote the agent, because it is stated that "kṛt-suffixes added to indeclinables denote the action (*bhāva*)," and thus the rule "kṛt-suffixes denote the agent" does not apply here; that rule applies only to those [suffixes] whose meaning is not otherwise specified.

By this, the following is refuted: that *samānakartṛkatva* (having the same agent) cannot be the [required] relation, because there would otherwise result the undesirable consequence of such usages as "he cooks in order to eat" (*bhoktum pacati*) having as their purport two actions with distinct agents, through the mutual non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the agent of the *tumun*-affix and the agent expressed by the verbal suffix. Furthermore, it is impossible in cases such as "it is cooked in order to be eaten" (*bhoktum pacyate*) or "one stands in order to eat" (*bhoktum sthīyate*).

Nor should it be argued that even in those cases there is no syntactic anomaly because one may supply (*adhyāhāra*) "by Devadatta," since the agent denoted by the third case (*tṛtīyā*) can then be construed as non-different from the agent; for it is established by experience that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs even without such an ellipsis. This is the direction of the argument.

However, the suffix *ṇvul* prescribed by the rule "tumunṇvulau" functions as a *kṛt* suffix denoting the agent according to the rule "kartari kṛt," and the relationship between the two actions is exactly as previously stated. Thus, they maintain that from the sentence "He goes to see Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ darśako yāti*), the understanding is: "The present-time act of going, which has Kṛṣṇa as its object, is for the purpose of a future act of seeing."

And this is logical: for even when one sees other people on the road while traveling with the specific aim of seeing Kṛṣṇa, there is no usage such as "he goes to see [them] knowing [them]," whereas there is usage such as "he goes to see Kṛṣṇa, not the Yavanas and so forth. Therefore, the modern logicians accept that the meaning expressed by the suffix *tumun* is the state of being the object of a desire dependent upon a desire qualified by having that same agent as its agent.

For this very reason, in the *Vyutpattivāda* on the fourth case (*caturthī*) as a kāraka, it is stated: "And here, 'to bring' (*āhartum*) is the meaning of the suffix *tumun*; [it refers to] bringing which is connected to its own object, which in turn is connected to being the purpose for the action expressed by the word co-occurring with it. Without the denotability (*vācyatā*) of "having that which is its own object as its purpose," the statement "connected to" would be incoherent.

Otherwise, since that [relation] would not be a restrictor of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), a counter-positivehood delimited by that relation would be unestablished; consequently, it would be impossible to convey the absence of a perception whose counter-positive is the Yavana and so forth as qualified by such a counter-positivehood. Nor can it be maintained that what is conveyed as the meaning of the nominative case-ending is simply the absence of being a locus of going qualified by a perception of the Yavana and so forth through the aforementioned relation, for this is impossible in cases such as "One stands to see Kṛṣṇa, but not the Yavana and so forth. This is the general direction of the argument.

In the system of the Grammarians (Śābdikas), however, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency, because they accept that in all cases the cognition is precisely of the action qualified by all its qualifiers, with the primary qualificand as its object. In examples such as *bhoktum icchati* ("he desires to eat"), the suffix *tumun* is applied by the rule *samānakartṛkeṣu*. The meaning of that rule is: when words expressing desire are used as adjuncts (*upapada*) which convey an object sharing the same agent as the meaning of the verbal root that serves as the base for the *tumun*, the suffix *tumun* is added to that root. This [rule] is intended to exclude cases where the adjunct is an action performed for the sake of another action.

The suffix *tumun* serves as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) when the desire for the action denoted by the base (*prakṛtyartha-kriyecchā*) is construed with the agent denoted by the base, through the relation of being the agent of that which has as its object the purpose of that [desire]. However, according to the opponent's view (*paramata*), this [relation] is not expressed by it. Furthermore, the relation of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is also included within the set of relations in order to prevent the use of the expression "he desires to eat" (*bhoktum icchati*) in cases where there is a desire for another person’s act of eating.

The inclusion of *samānakartṛkatva* (having the same agent) among the relations [of the infinitive suffix] is for the purpose of precluding such usage as *śaktim icchati* ("he desires power"). In examples such as *śaknoti bhoktum*, *dhṛṣṇoti paṭhitum*, and *jānāti paṭhitum*, the suffix *tumun* is applied by the rule *śakadhṛṣajñāglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhāstyartheṣu tumun*. In the first case (*śaknoti*), [the infinitive denotes] the meaning of the verbal root, which is *śakti* (capacity), synonymous with *sāmarthya* (ability).

In the first case, the relation of being the purpose (*prayojanakatva*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root is what is indicated by the suffix *tumun*. In the second case, the relation is either the state of being the object (*viṣayitva*) of the doubt that constitutes the lack of boldness (*aprāgalbhya*), or it is the state of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*) with respect to the aforementioned boldness. In the third case, the relation of being the object is indeed explicit.

In this case as well, the requirement of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) must be included within the relation everywhere. The relation here is, according to the view of others, that which is denoted by the suffix *tavya*. Here, the respective meanings of the verbal roots with which it is co-uttered (*samabhivyāhṛta*) are to be included within the meaning of the root *śak* (to be able). To illustrate: the function of the root *śak* consists in an operation conducive to the action of joining below the throat, and in the sense of "capacity. In that context, there is a primary denotation (*śakti*) regarding capacity, while in the other case there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In this regard, the infinitive suffix *tumun* and the base of the verb *bhuj* (to eat), etc., serve as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*).

In such a sense, the function [of the verbal root] occurs only in the case of an object-terminating suffix (*karmapratyaya*), and not in the case of an agent-terminating suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*), because there is no purpose [for it]. In that case, the operation (*vyāpāra*)—which is connected by the power [of the root] through the relation of being instigated (*prayojyatva*)—is construed with the aforementioned action (*kriyā*) through the relation of being produced (*janyatva*). Because rice and the like possess the fruit in the form of such an action, they are construed with the aforementioned action through the relation of being produced; and because rice and the like possess the fruit in the form of such an action, they have the status of an object (*karmatva*).

And thus, from the sentence "it is possible to eat rice," the understanding is that there is an action residing in the rice which is conducive to a conjunction in the throat produced by an operation prompted by capacity.

In the system of the logicians (tārkika), however, the understanding is that "rice-gruel is the substratum of such an action. Furthermore, in the Mīmāṃsā system, *śakti* (capacity) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). In the Nyāya system, it is a unique collection of causes conducive to their respective causes; as in the present case, [it consists of] contact with the blazing fire in the stomach and so forth, because gender and number are not perceived. Thus, it follows that suffixes such as *tumun* merely restate the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Likewise, the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is also precisely the abstract action (*bhāva*).

As for the argument that—based on the grammatical rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* [Pāṇini 3.4.21], which prescribes the suffix *-ktvā* and others—the agent is the referent of the meaning of the suffix; otherwise, in the sentence *iṣṭakāḥ paktvāhaṃ pāktvāhaṃ bhokṣye* ("Having baked the bricks, I shall eat"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*).

Nor should it be argued that [the application of the rule] does not occur because the agent is already denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*), for even though the agent of the act of eating is expressed, the agent of the act of cooking is not. This is because the rule "it occurs when [the case-relation] is not denoted" (*anabhihite bhavati*) is understood as a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion). For this very reason, it is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other works that in the example "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*), although the locus of the act of building the palace is denoted, the seventh case (*saptamī*) still applies because the locus of the act of sitting is not denoted. That [argument], however, is not correct;

Even so, this [objection] remains unrefuted because the occurrence of the accusative case in the expression *prāsāde āste* ("he sits on the palace") would still follow; furthermore, since the rule would be established by the phrase *samāne kartari* ("when the agent is the same"), the formulation *samānakartṛkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21) would result in being redundant. Therefore, both the state of having the same agent and the state of occurring earlier in time are merely indicated (*dyotya*).

Indication (*dyotakatva*) consists in making the intention (*tātparya*) regarding the connection between two meanings understood. To explain: here, the action (*bhāva*) exists only in its state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyāvastha*), and it is obtained through the verbal root (*dhātu*). Furthermore, the action that constitutes the meaning of the base of the suffix *ktvā* serves as a qualifier for another action. Because of the governing rule concerning "connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandha*), the relation between these two is one of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and posteriority in time. In this context, the suffixes *ktvā* and so forth serve to indicate the nature of that relation. In some cases, however, additional properties such as being produced (*janyatva*) or being non-pervasive (*avyāpyatva*) also appear.

However, because that [sequence] is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*māna*), it is not expressed by the suffix *ktvā* and the like. And thus, in cases such as "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), "I am satisfied only after eating, not after drinking," "having studied, he stays," and "the Lord remains having known," our understanding is the same as that of others.

And thus, the statement of the Mīmāṃsakas—that "the status of having a common agent (samānakartṛkatva) is obtained precisely through the cognition of the relation of coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the agent and the meaning of the verbal root, and therefore that [status] is not denotable by the suffix -ktvā"—is incorrect. However, textual passages stating that "common agency and anteriority in time are cognized" are not untenable, because such cognition exists as a relation (saṃsarga). Yet, there is simply no experience of a cognition where that [common agency] is the qualificand (prakāra). In the Sūtra, however, in the expression "samānakartṛkayoḥ," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (nirdhāraṇa), or it is a locative case.

The term ‘pūrvakāle’ (in the prior time) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. And thus, the meaning is as follows: according to the sense of the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*, the suffix *ktvā* is applied after a verbal root that denotes an action qualified by a prior time among two actions having the same agent. Therefore, "prior time" is a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of the *ktvā*-suffix; furthermore, "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is the relation that constitutes the mode of being a qualifier (*prakāratāghaṭaka*) of such a base-meaning with respect to the meaning of another verbal root.

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya resolves the doubt regarding the suffix *ktvā* in the example "He eats first, then he goes" by stating that the word *pūrva* here signifies "prior time," and not that the verbal root itself has that function; for this is expressed by the word *sva* (itself). However, this does not mean that the rule is governed by the maxim *uktārthānām aprayogaḥ* ("that which has already been expressed need not be used"), because if that were the case, the objection raised in the Bhāṣya—"Why does [the suffix] not occur here: *āsyate bhoktum*?"—would be untenable.

In that case as well, since the suffix *tumun* conveys the relation consisting of having that [action] as its purpose, it indicates the priority of time (*pūrvakālatva*) for the verb *āsate*; therefore, that [suffix] is not applicable there. Furthermore, if priority of time were not understood there, how could a doubt even find a foothold? That the formation is achieved by the present tense (*laṭ*) according to the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*) is another matter.

Kaiyaṭa’s commentary states: "If *ktvā* occurs after the root *ās*, then *tumun* occurs after the root *bhuj*, because [the former] is not expressive [of that meaning]. Regarding the example "having first eaten, he subsequently goes" (*pūrvaṃ bhuktvā paścād vrajati*), the meaning is: "having eaten before other eaters, he goes after other goers. Thus, since the state of being prior (*pūrvakālatva*) is understood only in relation to the action of another means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), this is not the scope of the present rule; rather, it falls under the rule "optionally when *agra-* is used as the first word" (*vibhāṣāgre prathamā*). This is clear from the Bhāṣya on this point.

However, in the case of "darśapūrṇamāsābhyām," there is no fault, because through the relation of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), the qualification of being prior in time is understood in reference to the *soma* sacrifice.

Thus, "pūrvakālaḥ" is a *karmadhāraya* compound; and they say that, just like the genitive case, the suffix *-ktvā* and others can also be said to express a relationship such as having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*).

In this context, "prior time" (*pūrvakālatva*) means being delimited by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). The action of going (*vrajana-kriyā*) is construed with prior non-existence through the relation of having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by its respective individuality (*tattad-vyaktitva*). Furthermore, "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) consists in occurring at a moment that is the locus of the destruction of the time-locus of that [action], while being qualified by not being the locus of the destruction of a muhūrta or other period that is the locus of the destruction of that same time-locus. By this definition, the aforementioned defect does not arise. In the case of the sentence "The Lord, having known, remains" (*īśvaro jñātvā tiṣṭhati*), since the destruction of the Lord's knowledge is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), such a destruction is not included in the definition of immediacy.

This is what must be understood here: in the expression "having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he goes," the suffix *ktvā* is used everywhere by taking the state of being prior in time relative to the action of going (*vrajana*), but not by taking it relative to the actions of eating and so forth.

That being the case, just as in examples such as "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), where there is no intention to express the number two—despite its being conveyed by the dual suffix in the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21)—just as when it is said, "Of these Brahmins, let the first one be brought," the very first one is brought and not some intermediate one; likewise here too, the suffix *ktvā* would apply only to the root *snāti*, and not to *bhuji* and so forth.

And thus, the connection of the acts of bathing and going is only with the act of departing (*vrajana*), and not of bathing and so forth with eating and so forth. For this very reason, even the reversed usage "having eaten, having bathed, having drunk, he goes" (*bhuktvā snātvā pītvā vrajati*) is justified there; this is clear from the Bhāṣya. [The meaning is that the suffix *ktvā* occurs after a word denoting an action that precedes in time between two actions performed by the same agent.]

As for what the Naiyāyikas say—that "immediately preceding in time" alone is sufficient, and that the word "immediately" (*avyavahita*) is used to exclude such usage when referring to a meal from another year—it is argued that this refers to *yogyatā* (logical fitness), which is determined by factors such as intention (*tātparya*), as well as by [temporal units like] a staff-measure (*daṇḍa*), a month, or a muhūrta. Thus, in cases such as "having eaten, he goes," because there is an understanding of the sequence "he goes after eating," and because there is no understanding that the eating occurs at a time prior to the going, such immediate succession does not even exist [in those cases].

In the case of eating during the rainy season (*varṣāntarīya-bhojana*), such an application is indeed accepted when there is an intention (*tātparya*); however, in the absence of such an intention, no cognition arises precisely because that [intention] is lacking. Furthermore, non-interruption (*avyavadhāna*) is generally respected as the default rule.

For this very reason, the statement "Having performed the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, one should sacrifice with *Soma*" prescribes the *Soma* sacrifice as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *Darśa* at a time subsequent to it. Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency with the established Mīmāṃsā doctrine, which holds that the hearing of the suffix *-ktvā*—which signifies priority in time—would have to be set aside in favor of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

And thus, the primacy of the action denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) remains its general rule, uncontradicted. Therefore, the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is "subsequent time. Furthermore, "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) does not consist in "occurring in a moment that is the locus of the destruction of that [action]," because this would be absent in cases such as "having stood, he sees," since standing exists even at the time of seeing; for this would contradict immediacy defined as "occurring in a moment that is the locus of the destruction of that [standing]. Rather, immediacy can be understood as "being the counter-positive of a prior absence existing at that same time," or as "having an origination in a moment that is the locus of the destruction of the moment which is the locus of that [prior action]."

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the expression "He sleeps having opened his mouth" at a time when the mouth is no longer open; nor that there would be the undesirable consequence of not using the expression "I am satisfied only by eating, not by drinking," because in both cases there is no difference in the lack of immediate succession (*ānantarya*); and [finally] that there would be the undesirable consequence of using the expression "The Lord remains having known," because the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* and others includes not only immediate succession but also properties such as being produced by that action (*tajjanyatva*) and being pervaded by it (*vyāpyatva*).

And likewise, in cases such as "having opened his mouth" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya*), because the usage occurs precisely with the intention of expressing pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) by means of a temporal (*kālika*) or other relation, there is no such usage when sleep belongs to another time, since it lacks that [temporal] connection. For this very reason, the modern Naiyāyikas maintain that the expression "having studied, he remains" (*adhītya tiṣṭhati*) is justified only by taking the state [of remaining] co-temporal with the study, and not by taking a state co-temporal with the cessation of the study.

That too is refuted by this: since the manifestation [of the relation] is possible precisely through the mode of being related—as explained above—it is improper to postulate that it is a denoted meaning (*vācya*). For this very reason, it is the relation as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) that is indicated here, not the relation as a word-meaning (*padārtha*); thus, there is a distinction from the *karmapravacanīyas*.

Furthermore, if those [repetitions] were to be expressed [by the suffix], then by the rule that the meaning of the suffix of *kṛt* (the verbal noun) must be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it would follow that that very [repetition] becomes the qualificand. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, because in the absence of the primacy of action (*kriyā-prādhānya*), there would be an impossibility of the occurrence of frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*) and duality; for if that [suffix] were to apply based on an action that has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta-kriyā*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as *pācaka* (a cooker); and furthermore, it would contradict the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) prescribing the formation of abstract nouns (*bhāva*). This is the general direction of the argument.

In expressions such as "I am going after having eaten" (*ahaṃ bhuktvā vrajāmi*), the instrumental case does not occur; for, according to the authority of the *Bhāṣya* and other texts, when the power (*śakti*) relative to the verbal action denoted by the finite verb—which takes the meaning of the suffix *-kta* as its primary qualificand—is expressed, the power relative to the subordinate action is also considered to be expressed. As Harivṛṣabha has stated:

"Where there are two distinct powers belonging to a substance—one pertaining to the primary and the other to the subordinate action—the power that rests upon the subordinate [action] conforms to the primary."

"The power whose primary object is the principal meaning is expressed by the suffix; when it pertains to a subordinate element, then, like that [principal], it is understood even though not explicitly stated. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, in the expression "paktvaudano bhujyate" ("having cooked, rice is eaten"), the accusative case does not occur after *odana*. Nor should it be argued that [the accusative] is unavoidable because the suffix *ktvā* (in *paktvā*) possesses an expectancy for an agent and an object due to its internal nature (*antaraṅgatayā*), since the nature of an action itself is non-existent without a relation to a *kāraka*, and because of the grammatical rule that a word is capable of connecting with another only when its requirements are fulfilled. For at that time, there is no cognition of a power (*śakti*) defined by the principal action, nor is there the state of being expressed (*abhihitatva*) by it. This is because the authority of the *Bhāṣya* [establishes otherwise].

There is no fault here, because grammatical derivations apply to cases other than indeclinables prescribed under the heading of "relation with a root-meaning" (dhātusambandha) and those formed with the suffix *ku*.

Furthermore, since the connection with another action was previously the object of cognition, the suffix *ktvā* is indeed correct; therefore, arguments such as its being "internal" (*antaraṅga*) are entirely inappropriate. However, in the example "Having cooked the rice, the village is gone to by Devadatta" (*odanaṃ paktvā grāmo gamyate devadattena*), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) does indeed occur. This is because the powers (*śakti*) determined by the primary action and the subordinate action do not reside in a single locus, and thus there is no expression of this [subordinate action] by virtue of the other having been expressed. This is the path accepted in the *Bhāṣya* and other works. And this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "svādumi ṇamul" (Pāṇini 3.4.26).

In this regard, the following should be understood: because the action expressed by the verb (ākhyāta) is primary, all elements presented as ending in the suffix *ktvā* are qualifiers of that [action] alone, and there is no mutual relationship between them, according to the maxim "And because subordinate factors exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*).

By this, the objection is refuted that—just as when it is said, "Bring these [men], starting with the first," the middle one is not brought, so too here a suffix should not occur after a word expressing a middle action.

For this very reason, the usage is not restricted, as in "having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he goes," or "he goes, having drunk and eaten," and so forth. As for the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*), it is grammatically correct because sleep exists even at a time subsequent to the opening of the mouth; such is the general direction [of the argument].
This concludes the investigation into the meaning of *kṛt* suffixes. Now begins the investigation into the meaning of nouns (*nāman*).
Now, since that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix possesses the status of a noun (*nāman*), its meaning is investigated.

In this regard, the meaning of a nominal base (*prātipadika*) ending in a *kṛt* suffix is the individual (*vyakti*) itself, because it is through linguistic usage—the crown jewel among the determiners of power—that the power [of the word] is determined specifically with respect to the individual. [Objection: But surely the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) regarding mere individuals is impossible, because it is impossible to grasp a convention (*saṅketa*) due to the absence of the presentation of all infinite individuals by a single word. Nor can it be argued that the apprehension of power need not apply to every individual, for if it were otherwise, even horses would appear when the word "cow" or the word "horse" is uttered.

Furthermore, in the case of another individual elephant-driver (*hastipaka*), having taken "elephant-driver-ness" as the delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), one might not have grasped the relation with the elephant regarding that specific driver; yet, upon seeing the elephant, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of remembering that [elephant] as well. This is because, according to the Mīmāṃsaka position, the knowledge of a relation with one individual cannot be the cause for the recollection of another individual. For in the Mīmāṃsaka system, the expressive power (*śakti*) of words resides in the genus (*jāti*), due to parsimony (*lāghava*); for if it were in the individuals, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) since individuals are infinite. [Note: Here the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the power of words lies in the genus, because of parsimony; for if the power were in the individuals, there would be complexity due to their infinity.]

They say that the evidence for the view that the denotatum of a word is the universal (*jāti*) consists of the rule *jātyākhyāyām ekasmin* (Pāṇini 1.2.58), the Vārttika located under the rule *sarūpāṇām* (1.2.64)—namely, "The mention of *aṇ* in the context of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) is not a general maxim; it is established by the fact that [the word] denotes the form (*ākṛti*)"—and the Bhāṣya statement, "Vājapyāyana [holds that the word denotes] the form. However, this is not correct;

for even though individuals (*vyakti*) are infinite, there is no burden of postulating an infinite number of word-powers (*śakti*), because one may accept the power as residing in the individual characterized by that universal, where the universal serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and its unity [ensures the unity of the denotation]. Thus, there is no complexity (*gaurava*).

In reality, however, based on the Bhāṣya on the *Sarūpa-sūtra*—which states, "It is not that for one whose primary referent is the form (*ākṛti*), the substance (*dravya*) is not also a referent"—the denotation must be precisely qualified (*viśiṣṭa*). This is because it is so experienced, and what is established by experience cannot be denied. Furthermore, gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*) are also the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). As stated: "One, two, three, four, and likewise five—these are all the positions regarding the meaning of a noun (*nāmārtha*) described in the treatise."

By this [definition], since it is understood that gender, number, case-role (*kāraka*), and so forth are the meanings of the nominal stem (*nāman*), it is logical that suffixes function as *dyotaka* (indicators), while the base (*prakṛti*) functions as the *vācaka* (signifier). A "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is a meaningful linguistic item distinct from a verbal root (*dhātu*), a suffix (*pratyaya*), a word ending in a suffix (*pratyayānta*), and words beginning with such forms. By taking this unified property of being a nominal stem as the delimiting factor for the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), one avoids the postulation of an infinite number of delimiters for expressive power, nor does one face an infinity of expressive powers themselves. Even if there were an infinity of expressive powers, there is no fault, because a complexity that results in a desired outcome (*phalamukhagaurava*) is not considered a defect.

Although, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it might seem appropriate to assume that case-endings (*vibhakti*) alone express number, nevertheless, this appropriateness must be abandoned because of the deviation from negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*); for instance, in expressions such as "bring the curd and honey," number and grammatical relation (*kāraka*) are perceived even in the absence of a case-ending.

In reality, neither the stem (*prakṛti*) nor the case-ending expresses number; rather, the entire complex ending in the case-suffix—as in "ghaṭaḥ" (pot)—denotes the pot qualified by number. As it has been said:
"The case-endings may be either denoters (*vācikā*) or indicators (*dyotikā*) of duality and so forth."
The delimitors of capacity are the respective serial orders (ānupūrvī); thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Even the word itself appears in verbal cognition as a qualifier, because in cases such as "Yudhiṣṭhira was," there arises the cognition that "someone denoted by the word Yudhiṣṭhira existed. And so it has been said:
"There is no cognition in the world that is not accompanied by words."
"All knowledge appears as if permeated by sound" (Vākyapadīya, Brahmakāṇḍa 123).

[This is so] because it would take on the form of distinct objects; and since that [power] is relational, it would follow that it is differentiated by the difference between its relata, leading to the consequence of an infinite number of powers corresponding to the differences between each individual instance.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the distinction between objects—such as "cow," "white," "moving," and "Dittha"—as words denoting genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and name (*saṃjñā*) would not be established, and consequently the simultaneous employment of terms like "cow," "white," and "moving" would be untenable; we say no. For the object is presented in the very form in which the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurred. And although that property (*dharma*) may be incapable of being denoted itself, it can serve as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) in the case of genus and so forth; thus, having made that [property] the delimitor, [the denotation occurs].

Since it is possible to grasp the power (śakti) with respect to all individual instances (vyakti) through the proximity of general definition (sāmānyalakṣaṇā-pratyāsatti)—which consists in being the substratum of their own function, genus, and so forth—there is neither the fault of infinity (ānantya) nor deviation (vyabhicāra). [The doubt that "due to the infinity of individuals, there would follow an infinity of powers" is dispelled by the phrase "neither infinity nor deviation."]

The intention here is as follows: by taking a property (*dharma*) as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the word's expressive power (*śakti*) is grasped; consequently, in reality, the individual (*vyakti*) qualified by that property and its form is understood, but not in the manner of that property being the mode (*prakāra*) [of cognition].
