This alone constitutes the nature of a universal (*jāti*) and so forth as a secondary indicator: that, having enabled all its own substrates to become objects of the grasp of expressive power by way of their own essential nature, it itself remains neither an object of the grasp of expressive power nor an object of cognition.

Just as in the expression "Devadatta’s house has crows," the act of cooking distinguishes that house from others by means of the grass and so forth characterized by that cooking; likewise, the universal (jāti), having established the individuals, distinguishes its own power from others by means of those individuals characterized by itself.

And thus, even though the individual instances capable of being denoted (*śakyavyakti*) are infinite, there is unity of the power (*śakti*) because of the unity of the genus (*jāti*), such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which serves as its indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is just as there is unity of the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), such as "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), despite the multiplicity of the individual instances (*vyakti*) that serve as the substrata (*āśraya*) for the relatum of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*). Since the difference in power follows only from a difference in the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), there is no burden of postulating an infinite number of powers. Nor does the word "cow" (*go*) produce the cognition of a horse.

Nor should it be argued that if [the relation] is impossible, there would be no resulting cognition having that as its qualifier; for it is possible—just as in the case of an elephant and so forth, where, through the apprehension of a connection with the mahout and so on, there is an appearance [of the object] in that form—because every relational entity, by taking some property as a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa), brings about an appearance qualified by that very property.

Is it not the case that being an *upalakṣaṇa* consists in being the object of a mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by that word, or merely in residing in that [word]? Not the first, because it would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor the second, because, just like "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), substance (*dravya*) and so forth also reside in a pot and the like; consequently, by virtue of the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the power (*śakti*), there would arise from the word "pot" a cognition having "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) as its qualifier.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the cognition of what is not denotable, we say no; for when [a property] such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) functions as the mode (*prakāratā*) in verbal cognition, the only factor that determines its being the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) for that word in that respect is precisely its being the delimitor of the objective determination (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatva*) within the cognition that constitutes the word's denotative power (*śakti*). And "being a delimitor of denotability" means being the delimitor of the objective determination in the cognition that is a constituent of the word's power. Thus, the cause is simply the knowledge of the power, which has as its relation a specific objective determination qualified by being delimited by that property through that particular relation.

Furthermore, in the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) for words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*), there is no fault, because it is accepted that pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) alone serves as the delimiting property of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*), and not substance-ness (*dravyatva*) or other such properties. This should be understood in the same way in all cases.

Nor should it be argued that where there is a grasp of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) such that the substance-word generates the cognition of a substance by way of its possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*), there would follow the cognition of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) as the qualifier (*prakāra*) because it is the delimiting factor of the qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatva*). This is because, even though substance-ness is a qualifier with respect to the qualificandum, the specific cognitive relation known as "delimiting factor of qualificandumhood" resides only in the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*). [Note: The reading *savīkāreṇādoṣāt* is appropriate here; the reading with the ablative ending in the objection *na ca* is not.]

There is no fault, because this is accepted as the method of the Teacher (Ācārya) for establishing [the object] in meditative concentration (*samādhāna*). This very thing is called the "delimitor of the subject" (*dharmitāvacchedaka*). For this very reason, even in the Nyāya system, although words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) lack a primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is qualified by being the substratum of sound (*śabdāśrayatva*), there is nevertheless a cognition [of it] in the form of being the substratum of sound. The author of the *Maṇi* (Gaṅgeśa) stated that there is no deficiency, because he accepts that only the apprehension of a relation having as its qualificandum that which is qualified by being the substratum of sound, etc., serves as the cause for recollection and other cognitions having that same qualification as their object.

As for the claim that if the property of being the substratum of sound is not accepted as the denotation of the word "ākāśa," then from the word "ākāśa" there would arise only indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); and that this "indeterminateness" means that in that respect [the substratum], the object presented by that word is not a qualifier (*aprakāratva*), rather than meaning a total absence of qualifiers in that respect—since it is necessary that the singularity and so forth presented by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) must necessarily be qualifiers in that respect; [we reply that] the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) is indeed entirely devoid of qualifiers.

Nor should it be argued that the recollection of a non-conceptual [perception] is untenable because the established doctrine maintains that memory possesses a form identical to that of the original experience; for there is no fault, since we accept the loss of the objective qualifier (*prakāra*) in such recollection. That, however, is not correct.

Because a thing distinct from a universal (*jāti*) cannot, by its own nature, function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to another word-meaning, verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) would be untenable in cases such as "one who goes through the sky" (*ākāśagāmī*). [As for example: whatever is the delimitor of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), the connection of another word-meaning like "blue" occurs only with the pot as delimited by that [pot-ness], and not with pot-ness itself. For this very reason, one does not use the expression "the pot is eternal" (*nityo ghaṭaḥ*) with the intention of connecting "eternal" with pot-ness.
Furthermore, there is the untenability of the restrictive rule that the connection of another word-meaning occurs only with that which is delimited by the delimitor of the relatum.

Nor does it follow that the usage "ākāśaḥ śabdāśrayaḥ" (space is the substratum of sound) would be untenable when space is understood from the word "ākāśa" as being the substratum of sound; for in that case, [it is understood] as being a substance other than the eight substances.

There is no fault [in our position], because we accept the denotative power (*śakti*) of that word even when it is characterized by being expressible as "space" (*ākāśa*); furthermore, the determination [of the meaning] occurs through the intended purport (*tātparya*). Nor should it be argued that a denotative power for a single substratum (*dharmin*) delimited by multiple attributes is unprecedented; for such an argument lacks a proving reason (*aprayojakatva*). There is no fault, because we simply admit that there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) wherein those very attributes serve as the delimiters of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*). This should be understood similarly in cases where a word like *dravya* (substance), which possesses a power delimited by a universal, is used with the intention of referring to gold or the like.

In the same way, it should be understood that even when one employs a word capable of denoting a thing qualified by a specific property with the intention of producing a cognition whose qualificandum is qualified by a general property, the same principle applies.

Just as it is logical that the word *svarga* (heaven), which is incapable of denoting a pleasure unmixed with suffering, possesses a secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) when applied to pleasure in general; for there is the empirical observation that no cognition occurs by abandoning a portion of the primary motivating factor (*pravṛttinimitta*). In such a cognition, regarding that specific form, the cause is the knowledge of the power (*śakti*) which apprehends the state of being the delimiting property of the objecthood (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatva*) as determined by the cognition of the constituent parts of that power. Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the meaning]. For this very reason, in cases such as "the hamlet is on the Gaṅgā," there is the presentation [of the bank] by way of its nature as a bank (*tīratva*), and so forth.

It is thus consistent that from the staff there is the presentation of the jar by way of its being a jar, and from the jar there is the presentation of the staff by way of its being a staff. [Note: Here, the term "jāti" (genus) is an illustration for any respective basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*); therefore, there is no defect even if "spatiality" (*ākāśatva*), "potness" (*ghaṭatva*), and so forth lack the status of being a genus. For if the denotative power (*śakti*) were restricted to the genus alone, then in cases such as "one should give a cow," there would be an inconsistency because it is impossible to give "cowness" (*gotva*).

Furthermore, some maintain that there is no cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because such a cognition occurs even when the basis for indication—the relation with the denotable object (*śakyasambandha*)—is not apprehended; moreover, it would involve the unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating two distinct functions (*vṛtti*) in every sentence that conveys a qualified cognition. Others, however, hold that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" resides in the universal (*dharma* = *jāti*) alone, rather than in the various individuals, because the latter would entail excessive complexity. Nor can there be a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding each individual, for if that were the case, one would have to resort to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for other individuals. [In this view, the definition holds: the universal is inherent (*samaveta*) in the individual (*sva* = *vyakti*), and the state of being the locus of that inherence (*tatsamavāyitva*) belongs to the individual.]

The relation [of the word] is "inherence-in-that-which-is-inherent-in-itself" (*svasamavetasamavāyitva*); this is the simplicity [of the theory that the word denotes the universal], given that the power [of the word] resides in the universal (*jāti*). [In this case, *sva* = the universal; its inherence is in the individual. Similarly, [the relation] is "inherence-in-itself" (*svasamavāyitva*)—this is the meaning of the relation—and thus there is simplicity.

Furthermore, even by the proponent of the individual (*vyaktivādin*), in order to avoid the faults of infinite regress (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it must necessarily be admitted that the individual is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); for this very reason, the establishment of a uniform cognition is achieved.

And thus, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), that [universal] alone should be the denotatum; for it is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a power (*śakti*) in the individual and the status of being its delimitant (*avacchedakatva*) in the universal. Just as, according to you, the state of being the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatā*) in the universal is itself undelimited (*niravacchinna*), so too the power resides in it in that very same way; therefore, there is no suspicion of cumbersomeness due to the introduction of [properties] such as "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*). For this very reason, it is logically consistent that in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the individual is a qualifier (*prakāra*) by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) alone.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *go* (cow) is not capable [of denoting itself], the apprehension of a power (*śakti*) devoid of a locus (*nirdharmaka*) is impossible—on the grounds that the initial apprehension of power consists of an inference, and there can be no inference lacking a property-delimiting locus (*dharmitāvacchedaka*). For in this view, we accept that the apprehension of power is precisely one in which the word is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and the cognition constituting the power is qualified by the universal *gotva* (cowness) and so forth; thus, there is no fault.

There is no rule that a universal (*jāti*) is a qualifier (*prakāra*) by its very nature solely through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); for in cases such as "I know the pot," one accepts that pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth function as qualifiers with respect to the cognition and other factors even through the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāritā*). For this very reason, there is no denotative power (*śakti*) in the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). [The underlying principle is: "A cognition does not apprehend the qualified without having grasped the qualifier. The meaning is that a cognition whose object is the qualifier does not penetrate the qualified;
the essential point is that the property of having the qualified as its object is necessarily dependent upon the property of having the qualifier as its object.

And thus, since on the theory of the denotation of qualified entities (viśiṣṭaśaktivāda) the apprehension of the qualified denotation necessarily involves the qualifier as its object, it is more appropriate—due to parsimony (lāghava)—to postulate that the state of having the qualifier as an object alone serves as the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) for the causality of the presentation of word-meanings and so forth, rather than postulating the state of having both [qualifier and qualificand] as objects. Therefore, the resulting conclusion is that the denotative power (śakti) must be admitted to reside in the universal (jāti) alone; for by the maxim "that which has not grasped the qualifier [cannot grasp the qualified]," it is necessary that the universal be the denoted meaning, and it is therefore fitting that the power resides in that very [universal].

But if this were so, there would be the following objection: in cases such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), the connection with actions like carrying or milking would be untenable. Nor can it be argued that there is no fault because, even if the genus (*jāti*) is precluded from direct connection, its connection is admitted through a mediated relation; for in cases such as "A cow is born" (*gauḥ jātā*), there would result the cognition of *gotvatva* (cowness-ness) and the like as the delimiting factor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*) within the genus-cow, which serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, this would entail the inclusion of that [genus-ness] within the primary denotative power (*śakti*). This is because of the rule that even a genus appears by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*) only as a qualifier (*prakāra*).

If it is argued that the denotative power (*vyakti-śakti*) of those words is indeed established because there is no dispute regarding their capacity to produce the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*), to this they reply: we disagree with you regarding the existence of a denotative power for the individual, but rather regarding its being the cause of the knowledge of that power. For this very reason, it is said that the power is "crooked" (*kubjā*) with respect to the individual portion, because the knowledge of that [power] is not required for that portion.

It is precisely because of this that the individual (vyakti) is not denoted. For the status of being denoted by a word is governed solely by the fact that the object of the knowledge of the word's power (*śaktijñāna*) is the very same object that serves as the determinant for the production of the verbal cognition (*śābdadhī*). Just as, although there exists a "crooked" power (*kubjaśakti*) with respect to the relational aspect (*anvaya*), having that relation as its object is not the determinant for the capacity to produce the knowledge of the power; likewise, although it exists with respect to the individual aspect, since having the individual as its object is not the determinant for the capacity to produce the knowledge of the power, there is no conventional usage of "denotability" (*vācyatva*) regarding the individual.
And because it is precisely the state of having "cowness" (*gotva*) as its object that is introduced [as the determinant], cowness and so forth possess denotability.

And thus, on this view, even the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*)—namely, that "the cow is denotable by the word *go*"—can be explained simply by the fact that the individual (*vyakti*) is not included within the delimiting factors (*avacchedaka*) of the causal relation between the cognition and the utterance. However, since its causality exists as a cognition having "cow-ness" (*gotva*) as its qualifier, without including the individual as its objective content (*viṣayatā*), the non-denotability of the individual is established. Consequently, the term "crookedness" (*kubjatva*) is applied to that aspect [of the potency]. On the other hand, according to the view that the apprehension of potency has the word itself as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the potency is called "crooked" precisely because it does not depend upon the cognition of that [individual].

Thus, in the theory of the expressive power residing in the individual (vyakti-śakti-vāda), regarding the aspect of the genus (jāti): "If the chest or the back becomes successively elevated and painful, when the provoked Vāyu produces this condition, one should designate it as Kumbaja."

Thus, the characteristics of a hunchback are set forth in Āyurveda. Just as such a person, being unable to perform any action with his deformed limb, accomplishes activities such as eating by means of his unimpaired hands, feet, and so forth; likewise, the potency (*śakti*) of a word—which is not present prior to verbal cognition, and for that reason is unknown in the word and not defined by the aspect of syntactic relation (*anvaya*)—does not assist in verbal cognition. However, when that potency is known, it certainly does assist in verbal cognition.

Although the state of being humpbacked as defined by the aforementioned characteristics is indeed a property of a conscious being, nevertheless, because of this common attribute, it is superimposed here upon the unconscious power (*śakti*); this is the essential point. Thus, it should be understood that "the Power is humpbacked."

As for what the Bhaṭṭas say—that from the word there is neither recollection nor experience of the individual (vyakti), nor is there a "crooked" (*kubjā*) power (*śakti*) residing therein, but rather an implication (*ākṣepa*); and that it is the universal (*jāti*) alone which implies [the individual]; and that this implication is an inference (*anumāna*), where there is no lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) because the universal implies the individual through identity (*tādātmya*) or as its substrate—this is not correct. For such a presentation of the reason (*hetu*) is not universal, and because the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is not presented from the word "cow" in such a form [as being the locus of the property to be proved].

Furthermore, if the denoted individual (ākṣepitavyakti) were to be construed as the object (karman) and so forth, there would be a violation of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). [Note: It should also be understood that this is for the purpose of excluding things such as space (*ākāśa*) or Caitra—which are presented through the cognition of one related member when hearing the word "pot"—from being objects of the verbal cognition produced by the word "pot."]

In order to prevent the cognition of a positive relation (*anvaya*) in cases such as "This smoke is burning," it must be accepted that the recollection of word-meanings produced by words is a cause of verbal cognition; otherwise, there would be no occurrence of the connection with other word-meanings implied [by the sentence]. By this, the view that "implication" (*ākṣepa*) is "presumption" (*arthāpatti*) is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that the requirement of being cognized by the same cognition (*samānasaṃvitsaṃvedyatva*) entails [the presence of the universal]; for in the cognition of a jar as "substance" (*dravyam*), there is no cognition of "jarness" (*ghaṭatva*). However, in cases such as "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is construed with the objecthood (*karmatva*) through a mediated relation consisting in its residing in the same locus as its own substratum; because, through that relation, the possession of cowness is pervaded by the cow and so forth via the relation of inherence (*ādheyatā*), and because it would otherwise be logically untenable (*anupapatti*) without the existence of a cow.

The view that—although an individual such as a cow appears in verbal cognition as a constituent of the relation by way of implication (ākṣepa), since the cognition has the individual as its qualifier through relations such as being the object of the act of bringing (ānayanakarmatva) or being the locus (ādheyatva)—nevertheless, one still resorts to implication in order to ensure that the individual qualified by "cowness" (gotva) appears within the aspect of the objecthood (karmatva) and so forth; and that the recollection of the universal from a word is strictly indeterminate (nirvikalpaka)—this [view] is also flawed, because of what was stated previously.

The followers of Maṇḍana maintain that there is indication (*lak�ṣaṇā*) with respect to the individual (*vyakti*) of that which has its power [of denotation] residing in the universal (*jāti*). Their view is as follows: through indication, the cognition is indeed one in which the universal is the primary object; thus, there is no contradiction with experience. This is because, just as words such as "blue" convey their meaning through indication by way of the quality of blueness—which is their direct denotation (*śakya*)—the word "cow" and others likewise convey their meaning through indication by way of the universal, which is their direct denotation. Indication occurs when an object is known under a form other than its own direct denotation.

"But this [usage] is merely common," you say. That is not so; for in the case of an individual (*vyakti*), is the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) unconditioned or conditioned? Not the first, because it is impossible. Nor the second; for on that view, one must admit that the universal (*jāti*) itself is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). And thus, since the appearance of the universal is established by its very status as the delimitant of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), the postulation of a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for it is redundant. Nor should one assume a primary power there in order to establish indication in the form of a relation with the primary meaning (*śakyasambandha*);
for in that case, since power would have no independent utility, it could not be established as a function (*vṛtti*).

Now, it might be argued that by the Gautama-sūtra, "The meaning of a word is genus, configuration, and individual," and by demonstrating through experience that even configuration (*ākṛti*)—in the form of a specific structure—is understood from words such as "cow," others accept that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the individual qualified by both genus and configuration. In that case, since the genus is a qualifier of the individual through the direct relation of inherence (*samavāya*), it possesses the status of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); however, since configuration, which consists of the conjunction of parts, is a qualifier through an indirect succession consisting of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it does not possess that status.
In expressions such as "oxen made of flour," there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the cow and so forth as qualified by the mere configuration (*ākṛti*).

And thus, in the theory that the genus (*jāti*) is the denoted meaning, since the configuration—which consists of specific conjunctions of parts—is infinite, it is more appropriate for the single genus alone to be the primary denotation (*śakyārtha*) rather than that [configuration].

Nor can it be argued that the universal residing solely in the conjunctions of parts is what is denoted, and its inherence [in the whole] occurs through a mediated relation involving its own substrata; for experience shows that cognition has the *ākṛti* (configuration) as its qualifier. Furthermore, the absence of usage regarding a bare universal unqualified by the individual does not prove the absence of linguistic power (*śakti*), because such non-usage is not a decisive reason (*aprayojakatvāt*).

If it is argued that there is never the contingency of using the expression "the cow is eternal" based on the mere universal (*jāti*) alone—because it is a matter of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that a universal, when presented through its own form by virtue of its expressive power (*śakti*), can only be construed with the substratum (the individual) denoted by the same word, and that such construal occurs only through the relation of being the locus (*āśrayatā*)—we say: no. For, in this way, it would be more appropriate to posit a qualified expressive power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) itself, rather than postulating that even the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is a cause for such a cognition, which would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, it is proper to maintain that there is a "crooked power" (*kubja-śakti*), and that the cognition [of the qualified object] arises through suggestion (*vyañjanā*); thus it is concluded.

In reality, however, since both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are presented through the very power of denotation (*jāti-śakti*) once that power is known, it depends on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*): sometimes the genus is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the individual is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and sometimes the individual is the qualificand and the genus is the qualifier. And thus, while the connection with the horse and so forth belongs to the genus through a mediated sequence (*paramparā*), the individual alone is the delimiting factor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedikā*). Consequently, in the view that [the genus] is connected through a mediated sequence, the previously mentioned defect does not apply.

For this very reason, the rules *jātyākhyāyāmekasmin* (Pāṇini 1.2.58) and *jātiraprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6) are consistent. Furthermore, for this same reason, the usage found in the Bhāṣya and other works—that when the genus (*jāti*) is predominant, it is a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*), whereas when the individual (*vyakti*) is predominant, it is a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*)—is also consistent. [Note: Here is the distinction: Since the formation of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is established by the rule *sarūpāṇāmekaśeṣaḥ*, it is proven that the individual (*vyakti*) is indeed the meaning of the word; however, it is not the case that the individual alone is so. This is because even though the word-meaning is the individual qualified by the genus (*jāti*), the commencement of that *ekaśeṣa* rule is nonetheless necessary.]

Since the author of the Bhāṣya has rejected the inclusion of the term *aṇ* [in Pāṇini 4.1.83], and since it is established in the original treatises (*ākara*) that the rule on "homogeneity" (*sarūpa-sūtra*) serves merely as a guide for the formal grammatical process (*śāstrīyaprakriyāmātra*), it follows that neither of these two [arguments] proves that the individual alone is the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Therefore, the reality is that those who maintain the view that only the individual is denoted have recourse solely to common usage (*vyavahāra*).

In reality, however, the word-meaning is indeed the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). Although from the Bhāṣya passage, "For one for whom the form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, the substance (*dravya*) is not the word-meaning," and so forth, it appears that the word-meaning consists of the form and the individual (*vyakti*) as distinct entities, nevertheless, upon considering the subsequent Bhāṣya—"For one [entity] is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), while for another it is primary (*pradhāna*)"—the expressive power (*śakti*) is determined to reside in the qualified entity.

This should be applied to all positions: since it is only the cognition of the word’s power with respect to a genus (*jāti*) that causes the understanding of an individual qualified by that genus, there is no understanding of the individual from words such as *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness). Others hold that only the cognition of the power residing in a genus, as expressed by a word not containing an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), is the cause for that [understanding of the] individual.

Thus, in cases such as *śukla* (white) and *śabda* (sound), which denote a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the quality (*guṇa*) is the denoted object; in *śakya* (capable) and *pācaka* (cook), it is the action (*kriyā*); and in *ḍittha* and the like, it is the word itself. In that regard, the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) occurs in this manner: "the word *ḍittha* has potency with respect to that which possesses the word *ḍittha*. Nor is there an impossibility of such an apprehension of potency, on the grounds that prior to the apprehension of potency, the qualification by that word cannot be grasped through any other means of knowledge. This is because that qualification is grasped through the general relation (*sambandhasāmānya*), or else there is no fault, just as in the case of the cognition of a future name (*bhāvisaṃjñā*).

And because the property of being the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka) is precisely the state of being a cognition whose qualifier is the word, related by the relation of denotative power (vācakatā), there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Now, one might object: "How can words such as *pācaka* (cook) be said to possess the power to denote action? Since the root *pac* has power with respect to the action and the suffix *aka* has power with respect to the agent, and since there is mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) between the two meanings presented by those respective words due to expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the word *pācaka* itself lacks any denotative power. This is not so; for examples such as *kumbhakāra* (pot-maker) and others, which fall under the category of "single-meaning integration" (*ekārthībhāva*), remain valid here.

In reality, however, because the rule *kartari kṛt* [Pāṇini 3.4.67] has a single homogeneous meaning, there is also a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) in words such as *pācaka*. For this very reason, there is no syntactic connection with the relation of subject and predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*) from words like *pācaka*; such is the general direction of the argument.

In reality, even though qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth may also be denotable, because of the presence of infinite extension (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is the very genus (*jāti*) residing in the quality that is the denotable meaning there as well. Likewise, in the case of "cook" (*pācaka*) and the like, it is the genus residing in the action; for although the acts of cooking jaggery, rice, and so on are distinct, one accepts a single genus-form called "cook-ness" (*pākatva*). Even in the case of "Dittha" and so forth, it is the genus residing in the word "Dittha" and the like; for the words "Dittha" and so on are manifold due to differences in their utterance by parrots and others. The denotation of the word "space" (*ākāśa*) and the like has already been explained.

Alternatively, they say that even "space-ness" (*ākāśatva*)—which is a genus or an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*)—is the denotable meaning, as it remains constant despite the distinctions between different cosmic cycles (*kalpa*).

Others hold that since a word necessarily denotes an individual qualified by a universal (*jāti*), it is possible for there to exist even in that case a *śakti* (denotative power) consisting in the capacity to convey meaning. Furthermore, regarding the cognition of an individual as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) with "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as the qualifier (*prakāra*), the cause is simply the knowledge of the *śakti* having "pot-ness" as its qualifier; thus, there is no complexity (*gaurava*). Nor does this imply that individuals are understood from words such as "pot-ness. For it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "It is not the case that for one who holds the universal to be the word-meaning, the substance is not the word-meaning; nor is it the case that for one who holds the substance to be the word-meaning, the universal is not the word-meaning. This is what others say.

In these three positions, although the gender (*liṅga*) is not directly denoted by the suffix, there is no lack of gender-distinction; for it is accepted that words possess their respective genders precisely by virtue of being suffixes that denote those specific genders. This is appropriate because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), suffixes such as *ṭāp* are prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the feminine" (*striyām*), and because of grammatical injunctions such as "after that [word ending in a short vowel], *śas* becomes *naḥ* in the masculine" (*tasmācchaso naḥ pusi*). The same should be understood regarding number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that even the gender (liṅga) is indeed the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāman*). For if it were the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), there would follow the consequence that either the state of being female (*strītvam*) or the female entity itself would be the primary referent. Even if the capacity [of the suffix] resides in the individual (*vyakti*), what is established by experience is the cognition of a "goat-cow" (*ajā*) as having attained identity with femininity, and not a cognition of a female entity as having attained identity with the class-property (*jāti*) of "goat-ness. [Note: The phrase "from the word *aja*" is to be supplied.]

Furthermore, since the feminine gender is understood even without the suffix *ṅīp* in words such as *vāk*, it is necessary that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself possesses the expressive power (*śakti*) for that gender; thus, there is the burden (*gaurava*) of postulating an additional power for the suffix *ṅīp*. Moreover, the grammatical rules for gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) are observed to apply to the nominal stem alone. For this very reason, the term "other than *ktin*" (*aktinaḥ*) in the Vārttika "from a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix marker, other than *ktin*" (*kṛdikārād aktinaḥ*) is purposeful. Otherwise, since the feminine gender would already have been expressed by *ktin*, the suffix *ṅīp* would not apply, and its inclusion in the rule would clearly be redundant.

For this very reason, in cases such as *vyāvakruṣṭī*, even though the suffix *añ* is prescribed for the feminine by the rule *ṇacaḥ striyām añ* [Pāṇini 5.4.14], the feminine suffix is nonetheless established. Nor can it be argued that, according to your view as well, a feminine suffix would not apply because the meaning is already expressed by the base (*prakṛti*) itself; for that which is expressed by the base does not function as a differentiator (*avyāvartaka*). Otherwise, the rules prescribing suffixes such as *ṭāp* would become redundant. This is the general direction of the argument. Now, one might object: "A woman is defined by her breasts and hair, while a man is said to be characterized by body hair."

If it is argued that there would be no occurrence of the feminine suffix because a gender-mark (*liṅga*)—defined by such characteristics as a specific configuration of parts—is sublated in insentient objects like a bedstead (*khaṭvā*), and furthermore, that in cases such as *dārān* (wives), the substitution of *n* for *t* would not occur because the referent lacks masculinity; [we reply: no, for the application is possible through superimposition (*āropa*). And some hold that the grammatical instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) is the authority for this superimposition.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, [explains]: the increase of the qualities of primordial matter (prakṛti)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is masculinity; decrease is femininity; and mere persistence is neuter-ness. For this very reason, even though there is increase and decrease, by taking mere persistence as the basis, the objection regarding the rule "the neuter is used for the general" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*) is resolved. Its meaning is that the neuter gender occurs when one intends to express mere persistence, which is common to all three states: increase, decrease, and equilibrium.

Since these three states exist in every category of object (*padārtha*), this [reason] is purely positive (*kevalānvayi*); and because the linguistic usages "this individual," "this thing," and "this category" proceed everywhere without obstruction, it is also grounded in the object itself. Thus, the Bhāṣya states: "In a single object, a difference in gender is observed due to a difference in words and due to a difference in constituent parts."

The meaning is that there is a single object [denoted by] *puṣyaḥ*, *tārakā*, and *nakṣatram*; this is because we observe a plurality of words [for the same thing]. Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa states that the gender (*liṅga*) is indeed distinct from the breast, hair, and so forth, because we observe a difference in gender when the phoneme *r* is added as a constituent part, as in the pair "kuṭī" (feminine) and "kuṭīraḥ" (masculine).

However, the expression "a word in the masculine gender" (*puṃlliṅgaḥ śabdaḥ*) should be understood through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the denoted object and the denoting word, or alternatively, as a derivative formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 5.2.127 (*arśa-ādy-ac*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the Self is thus unchanging, the word ‘Brahman’ would not incur neuter gender due to the absence of these [qualities]; for since everything is superimposed (adhyasta) upon the Self as its cause, those qualities exist there too by way of a traditional succession (paramparayā). For this very reason, there are such conventional usages as “the Self is Brahman” and so forth. Nor does this imply that increase and the like must necessarily be regarded as momentary, on account of the statement in the Bhāṣya: “Not even for a moment does any quality such as existence remain in the Self; it either increases until it has reached its full measure of growth, or it is joined with diminution. [This is not so.]

And thus, it should not be argued that the conventional usage of terms such as "possessing both genders" would be untenable; for conventional usage does not depend upon the existence of an object at the same time as the usage itself. For this very reason, conventional usage regarding past and future objects is logically consistent.

Nor should it be argued that even so, because contradictory properties such as growth (*upacaya*) cannot coexist in one place, a single entity would fail to possess all three genders; for, according to the authority of the lexicons (*kośa*) and other sources, there is no contradiction at all. It is to be determined from the grammatical treatises on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) and similar authorities that some words are denotative of an object qualified by only one gender, some by two genders, and others by all three. Thus, by the word *madhu*, only honey and the like—qualified by both growth and stability—are expressed, whereas Caitra and the like are expressed when qualified by growth alone; this too is to be determined from those very same sources.

And in these cases, the technical convention (*saṃketa*) for words such as *pum* and so on is established by the science of grammar (*śāstra*), just like [the technical terms] *vṛddhi* and so forth. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "One must necessarily adopt some established conclusion (*svakṛtānta*). In that context, since it would be more appropriate to employ a concise designation (*laghubhūta-sañjñā*)—similar to the *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha* designations—the fact that a cumbersome designation (*gurubhūta-sañjñā*) is employed indicates that when rules concerning [the substitution of] *natva* and so forth are to apply, even worldly gender (*liṅga*) is accepted as a cause (*nimitta*). In cases where such worldly [gender] is impossible, [the cause] is restricted to that which is technical (*śāstrīya*) alone.

But when that [application] is possible, [the term applies] to the worldly [object] as qualified by the scriptural [meaning], through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and not to the purely worldly nor to the purely scriptural, due to the force of the employment of the technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*). This is because, although the conventions such as "masculine" (*puṃs*) and so on are employed for the purpose of including other meanings—just as the technical name "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is used—they are not employed for the purpose of excluding other meanings. For this very reason, in cases such as "Look at the *cañcās*," one accepts that only the masculine and so on, as qualified by diminution, appear due to the inherent nature of the word's power; thus [it is stated]: "In the case of *lup*, it is like what is joined [to the suffix]."

The rejection of the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.51] by the rule "tadaśiṣyam" [Pāṇini 1.2.53] is thus consistent. Otherwise, since the status of being like the masculine (yuktavadbhāva) would extend even to non-existence, the grammatical operation conditioned by masculinity would not apply; however, in the case of its rejection, that operation does apply—thus there would be a difference in the result.

And thus, when [the term] *striyām* (in the feminine) or *paśunā* (with the animal) and so forth are employed, it refers only to the scriptural gender (*śāstrīyaliṅga*), not to the absence [of gender] and so on. But when used in reference to a male animal (*puṃpaśu*), it refers to the worldly [gender] as qualified by the scriptural [rule]. For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that since masculinity is intended to be significant in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), there is no sacrifice performed with a female animal.

In this context, the phrase "of masculinity" (puṃstvasya) means "of worldly masculinity" (laukikapuṃstvasya). Furthermore, according to the principle of the final section of the sixth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], namely "Or the goat [is the animal], because of the wording of the mantra," there exists—in the case of the specific animal, the goat, as well as in the case of the wording of the mantra—a factor that indicates the intention (*tātparya*) to express worldly masculinity. This is because in the mantra "of the omentum of the goat" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*), the term "of the goat" (*chāgasya*) which is recited there cannot apply to anything other than a goat, nor can it apply to a female.

Because the word *chāga*, ending in the vowel *-ā*, is not used for a female individual, it is held that its denotative power (*śakti*) resides in that which is qualified by a technical masculinity (*pāribhāṣika-puṃstva*) co-referential with worldly masculinity (*laukika-puṃstva*).

They further maintain that grammatical gender (*śāstrīya-liṅga*), like worldly gender, appears in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), because such is our experience and because of the authority of lexicons and other sources. However, in the *Vākyapadīya*, three types of genus (*jāti*) are stated; there too, the process of derivation is exactly as before:
"These three genera alone are established in some [theories]."
They are not opposed by the opposing classes of beings, such as humans and others.

Thus it has been stated. However, some maintain that gender (*liṅga*) is purely technical (*pāribhāṣika*) and resides in the word itself; for common usage such as "the word is masculine" cannot be considered figurative (*gauṇa*) in the absence of a subverting factor. Furthermore, the rule *bhāṣitapuṃskāt* is justified because the words are distinct due to the difference in their meanings. Difference in gender, however, is not a cause for [grammatical] distinction, since we observe usage such as "this is one word which possesses two genders. In that context, masculinity indicates the absence [of femininity], while the suffix *ṭāp* and others indicate femininity and so forth.

And that [gender], although residing in the word, accompanies the object denoted by the word as a delimiter of its meaning; for it is established by the science of grammatical gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) that a specific gender qualifies the capacity of a word to denote a specific object. This is because it is logically possible for gender to function as a differentiator of the object through the relation of being denotable by its own substratum. For this very reason, there is also a restriction on ritual application. Thus, in the case of the expression *paśunā* ("with an animal"), since masculinity functions as a delimiter, there is no sacrifice with a female animal.

Nor can it be argued that because the word *paśu* is eternally masculine, it excludes female animals—just as the gender expressed by words such as *padārtha* is common to all genders—since the phrase "bring a *paśu*" (*paśvānaya*) is seen in the Ṛgveda, which leads to the conclusion that its masculinity is intended to be significant; furthermore, this does not establish its eternal masculinity, as the matter is resolved according to the principle of the final section of the sixth book [of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra], namely, "Or rather, a goat [is meant], on account of the wording of the mantra" (*chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*).

Just as in the case of the expression "two rams for Sarasvatī" (*sārasvatau meṣau*), where there arises a doubt as to whether the base of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is feminine or masculine, the determination that both are included by means of the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation is resolved by the principle "when there is doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (*asandigdhe tu vākyaśeṣāt*), based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "This indeed is the divine pair."

Nor does it follow that, because a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) possesses a gender common to both sentient and insentient beings and a gender common to both male and female, there would be the undesirable consequence of giving the seal to Yajñadattā as well when there is an injunction such as, "Devadatta and Yajñadattā are to be brought, and this seal is to be given to her. There is no such fault, because the pronoun, by recalling the previously presented object through its specific form, refers back to that previously presented object as distinguished [from others]—just as it recalls Devadatta specifically by his identity as Devadatta—and likewise by his masculinity. Thus, there is no error.

For this very reason, although words such as *śukla* (white) denote a quality (*guṇa*) as an additional element when referring to a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), it is logical that they are dependent upon the substantive (*viśeṣya*) because they function as a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the gender and number expressed by the word denoting the substantive. For this same reason, when there is an intention to express only the general referent (*padārtha-mātra*), since the gender in the form of excellence or deficiency of a quality is not intended to be expressed, the rule "the neuter is used for the generic" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*) is appropriately established with reference to usage in a state of unavoidable equality.

They say that, according to the maxim of the "general singular number" (*autsargikaikavacana*), words such as *dāra* (wife), which do not abandon their gender (*ajahalliṅga*) and are invariably plural, are used in that way even when the gender does not determine the meaning—as if they referred to a single entity. Furthermore, they maintain that the "triplet" (*trika*)—namely, gender, number, and case-role—is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*), whereas number and case-role are indeed the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). This is because it is more appropriate to assume the expressive power (*śakti*) for the suffixes themselves in those two respects, rather than assuming such power for an infinite number of stems.

Others, however, maintain that number is indeed the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) itself, because in cases such as *dadhi* (curd) and *madhu* (honey), that [number] is understood even without a suffix. Furthermore, the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating an infinite number of delimiters for the expressive power (*śakti*) is not a defect, as it is "aimed at the result" (*phalamukha*). This is because, since the cognition is grasped even from the base alone, those [bases] must necessarily be regarded as causes of that cognition; thus, there is no need to postulate anything else.

However, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) must be avoided by accepting that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with specific case-endings is the cause for the cognition of those respective numbers. And they say that this [requirement] is necessary even for you [the opponent], in order to prevent the cognition [of number] from arising from the sentence "This is a jar" (*ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*).

Some, however, say that the *kāraka* (case-role) is likewise [to be understood in this way]. If it is objected that, if this were so, principles such as "In the cognition where the meaning of a noun is the qualifier (*prakāra*), the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a *su*-affix and the like is the cause" would be undermined, we reply: No; for this is consistent when one takes the meaning indicated (*dyotya*) by the case-ending into account. All these positions are clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sarūpa* rule and elsewhere; this is the general direction.
[Note: "The individual meaning, gender, number, and also the object [of action] and so forth—these five alone are the meanings of a noun; for some, the first three are [the meanings]. ]
Thus, the meaning is that there are five positions.
Herein is the distinction: mere number is the meaning of the case-ending (vibhakti), while the other four are the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika).
And so it has been said:

"Or the case-endings of the dual and so forth may be expressive (*dyotikā*) of gender and the rest. This is the intended meaning: one must accept that in words such as *ghaṭa* (pot), there is a distinct power (*śakti*) for each [gender, number, and case] as determined by their respective markers (*liṅga*). Furthermore, even though these meanings are presented by a single word, they enter into mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*) due to the variety of their mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). In that context, gender and number function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), while the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) functions as the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Alternatively, because the *kāraka* is also indicative (*dyotaka*), it may function as a qualifier.

If the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) were to possess a meaning qualified by gender and number, there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a separate expressive power (*śakti*) for that which is qualified by singularity and that which is qualified by duality and so forth; furthermore, there would be the impossibility of accounting for variegated cognitions (*citrabodha*), such as "the form of a cow" (*gorūpam*), where number does not appear. Some maintain that in the view where word-meanings are discrete (*viśakalita-padārtha*), such a cognition is accounted for because [the nominal stem] lacks the function of indicating the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-grāhakatva*).

Others, however, say that—just like a verbal root—the expressive power resides only in the qualified entity; since they accept a separate power even for that which is qualified merely by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so on, they maintain that the production of a cognition devoid of number and other such qualifiers is thereby accounted for.

Some, however, say that the following explanation must be accepted: "In the case of verbal cognition (śābdabodha) where the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is the qualifier (*prakāraka*), the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by suffixes such as *su*," and so forth; thus, the explanation is achieved by taking the meaning manifested (*dyotya*) by the inflection (*vibhakti*). Others, however, maintain that even in the absence of that [manifested meaning], there is simply the acceptance of the desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because since the manifested meaning functions as a qualifier, such a cognition does not exist at all. Nor can the matter be resolved through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because in cases such as "He says *jabagada*," the primary meaning (*śakya*) is not apprehended, and therefore a metaphorical indication—which consists of a relation to that primary meaning—cannot be apprehended. Furthermore, cognition occurs even without the consideration of sublation (*bādha*) and other such conditions.

Furthermore, in the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), if there is a distinction between the object of imitation (*anukārya*) and the imitation itself (*anukaraṇa*), or if that distinction is intended (*vivakṣā*), then even a word is the denotable meaning (*śakya*) of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For instance, in examples such as *paṭad iti kuru* ("Do this, making the sound 'paṭat'"), the difference from the sounds being imitated is established through the perception of contradictory properties, such as consisting of articulated sounds (*dhvani*) versus consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*). In cases such as the rule *bhuvo vuk*, however, the distinction is due to the intention (*vivakṣā*) [to treat the item] either as having a meaning as its referent (*arthapadārthakatva*) or as having a word-form as its referent (*śabdapadārthakatva*).

And thus, in that case, a denotative power (*śakti*) must necessarily be admitted both for the sake of bringing that [meaning] to mind and for the sake of establishing its status as an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). For this very reason, since it possesses "meaningfulness" (*arthavatva*)—defined as the capacity to convey meaning through a *vṛtti* (linguistic relation)—it attains the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); consequently, when suffixes such as the nominative (*su*) arise, the substitution of *jaś* (the replacement of *s* by *r*, etc. is established. However, when there is an intention to express their non-difference (*abheda*), it manifests in the verbal cognition itself as presented to the auditory organ; in that case, no independent assumption of a *vṛtti* is made.

For instance—the rule that "only that which possesses a *vṛtti* (linguistic relation) is the object of verbal cognition" is postulated in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And even under the rule that "that which possesses a *vṛtti* through either the relation of *nirūpakatā* (defining property) or *āśrayatā* (substratum) is its object," there is still no status as an object of verbal cognition for that [which lacks such a relation].

Now, if this were the case, it would necessarily have to be stated that, in order to exclude even a jar or the like—which is presented through perception—from being an object of verbal cognition, the cause of verbal cognition is the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) produced by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the *vṛtti*.

If it is asked: "Even though there is possession of a function (*vṛtti*) here and there is the presentation [of the word] through the auditory organ, how can it be the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), given that it is merely the object of such a presentation?"—to this they reply: It is established by experience that the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) in a general form—namely, "The phonemes beginning with *ga* have power toward some [object], because they are phonemes (*varṇatvāt*); the word 'night' (*nakta*) has power toward some [object], because it is a correct word (*sādhupadatvāt*)"—is the cause for a cognition in which the word is the qualifier (*prakāra*) by way of the relation of being denoted (*vācyatva*). This apprehension takes the form: "There exists some object denoted by that word."

For this very reason, when words whose meanings are unknown—such as the word *caitra*, *gavaya*, or *nala*—are heard, and a question is asked such as "What is the meaning of this?", one observes both the questioning and the subsequent answer, such as "A certain king by that name," provided through means like comparison (*upamāna*) or the statement of its definition. It is for this reason that they establish the authority of comparison (*upamāna*) and other means, since they convey that meaning through similarity and the like; and they establish the authority of lexicons (*kośa*) and so forth, since they convey that meaning through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words.

In this very way, the experience [of meaning] regarding words whose referents are not established is universally established; however, such a cognition does not occur in the manner of specific universals (jāti) and so forth, as it does with words like "jar" (*ghaṭa*), because such a cognition is impossible. This is due to the absence of any means for grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) in the form of "nal-ness" (*nalatva*) and so forth, which makes it impossible for the word to convey meaning through that form.

Nor should one accept the claim of the Neo-Naiyāyikas that beginningless, continuous streams of specific cognitions—whose objects are past Caitras, future Caitras, and so forth, as well as present objects that are not in contact with the senses—are to be postulated because otherwise such specific awareness would be inexplicable; for the reason (hetu) for this is unestablished. Furthermore, it would follow that there would be recollection of these objects even without hearing the words expressive of them. If the restriction [of memory] were dependent on the awakening factors (udbodhaka), then the very causality of cognition and mental impressions (saṃskāra) would be undermined.
Moreover, experience shows that cognition has the word as its qualifier (padaprakāraka). Otherwise, the aforementioned questions and so forth would be rendered impossible.

Furthermore, for those who hear of Caitra—who is well-known in another region—in Kāśī, there occurs an experience of cognition even though they have not grasped a specific relation [of denotation], just as in the case of words such as *nal*. If, in accordance with that experience, one were to admit the existence of a specific grasp of denotative power (*śaktigraha*) arising from beginningless latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), then for those very same people at a later time, upon seeing him on the bank of the Gaṅgā, there would be no cognition from the sentence "Caitra is not here. This is because [the required] knowledge of the absence of the counter-positive delimited by Caitra-ness, having the state of being on the bank of the Gaṅgā as the delimitor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), would be lacking.

This is because it is universally established that the cognition of Caitra as possessing that [quality], taking that very [quality] as the delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), acts as an inhibitor.

Furthermore, just as for those who have grasped the specific relations [between word and meaning], the recollection of the word would occur upon seeing that [object], and there would be no doubt such as "Is Caitra here or not?

By this, it is also explained that following every experience in the form of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so on, after the aspect of "knowability" is lost, there first arises an indeterminate recollection (*nirvikalpaka-smaraṇa*) regarding that universal (*jāti*); subsequently, by taking up the presentation of each respective object through its respective form, the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*) occurs.

Nor is it correct to claim that the apprehension of all objects would entail omniscience simply because of the occurrence of such an awakening; for memory is restricted to specific instances and times precisely by virtue of the awakening factor, which is itself determined by the force of its own result (the experience). Furthermore, this view is rejected because there is no evidence for postulating such a memory that contradicts actual experience.

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "The apprehension of the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as *varuṇa* occurs through the presentation [of the meaning] by words such as *pāśahasta* (rope-in-hand); nor is there any inconsistency because the apprehension of power for that [word *varuṇa*] would be impossible, since in the case of derivative (*yaugika*) terms there is no requirement to apprehend a power for the whole, and because the components—words such as *pāśa*—have their power apprehended in common usage; the same should be inferred for words such as *adṛṣṭa*. This is refuted because, since there is no presentation by words such as *pāśahasta* in the form of a specific universal (*jāti*), the apprehension of power cannot occur in that form.

Otherwise, when Varuṇa is present before one's eyes, for those who have grasped the word-potency (*śakti*) in words such as "Varuṇa"—just as in your own theory—there would arise the cognition "This is Varuṇa" even upon seeing a mere individual (*vyakti*), despite not seeing the noose (*pāśa*) and so forth, provided they have grasped that potency in words like "noose. For this very reason, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible in cases such as "Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa"; otherwise, it would not occur, just as in the case of "A pot is a pot."

The apprehension of the power (śakti) conducive to a cognition having the word as its qualifier has indeed been stated [previously]. And thus, from words such as "Nala," the resulting cognition occurs precisely in the form "the denotatum of the word 'Nala'," and so forth. Consequently, just as the universal *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) appears in the verbal cognition produced by words like "pot" through the relation of expressive power (*śakti*) as a qualifier of the denotatum, the appearance of the word itself is not untenable. In that case, however, the word-part does not possess the status of being an object of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*), because there is no evidence for it; the required effect is accomplished by the word's being merely the substratum (*āśrayatva*).

And thus, since a relation is defined by both its relata and therefore lacks any distinction in its capacity to present both relata, when the word itself is presented—just like a jar—by means of a power (śakti) delimited by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, and there is an intention to convey the meaning, the word appears as a qualifying attribute; hence there is no fault. In that case too, for those who have grasped the power specifically in the form of "jar-ness" and so forth, from words such as "jar," there arises a cognition in which both the word and the universal are presented as qualifiers.

However, from words such as "Nala" and others, because their unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*) are not presented in the manner previously described, the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) occurs with respect to an individual presented in a general form; consequently, there arises a cognition of the form: "There is some object denoted by the word 'Nala' and so forth, which has a mere individual as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and the mere word as its qualifier (*prakāra*)."

In expressions such as *‘gavityayamāha’* (he says this, being a cow), the intention (*tātparya*) is understood to reside in the word-form alone—either by virtue of the co-occurrence with the word *iti*, or by the force of grammatical rules such as *Pāṇini’s sūtra* 1.1.68 (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā*), or by the force of context and so forth, or by the force of syntactic fitness, expectancy, and so on. In that regard, in cases such as *‘ghaṭo nityaḥ’* (the pot is eternal) or *‘svargī dhvastaḥ’* (the inhabitant of heaven has perished), the mere form of the word itself is primarily conveyed by that power (*śakti*), just like the qualifying portion.

Even though the function (vṛtti) is present, a portion of the meaning is not conveyed due to a lack of intention; or, when there is an intention directed toward only a single part, such as "a pinch" (lava), the horse understood from the word *saindhava* is abandoned.

Nor is it incorrect to say that by the power of the object itself, through the force of *tātparya* (intentional import), the word also appears as the primary [object]; for the very nature of a cognition having that [word] as its qualifier and a particular individual as its qualificandum is what constitutes the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the effect of the knowledge of its [the word's] denotative function (*vṛtti*). Otherwise, in cases such as "The pot is eternal," there would be no secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Indeed, it must be stated that secondary indication is resorted to there precisely for the sake of a cognition [of the word] as the primary [object]; for in that case, secondary indication is accepted in accordance with the cognition [of the word] in the form of "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*), and so forth.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of "pot-ness" (rather than the pot itself). Here, since the letters qualified by a specific sequence constitute the word, even when only that [word] is presented, the sequence appears as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*); thus, the aforementioned fault does not arise. Because the individuality of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) does not appear, the word lacks the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and consequently, its primacy (*prādhānya*) is established by implication.

In the system of the Mīmāṃsakas, just as one accepts the recollection of a mere individual with its qualifiers lost due to all experiences having the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*) as their mode, there is no sublation to the recollection of a mere word with its qualifiers lost; for the co-utterance (syntactic connection) such as "pronounce [it]" is useful precisely for that loss of qualifiers.

Thus, there is no fault, because the knowledge of the word's power (*śakti*) itself is the delimitor of the causal status (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for a cognition where the word is the qualifier. It should be understood that, like the apprehension of power, there is also an apprehension produced by the function (*vṛtti*) through mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), as it is established by means of those impressions.

By this, the following [objections] are refuted: (1) that when one says "utter the word *go*," there would necessarily be the utterance of the modified form (*gav*), because only such a form is presented to the auditory organ; (2) that since the word itself is not the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), there would be no possibility of the accusative case-meaning and so forth being construed with it; and (3) that because the word itself is more rapidly presented through direct perception, there would be a misconception of self-referentiality even in cases such as "the cow exists. This is because, by virtue of the aforementioned intention (*tātparya*), the unmodified form alone is presented from the word through its linguistic function (*vṛtti*).

Nor does this intentional focus (tātparya) alone entail the total abolition of all linguistic functions (vṛtti), for that [intentional focus] is not a cause for linguistic function in general. Rather, in some cases it is the regulator of the validity of a cognition produced by a word, while in other cases it is so even regarding the mere understanding [of meaning]; thus, we shall explain in the section on the Vākya-sphoṭa that there is no way to account for [meaning] without a linguistic function (vṛtti).

This being the case, it is established that when there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*), the word is primary; in its absence, it is merely a qualifier of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*). For this very reason, in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the status of [the term] as a name (*nāmadheya*) is established; because it functions as a qualifier, the sentence-meaning is: "One should bring about the desired result by means of a sacrifice non-different from the *udbhid*. The understanding of it as a technical designation (*sañjñā*) arises from grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is because coreferentiality exists either between a qualifier and a qualificand, or between a name and the thing named.

In that context, since the well-known meaning of the word *udbhid* cannot be syntactically construed with the sacrifice (*yāga*) without resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and since the relationship of qualifier and qualified—as in "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*)—is impossible, the conclusion is reached in the second [alternative] by relying on the word's own denotative power (*padaparatva*). Furthermore, by the term "relationship of qualifier and qualified," there is expressed a relationship of delimitation and delimitedness (*paricchedya-paricchedaka-bhāva*) as determined by a relation other than direct denotation (*vācakatā*).

For it has been clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the question "What is the word here in 'this is a cow'? (*Pāṇini 1.1.1*), as well as in its commentary, the *Kaustubha*, and in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "vṛddhir ādaic" (*Pāṇini 1.1.1*), that there is indeed non-difference between the denoted and the denoter, just as there is between a quality and the possessor of the quality. Furthermore, the word *udbhid* denotes the sacrifice through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

And thus, after that cognition has occurred, once the apprehension of the word’s denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to a sacrifice delimited by the class-property of being a *udbhid*-sacrifice (a sacrifice of a different genus) has taken place, there arises elsewhere the presentation of the sacrifice by the word *udbhid* in that very same form; or else, it is of the nature of having the word itself as its qualifier—this is another point. In cases such as "vṛddhir ādaic" [Pāṇini 1.1.1], the sentence-meaning is "the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are non-different from the word *vṛddhi*. Since the previously mentioned logical inconsistency would arise if one were to understand the non-difference of the well-known referent of the word *vṛddhi* from the referents of the words *ādaic*, the term *artha* (referent) must be intended in both senses [as both the meaning and the word].
There, the sentence-meaning is the non-difference of the word qualified by its referent, through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

And thus, with respect to the named (saṃjñin), the non-difference from the term that constitutes the name (sañjñābhūtapada) is what must be enjoined in these cases. It cannot be argued that, instead, with respect to the term, only the non-difference from the named should be enjoined. For this very reason, one should not say that in the rule "vṛddhir ādaic," there is a mention of *ā*, *ai*, and *au* as subsequent [to the name]; for otherwise, faults would arise in rules such as "adeṅ guṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.1.2]. Furthermore, by the authority of the Bhāṣya—stating, for instance, that the word *vṛddhi* is placed first for the sake of auspiciousness—it is appropriate that the term which is the name itself be the thing enjoined, as is the case with the name-terms *ṭi*, *ghu*, *bha*, and so forth.

Furthermore, because it cannot be the object of a designation (*uddeśya*) due to its not being established by any other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), the establishment of a word through mere pronunciation does not constitute a counter-argument against its being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) in our system; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that [words such as] *paṇa* and so forth could not be enjoined. This is the direction of the argument. However, some say that precisely because of the aforementioned inconsistency, at that very time, words such as *udbhid* have their power (*śakti*) grasped in a general form as denoting that [specific thing], just like the word *nalada*, and it is by that very [grasping of power] that the comprehension occurs.

As for the claim that, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the case of a name (*nāman*), that is not correct; for, as explained above, the desired result is established through the already-established primary power (*śakti*) alone. Furthermore, if this were so, the status of being a name would be abolished. Indeed, it is precisely out of fear of *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* (indicating possession) in the case of a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) that the status of being a name is asserted. If that [fear of *lakṣaṇā*] persists even when something is a name, why abandon its status as a quality-injunction? For the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is required as the underlying reason here, just as it is in the case of a quality-injunction. Indeed, there can be no *lakṣaṇā* without such a reason. This is the general direction. For this very reason, even the fault of "repetition" (*kathitapadatva*) is sometimes not a fault.
The sun rises copper-red and sets copper-red as well;
for the great, there is uniformity in both prosperity and adversity.

In this regard, the statement in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* that "without the word *tāmra*, such a cognition does not arise" is consistent with what was stated by Bhartṛhari: "Just as the two powers of being the apprehended (*grāhyatva*) and the apprehender (*grāhakatva*) belong to light,
so too these two exist separately in all words."

The meaning of this is as follows: in order to exclude visual perception in the dark, it must necessarily be stated that the conjunction with light (*ālokasaṃyoga*) is the cause for the visual perception of a substance in general. And so, just as the pot and the light are both perceived through the very same conjunction of the pot and the light, likewise, the manifestation of both the word and its object occurs solely through the power residing in the word as directed toward the object.

Or, just as in the absence of the conjunction between the pot and the eye, through that very same conjunction with light, only the light itself is manifested, so too, when there is no intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the object, there is the cognition of the word alone by virtue of that [same] function.

But for you, even in the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (where the denoted meanings are subsequently connected), just as the relation appears in verbal cognition even without a *vṛtti* (semantic function) due to the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, so too—in the case of "the cow is eternal" or "the cow is non-eternal"—it appears either independently or as a qualifier by the force of intention (*tātparya*), expectancy, and so forth, through the very same general causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces verbal cognition, just like the property of cowness (*gotva*) and the like.

Since we observe that activity directed toward fire occurs simultaneously with verbal cognitions such as "There is fire on the mountain," and because of the Bhāṣya statement, "The verb *asti* (is) is present even when not explicitly employed, being synonymous with *bhavati* (exists)," it is postulated—just as the general causal complex of cognition itself possesses the capacity to manifest the present time by way of a specific qualification—that in every verbal comprehension, the word itself is the object of that verbal comprehension. [This is the essential conclusion of the Grammarians (*Śābdikas*) who maintain that the word is the object of verbal comprehension: that the meaning of the word, consisting of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) and its substratum, etc., is the object.]

Nor is there objecthood in mere cognition alone; for both the word and its sequence appear as distinct entities, just as they do in indeterminate (nirvikalpaka) cognition. Consequently, a qualified cognition arises in the form: "The cloth is denotable by the word 'cloth'. Furthermore, even in the Grammarian's (Vaiyākaraṇa) view—as in the view of others—by postulating a specific time or a specific unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) as the cause, it would not follow that at the time of using the word 'jar', all other words such as 'kalaśa' etc., which are denoters of the object 'jar', would appear [in consciousness].

Just as at the time of the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of cloth-ness, the substance-ness (*dravyatva*) does not appear; and because of the Vedic scripture, "The single-syllabled Brahman is *Om*," the statement, "The name *Rāma* consists of two syllables," and the requirement for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the rule "Vṛddhi is *āṬ*, *aiC*" [Pāṇini 1.1.1], there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its meaning. It is precisely the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) having the object as its qualificandum that is the cause for the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) of the word.
