Since identity (*tādātmya*) is constituted by both difference and non-difference, when one intends to emphasize the predominance of difference, linguistic usages such as "the object in the form of a cloth is not the word 'cloth'" become logically consistent; enough with this prolixity. [This is because] based on the experience of the manifestation of words, we postulate that the general causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābdasāmānyasāmagrī*) itself is what causes the manifestation of the word.

And thus, the causal efficacy of the word-generated presentation of a word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) is postulated only with respect to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose object is distinct from the word itself, by way of either the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) or the relation of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). Furthermore, regarding the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*), "being the meaning of the stem" is defined as "being the object of the cognition generated by the stem. Consequently, in cases such as *gām uccāraya* ("utter the cow"), there is no inconsistency in the connection of the accusative case-role (*karmatva*) and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that there is the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of all synonyms appearing as qualifiers (prakāra) in the cognition produced by the word "jar" due to a lack of a determining factor (vinigamakābhāva); for they say there is no such fault, because the general causal complex (sāmānyasāmagrī) for verbal cognition—which includes the knowledge of each respective word—is the cause of a cognition qualified by that respective word.

And thus, even though a word is presented through its occurrence (*vṛtti*), because that [word-base] lacks the status of being an object of the occurrence, it lacks *arthavattva* (meaningfulness) in the form of being a signifier of an object of the occurrence; consequently, due to the absence of *prātipadika* status, there is no production of case-endings in instances such as *bhū sattāyām* ("*bhū* in the sense of existence") or *gavityayamāha* ("he said 'cow'"). Even in the absence of that production, there is indeed grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) because the form is established (*pariniṣṭhita*). However, rules such as *bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.88] are correct only under the view that the distinction [between the base and the affix] is intended. And the determination between these two views is made in accordance with the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*).
Mimicry (*anukaraṇatva*) consists in being the producer of a cognition whose object is merely a word possessing the same sequential order [as the original].

It should not be argued that, if this were the case, those words listed in the *gaṇa* lists would lack the status of denoting action because they are mimics; for the term "being listed in the *gaṇa*" (*gaṇapaṭhitatva*) intended in the *bhūvādi* sūtra refers to the state of being denotable by a word listed in the *gaṇa*, and thus there is no fault—so they say.

However, some maintain that an imitation (anukaraṇa) brings to mind a word similar to itself through the relation of similarity; and although it is thus presented, by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, its status as a correlate in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)—just like a related item—is accepted due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), the force of experience (*anubhava*), and the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*). In this view, the defining property of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is simply "the nature of being a verbal cognition produced by an imitation, rather than by the presentation of a word-meaning generated by a functional suffix (*kṛtya*)."

Regarding the grammatical derivation (vyutpatti) such as "the suffixes [are] connected with the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthānvita*), they state that "being the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthatva*) consists in being the object of the cognition produced by the base. Consequently, there is no lack of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) for the accusative case and so forth in expressions such as "utter the word *go*" (*gām uccāraya*). Furthermore, they say that "being an imitation" (*anukaraṇatva*) consists in being the object of an utterance whose sole purport is a word similar to itself.

The apprehension of the primary signification (*śaktigraha*) regarding pronouns such as *tat* (that) is of the following form: "A word such as *tat* denotes that which is delimited by a property characterized by being the delimitor of the objective domain of the conceptual cognition (*buddhi*). In this case, although the objective domains of the signification reside in non-universal properties such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*), the signification is unitary because it is delimited by a single, recurring form. This is analogous to how the objective domains of the conventional denotation (*saṃketa*) of words like "pot"—which reside in various individual pots—are unitary with respect to that word's signification, because they are all delimited by the recurring property of "pot-ness."

However, there is this distinction: since there is an experience of a cognition (bodha) qualified by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth in those cases, it is accepted that these [qualities] are objects of the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*) by way of the objective relation known as *dharmitāvacchedakatā* (the delimitation of the subjecthood). Furthermore, within the cognition that is the object of the apprehension of the expressive power, these qualities possess the status of qualifiers (*prakāratva*). Similarly, words such as "animal" (*paśu*), which have the power to denote a tail possessing hair that is subsumed under the common property of "hair-ness" (*lomatva*), are objects of the apprehension of that power; by way of that objective relation, "hair-ness" and the like are accepted [as being denoted].

Since the state of being present in the mind (*buddhisthatva*) does not appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it cannot be the object of the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*) by way of that [verbal] objecthood; nor can it be a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition whose object is the content of the apprehension of expressive power. Therefore, it functions as a mere incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the property of being a delimitant of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedakatva*) consists in being the determiner of an objecthood residing in its own locus. Since the objecthood in question regarding "being present in the mind" is merely a co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [with the other properties], there is no possibility of a cognition having that [mind-presence] as its qualifier.

It is postulated, on the strength of the observed result (*phala*), that only that which is the object of the apprehension of power (*śakti*)—whether as the delimitor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) or as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—becomes the object of the cognition produced by that [apprehension], and that only that which is the qualifier (*prakāra*) becomes the object of that cognition.

Nor is there an impossibility of apprehending the power regarding *dharma* as something unprecedented (*apūrva*); for the apprehension of power remains intact with respect to "dharma" in general, which is presented through the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) consisting in being the delimitor of the object of a cognitive state (*buddhiviṣayatāvacchedakatva*).

However, if one does not accept general proximity (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*), then, upon observing the usage of words qualified by "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) and so forth as apprehended through a mode of cognition (*buddhiprakāratayā*), one grasps the word-potency (*śakti*) for that term in that instance. Thereafter, one determines a general pervasion (*vyāpti*) as follows: "Whatever word is employed by a cognition having as its object a thing delimited by such-and-such a property, that word possesses potency with respect to things qualified by that very property."

Immediately thereafter, there is no inconsistency because—by means of a reason such as "being employed by a cognition whose object is qualified by Caitra, the courtyard, and so forth, which has been grasped through perception"—one arrives at a certainty in the form of an inference (anumiti) regarding the denotative capacity for that specific word (tatpada) to signify something qualified by *caitratva* (the property of being Caitra), even though this was previously unestablished, due to the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and other contextual factors.

For this very reason, it is logically consistent that from that word (*tatpada*), one may sometimes have the cognition "a jar," sometimes "that which possesses a genus" (*jātimān*), sometimes "a jar possessing a genus," and sometimes "a jar present in the intellect."

Nor does the possibility of a unification (anugama) of the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for words such as "Hari" arise through a term like "being the object of a specific cognition," which serves as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of the elimination of polysemy (*nānārtha*); for, according to the previously stated method, even a single entity is experienced as being understood in multiple forms from words such as "tad" (that), and thus, while such [unification] might be accepted there, it is impossible to postulate it for words like "Hari" because no such experience occurs from them. For this very reason, those [words like "Hari"] possess polysemy.
Otherwise, there would result the contingency that from words like "Hari" too, a cognition in the form "Hari possesses a genus" or the like would occasionally arise.

Furthermore, there is no rule that when a property (*dharma*) appears in some manner, it must appear as qualified by its own delimitation (*avacchedakatva*), rather than being merely indicated (*upalakṣita*) by it. For this very reason, from the cognition "there is no possessor of a universal" (*jātimān nāsti*), there is no comprehension of the absence of a pot delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*) in its own form. And thus, one should not argue that because the status of being a subject-delimiter (*dharmitāvacchedakatva*) is apprehended only as qualified by "being present in the mind" (*buddhisthatva*), there would necessarily follow a comprehension of that [subject] as qualified by it; for such a rule applies only when the status of being a delimiter appears as a relational mode (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*).

However, since the apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) occurs precisely through the mode of the relation between the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*), there is no fault. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, from a word uttered at a certain time, there would follow the cognition of even that which is delimited by a property residing in another time or another place; for this is resolved by the fact that the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) is the cause [of such a cognition]. Furthermore, because there is no instance [of a word] standing in the place of an individual (*vyaktisthānīya*), and because the cognition of that which is delimited by the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is actually taking place, there is no ground for such an undesirable consequence.

In this way, it should be understood that the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is Caitra-ness and so forth, as characterized by a common property consisting of the delimitors of being the object of one's own address and the delimitors of being the speaker, respectively.

The Goddess said: "When you have been slain right here, the gods will quickly roar. In such cases, because the words uttered by the seer (ṛṣi) provide knowledge of the Goddess's speech as well—through the proximity of the general form consisting of that specific sequence of phonemes—the cognition of the Goddess and Mahiṣāsura via the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is established solely through the recognition of their respective roles as the speaker and the person addressed by such sentences. However, there is no cognition [of the non-speaking seer or his addressee] because they lack the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the supreme knowledge of the silent sage (*maunipuruṣa*) is not of such a nature, there would be no possibility of the silent sage being cognized by the word "I" in the sentence "I know that I am a learned man," since he lacks the status of being an utterer; for there is no fault, as the act of uttering serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the underlying mental reflection (*anusandhāna*).

Nor should it be argued that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* resides only in that which is delimited by the form serving as the delimitor of the object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatāvacchedakarūpa*), rather than in that which is delimited by the delimitor such as "the state of being addressed" (*sambodhyatva*); for the avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) follows simply from the absence of speaker-intention (*tātparya*). This is because, even when such intention exists—for instance, when the sentence "I am doing" is uttered by Caitra, or when the sentence "You go" is employed to inform someone other than the addressee—there occurs a comprehension of Maitra and others [as the referents], even in the absence of any error regarding their being the speaker or the person being addressed.

Because this would contradict all empirical experience; otherwise, if that were the intended meaning, it would result in the same usage being applied even to a single thing. The meaning of the word *sarva* is delimited by the totality (*yāvattva*) of objects that are the content of cognition. Here, *yāvattva* is a delimitation based on a number other than unity. Furthermore, there is a commonality among various instances of *yāvattva* insofar as they are the objects of cognition. In expressions such as "He eats all the rice," however, one should understand that the delimitation by a number residing in the parts is superimposed upon the whole.

However, where there is a cognition based on the word "all" alone—such as "all [things] qualified by potness and so forth are to be brought"—in that case, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is to be understood. Alternatively, some say that the primary denotative power (śakti) of the word "all" resides in those things possessing potness and so forth that are objects of cognition, by virtue of their being delimited by the "as-many-as-are-objects-of-cognition" (yāvattva). In expressions such as "all pots," however, they maintain that words like "pot" are employed for the sake of determining the specific referent.

The word *kiṃ* has its denotative power (*śakti*) in that which is delimited by a property that is the object of a desire to know (*jijñāsā*). For this very reason, a question-sentence containing the word *kiṃ* is logically consistent for the purpose of communicating one's own desire to know. Thus, from the question "Who cooks? (*kaḥ pacati*), there arises the understanding: "Cooking has as its agent [one] delimited by a property that is the object of a desire to know. Since the cessation of the desire to know regarding that [object] occurs precisely through a statement such as "The Brahmin cooks" (*vipraḥ pacati*), which generates the knowledge that is the object of that desire, such a statement serves as the answer immediately following such a question.

Nor should it be argued that "he cooks the object of cognition" (*prameyam pacati*) would also be a valid answer, because the knowledge produced by that [action] is likewise the object of such a desire; for there is no fault, since we accept that the word *kim* (‘what’), when expressing the intended object (*uddeśya*), has its denotative power (*śakti*) restricted only to a property delimited by a property that is pervaded by a property residing in the agent presented by the word co-occurring with it. Thus...

In expressions such as "Who is the Brahmin who cooks?", the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ*—which is co-occurrent with another word denoting the subject (*uddeśya*) qualified by its own meaning through non-difference (*abhedena*)—possesses a power (*śakti*) directed toward that which is delimited by a property pervaded by the property that delimits the referent of the word whose meaning is conjoined with its own meaning through non-difference. Therefore, in that case, the answer is "Caitra cooks," and not "A human being cooks."

Thus, in general, wherever there is a syntactic connection with the meaning of the word *kiṃ* (what), it should be understood that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word resides only in that which is delimited by a property pervaded by a property residing in that [referent]. However, in some cases, the power resides only in that which is delimited by a property pervaded by a property connected with its own [referent]; such [distinctions] are to be inferred accordingly.

Thus, in expressions such as "Who is this?", the word *kiṃ* (who), which denotes the predicate (*vidheya*), possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward that specific property (*viśeṣadharma*) which is sought after as the delimitor of the predication-ness (*vidheyatāvacchedakatā*)—as delimited by the property characterized by being the delimitor of the object-ness (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatva*) presented by the co-occurring term. For this very reason, the answer given there is simply "This is a Brāhmaṇa. In cases such as "Is the face the moon?", the indeclinable *kimaḥ* has the sense of "speculation" (*vitarka*). And speculation is a cognition consisting of the speaker's conjecture.
And thus, there is the cognition: "The face is the qualificandum of a possibility whose qualifier is the moon through non-difference.

Similarly, in cases such as "Is this wealth Caitra’s?", the cognition is: "The wealth is the qualificandum of a possibility whose qualifier is Caitra-ownership through a relation such as substratum-hood. In expressions like "What is the moon?", after the cognition of the possibility, the perception of the common property (sādharmya) such as "delightfulness" which grounds that possibility occurs by implication (arthāt). In "What is a cow?", that [word] also has the sense of censure. The denotative power (śakti) of the word *yat* resides in that which is delimited by a property characterized by being the delimitor of the objectness of the speaker’s intention, insofar as it is to be conveyed by that [word].

Therefore, for the communication of that meaning, there is a necessary dependence on that word (*tat-pada*), because without the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of that word, it is impossible to determine the word's expressive power (*śakti*) due to the failure to grasp the aforementioned inclusive property (*anugamaka-dharma*). Furthermore, even prior to the cognition produced by that word, the speaker’s intention (*abhisambandha*) regarding that which is to be expressed is easily grasped through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; thus, the cognition arising from that word does not depend on the apprehension of the word's expressive power.

In that regard, because the word *yat* occurring in the subsequent clause (*uttaravākya*) is capable of implying the word *tat*, there is no requirement to explicitly employ the word *tat* there. This is as in the example: "The lotuses have formed a union with the moon, which is superior in loveliness," and so forth. Thus, the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *tat* should be understood as residing in what is presented by the word *yat*. In such cases, the word *tat*—whether referring to something well-known, previously experienced, or already introduced—implies the word *yat* due to its inherent capacity; therefore, there is no need to employ the word *yat* there. This is explained in detail in the *Kāvyapradīpa* and other works.

The word *idam* has its denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to an object of direct perception; *etad* likewise; and *adas* has its power with respect to an object of indirect (non-perceptual) cognition.

The word *sva* (self/own) has its power with respect to that which is presented by a word co-occurring with it (*samabhivyāhṛta*). Here, "co-occurrence" (*samabhivyāhāra*) consists in being a constituent of the same sentence. Furthermore, that which is presented by the co-occurring word is understood specifically as the meaning of a word that functions as an agent (*kāraka*) or action (*kriyā*) within that co-occurrence. Consequently, in a sentence such as "Caitra’s brother sees his own son," there is no cognition of Caitra by the word *sva*. Likewise, in a sentence such as "Maitra sees Caitra, who is looking at his own son," there is no lack of comprehension regarding Caitra’s son.

For this very reason, in such instances as "Is the quality of causing the wheel's rotation in the jar produced by its own cause, the staff?", there is the cognition of the jar—which is the agent of the action supplied by ellipsis—by means of the word *nija*, which has the same meaning as its own term (*sva*).

But when the meaning of the genitive case is construed with the action (*kriyā*), there the word *sva* (self) also denotes that very meaning; as for example in such cases as: "Smoke possesses co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a fire that pervades itself. It is with this very intention that it is said: "By general rule, pronouns (*sarvanāman*) refer to the principal [element]. In this context, "referring to the principal" means "referring to that which is construed with the principal [element]."

A single word is capable of denoting that which is qualified by isolation (*kaivalya*) and other such properties. Isolation (*kaivalya*) is the state of being devoid of a second entity of the same class (*sajātīya*). This, in turn, is the non-counterpositiveness (*apratiyogitva*) of a difference residing in entities of the same class. Thus, in cases such as "This one person eats here," the cognition takes the form "He is the non-counterpositive of a difference residing in the agent of the act of eating whose locus is this place. Similar reasoning should be applied to other instances; in this way, all desired conclusions are established. This concludes the determination of the meaning of nouns (*nāmārtha*). Now begins the investigation into the meaning of case-endings (*sub-artha*).

Now, the meaning of the nominal stem (*subartha*) belonging to this [category] is determined; first, there is the investigation of the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamā-vibhakti*). In that regard, there are seven cases known as the nominative, accusative, instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive, and locative. Among these, the rule (*sūtra*) that establishes the expressive power (*śakti*) of the nominative is: "The nominative occurs in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-arthe prathamā*). That meaning which presents itself when a nominal stem is uttered is the meaning of that nominal stem. By this, all meanings—including the primary (*śakya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the metaphorical (*gauṇa*)—are included.

In expressions such as "Kṛṣṇa is beautiful" (*kṛṣṇaḥ sundaraḥ*), the case-ending (*vibhakti*) restates the meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛtyartha*); non-difference (*abheda*) is the relation (*saṃsarga*); and the resulting cognition is that "the beautiful one is non-different from Kṛṣṇa. Gender (*liṅga*), however, is the meaning of the nominal stem itself. It has been established in the *Nāmārthavāda* that the suffix (*pratyaya*) is merely indicative (*dyotaka*). Furthermore, it has been established in that same work that number (*saṃkhyā*) may be either denoted (*vācyā*) or indicated (*dyotyā*). In cases such as "The boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*) and "A *droṇa* measure of rice" (*droṇo vrīhiḥ*), one should understand that there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the words "lion," "rice," and so on, [respectively] for something similar to a lion and for a quantity measured by a *droṇa*.

In this sūtra, the term *prātipadika* includes not only the nominal stem itself but also that which is qualified by a suffix expressing gender derived from that stem, because of the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) stating: "When a nominal stem is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included. Consequently, the formation of the nominative case in forms such as *indrāṇī* is established; this is the general direction of the argument.

This *sūtra* also operates only in connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*), due to its association with rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.2), and because it is required in that very way. For this very reason, the rule "the first case is used when coreferential with a finite verb" (*tiṅsamānādhikaraṇe prathamā*) is established; for this same reason, the passage from the *Bhāṣya* and other texts stating, "the root *as-* exists even when not explicitly employed, provided it is followed by a word ending in a form of *asti*," becomes consistent. Where, however, a verbal action is not heard, one should understand that it must be supplied (*adhyāhāra*).

Regarding words such as *eka*, they say that since a usage that restates what is already known (*anuvādaka*) is more logical than a usage whose meaning is unconnected (*ananvitārthaka*), the singular number and so forth should be understood.

The vocative case (*saṃbodhana*) is also the meaning of the first case ending (*prathamā*), according to the natural force of the rule *sambodhane ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.47). In this context, "vocative" means making known; for this very reason, the linguistic usage "the person being addressed (*saṃboddhyamāna*) is Devadatta" is consistent. It is precisely for the purpose of making that [person] known that a sentence containing a word ending in the vocative case is employed, and its result is [the addressee's] engagement (*pravṛtti*), withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and so forth. In this regard, the inclusion of the prefix *sam-* is for the purpose of indicating completeness (*samyaktva*).

Therefore, it refers to that which is the object of the vocative case (*sambodhana-vibhakti*). [Fn: For this very reason, it is established that the vocative case is also a "kāraka" (case-role) case ending. The underlying idea is as follows: from the statement of Bhartṛhari, "They know that addressing (*sambodhana*) is merely bringing an already established entity face-to-face; for an entity that has attained face-to-face-ness is then employed in actions," and because of parsimony (*lāghava*), the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "addressing is face-to-face-ness for the sake of cognition" shows that here, addressing is precisely that face-to-face-ness manifested by turning one's face toward another.]

And that [number], like the number itself, is construed with the referent of the base (prakṛtyartha)—such as Devadatta—by way of the relation of being a locus (āśrayatva). Whether that [number] is the meaning of the case-ending (vibhaktyartha) or the meaning of the base is another matter. Furthermore, since it is stated that "the meaning of the base is employed in actions," its construal occurs specifically within the instigation (pravartanā) that constitutes the meaning of the optative suffix (vidhi), by way of its connection to that instigation.

Precisely because such a construal is accepted, there is no contradiction with the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that "there is only a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root. And that instigation is construed with the action of going by way of the relation of being its object (*viṣayatva*).

And thus, in cases such as "Devadatta, you go," the understanding is that the act of going has as its object an instigation directed toward the person denoted by the second-person pronoun *yuṣmad*, who is non-different from Devadatta who is present before [the speaker]. It should be understood that [this instigation] is also connected with the verbal action (*kriyā*). Consequently, in instances such as "Be a king, fight!; O Indra-śatru, prosper!", the vocative case ending is not employed, because even at this moment, the state of being a king is unestablished and therefore lacks the status of being a subject of restatement (*anuvādya*). For this very reason, the sentence "O King, fight! is used during the stage of childhood [when one is not yet a king].

Furthermore, the injunction "Become a king, O youth" is not applied during the state of being a king; and words such as "O" (*he*) serve to indicate the intention of addressing someone. As for insentient objects, however, the usage is figurative, based on the superimposition of sentience.

And in this context, the vocative is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root, and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the action. Therefore, in cases such as "O Rāma, protect me" (*rāma pāhi*), the cognition is that the act of protection has as its object the vocative directed toward one related to Rāma. This is because the vocative case-ending has as its domain that which is already established (*anuvādya*); and since that which is established requires something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and since the enjoined is of the nature of an action, it is only logical that the connection occurs precisely with that [action].

In expressions such as "O Devadatta, you are handsome," it should be understood that the verb "are" (*asi*) is to be supplied. For this very reason, in cases such as "Fie on you, fool! (*dhik mūrkha*), the nominative case is used when a verb is supplied; the understanding is that there is an act of censuring directed toward the person addressed, who is a fool. The censure of the act consists precisely in its being performed by an extremely contemptible fool. In the absence of such an act, the accusative case is used, and the understanding is simply that there is a censure related to the fool.

For this very reason, in examples such as *vrajāni devadatta* ("O Devadatta, let us go"), the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19) successfully establishes the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because the utterance constitutes a single sentence according to the rule *ekatiṅ vākyam*. However, if [the vocative] were not a qualifier with respect to the action (*kriyā*), this would not be established. As for the claim that in *rāma pāhi* ("O Rāma, protect [me]"), the meaning is "protection performed by Rāma, who is the person being addressed," where the address (*sambodhana*) is a qualifier of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), and the base-meaning is a qualifier—through identity—of the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*); [we reply: if understanding occurred according to the aforementioned method, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage *bho brāhmaṇāstvaṃ paca* ("O Brahmin, you cook").

Nor does this lead to the occurrence of the first person in cases such as "rāma pāhi" (O Rāma, protect), because in the rule *yuṣmadyupapade* [Pāṇini 1.4.105], the term *yuṣmad* is intended to signify its meaning; and since the meaning of *yuṣmad* is that which is being addressed, the word "rāma" also possesses that meaning, and thus there is no fault. This is not so, for in examples such as "hi rāma śivo gacchati kāśīm" (Indeed, O Rāma, Śiva goes to Kāśī), it is impossible to state that the meaning of the suffix is subordinate to the meaning of the word [to which it is attached].

Furthermore, if [the pronoun] *yuṣmad* were intended to refer to its primary meaning [the person addressed], then in the sentence "O Rāma, you are going" (*he rāma bhavān gacchati*), the second-person suffix would be improper; for although the meaning of *bhavat* is common to both those who are being addressed and those who are not, in the present case, due to its co-occurrence with a vocative, it refers exclusively to one who is being addressed. On the other hand, if it were not intended to refer to the primary meaning, then in cases such as "O Rāma, protect me" (*rāma pāhi*), the second person would be difficult to justify; for if one were to supply the word *tvam*, its coreferential relation with the meaning of the verb would preclude its coreferential relation with the word "Rāma."

As for the argument that [in the sentence] "O Brahmins, you cook," there might be such a case, that is not so. Is the agency here attributed to all the Brahmins being addressed, or to only one of them, or to someone other than those being addressed? Not the first, because it would result in the impossibility of using the singular form "you" (*tvam*). Not the second, because since there is no fruit in informing the others, informing them would result in being useless.
However, if the intention is to convey distinct actions—as in "You eat" or "You bathe"—then this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). By this, the third alternative is also refuted.

Furthermore, due to the inherent nature of linguistic power (*śabdaśakti*), when there is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of a word ending in the vocative case, it is established by worldly convention that the pronoun *yuṣmad* refers only to what is indicated by that [vocative] word; therefore, it is impossible to state that anything other than that is the meaning of the word *tvam*. For this very reason, in your own view, in such cases as "O Devadatta, he cooks," the person being addressed does not possess the status of the agent (*kartṛtva*), because by the inherent nature of linguistic power, the meaning of the word *idam* (in "he") is necessarily distinct from the person being addressed. This is the direction of the argument. Thus ends the investigation into the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamāvibhakti*).
Now begins the investigation of the meaning of the second case-ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*).

The case-endings beginning with the second are of two kinds: *kāraka*-case-endings and *upapada*-case-endings. Among these, there are six *kārakas*: the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the point of departure (*apādāna*), and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). In this context, the state of being a *kāraka* consists in being connected with an action. For this very reason, in such expressions as "he asks the son of the Brahmin the way," the Brahmin does not possess the status of a *kāraka*, because he lacks connection with the action.

Otherwise, just as in the case of a son qualified by "handsome" (*sundara*) and so on, where the handsome qualities constitute the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in the action) because they are pervaded by the action, so too would the son—who is qualified by his relation to Brahmā—possess that same status because he is pervaded by the action. Furthermore, the handsome qualities and so on possess connection with the action either through the logic of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the red cow), or else they possess connection with the action by virtue of being non-different from that which is directly connected to the action; for there is no evidence for assuming a relation other than this, and because a relation based on difference is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

As for the claim that "kārakatva" (the status of being a grammatical participant) consists in being connected with the meaning of an affix that denotes another action, that is not correct; for in cases such as *pakva* ("cooked"), the meaning of the affix would fail to qualify as a *kāraka*.

By this same reasoning, the view that "kārakatva" consists in being connected with the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that is itself connected to an action is also refuted; for in cases such as *pakva odanaḥ* ("cooked rice"), the rice (*odana*) and so forth would fail to attain the status of an object (*karman*).

Furthermore, the essential point here is this: the general definition of a *kāraka* (participant in action) is "the state of being a producer of an action. This state of being a producer consists in the nature of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*). And the nature of being a cause is the possession of a property that is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence co-located with the effect, as delimited by the time-point immediately preceding the effect, provided that there is no other way of accounting for the effect (*anyathāsiddhi*). Consequently, in such cases as "Caitra cooks the rice," Caitra is not a *kāraka*, because he lacks the state of being a producer of the action due to his being otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*).

The recipient (*sampradāna*), however, is a generator of the action by way of manifesting consent. This is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): when consent exists, the act of giving proceeds; in its absence, the act does not occur.

Similarly, in cases such as "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) factor also possesses the quality of being a generator of the action, since it is a cause for the act of staying; thus, its status as a generator of action remains intact.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the status of being a *kāraka* would not apply because the jar, being unproduced, lacks the capacity to produce the action; for there is no fault here, since the capacity to produce residing in the potsherds is superimposed upon the jar, or because the jar possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) in its conceptual form (*bauddhārtha*). Likewise, even the ablative (*apādāna*) possesses the capacity to produce the action, because in the absence of a tree, the separation of the leaf would be impossible. The Naiyāyikas, however, define *kārakatva* as the state of being connected with the action through the mediation of the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*). The precise formulation is: the state of being the substratum of a cognitive content (*viṣayatā*) which is itself determined by a cognitive content of the meaning of a case-ending, which in turn is determined by the cognitive content of the action.

In the expression ‘*stokaṃ pacati*’ (he cooks slightly), they argue that the term *pariṣkurvanti* (they explain/rectify) is used to exclude *stoka*—which is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*)—from being a *kāraka*, on the grounds that it does not connect with the action through the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*). However, in cases such as ‘*caitrasya taṇḍulaṃ pacati*’ (he cooks Caitra’s rice), since Caitra does not connect with the action through the meaning of a case-ending, he lacks *kāraka*-status. This [explanation] is incorrect; for in examples such as ‘*kaṭe āste*’ (he sits on a mat) and ‘*sthālyāṃ pacati*’ (he cooks in a pot), the mat and the pot connect with the action by way of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) respectively, and thus do not connect with the action through the meaning of a case-ending. Consequently, they would fail to attain *kāraka*-status. Furthermore, this would also result in the agent himself failing to attain *kāraka*-status.

And agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the locus of the operation expressed by the verb stem under discussion. By this, all agents—including the prompted agent (*prayojya*), the prompter (*prayojaka*), and unexpressed agents—are included. In the case of "He ties the horse to the beans" (*māṣeṣvaśvaṃ badhnāti*), although the horse possesses agency by virtue of being the locus of the operation conducive to contact below the throat, there is no occurrence of [grammatical] agency because it lacks the status of being the locus of the operation expressed by the verb stem under discussion. And objecthood (*karmatva*) consists in being intended as the locus of the result of the operation expressed by the verb stem under discussion, which is brought about by the operation that constitutes the primary meaning of that same verb stem.

This very quality of being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) constitutes the definition of an object (*karman*). In the example "He milks milk from the cow" (*gāṃ payo dogdhi*), the inclusion of the condition "being brought about by the agent" (*prayojyatva*) is for the sake of establishing the status of the milk as the object. In the example "He goes from Prayāga to Kāśī" (*prayāgāt kāśīṃ gacchati*), the phrase "the fruit of the action denoted by the root in question" (*prakṛtadhātvarthaphala*) is used to exclude Prayāga from being considered an object. The Naiyāyikas, however, define the object as that which possesses a fruit residing in a locus different from the operation delimited by the meaning of the verbal root. And such a fruit is...

They say that [the action of] *gam* (to go) is conjunction; [the action of] *tyaj* (to abandon) is disjunction; and [the action of] *pat* (to fall) is conjunction with a lower location. Since the action consisting of the lower location is included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the leaf is not an object [of the verb], and thus one says, "The leaf falls from the tree to the ground. However, in the view where the result is merely conjunction, the usage is "He falls from the tree to the ground.

And instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) consists in being the producer of a result without the intervention of an operation residing in itself. This very thing is "being the most effective means" (*sādhakatamatva*). In the example, "Vālī was killed by Rāma with an arrow," the definition applies to the arrow because it produces the result immediately after its own operation.

And the nature of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*) is: that factor (*kāraka*) which, for the sake of connecting the mere action with its object, is intended as the goal (*uddeśya*) within the action. For example, in the sentence "He gives a cow to the Brahmin," the definition applies because the arrow possesses the quality of producing the result immediately following its own operation.

And the state of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*) is the status of that *kāraka* which is intended as the goal with respect to an action for the sake of establishing a connection between the object of that action and the action itself. For example, in "He gives a cow to the Brāhmaṇa," the Brāhmaṇa is the intended goal of the act of giving for the sake of establishing a connection with the cow, which has become the object of the act of giving. The relationship between the cow and the Brāhmaṇa is one of ownership.

And the state of being an *apādāna* (ablative) is: the state of being the locus of a separation—which is not expressed by the root of the verb in question—produced by a specific action inherent in a specific agent. That very state is what constitutes the status of being a limit (*avadhitva*). Furthermore, this separation is not necessarily preceded by a real relation and need not itself be real; rather, it may also be preceded by a mentally constructed relation and be mentally constructed as well. This is because, in the case of examples such as "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra," the *Pañcamī* (ablative case) is established in the *Bhāṣya* precisely by resorting to a separation that is mentally constructed.

And the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) consists in being the substratum of the fruit and the operation [of the action] by means of either the agent or the object. For example, in "He cooks rice in a pot at home," the pot is the substratum of the fruit—namely, the softening (*viklitti*)—by means of the object (the rice), while the house is the substratum of the operation by means of the agent.

A relation such as owner-and-owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), which is distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a *kāraka*, is expressed by the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). In expressions such as "The king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the relation expressed by the genitive connects with the man through a relation of substrate-and-located (*āśrayibhāva*); for the cognition [arising therefrom] is: "The man possesses a relation characterized by the king."
In this context, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in each respective relation in its form as "relation-ness" (*sambandhatva*).

Thus, since "relation-ness"—which is the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—is present in [grammatical relations] such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*), there is indeed the status of being the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyarthatā*) in the form of "relation-ness. For this very reason, the genitive is established in examples such as *satā gatam* ("gone by the virtuous") and *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows [the use] of ghee") when "relation-ness" is intended to be expressed; such is the heart-intent of the ancient grammarians as recorded in the *Siddhāntakaumudī*.

The moderns, however, maintain that the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) and so forth is not denoted by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as a mere "relation-ness" (*sambandhatva*). For this reason, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "There are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive" is consistent. In the expression "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the meaning of the genitive is a collection consisting of the states of ownership (*svatva*) and proprietorship (*svāmitva*), and not ownership alone or proprietorship alone; for these reside in only one [of the two relata], whereas a relation is necessarily resident in both.
Furthermore, the relation which is the meaning of the genitive appears solely as a mode of connection (*saṃsargavidhayā*), and not as a qualifier (*prakāravidhayā*).

And thus, regarding the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puru�ṣaḥ*), they say that the man is qualified by the king through the relation of owner and owned; however, the statement in the root-text [that he is qualified] is made in accordance with his appearing as a qualifier (*prakāra*). As for the claim that "being a *kāraka* consists in being a producer of action," that is not correct, because in the previously cited example, the son would fail to attain the status of a *kāraka*.

If it is argued that even the questioner possesses the status of a producer because the act of questioning cannot be completed without him, even so, there is an over-narrow definition (avyāpti) regarding the recipient (saṃpradāna); for a gift can occur even when no recipient is present, and thus the recipient lacks the necessary condition of being invariably antecedent (niyatapūrvavṛttitva). Furthermore, there is an over-narrow definition regarding the agent and the object in cases such as "he is born" (jāyate) or "he does" (karoti).

Nor should it be argued that, just as a sacrifice is a producer [of the result] by means of the *apūrva* even in the absence of its own prior occurrence, so too the cognition of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and other factors is easily established as a producer of that [action] by virtue of its prior occurrence; for the status of being a producer of an action—defined by the condition of being invariably and non-otherwise established as a prior antecedent—is more cumbersome than the status of being connected with the action, which consists in being the locus of the objectivity that determines the verbal objectivity residing in the action.

Furthermore, the justification for the status of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is no more easily established in the case of a positive correlate (*anvayin*) than it is in the case of a producer (*janaka*). Even the claim that what is involved therein is a producerhood that is the determiner of an indivisible producedness (*akhaṇḍajanyatā*), which takes the form of an indivisible *upādhi*, is beset by a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*).

Furthermore, since the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed in the sense of the substratum (*āśraya*), and since the status of being a substratum of action excludes [the roles of] recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and point of departure (*apādāna*), it is more logical for the suffix to indicate "objecthood" (*viṣayatā*) by way of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the quality of being a generator (*janakatva*) as defined by the verbal root's action; for this [objecthood] is not something distinct, as it consists in a particular kind of essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*). And its connection with the action occurs either as a qualifier (*prakāratva*) or as the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*). For this very reason, the relationship of agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) as defined by the act of cooking is appropriately established in cases such as "Devadatta is a cook" (*pācako devadattaḥ*) and "the rice is cooked" (*pakvastandulaḥ*). For this same reason, [there is no contradiction] regarding the [roles of] the factors of action (*kārakas*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) occurs only with respect to the action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, in rules such as *kārakād dattaśrutayoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.148], the word *kāraka* is uttered with a specific accent (*svarita*); by this, the sixfold set beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*) mentioned in the governing heading (*adhikāra*) on *kārakas* is understood, and thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And so, the ultimate truth is that the state of being a *kāraka* consists in possessing the word *kāraka* through the relation of a particular convention (*saṃketa-viśeṣa*).

In this regard, the aphorism defining the characteristic of the object (*karman*) is: "The object is that which is most desired by the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.49). The term *kartuḥ* is a genitive in the sense of the agent; it is derived from the root *āp* with the suffix *san*, followed by the suffix *kta* in the present sense according to the rule "matibuddhi... (3.2.188), for the author of that [rule] states that "desire" (*mati*) means "wish. Thus, the meaning is: the object is that which is sought to be attained by the agent. And here, "attainment" (*āpti*) refers to a relationship.

In this context, since a direct relationship between the agent and the object is impossible, an indirect relationship mediated by the action (*kriyā*) is understood. This is because there is no evidence for abandoning what is already present (the action) as a qualifier of the agent—which is already established—and instead postulating something that is not so established. Thus, the meaning is: "that which is intended to be related to the agent through the mediation of the action. Furthermore, the "relationship" consists of the nature of being produced (*janyatā*) and so forth, appearing as a relation (*saṃsarga*) between the result and the operation, as well as the nature of being the locus of that result.

And "being desired" (iṣyamāṇatva) means precisely being the intended object of that [agent's] operation. And thus, it follows as a conclusion that *karmatva* (the state of being an object) consists in being the intended object of desire by virtue of being the substratum of the fruit of the action denoted by the verbal root in question, which fruit is itself brought about by the operation that is the primary meaning of that same verbal root.

To explain: in the sentence "The potter makes a jar" (*kulālo ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the verb in question is the root *kṛ* (to do/make). Its meaning is the operation conducive to production, which is the primary element and does not serve as the locus of the mode of presentation (*prakāratva*) residing in another [element] that is the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*). The result of the meaning of this primary verb is "production" (*utpatti*). The status of being an object (*karmatva*) is established for the jar because it is the intended recipient (*uddeśyatā*) by virtue of being the substratum of that [result], according to the cognition: "The jar becomes the substratum of production. This is because the agent intends the jar as the locus of the result. Thus, the jar's status as the object is proven.

And being the locus of the result (*phalāśrayatva*) is to be understood by means of the relation that delimits the status of being a result (*phalatāvacchedakasambandha*). This relation that delimits the status of being a result is that relation by which there arises an intention whose qualifier is the state of being the locus of the result; and this [relation] differs according to the specific verbal roots (*dhātu*) involved.

For example, in the expression "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), inherence (*samavāya*) qualified by being the correlate (*anuyogitva*) is the relation that delimits the result. Since the property of being the delimitor of the objective content residing in the result—which belongs to the desire in the form "let the village be the locus of conjunction through that relation"—resides in inherence alone, only the locus of the result through that relation possesses the status of the object (*karman*), and not the locus of the result through a temporal (*kālika*) or other such relation, because that relation lacks the status of delimiting the result.

For this very reason, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) resides in two things, even though it exists in Caitra by way of inherence (*samavāya*)—just as it exists in the village—the expression "Caitra goes to himself" (*caitraḥ svam gacchati*) is not used, because inherence qualified by the state of being the locus (*anuyogitva*) does not exist in Caitra. Furthermore, its [the action's] status as having an object (*sakarmakatva*) is established because its result—namely, separation (*vibhāga*) produced by the agent-located activity—is present in the fruit [of the action].

Nor should it be argued that in a case where there is a disjunction caused by both Caitra and Maitra, even though the result in the form of disjunction exists in Caitra by virtue of its inherence as qualified by being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*), the undesirable consequence (*prayogāpatti*) would follow that "Caitra disjoins Maitra. This is because, in the case of intransitive roots (*akarmakadhātu*), the operation (*vyāpāra*) possesses co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the result; thus, in that context, the locus-hood of the result is intended to be by way of simple inherence (*samavāya*). Consequently, since the result does not exist in Caitra by way of inherence as qualified by subsisting in Maitra, there is no fault. Furthermore, this is because the agent-number (*kartṛsaṃkhyā*) takes precedence and sublates [the other].

By this, the following objection is refuted: "In cases such as *ratho grāmaṃ gacchati* ('the chariot goes to the village'), since the agent is insentient, desire is impossible; therefore, because the object [the village] lacks the quality of being the intended goal of the agent's desire, it would not possess the status of an *object* (*karman*). This is rejected because the state of being the intended goal (*uddeśyatva*), as characterized by that [desire], exists there as well, since the conjunction with the subsequent location is the intended goal of the operation of the chariot and so forth. Furthermore, they say that according to the system of the Bhāṣya, there is no harm, as one may superimpose sentience [upon the chariot], just as in the case of *kūlaṃ pipatiṣati* ('the bank wishes to fall').

And being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) consists in the action’s being the object of a desire preceded by a desire for the result, with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is the result itself; for the result possesses that status [of being the intended object]. Since the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) does not apply to the result itself (as there is no further result in it), it applies to what is distinct from that. For example, in *staṇḍulaṃ pacanti* ("they cook rice"). And thus, in that case, non-difference or identity is the meaning of the accusative. However, because they are the substrata of the result, rice and the like also possess the status of being intended objects. For this very reason, the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) is consistent.

For in that context, by virtue of its association with the agent (*kartṛ*), only the object of the root-meaning itself is grasped. For this very reason, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is not used for objects such as "softening" (*viklitti*). For this same reason, when Devadatta goes from Prayāga to Kāśī, the usage "he goes to Prayāga" (*prayāgaṃ gacchati*) occurs; otherwise, since Prayāga would also be the locus of the disjunction produced by Devadatta's activity, that [usage] would be unavoidable. It is quite clear, however, that Prayāga lacks the status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) of the root-meaning.

Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the locus of the result through a temporal or other such relation, because what is grasped is the locus of the result through the relation that delimits the nature of the result (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

Nor should it be argued that in the sentence "Caitra goes to the village" (*caitro grāmaṃ gacchati*), Caitra—who is the locus of the result consisting of conjunction with the village—would possess the status of an object (*karman*); for this is precluded by the subsequent technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, since the relation of being the relatum (*anuyogitā*) residing in the village is precisely what delimits the result, Caitra lacks that [relation] with respect to that result. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* explains the establishment of both objecthood and agency in the sentence "He kills himself with himself" (*ātmānam ātmanā hanti*) by means of the difference between the limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*) consisting of the body and the mind.

In the expression "the tree falls to the ground" (*vṛkṣād bhūmau patati*), the status of being a locus (*ādhāratva*) is intended by way of the agent and the object; however, when the intention is to express its being the direct substratum (*sākṣāt tadāśrayatva*), it should be understood as the object (*karmatva*). For this very reason, the rule prescribing the compound *dvitīyā-śrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.24) is consistent. In the case of "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), there is the status of object because it is the substratum of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning, which consists of origination (*utpatti*). In cases such as "he knows the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), there is the status of object because it possesses the fruit consisting of the destruction of nescience (*ajñānabhaṅga*) delimited by the object produced by cognition.

Nor is it untenable to say that one knows [the object] even when it has perished or is yet to come, because in those cases too, its existence is admitted in a subtle form; furthermore, there is no harm in admitting the occurrence [of cognition] even in the past or future, just as the Nyāya school accepts the existence of an object (viṣayatā) in the past, or just as one accepts the occurrence of a quality in a substance even during its destruction.

Alternatively, in cases such as "he knows" (*jānāti*) or "he desires" (*icchati*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to knowledge, desire, and so forth. And that [operation] is simply the contact between the mind and the eye (*manaścakṣuḥ-saṃyoga*) and the like, which generates the knowledge. For this very reason, expressions such as "the mind knows" (*mano jānāti*) are logically consistent. Furthermore, [in the case of desire], knowledge and the like are conducive to the desire; the relation that delimits the status of being a result (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is objectivity (*viṣayatā*). Or rather, the operation is simply the knowledge, desire, and so forth, which are the qualifiers (*nirūpaka*) of objectivity. Nor can it be argued how objectivity can be a result since it is not produced by knowledge; for there is no impairment [of its status], since the status of being a result—which will be explained immediately below—is present in that case as well.

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of including the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) in this sūtra? Even in its absence, when there is an expectancy as to by whom [the action] is to be accomplished, the meaning of the verbal root under discussion would be obtained through the rule of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), since the section on "factors of action" (*kāraka*) is governing. If it is argued that, in such a case, the agent itself would also incur the status of being an "object" (*karman*), because the designation of "agent" (which applies later) would sublate it—this is not so. For, in the absence of any evidence for such a restriction, the status of "object" would belong only to things like rice (*taṇḍula*), which are desired through the complete meaning of the verbal root consisting of an operation delimited by a result, and not to the result itself. Therefore, the mention of the "agent" is intended to ensure that the result also possesses the status of being an "object."

Furthermore, in the sentence "he keeps the cow away from the barley" (*yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati*), the barley would also [erroneously] have the status of an object (*karman*). In that context, the meaning of the verb *vārayati* is an activity conducive to the absence of an activity that produces a result such as eating. Nor does the rule "of those [roots] having the sense of warding off" (*vāraṇārthānām*) apply to both [the cow and the barley] due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*). However, when the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is included [in the rule], there is no fault, because [the barley] is not the locus of the result produced by the activity residing in the agent; so they say.

If it is asked, "For what purpose is the inclusion of the superlative suffix *tamap*? [the answer is: It is for the purpose of excluding the status of being an object (*karmatva*) from "milk" (*payas*) in examples such as "he eats milk-rice" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*). It should not be argued that even in the absence of *tamap*, there would still be the undesirable consequence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) because, in this instance, there exists the intention to express the connection of milk with the meaning of the root *bhuj* (to eat) through a relation produced by its own operation—namely, the production of softness and clarity—and because there is no intention to express it as the locus of the result (*phalāśrayatva*). For it is impossible to maintain two simultaneous intentions.

In the view that the meaning of a nominal stem consists of five factors (*pañcakaprātipadikārthapakṣa*), there is no fault, because the intention exists for both [the action and the object] to be conveyed by the word *payas* (milk) itself. This is because one understands [the meaning] as "the effort of wind conducive to causing milk to descend below the throat, produced by the activity consisting of making the milk soft and clear," and so forth. In that case, in the absence of the mention of the suffix *-tamap*, the accusative alone would apply due to its higher status. It should be understood that here, primarily, the status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) of eating and buying belongs to the rice (*odana*) alone, not to the milk.

Nor is it impossible to avoid the status of *karman* (object) for the milk according to the rule *tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam* [Pāṇini 1.4.50], because its activity occurs entirely without being intended; this is precisely what is obtained by the term *anīpsita*. However, if its status as such were primary (*mukhya*), then it would indeed be a *karman*; this should be understood. And primariness with respect to being intended consists in being the qualificand of a desire whose qualifier is the mode of that verbal root's meaning, while not being the object of a desire whose qualifier is some other property employed in that verbal root's meaning. And in the present case, [the milk] is falling downward...

Even though [the fire] is not the locus of the result in the form of an instrument (*karaṇa*), there is no fault because it is indeed the object of a desire characterized by the modes of being soft, clear, and consistent. However, if the word "real" (*satya*) were absent, then in the sentence "He wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the fire would also incur the status of an object (*karman*). Nor does this imply that the rule "of those [roots] meaning warding off" (*vāraṇārthānām*) is redundant; for that rule finds its application in connection with verbs such as *vārayati* when they possess the aforementioned meaning [of preventing].

In this context, "prevention" (*vāraṇa*) is an operation conducive to the absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Nor does this contradict the *Vṛtti* and other works which state that "prevention is the obstruction of activity," for verbal roots possess multiple meanings. [This is the underlying point: By the rule *parau bhuvo’vajñāne* (Pāṇini 3.1.55), the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed after the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *pari-* in the sense of contempt (*avajñāna*). And since this meaning is already established by the lexicon stating, "disregard (*anādara*), defeat (*paribhava*), humiliation (*parībhāva*), and insult (*tiraskriyā*"), the further prescription of *ghañ* in the sense of contempt becomes redundant; thus, it serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) that verbal roots have multiple meanings.

Moreover, if the root *kurda* meant "only in the sense of playing," then the inclusion of the word "only" (*eva*) would be redundant, since verbal roots do not possess multiple meanings [in that restricted case]. [However, this is not so] because they do possess multiple meanings. For me, however, there is no fault, because fire lacks the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of a desire whose mode (*prakāra*) is the absence of contact. For the desire is not "May fire not be in contact with the boy," but rather "May the boy not be in contact with fire. And this has been indicated right here in the Bhāṣya.

And thus, the refined meaning of this sūtra is as follows: *karmatva* (the state of being an object) consists in being either (1) the result delimited by the delimitor of the root-meaning (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*), or (2) the locus of the result of the root-meaning through a relation that is delimited by the result brought about by the agent’s activity (*kartṛvyāpāraprayojyaphalatāvacchedakasambandha*). Here, "result-ness" (*phalatva*)—in the context of co-occurrence with an agentive suffix—is the property of being the meaning of that root which serves as the locus of the mode (*prakāratā*) qualified by the predication-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of that same root; however, there is no inclusion of "causality" (*janakatva*) here. For if [causality] were included, it would lead to a contradiction with the Bhāṣya and other texts which establish *karmatva*, since in cases such as *āste* ("he sits"), the term is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) for the act of seeing and so forth preceded by sitting.

In sentences such as *devadattaḥ pacati* ("Devadatta cooks") and *karoṣi* ("you do"), which mean "an effort conducive to the arising of the action of cooking, having Devadatta as its agent and the rice as its object, has you as its agent," and in sentences such as *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("see, the deer runs"), the phrase *taddhātu-* (belonging to that verbal root) is used to exclude the status of being a "result of the action" (*kriyāphala*) from the cooking or running itself.

For if that were not the case, Devadatta would be the "object" (*karman*), and consequently, a second-case suffix (*dvitīyā*) would have to appear after it—as in *pakva odanaḥ* ("the cooked rice is fit")—because a designation (*saṃjñā*) that conforms to the primary element is stronger [and thus overrides others]. Nor can this be sublated by his being the "agent" (*kartṛ*) of the meaning of the verbal root, because this [designation of agent] is also to be understood as distinct for each specific action.

Therefore, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to the word *puṣpa* in the expression "he desires flowers" (*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*), nor to the word *hari* in expressions such as "devotion is pleasing to Hari" (*haraye rocate bhaktiḥ*), which has the meaning "he pleases Hari" (*hariṃ prīṇayati*); for in connection with those [verbs], the term *sampradāna* (recipient) refers to the locus of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning.

Now, one might object: if the term *tamap* (the superlative suffix) is employed, then [the designation of "object"] would apply only in cases where there is an explicit mention of the agent's pleasure (*prīti*), such as in "he eats milk-rice" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), and not in cases like "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*) or "he sees the sun" (*ādityaṃ paśyati*). Nor should it be argued that even in those cases, excellence relative to the action certainly exists, since the action itself is desired for the sake of its result and thus becomes "desired" (*īpsita*); for even in the case of "seeing" and so forth, a result in the form of manifestation (*prākaṭya*) indeed exists. This objection cannot stand, because the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) must belong to the same class.

For a *kāraka* is of the same class as other *kārakas*, not an action (*kriyā*). Nor should it be argued that even an action possesses the status of an object (*karman*) in relation to [the agent's] desire for non-perception and so forth, because there is no evidence for such a status appearing in all instances. Furthermore, if this were the case, since an action would also be the most desired (*īpsitatama*), it would be impossible for it to possess a degree of excellence relative to that [action]. To this, they reply: "By such indications as *he looks at the forehead and the hen* and *that by which he desires non-seeing*, it is made known that the technical designation of 'object' (*karmasaṃjñā*) applies even when the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is not explicitly mentioned."

In this context, the rule that establishes the expressive power (*śakti*) of the second case (*dvitīyā*) for the object (*karman*) is: "The second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*). Here, by the word *karman*, only that which is designated as "object" (*karmasaṃjñaka*) by the rules of this very grammar is understood, because there is no qualification [to the contrary]. In this regard, the meaning of the base (*āśraya*) is the referent of the second case prescribed for the object as taught by the rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*). This is because, according to the authoritative statement of the masters—"the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise"—the result (*phala*) is already expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself.

Because [the object] is obtained [from the verbal suffix], and because even "being most desired"—which constitutes the primary objective (mukhyoddeśyatā)—does not appear from that [suffix], as it is obtained through the mode of the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha). In that context, the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is the qualifier by way of non-difference, and the result is the qualificand by way of being inherent (ādheyatā). Thus, in cases such as "he worships Hari" (*hariṃ bhajati*), the cognition is: "an activity that generates pleasure residing in a locus non-different from Hari. For the meaning of the root *bhaj* is indeed "an activity that generates pleasure."

Nor can it be argued that, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the meaning [of a word] is merely the substratum (the individual), because the potency must be admitted to reside in the form (*ākṛti*) alone due to parsimony (*lāghava*); for if the potency were accepted as residing in the individual (*vyakti*), there would result a redundancy (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiting factor of the denotable (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). This has been established as the final position (*siddhānta*). Even so, since the cognition of the substrate (*dharmin*) necessarily follows from that [cognition of the form], the potency—defined as the capacity to produce cognition—is unavoidable in that case.

Otherwise, if there were the consequence that a case-ending conveys only the property (*dharma*), then in expressions such as "drive the cow" (*gāṃ vāhaya*), there would be the consequence that the act of driving could not be construed with the referent. Furthermore, we have already explained at length that for us, *śakti* (denotative power) is precisely this capacity to convey meaning. Moreover, since it has been determined that compounds whose meanings include the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and others have the substratum (*dharmin*) as their primary referent, that alone is logical. This is also supported by the natural sense of sūtras such as "in the object" (*karmaṇi*).

By the introduction of the technical designation "kṛt" and so forth, it is understood that the case endings (*vibhakti*) are grammatically correct when their meaning is construed non-differently with the meaning of the verbal root itself in other instances; this is because the rule teaches the correctness of the case endings precisely in such a way. For this very reason, the passages from the *Bhāṣya* and other texts which establish that the *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes) and *sup* (nominal suffixes) have the same referent (*samānārthatva*) become consistent. Furthermore, it has been established in the *Ākhyātavāda* that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the *tiṅ* suffixes resides in the substratum (*dharmin*) alone. Moreover, since "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), there is no complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiting property of the denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). This is because, even though it is complex, its status as a delimiting property has already been established.

Nor can it be said that the "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatā*) is differentiated by the difference in the perceiver or the difference in the related entity—otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of apprehending the "substratum-ness" of a jar and so forth—and thus there is an infinite plurality of powers (*śakti*); for if a cloth were apprehended, that would simply be an accepted consequence, and if it were not apprehended, there is no reason to suspect a fault. This is precisely the way of those who maintain the oneness of inherence (*samavāya*), as well as those who maintain the oneness of qualities such as whiteness.

Or, let it be that the substratum-hood (*āśrayatva*) is manifold; nevertheless, since the delimitor of the objecthood of the cognition regarding the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) at the outset is the property of being the substratum-hood itself—which serves as the delimitor of the delimitor of the denotablehood (*śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*)—and this is unitary, there is no infinity of denotative powers (*śakti*).

As for the claim that, since the locus (*āśraya*) is the denotable meaning (*śakya*), the state of being contained (*ādheyatva*) must be accepted as the relation (*saṃsarga*); and that consequently, the cognition [of the object] would result even from the sentence "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*); and that the co-occurrence with the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is not the cause of such a cognition, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—since at the time when the accusative is understood to denote the object (*karmatva*), such a cognition arises even from "The rice cooks"—that is not correct. For even if the objecthood (*karmatva*) were the denotable meaning, the undesirable consequence of such a cognition arising from that [sentence] would be difficult to avoid.

Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because the causality [of the word] for a verbal cognition whose relation is "residing-in" (ādheyatā) and whose qualificandum is a jar consists in being a cognition produced by a word following a word denoting a jar; nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of one who has acquired a contrary linguistic habit (viparītavyutpanna) from the string "ghaṭaḥ karmatvam," since such a cognition arises from that string for those who have mastered the co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) such as "karmatvaṃ ghaṭaḥ" and "am ghaṭaḥ."

Because the state of deviation remains as it was; for even from the expression "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), there would result an understanding contrary [to the intended one]. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of such an understanding occurring even for one who lacks proficiency (*vyutpatti*). [Note: Proficiency is a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the study of one's own respective treatise. For example, according to those who have studied the Grammarian’s system (*Vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), only items ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) and the like possess the status of being a "word" (*pada*), and not even that which possesses expressive power (*śaktimat*). However, the point is that for Logicians (*Tārkikas*), even that which possesses expressive power is a word.

If you argue that, in the case of an understanding produced by a particular co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), the apprehension of the capacity of that co-occurrence to produce such an understanding is also a cause, then we have no objection.

The distinction is this: for others, [the word] enters [into the definition] by way of its sequence (*ānupūrvī*) being composed of words that convey the status of being an object (*karmatva*); for us, however, it enters by way of being a word that conveys an object. Nor should it be argued that in your view there is no entry of a word denoting the locus (*āśraya*), because that [locus] is the denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*) of that [word]. And thus, it should not be said that there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of objecthood even from "It is cooked by Devadatta" (*devadattena pacyate*), because there is no fault; for we accept that the delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—namely, the state of being the locus and the respective capacities (*śakti*)—are distinct in the case of the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and so forth.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence that the second and subsequent [moments] would become mere synonyms. Alternatively, let it be granted that [the object] enters into the causal relation by virtue of being an "object" (*karman*) in the sense of being the locus of the result; for even if the result is impossible [to produce], it serves to distinguish [the cause] from others simply by its residing in that [locus]. Thus, there is no fault.
