As for the claim that because one experiences the cognition [of an object] as "karmatva-ness" (the property of being an object) and so forth, it must therefore be denotable (*śakyatā*) in those respective forms—that too is not correct. This is because such a cognition is dependent upon a specific linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) and is thus not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatva*), and furthermore, because no one actually experiences it in that way. Nor should it be argued that the substratum (*āśraya*) itself is not denotable because it is obtainable through other means; for even if it is obtained as "greenness" (*haritva*) and so forth, it is not obtained as "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*).

By this, the objection that—since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) also possesses that meaning (the action)—there would result an option with the nominative case prescribed for the meaning of the nominal stem—is refuted, because [the action] is not the meaning of the stem in the sense of being its substratum (*āśraya*). In this very manner, it should be understood that all case-endings denoting grammatical relations (*kāraka-vibhakti*) have as their content the substratum (*dharmin*).

Now, does the statement "non-acquisition as the substratum" (āśrayatvenālābhaḥ) not simply mean that the status of being a substratum (āśrayatva) is not acquired? And if so, then it is appropriate that the expressive power (śakti) resides there [in the substratum] itself. The grammatical rule "the second case ending is used for the object" (karmaṇi dvitīyā) and others, however, presuppose an identity between the expressive power and its locus (tadvatsatādātmya). Otherwise, in accordance with rules such as "for one and two" (dvayekayoḥ), it would follow that the singular number and other suffixes would denote a substratum qualified by number.

However, regarding verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and primary derivatives (*kṛt*), such as in "the mat was made" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*) or "Devadatta cooks somewhat" (*devadattaḥ pacatikalpam*), it has been established in the *Ākhyātavāda* that they denote the substratum (*dharmivācakatva*) or indicate it (*tallakṣakatva*), due to the requirement of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in their syntactic connection and in accordance with rules such as "when *yuṣmad* is the subordinate word" (*yuṣmadyupapade*). Furthermore, the meaning of the rule "provided it is not already expressed" (*anabhihite*) is "provided that those respective powers (*śakti*) have not been denoted. Since the power exists even in the verbal suffix by way of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*), there is no fault. Its [the suffix's] connection is with the fruit (*phala*), which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), through the relation of being a determiner (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*).

Alternatively, even if [the suffix] has the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it functions as a qualifier of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), just as in cases such as *rama* (accusative singular). For this very reason, compounds such as the possessive (*bahuvrīhi*) whose meaning is that [suffix] have as their primary referent the substratum (*dharmī*). Or rather, their status as such is due to their having as their meaning only the base of the case-ending. For this same reason, even in the view of others, the fact that a possessive compound with the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyartha-bahuvrīhi*) conveys the substratum is logically consistent.

Nor is there any complexity (gaurava) in the view that the reality (*tattva*) is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the denotability (*śakyatva*) of that [reality], because this has already been answered; and because it is precisely that [reality] which, through identity (*tādātmya*), serves as the delimitor. Furthermore, even if the instances of substratum-hood (*āśrayatā*) are manifold, there is no complexity, since the universal "substratum-hood-ness" (*āśrayatvatva*) is itself an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*). If it is argued: "In this view, the universal 'substratum-hood-ness' would also have to be denotable, for even if it is not denotable, it is possible for it to be the delimitor of denotability—just as, for example, that which is not the object of a definition (*alakṣya*) can be the delimitor of being the object of a definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*)," we reply: True. For this very reason, Hari stated another alternative: "Or rather, it is simply the capacity (*śakti*)."

And this second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs only when the object (*karman*) has not been expressed by a *kṛt* suffix or the like, according to the rule "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*). Therefore, in examples such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), the second case does not occur; for the phrase "when not already expressed" is a qualifier specifically of the object and so forth, due to their immediate proximity. By this, the objection that the second case would still occur because the number one (*ekatva*) is not expressed even though the objecthood (*karmatva*) is expressed by the *kṛt* suffix is refuted. This is just as, although the number is expressed by words such as *eka*, the second case is employed to convey the objecthood and other relations.
The detailed explanation—that the understanding of number can also occur through the nominative case—should be consulted in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

Furthermore, there is another rule that teaches the status of being an object (*karmatva*): "And likewise that which is connected [to the action] though not intended. In this context, "not intended" (*anīpsita*) means not being the primary goal (*anuddeśyatva*). An example is: "He eats poison because he is dependent on others. This "not being the primary goal" should be understood, by virtue of proximity, as applying only to the agent of the verb whose meaning constitutes the locus of the result for the sake of which something is made an object. And "being so connected" (*tathāyukta*) means being the locus of the result of the meaning of the verb in question.

In such instances as "Devadatta eats rice with poison" (*viṣeṇaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*) or "Devadatta goes from Prayāga to Kāśī" (*prayāgāt kāśīṃ gacchati*), the poison (*viṣa*) and Prayāga do not possess the status of an *object* (*karma*).

Here, the intention is that the locus (*viṣaya*) is construed with the action itself (*vyāpāra*) through the relation of being produced by its own operation; thus, it does not possess the status of being the substratum of the result (*phalāśrayatva*).
Consequently, the refined definition of the sūtra is: "that which is the substratum of the result of the verbal root's meaning, provided it is in no way intended [as a goal]."

In examples such as *payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats rice with milk"), the "sat" portion [of the definition] is included to exclude the status of "object" (*karmatva*) from the milk. For this very reason, the mention of the term *anīpsita* ("not intended") in this sūtra is purposeful; otherwise, by the maxim of the curd and Kauṇḍinya (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*), the application of this rule would be established as occurring only in the case of what is not intended, so what would be the use of that term? Otherwise, [the rule] might apply even to a non-primary intended object (*amukhyoddeśya*), and thus that term is used to exclude such cases.

Furthermore, there is a sūtra that explains this: "And that which is unmentioned" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.51). Here, the word "connected" (yuktam) is carried over from the preceding sūtra. In this context, when there is an expectancy as to "by what," the connection is made with the immediately present object (karman). Thus, the meaning is as follows: that object which is not intended to be expressed in the form of an ablative, dative, locative, or [direct] object, but is instead intended to be expressed as a relation, and which stands in a relationship to the action denoted by the verbal root as its instrumental cause—that is the [unmentioned] object. For this very reason, the instrumental and the causal factors are not included here, because they lack the quality of being "connected with the object. And this—

"Of the roots *duh* (to milk), *yāc* (to beg), *pac* (to cook), *daṇḍ* (to fine), *rudh* (to obstruct), *pracch* (to ask), *ci* (to gather), *vr̥* (to choose), *śās* (to instruct), *sū* (to bring forth), *ji* (to win), *math* (to churn), and *muṣ* (to steal)—as well as for *nī*, *hr̥*, *kr̥ṣ*, and *vah*—that which is connected with the object is called 'unexpressed' (*akathita*).

Thus, this rule applies only in connection with the specifically enumerated verbal roots. "Connected with the object" means being related as a cause to the meaning of the root in question, which is centered on the object.

And thus, the refined meaning of this sūtra is as follows: the state of being the secondary object (*gauṇakarma*) of any one of these [verbs] consists in its being construed as related to the operation of the meaning of any one of these [verbs], which is produced by an operation whose primary meaning belongs to another of these [verbs]. Furthermore, its "secondary" status is known from linguistic usage such as "in the case of the secondary object of *duh* and so forth. And thus, the meaning of the accusative case prescribed for this object is "relation."

An illustrious example of this is: "He milks the cow for milk" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*). Here, the meaning of the root *duh* (to milk) is an activity conducive to an activity that is itself conducive to the separation of a liquid substance residing within [the cow]. Among these, the activity conducive to the separation resides in the cow; because the milk is the locus of the result produced by both the activity of the agent and the activity of the cow, it possesses primacy (*prādhānya*), whereas the cow possesses secondary status (*gauṇatva*) due to the opposite being the case.

In this regard, although the status of the object (*karmatva*) is established either by the rule "that which is thus connected" (*tathāyuktam*) or by "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*), nevertheless, this [present rule] is intended to prevent the application of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is an intention to express the relation of "remainder" (*śeṣatva*). Since the relation residing in the milk (*payoniṣṭha*)—namely, the relation of separation—is itself the delimiting factor of the result (*phalatāvacchedaka*), the cow does not have the status of an object merely by being the locus of separation.

Thus, the understanding is as follows: the operation residing in the cow is conducive to that operation which is conducive to the separation residing in the milk, and that [separation] is related to the cow.

However, when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is specifically an operation conducive to a separation residing in a liquid substance, then, if there is an intention to express the status of the *apādāna* (ablative), the fifth case alone is used, as in *goḥ*. If that [status] is not intended to be expressed, however, it is precisely the status of the *karman* (object) by this rule. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. Furthermore, this non-intention to express the status of *apādāna* and so forth should be understood as follows: namely, the intention to express two distinct operations for the verbal root, along with the non-intention to express the state of being the limit (*avadhi*) of the separation and so forth that constitute the meaning of those operations.

In the expression "He begs Bali for the earth" (*baliṃ yācate vasudhām*), the meaning of the root *yāc* (to beg) is an activity conducive to an activity that brings about the cessation of one's own ownership (*svatva*). Among these, the first activity resides in Bali, while the activity conducive to it—consisting of such things as the desire expressed in the words "let it be given"—resides in the beggar. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The activity residing in the beggar, which is conducive to that activity belonging to Bali which brings about the cessation of ownership residing in the earth. Some maintain that if the meaning were merely an activity conducive to the cessation of ownership, then Bali would be considered the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) when there is a consideration of his being the locus of the separation (*vibhāga*) from the substance possessed of that ownership.

Others maintain that [the recipient] possesses the status of *sampradāna* (the indirect object) because they are intended by the act of requesting (*yāc*). As for the claim that "requesting" consists in the desire to give with reference to oneself—that is incorrect; for it would fail to account for the usage, "He requests a girl for the sake of a son," since in this case the gift is intended for the son. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the expression "Devadatta requests" even when he lacks the desire to have himself as the recipient, simply because he might hope to obtain a reward and thus say, "Give [it] to me. This is the general direction of the argument.

In the expression "the undisciplined person requests discipline" (*avinītaṃ vinayaṃ yācate*), the meaning of the verb *yācati* (he requests) is an action conducive to an action conducive to acceptance (*svīkāra*). Acceptance, moreover, is a specific type of cognition that generates the utterance of words such as "I shall certainly do this. The relation that delimits its status as a result is objectivity (*viṣayatā*). Thus, discipline (*vinaya*) is the primary object; when the meaning consists merely of an action conducive to acceptance, the undisciplined person functions as the recipient (*sampradāna*). This very process is what they call entreaty (*anunaya*).

And thus, the understanding is that there is an activity residing in Devadatta which is conducive to an activity favorable to the acceptance of the subject matter of discipline (*vinaya*), and which is connected with one who has not yet departed.

In the case of "He cooks rice-grains into porridge" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the root *pac* is an activity conducive to softening (*viklitti*) which produces origination (*utpatti*). In that context, the rice-grains and the porridge are construed as the substrata (*āśrayatā*) of the origination and the softening, respectively. Because both activities have the porridge as their intended object (*uddeśyatva*), the porridge is the primary element (*pradhāna*). The understanding is: "The activity is that which produces the softening related to the rice-grains and so forth, which in turn produces the origination residing in the porridge."

But when the meaning is an operation conducive to the production [of rice] resulting from softening (*viklitti*), then one says, "He cooks rice-grains into boiled rice" (*taṇḍulān odanaṃ pacati*). The meaning is that he produces boiled rice, which is a transformation of the rice-grains, by means of softening. This is the general direction: if the verbal root expresses merely the operation conducive to softening, then the rice-grains alone possess the status of the object (*karman*).

In the expression *gargāñ śataṃ daṇḍayati* ("He fines the Gargas a hundred"), the meaning of the root *daṇḍ* is an action consisting of a command (*śāsana*), which is conducive to an operation that is itself conducive to the act of giving (*dāna*) where the Gargas are the recipients (*sampradāna*). "Command" (*śāsana*) means restraint (*niyantraṇa*). Here, "a hundred" (*śatam*) is the primary object because it is the intended goal (*uddeśya*). If the root were to mean merely an operation conducive to giving, then—provided the status of being the locus of separation (*vibhāga-āśrayatva*) is not intended—the Gargas would have the status of an ablative (*apādāna*); if that [status as locus of separation] is not intended, they have the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*).

In the sentence "He shuts the cow in the pen" (*vrajam avaruṇaddhi gām*), the meaning of the root *rudh* (to obstruct) is an operation conducive to a conjunction with a subsequent location, which is delimited by the relation of being the locus (*anuyogitā*) for the obstruction of movement to another location at a later time. Delimited by the relation of being the locus, that [conjunction] resides in the pen (*vraja*). The cow is the primary element because it is the object of reference (*uddeśya*). If the meaning were a conjunction with a subsequent location delimited by the relation of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*), then, when there is an intention to express its status as the substratum of the action through the medium of the object (*karman*), it possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

In the expression *māṇavakaṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* ("he asks the boy the way"), the meaning of the root *pṛcch-* is an activity conducive to making known the object that is the subject of the question. That activity consists of a desire or similar mental state such as "by which path should one go? Since the boy (*māṇavaka*) is the locus of the act of making known, and the path (*panthān*) is the object of that knowledge, their respective statuses [as recipient and object] are to be understood. If the meaning were merely an activity conducive to knowledge in general, the boy would have the status of a *sampradāna* (recipient).

In the expression "he gathers fruits from the tree" (*vṛkṣam avacinoti phalāni*), the meaning of the root *ci* (to gather) is an operation subordinate to grasping, which is itself conducive to an operation conducive to separation (*vibhāga*). Because the tree is the locus of the operation conducive to separation, it possesses the status of an *apādāna* (ablative). In the expressions "he tells the Dharma to the boy" (*māṇavakaṃ dharmaṃ brūte*) or "he instructs him" (*śāsti*), the meaning of the root *brū* is an operation conducive to an operation that generates comprehension; whereas the meaning of the root *śās* is an operation conducive to an activity that culminates in engagement [with the Dharma]. However, when the meaning is an operation conducive to knowledge in the sense of being its object (*viṣayatayā*), then the boy possesses the status of a *sampradāna* (dative).

In the expression "He defeats Devadatta a hundred times" (*śataṃ jayati devadattam*), the meaning of the root *ji* (to conquer) is an action called "overthrowing" (*parābhava*) that is conducive to the production of ownership (*svatva*). If the root were to mean merely an action conducive to the production of ownership, then [Devadatta] would be either the ablative (*apādāna*) or the recipient (*sampradāna*).

"'One should churn nectar from the ocean of milk'—the meaning of the root *manth* (to churn) is an operation conducive to the production of the essential portion residing within a liquid substance. 'Production' (*utthāna*) here means conjunction with an upward location. If the root is intended to signify merely the operation conducive to production, then there is the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) when one intends to express its being the substratum of the action by way of the object; or there is the status of an ablative (*apādānatva*) when one intends to express its being the substratum of disjunction."

In the expression "he steals a hundred from Devadatta" (*devadattaṃ śataṃ muṣṇāti*), the meaning of the root *muṣ* (to steal) is an activity conducive to both the ignorance of another and the taking of that person's property. However, when the meaning is restricted solely to the activity conducive to taking, then Devadatta possesses the status of an *apādāna* (ablative).

In the expression "He leads, carries, drags, or takes the goat to the village," the meaning of the root *nī* (to lead) is an operation conducive to an operation that is itself conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location (*uttaradeśa-saṃyoga*). That same [operation], preceded by the seizing of the shoulder and so forth, is the meaning of *vah* (to carry); a specific operation conducive to motion is the meaning of *kṛṣ* (to drag); and bringing to another place preceded by forceful seizing is the meaning of *har* (to take). Because the leading of the goat is the intended goal (*uddeśya*), the goat is the primary object (*pradhāna*). If [the verb] were to signify mere motion, the village would be understood as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

But when the connection with the village goat (*grāmīyājā-saṃyoga*) alone is the intended object (*uddeśya*), then the village itself is the primary factor (*pradhāna*). By this, the Mīmāṃsā texts—which state that in the passage "He pours curd into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas," the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the milk because of its primacy—are explained. Alternatively, their interpretation may be justified by taking the functional primacy (*arthaprādhānya*) of the milk, which results from the arrival of the curd in place of the milk. For this very reason, the employment of the locative case (*saptamī*) is meaningful; such is the direction of the argument.

Furthermore, it is stated: "When used in conjunction with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the location (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and the distance to be traversed (*gantavya-adhvā*) should be designated as the object (*karman*). "Location" refers to places such as Kuru, Pañcāla, and so forth. By the term "intransitive," roots that lack an object distinct from place, time, and the like, as well as those whose objects are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita-karman*), are included. Consequently, even in the expression "he cooks for a month" (*māsaṃ pacati*), the distance to be traversed refers to a measure of space such as a *krośa* and the like; and "state" refers to words ending in primary suffixes (*ghañ*, *ac*, etc. derived from verbal roots expressing states of being and the like.

In expressions such as *kurūn svapiti* ("he sleeps in the Kuru country"), *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"), *krośaṃ śete* ("he lies down for a league"), and *godohaṃ āste* ("he sits while the cows are being milked"), the meaning of the accusative case is "relation" (*sambandha*), because these forms are employed when one intends to express the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*). When the status of being a "locus" (*adhikaraṇatva*) is intended, however, the locative case alone is used. Furthermore, it should be understood that the definition of this [specific] type of "object-ness" (*karmatva*) is the state of being a locus intended as being related to the meaning of this verbal root.

Regarding the status of being an object (*karmatva*) as taught by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇi kartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), it consists in being the locus of the respective verbal root-meaning's activity produced by the activity denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Since the definitions of "object-ness" differ according to the specific verbal roots involved, there is no risk of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) or other such defects in these definitions. In the definition of "object-ness" formulated for roots ending in *ṇic* that contain the roots *hṛ*, *kṛ*, or *ghaṭ*, the qualification "provided it is not denotable by a word ending in the third case" (*tṛtīyāntapadānabhidheyatve sati*) must be added.

In such cases as "tena devadattena hārayati kaṭam" (Devadatta causes the mat to be carried by him), there is no over-extension [of the definition]. However, in the case of causative forms of the roots *abhivad* and *dṛś*, being so [causative], the object-hood (*karmatva*) consists in being the locus of the fruit conveyed by that root which has a reflexive suffix (*ātmanepada-pratyaya*). In examples such as "vaikuṇṭham adhiśete," "adhitiṣṭhati," "adhyāste," "upavasati," "anuvasati," "adhivasati," or "āvasati," the locus (*ādhāra*) is the meaning of the accusative case.

In the case of connection with a *dhātu* (verbal root), this very status of being a locus (*ādhāra*) is what constitutes the status of being an object (*karman*). This is evident from the natural sense of the sūtras "adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma" [Pāṇini 1.4.46] and "upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.4.48], while the term "ādhāra" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Furthermore, in the case of the root *upa-vas*, one should understand that the locus of the act of fasting—distinct from its meaning of "eating"—is the object. Consequently, there is no over-extension [of the definition] in cases such as "he fasts in the forest" (*vane upavasati*). Moreover, the status of being the object of the root *abhi-ni-viś* should be understood as being the locus of the meaning of that root which is not denoted by a word ending in the locative case.

In expressions such as ‘he is angry with’ (*abhikrudhyati*) or ‘he bears malice toward’ (*abhiduhyati*), one should understand that the relation is that of being the object (*viṣayatā-sambandhitva*). Furthermore, the cognition in cases like ‘he is angry with Hari’ (*haraye krudhyati*) is to be understood according to the method that will be explained later. In connection with the root *div* meaning ‘to play,’ as in ‘he plays for a hundred’ (*śataṃ dīvyati*), its status as an object (*karmatva*) should be understood simply as being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) for the action of that root, which is not presented by a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*). And the definition of an object common to all [verbs] should be understood as the possession of the word ‘object’ (*karma*) through the relation of a specific convention (*saṅketaviśeṣa*).

It should be understood that even the transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) of roots consists in their having as their meaning a sense connected with an object designated as such (*karmasaṃjñaka*) by this very treatise.

As for the claim that transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting a result that resides in a locus different from the operation, and that the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in denoting a result that resides in the same locus as that operation—that is not correct. For [in that case], there would be no transitivity for verbs such as *adhyāste* ("he sits upon"), and there would be the unwanted consequence of its being intransitive. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, because it would entail the occurrence of object-terminations (*karma-pratyaya*) in instances such as "the grounds were sat upon by chamberlains wearing glittering jewels" (*adhyāsitā bhūmayaḥ...*) and "the dice are played" (*dīvyante akṣāḥ*), and it would also entail the occurrence of terminations in the abstract sense (*bhāve*) in those cases. Furthermore, the state of being intransitive consists in the fact that the meaning of the root does not admit of a connection with an object-denoted meaning; such is the direction of the argument.
1 [The author introduces the Naiyāyika position in order to refute it, beginning with the words "As for that which... and so forth.

This is the underlying meaning: in order to avoid the fault [of over-extension] in the case of "Caitra goes to Caitra," the Naiyāyikas employ the adverbial qualifier "inherence in something other" (*parasaṃyuktatvam*). Their intended meaning is that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs only to that which is the substratum of such a result as is produced by an activity inherent in something distinct from the referent intended as the base of the accusative case.]

In the present case, since the difference having Caitra—as intended as the second primary factor (*dvitīyāprakṛti*)—as its counter-correlate does not exist in Caitra himself, that which is the substratum of the result consisting of conjunction produced by the operation inherent in him cannot possess the status of an object (*karman*). However, because the village is the substratum of the result produced by the operation inherent in Caitra—just like the difference having the village as its counter-correlate—the status of the village as an object is established. As for the view that "the status of an object consists in being the substratum of a result, delimited by the meaning of the verbal root, which is produced by an action inherent in another (*parasamaveta*)," the inclusion of the qualifier "inherent in another" prevents the usage "Caitra goes to Caitra."

This is the distinction: by means of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*), "remoteness" (*paratva*) is understood in relation to the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*); by means of the verb (*ākhyāta*), that [remoteness] is made known in relation to that which is correlated with the number of its own meaning. And that [remoteness] is construed with the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). This is for the purpose of excluding the status of being an object (*karmatva*) for the preceding location in the cases of *gam* and *pat*, and for the following location in the cases of *tyaj* and *spand*.

Regarding the phrase "the delimitor of the root-meaning" (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*): thus, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the [delimitor] for *gam* (to go), downward conjunction (*adhaḥ-saṃyoga*) for *pat* (to fall), and likewise, disjunction (*vibhāga*) for *tyaj* (to abandon). Since there is no such fruit for *spand* (to vibrate), there is no fault. Nor does it follow that "abandoning" and "going" would become synonyms; for in those cases, since the action and its fruit are already obtained by the verbal root itself, the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the locus (*ādheyatva*) and the distinction (*bheda*). Even though the fruit is a part of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśa*), its connection with the meaning of the second case occurs due to the uniqueness of linguistic convention (*vyutpattivaicitryāt*).

Alternatively, the fruit (phala) may be denotable by the verbal root independently. And "being the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root" consists in being the qualifier in a cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of the verbal root and whose relation is "being the producer" (janakatva). Or, it consists in being either the qualificandum in a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the verbal root and whose relation is "being produced" (janyatva), or [the former]. For this very reason, there is no defect even when the fruit is the qualificandum in the case of an object-terminating verbal suffix (karmākhyāta).

In that regard, in expressions such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the meaning of the verbal root is delimited by conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Within this, the referent of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—namely, the village—conjoins with the action through the relation of subsistence (*vṛttitva*) and with the difference (*bheda*) through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), both by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to an action that is coreferential with a difference from the village and which generates a conjunction subsisting in the village. Similarly, in the case of the verb in the passive voice (*karmākhyāta*), the meaning of the suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) includes both difference and the property of being located (*ādheyatva*). Here, the property of being located relates to the factor of the result (*phala*), while the difference relates to the action through the aforementioned relation; furthermore, the result relates to the difference by way of counter-correlativity—this is to be inferred.

Now, regarding the difference (*bheda*) of the action, does its connection [with the object] occur by way of a general counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāsāmānyena*), or by way of a counter-correlativity delimited by the delimitor of the relatum-ness (*anvayitāvacchedakāvacchinnapratiyogitayā*)? If you say: "Not the first, because it would lead to the absurdity that 'Caitra goes to Caitra,' since the difference from Caitra delimited by duality (i.e., Caitra and another) exists in Caitra as well. Nor the second, because it would not lead to the [absurdity in] cases such as 'Devadatta goes to substance'"; we reply: No, for there is no fault, since the connection occurs through a counter-correlativity delimited by the specific individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*) that is connected with the result (*phala*).

In examples such as *grāmaṃ gamayati yajñadattam* ("he causes Yajñadatta to go to the village"), the operation of the root-meaning of the simple root *gam* (to go) constitutes the result (*phala*) with respect to the operation denoted by the causative (*ṇic*) suffix, and the aforementioned state of being a delimitant (*avacchedakatva*) also exists; thus, one should understand that the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) possesses the status of an object (*karman*).

However, in connection with verbs such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), there is no fault, because the rule [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.52] beginning with *gati-buddhi-* serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*). The essential point is that since the status of being an object differs according to the difference in action, the definition must be formulated so that it incorporates an action distinct from that of the causative forms like *pācayati*.

Nor should it be argued that, by adding the qualification "inherence in another" (*parasamavetatva*), there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of action (*karma*) to Caitra in a case where there is a conjunction resulting from the actions of both Caitra and Maitra—since the action inheres in the other (Maitra) and Caitra possesses the fruit consisting of the conjunction produced by that action—and that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the usage "Caitra goes to himself. This is because the definition differs according to the difference in the action.

That which possesses a certain kind of result produced by an action inherent in another is the object (*karman*) of that action; and since Caitra’s own action does not inhere in another, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in taking that [action] as a basis. On the other hand, being such [an object] with respect to Maitra’s action is indeed desired, because the usage "Maitra goes toward Caitra" occurs precisely in that case. By this, the undesirable consequence regarding usage is also prevented, because a verbal cognition in the form "the substratum of an action residing in someone other than Caitra, which produces a conjunction residing in Caitra" is impossible.

Because one's own action cannot reside in another, and because an action residing in another cannot exist in oneself, in expressions such as "he makes a pot," there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the objectness (*viṣayatā*), similar to cases like "I infer Brahman" or "I know [it]."

Thus, in cases such as *jānāti* ("he knows"), the status of being "figuratively transitive" (*gauṇasakarmakatva*) consists in having as their meaning that which is related to the sense of the nominal suffix, namely a state of being an object distinct from being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*). For this very reason, even when one is not eating, in the usage *bhojanāya yatate* ("he strives for food"), since the intended recipienthood expressed by the dative case—which is related to the meaning of the nominal stem—is construed only with the meaning of the root *yat*, the root *yat* does not possess a direct object; nor is there any usage such as *bhojanaṃ yatate*.

As for the claim that the word *ghaṭa* refers to the potsherd (*kapāla*), because it possesses the result in the form of the pot, it has the status of an object (*karmatva*); and although the potsherd is already established, it should be understood as the object of volitional effort (*kṛti*) in its capacity as a pot—this is not correct. For the pot is not the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and furthermore, the usage "he makes the potsherd into a pot" (*kapālaṃ ghaṭaṃ karoti*) would result in an undesirable consequence. Nor is it tenable to say that the status of being an object consists in being the substratum of the result in the form of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), because then the expression "he knows that [pot] which has perished" (*naṣṭe ghaṭe taṃ jānāti*) would be impossible.
If it is argued that "cognizedness" is merely another name for "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*), they reply that this is acceptable, as it is what we intend.

In this regard, the following must be asked: Is the power (śakti) [of the accusative case] postulated to prevent the cognition [of duality] from sentences such as "Caitra goes to Caitra," or rather to prevent its grammatical correctness (sādhutva)? It cannot be the first: even if that [duality] were the denotable meaning (śakyārtha), one would necessarily have to postulate another causal relation—namely, that the presence of the operation (vyāpāra) conveyed by the verbal root is the cause for a cognition having that [duality] as its qualifier—in order to prevent its connection elsewhere. Compared to that, it is simpler not to postulate the power there, but rather [to hold that] the cognition has as its qualifier the result (phala) which is conjoined with the state of being the denoted meaning of the second case.

Let it simply be stated that [the cause] is the status of being the cause for the establishment of an operation whose locus is other than the meaning of the word ending in the second case (dvitīyāntārtha). Since you too must necessarily accept a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in accordance with the connection with the result (*phala*), there is no additional burden for me by including merely "having a locus other than the meaning of the word ending in the second case" within the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of its generative capacity (*janakatā*). For you, however, the burden is evident, due to the postulation of a denotative power (*śakti*) in the sense of difference (*bheda*) and the further postulation of a distinct causal relation between that [difference] and its consequence.

Nor is there a deviation [in the rule] in the case of "na caitra-maitrau parasparaṃ gacchataḥ" (Caitra and Maitra do not go to each other), because the operation resides in the meaning of the second-case ending; for what is intended is the cognition of an operation whose counter-correlativity-limiting factor is the mutual absence residing in the meaning of the second-case ending.

Nor should it be argued that because there is no grasp of the expressive power (*śakti*) when there is a difference [between words], and because there is no cognition from the expression "Caitra, Caitra," there is no such causal relationship [between word and meaning]; for even the grasp of that [word] as the cause is itself a cause for cognition, and thus remains unimpaired. For this very reason, one who has acquired a contrary linguistic habit (*vyutpanna*) has the cognition "pot-ness" from the expression "ghaṭaḥ karmatvam," but lacks cognition from the expression "ghaṭam ānaya."

Furthermore, in this way, the very possibility of [expressing] difference would not be established, because the desired cognition for one who has acquired a contrary linguistic habit from the expression "Caitra, Caitra" [would not arise]; and because for one who possesses the apprehension of a power residing in another, there is no cognition due to the lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). For a word like "cloth" does not become denotative of cloth simply because one who has apprehended the power of the word "pot" in a pot cognizes a pot.
Nor is the latter [alternative] possible, because that is precluded by the technical designation of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, the "object-ness" (*karmatva*) as defined by you is not the determinant for the occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) or for its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), because this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the accusative does not arise in expressions such as *ghaṭaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the pot") when used with transitive verbal roots (*saviṣayaka-dhātu*).

Nor can it be argued that this [definition] applies only to cases other than those involving an object (*saviṣaya*), while in those [transitive cases], the relation is simply through "objecthood" (*viṣayatā*); for this would result in over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as *kṛṣṇāya rocate* ("it pleases Kṛṣṇa"), *devadattāya krudhyati* ("he is angry with Devadatta"), and *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers"). Moreover, there would be under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *devadattam abhikrudhyati* ("he is angry at Devadatta") and *vaikuṇṭham adhitiṣṭhati* ("he dwells in Vaikuṇṭha").
Now, if it is argued that conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) itself is what determines that [relation], then the statement that difference is the denotable meaning is fruitless.

Furthermore, it has been stated that in cases such as "he knows the jar," there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the objecthood; however, this is improper, as it is based merely on one's own whim.

Furthermore, since the *Bhāṣya* and other works state the restrictive rules in the sequence: "the second case is correct only when [the object] is an action (*karman*)," and "only the second case is correct when [the object] is an action," this indicates that even figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is incorrect in other instances. For this very reason, there is the practice among your own elders that "there is no figurative indication in nominal case-endings (*sub-vibhakti*). Moreover, in the rule concerning the object (*karman*), because it is more logical to accept only the technical definition of "object" as prescribed within our own grammatical system according to the maxim of "the artificial and the non-artificial" (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), the scope of the term is not taken to include figurative objects.

Furthermore, there is the problem of pervasion (*vyāpti*) of your proposed definition with respect to the fruit (*phala*). Consequently, expressions such as *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly") would be impossible. Nor can this be justified by the rule stating that "adverbs ending in the accusative case are neuter," because no such rule exists; moreover, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the instrumental case would not apply in instances such as *somena yajati* ("he sacrifices with soma"). Furthermore, in this view, the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) would also be redundant, as it is more appropriate to define [the object] simply as that which possesses the fruit of the verbal root's meaning. And the state of being the fruit of the verbal root's meaning consists in being the substratum of the "being-produced-ness" (*janyatā*) as qualified by the verbal root's meaning.

Alternatively, they say that [the meaning of the accusative] is the state of being connected with the operation denoted by the verbal root (dhātvartha-vyāpāra) through either the relation of being a qualifier (prakāratā) or the relation of being a qualificand (viśeṣyatā).

As for the claim of the Mīmāṃsakas that "sādhyatva" (the state of being something to be accomplished) is the meaning of the accusative, it has been stated: "By direct statement (śruti), the accusative is understood to express that which is to be accomplished."

And thus, in such cases as "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the meaning is: "one should bring about the rice by means of threshing. Although the rice grains are already accomplished entities and are the instruments (*sādhana*) of the action, nevertheless, what is to be understood here as the "state of being the object to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) is precisely their status as things to be refined (*saṃskāryatva*), insofar as they serve as the means for producing a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*). In the case of "one offers the flour-gruel" (*saktuñjuhoti*), however, since the flour-gruel (*saktu*) is neither something that has already come into being nor something useful for what is yet to be produced, the previously mentioned state of being the object to be accomplished is impossible. Therefore, in order to convey the cognition of an activity conducive to the oblation consisting of flour-gruel, the instrumental sense of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is indicated by the accusative case-ending. And thus, the meaning is: "one should bring about [the result] by means of the flour-gruel."

Although, according to the aforementioned principle, there is grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutva*) in the case of *lakṣaṇā*, nevertheless, because grammatical correctness is established even in other senses by rules such as Pāṇini’s *supāṃ suluk* [7.1.39], *bahulaṃ chandasi* [7.1.103], and *tṛtīyā ca hośchandasi* [2.3.3] regarding the Vedic language (*chandas*), they say there is no fault. In that regard, the state of being an object (*sādhyatva*) is simply a particular power (*śaktiviśeṣa*), so there is no contradiction whatsoever. This much is the distinction: in the Veda, the power of being an object (*karmatva-śakti*) is co-extensive (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the previously mentioned state of being something to be processed (*saṃskāryatva*). Enough of this prolixity. Now, the meaning of that [term] which functions as an upapada-case is investigated.

In this regard, the general meaning of case-terminations used as *upapada* (governing words) is "relation" (*sambandha*), because they serve as exceptions to the genitive case of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). We shall explain their specific meanings in their respective places. In the example "The cowherd girls [are] on both sides of Kṛṣṇa" (*ubhayataḥ kṛṣṇaṃ gopyaḥ*), the understanding is that they are situated on both flanks in relation to Kṛṣṇa.
In "Fie upon the non-devotee of Kṛṣṇa" (*dhik kṛṣṇābhaktam*), the sense of "fie" is censure; the understanding is that there is censure in relation to the non-devotee of Kṛṣṇa.

"Uparyupari, ado'dhaḥ, adhyādhi, or lokaṃ"—the meanings of the doubled terms beginning with *upari* are, respectively, the state of being in the proximate upper part, the state of being in the proximate lower part, and the state of being in the proximate vicinity. Since the doubling is prescribed to express proximity (*sāmīpya*), the relation consisting of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) is the meaning of the second case ending. The resulting cognition proceeds in the manner: "that which exists in the upper part proximate to that which has the world as its counter-correlative," and so forth.

In the expressions "the cowherds [are] *abhitaḥ* or *paritaḥ* Kṛṣṇa," the meaning is: "by parts" (*khaṇḍaśaḥ*) and "with attachment" (*saktyā*), that is, by delimiting all the limbs (*sarvāvayavāvacchedena*). The connection with the object denoted by the second case (*dvitīyārtha-sambandha-anvaya*) applies to every single part of him. Thus, the meaning is: "by delimiting all the limbs belonging to Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, *abhitaḥ* can also mean "in front of" (*ābhimukhye*); thus, the meaning is "facing Kṛṣṇa."

In the expression "samayā" or "nikaṣā grāmam," the indeclinable [term] has the sense of proximity; the meaning of the accusative case is "being characterized by" (nirūpitatva). Thus, the cognition is: "that which possesses proximity as characterized by the village. In the expression "hā kṛṣṇābhaktam," the word "hā" signifies grief; the cognition is: "grief related to that [person]. In expressions such as "hā pitaḥ kvāsi," the meaning is that the existence of the father—who is the object of the question addressed to him—is an object of lamentation. For this very reason, the second case ending is not used for the father.

Because of the absence of connection with the word *hā* [in the sense of grief]. In expressions such as "it does not occur to the hungry person" (*bubhukṣitaṃ na pratibhāti*), the meaning is the absence of the manifestation of some object related to the hungry person. *Pratibhā* is instantaneous flash-forth (*sphūrti*). In the phrase "Hari is between you and me" (*antarā tvāṃ māṃ ca hariḥ*), the word *antarā* has the sense of "middle"; its nature as a limit (*avadhi*) is the relation expressed by the second case ending (*dvitīyārtha*). Thus, the cognition is: "Hari resides in the middle, having you and me as its limits."

In the expression "antarā hariṃ na sukham" (no happiness without Hari), the meaning of the word *antarā* is absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*). The meaning of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*), which connects with the absence. The word *hari* is used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote "one who possesses devotion to Hari" (*haribhakta*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "an absence whose counter-correlative is a happiness residing in one who lacks devotion to Hari. Similarly, the word *antareṇa* also has this dual sense; even when joined with the counter-correlative, the second case ending is employed.

In the expression *'japamanuprāvarṣat'* ("It rained following the recitation"), the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the relationship of the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*), as well as causality (*hetu*). The prefix *anu* indicates a specific type of relationship. The state of being the indicated (*lakṣyatva*) consists in being the object of a cognition produced by [another] cognition. For, by means of the cognition of the recitation, the activity [of raining] qualified by a specific time is made known through the cognition of the time of the recitation. It is for this very reason that this serves as the answer to the question, "When did it rain? In that context, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) connects with the cause (*hetu*) by way of non-difference (*abheda*).

And that [function of *anu*] occurs when there is knowledge of a portion of the locus (*lakṣya*). Since even between two word-meanings, such as in the case of the particle *eva*, a mutual connection is observed, the cognition is: "The raining is the object of a cognition produced by a cognition whose cause is non-different from Japa. In the phrase "the army has encamped along the river" (*nadīmanvavasitā senā*), the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is accompaniment (*sāhitya*), which is indicated. The cognition is: "It is connected with the river. In "the gods are inferior to Hari" (*anuhariṃ surāḥ*), the meaning of the second case is a relation of inferiority consisting of a state of being lower; it is what is indicated. The cognition is: "They possess an inferiority having Hari as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). In the case of "upari" (above), it is exactly the same.

In the expression "the lightning flashes toward (*prati*), around (*pary*), or after (*anu*) the tree," the meaning of the accusative case (*dvitīyārtha*) expressed by *prati* and the other prepositions is "being the object of indication" (*lakṣyatva*). The tree is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) because the lightning is known through its illumination; for by means of it, the lightning is made known as delimited by a specific direction. The resulting cognition is: "The flash of lightning is the object of the cognition produced by the cognition of the tree.

In the expression "devoted to Viṣṇu" (*bhakto viṣṇuṃ prati*), the meaning of the accusative case is "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*). This [meaning] connects with one part [of the compound], namely "devotion" (*bhakti*). The resulting cognition is: "One who is the locus of devotion having Viṣṇu as its object."
*Lakṣmīḥ hariṃ prati* ("Lakṣmī [is] toward Hari"): here, *svatva* (ownership) is the meaning of *prati*. The cognition is that of ownership having Hari as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*).

In the expression *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati* ("He waters tree after tree"), the repetition is due to *vīpsā* (distribution). By the term *vīpsā*, what is expressed is the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*)—residing in each individual sense-object (*prakṛtyartha*) present in the mind—which is the object of the speaker's desire to convey. And since trees and the like, qualified by such pervasiveness, are not subordinate to the act of watering because they serve as the locus for the pervasion residing in themselves, words such as *prati* function here as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*), because it is appropriate for them, by virtue of being *karmapravacanīya*s, to delimit the relation.

Although in cases such as "he waters tree after tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ siñcati*), even in the absence of *prati*, there is an application [of the action] through that very relation by virtue of the intention grasped through other means of knowledge, nevertheless, when *prati* is present, it too is a determiner of that [intention]; it is on this basis alone that it possesses the status of delimiting the relation. In that context, although trees and the like are the objects of the watering, the dative case alone—which functions as an upapada-vibhakti caused by that [relation]—is employed, because it is more internal (proximate) due to its connection with what is indicated by *prati*.

For this very reason, in expressions such as *pratyarthaṃ śabdaniveśaḥ* ("the application of words with respect to each object"), although the object (*artha*) possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as defined by the action of application (*niveśana*), the analysis (*vigraha*) shown in the Bhāṣya and other works is simply *artham arthaṃ prati*. By this, the view that the accusative case here is used solely for the object (*karman*)—based on the maxim "the case ending denoting a kāraka is stronger than the case ending of an upapada"—is refuted; for that maxim applies only when the simultaneous connection of both meanings is firmly established in the intellect. Furthermore, even if there is a connection through the relation of what is indicated (*dyotya*), there is no connection [of the object] as a substratum (*āśrayatva*). In the context of a compound (*vṛtti*), however, *prati* alone is the indicator of the distributive sense (*vīpsā*).

Furthermore, if the second case (*dvitīyā*) were used for the object (*karman*), there would be no possibility of the usage *prativṛkṣaṃ siñcati* ("he waters each tree"), because there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the word *prati* and the object.

By this, the argument of Haradatta and others—that here the second case is indeed used for the object, while words such as *pari* merely qualify the action (*kriyāviśeṣaka*)—is refuted; for if they were qualifiers of the action, the designation *karmapravacanīya* would not even apply, since the term is etymologically restricted to that specific sense. Moreover, in the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), Haradatta himself has stated that the function of these particles is precisely to delimit a relationship (*sambandhaparicchedakatva*).

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya also states: "Why, then, is this stated? It is not for the purpose of subverting the technical designations (sañjñās) such as *upasarga* and so on, because there is an absence of connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*). Having said this, it concludes with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "it is for the sake of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). In the example *vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati* ("he waters toward the tree"), the question arises: since the second case is already established by the status of being an object (*karman*) when there is a connection with an action in some instances, what is the purpose [of the rule]? My impression is that the answer is as follows: it is necessary both for the purpose of subverting the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which would otherwise be obtained through its internal applicability (*antaraṅgatva*) due to the connection with the relation delimited by *prati* and other such particles, and for the purpose of [providing the case ending] where there is no object (*akarmaka*).

Regarding the statement, "Let that which belongs to me here be given," the word *yat* (that which) denotes a portion by virtue of being present in the mind. The understanding is as follows: the existence of this act of measuring (*adhikaraṇa*)—which has as its agent the portion related to me—is the object of the instigation (*preraṇā*), and the giving has that [existence] as its object.

In the expression "sarpiṣo 'pi syāt" (even a drop of ghee might be), here too the particle *api* indicates the subordinate element (*apapada*), namely the "drop. The truth is this: by means of the verbal suffix *-ti* in the word *syāt*, which denotes the general agent, its specific instance—the drop—is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). The term "ghee" (*sarpiṣaḥ*) connects with the indicated drop through the relation of part to whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*). Furthermore, the drop connects with the action as its locus (*ādheyatā*) and through the relation of rarity (*daurlabhya*). In this case as well, it is the particle *api* alone that makes the intended meaning clear.

And thus, the cognition is that "existence" (sattā) is the object of the possibility (sambhāvanā), which has as its agent a single entity non-different from that [existence], and whose difficulty is caused by the difficulty of obtaining even a single drop of a constituent part of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).

In the expression "api stuyād Viṣṇum" ("he might praise Viṣṇu"), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes possibility. The particle *api* indicates the feasibility (*śakyatva*) of the action by virtue of being the object of the possibility expressed by the optative. The cognition is: "praise having Viṣṇu as its object and this person as its agent is being conceived as impossible. Alternatively, when the possibility of the feasibility of praise directed toward Viṣṇu is considered, it results in the sense that [the praise] is feasible because there is no certainty regarding other objects.

By this, the legal treatises (*dharmaśāstra*) are explained such that in expressions like "even one who has mastered the Vedānta," the use of the particle *api* does not intend its own literal meaning. In such cases, what is suggested is propriety as an object of possibility; and since the performance of what is merely possible and appropriate is improper, it should be understood that there is no intention toward the literal sense.

Alternatively, the suggestion (*sambhāvanā*) regarding possibility and so forth, even when directed toward an action, is what is indicated; however, the *liṅ* suffix [is used] in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and the like. Thus, even in the case of suggestion, the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) stating "when a *karmapravacanīya* [is present]" holds exactly as it is heard. In the first view, however, the meaning of that [rule] should be understood as: the word "api," when occurring in the domain of suggestion.

In *api stuhi* ("even praise"), the fact that praise is the object of the inclination toward action (*icchā-pravṛtti*) is also indicated. The understanding is: "praise which is the object of an inclination. In *api stuyād vṛṣalam* ("he might even praise a low-born man"), the censurability (*garhyatva*) inherent in the action is indicated by *api*. The understanding is: "a censurable praise having a low-born man as its object. When praise is censurable, the censurability of its agent follows as a consequence; that very point is restated by such expressions as *dhig devadattam* ("shame on Devadatta!").

In the expression "māsam adhīte" ("he studies for a month"), the referent of the word *māsa* (month) is a collection of thirty days, and its relation to that [action] is the state of being a pervader (*vyāpakatva*) of the thirty-day duration. Since the number thirty and so forth are obtained from the word *māsa* itself, only the property of being a pervader is the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*). Consequently, even if the study is connected with the thirty days only at certain times, the use of that expression remains justified. Furthermore, this pervasiveness consists in being delimited by a property that is not a limiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva`) residing in the locus of the thirty-day duration and non-coextensive with its counter-correlate; and this [pervasiveness] is construed with the act of studying and so forth.

By means of the qualification "non-co-occurrent with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*), the aforementioned usage is justified even when there is an absence of study during a sub-period such as a single day within the month. Furthermore, the word "month" (*māsa*) refers specifically to thirty days; it does not refer to an indivisible entity persisting for that duration. Otherwise, if it referred to such an indivisible time, the usage "he studied for a month" (*māsam adhīta*) would result even if one studied for only a single day, because there would be an absence of study non-co-occurrent with its counter-positive during such an indivisible period.

A "month" (*māsa*) and a "day" (*dina*) refer to an indivisible entity (*akhaṇḍavastu*) that persists from sunrise until the end of sunrise, and not to a collection of actions. If it were otherwise, each individual action or manifestation would also possess the status of being the locus of a month; consequently, since the absence of study—which has a different locus than its counter-positive—would exist therein, there would be the fault of sublation (*bādhā*). In expressions such as "he sleeps for a day," the word "day" refers either to a collection of thirty *daṇḍas* (forty-eight minutes) or to a collection of moments (*kṣaṇakūṭa*) from the time of sunrise until sunset.

Therefore, such an application [of the rule] does not occur in dreams involving a single staff and so forth. Furthermore, due to the force of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the specific quality of "thirty" (days) shines forth there; by this, the claim that even in a case where study spans a single month, the expression "he studied for a month" is justified because the absence of study in other months does not obstruct the fact that the study pervades the month, is refuted.

Similarly, in cases such as "the river is crooked for a *krośa*," there appears in the quality of being crooked (*kuṭilatva*) the property of not being delimited by the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence that resides in something possessing the nature of a *krośa* and is non-co-referential with its counter-correlate.

Furthermore, since [units of distance] such as a *krośa* are simply spatial entities (*deśatva*) characterized by specific numbers delimited by objects such as staffs present in the mind, there is no fault whatsoever. [Objection: Now, just as in "he sits for a month" (*māsam āste*), even in "he studies for a month" (*māsam adhīte*), the accusative case would be established by the status of object (*karman*) according to the rule "that which is desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsita*)—provided that the verbal root's function (*vṛtti*) is accepted as extending up to the completion of the action (*vyāpana*). Thus, the rule "of time and distance" (*kālādhvanoḥ*) would be redundant. As Hari has also stated: "Time, state (*bhāva*), distance, and space acquire the status of an object when they are connected with all intransitive verbs through the inclusion of another internal action. [Response: This is not so. For in examples like "he studies for a month," the verbal root does not denote the mere act of studying; rather, it denotes the act of reaching the end of the study (*pāṭhasamāpti*). Since the root does not denote the mere act of sitting (*āsana*) in "he sits for a month," the status of object is not established by the rule "that which is desired by the agent. Therefore, the rule "of time and distance" is indeed necessary. Furthermore, in the case of "he sits for a month," the status of object is established by the rule "the time of an intransitive verb" (*akarmakāṇāṃ kālaḥ*). However, in the case of "he studies for a month," since the root denotes the act of reaching the end of the study, the status of object is not established by that rule either. Consequently, the status of object must be established by the rule "of time and distance. Thus, the rule is not useless. If it is argued that although the term "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) is mentioned here, by parity of reasoning there is no obstacle to including even transitive roots (*sakarmaka-dhātu*) within its scope when their [transitive] meaning is internalized; and that for this very reason, an objection was raised in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra stating, "This is indeed a natural object" (*prākṛtam evaitat karma*); [the answer is: True, but the solution is already provided in the Bhāṣya itself: "Where there is a connection with an action (*kriyā*), this [rule] must be stated for that purpose."

Nor should it be asked, "How then is the example *māsam adhīte* (he studies for a month) to be explained? For it is appropriate to explain that *atyantasaṃyoga* (absolute connection) is intended where there is no desire to express the relation between an action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), since this [term] is necessary even for the purpose of connecting with an action in order to override the genitive case when one intends to express a general relationship.
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the second case-ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*) in the *Subarthavāda*.
Now begins the determination of the meaning of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*).

The agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) are the meanings expressed by the third case (*tṛtīyā*) of the kāraka, according to the natural sense of the rule: "The third case is used for the agent and the instrument" (Pāṇini 2.3.18). Among these, the rule defining agency is: "The independent is the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.54). Since this occurs within the section on *kārakas*, its meaning is that that which is independent with respect to an action is designated as the "agent."

And autonomy (*svātantrya*) is that which delimits the status of being an operation (*vyāpāratāvacchedaka*); it consists in being a substratum of the primary qualificandumhood (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*)—which is of the nature of a qualificandumhood determined by that [operation]—while not being a locus of a modehood (*prakāratā*) determined by that [operation], provided that this occurs through a relation other than [the one] that relates to the meaning of that verbal root. Furthermore, in the phrase "residing in the meaning of that verbal root" (*taddhātvarthaniṣṭha*), the "meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*) must be understood as the very denotation (*śakya*) of the root itself, independent of any indicators of intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

Therefore, even though the suffix *ṇic* is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), in examples such as "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook" (*devadattena yajñadattaḥ pācayati*), the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) is established for both the substratum of the prompted activity (*prayojyavyāpāra*)—which is the meaning of the root *pac*—and the substratum of the prompting activity (*prayojakavyāpāra*). A specific relation is introduced [in the definition] to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the substratum of an activity that exists through a temporal (*kālika*) or other such relations.

By this, the objection that the term *svatantra* ("independent") is non-excludent because all factors involved in an action accomplished by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) possess independence with respect to their own respective operations is refuted; for the aforementioned kind of independence does not exist simultaneously in all of them. It should be understood that by the inclusion of two components in the definition of primary predication (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the possessor of color (*rūpavat*), which is the substratum of color and so forth—such as in the case of "he goes toward the colored"—since primary predication does not belong to the fruit consisting of conjunction with a subsequent location, nor to the color itself.

In this context, it should be understood that "in co-occurrence with a verbal suffix denoting an agent" (*kartṛ-pratyaya-samabhivyāhāre*) is also a qualifying condition. By this, in examples such as *pakvastāṇḍulo devadattena* ("the rice is cooked by Devadatta"), even though the result (*phala*) is the primary qualificand, Devadatta’s status as the agent is established. Here too, since the operation (*vyāpāra*) is obtained from another source [namely, the verbal root], the meaning of the third case is merely the locus (*āśraya*). And the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed there through identity (*abhedena*). That [locus] then conjoins with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) via the relation of being located therein (*ādheyatā-sambandha*). Thus, in cases such as *caitreṇa supyate* ("it is slept by Caitra"), the understanding is that sleep resides in a locus non-different from Caitra, and so forth.

As for the claim that "agency" (*kartṛtva*) with respect to a particular action consists in being the locus of an effort conducive to that specific action—since in the word *kartṛ*, the verbal root *kṛ* denotes effort (*kṛti*) and the suffix *tṛc* denotes a locus (*āśraya*), such a meaning is obtained through the force of the etymological derivation (*yogārtha*)—and that the term "conduciveness" (*anukūlatva*) is employed instead of "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*) because, even when an effort directed toward lifting a very heavy burden exists, one does not conventionally designate someone as the "agent" of that action if the action is not accomplished; furthermore, since the locus is already obtained by the base itself (*prakṛti*), effort alone is the meaning: that is not correct.

Furthermore, since the obtainability of *kṛti* (volitional effort) from a verbal root has already been established in the case of finite verbs (*ākhyāta*), and because that [effort] cannot be obtained from the base (*prakṛti*) as its substratum (*āśrayatva*), there would be an over-extension (*avyāpti*) to non-sentient things in cases such as "the stick cooks" (*daṇḍaḥ pacati*). [Note: It should be understood that the remainder of the argument is that volitional effort resides only in sentient beings. If it is argued that the definition applies to the substratum in those cases, that is improper, as it is merely a matter of one's own whim. Moreover, even if the cognition [of agency] could be accounted for through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no evidence for its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) therein. By this, the view that agency in non-sentient objects is merely figurative (*gauṇa*) is also refuted.

Because no difference is observed in the grammatical operations prescribed by the treatises, and because commentators and others employ [the term] with uniform consistency, that [objection] is untenable based on your mere assertion. Furthermore, it has been established in the *Ākhyātavāda* that the root *kṛ* does not denote "action" (*kṛti*) at all. As for the argument that [it is so called] because of the usage "it arose from me, but it was not done by me"—[the word] *nāntarīyakam* is derived as follows: *antarā-bhavam* means "occurring in between," from which the suffix *cha* (forming *antarīya*) is applied according to the rule for the *gahādi* group. *Antarīyam* itself is *antarīyakam*. [The compound] *na-antarīyakam* becomes *nāntarīyakam*; the absence of the elision of the *n* results from the compound formed by the rule *saha supā*.

If one were to include even the agency defined by the eating of sugar situated within flour-cakes—which are produced by an effort that is invariably concomitant [with the sacrifice]—then it would follow that the agent of a sacrifice and the like would possess the agency of heaven and the like, because the effort toward the sacrifice has heaven and the like as its object by virtue of being its intended goal (*uddeśyatayā*). That is not so; for there is no common linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding "objectness" (*viṣayatā*) in the sense of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*), and thus there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case. Furthermore, in the context of effort (*kṛti*), the object of the action (*kriyā*) is not included [in the definition]; and although the effort toward a sacrifice may have heaven and the like as its object by virtue of being its intended goal, it lacks the quality of being conducive to heaven (*svargānukūlatva*).

This is because only a specific kind of favorability (*anukūlatā-viśe�ṣa*) is posited [as the definition]. Some also maintain that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in the state of desiring (*iṣṭatva*) to be the locus of such an act as eating sugar.

As for the claim that agency is "the state of being the impeller (*prayoktṛ*) of the entire set of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*)," that too is not correct, because it fails to apply (*avyāpti*) to insentient things. Furthermore, the state of being the impeller of the set of causal factors means "being the generator of an activity produced by other causal factors. And if this were the case, [the definition] would fail to apply to an instrument (*karaṇa*), since that which generates the result produced by the object (*karman*) [would itself be considered the agent].

There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to [instruments] such as an axe. Nor can it be argued that this fault does not arise because of the qualification "being not prompted by another causal factor," defined as the absence of an operation produced by another causal factor; for instruments and the like possess operations in the form of conjunctions produced by agents such as persons. Consequently, there would be no status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) for those things prompted by God (*īśvara*). This is the direction of the argument.

If it is argued that, in such cases as "the jar comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the jar and so forth cannot be the agent because they do not exist prior to their production and thus cannot be the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root, we say: no; for according to the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), there is no absolute non-existence of the effect. Rather, even at the time when the causal complex for destruction is present, the effect exists but remains latent; when the causal complex for production is present, it becomes manifest.

And thus, even in the case of a jar or similar objects, their status as agents will be established by virtue of their existence in a subtle state prior to production, thereby serving as the substratum for the operation denoted by the verbal root; for there is no fault in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). Even in other philosophical systems, it should be understood that in such cases, the intention to serve as the substratum for the operation of the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) alone is the determinant of agency. Furthermore, according to this view, independence (*svātantrya*) should be understood as consisting in either being the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal root or being the material cause that serves as the substratum for that operation.

However, some say that the existence of an external object (*padārtha-sattā*) is not the cause of cognition; rather, it is simply the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). For this very reason, there is cognition even from such expressions as "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*). And thus, there is cognition in the present case as well. Consequently, they maintain that there is no fault in the present instance either.

Regarding this, some hold that the state of being the locus of the verbal root's meaning—the activity—is either direct or indirect. Of these, the first is well-known [in ordinary usage], while the second is seen in such cases as "he plows with five ploughs" (*pañcabhir halaiḥ karṣati*).

For in that case—by the relation of being the prompter (*prayojakatva*) of its own substratum, the agent possesses the status of being the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha-vyāpāra*). Otherwise, since the operation of the prompted agent would also be denoted by the root, and because there would be a plurality of its substrata, the use of the plural number would result. Furthermore, if the operation of the prompter were also directly expressed by the root, the suffix *ṇic* would be required; this is precisely the meaning of the traditional maxim that "the causative sense is included within [the root]. That is not so; for if the causative sense were included within [the root], it would follow that the transitive character (*sakarmakatā*) of the root would be destroyed.
For this very reason, they say that when transitive roots have their causative sense included within them, they become doubly transitive (*dvikarmaka*).

Therefore, even the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is included there as its meaning; however, this applies only where there exists an indicator of that meaning even without the suffix *ṇic*. For example, in the expression "he ploughs with five ploughs" (*pañcabhir halaiḥ kṛṣati*). In some cases, however, it refers to sitting silently in a secluded place and so forth. Thus, the truth is simply that the root *kṛṣ* (to plough) has the operation of the instigator included within its own meaning (*ṇyartha-antarbhāveṇa lakṣaṇā*). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. If, however, there is a usage there even when devoid of a second object (*dvitīya-karma*), then it should be resolved by resorting to the view that the operation of the instigator alone constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Such is the direction of the argument.

And agency (*kartṛtva*) is based on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). Therefore, when the operation of the cooking pot and so forth is intended to be expressed as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), one says "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*). In this way, even for a single entity, agency, objecthood, instrumentality, and so forth occur due to the difference in limiting conditions (*upādhi*); as in the expression, "you create yourself by yourself. This was stated by Hari:

By this, the statement of Vācaspati—that for the self whose nature is consciousness, there can be no knowledge of its own nature because if it were self-luminous by virtue of being an object, there would be a contradiction between agent and object, and because if there were non-difference, there could be no relation of container and contained nor a relation of object and subject—is refuted; for agency and the like, which are conditioned by specific adjuncts such as words, cannot possibly be predicated of [the self] in perception and other means of knowledge.
