If, however, the words "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) are intended to indicate their respective substrata and objects; or if the phrase "in the case of self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatve*) means "in the case of being designated by the term 'self-luminous' (*svaprakāśa*)," for the etymological derivation of the word *svaprakāśa* is "that which illuminates itself" (*svaṃ prakāśayati*), then [the position] is perfectly correct—so enough of this prolixity. And the sūtra indicating the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is: "The most effective means is the instrument" (*sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*, Pāṇini 1.4.42). Its meaning is as follows: when the accomplishment of an action is intended to be immediate, without being interrupted by the operation of anything other than the operation of the agent, that [means] is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

In order to exclude cases such as "Caitra cooks with rice" (*caitraścaitreṇa pacati*) or "The wood cooks with Caitra" (*kāṣṭhaṃ caitreṇa pacati*), the phrase "dependent on the activity of the agent" (*kartṛvyāpārādhīna*) is used. However, when the accomplishment of the action is intended to be expressed even without the intervention of the activities of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth, then their status as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) is indeed accepted. As Hari said:
"In reality, that [instrumentality] cannot be designated, for a thing does not have a fixed status;
since we observe the intended expression 'it is cooked in a pot' (*sthālyā pacyate*)."

Thus, the meaning of the ablative case of cause (*kāraṇavibhakti*) is "operation" (*vyāpāra*). In that context, some hold that the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed as being located within it (*ādheyatayā*), and that the operation is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) by way of the relation of "having an immediate subsequent origination qualified by its own causality" (*svaniṣṭhajanakatānirūpitāvyavahitottarotpattikatvasambandha*).
For this very reason, [they say]:
"The substratum (*āśraya*), the limit (*avadhi*), the object of reference (*uddeśya*), the relation (*sambandha*), or indeed the capacity (*śakti*) [are the meanings]."
Others maintain that the statement of Hari (the author of the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*) regarding the determination of the meaning of case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*) is thus consistent.

However, in connection with the verbal root *div*, this very definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*), qualified by the condition of not being presented by a word ending in the accusative (*dvitīyāntapadānupasthāpyatva*), should be understood. In the example "He recognizes his father as his father" (*pitrā pitaraṃ saṃjānīte*), the third case-ending has the sense of the object (*karman*).
Now, the understanding [of the meaning] in the case of third-case endings used as *upapada* (prepositional) case-endings is set forth.

In the expression *prakṛtyā cāruḥ* ("naturally beautiful"), *prakṛti* refers to a specific quality that persists as long as its substratum exists. Therefore, the meaning is "one who possesses beauty connected to that [nature]. The meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is relation. In the expression *prāyeṇa yājñikaḥ* ("mostly a ritualist"), the word *prāya* has the sense of "much"; and that which possesses muchness is conduct and so forth. Thus, the cognition is: "one who possesses the status of a ritualist connected to conduct that possesses muchness. And the relation is that of the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpaka-bhāva*).

Alternatively, the word *prāya* signifies possibility (*sambhāvanā*), meaning "one who possesses the status of a sacrificer (*yājñika*) as a possible attribute. Indeed, the word *prāya* is seen used in that sense in such expressions as, "He generally departs when Cakrapāṇi [Viṣṇu] does," or "In this lineage, there are generally many sacrificers (*yājñikas*)," where it denotes plurality. The understanding here is "the sacrificers possess plurality.

In the expression "Gārgya by lineage (*gotra*)," the meaning is "one who possesses the state of being Gārgya related to a lineage. The relationship is one of general property and its particular instance (*sāmānya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*).

In "he buys grain for two *droṇas*," the understanding is that the act of buying has as its object grain delimited by two *droṇas*. In "he goes with ease," the understanding is that the going is a producer of ease.

In "Sutīkṣṇa by name," the meaning of the third case is a relation consisting of being made known; the understanding is that he possesses the quality of being very sharp (Sutīkṣṇa) as made known by the name.

The same applies in the case of "tamed by conduct" (*caritena dāntaḥ*). In expressions such as "the king named Suratha," the meaning of the word *suratha* is "one denoted by the word *suratha*. The indeclinable *nāma* has the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). The referent of the word *nāma*, namely "name," is construed with the word that is a constituent part of *suratha*. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one denoted by the word *suratha*, which is distinct from [the mere] name. Alternatively, the word *suratha* refers to the word-form itself; the cognition is: "a king who is distinct from [any other] word *suratha* that is not a name."

Alternatively, the word *nāma* (by name) also serves as an indicator of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the referential nature of the term. This is likewise the case even in non-compounded names such as *candrakalā* ("Moon-Phase"), where the name is used [as a qualifier]. In such instances, non-difference (*abheda*) is the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Similarly, when one intends to express that [qualities] such as being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) or being delimited (*avacchedyatva*) are relations, the third case is to be understood as applied to words like *paṭatvena* ("as a cloth") due to their status as *prakṛti* (base nouns), etc., in expressions such as "being produced" (*janyatva*), "being a qualifier" (*prakāratva*), "absence" (*abhāva*), and so forth. In the sentence "The lesson was studied in a day or a *krośa*," the meaning of the third case is a relation [of measurement], which attaches to the destruction (*nāśa*) that is a part of the pastness denoted by the suffix *-kta*.

And the fact that [the cessation] is preceded by the attainment of the fruit is what is illuminated. Thus, the understanding is: "The study concerning the *anuvāka* is the counter-positive of a cessation which is preceded by the attainment of a fruit related to the day."

In expressions such as *putreṇa sahāgataḥ* ("he has come with his son"), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is applied by the rule *sahayukte'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.18), where "non-predominance" (*aprādhānya*) consists in being a qualifier of the sense of *saha*. This is because, in expressions such as *kriyāpradhānam* ("predominant in action"), the word *pradhāna* is observed to have the sense of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, the meaning of the word *saha* is the state of being simultaneous with the referent of the word co-occurring with that which is connected to itself. And when used in connection with an action, the meaning of the third case ending is precisely the status of being the agent (*kartṛ*) of that respective action, and so forth.

And thus, in cases such as "the teacher is fat with the student" (*śiṣyeṇa saha sthūlaḥ*), "he has come with the student" (*śiṣyeṇa sahāgataḥ*), and "the cow belongs to the teacher with the student" (*śiṣyeṇa sahopādhyāyasya gauḥ*), the understanding proceeds respectively as follows: [the teacher] possesses fatness simultaneous with the fatness residing in the student; [he] possesses an act of coming simultaneous with an act of coming whose agent is the student; and [the cow] possesses the ownership of the teacher simultaneous with the ownership related to the student. In the last case, the relation expressed by the genitive case itself is what connects with the meaning of *saha* (together/with), because that is how it is experienced.

In some cases, its meaning is "occupying the same location"; for this very reason, even when sesame is sown in that same field after the sowing of beans, one says, "they sowed beans together with the sesame. Others say that in this very context, as found in the Bhāṣya and other works, the meaning is merely "simultaneity," though this is based on the intended sense (*tātparya*).

Others, however, hold that the meaning of the word *saha* is "concomitance" (*sāhitya*). Thus, there arises the cognition: "The father, who possesses concomitance with the son who follows [the lineage] of the father and so forth, has arrived. And this concomitance is either an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) co-located with the status of being the substratum of the action and so forth expressed by the co-occurring term, or it is a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*); this is another matter. Since this property (*dharma*) is also accepted as being cognized by the same cognition as the aforementioned concomitance, there is no fault even though the cognition having that as its object is established by experience.
For this very reason, the introduction of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) for the father, as stated in the Bhāṣya, is consistent.

Otherwise, even if the meaning of *saha* (together) were construed with the action and so forth according to the previously mentioned view, the resulting objection would be entirely irrelevant because of that very construction; thus they say. Likewise, the third case ending occurs even when joined with the word *saha*, which denotes existence (*vidyamānatā*), as in "The she-ass carries the load together with her ten sons" (*sahaiva daśabhiḥ putrair bhāraṃ vahati gardabhī*). [The intention here is this: the word *saha* ends in an elided locative case (*luptasaptamyanta*); that locative is present, and there is also the ellipsis of the word *api*. By this, the stated meaning is obtained.]

*Keccu*: Here, the word *vidyamāna* (existing) is to be supplied. Thus, they have established that the accomplishment of the coexistence (*sāhitya*) is brought about by the action of "existing. The meaning is: "even though there is the existence of ten sons.

In this way, even if the correlate of the sense of "together" (*saha-artha*) lacks grammatical primacy (*śābda-aprādhānya*), it nonetheless possesses semantic primacy (*ārthaprādhānya*). Therefore, it should be understood that when it is said of two people of equal status, "one must come with the other," distress is observed [in the one who remains].

In the expression "one-eyed with the eye" (*akṣṇā kāṇaḥ*), [the meaning is] one who possesses an eye that has undergone destruction. The referent of the word *kāṇa* is one who possesses an eye; the referent of the word *cakṣus* (eye) is the eyeball (*golaka*); and the meaning of the third case suffix (*tṛtīyā*) is a relation consisting of being caused by a modification [of that eyeball]. The resulting cognition is: "one who possesses an eye, which possesses the destruction [of its function] caused by a modification of the eyeball.
Similarly, in cases such as "lame with the foot" (*pādena khañjaḥ*), the meaning is "one who possesses a foot characterized by a deficiency in its configuration caused by a modification of the foot.

In expressions such as "ten-faced with the body" (*kāyena daśavaktraḥ*) or "three-eyed with the face" (*mukhena trilocanaḥ*), the third case suffix should be understood as arising from the category of *prakṛtyādi* (words like *prakṛti*, etc.).

In expressions such as "the ascetic by means of matted hair" (*jaṭābhis tāpasaḥ*), the meaning of the instrumental case is the relation of being made known (*jñāpyatva*). The resulting cognition is: "one who possesses the state of being an ascetic as made known by matted hair. In expressions such as "a jar by means of a stick" (*daṇḍena ghaṭaḥ*), the meaning of the instrumental case is the cause (*hetu*). And "being a cause" consists precisely in causality, which is defined as being invariably antecedent and not otherwise established; or it may be an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) co-located with that [cause]. The relation between the meanings of the stem and the suffix is identity. Furthermore, the meaning of the suffix is construed with the other [meaning] through the relation of being produced (*janyatā*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "a jar produced by a cause non-different from a stick."

In expressions such as *adhyayanena vasati* ("he dwells for the sake of study"), even the fruit—namely, the study—is intended as the cause (*hetu*) by means of its own cognition (*svajñānadvārā*). Thus, when there is a desire to express that study, though it is itself the fruit of dwelling, is the cause of the dwelling by way of its own cognition, the third case ending is employed. The resulting understanding is: "The dwelling has study as its non-different cause and shares the same agent. However, although places such as Kāśī are the cause of the study, the seventh case ending is used when there is a desire to express them as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

In fact, because in the sūtra "hetau" (Pāṇini 2.3.23) the result (*phala*) is also intended to be expressed as a cause (*hetu*), the establishment of the understanding—attested by experience—that "residence generates the result consisting of study" is achieved. This is to be understood through easy knowledge. In the expression "he gives [it] to the maidservant" (*dāsyā saṃyacchate*), the meaning of the third case is the objective (*uddeśya*); for in connection with the root *dāṇ*, when referring to the conduct of the unrefined (*aśiṣṭa*), the rule prescribes the third case in the sense of the fourth. The resulting cognition is: "The giving, performed by the lover, has the maidservant as its objective. Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the third case-ending.
Now begins the determination of the meaning of the fourth case-ending used in the sense of a *kāraka*.

The meaning of the dative case of the *kāraka* is "recipient" (*sampradāna*), according to the rule "the dative is used in the sense of the recipient" (Pāṇini 2.3.13). And the rule that defines the state of being a recipient is "that which one intends to connect with the object of the action is the recipient" (Pāṇini 1.4.32). Its meaning is: "a recipient is that which one desires to relate to the object of the verbal root's meaning. Furthermore, this connection with the object consists in being the determinant of the result residing in the object, and so forth.

And thus, it follows that the recipient (*sampradāna*) of a particular verbal root is that which is the object of the desire [of the agent] by virtue of being the determiner of the fruit residing in the respective object (*karman*). By the term "residing in the object" (*karmaniṣṭha*), the fact that the object is the cause for the dative case is demonstrated; thereby, it is understood that the scriptural statement regarding the dative (*caturthī-śruti*) possesses greater force than the scriptural statement regarding the object (*karma-śruti*).

For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that in the injunction, "When the Soma has been purchased, he gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa," the giving of the staff is not a mere disposal (*pratipatti*), but rather, by the dative scriptural statement—which is stronger than the accusative—it serves as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the Maitrāvaruṇa.

On this point, some maintain that the meaning of the dative case is the object of the agent’s desire, since the connection of the result with the verbal root is obtained through the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and by virtue of the relational constraints (*saṃsargamaryādā*). This very [object] is called the "intended recipient" (*uddeśya*). Thus, in the sentence *viprāya gāṃ dadāti* ("He gives a cow to the Brahmin"), the meaning of the dative case is construed as the "qualifier" (*nirūpakatva*) with respect to the "property-ownership" (*svatva*), which is one part of the meaning of the verbal root *dā*—namely, the activity consisting of both the production of ownership and the cessation of [the giver's] previous ownership. Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "An activity conducive to both the production of ownership and the cessation thereof, which is qualified by ownership that is not yet determined by an object of desire identical to the Brahmin."

As for the claim that the meaning of the dative case is the state of being the object of the agent’s desire as determined [by the action], and that this relates to the ownership which is delimited by the meaning of the root *dā*, while the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) that generates ownership is the meaning of the root *dā*: [this is incorrect].

And thus, they say that the understanding is: "the agent of the renunciation which produces ownership residing in the cow, which is the object of desire as determined by the Brahmin. But that is not correct; for it would result in the violation of the established relation of non-difference between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a case-ending. Furthermore, it would violate the natural sense of the sūtra which teaches that the recipient (*sampradāna*) is the object of desire. This [position] is to be questioned, however, because it is untenable in cases such as "one should give the *śrāddha* to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ śrāddhaṃ dadyāt*), since it is contradicted that ownership resides in the ancestors.
For this very reason, Śūlapāṇi and others maintain that the *śrāddha* is indeed a "portion" (*bhāga*) with respect to the ancestors, whereas it is a "gift" (*dāna*) with respect to the Brahmins.

Therefore, the meaning of the dative case is either *uddeśyatva* (the state of being intended as a recipient), which consists in a relation of essential nature (*svarūpasambandha*), or a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) that has that [relation] as its locus. The verbal root-meaning (of the verb *dā*, "to give") connects with this [meaning of the dative] by way of being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the *uddeśyatā* (recipient-ness) residing in itself. And the meaning of the root *dā* is an act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) conducive to the cessation of one's own ownership and the production of another's ownership.

Nor should it be argued that relinquishment is not the cause of another's ownership, since that status belongs only to the acceptance (*pratigraha*) and so forth; for the universal consensus of people—that regarding a cow relinquished with a Brahmin as the recipient, there arises the cognition "This cow is the Brahmin's, not mine"—is itself the proof [of our position].

For this very reason, when wealth has been relinquished for the sake of a recipient residing in a foreign land, even if that recipient dies before accepting it, that wealth is divided as paternal inheritance by the intended recipient’s sons and others; otherwise, there would be no sin in those strangers taking that wealth—just as one might take grass from a forest—even as they would have been none for the intended recipients themselves.

Nor is such acceptance useless; for, according to the Smṛti text, "When [the gift] has been obtained, the merit is eightfold," acceptance serves the very purpose of bringing about that state [of eightfold merit], as it is the cause of the excellence of the fruit for one who gives wealth after it has been accepted. Acceptance is indeed not a fault in the case of sesame seeds, horses, and so forth, which are given out of satisfaction, provided they are accepted for the sake of an unseen spiritual result (*adṛṣṭa*).

Nor should it be argued that in a case of joint ownership (*saṃsṛṣṭi*), since a common property right (*sādhāraṇasvatva*) arises after the destruction of the individual property rights (*asādhāraṇasvatva*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "he gives" (*dadāti*) being applicable there; for there is no fault here because of the qualification "conducive to [the recipient's] property right. In that case, there is no destruction of property right, but merely the arising of another's property right. Others hold that the arising of a property right in one who already possesses a property right occurs because the desire existing therein acts as an excitant (*uttejaka*).
Still others maintain that such a usage does not occur because of the absence of renunciation (*tyāga*).

Nor is there a fault in the case of indifference (*upekṣā*), because in that case there is necessarily no arising of another's ownership (*parasvatva*). For this very reason, such a formulation is not used in the case of sale, since sale does not produce another's ownership; rather, it is purchase alone that produces it, for the term "purchase" (*kraya*) denotes precisely the act of taking possession preceded by the payment of a price.

If it is asked, "What then is ownership (*svatva*) here?", the ancients maintain that it consists in being the object of such means as purchase, gift, and so forth, which serve as the basis for using the thing as one pleases provided it is not prohibited by scripture. Furthermore, they hold that this [ownership] is not perceptible by the external senses, because acts such as receiving a gift are specific types of mental cognition and are thus unfit to be apprehended by the external senses.

The Navyas, however, maintain that ownership (*svatva*) is a distinct category (*padārtha*), because the linguistic usage of ownership persists even after its destruction by acceptance (*pratigraha*) and other means; furthermore, because of usages such as "ownership perishes through giving" and "ownership arises from acceptance," it is established as a separate entity. Moreover, it is perceptible by the external senses, since there is the common expression, "I see my own [property]. And in the direct perception of that ownership, the cause is a cognition in the form "this is mine," which possesses the property of being suitable for disposal at will (*yatheṣṭaviniyojyatva*)—a property pervaded by the ownership belonging to that [person].

Therefore, they say that when there is no apprehension of that [the object], there is no apprehension of its being fit for disposal according to one’s will, nor of the non-deviation of the owner’s property-rights regarding it.

Property-right (*svatva*) is indeed inferable. However, the newer scholars maintain that the cognition "I see my own [property]" does not involve a perception of empirical objectivity (*laukika-viṣayatva*) regarding the qualifying element (the ownership), just as in the case of "I see fragrant sandalwood.
And thus, the understanding is that the previously mentioned act of relinquishment has as its intended recipient a person non-different from a Brahmin.

And thus, there is no fault even in such cases as "one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ śrāddhaṃ dadyāt*), because in that instance the ancestors themselves are the intended recipients (*uddeśya*). In the sentence "the teacher Khaṇḍika gives a slap to him," the meaning of the root *dā* (to give) is an activity conducive to a specific type of contact; here, "slap" (*capeṭā*) refers to the palm of the hand extended. In expressions such as "one should not impart knowledge (*mati*) to a Śūdra," the root *dā* signifies "informing" or "teaching"; by the word "knowledge" (*mati*), the scripture that produces it is meant. It should be understood that when the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is intended, the expression "the cloth of the washerman" (*rajakasya vastram*) is also grammatically correct.

Some, however, maintain that since "object-ness" (*karmatva*) is defined in relation to an action, and because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the context of a *kāraka*," the meaning of the sūtra is: "That which one intends to reach by means of an instrument that is the object of that very action—by virtue of being a recipient of the fruit produced by the connection with the object of that action—is the *saṃpradāna*. And the fruit produced by the connection with the object is, for example, the happiness of a Brahmin resulting from the acquisition of a cow. This [fruit] appears in its specific form through the force of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) and through intention (*tātparya*).

The meaning of the dative case is that which is intended as the goal (*uddeśya*) by virtue of being the recipient of a fruit produced through a connection with an action. Thus, the understanding is as follows: "An operation conducive to both the arising of ownership residing in the cow and the cessation of one's own previous ownership, [an operation] directed toward that which is non-different from the Brahmin and is intended as the locus of pleasure produced by a connection with the cow. In this way, the purposefulness of the rule *karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 1.3.54) is clearly established.

Similarly, regarding the phrase *kriyayā yam*, they say that the meaning intended by the dative of attainment (*sampādya-caturthī*) is the object intended as the locus of the fruit produced by the action, and the fruit consists of the attainment of pleasure and so forth. That is not correct.

Regarding the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* [Pāṇini 2.3.12] and so forth, the following is the intention: In the context of the rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti*, the venerable Commentator (the Bhāṣyakāra) has rejected this sūtra by first establishing the dative case in *grāmāya* even without including the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) there, and then establishing the accusative case in *grāmam* by means of the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā*.

Although the mention of "action" was rejected in that specific instance, since its result is achieved by another means, there is no need to formulate a new statement merely to reject that particular wording.
Non-difference is the reality—the meaning of the second and fourth cases is merely the object (*karman*) according to the view of the *Sūtra*. The cognition is: "going has the village as its object.

According to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, however, since the designation "recipient" (*sampradāna*) applies by the rule "that which one intends through the action," the fourth case is used; thus the cognition is: "an undertaking whose object is an activity conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location, having the village as its recipient. [This interpretation is incorrect] because such a meaning is untenable due to its contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* and other texts that refute [this analysis], and because there is no evidence for such a verbal cognition.

In this sūtra, the word *karmaṇā* is repeated; and as it is repeated, it refers to the action (*kriyā*). Consequently, because the status of recipient (*sampradānatva*) applies even to that which is the goal of an action devoid of an explicit object, forms such as *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband") are established. The understanding [of the sentence] is: "lying down having the husband as its goal."

In the sentence "He sacrifices a beast to Rudra" (*paśunā rudraṃ yajate*), the meaning of the instrumental case is the locus of the result, while the meaning of the accusative case is the intended recipient (*uddeśya*). The resulting cognition is: "A gift whose object is the beast and whose recipient is Rudra. [The implied meaning is: "An operation conducive to the cessation of ownership residing in the beast, which has Rudra as its intended recipient. This is based on the Vārttika: "The designation 'instrument' (*karaṇa*) applies to the object (*karman*), and the designation 'recipient' (*sampradāna*) applies to the object."

"Bhakti pleases Hari" (*haraye rocate bhaktiḥ*): the meaning of the root *ruc* is an activity residing in the same locus as [the pleasure], which is conducive to a pleasure delimited by the relation of being an object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). The meaning of the dative case is the relation consisting of the substratum (*āśrayatva*), in accordance with the natural sense of the rule *rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.33). [Note: Here, prior to "rucyārthaḥ," the reading "rucir artho yeṣāṃ te" must be supplied, otherwise there would be an inconsistency in the text. Thus, [it is] "those whose meaning is *ruc*" (*rucyarthaḥ*).

This is an exception to the general genitive case (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*); here, the status of being a recipient (*sampradāna*) consists precisely in the relationship with the fruit of a verb meaning "to please" (*rucy-artha*). Thus, [in the example *hariṃ rocate bhaktiḥ*], the meaning is: "the activity residing in the devotee which is conducive to that pleasure which is directed toward Hari as its object. However, since the verb *abhilaṣati* ("to desire") signifies an activity that is not co-referential with the pleasure delimited by that relationship, it does not have the sense of "to please"; therefore, in expressions such as *harir bhaktim abhilaṣyati*, Hari does not possess the status of a recipient.

In the expression “*gopī smarāt kṛṣṇāṃ ślāghate*” (The cowherd girl praises Kṛṣṇa out of love), the meaning of the root *ślāgh* is praise (*stuti*) which has cognition as its result. Praise, in turn, consists of the employment of words that communicate the possession of virtues. The ablative case in *smarāt* expresses cause. The sense of the dative case—the status of being the object—connects with the cognition. This is understood from the natural force of the rule *ślāgha-hanuṅ-sthā-śapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.34] and by the word *jñīpsyamāna*, which indicates that only the object of the primary causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is intended to be grasped.

And thus, the understanding is that this is a hymn performed by the cowherd women (gopīs), caused by love (smara), and having the awakening of Kṛṣṇa as its fruit; whether the hymn is directed toward oneself or another, however, is to be understood from the context and other such factors.

For this very reason, there is also the expression "Kṛṣṇā praises herself. With this very point in mind, the ancient commentators explain the meaning as: "She speaks of herself or another as praiseworthy. However, when Kṛṣṇā alone is the object of praise, she is the object (*karman*) precisely because she is the other [than the agent]. In the case of *hanute*, the root *hnu* signifies placing oneself in a location from which one is not visible to others. The word "herself" (*ātmānam*) is to be supplied as the object. Furthermore, it should be understood that her remaining in such a state is due to the fear of her co-wives.

And thus, the understanding is that the activity of the cowherd girls consists in an operation conducive to their remaining in a state where they are the object of a cognition whose locus is Kṛṣṇa. The meaning of the root *sthā* (to stand) is a state of standing that is conducive to making one's own intention known. The meaning of the root *śap* (to swear) is the performance of an oath that is conducive to making one's own intention known. [The resulting cognitions are: "A state conducive to a cognition having Kṛṣṇa as its object," and "The performance of an oath conducive to a cognition having him as its object. And so it is said that here, the status of being a recipient (*sampradāna*) is to be understood as being the substratum of the fruit of the verbal action denoted by roots such as *ślāgh* (to praise).

Others, however, argue: "If [the rule] were established simply by saying 'thus being made known' (*jñāpyamāna*), then the inclusion of the suffix *san* would be redundant. Since it has been stated that 'the agent of the causative (*ṇyanta*) is the object,' it is already established that the term *jñāpyamāna* refers to that very [agent]. Therefore, by the term *jñīpsyamāna*, what is grasped is that whose activity is conducive to the activity conducive to the cognition of the object; furthermore, because it is presented first, it is more appropriate to understand the term as referring to the object of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*)."

Since that [desire] is also the object of the desire for the person to be made to know, there is no impossibility of the production of knowledge. They say that the meanings of *ślāgh* (to praise) and so forth are for the purpose of making someone understand by means of praise and the like; that is, one makes another understand Kṛṣṇa through praise, one makes another understand Kṛṣṇa as characterized by censure, and one makes another understand Kṛṣṇa through a state of being or an oath. Many hold that, according to the natural sense of the suffix *san*, both [the agent of the action and the one who desires to know] are grasped by the word *jñīpsyamāna* (the one to be made to know).

In the sentence *bhaktāya dhārayati mokṣo hariḥ* ("Hari holds liberation for the devotee"), according to Pāṇini’s rule *dhāreruttamarṇaḥ* (1.4.35)—where *uttamarṇaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has the highest debt"—the devotee (*bhakta*) is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). This is because of the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), which results in the placement of the past participle (*niṣṭhānta*) at the end of the compound; here, *uttamarṇaḥ* refers to the owner of the wealth. In this context, the root *dhṛ* (in *dhārayati*) means "to hold," and when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), its meaning becomes "to cause to remain" (*avasthānānukūla*). The sense of connection (*sambandha*) is the meaning of the dative case.

And thus, the understanding is that the operation residing in Hari is conducive to the persistence of the state [of liberation] which has as its object the liberation of the devotee. This status of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*) should be understood as the state of being related to the substratum of the persistence that is the meaning of the root *dhṛ* (to hold/maintain).

If it is objected: "Indeed, what is called 'debt' (*ṛṇa*) is either the taking of another's property given by someone else after having promised to give another similar substance, or it is a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the debtor which is produced by that [taking] and is to be destroyed by repayment; in either case, there is no application here, because liberation lacks the aforementioned nature of debt, and consequently the devotee lacks the status of a creditor (*uttamarṇa*)."

They say that because there is a legal transaction regarding debt (*ṛṇavyavahāra*) even in that case, due to its being necessarily repayable. Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya, however, says: "The meaning of the root *dhṛ* (to owe) is a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) resulting from the taking back of a substance previously given, preceded by an agreement to give another substance; and the agency connected with the giving of that substance is the meaning of the dative case."

In the expression *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers") as well, the relation is the meaning of the dative case. The understanding is that there is a desire characterized by a relation to the flowers. Being the desired object (*īpsitatva*) consists in being related to the fruit of the action denoted by a verb meaning "to long for"; this is its status as a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*). Its status as a recipient is precisely its being the locus of the fruit of the action denoted by a verb meaning "to long for. However, expressions such as *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers") are to be understood as the objects of an implied action such as "seeing" (*dṛśya*) and so forth. But when the residual relation (*śeṣatva*) is not intended to be expressed, the genitive alone is used. For this very reason, others maintain that the rule *spṛherīpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.36) is consistent.

In the expressions *haraye krudhyati*, *druhyati*, *īrṣyati*, and *asūyati*, Hari is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) according to the rule: "The one toward whom there is anger [is the recipient] in the case of roots meaning anger, malice, envy, and censure" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.37). In this context, anger (*krodha*) is a specific modification of the mental state (*cittavṛtti*), which is the meaning of the root *krudh*. If anger were defined merely as a specific kind of cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*), then the root would incur transitivity. Malice (*droha*) is the desire for harm directed toward an object; here, "harm" (*apakāra*) refers to an action that produces suffering.

This [root *krudh*] is also intransitive (*akarmaka*), because its object is subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root itself. When these two [roots, *krudh* and *duh*] are employed, the relation [denoted by] the fourth case (*caturthī*) is the sense [of the suffix]. The cognition is: "anger related to Hari" and "the desire to do harm related to him. In the employment of these, the status of being the recipient (*sampradāna*) consists precisely in being related to one's own object through the relation of being the objective domain (*viṣayatā*). Envy (*īrṣyā*) is hatred directed toward excellence. Malice (*asūyā*) is the superimposition of the fault of being produced by hypocrisy and the like onto qualities such as purity and conduct. In the employment of these, the object (*karman*) is the sense of the fourth case.

The understanding is that [the object of] *druhyati* is hatred directed toward the excellence of Hari’s deeds, and [the object of] *dviṣati* is the manifestation of faults regarding qualities residing in Hari. It should be understood that the status of being a *saṃpradāna* (recipient) consists in being the locus of the result of the action denoted by that verbal root, while simultaneously being the object of the anger that constitutes the meaning of that same root. By the inclusion of the "simultaneity" (*satyantena*) condition, examples such as "she is jealous of her wife" (*bhāryām īrṣyati*)—meaning "may no other see her"—are excluded. In cases such as "even Pratāpa bears malice toward Mitra," one should understand that there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of sentience [upon the non-sentient].

In the expressions *kṛṣṇāya rādhyati* ("he deliberates regarding Kṛṣṇa") and *īkṣate* ("he considers"), the meaning of the two verbal roots is the deliberation upon the object of inquiry. Kṛṣṇa is construed with that single part which is the object of inquiry. The meaning of the dative case is the relationship [between the root-meaning and Kṛṣṇa]. In connection with these [roots], the status of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*) is to be understood as consisting in being related to the object of inquiry, which is the root's own meaning.

In the expressions "he promises a cow to the Brahmin" (*viprāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti*) or "he assents" (*āśṛṇoti*), the meaning of the verbal root is the acceptance (*abhyupagama*) produced by an instigation (*pravartanā*). The meaning of the dative case is the state of being the locus (*āśrayatva*), which is connected with the instigation. The resulting cognition is: "An acceptance residing in Devadatta, produced by an instigation residing in the Brahmin. It should be understood that in connection with these [verbs], the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) consists in being the locus of the instigation directed toward one's own interest.

In the expression "he encourages the *hotṛ* by chanting" (*hotāram anugṛṇāti*) or "he responds to him" (*pratigṛṇāti*), the meaning of the verbal root is encouragement (*protsāhana*), characterized by an activity conducive to joy directed toward the act of chanting whose object is the *hotṛ*. Furthermore, the *hotṛ* is construed with the chanter (*śaṃsitṛ*) as non-different. Due to the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the object, the *hotṛ* is the object (*karman*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "An activity conducive to joy, having as its object the chanter who is non-different from the *hotṛ*. It should be understood that this status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) consists in being the locus of the chanting that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root.

In the expression "bought for a hundred" (*śatena śatāya vā parikrītaḥ*), the meaning of the dative case is identical to that of the instrumental of instrument; furthermore, the operation of the "hundred" is simply the act of giving. Thus, in this context, the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) should be understood as precisely the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) as conveyed by the word ending in the third case.

In the expression *phalebhyo yāti* ("he goes for the sake of fruits"), the word *āhartum* ("to fetch") is to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). The meaning of the dative case is the object (*karman*) in the form of that which serves as the substratum for the fruit [of the action]. Now, an objection may be raised: since the mental presence (*upasthiti*) of a word-meaning generated by a word is a necessary factor for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), how can there be such a cognition in cases like *phalebhyo yāti*, given that the act of fetching—which is what connects with the meaning of the dative—is not present in that manner? Nor can one simply supply the word *āhartum* from the context; for supplying a word is either an inference (*anumāna*) or a presentation brought to mind (*upanītabhāna*), and thus it remains a non-usage (*aprayoga*).

For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the word *sthānin* ("that which remains unexpressed") in the rule prescribing the fourth case (*caturthī*) under discussion—namely, Pāṇini 2.3.14: *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*—"and [the fourth case is used] for the object of that whose subordinate word (*upapada*) has the sense of an action, provided it remains unexpressed."

It should not be argued that the word *prayoga* (usage) serves the purpose of denoting utterance; for if, as in the rule "the object desired by one who longs" (*spṛherīpsitaḥ*), the rules such as "when *yuṣmad* is the attendant word" (*yuṣmadyupapade*) were applicable both to the uttered word and to the supplied word, then the phrase "also when the original form exists" (*sthāninyapi*) would be rendered redundant. Therefore, the term *sthānin* (original form) has no known meaning [in this context]. Thus, even if the word itself is not supplied, its purposefulness lies in supplying the mere sense for the sake of the second person (*madhyama*).

If it is argued that [the rule] would not apply there because it is conditioned by a word (*pada*), we say no; for, precisely due to the lack of capacity in the mention of the *sthānin* (the element to be replaced), even in the absence of an apprehension generated by a word, it is accepted that the object becomes the content of verbal cognition through the mere implication of its meaning (*arthamātrādhyāhāreṇa*). Since it is indeed presented by the dative case itself through its own function (*vṛtti*), there is no harm to the apprehension brought about by that function. This is clear in the *Kaustubha* on the *aiuṇ* sūtra. Furthermore, in examples such as "the desired object of the root *spṛh*" (*spṛherīpsitaḥ*), there is indeed an implication of a word (*padādhyāhāra*).

In this regard, it is established that the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a meaning occurs only when there is a capacity for comprehension (*gamaka-sattva*), whereas the ellipsis of a word (*pada-adhyāhāra*) occurs in all cases. Thus, the understanding is: "The vehicle is that which brings about the fruit as its object. As for the view that there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word 'fruit' in the act of bringing the fruit as the object, and that the meaning of the dative case is the fruit; or alternatively, that its meaning is merely the action, while the relation between the preceding and following [words] consists in being the motivator of the objecthood—this is not correct. For since the term 'object' (*karmaṇi*) is explicitly stated in the Sūtra, there is no evidence for the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of such a meaning. This is the general direction of the argument.

In the expression *yāgāya yāti* ("he goes for the sake of sacrifice"), the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is a sacrifice delimited by future time. The meaning of the dative case (*caturthī*) is the fruit and the relation of being its producer. The resulting cognition is: "the going is the producer of a future sacrifice."

In the expression "I do not consider you as a blade of grass, nor [do I consider] a blade of grass [as such]," the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) and the dative case (*caturthī*) denote the object (*karman*). The base word (*prakṛti*) possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) similar to its own primary meaning. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "the absence of the knowledge that [you] are a non-agent with respect to an object similar to a blade of grass which is non-different from you. This results in the understanding: "the absence of a knowledge whose qualificand is you and whose qualifier is the state of being similar to a blade of grass. Furthermore, this [absence of knowledge] is necessarily caused by extreme inferiority. When the verb *man* (to think/consider) is used in conjunction with the dative case, its meaning is "to perceive" (*budhyate*), due to the inherent nature of the linguistic capacity (*śabdaśakti*).

In the expressions *grāmaṃ gacchati* (he goes to the village) or *grāmāya gacchati* (he goes for the village), here too, the meaning of both the second and fourth cases is simply the object (*karman*). Others, however, maintain that in this context, the meaning of the fourth case is the "intended recipient" (*uddeśya*), while the meaning of the root *yā* (to go) is the act of perceiving or requesting with respect to an activity conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location. Thus, since the perception and so forth directed toward the village constitute the "artificial object" (*kṛtrima-karman*)—being that which is intended by the activity conducive to conjunction with it—the village possesses the status of the "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*). There is no fault here, because although the village is the locus of the result [of conjunction], its status as such is not intended to be expressed; rather, its status as the intended recipient is what is intended to be expressed.
And thus, the understanding is that "seeing" and so forth have as their object an activity conducive to conjunction with a northern direction, which has the village as its intended goal (*uddeśya*).

Any over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be avoided by means of non-mention (*anabhidhāna*). However, in cases such as "he goes to the village," they say that the meaning is simply an activity conducive to conjunction.
This concludes the investigation into the meaning of the fourth case-ending (*caturthī-vibhakti*) as a *kāraka*.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the case-terminations used as *upapada*s (governing words). Next, the meaning of the case-termination used as an *upapada* is stated.

In the example "odanaḥ viprāya" ("rice for the Brahmin"), the sense is *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that). *Tādarthya* is a relation characterized by being an auxiliary. In some cases, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) connects with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) through a mediated sequence. As in the present instance, the connection occurs precisely through the state of being the non-separation from the "producedness" residing in the eating performed by the Brahmin as agent. The resulting cognition is: "The rice is the generator of the eating performed by the Brahmin. However, in some cases, the connection is direct. For example: "He worships Hari for the sake of liberation" (*muktaye hariṃ bhajati*).

In this case, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs precisely through being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the state of being produced (*janyatā*) residing in itself. The resulting cognition is: "Worship of Hari is the generator of liberation. Alternatively, the cognition is: "The residence possesses the state of being an auxiliary (*upakārakatā*) as determined by study."

In the expression "devotion conduces to knowledge" (*bhaktir jñānāya kalpate*), the dative case signifies a relationship. The understanding is that there is an origination related to knowledge, having devotion as its agent. However, according to the rule for the dative denoting purpose (*tādarthya*), the understanding is that there is an origination producing knowledge, having devotion as its agent. When a distinction between the material cause and the effect is intended, the dative is used after the word denoting the effect; but when non-distinction is intended, the nominative is used because of [the effect's] agency, as in "devotion conduces to knowledge" (*bhaktir jñānaṃ kalpate*).

But when there is the intention to express the status of the source (*apādānatva*) according to the rule *janikartuḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.30], then the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used: *bhakteḥ jñānaṃ kalpyate* ("knowledge arises from devotion"). Since the agency (*kartṛtva*) of knowledge is already expressed [by the suffix], the first case (*prathamā*) alone is used for it.

The essential point here is this: the meaning of *kalpate* and similar forms is "undergoes transformation" (*pariṇamate*). Transformation, moreover, is the attainment of another form. When that other form—a part of the whole—is construed non-differently with a word denoting a modification such as "knowledge," the dative case would normally be required; however, by the rule *klṛpi saṃpadyamāne ca*, the fourth case (dative) is prescribed. Thus, the meaning is that when used in conjunction with a verbal root having the sense of *klṛp*, the fourth case is employed for a word expressing that which is being produced.

And thus, in this context, the fourth case (caturthī) has fulfilled its purpose; however, when there is a desire to express the non-difference between those two [the cause and the effect], it is superseded by the first case (prathamā) due to its higher status. They say that if the meaning is merely the arising from the beginning of the Kalpa, then the fifth case (pañcamī) and so on apply according to the aforementioned rule. In the example *vātayā kapilā vidyut* ("A tawny lightning flash is a portent of wind"), the relationship consisting of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*) is the meaning of the fourth case. The understanding is: "The tawny lightning flash is an indicator of wind. Here, the fourth case is used by the rule *utpātena jñāpite ca* ("The fourth case is used when something is indicated by a portent"). A portent (*utpāta*) is a physical change that indicates the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of living beings.

In the expression *viprāya hitam* ("beneficial for the Brahmin"), the meaning of the dative case is relation (*sambandha*). The word *hita* (beneficial) has the sense of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*). Thus, the cognition is: "that which is a means to a desired end related to the Brahmin. In the expression *haraye namaḥ* ("salutation to Hari"), the dative case is used according to the rule *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alaṃ-vaṣaḍ-yogācca* [Pāṇini 2.3.16]. The meaning of the word *namaḥ* is bowing (*nati*). This is an activity conducive to the communication of the knowledge that [the speaker] is inferior [to the object of salutation]. In this context, by virtue of the diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), the word *namaḥ* itself denotes the act of bowing, which is the inferiorizing activity.

It is perceived as being colored by its status as having a specific person who employs it as its locus and by its being the terminus of the act of salutation. This is because words uttered by another do not produce the cognition of "I bow. And that activity is, in some cases, the conjunction of the hand and the head, and in other cases, the very employment of such a word. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "An activity residing in the employer, which is conducive to the communication of a knowledge of inferiority relative to Hari as the limit."

In expressions such as "This is the *arghya* offering; salutation (*namaḥ*) to Śiva," the meaning of the word *namaḥ* is renunciation (*tyāga*). And renunciation is a specific kind of activity conducive to both [the recipient's] acquisition of ownership and the donor's cessation of ownership. This is because, according to authoritative sources such as "Śiva would not accept [it as] his own," the deity also possesses ownership over the substance.

The meaning of the dative case is a relation consisting of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*). And being the intended recipient is a specific form of objective directedness (*viṣayatā*). Thus, the cognition is: "The *arghya* is the object of an act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) directed toward Śiva. In the view that the deity is insentient, however, relinquishment is an activity conducive to the loss of one's own ownership. And this [act] is perceived as being specifically qualified by having its performance by oneself as taught in the Veda, due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), because when the word *namaḥ* is uttered by another person, no relinquishment belonging to someone else is perceived.

There is no fault here, for the word *namaḥ* is employed precisely by superimposing ownership upon those various substances belonging to the sacrificer, as they are offered by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Furthermore, the dative case used here for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) need not be suspected [of being ungrammatical], because the referent of the word *namaḥ* lacks the nature of an action (*kriyā*). It is said that because of the phrase "as enjoined by the Veda," the word *namaḥ* is not employed in sacrifices where the intended recipient (*uddeśya*) is something other than a deity.

In the expression *namaskaroti devān* ("he pays homage to the gods"), the accusative case is used to denote the object (*karman*) because of the maxim: "The case ending based on the *kāraka* (syntactic role) is stronger than the case ending based on an adjunct (*upapada*). The underlying rationale for this maxim is that since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is primary while the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāmārtha*) is secondary, and between the primary and the secondary, it is more appropriate for the meaning to be determined by the primary factor.

[Objection: But how can the gods (*deva*) be the object (*karman*) here? Nor should it be argued that they are the object because they are the locus (*āśraya*) of the cognition of inferiority—which is the fruit of the act of salutation (*namaskāra*), consisting of an activity conducive to bringing about such a cognition—since this would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a neutral observer looking on would be an object. [Response: This is not so; there is no fault, because the delimiting relation of the fruit (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is inherence (*samavāya*) as co-located with the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) whose object is oneself. [In this view,] "self" (*sva*) refers to the fruit, which is the cognition of inferiority; and since one is the locus of inferiority through the relation of being a limit (*avadhitā-sambandha*), one is the object, according to others.

If it is objected: "Even in this case, since words such as *namo haraye* require that the word *namaḥ* must necessarily be expressive (*vācaka*), then even though it is the substratum for the cognition of the meaning of the word *namaḥ*, how can it be the object (*karman*) given that it is not the substratum of the result of the verbal root's meaning? The answer is: there is no fault, because it is accepted that when used in connection with the root *kṛ*, a word listed among the *sākṣāt-prabhṛtis*—being designated as a particle (*nipāta*) and so forth—is merely indicative (*dyotaka*). In examples such as *haraye namaḥ*, however, it is listed among the *svarādi* group; but in the present case, it is not. For this very reason, the formation of compounds and the like is established.

Nor does this [objection] hold, for even though there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the word *namas*, how could the case-ending of the subordinate term (*upapada-vibhakti*) not apply? It applies simply by virtue of the connection manifested by that [suffix]. However, when even this object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), then the genitive is set aside and the dative alone is used by the rule "namaḥ-svasti-... (Pāṇini 2.3.16).

As for the claim that this principle applies only when a single word functions as both an oblique case (upapada-vibhakti) and a case expressing a grammatical relation (kāraka-vibhakti), that is not correct; for it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the rule *namo-varivas-śvaso 't* [Pāṇini 3.1.22]. For in that context, the venerable Teacher [Patañjali] introduced this very principle in order to prevent the occurrence of the dative case in the example *namasyati devān*. By this, it follows that due to its association with *svasti*, only the word *namas* denoting a substance (*satvavācin*) is to be understood.

The argument that in examples such as *namasyati*, [the word *namaḥ*] does not denote a substance (*sattva*) because it is designated as a particle (*nipāta*) by virtue of being a "maker of existence" (*satvakaraṇa*), is refuted. For even in cases like *namasyati*, since it denotes an action, it would not denote a substance; thus, the rule [P. 2.3.16] would fail to apply, leading to a contradiction with the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term *yoga* (connection), the dative case is prescribed merely when there is a connection [with a verb], so that in the absence of an intention to express the status of being an object (*karmatva*), one finds forms such as *namasyati devebhyaḥ*. Moreover, because of the great designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) "indeclinable" (*avyaya*), even those words listed in the *svarādi* group possess a connection with gender, number, and grammatical relations (*kāraka*). This is the general direction of the argument.

In expressions such as *prajābhyaḥ svasti* ("May there be well-being for the subjects"), the word *svasti* signifies auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and the dative case expresses the relation (*sambandha*). In instances where there is an expression of a wish for auspiciousness, such as *svastyastu gobhyaḥ* ("May there be well-being for the cows"), the dative case is used when the meaning of the word *svasti* is construed [with the verb], whereas the genitive case is used when it is construed with the action (*kriyā*). In that context, when the dative ending is present, the understanding is: "The coming-into-being (*bhavana*) of auspiciousness, which has as its agent the cows related to the objects of the wish. When the genitive ending is present, the understanding is: "The coming-into-being of auspiciousness, which has as its agent the object of the wish and is related to the cows."

As for the claim that "the meaning of the word *āśis* (blessing) is *svasti* (well-being), and that is a desire directed toward the welfare of another, while the relationship with that which possesses the welfare is the meaning of the dative case"—that is not correct. For it would result in the non-occurrence of the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in forms such as *bhūyāt* (may he be); furthermore, it would result in the non-occurrence of the dative in expressions such as *svasti vṛṣalāya* (well-being to the outcaste), since in that context the word *svasti* has the sense of "acceptance" (*aṅgīkāra*). This is because authoritative sources state that its meaning is precisely the acceptance of auspiciousness. This is the general direction [of the argument]. The words *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* are explained by the word *namas*, which signifies renunciation (*tyāga*).

In the expression "alam daityebhyo hariḥ" (Hari is a match for the Daityas), the meaning of the word *alam* is "capacity," and the meaning of the dative case is a relation consisting in being connected with the act of slaying the Daityas and so forth. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Hari is the possessor of a capacity that is related to the slaying of the Daityas and so forth.
This concludes the determination of the meaning of the dative case as an upapada (governing word).
Now follows the investigation into the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī-vibhakti*).

The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), which is a kāraka-case, is the *apādāna* (point of departure). This is established by the rule: "The fifth [case-ending] is used for the *apādāna*" [Pāṇini 2.3.28]. And the definition of that is given by the rule: "That which is fixed (*dhruva*) in relation to separation (*apāya*) is the *apādāna*" [Pāṇini 1.4.24]. Here, *apāya* means disjunction, that is, the absence of a relationship. Furthermore, this [absence] is not necessarily preceded by an actual, real relationship, but may also be preceded by a relationship imagined by the intellect (*buddhi-parikalpita*). In the same way, it should be understood that even non-existence (*abhāva*) is to be understood as being imagined by the intellect.

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya’s rejection of the term *jugupsāvirāma* and others—by relying on their characterizing cessation (*nivṛtti*) preceded by loathing (*jugupsā*) and so forth—is justified; likewise, the application of the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* [Pāṇini 2.3.41] and usages such as *yato yato virajyate* become consistent. Furthermore, the specific movement that produces that [cessation] is also considered here to be "departure" (*apāya*), according to the clear intention of Hari: "Movement without a limit (*avadhi*) is not called departure. The meaning of that is that an action cannot be denoted by the word *apāya* unless it possesses the quality of being conducive to a separation capable of connecting with a limit.

The word *ayāya* (in the sūtra) is repeated, and the word *anveti* (follows) is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhriyate*). Therefore, its meaning is: that which is constant (*dhruvam*) when there is departure (*apāye*), being the non-substratum of the action consisting of going (*gati-rūpa-apāya*) that follows the departure—that is the *apādāna*. And thus, the resulting definition is: that which, while not being the substratum of the specific action denoted by the root in question—which produces disjunction (*vibhāga*)—by means of the relation that delimits the status of being an operation (*vyāpāra-tāvacchedaka-sambandha*), is nevertheless the substratum (*āśrayatayā*) that follows the separation (*viśleṣa*) denoted by that [action]. This is the established conclusion.

The term "real" (*satyam*) is included to exclude the agent. The phrase "supplied by the verbal root under discussion" (*prakṛtadhātūpāttā*) is used to include cases such as "he falls from a running horse" (*dhāvato'śvāt patati*) and "he falls from a horse falling from a wall" (*kuḍyāt patato'śvāt patati*). The phrase "that action" (*tatkriyā*) is used to include cases such as "two rams move away from each other" (*parasparānmeṣāvapasarataḥ*). In expressions such as "one should desist from this and that" (*nivarteta tatastataḥ*), the meaning of the verbal root—which consists of the absence of activity—exists in the limit (*avadhi*) as a qualifier delimited by the relation of objectness (*viṣayatā*); therefore, the specific relation is specified in order to avoid the over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition to such cases.

The qualificandum portion [of the definition] is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a neutral (*udāsīna*) entity. And that [neutral entity] is precisely the limit (*avadhi*), such as the one who is afflicted (*ārta*). Limit-hood (*avadhitva*) is either a specific kind of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) that is co-located with the state of being the substratum of the aforementioned separation (*viśleṣa*), or it is a distinct category of reality (*padārthāntara*). In this context, since separation is already obtained from the verbal root, the limit is the meaning of the ablative case by virtue of its being a limit.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for its manifestation as a limit (*avadhi*), because the mention of the word *dhruva* (fixed/constant), which serves as an indicator of that limit, constitutes such evidence. Otherwise, since the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) would already be established by the rule "the ablative is [used] in the sense of separation" (*apāye 'pādānam*), which defines the ablative as that which is connected with the action of departure, the mention of *dhruva* would clearly be redundant. Nor can it be argued that the term is intended to prevent the status of an ablative from applying when a tree is connected to the action of falling by a general relation (*sambandhasāmānya*), because such a meaning cannot be obtained through the primary denotative function (*vācyavṛtti*). Furthermore, this interpretation is supported by the fact that it accounts for the absence of the status of an object (*karman*) in examples such as "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*).

Nor would that [rule] be intended to exclude the status of the *apādāna* (ablative) for the agent, the *parṇa* (leaf), because even if there is a connection with the operation conducive to that [separation], there is no connection with the separation itself; and furthermore, because the designation of *kartṛ* (agent) sublates it due to its higher priority. For this very reason, Hari stated that the ablative (*pañcamī*) has the *avadhi* (limit/source) alone as its meaning, in the passage beginning: "The locus, the limit, and the object."

By this, the view that "separation" (*vibhāga*) and "substratum" (*āśraya*) are the meanings of the ablative case is refuted. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the term] "vṛkṣāt" being understood as "separation" in expressions such as *vṛkṣādvibhajate* ("he separates from the tree"). If, in that case, the limit alone (*avadhi*) were the meaning of the ablative, why resort to the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) fallacy? For according to your own system, the ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) of the ablative in that context would follow; moreover, in the Nyāya system, you yourself have stated the ungrammaticality of the accusative in cases like *ghaṭaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the pot"). Finally, since the definition "the *apādāna* is that which possesses departure" (*apāyavat*) would suffice, the inclusion of the term *dhruva* ("fixed") would be redundant, and because separation is already obtainable from the verbal root itself.

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*), the tree would incur the status of an object (*karman*) by virtue of being the locus of separation (*viśleṣa*), just as in the case of "he abandons the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ tyajati*). This is because, with respect to the relation that delimits the result (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), the tree is not the locus of that [result]; for that [status of being an object] belongs only to that which is the locus of the separation residing in the agent (*kartṛ-niṣṭha-vibhāgīya-sambandha*). In cases such as "he abandons the tree," since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is precisely the separation that is non-co-located with the activity (*vyāpāra*), the status of being an object indeed occurs.

By this, the following view is refuted: that "separation" (*vibhāga*) alone is the meaning of the ablative suffix (*pañcamī*), that its relation with the meanings of the base and the suffix is "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*), and that the separation connects with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) by way of the relation of being produced (*janyatā*). This is because it would entail abandoning the well-established relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) between the meaning of the case-suffix and the meaning of the base; furthermore, since the definition "the *apādāna* is that from which there is departure" (*apāya*) already suffices, the other [elements of the definition] would become redundant.

And thus, in expressions such as "the leaf falls from the tree," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) has as its meaning the limit (*avadhi*) functioning as the point of departure. Therein, the meaning of the base (the stem *vṛkṣa*) is a qualifier by way of identity (*abheda*). And that [meaning of the base] is a qualifier of the "separation" (*vibhāga*), which is one part of the meaning of the root *pat*—namely, the action consisting of an operation conducive to a separation that is itself conducive to a conjunction [with another locus]. The resulting cognition is: "An operation residing in the leaf, which is conducive to a separation having the tree as its limit and conducive to a conjunction located in the ground. One should not object that, even if this were the case, the expression "it flows from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt syandate*) would be improper; for we accept this as a desired outcome (*iṣṭāpatti*), just as in the case of "he moved from his seat" (*āsanāccalitaḥ*). However, if the root were intended to denote mere action (*kriyāmātra*) without the sense of separation, then the form would simply be "it flows on the tree" (*vṛkṣe syandate*).

In expressions such as "lightning flashes from the cloud" (*valāhakād vidyotate*), there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the act of flashing as being preceded by an emergence. Emergence is an action that produces separation. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The flashing, which occurs subsequent to an action producing separation having the cloud as its limit, resides in a substratum whose nature is lightning. This is called an instance where the object [of the metaphor] is explicitly mentioned (*upāttaviṣaya*).

However, when one keeps in mind an arrival whose existence is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasaddharma*) and, in response to the question "Where have you come from?", answers "From Pāṭaliputra," then—according to the view that does not accept that the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) generated by words is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)—the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs only with the arrival presented through direct perception. According to other views, however, it should be understood that the connection is with the arrival presented from a word remembered by way of its relation to the directly perceived object.
It is with this very intention that they say: "Even an action that is being understood (*gamyamānā*) is the motivator for case-endings (*kārakavibhakti*)."

However, some maintain that even when words are supplied (*padādhyāhāra*), because the word itself is not explicitly uttered, this [example] falls under the very category of "even though it is understood" (*gamyamāna*).

In that context, the word *kim* signifies the object of the question. Thus, the understanding is that there is an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to a division delimited by the object of the question. In both the interrogative sentence and the answer, [the phrase] "delimited by Pāṭaliputra" and so forth is supplied.

This very [operation] is called "the action required" (*apekṣitakriya*). On the other hand, they say that in "He falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt patati*), the object is explicitly indicated (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*).

1. [Note: Here, the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative source) is established by the rule *jugupsā-virāma*. The meaning of this is that whatever object is intended as the domain of disgust (*jugupsā*) and so forth is the *apādāna*. The meaning of the root *jugups-* is censure (*nindā*), which consists in the cognition of something as a means to an undesirable end. The meaning of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is "being the object" (*viṣayatva*) and so forth, or else it is the power (*śakti*) of being an *apādāna*.]

By accepting that the verbal root (*dhātu*) has an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for cessation preceded by such censure, the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is established by the rule *dhruvamapāye* itself. In this very manner, the author of the Bhāṣya rejects this Vārttika and the subsequent sūtras. In expressions such as *adharmājjugupsate*, *viramati*, and *pramādyati*, the meaning of the root *jugupsati* is censure consisting of the cognition that [the object] is a means to an undesirable end. The meaning of the fifth case suffix (*pañcamī*) is the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*). The resulting understanding is: "The cognition that non-dharma (*adharma*) is a means to an undesirable end."

The meaning of *viramati* (he desists) is the absence of an effort (*kṛti*) qualified by a destruction that resides in the same locus as that effort. Furthermore, in all cases, the effort appears as having a single object due to the force of expectancy. This qualification [of the absence] is by way of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a body belonging to the same class as the body understood from the coreferential agent-noun. This is because words such as "Caitra" convey a qualified self, and thereby convey the body as well. And this "belonging to the same class" is precisely by way of the universal such as "Devadatta-ness" presented by words such as "Devadatta."

Therefore, even when unrighteousness (*adharma*) is being committed with the delimitation of a future body, the linguistic usage "Devadatta desists from unrighteousness" is established by taking the present body as the locus. Nor is there the usage "he desists" by taking the destruction of the final occurrence delimited by a childhood body, while one is currently committing unrighteousness delimited by a youth body. Nor is there the usage "he desists" when one commits unrighteousness in both prior and subsequent times but does not commit it for a mere moment in the middle; for the destruction of that action (*kṛti*) must reside in the same substratum as the action itself.

Nor does the usage cease by taking the destruction of the final effort delimited by that respective body as the basis; rather, the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is simply "object-hood" (*viṣayatā*). Thus, the cognition is: "Devadatta is characterized by the absence of effort qualified by the destruction of an effort that is not co-located with an effort having demerit as its object. Similarly, the meaning of the ablative in the case of *pramādyati* ("he neglects") is the absence of the knowledge that [an action] is a means to a desired end, qualified by entitlement (*adhikāra*), through the two relations of being in the same locus and occurring at the same time; this meaning, namely "object-hood," connects with the knowledge of being a means to a desired end. In this context, whatever is intended as the object of disgust (*jugupsā*) and so forth is the *apādāna*.

In expressions such as *corād bibheti* ("he fears the thief") or *trāyate* ("he protects"), fear (*bhaya*) is the cognition of something undesirable, while protection (*trāṇa*) is the activity conducive to the removal of that [fear]. The meaning of the ablative case here is the cause (*hetu*). This is evident from the natural sense of the rule: *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.25). And this [cause] connects with the "undesirable" portion, which is one part of the meaning of the verbal root. The phrase "the cause of fear" means "the cause of the undesirable," which is one part of the meaning of fear.

1 [Note: By writing "In the opinion of the author of the Mañjūṣā, the cognition has the form 'the thief is the source of the undesirable knowledge'," the authors of the Kāśikā have given meaning to the statement: "The turban of one has been placed upon the head of another."]

[Objection: Regarding the cognition of an undesirable thing caused by a thief—surely, for one for whom an undesirable thing caused by a thief is not established, yet he still suspects his own undesirable outcome to be caused by that [thief], the usage "this person fears the thief" would not occur, because the fact of being caused by a thief is sublated in respect to that person's undesirable outcome. [Response: No; there is no fault, because it is due to the superimposition (*āropa*) of the state of being caused by a thief upon another person's undesirable outcome which is caused by that [thief], or upon that person's own undesirable outcome.

Here too, when there is an intention to express the relationship [of the genitive], the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) occurs after the word *cora* (thief). For this very reason, the usage in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, "From whom do even the gods fear when he has become enraged in battle? (*kasya bibhyati devāśca jātaroṣasya saṃyuge*), is consistent. Alternatively, the syntactic connection should be understood as "from whom [does fear arise] in battle" (*kasya saṃyuge*).

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "being caused by" (*prayojyatva*) combined with "the state of being a producer of harm" (*apakārakatva*). This [meaning] is construed with the notion of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). Therefore, there is no fault in cases where an undesirable outcome dependent on a thief is not well-known, because fear exists due to the possibility of an undesirable outcome caused by the thief; for there exists the possibility [expressed as]: "The thief might cause me harm. In this way, the validity of even such a sentence as "He fears even his friend, through mistaking him for an enemy" is logically consistent.

And thus they say: when used with a verbal root meaning "fear," the apprehension of something as being the cause of fear is one sentence-meaning (the basis of the ablative); when used with a verbal root meaning "protection," that which causes the undesirable is the other sentence-meaning. Furthermore, the cognition [arising] is: "an operation conducive to the cessation of the undesirable caused by that. Nor is it the case that the fifth case (ablative) would not apply because fear produced by thorns and the like is not well-known; for that is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). If the fifth case is desired there, the usage occurs precisely by superimposing the status of being a cause upon it.

In the same way, the logical consistency of such expressions as "space does not see" or "space does not perceive an atom" is maintained by superimposing agency and other such qualities upon space in relation to seeing and so forth, and then negating those very qualities; this is because of the cognition [of the negation], just like the statement "the horn of a hare is not non-existent. For in that case, the negation is made of the existence of a hare's horn which is presented by the force of the word itself, according to the accepted principle: "Indeed, even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent, a word produces a cognition."

However, the ascertainment of unfitness (*ayogyatāniścaya*) is not an obstacle to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Otherwise, for one who has acquired a different linguistic proficiency (*vyutpanna*), the words of an opponent would be as mute as silence. If the opponent did not apprehend the sentence-meaning from the words, even the discourse intended to refute that [position] would be cut short. Others maintain that verbal comprehension can be "voluntary" (*āhārya*).
