For this very reason, they say that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*) of expressions such as "the horn of a hare does not exist" is indeed accepted.

In the expression "he fails because of his study" (*adhyayanāt parājayate*), the meaning of the verbal root is the absence of effort (*kṛtyabhāva*) which is co-located with the cognition of the non-accomplishability of the effort (*kṛtyasādhyatvadhī*). The meaning of the ablative case is the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*). And the fact that both [the cognition and the absence of effort] have the same object is obtained through the force of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Thus, the understanding is: "The absence of effort residing in Devadatta is co-located with the cognition of the non-accomplishability of the effort whose object is study. In the expression "he defeats the enemies" (*śatrūn parājayate*), the meaning of the verbal root is an activity conducive to contempt (*tiraskārānukūlo vyāpāraḥ*).

As for the claim that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the undesirable (*aniṣṭa*), the meaning of the ablative suffix (*pañcamī*) is being produced (*janyatva*), and that in the rule *parājerasoḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.26), the word *asoḍhaḥ* signifies an object intended as a means to the undesirable—this is not correct; for since the desired meaning would already be established by the recurrence of the term *hetu* (cause), the inclusion of *asoḍhaḥ* would result in redundancy, and furthermore, the meaning you have described cannot be obtained from the word *asoḍha*, which ends in a past passive participle (*kta*).

In the expression *yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati* ("he keeps the cow away from the barley"), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an activity conducive to the absence of an activity that produces results such as eating. According to the rule *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.27), the barley (*yava*) functions as the *apādāna* (ablative point). In this context, the term *īpsita* means "the object of desire by virtue of being the locus of the result that delimits the meaning of the verbal root whose sense is 'warding off'. In the example, because the cow desires the barley by virtue of being the locus of the result—namely, conjunction—which delimits the meaning of the verbal root, the barley possesses the status of *apādāna*.

In that case, due to the peculiarity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), it is only the absence of the activity of eating—which culminates in the act—whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the property of "eating-ness" that appears [in the cognition]. Furthermore, due to the force of intention (*tātparya*), the denotative power (*śakti*) resides specifically in this [delimited form]; thus, some maintain that having multiple meanings (*nānārthatva*) is indeed acceptable. And so, the resulting cognition is: "an activity conducive to that absence of the activity of eating—which produces a conjunction residing in the barley and which is [otherwise] present in the cow. However, if there is the usage "he restrains [the cow] even though it is eating the forbidden [barley]," then [the meaning] is simply an activity qualified by a desire whose mode (*prakāra*) is such an absence.
It should be understood that this refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

On this point, some maintain that where the consumption of poison by Caitra and others occurs as an unavoidable consequence (*nāntarīyakatayā*) and not by his own will, the suffix *san* is employed in order to prevent the usage "he wards off Caitra from the poison" (*viṣād vārayati caitram*)—which would otherwise apply to the agent of the activity that prevents such consumption. For this very reason, in such cases, the only usage is "he wards him off from the poisoned food" (*saviṣād annād vārayati*).

And it should not be argued that [the example] "one does not prevent the blind man from the well" is invalid; for it must be said that although falling into the well is not an object of the blind man's desire as such, it is nonetheless an object of his desire insofar as he desires to go toward that location in front of him. Thus they say.

Kṛṣṇa hides from his mother; here, the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is established by Pāṇini’s rule [1.4.28]: "That from which one desires non-perception through disappearance. In this context, "disappearance" (*antardhi*) is defined as staying in a particular location for the purpose of bringing about the absence of being seen by another, such absence being produced by an operation distinct from the other's own activity. This alone is the meaning of the term *antardhi* in the Sūtra. The meaning of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), namely "occurrence" (*vṛttitva*), connects with the "operation" which is a part of the verbal root's meaning.

The meaning of the verb *adhīte* (he studies) in the expression ‘*upādhyāyād adhīte*’ (he studies from the teacher) is an operation conducive to the acceptance [of the text] preceded by a rule [of recitation] subsequent to its utterance. The meaning of the ablative case is the relation of occurrence (*vṛttitva*), which connects with the utterance, which is a part of that [operation]. The meaning of the verb *adhīte* in ‘*upādhyāyād adhīte*’ is an operation conducive to the acceptance [of the text] preceded by a rule [of recitation] subsequent to its utterance. The meaning of the ablative case is the relation of occurrence, which connects with the utterance, which is a part of that [operation].

In the phrase "beings are born from Brahman," the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamyartha*) is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). [Note: "Birth" (*jani*) is the act of being born; "the agent of that" is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound. Because it ends in the suffix *tṛn*, there is no prohibition against the compound. Now, one might object that the rule "na lokāvyaya... would prohibit the genitive; however, according to the established doctrine, that prohibition applies only to the genitive used for grammatical relations (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*), so there is no obstacle to the application of the genitive used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).]

In reality, however, the author of the *Manoramā* maintains that a compound with the word ending in *-tṛc* is easily formed even with a genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). This is because of the natural sense of the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30). For it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources that in this context the word *prakṛti* refers to the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Thus, the understanding is that origination (*utpatti*) is a state residing in progeny (*prajā*), produced by a material cause non-different from Brahman.

2 [The authors of the Vṛtti, however, say that in accordance with this usage, in the rule "the source of the agent of birth is the *prakṛti*," the word *prakṛti* includes the cause (*hetu*) in general. In examples such as "joy arises from the son" (*putrāt pramodo jāyate*), the ablative case is used for the cause (*hetu*) due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "optionally when denoting a quality, provided it is not feminine" (*vibhāṣā guṇe'striyām*, Pāṇini 2.3.25). Others hold that it is by means of the superimposition (*āropa*) of the status of being a material cause (*upādāna*).

In expressions such as "The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," the meaning of the root *prabhavati* is "first manifestation. The sense is: "the first manifestation having the Himavat as its cause and the Gaṅgā as its agent. Regarding this, some others say that the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "locus-ness" (*adhikaraṇatva*). The author of the *Vyutpattivāda* says that the meaning of the ablative case is "dependence upon a relation" (*sambandhādhīnatva*).

According to the *Tārkikaratnākara*: identity (*tādātmya*) is the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*); the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the state of being perceptible with respect to a location not separated from the location delimited by the absence of perceptibility. Identity is construed with the "location" that is a constituent of the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, the meaning of the verbal root is the first external conjunction (*bahiḥ-saṃyoga*) which is non-different from the Himavat mountain and is not separated from the location delimited by the absence of perceptibility.

In the present context, the external object is *rasātala* (the netherworld). The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "occurring in the moment immediately following the destruction of the conjunction. The meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) is "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The Gaṅgā is that which possesses substratum-ness of its first conjunction with the earth, occurring in the moment immediately following the destruction of the conjunction whose relatum is Himālaya. This is because the meaning of the ablative is "source" (*prabhava*), according to the natural sense of the rule *bhavaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.31); for there, "source" (*prabhava*) is defined as that from which something originates (*prabhavati asmāt*).

In expressions such as "he looks from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*), the understanding arises through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a word ending in *lyap*, such as "having ascended" (*āruhya*). The meaning of the ablative case is the object of the supplied action. In cases such as "he looks from the seat" (*āsanāt prekṣate*), the meaning of the ablative is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the supplied word ending in *lyap*, such as "having sat down" (*upaviśya*). Here too, there is only an ellipsis of the word itself; for in the Vārttika rule "when *lyap* is elided, [the case of] the object [is used]," the word "elision" (*lopa*) refers precisely to non-utterance.
Others, however, explain the phrase "he struck the chest of the odd-eyed one" (*ājaghne viṣamavilocanasya vakṣaḥ*) by supplying a word ending in *tumun*, namely "in order to pierce" (*bhettum*).

Thus concludes the investigation of the meaning of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-vibhakti*). Now, the case-endings of the locative adjunct (*upapada*) are being defined. Consider the example: "The village is at a *yojana* from the forest," or "at every *yojana* [from the forest]. Here, the meaning of the fifth case is "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*). However, the meaning of the first and seventh cases is a relation such as "subsisting in a location immediately following [the point of reference]. Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "The village subsists in a location that is immediately following the *yojana* which is itself immediately following the forest."

In the expression "in the month from Kārttikī to Āgrahāyaṇī," the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "immediately following without an interval" (*avyavahitottaratva*) having its own [constituent] as the antecedent. The meaning of the locative case (*saptamī*) is "occurring in a time immediately following [the antecedent]. The resulting cognition is: "Āgrahāyaṇī occurs in a time immediately following the month consisting of thirty lunar days (tithis) that follows the constituent [period] of Kārttikī."

In the phrase "another is a friend, or the other is different from Kṛṣṇa," the ablative case (pañcamī) is employed by the rule *anyārāditarartedikśabdāccuuttarapadājāhiyukte* [Pāṇini 2.3.29]. In that rule, the word *anya* is taken as representing the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). Its meaning is "that which possesses difference. Furthermore, the word *anya* is *bhāvapradhāna* (predominant in its abstract state); the sense is that it signifies the quality of "otherness" (*anyatva*).

For this very reason, there is the establishment of such expressions as "the difference from the jar" (*ghaṭād bhedaḥ*) and "different from the jar" (*ghaṭād bhinnaḥ*). Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as "the jar is not the cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), there would likewise result the use of the ablative case, since that [word *na*] also has difference as its meaning; for [in the rule], only those words similar to it which have a different meaning and which convey gender and number are intended to be included. For this very reason, the word *itara*, which has that same meaning, is mentioned as a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*). Its purpose is to indicate that only such words as these, which have that specific meaning, are to be understood.

Nor should it be said that the word *itaras* is used for the sake of including the sense of "lowly," as in the rule *itarastvanyanīcayoḥ*; for, by virtue of simplicity—which avoids postulating a prescriptive statement—and by way of association (*sāhacarya*), only the sense of "other" is grasped. Furthermore, this is already established by the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), just as in the case of expressions such as *asmāt tāro mṛduḥ*. Nor does the application of that rule succeed even when the sense is "other," because the mutually opposed properties—such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—that serve as the basis for differentiation (*nirdhāraṇa*) are not denoted; and because a difference characterized by mutual opposition cannot function as a differentiator when it resides in both members of the relation.

Furthermore, since the negative particle (*nañ*) is merely indicative, the words *ghaṭa* and so forth themselves possess the figurative sense (*lākṣaṇikatva*); consequently, the ablative case (*pañcamī*), which is based on difference (*bheda*), does not apply. Nor does the application of the ablative follow from the rule in the lexicon stating "the word *eka* means 'other' (*anyārtha*) and 'principal' (*pradhāna*)," as in the example "a cloth is one [different] from a jar" (*ghaṭādekaḥ paṭaḥ*); for such an occurrence is accepted. The same applies when the word is used in the sense of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Nor should it be argued that there would be no application [of the suffix] in cases such as "ghaṭīyo bhedaḥ" (the difference belonging to the jar), on the grounds that the suffix *cha* prescribed after a word ending in the genitive case is not applicable here. For when the meaning of the word *idam* ("this") is construed with the sense of "belonging to this" (*ghaṭasyāyam*), that suffix is easily obtained; since *idam* denotes what is proximate and present in the mind, it lacks the status of having another [external] referent. Precisely for this reason, these [words] are called pronouns (*sarvanāman*) because they possess all meanings (*sarvārthatva*). For that [status] consists in denoting all objects in a single uniform manner. As for their cognition in specific forms, that occurs through the force of context and so forth, and is merely a secondary mental process (*pārṣṇika-mānasa*). By this, the objection that one should have said "ghaṭāt saḥ" is refuted.

In reality, however, the difference of a jar is from a cloth, and not from the jar itself; thus, regarding such usages, there is no objection to the desired conclusion. As for the expression "the difference belonging to the jar" (*ghaṭīyo bhedaḥ*), they say that the suffix *cha* is applied here in the sense of "that which has come from that" (*tata āgataḥ*), according to Pāṇini 4.3.74.

It should not be argued that the word *bhinna* does not have a different meaning [from *bheda*], because in expressions such as *ghaṭaṃ bhinatti* ("he splits the jar"), the root *bhid* is established as having the sense of an operation conducive to the disjunction of parts, and because the suffix *kta* exists [in *bhinna*]. This is because, in accordance with usages such as *ghaṭāt paṭaṃ bhinatti* ("he distinguishes the cloth from the jar"), it is accepted that roots have multiple meanings and thus can also have the sense of a cognition whose qualifier is mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). However, it does not have the sense of an operation conducive to difference (*bheda*), because difference is eternal.

It should be understood that when there is a desire to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the object (*karman*) itself merely by means of its having the sense of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), such usages as *ghaṭād bhidyate* ("it is differentiated from the pot") and *ghaṭād bhinnaḥ* ("different from the pot") occur; however, because there is an absence of the sense of separation (*vibhāga*), the rule *dhruvam apāye* (Pāṇini 1.4.24) does not apply here.

As for the claim that the inclusion of the term *itarat* (the other) is for the sake of denoting distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), and that for this very reason the ablative case occurs in expressions such as "the jar is distinct from the cloth," and that this [ablative] does not signify "otherness" because distinctness is accepted as a separate quality—this is incorrect; for distinctness is not accepted as a quality. For this very reason, the expression "color is distinct from taste" is justified. Furthermore, this is established by the rule *pṛthagvinā* [Pāṇini 2.3.32]. The meaning of the ablative case here is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*).

In the expression "Happiness does not arise without Kṛṣṇa" (*ṛte kṛṣṇāt na utpadyate sukham*), the meaning of the word *ṛte* is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), and the meaning of the ablative case is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*). Furthermore, the word "Kṛṣṇa" is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇika*) to mean "devotion to Kṛṣṇa" and so forth. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The absence of the production of happiness by [the agent] is caused by the absolute non-existence of that which has devotion to Kṛṣṇa as its counter-correlative. In the expression "Suffering [arises] without Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇād ṛte duḥkham*), the meaning of the word *ṛte* connects with the other term through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The cognition is: "Suffering is co-located with the absolute non-existence of Kṛṣṇa. In the expression "A man is pitiable without Kṛṣṇa," the meaning of that [word *ṛte*] is "possessing absolute non-existence"; the cognition is: "A man is pitiable due to the absolute non-existence of Kṛṣṇa. In expressions such as "He is not an archer without Kṛṣṇa," the meaning is "possessing difference"; the cognition is: "He is not an archer who is non-different from Kṛṣṇa. With this [usage of *ṛte*], the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) also occurs, as in "The tree fell without the wind. Here, the cognition is: "The tree, which possesses the absence of wind, is the locus of falling.
The acquisition of the absence of being produced by the wind in the falling of the tree, however, is obtained through the force of the context (*ārtha*).

Others, however, say: the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of a producedness (*janyatā*) as determined by a generative power (*janakatā*) residing in the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*). This [state of being the counter-correlative] is construed with the word-meaning "absence" (*abhāva*) in the phrase *ṛte* (without). That [absence] is construed with "falling" (*patana*). And that [falling] is construed with "tree. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "the falling, which has the tree as its agent, is characterized by the absence of being produced by the wind."

In the expression "to the east of the village" (*pūrvo grāmāt*), "easternness" (*pūrvatva*) consists in being a location proximate to the mountain of sunrise (*udayācala*). The sense of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), namely "limit" (*avadhi*), is construed with that which is proximate, which is a part of that [location]. Similarly, "westernness" (*paścimatva*) consists in being a location proximate to the mountain of sunset (*astācala*). "Southernness" (*dakṣiṇatva*) consists in being a location proximate to the right hand of one standing facing the direction of the sun's rising. Likewise, "northernness" (*uttaratva*) consists in being a location proximate to the left hand of one so situated. The understanding occurs in this sequence: "being a location proximate to the mountain of sunrise, having the village as its limit," and so forth.

In the expression "Phālguna is prior to Caitra," the meaning of the word *pūrva* (prior) is a time that is a non-locus of both the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). By virtue of the speaker's intention, the referent of the word *caitra* is construed as the counter-correlative, as the counter-correlative in relation to the destruction, and as [the basis for] time—respectively through identity, as the counter-correlative, and as being immediate—and so forth; for a single entity may be construed in multiple ways due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Phālguna is that which occurs in a time immediately following Caitra, which is a non-locus of both the counter-correlative identical to Caitra and its destruction."

In expressions such as "Māgha is prior to Caitra," it should be understood that, depending on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), Caitra is construed with time through its being separated by thirty days and so forth, as appropriate. However, if the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) is accepted, then the meaning of the word "prior" is the time that serves as the locus of that absence. In cases such as "Caitra is posterior," the meaning of the word "posterior" is the time that serves as the locus of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). And Caitra is construed with that destruction as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and with time through its being immediate [to it] and so forth, according to the intention, as before.

In the expression "Valabhadra is prior to Kṛṣṇa," the word *kṛṣṇa* is used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) with respect to the time of his birth; the understanding is that [Valabhadra] originates at a time which is a non-locus for both the origination and the destruction of Kṛṣṇa's time. In expressions such as "posterior to Kṛṣṇa," the understanding is that [the object] exists at a time that is a locus for the destruction of Kṛṣṇa's time of origination. In expressions such as "Kāśī is to the north of Prayāga," "northerliness" (*uttaratva*) consists in being a location possessing a conjunction with a conjoined [object]. And this [northerliness], by virtue of its intention (*tātparya*), appears in those respective usages through its various forms, such as "easternness," "southernness," "westernness," and so forth.

In such instances as "The Gaṅgā is further than my house; that same [Gaṅgā] is nearer to me than Kāśī," the meanings of the words *para* (further) and *apara* (nearer) are, respectively, being situated in a distant place and being situated in a proximate place. The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is the relation known as "limit" (*avadhitva*). Consequently, the cognition arises in this sequence: "The Gaṅgā possesses a distance relative to me, having my house as its limit," and so forth. However, in the word *mama* (my), there is no ablative case; for, according to the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), one accepts a particular case-ending for a word only from that word which gives rise to the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for it. Thus, since the expectancy for the word expressing distance arises from the word *gṛhāt*, the ablative is applied there, and not to *mama*.

It is quite clear that words such as *parā* (the other side) possess a fixed expectancy (*niyatākāṅkṣā*) only with respect to a limit (*avadhi*), and not with respect to a related object (*sambandhin*).

This has already been explained by the words *prāk*, *pratyak*, *pūrva*, and so on, in the context of "east of the village" and similar expressions. In the expression "Hari is to be served from/beginning with birth" (*bhavāt prabhṛti ārabhya vā sevyo hariḥ*), the indeclinables *prabhṛti* and *ārabhya* have the meaning of "starting from. "Commencement" (*ārambha*) is the connection with the first moment; and when connected with another action, its relation (*saṃsarga*) consists in its pervading subsequent time, due to the very nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvabhāva*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Hari is the object of service that begins at the first moment connected to birth and continues to pervade subsequent time."

Starting from the first moment, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the operation conducive to the connection [between the object and the agent] up until that point. For this very reason, the first moment possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*). It should be understood that even when the status of being an object is not intended to be expressed, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) alone is used, overriding the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). In the expression *grāmād bahiḥ* ("outside the village"), by the word *bahiḥ*, there is expressed—according to the speaker's intention (tātparya)—either a place or a time that is not the locus of the delimitor of the referent associated with the co-occurring word, or the object situated therein. Thus, the cognition is: "a place not being the locus of the property of being a village (*grāmatva*) which is related to the village," or "the object situated therein."
In the expressions "apa hareḥ" (away from Hari) and "pari hareḥ" (around/beyond Hari), the words *apa* and *pari* have the same meaning as the word *ṛte* (except for).

In the expression "āmukteḥ saṃsāraḥ" (the cycle of existence until liberation), the sense of the prefix *āṅ* is that of a limit (*maryādā*). In this context, the limit is of two kinds: temporal and spatial. Temporal limit-hood consists in the state of not being the locus of that object denoted by the word co-occurring [with the limit], which exists at a time that is the locus of its own prior absence (*prāgabhāva*). Furthermore, the term "liberation" (*mukti*) refers to the prior absence of the time that is the locus of liberation. In that case, the meaning of *āṅ* is pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and the meaning of the fifth case suffix (*pañcamī*) is the state of being delimited (*nirupitatva*).

The relation of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) is construed with "saṃsāra" (the cycle of worldly existence) by means of the relation of being the locus (*āśrayatā*) qualified by the non-occurrence of its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) in that which is pervaded by it (*svavyāpya*). The resulting cognition is: "The cycle of worldly existence possesses a pervasion qualified by the non-occurrence of its own counter-positive, as determined by the prior absence of the time that is the locus of one's own liberation. Regarding the use of the word *antareṇa* to convey this same meaning, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is employed. This is in accordance with the rule: "The second case is used after *ubha*, *sarvatas*, and words such as *kārya*, *aviguṇa*, *paryādi*, when followed by a doubled suffix (*ḍit*), and it is also seen in other instances. [Note: The reading within the square brackets is from a manuscript source relevant to the present context.]

By this, the meaning is "the second. From the full moon of Kārttika until the full moon of Vaiśākha, as long as the cold is immeasurable. Here, the meaning of the word *yāvat* is pervasiveness (*vyāpakatvam*), and the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyārtha*) is being delimited (*nirupitatvam*). By the word *vaiśākhī*, there is indicated (*lakṣyate*) the time which is the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of Vaiśākha, which is co-located with the destruction (*adhvaṃsa*) of Kārttika; this is because of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the word *yāvat*, which has the sense of a limit (*maryādā*), with the word *kārtikī*.

Alternatively, by the term "Kārttikī," its destruction (*taddhvaṃsa*) is indicated. Its connection occurs with the time that is the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of Vaiśākhī, through the relation of being its substratum (*āśrayatā*). Consequently, there is no fault even if cold is absent during the months preceding Kārttikī—which are the loci of the prior non-existence of Vaiśākhī—even though such absence exists.

Pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) consists in possessing a property that is not a delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) for the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence residing in a time that belongs to the same class as the time of its own counter-positive within its own locus. Here, "self" (*sva*) refers to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of Vaiśākhī; and "belonging to the same class" (*sājātya*) is by way of the category of "lunar-day-ness" (*tithitva*) and so forth, which is the deliminator of the nature of the object denoted by the term "counter-positive. Consequently, there is no fault even if coldness is absent from certain staffs or other objects that serve as the locus of the prior non-existence.

In passages such as "Having begun [the rite], one should worship until that tenth day," the *tithi* (lunar day) is indeed a specific, indivisible portion of time, and not a mere accumulation of actions; for it is impossible for acts such as worship to occur over such an extent of time. Furthermore, the object denoted by the word expressing the limit (*avadhi*) co-occurring with the term "as long as" (*yāvat*)—which serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the "extent" (*yāvatva*) and is a pervader (*vyāpaka*)—is presented precisely in its own form, due to the force of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Consequently, there is no loss of pervasiveness even when including future or past Vaiśākhas and so forth.

Pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is construed with "cold" (*śīta*) by virtue of being a substratum (*āśrayatā*) qualified by the state of occurring at a locus where the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of something occurs, provided that such non-existence has a pervadedness (*vyāpyatā*) defined by itself.

And thus, the understanding is that [the term "until"] has as its delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*) the property of not occurring in that which is the counter-positive of a prior absence residing in itself, as determined by a time that is the locus of the prior absence of Vaiśākhī, which is co-locative with the destruction of Kārtikī. Furthermore, the state of being a spatial limit (*deśagatamaryādātva*) consists in not being the locus of those things that reside in the space intermediate between the referent of the word "limit" (*avadhi*) co-occurring with it and another referent. For example, in such cases as "He comes from Prayāga as far as Kāśī. Here, by the word "Kāśī," the space intermediate between Prayāga and Kāśī is indicated (*lakṣyate*).
The word "Prayāga" serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

Alternatively, the term *prayāga* indicates the region to its north, and the term *kāśī* indicates the region to its east; the meaning of "pervasion" (*vyāpakatvam*) is "as far as. Its connection with the act of coming occurs through being a locus characterized by the absence of occurrence in any location other than those [regions] that are pervaded by it (the regions indicated). Thus, the result is: "The act of coming is such that it pervades the regions to the north of Prayāga and to the east of Kāśī, and it does not occur in any location other than those."

In the expression "Brahman up to the end" (*ā sakalāt brahma*), the prefix *ā* signifies inclusion (*abhividhi*). The resulting cognition is that Brahman is all-pervasive (*sakalatva-vyāpaka*). This [inclusion] is also of two kinds: temporal (*kālika*) and spatial (*daiśika*). Regarding the first, an example is: "The cold lasts until the month of Caitra from the month of Kārttika. Here, what is conveyed regarding the cold is its pervasiveness over the time that is the substratum of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the time subsequent to Caitra, which itself is the substratum of the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of Kārttika. By the word "Caitra," the time that is the substratum of the prior non-existence of the time subsequent to Caitra—which is the substratum of the destruction of Kārttika—is indicated, as explained previously. The meaning of "until" (*yāvat*) is pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*).

An example of the latter [type of *yāvat*] is: "It has rained as far as Pāṭalīputra from Kāśī. [Note: The form *vṛṣṭo* is an imitation [of the original], and therefore it is not incorrect. Here, there is the state of pervading the western region having Kāśī as its limit and the eastern region having Pāṭalīputra as its limit. By the word *yāvat*, that which is qualified by non-occurrence in the eastern region of Pāṭalīputra and qualified by non-occurrence in the western region of Kāśī is made known. The method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is to be inferred in the manner previously stated; such is the direction [of the analysis].

In the expression *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇāt prati*, the meaning of *prati* is "possessing similarity"; the cognition is that [Pradyumna] possesses a similarity whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is Kṛṣṇa. In the expression *tilebhyaḥ prati yacchati māṣān*, the meaning of the verb *yacchati* as co-occurring with *prati* is "giving back after having first taken. Thus, the cognition is that there is a giving back of the beans (*māṣa*), which have them as their object, preceded by a taking that has the sesame seeds (*tila*) as its relation.

"Bound because of a hundred"—here, the meaning of the ablative case is the cause (*hetu*). The understanding is that there is an action of binding caused by a hundred. By this, examples such as "bound because of cowardice" (*jāḍyād baddhaḥ*) and "possessing fire because of smoke" (*dhūmād agnimān*) are explained. [Note: Here, the intention of the author of the present work is that the ablative is used because the relation of produced and producer residing in the hundred is superimposed upon the object. Thus, even though smoke and the like do not possess the status of being a producer of fire, the anomaly of the ablative case is removed. Accordingly, in this view, the cognition is: "fire caused by smoke."]

The assertion that even an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is included by the word "cause" (*hetu*) is utterly inconsistent; for the *Abhidhānakośa* establishes that the word "cause" has the meaning of "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa*), stating: "A cause is not a non-efficient cause, but a seed. Furthermore, in common usage, the word "indicator" is never employed in the sense of an efficient cause.

In the *Laghuśabdenduśekhara*, however, it is explained that "the word 'smoke' is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the sense of its own cognition, and the word 'possessing fire' is used figuratively in the sense of the object of its own cognition."

This is its intention: because the cognition of smoke itself is the cause for the cognition of that which possesses fire, the relation of cause and effect residing in the cognitions is superposed upon the object. In this view, the understanding is: "the mountain, which is the object of the cognition of fire caused by the cognition of smoke.
Between the two views mentioned previously, the position that the relation of produced and producer residing in the cognitions is superposed upon the object appears to be the more sound one.

The authors of the *Cintāmaṇi*, however, maintain that the word *vahni* (fire) is indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) of the cognition of fire, and the word *dhūma* (smoke) is indicative of the cognition of smoke; the meaning of the ablative case is causality (*hetutva*) in the form of being a generator. The causality, which is construed with the cognition of smoke—the primary referent—is connected to the cognition of fire (the referent of the word *vahni*) by way of the relation of "determinateness" (*nirūpakatā*). The possessive suffix (*matup*) signifies either the possessor of the objecthood (*viṣayatāvān*), or the objecthood itself (*viṣayatā*), or else the word *vahni* is indicative of the cognition of fire, and the possessive suffix signifies the locus (*āśrayatva*) as its meaning. Alternatively, they say that the word *vahni* is indicative of the fire as it is being cognized, and the possessive suffix signifies the conjoined (*saṃyogin*).

And thus, according to this view, the cognition is: "The mountain possesses a relation whose object is the cognition of fire, which has as its locus of being produced the generative capacity residing in the cognition of smoke.

However, the author of the *Dīdhiti* says: "The meaning of the ablative case [in 'dhūmāt'] is 'being made known by a cognition'; the word 'smoke' (*dhūma*) retains its primary sense; for this very reason, in sentences such as the *udāharaṇa*, it is shown that smoke alone is the means of proof (*gamaka*), and its purpose—such as the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—is demonstrated. The word 'fire' (*vahni*) also retains its primary sense; for this very reason, there is the expression of what is desired to be known (*jijñāsitābhidhāna*), because it is fire itself that is desired to be known, not the cognition of fire," so they say.

In this view, the cognition is: "Fire is that which is made known by the cognition of smoke. By words such as *dhūma* (smoke), the cognition thereof is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the expressions *pṛthak*, *vinā*, *nānā*, *rāmam*, *rāmāt*, or *rāmeṇa*—here, the meaning of the fifth, second, and third case endings is the relation consisting in being an instrument (*prayojakatva*). Whether separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is a quality (*guṇa*) or a difference (*bheda*) is another matter. *Vinā* and *nānā* have meanings identical to the word *ṛte*. In the expression *stokena* or *stokāt muktaḥ* ("released with little effort"), the third and fifth cases signify the instrumental sense (*karaṇa*). The substantive, such as *yatnena* (by effort), must be supplied. The resulting cognition is: "The object of release has as its instrument an effort non-different from a small degree."

Others, however, maintain that the word *stoka* refers to a property (*dharma*), for it is through the entry of this property that the linguistic usage "a small [quantity]" (*stoka*) applies to the substance. Furthermore, the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is connected to the meaning of the third case—the operation—by way of a mediated relation, namely, "residing in what resides in its own locus" (*svāśrayavṛttitva*). And the locus, which is the referent of the third case, is connected to the action by way of the relation "being produced by an operation residing in its own locus. This is what they say.

In the expression *grāmasya dūrāt*, *dūreṇa*, or *dūraṃ gataḥ* ("gone far from the village"), the third, fifth, and second case endings denote the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). The meaning of the word *dūra* is "residing in a distant location," while the meaning of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is "relation" (*sambandha*). Furthermore, this [meaning of] residing in a distant location is construed with the act of going by way of being its locus (*āśrayatā*). Nor does this contradict the grammatical rule that two nominal meanings are construed as identical (*abheda-anvaya*), for such a rule is accepted only regarding the construal of the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) of the cognitions produced by the nominal stems; moreover, this is justifiable in cases like the word *prāc* ("eastern"), which primarily denotes the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*). Others, however, say that the meaning is "that which resides in a distant location."

By this, the usage of *grāmasyāntikam*, *antikāt*, or *antikena* is explained. The meaning of *antika* (near) consists in its occurrence in a proximate location and so forth. Thus concludes the determination of the meanings of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-vibhakti*). Now follows the determination of the meanings of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*).

The meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is a relation (*sambandha*) in its nature as a relation. [Note: Here is the summary—by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*, the genitive is prescribed for a relation such as the state of owner and owned, which is distinct from the meanings of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). That relation is the meaning of the genitive both as "relation-ness" (*sambandhatva*) and in its specific forms. By the force of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), it is perceived sometimes in its specific form and sometimes as "relation-ness."]

Furthermore, the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is the relation of action and its factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*) as a specific type of relation. For this very reason, even though a garment may possess various relations such as being simultaneous [with Caitra], the expression "this is not Caitra's" is logically justified. Otherwise, since there would be an absence of Caitra’s relation to it and an absence of difference from that which possesses such a relation, the inappropriateness of that usage would be evident.

If, however, the meaning of the genitive case is the relation in its various specific forms, then there is no inconsistency in the usage "this is not Caitra’s," because the absence of the property delimited by being the owner (svatva) and so forth exists in clothes belonging to others. Precisely because it is denotable in those various specific forms, the *Mahābhāṣya* passage—"one hundred and one meanings of the genitive"—found under the rule "ṣaṣṭhī sthāne yogā," becomes consistent.

If, on the other hand, it were [denoted] solely as the generic property of relation (*sambandhatva*), then, due to the unity of the expressive power delimited by that generic property, the aforementioned *Bhāṣya* would be untenable.

From the second case onwards, however, the understanding of the relation between action and its factors occurs in the form of specific properties such as "objectness" (*karmatva*) and "actionness" (*kriyātva*), in accordance with experience. But in cases such as *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), there is an understanding of the action-factor relation in its specific form.

Regarding cases like *mātuḥ smarati*, the modern grammarians (*śābdika*) and logicians (*tārkika*) such as Miśra and others maintain that if one were to accept an understanding of the action-factor relation in its specific form, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*bādhaka*) of requiring a second case ending; therefore, they hold that the action-factor relation is understood solely as a "relation" (*sambandhatvena*).

The predecessors, however, maintain that here too, a relation—whether it be the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) or the state of being a cause (*nimittatva*)—rooted in the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), presents itself as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) either by way of a relation or by way of a qualifier itself. As Bhartṛhari has stated:
"A relation, distinct from the case-factors (*kāraka*), which is preceded by [the relation between] action and its factors, is expressed whether the action is explicitly mentioned or not."

In this view, every relation whatsoever is rooted in the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva). Even the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) in the expression "the king's man" is preceded by the relationship between action and its factors. Indeed, the Bhāṣya itself provides the authority for this point, stating: "For since the king becomes the master of the man by giving him wages. Thus, the Bhāṣya, which conveys the meaning that "since the king becomes the master of the man by giving him wages," is the very proof here.

For action indeed brings about a mutual relation between substances whose natures are already established, which otherwise would not possess such a relation and would be as if without support. They say that while in the case of "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*) action is explicitly heard, in cases such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), an unexpressed action such as giving (*dāna*) is inferred.

This is what must be understood here: in the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the king and so forth are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the relation, and the relation is a qualifier with respect to the man. The resulting cognition is "a man who possesses a connection with the king. Thus, although the relation of owner and owned resides in both [relata], the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is introduced after the word "king" alone—the denoter of the qualifier—and not after the word "man" and so forth, because of the requirement that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) must be predominant with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).

Although, according to the Bhāṣya view, the relation denoted by the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhyartha-sambandha) appears solely as a relational object (*saṃsargatayaiva*), nevertheless, since a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) is defined by both its relational object-ness (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*) and its qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*), its predominance—consisting in possessing an object-ness that defines the mode-ness—is indeed intact. However, this would not be possible if the genitive were applied after words such as *puruṣa*. Furthermore, because the qualificandum, such as *puruṣa*, must necessarily be either a *kāraka* or the meaning of a word expressing a *kāraka*, it is not "non-residual" (*aśeṣa*); therefore, the genitive does not apply from it.

In reality, however, due to the very nature of the power of words, the relation is perceived as being manifest (*udbhūtatayā*) in the qualifier alone; thus, the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arises from the word expressing the qualifier itself. As it was said by Hari:
"Although this [relation] is [inherently] present, it is distinguished among the qualifiers because they exist for the sake of another;
and while being denoted therein, it is also utilized for the sake of the principal."

The intention is as follows: in the view that does not accept non-difference (*abheda*) as a relation in its capacity as a mode (*prakāratayā*), because there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "the jar is not blue" (*anīlo ghaṭaḥ*), one must resort to [non-difference] as being accompanied by difference (*bhedasāhitya*). Since that which is accompanied by difference is necessarily a relation, and since the expectancy for that [relation] arises only in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the relation is perceived as manifest only there; thus, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs only there.

However, when the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is not in proximity to another word, there is no expectancy for a relation that would determine its status as a qualificand, precisely because it is self-contained (*svaniṣṭhatva*). Self-containment means appearing as the locus of the particularity (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of its own meaning, or possessing that state.

Even a relation that has partially entered the path of cognition through the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth when [the term] is subordinate—though it serves the purpose of the principal—is still [present], because a relation is "two-located" (*dviṣṭhatva*). This is according to the natural sense of the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50), as the ancients maintain.

But is this not incorrect, since by means of the genitive case, specific relations appear precisely in their respective forms? For this very reason, even when a relation such as conjunction exists, one says, "This garment does not belong to Caitra," with the intention of referring to a specific relation.

If it is argued that for this very reason the *bhāṣya* on the rule "ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā" [Pāṇini 1.1.46]—which states "there are one hundred and six meanings of the genitive," such as "immediately after" or "in proximity"—as well as the *bhāṣya* on the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" [Pāṇini 8.3.59]—which states "even a single genitive case is divided according to the difference of its objects"—are both consistent [with the view that the genitive has many meanings], then that is true; however, in the rule "ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe," the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to that which is other than what has been previously mentioned.

And that [denotation] occurs both as those respective forms—such as the relation of ownership (*svatva*) and so forth—and as the form of "relation-ness" (*sambandhatva*), as well as "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth; for it is established by experience that from words such as "object" (*karman*) there arises a cognition of the substratum precisely as a substratum, and it is for the sake of such a cognition in those respective forms that the rules for the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others are prescribed.

In that regard, since there is no subverting factor, according to the maxim that "a universal is never devoid of its particular instances," cognition occurs precisely in those respective forms. Sometimes, however, it is produced by the genitive case even as a relation, as in "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*), and so forth. They say that when there is cognition in those respective forms, because obstructing factors such as the accusative case are present, cognition occurs only as a relation.

However, some [hold that] because the remaining category (padārtha) has a nature other than what has been stated, and because it is appropriate for the limit (*avacchedaka*) and the limited (*avacchinna*) to be of the same genus (*sājātya*), the relation which is the meaning of the genitive case is simply another relatum (*dharmin*) in its capacity as a related entity. The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed with the relation—which is a part of the meaning of the suffix—by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). And the meaning of the suffix is construed by identity with the other category, which is the substratum (*anuyogin*).

Alternatively, [the meaning of the suffix] is the object that serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the relation. In this way, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed only through identity (*abheda*). Furthermore, that [meaning of the base] is construed with the meaning of the other word only through the relation of being the correlate (*anuyogitva*)—which is itself not mediated by anything else—that is characterized by the counter-correlation (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by its own delimitor (*svāvacchedaka*), due to the peculiarity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). And thus, the number denoted by the suffix is construed with the meaning of the suffix itself, just like [the meanings of] other case-endings.

Consequently, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is such that the cause for a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is the number denoted by a case-ending is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by that case-ending.

In your view, however, for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the number expressed by the genitive case-meaning (*ṣaṣṭhyarthasaṃkhyāprakārakaśābdabodha*), one would have to postulate yet another causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāvāntara*) wherein the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the base (*prakṛti*) is the cause. Nor can it be argued that the relation itself is what is construed with that [number], because this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of forms such as *rājñoḥ* (of two kings) when intending to refer to two relations belonging to a single king. Furthermore, regarding the verse of Harisvāmin, "The relation is indeed the power (*śakti*) itself," they explain that the word *sambandha* there ends in the suffix *ac* added after the class beginning with *arśas*.

Alternatively, regarding the view "or it is simply the capacity (*śakti*)," one should understand that in this other opinion, the relation itself is the meaning. Furthermore, that relation is also merely a qualifier (*prakāra*), because it is a word-meaning (*padārtha*). By this, the position that the capacity resides in [the property] such as "object-ness" (*karmatva*) is refuted; for in that case, there would be no distinction between the scope of the accusative and other cases versus the genitive. As for the view that the capacity resides in the substratum (*dharmin*), the proposed regulation—that the accusative occurs when the substratum is to be conveyed and the genitive when a property (*dharma*) is to be conveyed—is also rejected. This is because even if the capacity resides in the property, a regulation could still be possible: the accusative and others would apply when there is cognition by way of "object-ness-ness" (*karmatvatva*) and so on, whereas the genitive would apply when there is cognition by way of "relation-ness" (*sambandhatva*).

However, there is this distinction: according to the view that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the substratum (*dharmin*), when the intention is to express the substratum as being related, or when the intention is to express the mere attribute (*dharma*) through its difference [from the substratum], the genitive alone is used, because both are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). But according to the view that the expressive power resides in the attribute (*dharma*), it is only when the intention is to express the attribute as being related. Enough of this. And thus, in the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the understanding is: "the man possesses ownership as characterized by the king."

However, in the absence of a specific relation or intended meaning, the relation itself, as a relation, is the meaning of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*); thus, there is the cognition: "the person is related to the king" (*rājasambandhī puruṣaḥ*).
In cases such as "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*), the cognition is: "the agent of remembrance related to the mother.

In "he dwells for the sake of food" (*annasya hetor vasati*), the meaning of the genitive is "being produced" (*janyatva*); the cognition is that the dwelling possesses a state of being produced, which is not determined by a producer residing in the food that is non-different from the cause.

In the expression "to the south of the village," "in front of," or "above," the meaning of *dakṣiṇataḥ* and so forth is the state of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) of the southern region, the state of being the locus of the area in front of the village, and the state of being the locus of the upper region, respectively. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) signifies a relationship (*sambandha*). In the mantra: "I shall give the command for the fat of the oblation of the omentum of the goat for Agni," the genitive in *medasaḥ* expresses the object (*karman*), while the genitives in *chāgasya* and *vapāyāḥ* express the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) and the general relationship (*sambandha*), respectively. Thus, the understanding is: "The command is directed toward the fat, which is the oblation related to the omentum that constitutes a part of the goat."

In the expression *kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ* ("the action of Kṛṣṇa"), the agent (*kartṛ*) is the meaning of the genitive case; the understanding is that the action has Kṛṣṇa as its agent (*kṛṣṇakartṛkā kṛtiḥ*).

In the expression *jagataḥ kartā kṛṣṇaḥ* ("Kṛṣṇa is the creator of the world"), the object (*karman*) is the meaning of the genitive case; the understanding is that Kṛṣṇa is the locus of the activity conducive to the production of the world, which has the world as its object (*jagatkarmakotpattyanukūlavyāpārāśrayaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ*). [Note: Logicians (*tārkikāḥ*), however, hold that the meanings are agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*). The meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed there through the relation of inherence (*ādheyatā-sambandha*). Agency and so forth are construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through the relation of being the determiner (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*).]

They say that the understanding is as follows: "Kṛṣṇa is the possessor of an effort (kṛti) which is the specifier of the agency (kartṛtā) [in the act] of creating the world, and he is the possessor of an effort which is the specifier of the objectness (karmatā)—which consists in being the objective domain of the world's functioning.

As for the claim that there is a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) of the genitive case in the words "agent" and "object" [in the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ ṣaṣṭhī*], that is not correct; for since there exists a grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*) such as *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65] which teaches the primary denotative power (*śakti*), secondary indication is inappropriate. To say that this [rule] does not teach the primary denotative power is empty talk; otherwise, rules such as *śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī* would also fail to teach primary denotative power, and because of the traditional maxim of the elders that "there is no secondary indication in the case of nominal suffixes" (*suvibhaktau na lakṣaṇā*). This is the general direction [of the argument].

In expressions such as *rāhoḥ śiraḥ* ("the head of Rāhu"), however, the genitive case is justified by superimposing a distinction—namely, that this [head] is a member belonging to a single state, whereas the head [ordinarily] is associated with multiple states; this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ādyantavat*.
Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhakti*).
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the locative case (*saptamīvibhakti*).

The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the meaning of the seventh case (*saptamī*), according to the rule "the seventh case is used for the locus" (*adhikaraṇe saptamī*). And the rule "the locus is the substratum" (*ādhāro 'dhikaraṇam*, Pāṇini 1.4.45) provides the definition of locus-ness. In that context, because the section on *kārakas* is under discussion, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only the substratum of the action (*kriyā*) is understood. Since the direct substrata of the action—the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*)—are already designated by their own specific technical names (*saṃjñā*), it is the indirect substratum that is grasped here.

Nor should it be argued that those two [the agent and the object] themselves could serve as the locus through a mediated succession; for the status of being the "most desired" (*īpsitatamatva*)—which constitutes the primary objective (*mukhyoddeśyatva*) of the agent—is absent here, since this requires the possession of a result produced by the action of the agent conveyed by the verbal root. Furthermore, due to the force of the word *svatantra* (independent) in the rule defining the technical term "agent," the locus is not understood through a mediated succession in the sūtra for the designation of the agent. And such a mediated succession occurs only by way of the agent or the object.

Although, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), all case-factors (*kāraka*) are present through the action, nevertheless, by the force of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*), [grammatical] explanation, and experiential evidence (*anubhava*), only those two [the agent and the object] are grasped. And thus, it follows that the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) consists in being the substratum of the action by way of the agent and the object.

Nor should it be argued that, since the status of the object (*karmatā*) of the result has been previously established, it would be unavoidable for rice and the like—which are the substrata of the action by way of the result serving as the object—to be considered loci; for even the status of being the substratum of the result produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) serves as the basis for the technical designation of "object" (*karman*), and thus that [designation] precludes [the application of the term "locus"] to such things.

However, it is entirely impossible for rice (*taṇḍula*) and the like to be the substratum of an action by way of the agent (*kartṛ*), because the term "substratum" (*ādhāra*) intends to mean that the status of being an agent is mediated specifically through a relation that directly governs the occurrence [of the action], and because relations such as temporal ones are over-extended; thus, they are not accepted as governing the status of being a substratum in cases other than those involving the usage of time (*kāla*). In this context, when one intends to express that something is the substratum of an action by way of the agent and so forth, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used; when one intends to express that it is the direct substratum of the result (*phala*), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used.

For this very reason, both "he goes to the village" (*grāme gacchati*) and "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*) are correct. For this very reason, expressions such as "he touches the heart" (*hṛdayaṃ spṛśati*) and "touching the heart" (*hṛdispṛk*) are consistent with grammatical usage. Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence that Devadatta would be considered the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in sentences like "Devadatta is cooking" (*devadattaḥ pacati bhavati*), on the grounds that one intends to express his being the substratum of existence by way of the act of cooking; for the terms "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) refer only to those [factors] distinct from the action itself, according to the maxim of the curd and Kauṇḍinya (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*). Therefore, there is no fault.

Others, however, say that if it were stated as a reality, it would result in the acceptance of an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); otherwise, they say it is not so simply because it is not expressed. Furthermore, regarding the statement "there is no desire for liberation," there is no failure to establish its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). They say this is because the desire conveyed by the suffix is already established, and thus the explanation holds by taking that [established desire] as the basis.

As for the argument that in cases such as *pacati bhavati* ("he becomes cooking"), since the intention is to express the state of being the locus of existence (*bhavana*) by means of the act of cooking (*pāka*), the application of the term "agent" (*kartṛtva*) alone occurs because its connection to the cooking is more immediate (*antaraṅga*); and in cases such as *mokṣe icchāsti* ("there is a desire for liberation"), since the intention is to express the connection with the verb "to exist" (*asti*) through a desire for an established object (*siddha*) denoted by the suffix, it is easy to justify [the desire] as the "locus" (*adhikaraṇatva*). For the application of "object" (*karmatva*) does not occur by taking that [desire] as the basis, because it is not an action (*akriyatvāt*). However, when the intention is to express the connection there through the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), then because it is an action, the genitive case applies by virtue of it being an "object," just as in the case of the sixth case. That is not correct.

In reality, even if the action (*kriyā*) is construed with [the agent] through a relationship mediated by the agent, there is no evidence for its construction with the meaning conveyed by the word denoting the agent; thus, factors such as "inner-ness" (*antaraṅgatva*) remain unavoidable. Therefore, the truth is simply this: the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs when the meaning of the word *icchā* (desire) is construed [with the object], whereas the locative case (*saptamī*) occurs when it is construed with the action through a relationship mediated by that [desire].

If it is asked, "Since the meaning of case-terminations denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), object (*karman*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is merely their substratum (*āśrayamātra*), from what does their distinction arise?", understand that it is due to the difference in the relatum (*nirūpaka*), the difference in the relation (*sambandha*), and because each specific case-ending conveys only that which is qualified by its respective technical designation (*saṃjñā*). In that regard, for the agent, the relatum is the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root; for the object, it is the fruit (*phala*) of that [operation]; and the relation is simply the state of being contained (*ādheyatā*).

It should be understood that there is a distinction in the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*): in the case of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the relation is "being produced by its own operation," whereas in the case of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it is "having its agent residing therein," and so forth.

In this context, the locus (*adhāra*) is threefold: the contiguous (*aupaśleṣika*), the objective (*vaiṣayika*), and the pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*). Among these, the first is that which is connected to the agent or the object through relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*); the second is that which is connected to them through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*); and the third is that which is connected through the relation of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*). In the example "He sleeps on a mat" (*kaṭe śete*), the understanding is that the act of sleeping resides on the mat by virtue of the relation of being the action of an agent residing therein (*svavṛttikartṛkatvasambandha*).

In the example "There is a desire for liberation" (*mokṣe icchāsti*), the understanding is that existence has desire as its agent, residing in liberation by virtue of the relation of being the action of an agent whose object is itself (*svaviṣayakartṛkatvasambandha*).

In the case of "The Self exists in everything," the understanding is that existence has the Self as its agent, occurring in all things through the relation of being the agent which pervades its own locus. In expressions such as "The tree at the root is conjoined with the monkey" or "it exists," when there is a co-utterance with an action whose agent possesses a non-pervasive property, the action is construed with the verb through the relation of having as its agent that which is the locus of the property delimited by itself and residing in itself; this is due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Even where a verbal form for the action is not heard, it must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*); such is the general direction.

In the expression *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("one who has studied grammar"), the suffix *kta* is not used in the sense of the object (*karman*). If it were so, since the object would already be expressed, the locative case would not occur according to the rule "an addition regarding the object of a word ending in *kta* when followed by *in*" (*ktasyenviṣayasya karmaṇyupasaṃkhyānam*). Therefore, the suffix *kta* is applied here by the rule "the neuter in the sense of the abstract state" (*napuṃsake bhāve*), because that suffix applies even to transitive verbs.

Even according to the view that its application occurs only to intransitive roots (*akarmaka*), since the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarmakatva*), the suffix *kta* is first applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Subsequently, even when a connection with an object arises, there is no evidence for the revocation of the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) that has already occurred based on the internal factor (*antaraṅga*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the usage "pacyate taṇḍulaṃ devadattena" (the rice is cooked by Devadatta), because the intention to express [the object] exists precisely in accordance with actual usage; otherwise, under the position that "first the verbal root is joined with its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)," the form "vijayati" would result in the use of the *parasmaipada* ending.

In the analysis (vigraha) "adhītam anena" ("this has been studied by him"), the suffix *ini* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.88 (*iṣṭādibhyaśca*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). It should be understood that, as in examples such as "he has studied grammar" (*adhītavān vyākaraṇam*), the relation of a case-factor (*kāraka*) can occur even with respect to a subordinate action (*guṇībhūtakriyā*). The locative case here signifies the object (*karman*). Thus, the cognition is: "the agent of the act of studying whose object is grammar.

If it is argued that since the verb "exists" (*asti*) must necessarily be supplied, the locative case is established here because [grammar] is the locus of the operation (*vyāpāra*) by way of the agent, we say no; for this [supplying of the verb] is necessary specifically to prevent the accusative case from applying when [grammar] is construed with the act of studying, on the grounds that it is the object (*karmatvena*).

In expressions such as *carmaṇi dvīpinam* ("for the sake of the skin, a leopard"), the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the locative case. The understanding occurs in the manner: "the act of killing, which has the leopard as its object, results in the acquisition of the skin. It should be understood that the skin possesses the status of being the fruit because the action of killing is dependent upon a desire directed toward obtaining it.

In the expression *goṣu duhyamānāsu* ("while the cows are being milked"), the locative is used by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). The meaning of that rule is: when one action is indicated by another action, the locative case is used after the word expressing the indicating action.

[Objection: Is it not observed that the relationship between the signified and the signifier is based on repeated observation, as in the case of fire and smoke? Therefore, the appropriate example for this would be such as "when the sun has risen, darkness has perished," and not this one—"he arrived while the cows were being milked"—since [in the latter case] the time is not repeatedly observed. [Reply: No; for there is no impairment of its status as a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator), since an action whose place and time are already known serves to delimit another action whose place and time are not yet known.

Others, however, state that this specific time is the substratum for this particular instance of going because it is the substratum for the *godohana* [water-pot] used for this [sacrifice]; they assert its status as a prover by way of a negative inference (*vyatireki-anumāna*), according to the principle: "Wherever there is an absence of being the substratum for this going, there is an absence of being the substratum for this *godohana*."

It should be understood that "indicative-ness" (*jñāpakatva*) is indeed the cause for the application of this grammatical treatise, as it is made known by the employment of specific words; it does not depend on the necessity of its apprehension through some other means of knowledge (*māna*). In this context, the example of location (*deśa*) is found in such instances as "when a quality exists, substantiality exists" (*sati guṇe dravyatvam asti*). And "indicative-ness" is the meaning of the locative case; there, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with [the indicator] through a relation mediated by the action that serves as the cause for its own application.

For this very reason, its connection is only with the action (*kriyā*), because it conforms to the meaning of the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.37), which states that the locative case is used for that which possesses a "being made known" (*jñāpyatva*)—as defined by the "making known-ness" (*jñāpakatā*) residing in another action—through a relationship mediated by the action itself.

And thus, [the cow] is the substratum of going, possessing a "being made known-ness" as defined by the "making known-ness" residing in the cow who is the object of the present act of milking, through the relationship of being the substratum of the action whose own substratum is [the cow].

This is the understanding [of the rule]. In examples such as "The guest has arrived while the cows are about to be milked," one should understand that even a future milking, when it has ascended to the level of cognition (*buddhi*), serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In that case, the cognition of the guest's arrival as being prior in time to the future milking is derived from the meaning of the sentence (*ārtha*).

Alternatively, by virtue of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the sense of the suffix *sat* (present participle), which consists in being a "cognizer" (*jñāpaka*), is construed through the relation of "being cognized" (*jñāpyatā*) as determined by its own selfhood (*svanirūpita*) and as co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the occurrence at a prior time (*pūrvakālavṛttitva*). For this very reason, they say that in cases such as "when water is drunk, thirst is quenched," even the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) appears as a relation when used in conjunction with a past-tense form of the root *kṛ*.

As for the claim that the meaning of this locative case is the occurrence of the present time and so forth in relation to the action that serves as the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the nominal stem ending in a *kṛt* suffix; and that, consequently, the cognition in such cases takes the form "he has arrived at the time related to the milking of the cow, which is the object of the present milking non-different from the cow"—that is not correct. Why? Because it contradicts the natural intent (*svarasa*) of the Sūtra, and because it would entail the postulation of an infinite number of linguistic powers (*śakti*), since [the locative] would have to express the occurrence of a subsequent time and so forth in examples such as *goṣu dugdhāsu* ("when the cows have been milked"). This is the general direction of the argument.

Nor should it be argued that in such cases as "the milking has come [for] the cows" (*gavām dohe āgataḥ*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the locative case not arising after the word *doha* (milking), while it would arise after the word *go* (cow). This is because, by supplying the word *satī* ("being"), the existence (*sattā*) of the agent of milking remains intact as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). By this, expressions such as "one should perform the *nāndīmukha* rite at a wedding" (*vivāhe nāndīmukhaṃ kuryāt*) are also explained, through the supply of the word *kariṣyamāṇe* ("when about to be performed"). By this, passages such as "one should bathe during an eclipse of Rāhu" and "his actions perish when He, the higher and the lower, is seen," are likewise explained, through the supply of the word *satī*.

The status of lunar eclipses and the like as causal conditions (*nimitta*) follows from the logical principle of the co-utterance of the established and the to-be-established; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding the word *kṣīyante* ("are destroyed"), it should be understood that because the *ya*-affix is used in the sense of a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*), the very meaning of the action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) is superimposed upon the object itself. This should likewise be understood in the case of: "The knot of the heart is split asunder; all doubts are severed."

Others, however, maintain that this Sūtra applies only where there is the employment of words for the purpose of establishing the connection with a specific time and so forth for an object already established by other means of knowledge (*māna*), as is evident from the natural sense of the Sūtra and its Bhāṣya. Consequently, cases such as "the *nāndīmukha* [rite] at a wedding" or "during an eclipse of Rāhu" are not examples of this; rather, in those instances, the word "wedding" indicates the time preceding it, and the word "eclipse of Rāhu" indicates the time during which it occurs, so that the locative case is used in the sense of a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*).
They further state that the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) follows by the very logic already stated.

In the expression “*rudati rudato vā prāvrājīt*” (“he went forth [into homelessness] while [his son] was weeping, or as he was weeping”), the meaning of the genitive and locative cases is that of being a *jñāpaka* (an indicator). The indicated (*lakṣya*) meaning of the verbal root is the act of going forth qualified by disregard (*anādara*). Here too, the genitive and locative cases serve to indicate the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-grāhika*). Furthermore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), this disregard refers specifically to the son and others. The qualification [of the act of going forth] is established through both coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and posteriority in time. Thus, the resulting cognition is: “the act of going forth, qualified by disregard, which is indicated by the son and others who are the agents of weeping.”

Regarding the statement, "Among men, or among men, the twice-born is the best," the genitive and locative cases are used by the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41). According to the authors of the Vṛtti, the meaning of that rule is: "Since selection (*nirdhāraṇa*)—the separation of one part from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*saṃjñā*)—occurs from [a whole], therefore the genitive and locative cases are used. In this context, within the phrase "by means of genus, quality, action, or name," the word "of a qualified [whole]" (*viśiṣṭasya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis; or else, the third case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

Separation (*pṛthakkaraṇa*) consists in making something the object of a cognition whose qualifier is the possession of a property excluded from what is other than itself. The ablative case in *yataḥ* connects with the exclusion (*vyāvṛttatva*) that constitutes the factor of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Thus, it follows that the sixth and seventh cases [respectively] signify that which possesses a property excluded from whatever is delimited by a property other than itself, as characterized by a genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

Why is the word *yataḥ* used? It is so that a case-ending (*vibhakti*) might not arise from that which—being qualified by genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is the locus for the communication of a property (*dharma*) excluded from others. Nor is it appropriate for the ending to arise from the qualifier alone, as in the case of the genitive; for there is the possibility of an exception even to the nominative, as in the rule "from words meaning 'far' or 'near'" (Pāṇini 2.3.35).

Furthermore, in examples such as *narāṇāṃ kṣatriyasya śauryam* ("the bravery of the Kṣatriya among men"), the Kṣatriya possesses the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). In cases such as *asti ca narāṇāṃ vipraḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* ("there is a Brāhmaṇa who is the best among men"), there is a cognition of one qualified by Brāhmaṇahood as possessing the quality of excellence, which excludes others such as non-Brāhmaṇas. Even in cases such as *narebhyo rākṣasaḥ krūraḥ* ("the Rākṣasa is more cruel than men"), where there is an intention to express the state of being extremely cruel—excluded from others such as men—with respect to one qualified by Rākṣasahood, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and locative (*saptamī*) case endings do not apply; for the ablative (*pañcamī*) is prescribed by the subsequent rule, "The fifth [case ending occurs] when there is distinction" (*pañcamo vibhakteḥ*), which serves as an exception (*apavāda*).
