Furthermore, the relation termed "exclusion" (*vyāvṛttatva*) is the meaning of the ablative case used for selection (*nirdhāraṇavibhakti*). Exclusion, moreover, is the state of not being the counter-positive of the absence of that which is delimited by the delimitor of the property to be predicated (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*). By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from taking the absence of "one-ness" delimited by "duality" and so forth. And this [exclusion] connects with the delimitor of the property to be predicated in cases where it is co-referential with the predicate through identity; however, in cases where it connects through difference, it connects with the predicate itself, due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

And in the case of a negative (abhāva), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), specifically by way of the relation of being located (*ādheyatā*) as determined by the locus (*ādhāratā*) delimited by its own delimitor (*svāvacchedaka*), which is itself qualified by a difference (*bheda*) delimited by "being a Brahmin" (*vipratva*) and so forth, due to the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); for otherwise, the absence of excellence (*śreṣṭhatvābhāva*) related merely by the relation of being located would be contradicted in respect to that which is delimited by "humanity" (*naratva*).

Since being the locus delimited by its own delimitor (*svāvacchedakāvacchinnādhāratva*) and so forth function as relations, the expression "this cow of the cows is rich in milk" (*gavāmiyaṃ sampannakṣīrā*) is not used; rather, the expression "among these cows, this one is rich in milk" (*etāsāṃ gavāmiyaṃ sampannakṣīrā*) alone is used. In that case, because of the qualification "distinguished by the difference from those delimited by Brahminhood (*vipratva*), etc. through the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the expression "the dewlap-bearing [cow] among cows is rich in milk" (*gavāṃ sāsnāvatī sampannakṣīrā*) is not used. Furthermore, because the predicate (*vidheya*) is construed with the delimiter of the subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), the expression "the black [cow] among animals is rich in milk" (*paśūnāṃ kṛṣṇā sampannakṣīrā*) is not used.

And thus, the cognition occurs in the following sequence: "The Brāhmaṇa is distinct from that which possesses excellence which is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in men by means of such a relation. In the expression "Bravery among men resides in the Kṣatriya," the cognition is: "There exists a presence residing in the Kṣatriya, which is the agent of bravery that is the counter-positive of an absence residing in men by means of such a relation. The plural number in "nṛṇām" (of men) is used with the intention of emphasizing the distinction between the individual parts; however, it should be understood that the singular number may also be used when the distinction between the parts is intended to be concealed.
It is for this very reason that the *Gītā* passage, "The dual [is superior] to the collective," is consistent.

Although the locative case is established when one intends to express the cow-herd as the locus (*ādhāra*), and the genitive case is established when one intends to express the relationship between part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*), it is more appropriate to state that very same case-meaning [the relation of inherence] in accordance with the parsimony (*lāghava*) of not having to prescribe either of the two alternative cases.

As for the cognition of the absence of the quality of "having much milk" in cows other than Kṛṣṇa and so forth, this is merely a matter of inference (*māna*), just as when it is said, "Devadatta sees with his left eye," it is understood that he does not see with his right.

For this very reason, in a sentence containing a locative of locus (*adhāra-saptamī*), such as "the black cow existing in the herd is one that yields much milk," the cognition of that [relation] is consistent; nevertheless, because it is impossible to state this type [of relation] in the examples for the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* [Pāṇini 2.3.42], which is an exception to this, and because the aforementioned type is indispensable, we have adopted this very same method for the sake of uniformity with that [rule], and because, in cases such as "Puruṣottama," there is an absence of semantic expectancy (*sāmarthya*) established by experience.

Furthermore, [this view] would result in the impossibility of forming compounds and would render the statement that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule prescribing the ablative case (*pañcamī*) inconsistent; moreover, even for me, there exists the status of a restatement (*anuvādatva*) regarding the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). As for the phrase "she who exists in the herd of cows" (*gomaṇḍale vartamānā yā*), the understanding arises only by supplying the word *gavām* (of cows) ending in the locative case used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa-vibhakti*). Or, let it be so in some instances, but they say there is no rule that it must always be so everywhere.

If it is objected that in such cases as "Water is viscous because it is different from fire," there is no possibility of determination (*nirdhāraṇa*)—since water and earth distinct from water are unestablished, and since the property of being the counter-positive of an absence residing in both water and earth is contradicted in respect to viscosity—the answer is no; for even there, the difference from water is not contradicted in respect to that which is delimited by the coexistence (*sāhitya*) pervading both, and the property of being the counter-positive of an absence residing in what is so delimited is likewise not contradicted in respect to viscosity.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, because the property of being delimited by a co-occurrence (sāhitya) pervading both exists in the water, the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* would indeed apply; for since the non-difference (*abheda*) of the substratum of the co-occurrence pervading both also exists [in the water], that [rule] does not apply.

By this, the usage of the Bhāṣya—such as "Among the inhabitants of Sāṃkāśya and the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra, the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra are the most handsome"—is explained. However, in cases such as "Among men, the twice-born is the best," they say that the connection is expressed by the combination of the indeclinable *madhye* and the case ending, just as in the case of the vocative in expressions like "O Caitra! [where the connection between the person and the address is conveyed by the combination of the word and the case ending].

In the expression "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed by the rule *pañcamī vibhakte*. For in that context, "vibhakta" means "divided" or "distinguished. The phrase "and where there is selection (*nirddhāraṇam*)" is understood to follow from the previous rule. Selection occurs where there is a distinction in one respect between that which serves as the basis of selection (*nirddhāraṇāvadhi*) and that which is being selected (*nirdhāryamāṇa*), even though they are non-different in some other respect.

Just as in the example "the Brahmin is the best among men," there is a distinction [of the best] from that which is non-distinct in its nature as a man; so too, since distinction exists in the case of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), by virtue of the force of the mention of the distinct case-ending, this [rule] applies only where there is indeed distinction and not non-distinction through any assumed form. Thus, the meaning of the sutra is: the ablative case occurs when there is the communication of something qualified by a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which possesses a property excluded from others (its own and those of the rest), and which bears a distinction relative to the substratum of the delimitor of the limit of selection.

In cases such as "Among the inhabitants of Sāṃkāśya and the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra, the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra are the most handsome," although there exists a difference from the Sāṃkāśyakas—who serve as the limit of the selection (*nirdhāraṇāvadhi*)—among the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra who are being selected, there is no fault because there is no actual difference [between the selected and the limit]; for there also exists a non-difference (*abheda*) with respect to the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra, which is the substratum of the co-existence (*sāhitya*) that delimits the state of being the limit of the selection. Thus, since difference itself is absent, there is no defect.

However, being a resident of Sāṃkāśya (*sāṃkāśyakatva*) is not the delimitor of the basis for exclusion (*nirddhāraṇāvadhitāvacchedaka*), because it would result in the redundancy of the word *pāṭaliputraka*. Here, the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is simply "exclusion" (*vyāvṛttitva*). The resulting cognition is: "The inhabitants of Mathurā possess greater wealth than those excluded from being inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra."

The Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*), however, having recognized the similarity between the people of Sāṃkāśya and those of Pāṭaliputra in terms of their beauty, employs this expression: "The people of Pāṭaliputra are more beautiful than the people of Sāṃkāśya. In that case, since there is the perception of a separation consisting in the absence of a relationship created by cognition, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is established precisely as the ablative (*apādāna*). Here, the word "separated" (*vibhaktāḥ*) is to be supplied; the understanding is: "The people of Pāṭaliputra, possessing a separation relative to the people of Sāṃkāśya, are more beautiful."

In this context, the relation that serves as the counter-correlate to the separation (*viśleṣa*) is precisely the state of having a common substratum in a single attribute. And the cause of that separation is precisely the state of being more beautiful. This is universally accepted because, once that [superiority] is perceived, the perception of beauty belonging to the same class [as the object of comparison] no longer arises due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

In cases such as *gavāṃ kṛṣṇā* ("the black one among cows"), however, there is no cognition of separation; for even when the fact of possessing abundant milk is known, the cognition of its being a cow does not cease. Regarding the examples of this sūtra, there is no intention to express a connection between the meanings of nouns (*nāmārtha*) without a connection to an action (*kriyānvaya*), because such a relation is not denoted. Therefore, there is no contingency of using the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). In this view, since the exclusion of those from Sāṃkāśya is understood by implication (*ārtha*) from the quality of being more handsome, they have rejected this sūtra.

In the usage *pāṭaliputrakamādhurāv ādyapaṇḍitau* ("The first scholar is from Pāṭaliputra and the other from Mathurā"), the ablative case does not occur at all; this is the general direction [of the analysis]. Regarding the expressions *mūlenāvāhayed devīm śravaṇena visarjayet* ("One should invoke the Goddess under Mūla; one should dismiss her under Śravaṇa") and *mūle śravaṇe vā*, the words *mūla* and *śravaṇa* indicate the time conjoined with those respective lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). The meaning of the third and seventh cases here is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The understanding proceeds in this manner: "The invocation has as its object the Goddess and has as its locus the time conjoined with the Mūla lunar mansion," and so forth.

"He will eat two days from today," or "He will eat after two days. Here, the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is the state of occurring in a time immediately subsequent to itself. The second [meaning], namely the state of being immediate to the time expressed by the coreferential term (*samabhivyāhṛtakāla*), is a qualifier of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). The first, however, is its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), serving as a qualifier of the action (*kriyā*) due to the diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Therefore, the meaning is: the locus of that eating which occurs at a time two days subsequent to this day, following an eating whose locus was this very day.

In the sentence, "Standing here, he should pierce the target at a distance of one *krośa*," the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is both the state of being located in a space immediately following [the speaker] and the state of being located in another space mentioned in conjunction [with it]. The syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is as before. The resulting cognition is: "The act of piercing has as its agent a person who is the locus of staying in this place, and has as its object a target situated in a *krośa* interval immediately following this place. Here, the case-ending is prescribed by the rule *saptamī-pañcamyau kārakamadhye* (Pāṇini 2.3.7). In that rule, by the word "kāraka" (factor of action),...

The meaning of that power (*śakti*) is said to consist of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) and so forth. Regarding the two powers, the meaning of the rule is that the seventh and fifth case endings are used for those [powers] which are time (*kāla*) and path (*adhvan*). However, some say that the meaning is simply "occurring in the time immediately following" [the first power], while in the subsequent case it is simply "occurring in the space immediately following" [the first power]; they further claim that the state of being situated between the two powers is a factual basis (*vastusannimitta*) for time and path.

In the examples *adhibhuvi rāmaḥ* ("Rāma is over the earth") and *adhirāme bhūḥ* ("the earth is over Rāma"), the cognition is that Rāma possesses ownership (*svāmitva*) as defined by the earth, and the earth possesses property (*svatva*) as defined by Rāma.

Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the seventh case-ending (*saptamī-vibhakti*). Now follows the determination regarding the intention or non-intention of expressing number (*saṅkhyā-vivakṣā-avivakṣā-nirṇaya*). The meaning of these *sup* (nominal) suffixes is also number—specifically singularity, duality, and plurality—either by way of their formal character as singular, dual, and plural endings, or by way of those respective meanings themselves. This is evident from the natural sense of the rules: "The dual and singular endings are used for one thing" (*dravyekayoḥ dvivacanaikavacane*) and "The plural ending is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) [Pāṇini 1.4.22]. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "The meanings of the *sup* suffixes are the object and so forth, as well as number; and the same applies to the *tiṅ* (verbal) suffixes."

It should be understood that here too, the word "api" (also) includes number (*saṃkhyā*), and later on, the word "ca" (and) includes the object (*karman*) and so forth. In that regard, according to the view that the meanings [of the suffixes] are the object and so forth, number is construed only with the meaning of the suffix. However, according to the view that the meaning of the suffix is "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth, it is construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); in that case, in some instances it is construed with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the base-meaning, and in others it is construed with the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the base-meaning.

For this very reason, the singular number in the sentence "the rice has ripened" (*sampanno vrīhiḥ*)—which intends multiple grains of rice—is appropriate; for there, the word is connected either to the universal *vrīhitva* (rice-ness) through that [individual] as its locus, or else it is connected directly to the meaning of the base itself through a mediated relation consisting in being the locus of its own locus. It is with this very intention that the ancient masters proclaimed: "The singular number is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*)."

For this very reason, even when used in co-utterance with the plural form "the Vedas" (*vedāḥ*) as in "the Vedas are a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam*), the singular number is employed because it is construed with the delimitor of the general property (*prakāratāvacchedaka*)—namely, the nature of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*). The result of this, however, is simply to establish that all [Vedas] belong to the same class of means of valid cognition.

In cases such as "a hundred Brahmins" (*śataṃ brāhmaṇāḥ*), however, the singular number is used solely with the intention of denoting the unity of the collection, based on the authority of the *Kośa* which states, "The numbers twenty and so forth always [denote] singularity. It never denotes plurality based on each individual member; here, the number is construed with the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*) due to the very nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*). In other instances, however, the usage is determined according to conventional practice; therefore, one should not raise objections such as "the pots are blue" (*ghaṭā nīlaḥ*).

For this very reason, the usage is established as "Agni and Soma are the deities" and "The ancestors are the deities. They say that in the first case, because the intention is to convey the status of a single deity, the singular number alone is used; whereas in the second case, because the intention is to convey each one as distinct, the plural number alone is used. However, in cases such as *dārāḥ* ("wife"), because the plurality of the parts is superimposed upon the whole (*avayavin*), the plural-ending form is used even when referring to a single individual.

Furthermore, in those cases, the case-ending (vibhakti) has as its basis only the plurality that is superimposed [upon the single object], and not even the singularity inherent in the object itself, according to the authority of the *kośa* and other sources. However, where the *kośa* and such authorities are indifferent, one may proceed according to usage as desired.
By this, usages such as "the teachers say" (*ācāryāḥ kathayanti*) and "the gurus have arrived" (*gurava āgatāḥ*), even when referring to a single individual, are justified.

As for the claim that, through a non-abandoning indication (*ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā*), words such as *dāra* (wife) denote individuals qualified by various attributes, and thus the number [denoted by the suffix] conjoins with the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*)—that is not correct; for it would result in the plural suffix following such a word being incoherent, since it would be directed toward a primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*). If, however, it is argued that there is no usage whatsoever of such words with only the primary meaning except through conventional indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), then let there simply be a direct denotative power (*śakti*) in that form; what is the use of indication? Furthermore, it should be understood that lexicons and the like serve to indicate the intention (*tātparya*) precisely regarding such a denotative power.

As for the claim that in such cases plural endings and so forth are used merely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), that too is not correct, because there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) to that effect. Furthermore, even in your own view, since there is no evidence for the constant presence of superimposition (*āropa*), it would follow that when such superimposition is absent, one should employ the singular ending; however, this is not the case, because we accept a fixed superimposition based on the authority of lexicons (*kośa*) and the like, and because we accept that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the object as qualified by various attributes.

However, in the case of *aneya* ("to be brought"), because the certainty of unfitness (*ayogyatāniścaya*) does not act as an obstacle to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is an application of plurality (*bahutva*) even to a single individual. For this very reason, the experience of pain arising from being reviled and the like, as well as the experience of pleasure arising from poetry such as *rūpaka*, are logically consistent. Furthermore, regarding the rule "the plural suffix" (*bahuvacanam*, Pāṇini 1.4.21), its meaning is that the plural suffix occurs when there is a cognition characterized by plurality. As it has been said: "For a word indeed produces a cognition even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent. Thus, verbal cognition is necessarily *āhārya* (voluntary or superimposed).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Bring the wives" (*dārān ānaya*), the consequence that many [wives] would be brought is not to be urged as a fault, because only a cognition that is not overridden by a non-authoritative cognition (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*) that is not induced (*anāhārya*) functions as an instigator of action. However, when such an expression is used precisely with the intention of denoting a plurality residing in the individuals (*vyakti*), then indeed many are brought. They say that the determination of this [meaning] arises from the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) and so forth. As for the claim that in such cases there is merely the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) and no verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), that is not correct; for if this were the case everywhere, it would follow that verbal comprehension is entirely abolished. This is explained in detail elsewhere.
In connection with the topic of number, the intention or non-intention regarding the number of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) is now examined.

As for what the Mīmāṃsakas maintain—that in such cases as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the singularity is intended because it qualifies the predicate—this is as follows: Singularity, being constrained by the factor of action (*kāraka*) which is conveyed by the same suffix, is proximate to the nominal stem, and is primary; thus, disregarding the meaning of the nominal stem itself, it is understood as an auxiliary to the action. Consequently, it enters into a relationship with the specific action not provided by the sentence [but by the context], subsequently connecting with the animal through the sense of the object, according to the logic of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇādhikaraṇa*).

And thus, because singularity is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*), the sacrifice is performed with only a single animal qualified by that [singularity], and not with multiple animals. In this way, everything that qualifies the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is intended to be expressed. However, in cases such as "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), the singularity residing in the cup (*graha*), which is the objective (*uddeśya*), is not intended to be expressed; otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). To explain: in the injunction "The nine cups belong to Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyā navagrahāḥ*), the cleansing is enjoined with reference to the cups already established by that injunction.

In that context, if there were an intention to express singularity, the meaning would be "he cleanses the cup" and "that one [cup]. In this way, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by the multiplicity of the objects of reference (*uddeśya*) is quite evident. Furthermore, the accusative case in the word *graham* indicates the predominance of the cup, characterized by its being the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*). The same applies to singularity as well. Thus, if singularity were intended just like the essential nature of the cup itself, then—according to the principle that "an accessory (*guṇa*) is repeated for each principal (*pradhāna*)"—the accomplishment of the cleansing would apply to every cup; therefore, the intention to express singularity would be entirely futile.

If, however, the cups (*graha*) were subordinate (*guṇatva*) like the animal (*paśu*), then—since the primary act could be accomplished by any one of them and because it is illogical for the primary act to repeat itself for every subordinate—the number would be intended as a defining characteristic, just as in the case of the animal. Now, if it is argued that subordination here consists either in being a preparatory rite (*saṃskāraka*) or in being something to be prepared (*saṃskārya*), or that there is an injunction for the cleansing (*sammārga*) by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the cups qualified by singularity—just as there is an injunction for an animal qualified by singularity—even so, since each individual cup possesses singularity, the aforementioned contingency would indeed apply.

Nor should it be argued that there is an injunction for cleansing qualified by singularity, and that this qualification occurs through the relation of "having an action whose object is its own substratum"; for even so, in accordance with the predominance expressed by the accusative case, the principle that "the subordinate (guṇa) repeats with each principal (pradhāna)" would entail the application of the cleansing to every [cup]. Therefore, they say that the number residing in the objective (uddeśya) is indeed not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), just as, in the present case, the nature of being a cup (*grahatva*) is not intended to be significant.

That cannot be accepted by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), because in the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35], it is universally agreed that when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix characterized by having a *val*-initial letter is referred to (*anūdyate*) for the purpose of prescribing *iṭ*, there is an intention (*vivakṣā*) to treat the *val-āditva* as a qualifier of that *ārdhadhātuka*. Nor is there any fault in this even regarding the planets (*grahas*), as it has been stated that there is no deficiency in expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) there and no resulting fruit (*phala*). Therefore, is the qualifier of the thing being referred to necessarily intended? No; it is not.

This is because, in rules such as *upeyivānanāścānanūcānaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.106), it is accepted that while the negative particle (*nañ*) and other elements are intended to be significant, the element *upeyi-* is not;
and because in rules such as *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), singularity is intended to be significant.

Thus, there is no fixed rule that a qualifier must be intended as singular; for instance, in the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.42), singularity is not intended. If it were so intended, the form *bhinna* would not result in the occurrence of two *na*s. Nor can this be obtained through a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), because such an assumption involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and lacks any authoritative basis (*māna*). This is because the particle *ca* in the phrase *pūrvasya ca* functions like the word *eka* in the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84).

Furthermore, in that case, there is no contingency of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding the non-perception of oneness; nor is there a contingency of multiple applications (*āpatti*) simply because the purpose of the treatise is fulfilled by a single [application], since in the word *bhinna*, there is no contingency of two negatives (*na-dvaya*). This is because, as in the case of *savarṇadīrgha* and other rules, oneness arises for both. However, for me, there is no fault due to the difference in sentences (*vākya-bheda*), and it must be said that in that instance the particle *ca* serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). For, according to the previously stated method, it is possible to say that the particle *ca* has the purpose of enjoining a partial element (*ekadeśa-vidhānārthatva*); thus, there is no evidence for a difference in sentences in your view.

Therefore, if, in accordance with the requirements of the subject matter (*lakṣya*), a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is indeed accepted and the particle *ca* is said to be merely indicative of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*), then the desire to express singularity (*ekatvavivakṣā*) is entirely redundant; for even according to me, the two occurrences of the negative particle (*na*) are obtained through the split in the sentence. Since the purpose of the treatise is fulfilled by one [instance], there is no contingency of many [names].

If it is argued that, since such non-restriction exists, one might maintain that singularity is intended in rules such as *ād guṇaḥ* (P. 6.1.87) and thereby reject the mention of the word *ekaḥ* in *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (P. 6.1.84), we reply: this is acceptable, for the *Bhāṣya* rejects that very point. Furthermore, in this view, the statements of Kaiyaṭa and others—such as that in *asya cvau* (P. 7.4.32) and similar rules, shortness (*hrasvatva*) and so on are not intended because they qualify the subject of an enunciation (*anuvādya*)—are indeed to be reconsidered. This concludes the investigation into the intentionality and non-intentionality of number. And thus ends the determination of the meaning of *sub*-suffixes.

The Determination of the Power of Compounds 1. [Note: Anticipating the objection that "since the meaning can be established through the power of the individual words alone, the acceptance of a power residing in the compound as a collection of words is fruitless," the author begins to establish the power of compounds in order to refute this view—starting with the word *atha*. While it would have been necessary to first provide a definition of the general category of compounds (*samāsa-sāmānya*), which enters as a constituent element when the power of compounds is to be determined, this was omitted in the root text; therefore, something is now presented on that subject. **The Definition of Compound (Samāsa)** A compound (*samāsa*) is a specific type of nominal stem (*nāma-viśeṣa*). It is a single word (*eka-pada*) consisting of two or more nominal stems (*nāman*) that are connected by mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and possess syntactic congruence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). In this context, "nominal stem" (*nāman*) refers to a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*). "Connected by mutual expectancy" means that the meanings of the constituent parts require one another for their completion. "Syntactic congruence" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs when the meanings of the constituents refer to the same object (*ekārthaviṣayatva*). "Coreferentiality" (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) occurs when they do not. The term "compound" (*samāsa*) is derived from the verbal root *as* (to be) with the prefix *sam* and the suffix *ghañ*; it denotes a state of being joined together (*samasta*). Because such a state arises from the proximity (*sannidhi*) of the constituent parts, it is called a "compound. This [definition] is intended to exclude [formations] such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's servant), where there is mutual expectancy but no syntactic congruence or coreferentiality. It also excludes [sentences like] *rājñaḥ puruṣo bhāryā ca* (the king's servant and wife), where there is syntactic congruence between "servant" and "wife," but no mutual expectancy between "king" and "servant. Furthermore, it excludes [expressions like] *rājapuruṣaścaitraḥ* (Caitra, the king's servant), where there is coreferentiality between "king's servant" and "Caitra," but no mutual expectancy between "king" and "servant. Thus, a compound is a single word formed by the combination of two or more nominal stems that are mutually expectant, possess syntactic congruence, or are coreferential. Alternatively, a compound may be defined as a single word consisting of two or more nominal stems that are connected by mutual expectancy and possess either syntactic congruence or coreferentiality. This definition serves to exclude [formations like] *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, *rājñaḥ puruṣo bhāryā ca*, and *rājapuruṣaścaitraḥ*. The state of being a compound (*samāsatva*) consists in possessing the status of a compound word by virtue of the relationship established through conventions such as those of Pāṇini and others. Furthermore, this definition pertains exclusively to the subject matter of the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). Therefore, even if it were to have a contrary meaning elsewhere, there is no fault. For this very reason, there is no harm in saying that this is a technical term (*pāribhāṣika-pada*); indeed, it can be stated that this is a technical term.

Alternatively, let it be defined as follows: "A compound (samāsa) is a collection of preceding words [forming a name] which is not the object of a cognition whose qualifier is the state of being immediately preceded by an inflection that has the fruit of producing a comprehension of meaning. In cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, even if there exists for some person a mental connection (*anusandhāna*) with an inflection on the word *rāja* and so forth, since that [inflection] lacks the fruit of producing a comprehension of meaning, there is neither impossibility (*asambhava*) nor lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

It should not be argued that there is no over-extension [of the definition] in cases such as "dadhi sundaram asti" because verbal cognition arises only when there is the recollection of the respective case-endings, whereas in the case of compounds, there is no fault because verbal cognition is admitted to arise even without the recollection of the case-ending in the prior member; for there would still be over-extension in cases like "dadhi sundaram," since cognition arises even for one who does not know the case-ending.

If it is argued that there is no over-extension because comprehension is not admitted to occur without the connection of case-endings, we say no; for, in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), one could likewise assert this for compounds as well, which would result in the fallacy of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*).

Nor should it be argued that the determining factor is this: in a compound (*samāsa*), since the requirement for verbal cognition consists in the mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between two words characterized by an uninterrupted sequence of prior and posterior, the consideration of case-endings (*vibhakti*) is not required; whereas in a non-compound (*asamāsa*), since expectancy consists in the base (*prātipadika*) being the object of a cognition whose qualifier is an immediately preceding case-ending, the consideration of case-endings is required. This is because such an argument fails due to counter-examples in compounds where the case-ending is not elided (*aluk-samāsa*). For instance, consider *paryabhūṣat* and *pacatabhūjjatā*.

Because [the definition] would suffer from the fault of being over-narrow (*avyāpti*) in such cases as these, and to avoid this by treating them as non-examples (*alakṣya*) would merely reveal that they are devoid of any connection with cognition.

However, some logicians (*tārkika*) maintain: "A compound (*samāsa*) is such a sentence in which the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth, following a particular great sentence, produce a cognition possessing a subject-object relation (*viṣayatā*) toward its own meaning as determined by a subject-object relation toward a particular referent. In other words, the nature of being a compound is the state of being a sentence that conveys such a cognition."

For in cases such as *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa"), there arises the cognition of one's own meaning as qualified by the meaning of the prior member, through the cognition of its being dependent on that [prior member]. They say that although a term like *pācaka* ("cook") is a sentence whose meaning is the agent of the action of cooking, it is not a "great sentence" (*mahāvākya*) because it lacks the status of a great sentence—defined as the capacity to convey a meaning obtainable from multiple names contained within itself—and thus there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such cases. More details should be understood from that very source.

Now, the power (*śakti*) of compounds whose base is a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is investigated; therein, first, the theory of *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) is defined.

In this regard, there is the rule: "The grammatical operation concerning words applies when they possess semantic capacity" (Pāṇini 2.1.1). Here, semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) means the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Regarding the question, "What indeed is called 'unification of meaning'?": "The statement that words which have separate meanings attain unification of meaning is what is meant by 'semantic capacity. But where? Where are they of separate meanings and where are they of unified meaning? In the sentence 'the king's servant' (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), they have separate meanings; in the compound 'king-servant' (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), they have a unified meaning," according to the *Bhāṣya*.

The meaning of this is as follows: "having a single referent" (*ekārthatva*) means having as its referent an object that is the domain of a single mental presentation (*upasthiti*). Otherwise, even the word *ghaṭa* would not have a single referent, since it possesses multiple referents in the form of the pot, potness, and their relation. Similarly, "having distinct referents" (*pṛthagarthatva*) means having as its referents objects that are the domains of multiple mental presentations. It is precisely to suggest this that [the author] said "of those with distinct referents" (*pṛthagarthānām*), and not "of those with multiple referents" (*anekārthānām*).

With the intention of showing that the suffix *cvī* is untenable because the compound (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*) are different, there is the introductory question in the Bhāṣya: "But where... (*kva punaḥ*), and so forth.

The intention of the latter [author] is this: for those who hold that the effect [of grammatical operation] arises from words (kāryaśābdika), they believe that this *vṛtti* is produced solely from the sentence (*vākya*).

Even in the other view, the suffix *cvī* is employed by relying on the determination of its belonging to the sentence due to similarity. It is precisely the meaning of the suffix *cvī* that is explained by the rule "of words with separate meanings" (*pṛthagarthānām*). To indicate this very point, the suffix *cvī* was not mentioned in the rule "in a compound, however, of those that have become one meaning" (*samāse punarekārthībhūtānām*).

The point is this: in a sentence (*vākya*), when word-meanings are presented by individual words, there arises through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors a cognition of a qualified meaning in which the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) has been established; it is not so in a compound (*vṛtti*). Rather, in a compound, the very presentation of word-meanings—arising from the powers of the constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*) aided by the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*)—is everywhere invariably directed toward a qualified object characterized by the relationship of qualifier and qualified. (Note: The ellipsis "saṃsṛṣṭārthaṃ samartham" is supplied from the *Mahābhāṣya*.)

Furthermore, in the system of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), there is no apprehension of the expressive power (śakti) for the qualified entity [as a whole] in that case. Thus, the apprehension of the power of a word such as *rājapuruṣa* takes the form: "the word *rājapuruṣa* is expressive of a person possessing a connection with a king. Through the discrimination between what is already established and what is not yet established, this qualified power ultimately resolves into the mere relation and so forth, which were previously unestablished.

It must be stated: if one accepts the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) regarding the relational component (*saṃsargāṃśa*), what is the distinction between sentence-function (*vākya-vṛtti*) and complex formation (*vṛtti*)? For in the case of the former, by virtue of the result [of usage], at the time of the presentation of word-meanings, one assumes the non-occurrence of excitants (*udbodhaka*) for the relational component as a rule; thus, there is a subsequent cognition of the relation between two word-meanings that have been presented separately. In the case of complex formation, however, because one assumes excitants for the relational component as well at the very time of the presentation of the word-meanings, the presentation is necessarily qualified [by the relation]; this is the distinction.

For this very reason, in expressions such as *prāptodakaḥ* ("one who has obtained water"), there is a cognition based on the reversal of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*). In that case, both the meaning of the unexpressed genitive case and the relation (*saṃsarga*) are accomplished by the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) of the compound, because they cannot be obtained through any other means; furthermore, since the king and so forth can be presented through their already established individual powers, it would be redundant to postulate a collective power for them.

Furthermore, grammatical conventions such as the co-referentiality (*abhedānvaya*) between a name and its referent have as their objects names and referents that are presented separately. For this very reason, there is no application of qualifiers such as "of the wealthy" to the king—who is a single part of the compound *rājapuruṣa*—as there would be in a sentence; for [the king] is merely a part of the meaning of a word.

Nor should it be said that the status of being the meaning of the word "king" (rāja-padārthatva) does not belong to him [the king] at all; for there is no fault, since the requirement is that the qualificand (viśeṣya) must be presented as not already connected with anything else when it is to be connected with a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). In cases such as *rājñaḥ* ("of the king"), however, there is no obstacle to the connection with a qualifier, because the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are presented separately and then conjoined. It should be understood that this very principle is the basis for the linguistic maxim: "The meaning of a word conjoins with the meaning of another word, but not with a mere part of the meaning of a word."

For this very reason, unlike the expression "the king's man and the horse" (*rājñaḥ puruṣo 'śvaś ca*), one does not say "the king-man and the horse" (*rājapuruṣo 'śvaś ca*); for that which is construed as a qualifier in one instance cannot be construed as a qualificand in another. Similarly, unlike the expression "the king's man [and] the wife's [man]" (*rājñaḥ puruṣo bhāryāyāś ca*), which generates a cognition possessing a dual objective relation (*viṣayatā*), one does not say "the king-man and the wife's [man]" (*rājapuruṣo bhāryāyāś ca*). This is because [the object] is presented only through its qualification by a single qualifier. For this very reason, the sentence "he who is the king's man is the wife's [man]" does not produce such a cognition.

However, the usage "the king’s man is the wife’s" (*rājapuruṣo bhāryāyāḥ*), which possesses a cognitive state whose object is a qualified-qualificative relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*) that makes known the wife's relation to one already qualified by the relation to the king, is indeed acceptable—just like the usage "the king’s man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣaḥ sundaraḥ*). Nor should it be argued that, because the principal member (*pradhāna*) is thus accompanied by a qualifier, the conventional designation "compound" (*vṛtti*) would be lost; for according to your own view, in a compound there is simply no connection of a qualifier with the bare substantive (*viśeṣya*). Such usage is justified because qualities such as "handsomeness" do indeed reside in the mere individual, such as the man.

As for the objection: "Difference (*bheda*)—[note: here 'difference' means mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)]. Now, if difference were the denoted meaning, would it be understood as the difference of the referent of the word 'king' in the man, or the difference of the man, or the difference of the man qualified by the king, in the king? Among these, the first alternative is not possible, because when the king has become a qualifier of the man, there is no co-referentiality (*ekatra anvitatva*) with the qualifier; and because the difference of the king exists in every man related to the king, that difference would fail to function as a differentiator (*avyāvartakatva*)."

Not the second [alternative], because a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the delimitor of co-presence (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), namely *puruṣatva* (the nature of being a person), is sublated (*bādhita*) in the case of the king; furthermore, a difference having that as its counter-correlate would fail to serve as a differentiator (*avyāvartakatvāt*). Moreover, in expressions such as "the king's wealth" (*rājadhanam*), although there exists a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by *dhanatva* (the nature of being wealth) within the meaning of the prior member, this cognition is of no use for the intended understanding.

If it is argued that for this very reason there is no fault even in the third view—since the cognition of that [relation] follows [from the words themselves]—we say no; for there is no fault because the cognition is "related to the king. Furthermore, the relation (*saṃsarga*) is not denoted by the first word. And thus, the cognition would be: "the person is related to the king who is distinct from the non-personal owner," or "the person is distinct from one who does not belong to the king. This is not so, because it contradicts experience, because it is unnecessarily complex (*gaurava*), and because it is impossible to establish that difference and so forth are denotable in a copulative compound (*dvandva*) such as "Rāma and Kṛṣṇa."

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the expression "Devadatta’s man" (*devadattasya puruṣaḥ*) would not apply when one intends to express merely Devadatta’s relation [to the man], whether in the case of an elephant or a horse owned by both Devadatta and Yajñadatta, or in the case of a wife whose owner is Devadatta. Likewise, the expression "Draupadī is Yudhiṣṭhira’s wife" (*yudhiṣṭhirasya bhāryā draupadī*) would not apply.

By this [argument], it follows that only difference (*bheda*) is the expressed meaning, and the resulting cognition is "a man distinct from one who is not the king's. Consequently, precisely because of this contradiction, expressions such as "the king’s man is the wife" (*rājapuruṣo bhāryā*) do not occur. As for the relation (*saṃsarga*), however, it is merely to be inferred.

Alternatively, it may be that the relation itself (*saṃsarga*) is the primary meaning; the cognition would then simply be "related to the king. On this view, the exclusion of what does not belong to the king (*arājakīyabheda*) is to be inferred, and thus the objection that there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to contradiction with that [exclusion] is refuted. Furthermore, because both difference (*bheda*) and relation (*saṃsarga*) are subject to deviation, and because there is no simultaneous presentation (*apṛthagupastiti*), there can be no connection by way of the relationship between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśyavidheyabhāva*); for such a connection requires their separate presentation (*pṛthagupastiti*).

Intending exactly this, at the occasion of defining the defect known as *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa*, the author of the *Pradīpa* states: "In cases where the denotata and the predicated element are presented separately by two distinct words, there alone does such a syntactic connection [of the predicate with the subject] occur. However, in a compound, there is no separate presentation from the word; and when there is no separate presentation, there is no such grammatical convention (*vyutpatti*)."

As for the claim by the Mīmāṃsakas that there is a lack of syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*) because even the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) do not connect with each other directly due to their connection with the verb, that is not correct; for, according to the principle of the *aruṇā* (red) factor and others, since every case-factor (*kāraka*) connects with the action, there would be no formation of a compound such as *paramakāraṇena kṛtam* or *paramakārakeṇa kṛtam*. If it is argued that the competency in those cases is produced by a subsequent mutual connection (*pārṣṇika*), then that is true here as well.

Furthermore, in examples such as "Rāma went to see Kṛṣṇa" (*draṣṭuṃ gataḥ kṛṣṇam*) or "Rāma resorted to the teacher’s family" (*śrito gurukulaṃ rāmaḥ*), there is no compound, because there is no *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) due to the lack of mutual connection between Kṛṣṇa and the one who has resorted [to him]. For this very reason, since the compound possesses meaning, its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established.

As for the claim that there is *ekārthībhāva* because both "king" and "man" are presented by the word *rāja-* and both are presented by the word *puruṣa-*, resulting in the cognition "the king-man who is non-different from the king," that is not correct; for it would entail the recurrence of the cognition, which contradicts actual experience.

Intending exactly this, Kaiyaṭa has stated that although the words in a sentence have separate meanings, there arises a cognition of a qualified meaning through the relation of qualifier and qualified by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors; however, in a compound (*vṛtti*), the qualified meaning alone is denoted by the two words "rāja-puruṣa."

If it is argued that, since the knowledge of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), a qualified cognition would be impossible without the separate presentation of the word-meanings, we say no; for it is possible, just as there is a recollection of a jar qualified by "jar-ness" from the word "jar," and because its status as a cause depends solely on its having the qualifier as its object. For this very reason, the direct perception of a qualified volition (*viśiṣṭakṛtisākṣātkāra*) is established, as is clear in the *Anumānadīdhiti*. Furthermore, there is no requirement for a presentation produced by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), because the presentation of a word-meaning is itself a form of memory (*smṛti*).

Now, one might ask: is this specific meaning of the *vṛtti* established by worldly usage (*lokavyavahāra*), or is it accessible through the treatise (*śāstra*) alone? On this point, some say: it is established by worldly usage. For no new prescription of meaning is being made here in this treatise; rather, the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) beginning with "acatura" [Pāṇini 5.4.77] applies to that which has the sense of "and" (*ca*).

It exists; thus, by restating a meaning already established in common usage—that "it is a *dvandva*"—the purpose is merely to prescribe the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *dvandva*. If the meaning itself were also being prescribed, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, the governing rule for optionality (*vibhāṣā-adhikāra*) would have to be applied in order to prevent the application of a sentence that has the same meaning as the compound itself. For me, however, since the occurrence or non-occurrence of a compound is established by its very nature, that [application of the rule] is not necessary. Moreover, a definition of the compound would also have to be formulated, because the fact of possessing a unified meaning is something known solely through the treatise (*śāstra*). But for me, even that is established from worldly usage alone; so they say.

Others, however, say that the meaning of the sūtra is as follows: [a compound] is to be understood solely through the treatise (*śāstra*); multiple nominal stems (*subanta*) function in the sense of *ca* (conjunction); and when they function in the sense of *ca*, they receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *dvandva*. [Note:

The state of "integration of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) consists in the fact that words observed in common usage—which, based on certain words, have as their objects distinct individual cognitions—generate a single unified cognition through a specific power directed toward a qualified object.

The fact that such words possess that [quality] should be understood through their similarity. The inclusion of the word "of those seen" (*dṛṣṭānām*) at the end is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the case-ending itself. For, while the meaning of a case-ending is conveyed by that very case-ending, it is not so conveyed by any other word; thus, because the case-ending lacks such a denotative function, the over-extension remains unavoidable if the rule were applied to the ending alone.

In expressions such as ‘*upagor apatyam*’ (the offspring of Upagu), it is observed in common usage that the meaning consisting of the offspring is the object of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the word ‘offspring’ (*apatya*). Consequently, this would result in the inclusion of forms like *aupagava*. To prevent this, the inclusion of the term ‘*yat kiñcit*’ (whatever) is introduced. Just as the conventional usage of the term ‘word’ (*pada*) with respect to non-existent things is figurative (*gauṇa*), so too is the conventional usage of words as having a single unified meaning figurative; it is to indicate this that the aforementioned designation is made.

This very "integration of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is what is designated as *ajahatsvārtha* (not abandoning its own meanings) in the treatises. [The term *ajahatsvārtha* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: those meanings which do not abandon their own respective words are *ajahatsvāḥ*; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with multiple members; then, that [compound] in which the meanings are *ajahatsvāḥ* is *ajahatsvārthā*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*. It is thus treated as having the nature of not abandoning its own meanings.

And this unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—by virtue of the restatements in the sūtras "anekamanyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24) and "samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.1)—is superimposed even upon the non-worldly analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*). For this very reason, when the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) applies, the elision of case-endings (*vibhakti-luk*) and so forth is established through the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) based on meaningfulness; furthermore, in accordance with rules such as "ṣaṣṭhī" (Pāṇini 2.3.50), there is also distinct meaning (*pṛthagarthatva*) for the purpose of accounting for the genitive and other cases based on the presentation of difference (*bhedopasthiti*).

Nor is there any contradiction, because according to the authority of the treatises (*śāstra*), there is no contradiction between two conceptual entities; furthermore, this is a merit rather than a defect, based on the maxim that "this is an ornament of supramundane establishment. If it is objected: "In this view, the conventional usage [of grammar] such as 'the *tatpuruṣa* is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the *bahuvrīhi*' would be destroyed; for in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, being a generator of a cognition whose object is an external referent constitutes its externality (*bahir-aṅgatva*). But in this view, that is not the case, because even when the meaning of another word is involved, the own-meaning of the constituent words themselves exists due to their having a qualified denotation (*viśiṣṭa-śakyatva*)," we reply: No.

This is because, compared to the apprehension of the speaker’s word-meaning relation (*śaktigraha*) which has as its object only the perceived meaning of the sentence containing the constituent words of the compound itself, the apprehension of the word-meaning relation belonging to the term designated as a *bahuvrīhi* is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), since it has as its object the external referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) which is distinct from the perceived meaning of the sentence formed by the constituent words; thus, there is no flaw [in the argument].

By this, it is also explained that a *karmadhāraya* compound is simpler than a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. This is because, compared to the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of a word designated as a *karmadhāraya*, the apprehension of the expressive power of a word such as a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* is more complex, as it involves an additional object of cognition in the form of the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, which is not part of its own [constituent] structure.

And thus: [The underlying point is this: It is heard in scripture, "One should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to perform a sacrifice. In that context, the term *niṣādasthapati* is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*; [the analysis being] the chief (*sthapati*) of the *niṣādas*. The word *sthapati* is a synonym for "master" (*svāmin*).

Regarding the compound *niṣādasthapati*, there arises a doubt as to whether it is a *bahuvrīhi*—meaning "one whose chief is a Niṣāda"—or a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound)—meaning "a Niṣāda who is also a chief. In the case of the *karmadhāraya*, since the Niṣādas lack the qualification for Vedic rites, they would be unable to perform sacrifices; consequently, one would have to assume that they must first study the Veda, which would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because there is an absence of expressive power (*śakti*), and because there is greater complexity (*gaurava*) in assuming a sentence-level indication (*vākya-lakṣaṇā*), the *karmadhāraya* alone is preferred due to its simplicity (*lāghava*). This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the assumption of such complexity—pertaining to the study of a previously unknown branch of knowledge at a later time—is not a fault, as it is merely a consequence of the result (*phala-mukha*). If it is argued that this contradicts the theory of those who maintain that compounds possess inherent expressive power (*samāsa-śakti-vādin*), on the grounds that even in a *tatpuruṣa* compound there would be no room for such complexity, do not say so.

Since the word *niṣādasthapati* is capable of signifying all three—(1) a carpenter who is a Niṣāda, (2) a carpenter related to a Niṣāda, and (3) another person whose master is a Niṣāda—it possesses multiple meanings. According to the maxim, "In the case of multiple meanings, the specific meaning is understood through the intended purport (*tātparya*)," when a doubt arises as to where the purport lies, the purport of the term *niṣādasthapati* is determined to reside in the first-mentioned meaning. This is because the apprehension of the compound's power (*śakti*)—which has as its object only those meanings presented by the individual powers of the constituent words—is more immediate (*antaraṅga*), and thus there is a parsimony of cognitive effort (*upasthitilāghava*) regarding that very first-mentioned meaning.

The meaning of this section is as follows: there is an apprehension of the specific intended meaning [of a word] when it is based on the apprehension of the word's power (śakti) directed toward an external object, because the apprehension [of the word itself] would otherwise be delayed.

Regarding words such as *niṣādasthapati*, although they possess multiple meanings—namely, a *sthapati* who is a *niṣāda*, a *sthapati* related to a *niṣāda*, or another person whose master is a *niṣāda*—the principle that "there is an apprehension of the specific intended meaning despite the multiplicity of meanings" applies. Thus, when doubt arises as to where the intention lies, it is determined to lie precisely in the sense of being a *niṣāda*, in accordance with the parsimony (*lāghava*) of the apprehension of the word's power and the presentation of the word-meaning.

Even when there is an intention (*tātparya*) on the part of others, since figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is unavoidable—just as in the case of the expression "enter with the staffs" (*ayaṣṭīḥ praveśya*)—it is the intention alone that remains as the final factor to be postulated; thus, there is no fault. It is with this very point in mind that it has been said: "The consideration of whether [the apprehension of] expressive power (*śaktigraha*) is internal or external belongs to a moment situated not far before the completion of the verbal cognition."
Thus concludes the Emergence of the Grammarians' View by Dīkṣita. Now follows the determination of the *ajahatsvārtha* [view],
and then the determination of the *jahatsvārtha* [view].

Alternatively, since it is established by the experience of all that even children who do not know the individual component powers (*avayava-śakti*) or the secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) possess understanding through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) alone, and since such a power must necessarily be postulated according to the method previously stated, it is possible to have the cognition of a person qualified by a king through that very power; therefore, the capacity of the words *rāja-puruṣa* to produce that cognition need not be postulated again, just as in the case of the word *vṛṣabha* (bull) and so on. This is because the status of being a denotative power (*śaktatā*) is restricted to that specific sequence which lacks inclusion within any other sequence.

Otherwise, even from words such as *rāma*, there would result the unintended presence of the word-meanings of the constituent parts—such as the substance (the four-faced Brahmā) or Nārāyaṇa—as well as the resulting verbal cognition; furthermore, there would be the unintended production of intermediate case-endings (*sub*), the unintended occurrence of the *ja*-class suffixes in words like *dhana*, and the unintended application of the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) in expressions like *paṭujātīyāya*.

In a sentence, however, the words themselves possess meaning. For instance, regarding the sense "a person who has a connection with a king," rather than postulating two distinct capacities (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for the two specific word-sequences "rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ" and "rājñaḥ," it is more parsimonious (*laghīyas*) to simply postulate a capacity for the individual words. Furthermore, "having a single meaning" means having the capacity to convey a single unified sense. As for the suffix *cvī*, it functions exactly as before.

Nor does the loss of meaningfulness for those elements included within a *vṛtti* entail the loss of their status as *prātipadika*s or *pada*s based on that [meaningfulness], because in compounds and the like, those two statuses are accepted at that time precisely because they are dependent (*upajīvya*) upon it; furthermore, even the meaning that is dependent is sublated by the authority of the rule "samartha" (Pāṇini 2.1.1). However, rules such as "sāsya devatā," "kartari kṛt," and "cārthe dvandvaḥ" take recourse to imaginary meanings, just as in the case of "laḥ karmaṇi."

Nor should it be argued that because the verbal roots, nominal stems (*pratipadika*), and so forth that constitute a compound (*vṛtti*) are devoid of meaning, there would be no occurrence of the substitution of *ā* for *i* in words such as *pathin* and *mathin*—as prescribed by the rule *pathimathoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.85]—since the principle of "the inclusion of what has meaning" (*arthavadgrahaṇa*) excludes what is meaningless. This objection is invalid; for, based on the authority of the Bhāṣya and other works on rules such as *pratyayottarapadayośca* [Pāṇini 7.2.98], the grammatical system functions by superimposing the meanings that existed prior to the formation of the compound, and thus its operation remains unimpaired.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts what is stated in the *Bhāṣya* regarding such cases as *vāpyaśvaḥ*, where one might suspect the application of the rule *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe* [P. 1.1.11] for *pragṛhya* status, only to conclude that there is no fault because the term is devoid of meaning (*ānarthakya*) in a *jahatsvārthā* compound; for that [Bhāṣya statement] is possible because, like other rules, this one may also apply by taking up the superimposed meaning (*āropitārtha*). This is not so, because in that context, by the force of the mention of "meaning" (*artha*), such a [superimposed] meaning is not grasped; this is clear from our own *Śabdenduśekhara*.

As for the claim that the paribhāṣā "the mention of a meaningful element" (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not exist at all: this is refuted by the specific inclusion of forms such as *añ*, *ṭhañ*, and *dayādi* in rules like "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ" [Pāṇini 4.1.15] and "dayāyāsaśca" [Pāṇini 3.1.37], which serve as its indicators (*jñāpaka*). [Note: Here, the reading "... from the inclusion of a specific form, and not elsewhere of that which constitutes a mere part... appears more consistent with the context; otherwise, the intended meaning would not follow.]

If it is argued that there is no fault because the apprehension of only those [sounds] that occupy multiple locations is thereby indicated, that is not correct; for the *arthavat* paribhāṣā cannot be rejected on the basis of established worldly logic (*laukikanyāya*). Furthermore, in your view, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) of the absence of *vṛddhi* in forms such as *aprauḍhaghaṭa*; thus, this argument is trivial.

Nor should it be argued that it is contradictory for words to possess meaning prior to the compound and to be meaningless thereafter; for this is logically consistent with the way a single gem may act as an obstacle or not act as an obstacle depending on the presence or absence of a counteragent. In cases such as *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"), however, the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) exists precisely by including the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) within it; thus, there is no destruction of the distinction between etymological and conventional (*yoga-rūḍhi*) meanings.

In cases such as the word *aśvakarṇa* (referring to a specific type of tree), since the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) does not enter into the primary denotative power (*śakti*), there is only pure conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). However, in expressions such as "one whose mind is attached to truth like Śiva," because multiple meanings are conveyed through several compounds uttered simultaneously (*tantra*), there is a cognition of multiple meanings.

And here [in the commentary], one should supply the correct reading: "The nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva [is attributed] to the syllable *Oṃ* by its components *a*, *u*, and *m*," and so forth; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of violating the established sequence.

It should not be argued that there is a contradiction with the *Atharvaśikhā* and other texts—which establish that the syllable *Oṃ* (Oṃkāra) conveys the nature of Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, and so forth through its constituent letters *A*, *U*, and *M*—because in the traditional lists of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*) and elsewhere, sages have declared the consonant to consist of half a mora (*ardhamātrikā*). Consequently, even under such an interpretation, the following distinctions remain untenable: the two moras mentioned in the *Praśna Upaniṣad* together with the letter *M*; the three and a half moras mentioned in the *Atharvaśikhā*; and the further subdivisions of the final half-mora into *nāda*, *bindu*, *kalā*, and *vikalā* as stated in numerous Śrutis and Purāṇas.
Furthermore, since these are intended for meditative visualization (*upāsanā*), it is equally logical to conceive of them as consisting of the three phonemes (*varṇas*).

And thus, from the Lord’s statement, "Om is the single-syllabled Brahman," it should be understood that the *praṇava*, which is of the nature of an indivisible single syllable, denotes the consciousness of the one Lord as delimited by Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Brahmā, and Māyā.

Now, an objection may be raised: in this view, if the primary meaning of words such as "king" were entirely abandoned, there would be no cognition of that [specific] object, and there would instead be the bringing of any person whatsoever.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the linguistic usage "the meaning of the word *rājan* (king) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in relation to the person" would not be possible, we say no; for there is no fault in the first case, since the person related to the king is presented precisely as a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). [Note: Here, the word *sumanas* is feminine and always plural; therefore, the qualifier *niṣkīrṇāsu* is appropriate, as stated in lexicons such as: "Women are *sumanas*, flowers are *sumanas*... and so forth.]

[This concludes the section on trees and medicinal herbs in the second book of the *Amara-kośa*. Even when the flowers have been removed, the designation "campaka-bundle" (*campakapuṭa*) and similar terms are still employed; for such usage is justified by the mere persistence of a connection with something similar to that [original object]. And this very position is designated as *jahatsvārthā* ("abandoning its own meaning") in the treatises.

Although these two positions are both approved by the Bhāṣya according to the manner previously stated—and Kaiyaṭa has explicitly stated this, taking up the phrases "either *ekārthībhāva* is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), or *vyapekṣā*" and "of those having separate meanings," and as it is also treated in the Bhāṣya on rules such as "īdūtau ca saptamyarthe" [Pāṇini 1.1.19]—nevertheless, the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) view is not tenable; for there is the complexity (*gaurava*) of abandoning the established meaningfulness of the constituent parts and accepting that [meaningfulness] only as something superimposed.

The cognition of someone arising from the apprehension of a specific power [of the whole] does not suffice to prove that the constituent parts are meaningless. For if, on the grounds that someone likewise understands from a sentence, one were to conclude that the parts are meaningless there as well, it would contradict the Bhāṣya statement that "in a sentence, the meanings are not separate," and it would lead to the fallacy of the "half-old woman" argument (ardhajaratīya).

Intending this very point, Haradatta stated: "We do not favor the view that the function [of a compound] is *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning), which results in the meaninglessness of the constituent parts. The truth is that these two positions exist according to the difference between perceivers: for one who understands through the specific power [of the whole] preceded by ignorance of the power of the constituents, and for another who understands precisely through knowledge of that [constituent power]; thus, both are necessary. This concludes the determination of *jahatsvārthā*.

Furthermore, this *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) does not occur in cases such as *pacati*, because there is no evidence for it. For this very reason, the relation between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) is logically consistent in those instances. As stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "When there is *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) consisting of *ekārthībhāva*, only the compound (*samāsa*) is included; however, the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti-vidhāna*) and the treatment as a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) are not included. Here, the word "compound" (*samāsa*) [fn] refers to derivative formations (*vṛtti*) such as those ending in *kṛt*-suffixes. They are designated as "derivative formations" (*vṛtti*) because they possess the status of being the substratum of a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) that generates a single presentation (*ekopasthiti*).

Since the meaning of the sūtra—"one who is capable of denoting a compound sentence is *sādhu* (grammatically correct)"—is obtained from the Bhāṣya, the term "compound" (*samāsa*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all types of derivative formations (*vṛtti*).

Furthermore, the status of being a rule whose objective is a word (*padoddeśyakavidhitva*) exists in all five types of derivative formations: primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), collective nouns (*ekaśeṣa*), and verbs with prefixes (*sanādyanta-dhātu*). Thus, it is an indicator for all derivative formations. For this very reason, the mention of "a rule concerning words" (*padavidhi*) is purposeful; for it is intended to include every rule that has a word as its objective. We shall explain the remainder later.

Even though all words are eternal, indivisible, and partless, the treatise (śāstra) serves merely as an indicator. Just as in a painting, the tail and other features of a gavaya or similar animal depicted there lead to the cognition of the actual tail and so forth through their similarity, and thereby bring about the cognition of the actual animal; likewise, through the similarity between bases (prakṛti), suffixes (pratyaya), and so on, there arises the cognition of the actual word and sentence by means of the cognition of the bases, suffixes, and so on contained within the indivisible word and sentence. The treatise, however, is merely a pointer.

They say that [the formation of compounds] is merely an analytical description based on the fabrication of divisions such as *prakṛti* (base) and *pratyaya* (suffix), according to the maxim of the "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavayanyāya*). Even for them, in order to exclude the connection with qualifiers and so forth—just as in the case of *pacati* and similar forms within a *vṛtti*—the state of "becoming one meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), characterized by a distinct type of grammatical expectancy (*vyutpatti*), is indispensable. Enough of this prolixity.

As for those who maintain the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvādins*), they hold that here "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists precisely in mutual expectancy in the form of reciprocal connection, because it has been established as such in rules such as *isusoḥ sāmarthye* [Pāṇini 8.3.44], and also out of deference to the rule regarding the treatment of a suffix as if it were part of the preceding element (*parāṅgavadbhāva*).

Otherwise, if the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) were applied here, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), as this [rule] would apply to the compound alone for the sake of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning). Furthermore, if that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) did not operate there, then in examples such as *ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāvṛtāvṛdhāvṛtaspṛśaḥ*, the word *ṛtena* and so on would incur the fault of having an acute accent on the first syllable by the rule *āmantritasya ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.198], because *mitrāvaruṇau* would be a vocative (*āmantrita*) following another vocative ending in the nominative case of the genitive-accusative relation (*sambandhodhana*).

Nor should it be argued that this fault does not arise because of the *Vārttika* stating "the apprehension of its cause must be made," which means that whatever expresses the cause of that meaning of the vocative should behave like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavat*). This is because the refutation of that rule by relying on the *samartha-paribhāṣā* (the maxim of semantic competency) is the more logical course; for in the case of *ṛtena mitrāvaruṇau*, there is no mutual semantic competency (*parasparam-asāmarthyāt*) due to the connection of these two with the word *āśāthe*, which has the sense of *ānaśāthe*.

However, because there is a connection with the *pārṇika* (the suffix *ṭhak*) in the two [words] *mitrāvaruṇau* and *ṛtāvṛdhau*, they indeed possess the required semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). This is clear from the *Vedabhāṣyakaustubha*; such is the direction [of the argument].

For this very reason, there is no compound in cases such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man") or *devadattasya bhāryā* ("Devadatta's wife"). Nor is there a compound in *ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the prosperous king's man"), because the word *rāja-* [in *rājapuruṣa*] refers by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to one related to the king; thus, being a part of the referent of the word *rājan*, the qualifier cannot be connected to it.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in expressions such as "the hamlet on the beautiful Gaṅgā," where there is an application of qualifiers like "beautiful" to the indicated sense, so too in the present case the application of such qualifiers would be unavoidable; for even there, since the word *gaṅgā* itself has the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "the bank of the beautiful Gaṅgā," other words serve merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Nor does this [position] conflict with the restriction—"a word-meaning conjoins with another word-meaning, but not with a word"—which is rooted in the following causal relation: "with respect to a verbal cognition delimited by its nature (śābdabuddhitva), where the primary qualificandum-ness (mukhyaviśeṣyatā) is determined by a qualificandum-ness residing in some word-meaning, the cause is the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by some word," as is seen in examples such as "Caitra’s grandson. This is the intended meaning.

The objection that the application [of the rule] is unavoidable remains; for in that case, one must state that "grandsonhood" (*naptṛtva*) consists in being a male produced by one who is himself produced [by the father], and that Caitra’s application occurs in the element of "being produced" (*janyatva*), which is a part of that [compound meaning]. Even if one accepts the aforementioned grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) in order to prevent the validity of sentences such as "the pot is eternal" or "the cow is eternal"—where the intention is to apply the term "eternal" to eternal entities like *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) or *gotva* (cow-ness)—in cases such as "Devadatta’s grandson," it is intended that Devadatta applies only to the grandfather through the relation of "being defined by" (*nirūpitatva*). Therefore, regarding the causal relationship [between the cause and effect of understanding] mentioned above...

The essential point is that there is no fault [in the theory], because either the *prakāratā* (qualifierhood) delimited by the relation of identity (*abhedasambandha*), or the *viśeṣyatā* (qualificandumhood) residing in something other than that which is eternally expectant (*nityasākāṅkṣa*), is included within the defining condition (*kāryatāvacchedakakoṭi*) of the effect; for the *prakāratā* residing in Devadatta is not delimited by the relation of identity, or else, due to its being produced (*janyatva*) and thus being eternally expectant, it does not fall within the scope of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*). This is because such a [requirement] is not accepted in cases other than those involving related entities (*sasambandhika*).
