Alternatively—even in that case, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs with the grandson alone, through the relation of being a son produced by oneself. Similarly, in expressions such as "different from a jar" (*ghaṭād anyaḥ*), the connection also occurs with the "other" (*anya*) alone, through the relation of difference whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is itself; thus there is no fault. For this very reason, a compound indeed occurs in cases such as "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*). Both of these positions are clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*. Nor should it be argued: "Let the relation to the king alone be the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*), and let its connection with the person (*puruṣa*) occur through difference; what is the use of assuming a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the relatum? [This is because the relation itself cannot be connected to the person without mediation.]

In order to exclude the comprehension of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in cases such as "the rice cooks" (*odanaḥ pacati*), it is held that for a verbal cognition of a case-role (*kāraka*) whose referent is a noun-meaning related by a relation other than identity, the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a suffix prescribed for that [case-role].

Furthermore, the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*) consists either in possessing the word-form "suffix" through a specific conventional relation (*saṅketaviśeṣasambandha*), or in being a specific universal (*jāti*); thus, there is no lack of uniformity (*ananugama*). Nor does this lead to the untenability of a relational cognition—where the king or similar object is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the relation or similar object is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—arising in cases such as *rājasambandhaḥ* when the word *sambandha* is mistakenly perceived as a suffix; for, in reality, there is an absence of the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a suffix.

Likewise, in cases such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), it should not be argued that there would be an obstacle to the application of a relation of difference (*bhedasaṃbandha*) between the king and the object of the genitive case (*ṅas*) etc., when one is under the delusion that the genitive suffixes denote a relation; for, in the absence of the perception of a common property (*sādhāraṇadharmadarśana*), such a delusion cannot even arise.

If, however, you maintain that such an error exists based on experience, then there is no fault, because the cause of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) is that which is not apprehended as being distinct from the suffix (*pratyaya*). It is not stated that it must be "apprehended as a suffix," for we observe such cognition even in cases like *rājñaḥ paruṣaḥ* when the genitive case-ending and so forth are not presented as having the status of a suffix; therefore, enough with this investigation into delusion.

Furthermore, in the cognition of that [relation] as a non-difference (*abheda-saṃsarga*), the cause is a presentation (*upastiti*) produced by either the verbal root (*dhātu*) or the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In cases such as *nīlo ghaṭaḥ* ("the blue pot"), the case-ending of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-vibhakti*) serves the purpose of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Accordingly, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *anabhihite* states: "The mat itself is the object; because of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, the second case ending is applied to *bhīṣma* and so forth. Kaiyaṭa comments: "Even though *bhīṣma* and the others are not themselves objects, they must be accompanied by the very same case-ending as the word related to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), since they share the same status regarding grammatical operation and restriction (*ekayogakṣematvāt*)."
For this very reason, the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa* (Pāṇini 2.2.19) is consistent.

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as "the jar is not a cloth" (*ghaṭo na paṭaḥ*) or "the face is like the moon" (*candra iva mukham*), there would be no distinct syntactic connection (*bhedānvaya*) between the jar and the cloth, nor between the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the cloth, etc.; for there is no fault, since the requirement for the cognition of difference is the presence of an apprehension (*upasthiti*) produced by either a particle (*nipāta*) or a suffix (*pratyaya*), and because in the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) governing the cognition of non-difference, we have provided the qualification "other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktatva*) to exclude such cases.

Nor is there a fault for me [the proponent] due to the provision of a qualifier not exceeding the compound, because that would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because the purpose is accomplished simply by assuming that the established secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) has as its object the related entity. Furthermore, according to the view that particles are *dyotaka* (indicative), there is no obstacle to the secondary function of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) referring to what is other than a pot, and the word "moon" (*candra*) referring to its likeness.

Nor should it be argued that in the sentence "Devadatta brings the jar" (*devadatto ghaṭam ānayati*), when there is an intention [to convey identity], there would be the undesirable consequence of an identity-connection (*abhedānvaya*) between Devadatta and the jar; for this is not the case, because a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is the referent of a given name and whose relation is identity requires as its cause a presentation produced by a word co-occurring with that name, which occurs at a time other than the presentation of the meaningful case-ending following that name. Therefore, there is no fault in cases such as "the wealth of the king’s son" (*rājñaḥ sutasya dhanam*).

And by "possessing significance" (sārthakatva), what is intended is that which is produced by a meaning over and above [the mere] number. Therefore, there is no fault in cases such as "The Vedas are authoritative" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*) or "A hundred Brahmins" (*śataṃ viprāḥ*). In the first case, for the purpose of establishing that they possess the nature of being cognitions of a single kind, there is no fault even if the case-ending signifies singularity residing in the property that delimits the meaning of the base; and in the second case, there is no fault if it signifies that same meaning residing in the aggregate. [Note: Here, the reading "samānavacanatvaṃ samānaliṅgatvañca" (agreement in number and agreement in gender) is correct.]

Furthermore, its [the word *eka*’s] inclusion in the traditional recitation would otherwise be redundant. It is not the case that having the same number of words (*samānavacanatva*) and the same gender (*samānaliṅgatva*) is the determinant for the cognition of non-difference between two things; for there are counter-examples such as "The Vedas are authoritative" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*), "The king’s son’s wealth" (*rājñaḥ sutasya dhanam*), and "That which is coolness is the very nature of water" (*śaityaṃ hi yatsā prakṛtirjalasya*).
Alternatively, what determines such a cognition is the non-presentation of the object in a form incompatible with that produced by the name co-occurring with the other name.

And since the singularity residing in the delimitor of the primary meaning (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*) is not incompatible with the plurality residing in the individual (*vyakti*), there is no fault.

For this very reason, from a sentence such as *nīlo ghaṭaḥ* ("the blue pot") uttered with the intention of referring to the singularity of the individual object, there is no such cognition [of the universal]. Furthermore, contradiction (*virodha*) is to be understood as being caused by something other than gender (*liṅga*). [Note: Here, either the reading "ata eva" before "tena," or the reading "tena" itself, is required; otherwise, there would be the consequence of mutual incoherence. Thus, there is no fault in rules such as *tena tulyaṃ kriyā* (Pāṇini 5.1.115).

Thus, it should be understood that in the case of a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*) and in the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*), the employment of two words denoting the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is correct only when they possess the same gender (*liṅga*), the same number (*vacana*), and the same case-ending (*vibhakti*); no other usage is valid. Furthermore, the cognitive presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a name (*nāman*) must be understood as being delimited precisely by the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). Consequently, in expressions such as "the pot is eternal" (*ghaṭo nityaḥ*), there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the nature of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*) and eternity (*nitya*) without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Moreover, "non-difference" (*abheda*) in this context is identity (*tādātmya*), which consists in a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) residing in itself.

By this, they say that [the objection] is refuted: if non-difference were the absence of difference as delimited by the property of being a difference (*bhedatva*), it would be unestablished; if it were the absence whose counter-correlate is difference, then since the absence of the difference from blue exists in fire and so forth by way of duality and so on, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that "fire is blue" and the like.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the cause for a cognition of a relation—which is distinct from the suffix, the meaning of the noun-base, the type, and the form—is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the suffix prescribed in that context; for in cases such as *dadhi bhuktam* ("curd has been eaten"), if there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*), it would follow that the meaning of the nominative-terminated word *dadhi* would be construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of eating.

Nor is this [compound] necessarily a derivative ending in a suffix (*pratyayānta*) simply because a suffix has been elided, for the same principle applies to the base form (*prakṛti*) as well; moreover, with respect to the absence of a relationship between a cause and a more cumbersome effect, it is simpler to assume a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the related entity. Therefore, the indication applies only to the related entity. Since we accept indication in words such as *niṣ* when they mean "gone beyond" (*krānta*), there is no separate usage of words like *krānta* in compounds such as *niṣkauśāmbi*, because of the rule that "those whose meaning has already been expressed are not used again" (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*), as their meaning has already been conveyed.

And that [usage] is a conventional (nirūḍha) indication, because it conforms to a fixed intended meaning. Therefore, the objection that "in the absence of indication, such usage would result" is refuted.

If it is argued that in this view, because the compound would be devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), it would not possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), we say no; for by the force of the rule that "a meaningful word" [is a nominal stem], the status of being a nominal stem is accepted even for a meaningless aggregate, provided it is composed of elements that denote meaning. Otherwise, since meaningfulness would already be established through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of forms such as *adātuḥ*, the mention of "compound" would be superfluous. For this very reason, the exclusion of forms ending in suffixes (*pratyayānta*) serves its purpose, and there is no fault in cases such as *bahupaṭavaḥ* (many cloths) or *śaśaśṛṅgam* (hare's horn). Furthermore, in cases like *pacatakī*, the prohibition applies because it ends in a suffix; and since the mention of "compound" is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), there is no fault regarding a sentence (*vākya*).

1 [Note: "When there is no purpose [for the primary meaning], and when there is a cognition of the connection [between the primary and secondary meanings] preceded by the recognition that the literal sense is obstructed, then the indication (lakṣaṇā) is established. For example, in cases such as "known by the skin" (*tvacā jñātam*), there is indication of the word "skin" (*tvak*) and others in the sense of the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*). Here, there is no purpose whatsoever for the indication; rather, tradition alone is the authority here.]

As for the claim that in every compound there is *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in the final member (*uttarapada*), and that the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies to that alone—that is not so; for if the designation of a nominal stem applied to that [final member] alone, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) following the preceding member would not occur, because it is impossible for the mere final member to be a nominal stem since it ends in an affix (*pratyaya*). This is the general direction [of the argument].

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, however, since the non-difference between the word-meanings presented by the powers of the constituent parts can be understood as the very mode of relation (*saṃsarga*), there is neither [the need for] a primary power (*śakti*) nor a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In an indeclinable compound such as *upakumbham*, there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the words "near" (*upa*), "jar" (*kumbha*), and so on. The word "and so on" (*ādi*) serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the established linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that "suffixes convey their own meaning as residing in the word-meaning immediately adjacent to them"—a rule formulated to prevent the connection of case-role (*karmatva*) and so forth in expressions such as *dhavavantam ānaya* ("bring the one possessing *dhava* trees").

For this very reason, even in a collective dvandva compound such as *pāṇipādam* ("hands and feet"), there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the collective whole "hands-and-feet" in the final member of the compound.

As for the claim that there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the aggregate [of the two words], that is not so; because such a thing lacks the capacity [for indication]. For indication is indeed a relation with something else. Now, one might argue: "Indication is simply a relation with what is signified (*jñāpya*), and this alone is appropriate in accordance with examples such as 'the hamlet is on the deep river' (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). To explain: first of all, the word *gabhīra* ("deep") cannot indicate the bank, because that would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the word *nadyām* ("on the river"), for the bank is not the river. For the same reason, the word *nadī* ("river") also cannot indicate the bank, because that would result in a lack of syntactic connection with the meaning of the word *gabhīra*.

Nor can it be said that [the meaning] resides in each of the two words individually, because that would entail the failure to obtain a riverbank qualified by depth. Nor can it be argued that the word "river" indicates (*lakṣayati*) a deep riverbank while the word "deep" merely serves to capture the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), for there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) [to favor one over the other]. Nor can it be said that [the meaning] resides in each of the two words individually, because that would entail the failure to obtain a riverbank qualified by depth. Nor can it be argued that the word "river" indicates a deep riverbank while the word "deep" merely serves to capture the speaker's intention, for there is no decisive criterion.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that "an affix conveys its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base," this applies only to the word *nadī* (river) and not to the word *gabhīra* (deep), because the case-ending of the latter serves only for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvārtha*). This is because the Naiyāyikas accept [the word *gabhīra*] as having meaning by virtue of denoting non-difference (*abheda*), and the Mīmāṃsakas accept its meaningfulness according to the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*; furthermore, when there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *gabhīra*, it is possible for that very word to function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the word *nadī* (river) denotes a substance (*dravya*), the function [of denoting the relation] belongs to it alone in accordance with its direct connection [to the action]; for the word *gabhīra* (deep) also denotes a substance possessing qualities (*guṇin*) by nature, and thus it too possesses a direct connection [to the action]. Therefore, since there is no decisive reason [to prefer one over the other], and because it would be cumbersome to assume secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for both words, it is simpler to accept that function for the entire compound as a whole. If it is argued that this is precisely why secondary signification is accepted as "praise" (*prāśastya*) in arthavāda sentences, we say no; for then the fault of assuming secondary signification would apply even to corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), since their denoted meaning exists [as well].

Furthermore, in this way, because there would be no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) for determining whether [the relation] resides in each individual word, in the sentence as a whole, or in both the words and the sentence, there would be excessive complexity (*atigaurava*).

Moreover, regarding the phrase "a relation with that which is to be made known" (*jñapyasambandha*), its meaning is: a relation with an object that possesses the state of being made known (*jñāpyatā*), as defined by the state of being a signifier (*jñāpakatā*) residing in itself.

In that context, does "signifier-ness" (*jñāpakatva*) mean the capacity to produce the cognition of an object through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), or merely the state of being the object of a cognition that produces the cognition of an object?

Not the first [alternative], because it would result in the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) being applied to the sentence itself. Not the second, because if each individual phoneme were also endowed with meaning, it would follow that case-endings and so forth must be produced after them. Moreover, this being the case, one would have to state that even the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) constituting a word is the delimitor of the indication, which would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*). For me, however, since that [sequence] is absent in the sentence, it is not so; thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*). If the relation of the signified is taken as *lakṣaṇā*, then *lakṣaṇā* results in nothing other than the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the cognition "this is related to that," where "produced" (*janya*) is the final conclusion.

Furthermore, some maintain that even those things related to ether (ākāśa), which are indicated by words such as "jar" through relations like inherence (samavāya) and are thus presented [to consciousness], can become objects of verbal cognition.

Therefore, it is correct to define *lakṣaṇā* simply as "a relation with the primary meaning. And it is quite clear that this [relation] does not constitute a collective whole (*samudāya*). As for the fact that the combined action (*samāhāra*) is the object of the act of blowing and so forth, this is to be understood through a mediated relation (*paramparā*), such as "residing in what resides in itself" (*svāśrayavṛttitva*).

Alternatively, no collective sense (*samāhāra*) is understood there; therefore, there is no metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And thus, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is direct. As for the dual number and so forth, they exist because the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) teaches their correctness. However, the conventional usage of "collective copulative compound" (*samāhāra-dvandva*) and the like should be understood as figurative (*gauṇa*), because—just as with a collective—when a copulative compound consists of parts of living beings and so on, the rule prescribing the singular number applies, making it the cause for the singular ending. Similarly, even in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), there is metaphorical indication of the two [members] as qualified by association (*sāhitya*). For this very reason, the dual number and so forth are construed. But in the case of a collective, association is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); this is the distinction between the two.

Alternatively, there is no metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here either; for since the two meanings, which are presented through their respective powers by virtue of being mounted upon a single recollection, can undergo a connection such as duality, etc.—whether it be in the form of connection with a single action or in the form of being delimited by a single cognition [the meaning is established]. [Note: *Sāhitya* (togetherness) is the connection of one thing delimited by a single property with another thing delimited by that same single property, through a relation delimited by that same single property. And the "single property" consists in the nature of being a collection.]

And thus, in the usage "Worship the Lord and the teacher" (*īśvaraṃ guruñca bhajasva*), because there is an absence of co-occurrence (*sāhitya*) when the Lord and the teacher are construed with two distinct actions in the form of meditation and service respectively, there is no compound.

Similarly, in cases such as "Go for alms and bring the cow" (*bhikṣāmaṭa, gāṃ cānaya*), a compound occurs between the two because the alms are construed as the object of the action denoted by the root *aṭ* ("to wander"), and the cow is construed as the object of the action of "bringing. This is because co-occurrence is understood only subsequently, and it is improper to apply secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) prior to that.

Nor should it be argued that if there is no manifestation of conjunction (*sāhitya*), then when one intends the connection of one [of two things] with the action of the other—as in the sentences "Look at the *dhava* tree" and "Cut the *khadira* tree"—the usage "Look at the *dhava* and *khadira* trees; cut them" would result. This is because it is more appropriate for the connection to occur with respect to a single entity qualified by a single property, namely duality (*dvitva*). Nor should it be argued that the connection with duality is difficult to achieve without a conjunction that serves as the delimitor of the fitness (*yogyatā*) for that connection. This is because the presence of the delimitor of fitness is not required; rather, the rule is simply that the connection occurs only with that which is fit once it has been presented.

For this very reason, in cases such as "bring water with a jar," it is only that which is non-perforated (*acchidra*) that is construed by the force of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*); however, there is no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having "non-perforatedness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*). Furthermore, there is no deficiency [in the theory] if the delimitor of semantic fitness (*yogyatāvacchedaka*) for the connection with duality, cutting, and so forth, is simply the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*).

Now, it must be said that the number’s relation to the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) occurs through a pervasion-restricted (vyāpyatvaviśiṣṭa) inherence (paryāpti) with the delimitor of the relatum (anvayitāvacchedaka); for if it were related by mere inherence, then even from words such as *ākāśa* (ether), which denote a single individual, a dual ending would result. This is because, since duality and so forth have inherence in the ether of two jars and the like, it is impossible to claim that they do not exist in each individual ether—given the rule that "what is not inherent in each individually cannot be inherent in the aggregate"—since what does not reside in each member does not reside in the aggregate.

Nor should it be argued that the acceptance of *paryāpti* (collective inherence) is thus redundant, because there would be no loss [to the system] if the relation were simply an inherence qualified by being pervaded by the delimiting property of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka-vyāpyatva-viśiṣṭa-samavāya*). For, on the view that inherence is one, the inherence of duality residing in a jar exists even in a cloth; since that inherence is not pervaded by "jar-ness," this would lead to the unauthoritative status of expressions such as "two jars" (*ghaṭau*). However, if inherence is held to be manifold, then let *paryāpti* be simply those respective relations qualified by such pervasion.

Nor should it be argued that even so, since the duality residing in two jars exists in a single jar as well—by virtue of the relation of pervasion-based pervasion (*vyāpya-paryāpti*) with respect to jarhood—the expression "two jars" would result even when intending to refer to only one jar. This is not a fault, because a word expressing a property that resides distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) functions as a cause for conveying its own meaning as related to all of its substrata that are delimited by the delimitor of the relation of coreferentiality (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). Thus, there is no such error.

Nor should it be argued that one should simply accept that co-utterance with that [number] has the function of conveying its own meaning as connected to all members of its own substratum—what is the point of introducing the property of pervasion (*vyāpyatva*)? Furthermore, it cannot be said that this occurs "by way of collective predication" (*paryāpti*), because when there is a misconception of semantic competency regarding a sentence such as "there are two in space," a cognition of duality and so forth could arise with reference to only a single individual; thus, it would be impossible to postulate such a causal relationship. Moreover, [the notion of *paryāpti*] is untenable within the theory that maintains the oneness of duality and other numbers.

If this were so, then in cases such as "cut the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," the manifestation of their coexistence (*sāhitya*) would necessarily be required; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing two dualities (duality and so forth) that are subsumed under the properties of *dhava*-ness and *khadira*-ness which serve as the delimiters of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). And if that were the case, such an expression would be untenable when the intention is directed toward each individual *dhava* or *khadira* tree. To this we say: no. The rule regarding the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*) applies only where a single property serves as the delimiter of the relatum; it is only in such instances that there is a restriction on its being a relational property (*saṃsargatā*).

However, where there is suchness (*tathātva*) of multiple properties themselves, there it is so through the mere apprehension of the members (*parvan*). Or, because one accepts that inherence (*samavāya*) itself is the reality, there is no fault. This is precisely the way it is with words such as *puṣpavant* (the sun and moon), for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the manifestation of their coexistence (*sāhitya*) therein. Furthermore, if this were not accepted—that is, if the manifestation of coexistence were not admitted—the same untenability would persist. To explain: if there were a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) based on coexistence, since the two individual properties alone would be the delimiters of the relata (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), there would result the cognition of two distinct coexistences, each being pervaded by those respective [individuals]. Therefore, the method previously stated is the only recourse.

Nor should it be argued that, in such cases as "the two, wearing linen garments, should establish the sacred fire," the simultaneous connection (*samuccitya*) would not be obtained; for that is established by the sentence itself: "Whatever is to be done, that should be done together with her. Although there is no mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)—which consists of mutual connection—in a *dvandva* compound, nevertheless, the compound occurs by virtue of the rule "A *dvandva* is used in the sense of *ca* (and)" [Pāṇini 2.2.29]. It is clear from the Bhāṣya that there is no compound in the case of *samuccaya* (aggregation) and *anvācaya* (conjunction), because they are not denoted by the term *ca*.

As for the claim that "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists in being construed in a single form as the object (*karman*) and so forth with respect to a single action—introducing the phrase "in a single form" (*ekarūpeṇa*) in order to exclude cases such as "all was made by clay"—that is not correct, because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) within the *Samartha* Sūtra. Nor does this imply a failure of the case-ending's meaning to be construed [with the action], since there is a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes are construed with the meaning of their stem (*prakṛti*).

And here it must be stated that whatever is the *prakṛti* (base), the *dhava* and *khadira* are not its referents; and whatever are the referents of those two, those two do not possess the status of being the *prakṛti*. This is because it is accepted as a linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey the meaning of the element immediately preceding them. Furthermore, this "immediacy" is based on grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*). Thus, the meaning is: whichever suffix is prescribed after a particular element, it conveys its own meaning as pertaining to the meaning contained within that [preceding] element.

And here, a case-ending is prescribed for the aggregate of words (*padasamudāya*). In that regard, whether it refers to the meaning of the prior member, the subsequent member, or both, factors such as semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) serve as the determinants; thus, there is no fault in examples such as "half-a-pippali" (*ardhapippalīm*) or "look at the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaṃ paśya*). Likewise, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as "one who has brindled cows" (*citragu*), the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) belongs to the subsequent member alone, with respect to the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that if the word "cow" (*go*) were to indicate its owner (*gosvāmin*), there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with "variegated" (*citra*) therein—on the grounds that "a word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, but not with a part of a word-meaning"—because we accept that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs only after the mutual cognition of the two primary denotations (*śakyārtha*) has taken place.

There is no fault [in the analysis], because the word *go* (cow) itself indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the *citrapada* (the compound "variegated cow"), or because of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the word *go*. Others hold that due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), there is here a syntactic connection even with a single constituent part [of the compound].

Others maintain that by the word *go* (cow), the cow is denoted through primary power (*śakti*), while the owner is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and because of the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), there can be a mutual connection even between two things denoted by a single word. Thus, in this view, there is no necessity whatsoever for a "specific power" (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) or for "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). With this very point in mind, the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "Some maintain that semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) consists in mutual expectancy. This is precisely the position accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others.

Regarding this, they say: even in the case of words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), since the suffix and so forth can be accounted for through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which is qualified by lotus-ness, there would be the undesirable consequence of the abolition of conventional power (*rūḍhiśakti*). This is because understanding occurs even in one who is ignorant of the power of the individual components, because of sublation (*bādhaka*), because of the requirement of a restricted intention (*niyatatātparya*), and because authoritative persons employ the term "power" [in such cases]. If it is argued that [conventional power] is thus established, the same applies to the present case as well.

Furthermore, in cases such as "Kaṇṭhe kālaḥ" (Black on the neck) and "Dāsyāḥ putraḥ" (The son of a maidservant), since there is no evidence for secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the undesirable consequence of the connection with qualifiers such as "beautiful" would be unavoidable. Nor can it be argued that even there the word *dāsī* signifies the one related to the maidservant, for that would result in the cognition "the one related to the one related to the maidservant. Moreover, secondary signification of the genitive-ending [word] itself is difficult to establish, because its primary denotation (*śakya*) is absent. Even if the genitive were to signify the related party, it remains difficult to establish that the meaning of the word *dāsī* constitutes a single part [of that relation].

Furthermore, just as one might say "the man is related to the king" and "related to the wife," there would follow the undesirable consequence that "the king's man is related to the wife," and just as one says "the king's man is a horse," there would follow the consequence that "the king's man is a horse. If you argue that the derivation (*vyutpatti*) in a compound is entirely different [from that of its constituent parts], then the state of "becoming a single unified meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is established.

Furthermore, in the sentence *api ca kamaṇḍalupāṇiṃ chātram adrākṣīt* ("And he saw a student with a water-pot in his hand"), the word *kamaṇḍalu* would incur the application of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) by the rule *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.21). Nor can there be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), because [the case-ending] arises after the compound has been formed and thus is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Even if it were included by the principle of "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of its ends," there is no proof that it is a constituent part of the stem;
this is clear from the commentary of Bhartṛhari and Kaiyaṭa on the rule *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*.

Furthermore, in your view, it is difficult to provide a definition of "functionality" (*vṛttitva*) that applies commonly to primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), and so forth—meaning a definition characterized by being one of the following: a primary derivative, a secondary derivative, a residual formation (*ekaśeṣa*), a verb with prefixes or suffixes (*sanādyanta-dhātu*), or a compound formation (*vṛtti*). This is because, as previously stated, the property of being a "composite whole" (*samudāyatva*) would over-apply to a sentence (*vākya*), just as the capacity [to convey meaning] does. [Note: "Being one of several" (*anyatamatva*) means being distinct from each of those non-distinct entities.]

And thus, because the entire range of entities is included as the counter-correlates of difference (*bhedapratiyogin*), there is prolixity (*gaurava*); this is the sense. Furthermore, [the property of] being "one or another" (*anyatamatva*) is even more cumbersome. For me, however, it is easy to state that it is a collective entity (*samudāyatva*), just like the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

Furthermore, if you undertake the statement for the sake of preventing a sentence from having the same meaning [as a compound], that involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor is there metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the usage of a compound, because the distinction between "compound" and "otherwise a sentence" remains possible; thus, this [distinction] is not necessary for me either, since there is no metaphorical indication in a *karmadhāraya* compound. For me, however, the rule is that a word-formation (*vṛtti*) occurs when there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), whereas "otherwise it is a sentence" is merely a statement of a fact established by logic.

Furthermore, in cases such as *vāpyaśvaḥ* ("a horse at the pond"), there would be the undesirable consequence of [the word *vāpī*] being treated as a *pragṛhya*. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault here because the word *vāpī* possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its locus being a river, and thus it does not terminate solely in the sense of the locative case; for then the same fault would arise in examples such as *somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ* ("Soma is placed upon Gaurī"), since even there, due to the elision of the case-ending, the secondary signification of the word *gaurī* as "that which has Gaurī as its locus" would be equally necessary in order to account for the syntactic connection between the meanings of the two nouns. For me, however, there is no such fault.

This is because [the word *samudāya*] does not terminate merely in the sense of the locative case—namely, the capacity to produce a mental representation (*upasthiti*) as being unmixed with other [words].
It is with this very intention that the *Bhāṣya* states: "And there is no fault in the case of *ajahatsvārthā* [compounding], for the meaning of the whole (*samudāyārtha*) is denoted.

By this, the view that *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) consists solely in *jahatsvārthatā* (abandonment of own-meaning), while *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy) is what constitutes *ajahatsvārthā*, and that the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *īdūtau* [Pāṇini 1.1.19] supports only the theory of *vyapekṣā*, is refuted.

Furthermore, just as in the case of the expression "the man of the wealthy god" (*ṛddhasya devasya puruṣaḥ*), which is formed by a *karmadhāraya* compound—such as "the man of the wealthy god"—there arises a cognition characterized by a specific objective relation (*viṣayatā*) based on the principle that "the qualifier [resides] in the qualified" (*viśeṣye viśeṣaṇam*). In that case, there would also arise the undesirable consequence (*sādhutvāpatti*) of such a cognition being grammatically correct even when another qualifier is added, such as "and there is another qualifier therein. For me, however, there is no such fault, because the meaning of the word "wealthy" (*ṛddha*), having attained semantic unity (*ekārthībhūta*) within the compound, connects only with the state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) by that [god].

Furthermore, because a composite whole lacks semantic significance (*arthavattva*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) would be difficult to establish. Moreover, by relying on the method previously mentioned, the application of the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) in the subsequent sūtra would not be obtained. However, for me, that [application] is obtained through the force of the continued reference to the word "semantically significant" (*arthavat*); this is clear from the authoritative treatise (*ākara*). For you, however, even if that [word] were continued, since only *kṛt*- and *taddhita*-derivatives possess semantic significance, the opposite fault would indeed arise.

Furthermore, in the word *pūrvaśālā* occurring in compounds such as *pūrvaśālapriyaḥ*, there would arise the undesirable consequence of its being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, this fault does not apply when the rule of "behaving like a subsequent member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) is applied, because by the very mention of the condition for that rule, cases such as *ṛtena* are excluded from undergoing *parāṅgavadbhāva*. As for forms such as *mitrāvaruṇau*, they should be understood as Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Alternatively, because those two are the agents of the act of making the *ṛt* sound, they certainly possess the status of being its cause as well. For this very reason, regarding the rule *subāmantrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), it is asked: "What is the purpose of the term *asub*? [Consider the example: *karoṣyaṭayana*. This is not valid; it will not apply here due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). This is not a fault."

Having stated that [the rule] "that which is in grammatical apposition is as if non-existent" (*samānādhikaraṇam asarvavibhakti*) is negated by the rule "not when expressed by a verbal root" (*adhātvabhihitam*), [the author] says: "The genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be prescribed for the meaning of the vocative (*āmantrita*) with respect to whatever is its *kāraka*, or else the phrase 'having that as its cause' (*tannimitta*) should be included. This has the sense that "whatever is the *kāraka* with respect to the meaning of the vocative becomes as if it were a subordinate member (*pārāṅgavadbhūta*)."

This is consistent with what is stated in the Bhāṣya: "It should apply only in cases such as *madrāṇāṃ rājan, paraśunā vṛśyan*, but not in cases such as *kṣatreṇāgne svāyuḥ saṃrabhasva* and *mitreṇāgne mitradheye yatasva*, where [the rule] *kṣatreṇa mitreṇa* [would otherwise apply]. For if the paribhāṣā regarding semantic competency (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) were to apply here, the non-application [of the rule] would be due solely to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), and the aforementioned statement in the Bhāṣya would clearly be inconsistent.

As for what Kaiyaṭa stated regarding "kṣatreṇa" and so forth—that "there exists a semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) mediated by action"—that is not correct; for if one holds the theory of *vyapekṣā*, there would result the undesirable formation of a compound in cases such as "kṛtaḥ sarvo mṛttikyā" (the entire jar was made). Furthermore, in instances such as "bho devadatta" or "bhago devadatta," the word "bhoḥ" and others would certainly not possess the status of being subordinate members (*parāṅga*) [of a subsequent vocative].

Although two statements have been initiated in the Bhāṣya, nevertheless, the inclusion of the condition *tannimitta* (having that as its cause) alone is superior, because even in the case of "goṣu svāmin" (the owner of the cows), the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) would not be established [without this condition]. For this very reason, in examples such as "vastraṃ rājñaḥ puruṣāgaccha" (the king's cloth, O man, come), there is no status of being like a subsequent member. As for the Vedabhāṣya, however, it is simply not to be accepted due to its contradiction with the Phaṇibhāṣya (the Mahābhāṣya); such is the direction of the argument.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, however, since the non-difference between the two word-meanings presented through their respective component powers (*avayava-śakti*) can be apprehended as a relation (*saṃsarga*) itself, there is neither primary denotation (*śakti*) nor indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In an *avyayībhāva* such as *upakumbham*, there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the words *upa-kumbha* and so forth; the word *upa* and the like serve to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*).

Therefore, in cases such as "bring one who possesses a horse" (*dhavavantam ānaya*), there is no conflict with the established linguistic rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as residing in the meaning of the immediately preceding word, because this rule serves to prevent the connection of [the suffix's meaning] with the objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth [of the horse]. For this very reason, even in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) such as *pāṇipādam* ("hands-and-feet"), the final member (*uttarapada*) bears a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the collection of hands and feet.

As for the claim that there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the whole [of the compound], that is not so, because such a thing lacks the capacity [for denotation]. For indication is indeed "a relation with what is denotable" (*śakyasambandha*). Now, [the author] sets forth and refutes the Mīmāṃsaka position with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), and so on: "Indication is simply a relation with what is made known (*jñāpyasambandha*); this alone is appropriate in accordance with examples such as 'a hamlet on the deep river' (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). To explain: first of all, the word *gabhīra* ("deep") cannot indicate the bank, because it would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the word *nadyām* ("on the river"); for the bank is not...

[Objection: It follows that even in the word *nadī* ("river"), the bank qualified by depth (*gabhīra*) is not indicated [by indication], because the word *gabhīra* can itself function as the qualificand within the process of indication. Nor should it be argued that, since the word *nadī* denotes a substance (*dravya*), indication must reside in it alone due to its direct connection with that [bank]; for the word *gabhīra* also denotes a permanent possessor of qualities (*nityaguṇin*), and thus it too possesses a direct connection [with the bank].

Therefore, since there is no decisive reason [to prefer one over the other] and because there is complexity (gaurava) in assuming figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for both words, it should be accepted with parsimony (lāghava) that it resides in the whole sentence alone. If it is argued that for this very reason they say that figurative indication of excellence resides in an explanatory passage (arthavāda), we say no; for then figurative indication would also result in the case of corrupt words (apabhraṃśa), since that which is indicated by them exists. Furthermore, if this were so, since there would be no decisive reason [to choose between] each individual word, the whole sentence, or both, there would be excessive complexity (atigaurava) due to the resulting indication in both the two words and the sentence.

Moreover, the phrase "connection with that which is indicated" means a connection with an object that possesses the state of being indicated (jñāpyatā) as determined by the state of being an indicator (jñāpakatā) residing in itself.

In this context, what constitutes "indicative-ness" (jñāpakatva): is it the capacity to produce the cognition of a meaning through a linguistic function (vṛtti), or is it merely being the object of a cognition that produces the cognition of a meaning?

Not the first [alternative], because it would result in the absence of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the sentence. Not the last, because if even individual phonemes were to possess meaning, it would follow that case-endings and so forth must be produced for them. Moreover, this being the case, one would have to state that even the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) constituted by the words is the delimitor of the capacity to indicate (*lakṣakatāvacchedikā*), which is an excessive burden (*atigaurava*). For me, however, since that [sequence] is absent in the sentence, it is not so; thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*). If indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in a relation with the indicated (*jñāpya*), then indication results in the very presentation of the object as "this is related to that," which is the cognition of the indicator (*jñāpaka*); in other words, it is produced.

Furthermore, they argue that by such [a definition], even space—which is related to a jar or the like through inherence (*samavāya*) and other relations—would result in being an object of verbal cognition when it is presented [to the mind] as denoted by words such as "jar. Therefore, it is more appropriate to define *lakṣaṇā* simply as "a relation with the denotable" (*śakyasambandha*). And it is quite clear that this [relation] is not the aggregate [of meanings]. As for the fact that the collective whole (*samāhāra*) is the object of the act of playing and so forth, it should be understood through a mediated relation (*paramparā*), such as [the action] residing in its own substratum.

Alternatively, since no collective sense (*samāhāra*) is understood there, there is no metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is direct. As for the dual number and so forth, they do not apply because the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) indicates that such usage would be incorrect. However, the conventional designation of this as a "collective copulative compound" (*samāhāra-dvandva*) should be understood as figurative; for while in a copulative compound of body parts (*prāṇyaṅga*) and the like, the singular number is prescribed, here the copulative compound itself serves as the cause for the singular, just as it does in a collective sense. Similarly, even in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*), there is metaphorical indication of the two [referents] as qualified by their association (*sāhitya*); therefore, the dual number and so forth can be applied. In the case of a collective compound, however, the association is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), which is the distinction between the two cases.

Alternatively, there is no metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here either; for it is possible for two meanings, presented by their respective powers (*śakti*) from two words mounted upon a single recollection (*smṛti*), to be connected with duality and so forth—whether that connection consists in their being related to a single action, or in their being delimited by a single cognition, or in one thing delimited by a single property being connected to another thing delimited by the same property through a relation delimited by that same property. And this "delimiting property" (*ekadharma*) is of the nature of a collective totality (*samudāyatva*).

And thus, in the usage "worship the Lord and the teacher" (*īśvaraṃ guruñca bhajasva*), because there is an absence of co-occurrence (*sāhitya*) when the Lord and the teacher are construed with two distinct actions in the form of meditation and service respectively, a compound is not formed. This is because co-occurrence is understood only subsequently, and it is therefore inappropriate for it to be present at the time of the initial application of the defining rule (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nor should it be argued that if there is no manifestation of *sāhitya* (conjunction), then when one intends the connection of one action with either of two [objects], there would result the undesirable usage "Look at the *dhava* and cut the *khadira*"—just like the sentence "Look at the *dhava*, cut the *khadira*"—because it is more appropriate for the connection to occur in only one [of the two] as delimited by a single property, namely duality (*dvitva*).

Nor should it be argued that without *sāhitya* as the delimitor of the fitness (*yogyatā*) for the connection with duality, such a connection with duality is impossible; for the presence of the delimitor of fitness is not required, since the rule is simply that a connection occurs only with that which is fit once it has been presented.

For this very reason, in cases such as "Bring water with a jar," the word "jar" conveys the meaning of "that which is other than one with holes" by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a dual number even from words like "space" when referring to a single individual, because duality and so forth exist in a *paryāpti*-relation in the "jar-space" and the like, making it impossible to claim that they are absent in each individual space (since the rule holds: "what is not *paryāpta* in each individual cannot be *paryāpta* in the aggregate"), for what does not reside in each member individually does not reside in the aggregate.

Nor should it be argued that because there is neither one nor two, cognition [of such a negation] is impossible; for even in the case of a single entity, since the relation of absolute pervasion (*kevalaparyāpti*) exists, it is impossible to cognize a difference whose counter-positive-locus-delimitation is delimited by the delimitation of the counter-positive-ness conditioned by the relation of absolute pervasion. Furthermore, it cannot be said that a difference whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by the delimitation of the counter-positive-ness conditioned by the relation of pervasion-by-oneness (*ekatvavyāpyaparyāpti*) is simply non-existent (*aprasiddha*).

Because there is a rule that the pervasion (*paryāpti*) of duality and so forth must be delimited by a property residing in both [terms], there is no obstacle to the occurrence of the exclusion of that [duality]—delimited by a property residing in only one of them which does not delimit it—within that which possesses it.

Nor should it be argued that the very acceptance of *paryāpti* (collective pervasion) is useless, because there would be no harm if the relation were simply inherence (*samavāya*) qualified by being pervaded by the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). For, according to the view that inherence is one, the inherence of duality residing in a jar exists even in a cloth; since it would thus not be pervaded by "jar-ness," expressions such as "two jars" (*ghaṭau*) would result in being invalid. However, if inherence is held to be manifold, then let *paryāpti* be simply those respective relations qualified by such pervasion.

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, since the duality residing in two jars exists in a single jar as well—by virtue of its relation of non-pervasion with respect to the property of being a jar (ghaṭatva)—the linguistic usage "two jars" would result even when intending to refer to only one jar; for there is no such fault, because a word expressing a property that resides distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti) functions as a cause for conveying its own meaning only when it is construed with all of its substrates as delimited by the property that serves as the locus of the relation (anvayitāvacchedaka).

Furthermore, one might argue: "Let it be accepted that co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) possesses the capacity to convey its own meaning as connected to all its own substrata; what is the use of including 'pervasion' (*vyāpyatva*)? Moreover, why say 'by way of pervasion' (*paryāptyā*)? This must be answered: because from a sentence such as "there are two in space" (*ākāśe dvau*), when there is a state of error regarding semantic fitness (*yogyatā*), a cognition arises in which duality and so forth are construed with only a single individual; thus, it is impossible to postulate such a causal relationship [of co-utterance]. Furthermore, this is because [duality and the like] would be impossible under the view that maintains the identity of oneness (*ekatva*).

And thus, in cases such as "cut the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," the manifestation of their association (*sāhitya*) is necessary. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing two duality instances—each pervaded by the *dhava*-ness and *khadira*-ness that serve as the delimiters of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). If it is argued that this leads to the impossibility of such usage when the intention is directed toward a single *dhava* or *khadira* tree respectively, we say no; for the rule that such a collective pervasion (*paryāpti*) functions as the relation (*saṃsarga*) applies only where a single property serves as the delimiter of the relatum.

However, where there is suchness (*tathātva*) of multiple properties themselves, there it is so because of the apprehension of the mere [properties] alone; or, since one accepts that inherence (*samavāya*) itself is the reality, there is no fault. This is precisely the way it is with words such as *puṣpavant* (the sun and moon), for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the manifestation of their coexistence (*sāhitya*) therein. Furthermore, if this were not accepted—even if the manifestation of coexistence were admitted—the same untenability would persist. To explain: in the case of a connection with coexistence, since the two individual properties would be the delimiters of the relata (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), there would result the cognition of two distinct coexistences, each being pervaded by those [individual properties]. Therefore, the previously mentioned method alone is the refuge.

Nor should it be argued that, in such cases as "Wearing two linen garments, let them two establish the sacred fire," the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the two items combined would not be achieved; for that is established by the sentence-meaning: "Whatever is to be done, let that be done together with this. Although there is no semantic requirement for mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)—which consists of mutual syntactic connection—in a *dvandva* compound, nevertheless, the compound is formed by the force of the rule "A *dvandva* [is used] in the sense of *ca* (and)" [Pāṇini 2.2.29]. It is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that there is no compound in the case of *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *anvācaya* (subordinate conjunction), because they are not denoted by that rule.

As for the claim that "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists in being construed with a single action in a uniform manner—as in the case of [the objecthood] of *karman* and so forth—the phrase "in a uniform manner" is used to exclude examples such as "everything was made by means of clay" (*kṛtaḥ sarvo mṛttikayā*). That is not correct, because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) within the *Samartha-sūtra*. Nor does this imply a failure of the case-endings to connect with their meanings, since there is a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes are construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

And here it must be stated that the *prakṛti* (base) is not for the sake of the *dhava* and *khadira* trees, nor is the status of being a *prakṛti* possessed by those two for the sake of what they signify; for it is precisely the established linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey the meaning of the element immediately preceding them. Furthermore, this "immediacy" is based on grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*). Thus, the meaning is: whichever suffix is prescribed after a particular element, it conveys its own meaning as pertaining to the meaning contained within that [preceding] element.

And here, the case-ending is taught as belonging to the aggregate of words (*padasamudāya*). In that regard, whether it applies to the meaning of the prior member, the subsequent member, or both, factors such as semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) serve as the determinants; thus, there is no fault in examples such as "half-a-pippalī" (*ardhapippalīm*) or "look at the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaṃ paśya*). Likewise, in Bahuvrīhi compounds such as "one who has brindled cows" (*citragu*), the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) belongs to the subsequent member alone, with respect to the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). Nor is it the case that if the word *go* (cow) were to signify the owner of the cow, the connection with "brindled" (*citra*) would not occur therein—[for] "the meaning of a word connects with the meaning of a word, but [not with the word itself]."

The intention is that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is "by means of a portion of the word-meaning. Alternatively, one might say it is because [the word-meaning] is a portion of the referent; however, this is not correct, because it is accepted that *lakṣaṇā* (implication) occurs only after the comprehension of the connection between the two primary meanings (*śakyārtha*). There is no fault, either because the word "variegated" (*citra*) functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), such that the word "cow" (*go*) alone implies the owner of the variegated cows, or because *lakṣaṇā* applies to the owner of the variegated cows. Others hold that due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti-vaicitrya*), there is here a syntactic connection even with a single part [of the compound].

Others maintain that by the word *go* (cow), the cow is expressed through primary denotation (*śakti*), while the owner is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); furthermore, due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), there can be a mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*) even between two things denoted by a single word. Thus, in this view, there is no necessity whatsoever for a "specialized power" (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) or for "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). It is with this very intention that the venerable Commentator stated: "Some maintain that semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists in mutual expectancy. And it is precisely this position that is accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others.

Regarding this, they argue: even in cases such as the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"), since the suffix and so forth can be accounted for through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) directed toward that which is qualified by lotus-ness (*padmatva*), it would follow that the conventional power (*rūḍhiśakti*) is eliminated. This is because understanding occurs even in one who does not know the individual parts or their individual powers, because understanding occurs even without reflecting on sublation (*bādhādi*) and so forth, because of the necessity of following a fixed intention (*niyatatātparya*), and because the learned (*prāmāṇika*) employ the term "power" [in this case]. If this is argued, it applies equally to the present case as well.

Furthermore, in cases such as "Kaṇṭhe kālaḥ" (Black on the neck) and "Dāsyāḥ putraḥ" (The son of a slave-girl), since there is no evidence for *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the undesirable consequence of the connection with qualifiers such as "beautiful" (*sundara*) would be unavoidable. Nor can it be argued that even there the word *dāsī* indicates the "one related to a slave-girl," because that would result in the cognition "the one related to a slave-girl" (*dāsīsambandhī*). Moreover, it is difficult to justify *lakṣaṇā* in the final member of the genitive compound, as it lacks primary denotative power (*śakti*). Even if one were to assume *lakṣaṇā* in the genitive suffix itself to denote the "one related to [her]," it remains difficult to justify how the meaning of the word *dāsī* could constitute a single part (*ekadeśa*) of that referent.

Furthermore, just as from the expressions "a rough person related to the king" (*paruṣo rājasambandhī*) and "related to the wife" (*bhāryāsambandhī*), one might erroneously derive "the king's rough person is related to the wife" (*rājapuruṣo bhāryāsambandhī*); and just as from "the king's rough person is a horse" (*rājasambandhī paruṣo'śvaḥ*), one might erroneously derive "the king's person is a horse" (*rājapuruṣo'śvaḥ*). If it is argued that the derivation (*vyutpatti*) in a compound is indeed distinct [from its constituent parts], then the state of "becoming a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is established.

Furthermore, in the example *kamaṇḍalupārṇiṃ chātram adrākṣīt* ("He saw the student with a water-pot"), the word *kamaṇḍalu* would incur the application of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) by the rule *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.21). Nor can there be elision (*luk*) by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (2.4.71), because [the suffix] arises after a compound and thus is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This is because, although it is included under the term *prātipadika* by the maxim *tanmadhyapatati*, there is no evidence for its being a constituent part of that [stem]. This is clear from the commentary of both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the rule *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*.

Furthermore, in your view, it is difficult to state a definition of *vṛtti* (grammatical integration) that applies commonly to *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compounds; for the definition characterized as being "one of the five types of *vṛtti*"—namely, *kṛt*, *taddhita*, *ekaśeṣa*, *sanādyanta-dhātu*, and compound—is [inapplicable]. This is because, just like the aforementioned semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), the property of being a "composite whole" (*samudāyatva*) is over-extended (*atiprasakta*) to the sentence (*vākya*). [Note: "Being one of the five" means being different from each of those non-distinct entities.]

And thus, the sense is that there is complexity (gaurava) because the entire range of entities enters [into the definition] as the counter-correlates of difference; furthermore, the property of being "one or another" (anyatamatva) is even more cumbersome. For me, however, it is quite easy to state that it possesses a collective nature (sudāyatva), just like the state of unified meaning (ekārthībhāva).

Furthermore, if you undertake this statement to prevent the application of the term "sentence" (*vākya*) to a compound that has the same meaning [as a sentence], you incur unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor does the compound arise through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for since the distinction between a compound and a sentence is possible otherwise, this [distinction] is not necessary even for me, as there is no secondary indication in a *karmadhāraya*. For me, however, the rule is that a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) occurs when there is unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), whereas otherwise it is a sentence; thus, that [statement] merely expresses a meaning established by logic.

Furthermore, in cases such as *vāpyaśvaḥ* ("a horse at the pond"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the word being treated as a *pragṛhya*. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault here because the word *vāpī* possesses a secondary metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to that which is located in the pond, and thus it does not terminate solely in the sense of the locative case; for then [the rule] would fail to apply even in cases such as *somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ* ("Soma is placed upon the Gaurī"). There too, since the case-ending is elided, a metaphorical indication of the word *gaurī* as "that which is located in the Gaurī" must equally be admitted in order to account for the syntactic connection between the meanings of the two nouns.

But for me, there is no fault, because [the compound] does not terminate merely in the meaning of the locative case—which is the nature of that which generates the mental presence [of the referent] as being unmixed with others.

It is with this very intention that it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "And in the case of *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandonment of own-meaning), there is no fault, for the collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*) is denoted.

By this, the view that *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) consists solely of *jahatsvārthatā* (abandonment of own-meaning), while *ajahatsvārthā* is nothing but *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy)—and the claim that the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "īdūtau" [Pāṇini 1.1.19] supports only the theory of *vyapekṣā*—is refuted.

Furthermore, just as in the sentence "the man of the wealthy god" (*ṛddhasya devasya puruṣaḥ*), there is the fault of [the cognition] possessing a cognitive object (*viṣayatā*) characterized by the "qualificandness of the qualified" (*vaiśiṣṭyaviśiṣṭatva*)—as in the case of "the man of the wealthy god," which is formed by a *karmadhāraya* compound—wherein the qualifier [is related] to the qualificand, and therein yet another qualifier; even though such a cognitive object is present in the understanding, the undesirable consequence of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) would follow. For me, however, there is no such fault, because that which has become fused in meaning with "wealthy" (*ṛddha*) does not undergo further syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through its own qualificative character.

Furthermore, because a composite whole (*samudāya*) lacks semantic meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) would be difficult to justify. If one were to rely on the method previously mentioned [referring to the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*], then the application of the rule of "extension by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) in the subsequent sūtra would not be possible. For me, however, the attainment of that [extension] is clear from the *Ākara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*), due to the force of the continued reference to "meaningful words" (*arthavatpada*). But for you, even if that [reference] were continued, since only *kṛt*-affixes and *taddhita*-derivatives possess semantic meaningfulness, the opposite fault would indeed arise.

Furthermore, in the case of compounds such as *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the initial member (*pūrvaśālā*) being treated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, this fault does not arise if the rule of "behaving like the subsequent member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) is applied; for by the very mention of the cause [of that application] in the sūtra *ṛtēna tyādeḥ*, the application of "behaving like the subsequent member" is prevented in such cases. As for forms like *mitrāvaruṇau*, one should understand that they are Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Alternatively, because they are the agents of the increase that has *ṛt* as its object, they indeed possess the status of being the cause (*nimitta*) for that [prohibition]. For this very reason, regarding the rule *subāmantrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), it is asked: "What is the purpose of [the term] *asub*? [Consider: *karoṣyaṭayana*. This is not a valid example; it will not apply here due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). This is not a fault."

Having stated that [the rule] "that which is in grammatical apposition is as if lacking in capacity" (*samānādhikaraṇamasamarthavat*) is negated by the rule "not when expressed by a verbal root" (*adhātvabhihitam*), he says: "Alternatively, the mention of the genitive case and the vocative as being *kārakas* should be made; or rather, the mention of the cause (*nimitta*) for that [apposition] should be performed," meaning that whatever *kāraka* stands in relation to the object of the vocative in the genitive case, that alone becomes like a subsequent member (*pārāṅgavat*).

This is consistent with what is stated in the Bhāṣya: "It should apply only in cases such as *madrāṇāṃ rājan, paraśunā vṛśyan*, but not in cases such as *kṣatreṇāgne svāyuḥ saṃrabhasva* and *mitreṇāgne mitradheye yatasva*, where [the rule] would otherwise apply to the words *kṣatreṇa* and *mitreṇa*. For if the paribhāṣā regarding semantic competency (*samartha*) were to apply here, the rule would simply not apply due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*), making the Bhāṣya's statement clearly inconsistent.

As for what Kaiyaṭa stated regarding examples such as *kṣatreṇa*—"There exists a capacity (*sāmarthya*) characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) mediated by action; thus, there would be the treatment as if it were a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). Since over-extension has been ruled out here by this specific rule, in the preceding sūtra, capacity was understood to be exclusively 'integration into a single meaning' (*ekārthībhāva*). Otherwise, both types of capacity would have to be resorted to"—this passage from Kaiyaṭa’s work follows that sequence [of argumentation]. That is not correct.

In the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), there would be the undesirable consequence of compounding (*samāsa*) in cases such as *akṛtaḥ sarvo mṛttikyā* ("the entire jar was made by the potter's wife"). Furthermore, in examples such as *bho devadatta* or *bhago devadatta*, the word *bhoḥ* and others would certainly not possess the status of being a subordinate member (*parāṅga*) [of the following word]. Although two statements were initiated in the *Bhāṣya*, nevertheless, the option of taking the cause (*nimitta*) alone is superior, because even in the case of *goṣu svāmin*, the status of being a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) is not established. For this very reason, in cases such as *vastraṃ rājñaḥ puruṣāgaccha*, there is no status of being a subordinate member.
As for the *Vedabhāṣya*, however, it is simply not to be accepted because it contradicts the *Phaṇibhāṣya* (Patañjali’s *Mahābhāṣya*); such is the direction of the argument.

As for the objection that in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, if one accepts figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the first member (*pūrvapada*) as denoting the relation, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a *karmadhāraya*—since being a *samānādhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa* is precisely what constitutes that [type of compound]—it cannot be argued that a *karmadhāraya* occurs only where there is non-difference (*abheda*) in the state prior to compounding, whereas a mere *tatpuruṣa* occurs where there is difference (*bheda*). For such a definition would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to those *tatpuruṣas* and *karmadhārayas* that are mandatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), since they lack an analytical statement (*vigraha*); and even if an "unworldly" (*alaukika*) analytical statement were present, it is by nature incapable of producing a cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*).

Nor should it be argued that *karmadhāraya* status applies only where there is identical case-ending (*tulyavibhaktitva*) prior to the compound and not otherwise; for since the preceding state must be postulated solely in accordance with the speaker’s intention to express a non-compounded meaning, and since there is no difference in cognition regarding the compound sentence according to your view, it is impossible to postulate any distinction between them. That being so—

No; for a distinction is possible: *karmadhāraya* status applies where, while the meaning of the constituent member of the compound is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words constituting that compound—without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—by including [the meanings] of case-endings capable of arising after them; whereas in cases of coreferentiality through figurative indication by including those [meanings], it is otherwise. By the "existence" clause (*satyanta*), exclusions such as *pañcamūlī* are avoided.

Furthermore, in order to exclude expressions such as "the rice cooks" (*odanaḥ pacati*), the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is simply that "the cognition produced by the *sup*-inflection is the cause of any cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). This is due to parsimony (*lāghava*); there is no need to include specifications such as "by a relation other than identity" (*abhedātirikta-saṃsargeṇa*). In cases such as "bring the blue pot" (*nīlaṃ ghaṭam ānaya*), both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) are individually construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), while their mutual connection through identity (*abhedānvaya*) occurs subsequently (*pārṣṇika*). As stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The mat is also the object (*karman*), and Bhīṣma and the others are also [objects]."

Now, an objection may be raised: here, in the sense of "done by the supreme agent" (*parameṇa kārakeṇa kṛtam*), the formation of a compound with a fully inflected case-ending is untenable due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). If it is argued that semantic connection is established by assuming a connection through the mediation of the *pārṣṇika* (the subsequent member), then in postulating such a non-worldly (*alaukika*) construction, there arises the contingency of the disappearance of the case-ending caused by the connection with the verb, on the grounds that the cause has ceased. To this we say: no; for according to the authority of the rule prescribing compounds within the section on co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) terms, it is accepted that the effect persists even when the cause has disappeared.

In expressions such as "Caitra cooks," "the blue pot," and "he cooks slightly," the meaning of the nominative case and so forth is indeed non-difference (*abheda*). It should not be argued that since the appearance of non-difference as a relation is logically possible, it is cumbersome to postulate a specific denotative function (*vṛtti*) for the case-ending; for where the attributive case-ending has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding non-difference, there is no established linguistic rule (*avyutpatti*) whereby the sentence "the blue pot" could produce a cognition having difference as its qualifier. Therefore, rather than postulating that the knowledge of such a co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) is the cause of two distinct types of cognition, it is simpler to postulate a specific denotative function.

It should not be argued that, according to this view, from the sentence "A non-pot is not blue" (*aghaṭo na nīlaḥ*), there would only be the cognition of the absence of non-difference from blue, and not the cognition of difference from blue; for it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that when a negative particle occurs in such a co-occurrence, it conveys the absence—qualified by the relation by which the possession of a property was previously cognized in the locus—of that very property in that locus. This objection is invalid, because we accept the consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

The cognition of the difference from blue, however, is indeed objective. [Note: It is accepted by all that the absence of absolute non-existence has the nature of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and the absence of the absence of difference has the nature of the delimiting property of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). In this context, the author of the text accepts that the absence of non-difference has the nature of its counter-positive; thus, there is a third path. This is because, in this case, the absence of identity has the very nature of its counter-positive.

Furthermore, because there is no lack of co-referentiality among the entities, in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground," the cognition of the absence of that [jar] is established through the cognition of the absence of existence whose agent is the jar, just as the cognition of the absence of the jar [is established].

And thus, since there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) without mediating the meaning of the case-ending, the resulting impossibility of a construction such as "the person is non-different from that which is related to the king" remains exactly as it was. That too is not correct, because in cases such as "that curd stands" (*tad dadhi tiṣṭhati*), a [syntactic] connection would not be established. Nor can it be argued that understanding arises there through the recollection of the elided suffix, for understanding would not arise in one who is unaware of the elision (*luk*).
