And if it is argued that in that case the word "curd" (*dadhi*) does not possess the status of a noun (*nāman*), then it is equally true that the word "king" (*rājan*) likewise lacks that status because its case-suffix has been elided.

Nor should it be argued that, even when there is no apprehension of the word *dadhi* as having curd as its object (i.e., when it is not understood as *dadhi-karmaka*), the understanding of the connection with "seeing" (*darśana*) as having curd as its object does not arise during the state of mistaking it for a word ending in a case-suffix other than the accusative; therefore, since the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the verb *paśya* with a word such as *dadhi* ending in the accusative must necessarily be the cause [of the cognition], the reconstruction of the elided accusative suffix is indispensable. For the same would apply to expressions like *rājapuruṣa*, where, during the state of mistaking the compound for one composed of words ending in case-suffixes other than the genitive...

Because the cognition "the person related to the king" does not arise [from the compound *rājapuruṣa*], even in that case, the necessary reconstruction of the elided genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is required. If one attempts to resolve this by asserting that the knowledge of *tātparya* (intention) and so forth serves as the causal factor, then the situation is the same for us; such is the direction of the argument.

Furthermore, just as in cases like "the blue substance is the pot," in a *karmadhāraya* compound such as "the blue-pot-substance" (*nīlaghaṭo dravyam*), there would result the undesirable consequence of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the blue and the substance through the principle of "two things in one substratum" (*ekatra dvayam*). Nor can it be argued that when there is a cognition of a noun-meaning as the predicate delimited by identity...

It should not be argued that there is no fault because the cause [of the cognition] is the presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case; for then in cases such as *dadhi dravyam* ("curd is a substance"), such a cognition would likewise fail to arise. Furthermore, the status of being "ending in the nominative" is equally present here even when the nominative suffix is elided (*lupta*). Moreover, since the relation of subject and predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*) within a compound will later be refuted, it would be unavoidable—by that same logic—that the object of the word *nīla* (blue), like the compound itself, would have to be related as a mere qualifier (*śuddha-prakāratayā*).

Furthermore, just as in the case of "the learned Brāhmaṇa" (*paṇḍito brāhmaṇaḥ*), "cook" (*pācakaḥ*), or "reader" (*pāṭhakaḥ*), the notion of *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) is necessary to prevent the relation of subject and predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*) in compounds such as *paṇḍita-brāhmaṇaḥ* or *pācaka-pāṭhaka*. For when that [integration] exists, just as from the word *ghaṭa-paṭa* there arises only the presentation of the two meanings [pot and cloth] as conjoined with one another, and not their individual presentations, there is no fault because the individual presentation—which would otherwise govern such a relation—is absent.

For this very reason, regarding the passage "The first consumption belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer" (*vaṣaṭkartuḥ prathamabhakṣaḥ*), one might suspect that it results in an injunction of priority by means of a reference (*anuvāda*) to a consumption qualified by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer; however, [the Mīmāṃsakas] maintain that "first consumption" (*prathamabhakṣaḥ*) is a single, composite word. In that case, because of its unitary semantic flow (*ekaprasaratva*), it is not logical to enjoin priority through one part while aiming at a consumption qualified by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer through another part; for if that were so, the compound would not exist due to a split in the semantic flow (*prasārabheda*) and the resulting destruction of syntactic unity (*sāmarthyavighāta*).
By this, the view that priority is enjoined by means of a reference to mere consumption alone is also refuted.

Nor does the meaning [of the Mīmāṃsakas] imply that there is no *vṛtti* (grammatical compounding) because of the rule: "There is no compounding of words with qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇānām*), nor is there a connection of a qualifier with what has already been compounded. For even though the primary element (*pradhāna*) exists as something qualified, there is no deficiency [in the formation]. Therefore, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that this is an injunction for a different kind of consumption (*bhakṣāntaravidhi*).

Nor should it be argued that in this view, since there is an absence of the initial occurrence of the word denoting the subject (*uddeśya*)—such as its connection with the particle *yat*—and an absence of the subsequent occurrence of the word denoting the predicate (*vidheya*)—such as its connection with the particle *tad*, how can such a syntactic relation (*anvaya*) be established? For such a cognition is observed even in cases like "the first [instance] is the eating" (*prathamo bhakṣaḥ*) or "the Brāhmaṇa is learned" (*paṇḍito brāhmaṇaḥ*), which shows that [the aforementioned conditions] are not invariably concomitant.

Therefore, what is essential for the cognition of such a syntactic relation is simply the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a word denoting the predicate that is co-occurrent with the word denoting the subject and whose meaning is not [otherwise] connected [to that subject].

By this, the view that presentation as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is the regulating factor for being the predicate (*vidheya*) is also refuted, because [the word] presents [its meaning] as the qualificand from the very word itself. As for the claim by rhetoricians (*ālaṅkārika*) that there is a failure to apprehend the predicate (*vidheyāvimarśa*) even in the absence of immediate succession to the subject (*uddeśya*), as in the verse beginning "This is an insult" (*nyakkāro’yam*), the cause of its being a defect is not the non-apprehension of the status of being a predicate; rather, it is precisely the delayed apprehension thereof, preceded by the recollection of a reversed word-order. For in poetry, un-delayed apprehension is what is required of the subject. And this has been indicated in the *Bhāṣya*, *Kaiyaṭa*, *Kaustubha*, and other works on the *sūtra* defining the technical term *vṛddhi*.
In reality, by abandoning that general rule (*utsarga*), there would be nothing more than mere distress to the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*); thus, the matter has been explained at length elsewhere.

Nor should it be argued that, in such cases, the cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by words other than a single compound word containing the denotators of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), so that no fault exists even in examples like "the four-armed one clad in yellow" (*pītavāsāścaturbhujaḥ*). This is because accepting *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) is simpler than postulating a cumbersome causal relationship involving all the different types of semantic functions (*vṛtti*).

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as "The sacrificial post of the Vājapeya is seventeen aratnis long," "The priests proceed wearing red turbans," and "Although the sacrificer is one who takes four portions, the oblation must be made with five portions," there would be no injunction of the number seventeen, the color red, or the number five by way of restating the Vājapeya post, the aratni, and the turbans; for in these instances, since the dimensions of the post, the aratni, and the possession of the turban are already established through extended application (atideśa), the direct instruction (upadeśa) prevails over the extended application, and thus operates.

Previously, since there was no contradiction due to the acceptance of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), upon close examination it is understood that the purport (*tātparya*) lies only in the redness; thus, the conventional designation as an injunction of that much alone is used.

Nor should it be argued that, by this same method, in the case of "the first eating" (*prathamabhakṣaḥ*), there would likewise be no injunction of another eating; for they say that in that case, because both [elements] are taught directly, such a claim cannot be made.

As for the argument that even in a *karmadhāraya* compound, the qualified meaning is presented through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the latter member alone, and therefore there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by way of the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), that is not correct.

This is because a *karmadhāraya* compound is stronger than a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, and thus [the desired form] would not result. By this, the view that "unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is not necessary for a *karmadhāraya*" is refuted; such is the direction of the argument.

Furthermore, in the case of a *dvandva* compound, such as "a beautiful jar and a cloth" (*sundaraṃ ghaṭaṃ paṭaṃ ca*), unification of meaning is necessary to exclude [the application of] qualifiers like "beautiful" to the *dvandva* compound itself, just as they apply to the individual members.

Furthermore, just as in a *vigraha* (analytic statement), there would result the undesirable application of the word "ca" (*and*) even in a *dvandva* compound. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*: "Just as in a sentence there is the connection with one's own [possessions]—such as 'the king’s cow, horse, and man'—and just as there is the connection with ownership—such as 'the cow of Devadatta and Yajñadatta'—so it is not in a compound, as in 'the king’s cow, horse, and man' or 'the cow of Devadatta and Yajñadatta'."

Nor should it be argued that the word's function (*vṛtti*) applies only after the concomitance (*sāhitya*)—in the form of being connected to a single action—is subsequently understood; for such a function is necessary in accordance with the experience of perceiving a concomitance that consists of another entity pervading the objects being compounded, which is co-extensive with the connection to a single action and so forth in a single form. It is for this very reason that the formulation of the compound rule for that meaning in the grammatical injunction, "The *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of *ca* (and)" [Pāṇini 2.2.29], is logically consistent.

Nor should it be argued that the meaning of a *dvandva* compound is that it occurs when there is a "concomitance" (*sāhitya*) among the referents of the words, consisting in their connection with a single action and so forth, yet this does not constitute the basis for grasping its denotative power (*śakti*). For if there were connection with a single action, there would be no denotative power residing in the word itself, and furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the action being cognized twice. Moreover, by the principle of association (*sāhacarya*) in the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24), it is more appropriate that the rule serves as the basis for grasping the denotative power; otherwise, in the absence of such concomitance, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) could not be attributed to the aggregate in cases involving a *dvandva*.
Furthermore, the commentators and others accept that the grammatical correctness of a *dvandva* compound depends precisely on the understanding of its literary context (*sāhitya*).

Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-occurrence of the word "ca" (and) as a rule even in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) of a *dvandva*, because in that case—as in a *dvandva*—the connection with a single action is only understood subsequently. Nor can it be argued that [the word "ca"] serves as an indicator of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the connection with a single action, for we observe the connection with a single action even in the absence of such a word, as in the example: "Day after day, he leads away a cow, a horse, a man, and a beast."

Now, if "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) is the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*), then, in order to maintain the equivalence of meaning between the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and the analytical statement (*vigraha*), it is necessary that conjunction also be manifested in the compound (*samāsa*).
Furthermore, just as in the sentence "Look at the *dhava* and cut the *khadira*," there would result the undesirable usage "Look at the *dhava-khadira* and cut [it]."

Furthermore, in cases such as "Devadatta and Yajñadatta cook," where duality is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the manifestation of their association (*sāhitya*) is necessary in order to obtain the property that delimits the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). Nor can the duality conveyed by the nominal suffix (*sub*) itself serve this purpose; for in examples like "Caitra and Maitra go," there is no dual suffix, which would result in the impossibility of the duality being construed. Nor can the word itself be the conveyor of that [duality], because it is not so stated in the lexicons (*kośa*) or the *Bhāṣya*. Moreover, since the rule for the *dvandva* compound prescribes it for the sense of "and" (*ca-artha*), there is no justification for a dual suffix after a *dvandva*, just as there is none for the word itself.

Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the distinction between singular and dual number—as in "Devadatta and Yajñadatta cook" (*devadatto yajñadattaśca pacati*) and "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are cooking" (*devadattaśca yajñadattasya pacataḥ*)—the manifestation of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is necessary.

Moreover, when there is a connection with duality and so forth expressed by case-endings (*sub*), the manifestation of association (*sāhitya*) is necessary in order to obtain the delimiting property of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*).

As for what was stated—that when multiple properties serve as the delimiters of the relatum-ness (anvayitāvacchedaka), mere *paryāpti* (distributive possession) alone functions as the relation—this is not correct. For it would result in the grammatical correctness of the plural number in a *dvandva* compound of the words "time" (*kāla*) and "space" (*ākāśa*). This is because the plurality residing in time, space, and a jar would exist in both time and space through a pure *paryāpti*. However, if *paryāpti* that is pervaded by the delimiter of relatum-ness is taken as the relation, then even the dual number would fail to apply, since a *paryāpti* of duality or the like, which is pervaded by each individual property serving as the delimiter of relatum-ness, is unestablished.

Nor should it be argued that because the property of being a substratum (*anvayitva*) is delimited by as many instances as there are of its own locus, such a linguistic usage does not occur; for this cannot be postulated, since we observe that when there is a delusion regarding fitness from the expression "time and space" (*kālākāśau*), there arises a cognition of plurality having only two individuals as its object. Furthermore, numbers such as duality (*dvitva*) produced by relative cognitions (*apekṣābuddhi*)—such as "this is one, this is one"—do not exist; rather, they are certain specific properties subsumed under the genus "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*) which serve as delimiters.

The meaning is that this is the view of those who maintain that [the universal] is indeed one and the same. Furthermore, duality and so forth are impossible under the theory of oneness. However, there is no fault if the coexistence (*sāhitya*) does not appear, because it is accepted that the relation is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) qualified by the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*).

Nor should it be said that even when there is co-occurrence (*sāhitya*), the situation remains problematic; for by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the substratum (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), it is accepted that in the case of co-occurrence, there is a relation with all things that serve as its own loci. Thus, even in words such as *puṣpavant* (the sun and moon), it is co-occurrence itself that serves as the delimiting property of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). It is with this very intention that Amarasimha states: "By a single expression, *puṣpavant* refers to both the maker of day and the maker of night. The phrase "by a single expression" means "by way of a single capacity-delimiting property (*ekaśakyatāvacchedakaprakāreṇa*)."

As for the claim that the word *puṣpavanta* has a grasp of power (*śaktigraha*) in the form of a dual capacity toward both the moon and the sun, and that the delimitors of its effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) are "the state of being a recollection qualified by the mode of being the moon while being qualified by the mode of being the sun" and "the state of being such verbal cognition (*śābdatva*)," this is because one accepts that the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*) of that very power residing in both the moon and the sun is a collective (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) one with respect to both moon-ness and sun-ness; and [because] in a cognition qualified solely by the mode of being sun-ness and so forth, [the power does not reside] in that single property alone.

This is because the cause is a cognition that apprehends the complete distribution (*paryāpti*) of the delimitorhood of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatā*). In both cases, the effect-delimitor (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is simply the state of being a cognition having both properties as its qualifiers; therefore, from such a cognition, there is no understanding of only one or the other. Furthermore, in the case of a word with multiple meanings, since each individual property is understood even when it is delimited by the respective property, and since the complete distribution of delimitorhood exists in each individual property, there is no fault. That [objection] is not [correct]; [The reason is: because the cause is a cognition that apprehends the complete distribution of the delimitorhood of denotability. And in both cases, the delimitor of the effect-status (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the state of being a cognition whose qualifiers are both [properties]; hence, there is no cognition of only one or the other from that [cause]. Moreover, in the case of a polysemous word (*nānārtha-pada*), since there is a cognition of each [meaning] even when it is delimited by its respective property, and since the complete distribution of delimitorhood exists in each individual property, there is no fault. That [is not so];

This is because, in this context, we do not accept that pervasion (*paryāpti*) resides in multiple properties that have become qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) determined by a single objective determination (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in one and the same subject; for in the present case, since the moon and the sun are distinct, it is impossible for their respective objective determinations to be one.

However, where there is the manifestation of another property that exists distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) while taking multiple properties as the delimiters of the subjecthood (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), then it is necessary that the pervasion of the delimitor-hood (*avacchedakatā-paryāpti*) reside in the multiple properties even though they qualify different subjects.

Just as in the case of the cognition "the pot and the cloth do not exist," where the non-existence delimited by duality (*ubhayatva*) is apprehended, it is understood that the delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of such a non-existence is fully present (*paryāpti*) in both pot-ness and cloth-ness; so too in the present case, a denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the [referent] qualified by association (*sāhitya*) is necessary. In that regard, association itself is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and not the denotable object (*śakya*); this should be reflected upon according to the method explained in the section on the meaning of nouns (*nāmārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that in the case of "the pot and the cloth do not exist," it is duality (*ubhayatva*) alone that serves as the delimiting property of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), and not pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth; for such a cognition would fail to arise with respect to anything possessing merely one of the two. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Furthermore, regarding the experience of multiple meanings generated by words such as *puṣpavant*, the certainty that the knowledge of that word generates an experience of multiple meanings is the cause [of such experience], and it acts as an inhibitor when there is an experience of only one [meaning]; therefore, there is no fault.

For this very reason, one who lacks such a determinate cognition may sometimes have a cognition of only one [of the two meanings] even through the power of the word's denotative function (*śakti*); for even when the denotative function is grasped as delimited by both properties, a recollection of only that which is delimited by a single property is possible due to the influence of an awakening factor (*udbodhaka*), and even when there is a recollection delimited by both properties, a verbal cognition of only that which is delimited by a single property is possible due to the force of semantic competency (*yogyatā*).

That too is not correct, because it has been established that there is no capacity (śakti) distinct from the capacity to convey meaning (bodhakatā). Even if one who possesses the grasp of a word's capacity to convey meaning as delimited by a single property [such as gender] were to have such a cognition, the word would not be considered grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) in that context due to its contradiction with lexicons and other authorities; just as, for example, the word *dāra*, which denotes "wife," is not used in the singular and so forth.

In reality, however, the apprehension of the word-power (*śakti*) regarding the term *puṣpavant* is simply that it generates a cognition having both "moon-ness" (*candratva*) and "sun-ness" (*sūryatva*) as its modes; therefore, no cognition of either one alone arises from it. Furthermore, the phrase "by a single expression" (*ekayoktyā*) means "by a single word-power" (*ekayā śaktyā*), and the term "*puṣpavantau*" means "the two things denoted by the word *puṣpavant*."

Alternatively, the meaning of "by a single utterance" (ekayoktyā) is "by a single pronunciation. However, in cases where there are multiple meanings, the cognition of those multiple meanings does not occur without repetition. In the present case, however, because the denotable object (śakya) is one, both meanings are cognized simultaneously from what is uttered only once; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

As for the claim that "the object is simply the state of being the referent of a single cognition," that is not correct; for that too is apprehended subsequently, and because a cognition of that specific form contradicts experience, and because it would result in the application of a *dvandva* compound in the case of "the jar is the agent" (*ghaṭaḥ kartā*). If it is argued that "being the referent of a particular cognition" is what constitutes the object, then, due to the lack of a commonality (non-uniformity), this would lead to the postulation of an infinite number of powers (*śakti*).

By this, the view that "difference (*bheda*) is the object" is also refuted; for since difference is a universal-positive (*kevalānvayin*), it lacks the capacity for exclusion (*avyāvarttakatva*), and thus the designation "object" would become meaningless.

Nor is that [rule] intended to exclude *dvandva* compounds from the domain of *karmadhāraya*, because in cases such as "gone to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), there is the possibility of sublation by that [rule for *karmadhāraya*] just as there is by the *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa*. Otherwise, since distinction (*bheda*) exists within the domain of the *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa*, the *dvandva* would be difficult to prevent. It is another matter that the meaning of "conjunction" (*cārtha*) is association (*sāhitya*), but only among distinct things. Therefore, the essential point is that the rule is for the purpose of producing a cognition regarding association.

Furthermore, *sāhitya* (conjunction) is co-extensive with having a single time, a single instructor, and being the agent of a single action, and so forth; and among other word-meanings, it is co-extensive with being related to an action presented by a single word in a single form at a single time. For this very reason, common usages such as "done by the two together," "seen together," "given to the two together," and "the connection of the two together" are logically consistent. In a *dvandva* compound, however, everything appears without distinction.
It is for this reason that the Mīmāṃsakas maintained that because conjunction is understood in a *dvandva*, there is a single deityhood (*devatātva*).

However, where there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the former—as in "Cut the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," and so on—it is only the second [element] that appears. Even in the case of the first [element], its appearance is restricted to being the object of a single type of action, provided it is devoid of simultaneity. But in cases such as "One should perform the *śrāddha* for both parents," the sublation [of the restriction] is abandoned because the sublation would result in the scripture having a narrower scope, due to the [parents] being qualifiers of the objective (*uddeśya*). However, the restriction to being the correlate of a single action is universal. It is with this very intention that the ancients defined "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) as the state of being correlates of a single action in an equal manner.

The term *tulyavat* means "simultaneously" and "in a single form," with the same intention. This is an adjective [qualifying the conjunction] in the sense of *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection), due to the diversity of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*). For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya and other texts that the context (*prakaraṇa*) serves as the regulator is consistent. Furthermore, in a *dvandva* compound denoting either mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*) or collective aggregation (*samāhāra*), the aggregate (*samāhāra*) alone is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), and that aggregate, like a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), is indeed something distinct.

Nor should it be argued that the members of the aggregate themselves become the object of cognition only through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of [being part of] the aggregate; for if that were so, the genitive case based on difference—such as in "the aggregate (*samāhāra*) or collection (*samūha*) of jars"—would be untenable.

Nor is the distinction superimposed [upon the whole], for the correctness of the *dvandva* compound and its usage are established by that much alone. Therefore, the aggregate (*samudāya*), produced by the conjunction of distinct constituents (*samudāyin*), is indeed something additional; for the sake of a cognition having that [aggregate] as its qualificandum, *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) is necessary. In reality, however, when the collection whose constituent distinctions are manifest (*udbhūta*) is the qualificandum, it is an *itaretarayoga*; but when the collection whose constituent distinctions are not manifest (*anudbhūta*) is the qualificandum, it is a *samāhāra*—this is how it should be understood.

And thus, since the singular number is established simply because the aggregate (*samāhāra*) is a single entity, a specific rule for that purpose need not be commenced. For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya and other works—that the context [of the rule] serves as a restrictive factor—is consistent. And that [restriction] can only be based on the expressive power of the aggregate itself, because there would otherwise be no determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) if one were to resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of either one of the two constituent words.

Nor can it be argued that the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) whereby a suffix conveys its own meaning as residing in the object denoted by the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) serves as the determining factor for its application to the subsequent word (*uttarapada*); for this would fail to exclude the connection of the genitive case-meaning with *puruṣa* in examples such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*. Furthermore, this is contradicted (*vyabhicāra*) in cases like *sarvakaḥ*, where the suffix *ka* applies despite the absence of a preceding meaningful word.

Moreover, in instances such as *dadhiyad dadāti*, there would result the unintended connection of the meaning of the suffix *vatup* with the word *dadhi*, since the required proximity (*sāṃnidhya*) exists. In examples such as *dadhīyad bahugaḍur dadāti*, there would follow the unintended connection of the meaning of the suffix *bahuc* with *dadhi*, and the unintended non-connection of the same suffix with *paṭa*.

Moreover, if that were the case, there would be no possibility of forming a *dvandva* compound at all; for such a compound is prescribed only for multiple *sub*-ending words (*subanta*) occurring in the sense of conjunction (*cārtha*). Furthermore, even regarding the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), since—as explained by the aforementioned reasoning—the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) belongs only to the final member, there would be an absence of multiple *sub*-ending words occurring in the sense of another word; consequently, compounds such as *citragu* could not be established as *bahuvrīhi*.

Moreover, even in the case of words such as *ghaṭa*, since the meaning could be established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or primary denotative power (*śakti*) residing solely in the final phoneme—such as the suffix *-ac* derived from the verbal root *ghaṭ*—the very theory of a distinct power for the whole word would be undermined. Furthermore, even if [the final phoneme] merely serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the causal capacity for producing cognition remains necessary, and thus the existence of a distinct power (*śakti*) is unavoidable. Nor can it be argued that the power resides in the whole because comprehension occurs through the conventional usage of the whole even by those who do not know the individual parts or the power of the individual parts; for the same logic applies to the present case as well.

For this very reason, it is established by experience that although the meaning of the whole is understood through the derivation of the whole in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), there is an absence of the capacity for word-segmentation (*padavibhāga*) without the grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇavyutpatti*). Nor can it be argued that there is no [primary] denotative power (*śakti*) because understanding occurs even through the knowledge of the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the parts when the power of the whole is unknown; for if one who has grasped the power of words like *gaṅgā* in the sense of a bank were to understand the current through secondary indication, it would follow that the power of the word *gaṅgā* in the sense of the current could not be established. This is the general direction of the argument.

Moreover, in this way, there would be a violation of the linguistic rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as integrated with the meaning of the base; for the latter member alone cannot function as a base (*prakṛti*).

Nor is there any fault [in our position] because the term *prakṛtyartha* (meaning of the base) refers, by way of its function (*vṛtti*), to that which is the object of the cognition produced by the base; or rather, one might argue that "being a base" (*prakṛtitva*) does not consist in being the locus of pervasion (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatva*) there, but is merely the state of being its substratum (*tadāśrayatvamātra*), and this exists even in a single atom. However, this must be rejected, because in cases such as ‘bring the brindled cow’ (*citragumānaya*) or ‘look at the man with a staff’ (*daṇḍinaṃ paśya*), if there were an intention [to convey the whole], there would follow—without resorting to secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—the undesirable consequence of the connection of the act of bringing or seeing with the brindled cows or the staffs themselves.

Nor is there a lack of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the staff and so forth simply because they are parts of a single referent (*padārthaikadeśatva*), for their independence remains unimpeded—just as in examples such as "the king's harsh [servant]," where the king and others are independent. Otherwise, in cases like "he who possesses fire because of smoke," or the principle that "proximity is based on grammatical instruction" (*sannidhānaṃ cānuśāsanikam*), those [rules] would also be undermined.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) simply because of non-proximity (*anāsannatva*); for proximity does not consist in the absence of word-interventions. If it did, then even for a person who grasps the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the meaning "The mountain has fire; Devadatta has eaten," there would be no resulting cognition from the sentence "The mountain, the eater, has fire by Devadatta. Rather, proximity is merely the presentation of word-meanings generated by the words themselves. And that [presentation] certainly exists in the form of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) and so forth. For this very reason, verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is logically consistent in cases such as: "I worship the final lotus of the Blessed One, which resembles a lotus."

By this [definition], the state of being the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatva*) is defined as being the object of a presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a word occurring immediately prior to the suffix. This [state] belongs to both members in a *dvandva* compound, whereas in an *avyayībhāva* and other such compounds, it belongs only to the meaning of the preceding member. By including the requirement of "immediacy" (*avyavadhāna*), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the staff (*daṇḍa*) in the case of *daṇḍinam*—where the staff is the object of the cognition produced by the word *daṇḍa* occurring before the suffix—is refuted. However, this [definition] suffers from under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *bahupaṭuḥ* and *sarvakaḥ*.
Furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that in expressions like *dadhiyad dadāti*, the meanings of the suffixes *yat* and *vat* would have to be construed with the curd (*dadhi*).

Because the very status of being the limit for the application of a suffix (*pratyaya*) constitutes the base (*prakṛti*), and the state of being the qualificand in the presentation arising from the function of the base constitutes the "meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthatva*).

Now, what is the meaning of the statement "suffixes are connected with the meaning of the base"? Nor should it be said that its meaning is: "in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose object is the meaning of the suffix, the presentation generated by the base is the cause"; for such a causal relation cannot be grasped unless one has already acquired the notions of "suffix-ness," "base-ness," and so forth; and furthermore, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a cognition arising from the expression "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) for one who has not mastered that specific linguistic convention.

If it is argued that there is no fault because one must specify that, in the case of a cognition having "pot" as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and "objectness" (*karmatva*) as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by those respective words denoting objectness which are co-occurrent (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with those respective words denoting the pot, we say: no.

Even though, through the apprehension of various respective causes, there may arise in that manner or that other manner an understanding for one who is proficient, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of suffixes consists solely in their connection with meanings presented by the functions of their respective bases (*prakṛti*); and the grammatical correctness of each respective base consists solely in its connection with the meanings of the suffixes belonging to its own base, and not otherwise—this much alone is the subject matter under investigation.

If it is asked, "What is the proof for its correctness (*sādhutva*) in that very case?", [the answer is: when it is stated that the suffix *am* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the sense of the object (*karmatva*), that [meaning] is obtained through the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Nor should it be argued that this [principle of proximity] should apply even when there is a connection with a meaning included within the base itself; for if the stick were connected to the state of being the object, then expressions such as "see the man with the stick" (*daṇḍinaṃ paśya*) would result in being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) even without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The meaning is that, when there is a connection by way of the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), only a collection of words that generates separate mental representations (*pṛthag-upasthiti*) is grammatically correct (*sādhu*). This is understood from such indications as "one technical name (*saṃjñā*) [is used] for the sake of the subsequent operation" (*paraṃ kāryam*). In this manner, other components of analysis that determine correctness should also be inferred by the wise from the respective *sūtras*, the *Bhāṣya*, and other authorities. And it has been said in the *Hiraṇya*—[the relationship] is constrained by the distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) based on the relation between the qualified (*bhedi*) and the qualifier (*bhedaka*). [Note: In modern printed editions, the reading 'nibandhanam' is found.]
"Even in the absence of that [number], the cognition [of the meaning] is not here precluded.
This is the general direction.

Here, this should be understood: there is a rule that only a case-meaning (pratyayārtha) other than number does not enter into the relation of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). For this very reason, in expressions such as "the rice has ripened" (*sampanno vrīhiḥ*), there is no fault even though the number is construed with the genus (*jāti*).

Nor should it be argued that where the duality and so forth of the agent of cooking (the *pākakartṛ*) is sublated, while that [duality] of the act of cooking (*pākādi*) is not sublated, there would result the undesirable application [of a sentence] such as "see the two cooking" (*pacantau paśya*). This is because the action presented by the verbal root is presented precisely as having its distinctions removed; therefore, the connection of duality with it is untenable. For this very reason, they say that in forms such as *pacanti*, number does not connect with the meaning of the verbal root.

In reality, wherever there is a sublation of the connection with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there that connection occurs in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as well. For this very reason, in expressions such as *paṇḍitarūpa* ("of scholarly form"), the connection with excellence (*prāśastya*) occurs in scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*). However, where there is no sublation, it occurs in the qualificand alone. For this very reason, the ancient commentators’ resolution—that when the fruit of the verbal root-meaning connects with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by that [suffix] as its object (*karman*) or instrument (*karaṇa*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth would otherwise result for the root, yet this does not happen because it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*)—is consistent. This is the general direction.

And thus, a collective power (*śakti*) is necessary for the whole. By this, the view that a *dvandva* compound occurs by the force of the injunction even in the absence of semantic integration (*samarthya*) is refuted, because the capacity for *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) does indeed exist. For this very reason, there is no compound in cases of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or succession (*anvācaya*). In conjunction, indeed, there is a connection of mutually independent elements with a property delimited by another. The particle *ca*, however, merely indicates the intention (*tātparya*) regarding the connection of several things to a single action, and it also serves to illuminate the simultaneity of those two actions.

In passages such as "Day after day he carries away cattle, horses, men, and livestock," even in the absence of the word "and" (ca), the syntactic connection occurs—either as a predicate or as an attribute—by virtue of the intended meaning (tātparya).

For this very reason, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as "Devadatta cooks and laughs," where there is a conjunction of actions (*kriyā-samuccaya*). It should not be argued that in cases like "Worship both Īśvara and the Guru," there could be no conjunction because the two acts of worship do not occur at the same time—since the oneness of time consists in being the object of a particular cognition—and thus there would be no conjunction here. Rather, even in a conjunction, there is the manifestation of simultaneity (*sāhitya-bhāna*). For this very reason, they say that in cases of conjunction such as "Devadatta and Yajñadatta cook," the verbal suffix is invariably used in the singular number.

And thus, since there is no formation of a *vṛtti* (compound) for multiple *subanta* words in this sense, the very possibility of a compound does not arise; for that reason alone, there is no *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning) therein.

In a *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), the connection of one [word] with the others occurs at the same time as they are combined, delimited by a single property, because we experience it exactly so in cases such as "cut the dhava and the khadira trees. For this very reason, two instances of the particle *ca* are employed in its analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). [The meaning is that the particle *ca* implies the sense of "together" (*sāhitya*). By means of that, the mutual concomitance (*sāhitya*) of each with the other is understood.

And *cā* has precisely the meaning of "conjunction" (*sāhitya*). Nor does this result in the perception of two separate conjunctions by means of the two *ca*s, because that [conjunction] is manifested by the two *ca*s themselves. For this very reason, in cases of mutual association such as "Devadatta and Yajñadatta cook," there is always an imperative verb ending in the dual.
By this, the view that conjunction—pervading all four meanings—is itself the meaning of *ca*, is refuted.

And thus, in that case, for the sake of conveying that meaning, *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) is indeed indispensable. However, where—as in the case of *aharahar* and similar expressions—the intended sense is grasped through another means even without a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*), there the comprehension of concomitance (*sāhitya*) certainly occurs even when only a single *ca* is employed. For example: [The constituent parts of Sāṃkāśyaka are denoted by the word *Sāṃkāśyaka*, and the constituent parts of Pāṭaliputra are denoted by the word *Pāṭaliputraka*.]

This is evident in such examples as, "Of the inhabitants of Sāṃkāśya and the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra, the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra are the most handsome," and so forth. This point—that even when only one word ending in the dual suffix is used, the sense of association (sāhitya) is understood—is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on Pāṇini 5.3.57 (*dvivacanavibhajya*).

Because of the statement "delimited by a single property" (*ekadharmāvacchinne*), there is no such usage as *ajāgrāmau nayati* ("he leads the goat and the village") to express the meaning of *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* ("he leads the goat to the village").

For this very reason, the grammatical correctness of such statements as "The modified and unmodified [forms] nourish the body and they cause it to exist" is established. They say that when there is first an application of the word to the collective whole (samudāya) with respect to the action delimited by the mutual association (*sāhitya*), there subsequently arises a cognition of the individual application through secondary implication (*pārṣṇika*). Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as "That which is for Agni and for Prajāpati," because of the understanding of mutual association, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) would belong only to the combined entity. This is not so, because the particle *ca* primarily connects with the meaning of the suffix itself; thus, there is no fault, as there is a conjunction of the two statuses of being deities.

Furthermore, in that case, since it is established by grammatical usage (*vyutpatti*) that two items of equal prominence presented by a single word are construed with another element at one and the same time, and since this is already observed in cases such as *puṣpavant* (the sun and moon), it would result in the breakdown of the very nature of *samuccaya* (conjunction).

By this, the argument that a compound could arise in the case of *anvācaya* (subordinate conjunction) is refuted; for even if the subordinate nature is indicated there, it is indicated by only one [particle], and thus there is no absence of multiple *subanta* (inflected nominal) words in the sense of *ca*.

Generally, this [use of *ca*] occurs when there is a connection with a verb (*kriyānvaya*). However, where there is a connection with a verb and yet two *ca*s are present—as in "they cook and they laugh" (*pacanti ca, hasanti ca*)—there is no perception of being secondary (*anuṣaṅgikatva*), because mutual concomitance (*parasparasāhitya*) is understood. It is with this very intention that [the author] says: "In the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ*, the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) is for the sake of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). For in that context, it would have been established by merely saying "*ce dvandvaḥ*" (when *ca* occurs, it is a *dvandva* compound). But how could *ca* be a grammatical operation (*vṛtti*)? It is indeed a word (*śabda*). Since an operation is impossible upon a word, it will be understood as applying to the meaning (*artha*).

This being established, the purpose for which he includes the mention of *artha* (meaning) is this: so that it may be understood in this way—as stated in the Bhāṣya—that "the meaning [expressed] by *ca* is also the meaning [of the compound]. It is stated in the Bhāṣya that, by the force of the inclusion of *artha*, there is no compound in cases of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or sequential connection (*anvācaya*). For if the rule were formulated as *ca dvandvaḥ* (in Nyāsa), the meaning would be that a *dvandva* occurs when multiple *subanta*s (inflected nominal stems) are combined in a usage-suitable co-occurrence; such is the sense of that [Bhāṣya passage]. By this, the view that even in a *bahuvrīhi* the indication of the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) resides solely in the final member (*uttarapada*) is also refuted.

For this very reason, the commencement of the *aruṇā-ādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the redness) is justified. For therein, there arises the doubt: "Is the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) to be separated from the sentence and inserted into the context, or is it connected with the act of buying (*krīṇāti*) as its substrate because it serves to qualify it, thereby becoming an attribute of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) and so forth? In the case of a connection with the act of buying, the word "red" (*aruṇayā*) would function as the instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*). However, since that is not possible for something formless (*amūrta*), it has no connection with the act of buying; therefore, being separated from it, it is inserted into the context.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that whatever substance is used to perform an action is denoted by the term *aruṇā*. However, according to your own view, even words such as *ekahāyanī* would denote only qualities like being one-year-old or having reddish-brown eyes (*piṅgākṣitva*), since these qualities are incorporeal (*amūrta*) and thus cannot function as instruments (*karaṇa*) for the act of purchasing. Consequently, the doubt regarding the role of the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) alone would be rendered groundless. Furthermore, the capacity to denote a substance through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) is equally applicable to all three terms.

Furthermore, the established conclusion—that the placement of the substance mentioned in its own sentence is more appropriate than the placement of the substance mentioned in the context (prakaraṇa), because a sentence is stronger than context—is also untenable; for even those two [the context and the sentence] lack the capacity to denote a substance. Since figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) applies to the word *aruṇā* as well, the placement of the substance within its own word is possible, and thus the placement of the substance within the sentence is effectively ruled out from the start.

However, when a connection with words such as *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed), which are directly present [in the text], is possible due to their immediate mental apprehension (*śīghropasthiti*), there can be no connection with a figurative meaning (*lākṣaṇika*) that is apprehended with delay; this is because [the word] has no expectancy regarding the substance (*dravya*). Thus, it is established that there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *aruṇa* at all, and everything is consistent.

Furthermore, in the case of a bahuvrīhi compound expressing a sense other than the genitive—as in "the village reached by water" (*prāptodako grāmaḥ*)—according to your own method, after the cognition "water not different from the agent of reaching" arises, even if one were to assume a figurative indication of the village as being related to that [water], the intended meaning—"the village which is the object of the reaching whose agent is the water"—would remain entirely unestablished.

Nor can it be argued that the suffix *kta* in *prāpta* has an agentive meaning (*kartṛ*) but functions as a designation for the object (*karman*) [in the compound]; for the reason is that we accept the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) that "the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) through the relation of non-difference (*abheda*) is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by words having the same case ending. Otherwise, due to the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that the meanings of two co-referential nominal stems (*prātipadika*) are construed as non-different, there would result the undesirable cognition: "related to the object of the act of obtaining which is non-different from water."

Nor should it be argued that water’s agency is connected [to the action] through its relation to attainment (*prāpti*), for this would result in an unintended meaning such as "the agent of the attainment whose agent is water. Nor is it the case that the meaning of the *kta* suffix is not intended to be expressed, as there is no evidence for such a claim.

Furthermore, even if [the agenthood] is not intended to be expressed—[the sense being that this is said with the intention of expressing the meaning of the *kta* suffix]—in order to prevent such usage as "the rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*) when the intended meaning is "he cooks the rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), it has been established that for a verbal cognition where the meaning of a noun is the qualifier (the *prakāra*) by means of a relation other than identity, the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the suffix prescribed for that [agent]. Since this is already established, such a connection [of the rice with the action] is impossible.

If it is argued that after the cognition "the non-attainment [of the object] has the same agent as the water," the collection of objects (karmagrāma) is indicated, we say no; for the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is established elsewhere, and because of the statement "substantives (nāman) have substance (sattva) as their primary meaning," such a cognition is impossible.

In order to prevent the cognition "the jar possesses jar-ness which is non-different from eternal" (*nityābhinnaghaṭatvavān*) from arising in response to such expressions as "the jar is eternal" (*ghaṭo nityaḥ*), it is required that for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a nominal stem related by the relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*), there must be an expectancy for an apprehension (*upasthiti*) generated by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) functioning as the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatayā*). The point is that in the case of "the jar is eternal," since the jar is presented as the qualifier (*prakāratayā*), there can be no connection of "eternal" with it through the relation of identity.

Furthermore, because the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a noun delimited by its qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatāvacchinna*) serves as the cause [of semantic relation], and because it is impossible for the non-difference (*abheda*) with water to be construed with the agent [if the agent were expressed by the first member], one might argue that the word *udaka* indicates (*lakṣyate*) that which has become the object of the attainment (*prāpti*) whose agent is the aforementioned [agent], and that the word *prāpta* functions merely to indicate the speaker’s intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*). However, this should not be asserted, because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) [to prefer this over other interpretations], and because it would result in the abandonment of the well-established principle—seen in examples such as *citraguḥ*—that a word’s function as an indicator of intention applies specifically to a case where it denotes a meaning formed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its own primary denotation (*vācyārtha*). If, however, one accepts a different rule of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), then the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is established.
The same should be inferred for cases such as *ūḍharathaḥ*.

For me, however, there is no fault, because all types of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) have as their object words that produce distinct mental representations (*upasthiti*); and because the assumption of expressive power (*śakti*) regarding the relation (*saṃsarga*) and the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) occurs precisely by including the reversal of the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Having considered all this, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "In this regard, when there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) as the basis for semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), that specific distinction produced by the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) must be explained."

As for what the Mīmāṃsakas say—that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the analysis (*vigraha*) "this belongs to the variegated cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam*) is appropriate, and not "he whose cows are variegated" (*citragāvo yasya*)—because if that were the case, then just as in "the king’s servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) the meaning of the word ending in the nominative (*puruṣa*) is primary, so too here the variegated cows themselves would be primary rather than the referent of the genitive; yet it is established by experience that Devadatta and others alone are primary. For in this way, the identity of meaning between the derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and its analytical statement (*vigraha*) is maintained. That is not so.

Thus, even in the case of a *vigraha* (analytic expansion), because the relation denoted by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is related through a distinction, the resulting cognition is one characterized by a relational objectivity (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*) based on a distinct relation, which is in turn determined by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the relation, as in "one who possesses a relation with a brindled cow. In a compound (*samāsa*), however, it is characterized by a qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the relatum, which is determined by a mode-ness residing in the brindled cow; thus, the distinction remains in that state. This is likewise the case for *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compounds and others.

Furthermore, there is no strict rule that the meanings of a compound and its analytical expansion (*vigraha*) must not be identical; therefore, there is no fault even in our proposed analysis. Moreover, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* with a sense other than the genitive, even if one were to analyze it as "this [village] is the water which has reached," the meaning understood from the compound—that the village is the object of the reaching performed by the water—would remain impossible to convey.

Furthermore, your analysis of the compound *tvadīyavigrahasya* contradicts the injunctions of the sages, such as "the *bahuvrīhi* occurs when there is a sense other than the first case-ending" (*aprathamāvibhaktyarthe bahuvrīhiḥ*) and "the *bahuvrīhi* is the remainder; the remainder is [that which is] left after the three [case-endings]" (*śeṣo bahuvrīhis trikataḥ śeṣaḥ*). Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because only words ending in the nominative case enter into the *alaukika-vākya* (pre-grammatical sentence), for it is precisely those elements that have entered the *alaukika-vākya* that can be employed in the final, established form (*pariniṣṭhita*) under another alternative analysis. This is because it is improper to abandon what is already present and instead construct a worldly sentence (*laukikavākya*) composed of elements not so present.

For instance, in the case of the formation *kṛtasuviśvasu* and so forth, when the optional designation (*vibhāṣā-samāsa-saṃjñā*) has occurred, then, upon its being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktiluk*). But when that designation has not occurred, who could prevent that case-ending? Thus, by virtue of the subsequent grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) applying, the very hearing of that ending follows. By this, those who analyze compounds such as the genitive-tatpuruṣa as *rājā cāsau puruṣaś ca* (the king and he is the man) are refuted; for otherwise, the rules prescribing genitive compounds and so forth, as well as the rule prohibiting elision (*aluk*) and the rules for the tatpuruṣa such as *tulyārthatṛtīyā* [Pāṇini 2.1.30], would fall into the state of having no scope of application.

Now, one might argue: let the *bahuvrīhi* compound consist only of words ending in the nominative case; let there also be, as an alternative, the sentence "he whose cows are variegated" (*citragavo yasya*), but let the status of being the *vigraha* (analytic expansion) belong only to "of the variegated cows" (*citragavām*), because that alone possesses the same meaning. Otherwise, the determination of the word's power (*śakti*) would not arise from the *vigraha*. Similarly, in the case of *prāptodakaḥ*, the *vigraha* is simply "the village which is the object of the attainment whose agent is water" (*udakakartṛkaprāptikarma grāmaḥ*).

Nor does it follow that a *bahuvrīhi* must necessarily be a compound because it lacks an explanatory expansion (*vigraha*) consisting of non-compounded words; for the status of being a "necessary compound" (*nityasamāsa*) applies only when it is impossible to form a sentence containing the constituent words of the compound that conveys the same meaning as the compound itself. In the present case, however, such a possibility certainly exists. If it is argued that there is no apprehension of identity of meaning in all respects [between the compound and its expansion], we say no.

Just as the term *ākṣika*—meaning "one who has dice as the locus of his cultivation" (*akṣa-karaṇakabhāvanāśraya*)—is a gloss for "one who plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*), and although there is an absence of identical meaning regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, this gloss nevertheless determines the word's power (*śakti*); likewise, in the present case, resorting to such a strained interpretation (*kliṣṭakalpanā*) as "sayāt" is entirely useless.

Moreover, in response to the question "Who is Devadatta?", the desire for knowledge would not be satisfied even by the sentence *citraguḥ* (the one possessing brindled cows), just as it is not satisfied by the sentence *citragavām ayam* (this is of the brindled cows); such is the direction of the argument. Therefore, in every compound, the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is indispensable.

But surely, if one accepts the principle of *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) everywhere and accepts that very principle in the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, then the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ* would be contradicted. To explain: in that *Bhāṣya*, having raised the objection that in cases such as *rāmakṛṣṇau* there would be no compound due to a lack of *sāmarthya* because of the mutual non-connection [of the members], it is argued that since the formation is already established by the formulation "a *dvandva* is used when expressing multiple substrates simultaneously" (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacane dvandvaḥ*), the introduction of an alternative formulation (*nyāsāntara*) would result in its redundancy.

1 [In the analysis *adhikriyate śabdo yatra* ("that wherein a word is employed"), the meaning is "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*). Here, by proximity, the referent of the constituent words of the analysis is understood; thus, the word *adhikaraṇa* functions as a synonym for its referents. This was explained by the Teacher in the rule: *yuṣmadyupapade samānādhikaraṇe madhyamaḥ* ("when *yuṣmad* is the subordinate term and coreferential, the second person is used"). *Adhikaraṇa* here means the two items being expressed; the meaning is that when those two are denoted simultaneously by two words, a *dvandva* compound occurs. *Adhikaraṇa* = the two items being expressed; the sense is that when those two are expressed together by two words, a *dvandva* compound results.
The meaning is this: since "Rāma" denotes both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and "Kṛṣṇa" denotes the tree, the semantic compatibility consisting of their non-differentiation (abhedānvaya) remains unimpaired.

Nor does the irregularity of the *dvandva* compound *rāmakṛṣṇau* arise through the sublation of the rule by the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule "virūpāṇām api" (even for dissimilar forms), as in the case of "ghaṭakumbhau"; for, by the force of the injunction for *dvandva* and by the force of the rule "samānārthānām" (of those having the same meaning), *ekaśeṣa* occurs only when there is identity of meaning, even without simultaneous reference to a single substratum (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*). Now, an objection might be raised: since the injunction for *bahuvrīhi* by the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24) prescribes that multiple *sub*-ending words form a *bahuvrīhi* when they denote another word-meaning...

If it is argued that since all words such as *citragu* (the "one who has brindled cows") denote that [possessor], there would be the undesirable consequence of a *dvandva* compound due to the simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), and that this is avoided by the repetition of the cognition through the *bahuvrīhi*—which, by the maxim of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), does not suffer from sublation—[we reply: no; for that very point has been refuted in the Bhāṣya itself with the words, "This simultaneous expression of multiple substrates is painful and difficult to establish," and so forth.

In this context, there is the state of being an error because it is overcome by defects. To explain: the determination of the meaning of a word arises from the linguistic usage of elders. Furthermore, it is not observed in common worldly usage that the word *plakṣa* denotes the *nyagrodha* tree. Nor can the word *plakṣa* be taken as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the *nyagrodha* has already been established by the word *nyagrodha* itself.

Furthermore, it is untenable for the section on the singular form of *dvandva* compounds to serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*), because its purpose is fulfilled simply by prescribing the singular number in all cases where dual or plural numbers would otherwise apply; moreover, in your view, neither the notion of association (*sāhitya*) nor collective aggregation (*samāhāra*) is manifested [in such a compound]. Furthermore, if the analysis (*vigraha*) were thus, the use of the word "ca" (and) would be logically inconsistent.

"Difficult to establish" (*durupapādā*) means that its establishment is faulty or devoid of substance; that is to say, it lacks valid proof. For instance, one might argue: "In cases such as *dyāvākṣāmā*, since we observe that both members convey two meanings through mutual association in the *vyāsa* (analytic) form, it must be accepted that the same applies in the *samāsa* (compound). This, however, cannot be said, because *dyāvākṣāmā* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage.

Nor can it be argued that, due to the absence of mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*), neither the *ekaśeṣa* nor the *samāsa* would apply, and thus the rule is required for their establishment; for those [compounds] are established by the very force of the specific grammatical injunction itself.

Furthermore, the analysis (vigraha) "dhavau ca khadirau ca" ("the *dhava* and the *khadira* trees") is not [the correct one], because it is impossible to abandon the singular number that first occurs during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Nor is it the case that this is for the sake of ensuring the absence of compounding in cases of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and sequential mention (*anvācaya*), since the absence of compounding in those two cases has already been established, and because—as demonstrated by the previous direction—the Bhāṣya has settled the doctrine that the capacity for "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) alone [prevents compounding], thus leaving no fault. Nor is that [capacity] necessary for the production of dual or plural endings from a compound, since that is accomplished simply through the cognition of multiple meanings from the compound, as in the case of words such as *puṣpavant*.

Nor does this mean that in cases such as *aṅgavaṅgakaliṅgāḥ*, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.62] would not occur; for the meaning of that rule is indeed that the elision of the *tadrāja* suffix takes place when plurality is intended on account of the offspring (*apatya*).

It should not be argued that, without the simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), there can be no connection of plurality with the individual meaning of the *tadrāja* [patronymic] suffix, because that [plurality] subsists collectively (*vyāsajyavṛttitvāt*). For if the elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix occurs when plurality is the intended meaning, and if that plurality is produced by the very meaning of the *tadrāja* suffix itself—meaning that the connection with plurality occurs through the meaning of the *tadrāja* suffix alone—then there is no fault even if one does not accept [the aforementioned view]. This is because, as stated clearly in our *Śabdenduśekhara*, "there exists a co-inherence of plurality in each [individual member]."

In every respect, it is not tenable for case-endings (*vibhakti*) to enter into both worldly and non-worldly [compounds] by assuming simultaneous denotation of the locus (*adhikaraṇavacanatā*); this is the direction of the argument.

And thus, in a *vṛtti* that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), in all cases, from the compound word, there arises the presentation of a qualified object-entity through the component powers (*avayavaśakti*) assisted by the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*). In the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, even the "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*) is indeed the object of the collective power. Furthermore, in expressions such as "of whom" (*yasya*), the "meaning of another word" consists of the related party (*sambandhin*) and so forth, resulting from a transposition of the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).

In expressions such as *prāptodaka*, the presentation [of meaning] through the reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) from words like *prāpta*, as well as the presentation of the object which is the referent of the compound (*anyapadārtha*), is achievable only through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*). For this very reason, the grammatical treatises state that because [the meaning] has already been expressed (*abhihitatvāt*), case endings such as the accusative do not occur. Similarly, in a *dvandva* compound, the sense of conjunction (*sāhitya*) is also a function of the power of the whole alone. Thus, the conclusion of the position is that in the theory of "abandoning one's own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā*), there is exclusively the power of the whole everywhere, while the constituent parts (*avayava*) are indeed devoid of meaning.

And this single-meaningness (*ekārthībhāva*) occurs in the case of *kṛt* suffixes, *taddhita* suffixes, roots ending in *san* and others, *sub*-suffixes, *ekaśeṣa*, and compounds. Among these, it has already been established in the case of compounds. It also applies to *kṛdanta* forms, because they are rules (*vidhi*) that have as their locus words conditioned by an *upapada*; it is precisely there that the technical rule regarding semantic capacity (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) operates. For this very reason, the word "word" (*pada*) in the sūtra is purposeful. Otherwise, since all rules within grammar would be equally related to words, the inclusion of that term [in the sūtra] would clearly be redundant.
For this same reason, one does not say "a beautiful pot-maker" (*śobhanaṃ kumbhakāraḥ*).

Nor should it be argued that since the compound (*samāsa*) here is obligatory, its formation is already accounted for by the "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), and thus there is no evidence for the unification of meaning even when a compound is not formed; for in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, the compound is optional. Therefore, in order to exclude constructions such as *sundareṇa mūlakenāpadaṃśam* (when the compound is absent) or *mūlakenādreṇa copadaṃśam*, which would otherwise result in expressions like *mūlakasyopadaṃśanaṃ sparśanaṃ ca kṛtvā bhuṅkte* ("having performed the chewing and touching of the radish, he eats"), one must instead have *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ sparśaṃ ca bhuṅkte*. Thus, the unification of meaning is necessary.

The unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is absolutely necessary for the formation of compounds. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *tatropapadam* (Pāṇini 3.1.92): "In the case of *mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti* ('he makes a large pot'), the suffix *aṇ* would apply. This is not so; the term 'upapada' is made a technical designation (*saṃjñā*)—it means 'a word uttered near [another]' (*upoccāritaṃ padam*). Since there is now even a trace of a 'word' (*pada*), this becomes a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*). And a rule concerning words applies to those that are semantically connected (*samartha*); therefore, because of the lack of such connection here, the suffix will not apply."

However, in the case of *kevala-kṛt* compounds, there is no formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), because there is a lack of evidence for it. For this very reason, the counter-example *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat") is consistent with the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). But the connection with the word *śobhanam* ("beautiful") is not possible, due to the absence of *ekārthībhāva*.

Moreover, this [particle] does indeed possess the status of a *kāraka* by virtue of being an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), because even if it were such, it lacks the state of being eternally expectant (*nityasākāṅkṣatva*). Furthermore, it is quite clear that the connection of such a *kāraka* occurs with an expectancy that is to be aroused (*utthāpyākāṅkṣā*), and not with an expectancy already arisen (*utthitākāṅkṣā*). This is evident in the commentaries of Kaiyaṭa and Padamañjarī on the rule *kutsane ca supi* (Pāṇini 8.1.66).

Is it not the case that the meaning of the sūtra is: "Wherever *ekārthībhāva* (the state of having a single meaning) is established by another means of knowledge (*māna*), there [it is] a word-derivation (*padavidhi*)"? It does not mean, however, that "wherever there is a word-derivation, there is *ekārthībhāva*. Since *ekārthībhāva* is established by another means of knowledge through the cognition of a distinct meaning, why is it said that it is produced by the application of the *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) "without an upapada," and that therefore there is *ekārthībhāva*? True.

Regarding the doubt as to where there can possibly be an understanding of a distinct meaning [in a *kṛd*-affix], we—whose only eye is the grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*)—find no fault in inferring such a meaning in those cases where the application of a rule like "karmaṇyaṇ" (Pāṇini 3.2.1) is observed, either through association (*sāhacarya*) or otherwise.

In reality, however, due to the association with rules such as "karmaṇyaṇ" and for the sake of uniformity with rules such as "kartari kṛt," there is everywhere a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) within all *kṛt*-affixes.

For this very reason, the construction "pācakaḥ gamanasya" (the cooker [is] of going) is not employed. Nor should it be argued that, in order to exclude such usage in the sense of "cooking has going as its agent" (gamanakartṛ kaḥ pākaḥ), the same [restriction] would apply to verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) as well; for there is no flaw, since the rule "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning" (*kriyāpradhānamākhyātam*) teaches that the grammatical correctness of a form ending in a verbal suffix is secured only when the case-role (*kāraka*), which is the meaning of the suffix, stands in a relation of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) with respect to the action.

And with respect to the meaning of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), action alone is primary; that is to say, it is precisely action that is the principal element. For this very reason, in expressions such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), there is the cognition of a relationship between the factor (*kāraka*) and the action in the form of the "subject-to-be-indicated" (*uddeśya*) and the "predicate" (*vidheya*). However, there is no such fault in the case of nominal stems (*subanta*), because by the prohibition "not alone" (*na kevalaḥ*), a nominal stem cannot even be used without a case-ending whose meaning is connected to its own meaning. In other cases, however, there is indeed the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

It is precisely based on this that there arises the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that "a suffix conveys its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the stem," and the principle that "the stem and the suffix express [their meanings] together. The meaning of this is that the two meanings [of the stem and suffix] are indeed construed together, and not with anything else. Furthermore, whether that [construal] takes the form of a mental presentation (*upasthiti*) or the form of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is another matter.

For this very reason, when there is an intention to express the connection with the operation (*vyāpāra*), one does not say *ādi-pācaka* (a beginner-cooker). However, qualifiers of the result (*phala*) do indeed have a partial connection (*ekadeśānvaya*). This is because in the Bhāṣya on the rule *pūjanātpūjitam* (Pāṇini 2.1.67), regarding the example *dāruṇādhyāpakaḥ* (a harsh teacher), it is accepted that the meaning of the word *dāruṇa* (harsh) connects as a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatayā*) with the result, which is a single constituent part of the meaning of the compound word *adhyāpaka*.

Furthermore, since the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*)—when used in conjunction with an agentive suffix—is precisely the activity delimited by a result, it is necessary even in cases such as "he cooks well" (*śobhanaṃ pacati*) that there be a syntactic relation (*anvaya*) with a single part [of that meaning]. Nor is there any fault, for the root possesses separate expressive powers (*śakti*) for both the result and the activity, and they are presented [to consciousness] in exactly that way.

Therefore, it cannot be argued that there is a burden of complexity regarding the delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka-gaurava*). Otherwise, since a cognition of the result as delimited by an operation would necessarily arise when a verb is used in co-utterance with an object (accusative), one would be forced to postulate two heavy powers with complex delimiters. This is because, in such a case, the result and the operation would result in being construed respectively as the *uddeśya* (the subject) and the *vidheya* (the predicate). Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence of such usages as *viklidyate* ("it becomes softened") and *gacchati* ("he goes") meaning "one who possesses an operation that produces both softening and conjunction."

Even if one were to exclude such a cognition for those who possess knowledge of the causal relationship through the conceptualization of cause and effect, it would still be impossible to avoid the undesirable consequence that such a cognition arising in those who do not know that relationship would nonetheless be valid. Furthermore, the objection regarding complexity (*gaurava*) remains exactly as it was. For this very reason, the existence of a primary expressive power (*śakti*) in compounds and the like is established.

Therefore, the expressive power (*śakti*) of verbal roots resides both in the operation qualified by the result and in the result qualified by the operation. Furthermore, the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with various suffixes whose meanings are agent (*kartṛ*) or object (*karman*) serves as the regulator for the cognition of each respective meaning.
