In forms such as *pacati*, there is indeed an association between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) by way of the relationship between the subject (*uddheśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*). This must be accepted by those who maintain that "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) applies universally to compounds, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and so forth.

Nor would it follow that, in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, there could be no injunction of the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha)—namely, the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) which constitutes the fruit of that [sacrifice]—with reference to the production of heaven (*svargabhāvanā*) as the object. For the sacrifice (*yajati*) possesses a potency (*śakti*) toward heaven as its objective with respect to the operation (*vyāpāra*) in which relinquishment is the instrument. Although that operation has relinquishment as its content, nevertheless, let its presentation be solely by way of being the instrument; since it is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) in itself due to its nature as mere relinquishment, it cannot be the thing to be produced (*bhāvya*), and thus heaven alone, as something external [to the ritual], connects as the thing to be produced.

It must be stated that the causality (*kāraṇatva*) of a sacrifice consists in its being the producer of the object to be brought about by the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). This is because even instruments such as axes possess their status as instruments only by virtue of producing the act of cutting, which is itself produced by the operation of a person. Furthermore, although the quality of being an "object of prescription" (*vidheyatva*)—defined as being the object of the instigation (*pravarttanā*) understood from the injunction—is grasped through the word as part of the complete meaning of the verbal root (since it is the meaning of the base), nevertheless, just as in the case of the sentence "The priests move about with red turbans," where redness is not otherwise established and thus becomes the object of prescription, so too here, since heaven is of the nature of pleasure, it is [naturally]... [the object of desire].

This is because, by virtue of being intended (*iṣṭatvena*), one engages in that activity spontaneously; and since there is no fault in taking the qualification as "established" (*siddhatvena*)—as it culminates in the fruit—it is also necessary even in the Mīmāṃsaka position that holds that the meaning of the suffix is *bhāvanā*. For even for them, due to the proximity of being expressed by the same word, the instigation (*pravartanā*) which is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) culminates in its connection with that very *bhāvanā* expressed by it; thus, they must necessarily accept that the object of that [instigation] is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

There is indeed no connection [of the object] with the objective state (*viṣayatā*) delimited by "prescribability" (*vidheyatva*), which is an indivisible property (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) co-located with non-attainment (*aprāptatva*) characterized by being the object of instigation (*pravarttanā*). This is because verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) are established as being effective precisely in the absence of such an objective state. Thus, the Mīmāṃsaka position that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix is also untenable, since such a connection would result in an improper relation due to the meanings being presented by distinct words. Enough of this.

It is also necessary [to state that a word ending in a case-suffix is the cause] even for the formation of secondary (taddhita) suffixes, in order to exclude examples such as *sundarasyaupagavaḥ* ("the descendant of Upagu belonging to the handsome one") and *aupagavo devadattasya* ("Devadatta's descendant of Upagu"), and to ensure that the relationship between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*) is maintained. Since secondary suffixes arise from words ending in case-suffixes, its status as a rule conditioned by a word (*pada*) is quite evident. It is likewise necessary in the case of denominative suffixes (*sanādyanta*) to exclude examples such as *mahāntaṃ putrīyati* ("he treats the great one as a son"), *pipaṭhiṣati* ("he desires to study"), *gantum* ("to go"), *śobhanaṃ pipaṭhiṣati* ("he desires to study beautifully"), *sundaraḥ kṛṣṇati* ("the handsome one acts like Kṛṣṇa"), and *mahāntaṃ ghaṭayati* ("he fashions the great one").

In this regard, it is clear that rules such as *supa ātmanaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.8] are rules whose locus (*uddeśya*) is a word-form (*pada*). Although there is an absence of such a status in the rule for the suffix *san*, and thus no application of that technical principle (*paribhāṣā*), nevertheless—in rules such as *supa ātmanaḥ* [3.1.8]—because the phrase "from that [agent], when there is a desire for the object" (*tataḥ karmaṇa icchāyām*) is understood by way of textual continuity (*anuvṛtti*), one must assume that [the status of being a word-form] applies to the end of the *san*-derivative in accordance with the governing topic of meaning (*arthādhikāra*).

And thus says the Bhāṣya: "Or rather, the statement [of the rule] is purposeless because the suffix *san* is eternal. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa comments: "In this context there are two positions: the position of *vṛtti* (compound formation) and the position of *avṛtti* (non-compounding). Among these, by its very nature, it occurs that both the sentence (*vākya*) and the *vṛtti* exist. Because *vṛtti* has as its domain the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), while the sentence has as its domain mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), there is no possibility of a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) due to their having different meanings."

The *san* suffix prescribed by the two rules beginning with *guptij* (Pāṇini 3.1.5) does not apply here, because there is no evidence for it and because it is not a rule dependent on word-formation (*padavidhi*). For this very reason, the *yaṅ* suffix does not apply to the *kaṇḍvādi* group; for since *yaṅ* and the other such suffixes denote the same meaning as the root itself, they cannot be defined as having a distinct meaning, which is a requirement for a second element. Consequently, words such as *stoka* are construed with the meaning of their own base.

For this very reason, there is no *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) in cases such as "the root *kṛ* is subsequently employed" (*kṛñcānuprayujyate*, Pāṇini 3.1.40). However, in the case of the *kvip* suffix derived from nominal stems (prātipadika), *ekārthībhāva* does apply there, because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) in the sūtra "the *ky-aṅ* suffix [is used] for the agent" (*kartuḥ kyaṅ*, 3.1.11), and due to the association with what precedes and follows.

For this very reason, although [the formation of *avagalbhate*] is established by the rule "from all nominal stems" (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*), there is no obstacle to connecting the word *supaḥ* ("from a case-ending") with the rule "in the sense of conduct" (*ācāre*) for the item *avagalbha*; since that [suffix] would apply only when there is a unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), its purpose is clearly evident. However, in this [present context], due to the functional significance of the mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-grahaṇa-sāmarthyāt*), there is no connection with the word *supaḥ*. For this very reason, they say that in forms such as *rājānati*, elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) and so forth does not occur.

In this way, even in the case of the *ṇic* suffix derived from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), that [same rule applies] due to association (*sāhacarya*). This is because, by means of a word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra "sutyāpa" [Pāṇini 3.1.25], the *ṇic* is included; and since it is situated within the same section (*prakaraṇa*), that [rule] applies to it as well. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "hetumati ca" [Pāṇini 3.1.26]:

"The addition [to the rule] is: 'one performs that' (*tatkaroti*). [Thus], *sūtraṃ karoti* becomes *sūtrayati*. Here, in the sentence 'he composes the *sūtra* of grammar' (*vyākaraṇasya sūtraṃ karoti*), the genitive case is used; whereas in the form 'he grammaticalizes grammar' (*vyākaraṇaṃ sūtrayati*), the accusative case is used. How does this come about? That relationship between the *sūtra* and grammar which existed prior to the formation of the suffix ceases once the suffix has been produced. However, since the verb *karoti* possesses a functional connection (*sāmarthya*) with grammar, the accusative case will indeed apply. Thus the *Bhāṣya* is consistent.

In the case of a word ending in a *sup*-affix followed by *ṇic*, however, this [ekārthībhāva] is indeed clear; for there exists precisely the status of being a rule conditioned by words (*padavidhitva*).
Even in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, there is ekārthībhāva because the term "dvandva" is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra].

To explain: the rule that prescribes this is "sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau" (Pāṇini 1.2.64). For by the elision of the word *eva* from that rule, it is ordained that there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) among those possessing homogeneity with respect to the property of being a case-ending (*vibhaktitva*) in ordinary usage. Precisely for this reason, there is no single remainder even in forms beginning with *bhyām* for the two words *mātṛ*, one denoting "mother" and the other denoting "measurer," because of their heterogeneity in forms such as *au* and *jas*.

However, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) does indeed occur between the word *hariṇī* meaning "female deer" and the word *hariṇī* meaning "a woman distinguished by the color green," because even though there is dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) due to the application of the *puvadbhāva* rule in the case of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) and so forth, there is an absence of dissimilarity in the case of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). And this [retention] takes place precisely before the production of the case-ending, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), since similarity (*sārūpya*) is merely a defining condition (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the case-ending.

Is this not already established by the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application)? For *tantra* is indeed twofold: the *tantra* of words (*śabdatantra*) and the *tantra* of meanings (*arthatantra*). According to the principle that "the difference in words arises from the difference in meanings," the first [type of *tantra*] applies where, upon the utterance of a word through a single operation of the palate and lips, a hearer perceives two distinct words due to the absence of any determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*). According to the principle that "there is unity of the word despite the plurality of its meanings," the second [type of *tantra*] applies where, through a single word manifested by a single operation of the palate and lips, multiple meanings are understood due to the absence of a determining factor.

Alternatively, the first [type of *tantra*] occurs in cases involving a word-break (*sabhaṅga*), such as "the white horse runs" (*śveto dhāvati*). The second occurs when there is a single sequence (*ekānupūrvīkatva*) for two meanings, as in "O swan of the mind of the wise" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*). Furthermore, there is no evidence for the restrictive rule that "a word is uttered only once. For those who accept such a rule, "repetition" (*āvṛtti*) refers to the conceptualization of repeated recollection. In reality, however, it should be understood that the term "repetition" denotes what is governed by the word (*śabdatantra*), while the term "rule" (*tantra*) denotes what is governed by the meaning (*arthatantra*). And the common basis in both cases is simply the similarity of the words (*śabdasārūpya*).

If it is argued that since [the desired result] is established by that very [rule], the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is redundant, we say no; for it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) stating that "only one remains among those that are identical. Consequently, since it is observed that a word is applied to each individual object, that [restriction] is intended to exclude forms such as *ghaṭa-ghaṭau*. In the rule "of those that are identical" (*sarūpāṇām*), by resorting to the method of *tantra* (simultaneous application), another restriction is adopted: "only among those that are identical within the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktau*) is there *ekaśeṣa*. Thus, in examples such as *mātṛbhyām*, even the *tantra* established by common worldly usage does not apply.

And this restriction applies only when there is a desire to express [the members] together within the domain of *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning), because it is accepted that the operation of the restriction occurs only in the domain of *dvandva*, by carrying forward the term "in a *dvandva*" (*dvandve*). Thus, in the case of *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy), a sentence indeed remains; otherwise, because *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would be obligatory, a sentence would be impossible to obtain.

And thus, just as in the case of a *dvandva* compound, there is the manifestation of concomitance (*sāhitya*) even in the case of *ekaśeṣa*. Consequently, when concomitance is intended to be expressed, there is only *ekaśeṣa* for words of identical form, and not the employment of a *dvandva*; for instance, in cases such as *mānasa*, there is sometimes an employment by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application), and sometimes even separately, as in "the mind of the learned" (*vidvanmānasamāsa*).

However, if one were to accept a rule that does not include the phrase "in a *dvandva*" and instead excludes concomitance from its scope, then, because *ekaśeṣa* would—just like *dvandva*—sublate even the *karmadhāraya* compound, forms such as *mānasamānasa* would result in ungrammaticality, as would the resulting sentence.

Thus, when there is a cognition of a collective type (*sāhityaprakāraka*), the term *ekaśeṣa* (single remainder) is employed; in its absence, the term *tantra* (abbreviation) is used. Furthermore, with the intention that "repetition" (*āvṛtti*) refers to the repeated mental application (*anusandhāna*) within the system of words (*śabdatantra*), the linguistic convention "let one of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa* [be applied]" is established.

Furthermore, when there is a plurality of actions, there is indeed a *dravya-ekaśeṣa* (single remainder of substances), as in the example: "Let the dice be thrown, eaten, and played with. However, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *yuṣmadyupapade* (Pāṇini 1.4.105), the term *ekaśeṣa* refers to *tantra* (the method of simultaneous application) because it results in that same effect; thus, there is no contradiction. And this has been explained in exactly this way by the *Upādhyāyas*—that is, by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa Upādhyāya.

According to the teachers: since the rule "in a *dvandva*" is common [to both types of *dvandva*], it should be understood that *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) applies even in the case of a collective *dvandva* (*samāhāradvandva*). Nor does this entail the occurrence of the neuter gender, because the grammatical injunction for that [neuter gender] applies only to the collective *dvandva*. For this very reason, the usage "ghaṭaghaṭam" does not occur; otherwise, in the absence of *ekaśeṣa* regarding the collective *dvandva*, a [non-collective] *dvandva* would be unavoidable here.

Furthermore, even on the view that words are applied to each individual object (*pratyarthaśabdaniveśapakṣa*), in cases such as "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," the inclusion of all individuals is accomplished through *ekaśeṣa* alone; thus, the grammatical rule does not need to be repeated for each individual—this is another favorable consequence. Because the aggregate is singular, the singular number alone is to be understood here. However, since killing is precluded [as a general rule], it occurs only with respect to specific individuals, just as in the expression "a hundred Brāhmaṇas are to be fed."

Furthermore, it is explained in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that the term *ekavat* ("as a single unit") in the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.69) is not redundant; for its purpose is to ensure that specific rules do not apply to the domain of *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective compounds). Thus, in forms such as *rāmāu* (Rāma and Rāma), the two Rāmas qualified by their association (*sāhitya*) are understood through the very word *rāma* which remains as the residue (*śiṣṭa*).

As for the claim that cognition arises from the recollection of the second word "rāma," and that for this very reason the "ekārthībhāva" (integration into a single meaning)—in the form of the unification of multiple meanings into one—is compatible with *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of several identical words); that is not correct. For it would result in the impossibility of cognition for one who does not know the exclusion of the others, and it would entail a violation of the principle that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). The conventional usage of the term "ekārthībhāva," however, must be explained as being figurative, just as the term "staff" is applied to the person who is the cause [of entering the assembly].

In expressions such as "two and two, one and one," neither the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of a single form) nor the *dvandva* (copulative compound) occurs, because they are not prescribed [for such cases]. However, in cases such as "twenty" (*viṃśati*), the *ekaśeṣa* is indeed desired.

If it is argued: "Even if this sūtra were necessary under the view that 'the individual (vyakti) is the word-meaning' to prevent the use of a word for every single individual, it is redundant under the view that 'the universal (jāti) alone is the word-meaning'; for even from a single word, the cognition of multiple individuals endowed with a single form can occur—either through the co-occurrence of various case-endings or by virtue of speaker-intention (tātparya). We reply: No; for even under that [universalist] view, the sūtra is necessary in cases such as *akṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ* to ensure the cognition of multiple individuals endowed with diverse forms.

Nor should it be argued that, having accepted a universal (*jāti*) residing in a genus (*jāti*), the *sūtra* need not even be formulated for its sake; for if such a universal were the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) in all cases, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of polysemous expressions (*nānārtha*). Furthermore, the *sūtra* is indispensable for establishing the rule of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) when one intends a cognition qualified by "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) etc., in cases where the meaning of that [genus] is forgotten (*pramoṣa*).

This is because the term "forgetting" (*moṣa*) refers precisely to the non-coincidence of the awakener (*udbodhaka*) regarding that part, given that memory—which consists of a recollection whose latent impression (*saṃskāra*) concerning that object has been awakened—acts as the bringer of the content to mind.

By this, the view of those who maintain that "the word itself is also a means of knowledge in verbal cognition"—according to which the word, like the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, is a qualifier (*prakāra*), and thus the word common to both [the denoted and the denoter] alone serves as the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—is refuted. This is because the denotative power (*śakti*) is constituted by the object; since the object is not distinct from its difference, the word cannot subsist in multiple objects through a single relation, and thus it lacks the quality of being a recurring commonality (*anugatatva*). This is the general direction of the argument. The refutation of the position that "there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of words ending in case-suffixes," and so forth, is clear in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

In the case of *brāhmaṇaśca brāhmaṇī ca brāhmaṇau*, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) by the rule *pumān striyā* [Pāṇini 1.2.67]. The meaning of that rule is: when a woman is mentioned together [with a man], the male form remains, provided that no distinction is made other than the meanings of "female" and "male. Therefore, for *gaureṣa* and *gauścaiṣā*, the result is simply *etau gāvau*.

However, for those who explain that "the *ekaśeṣa* [occurs] when there is the existence of a specific distinction produced for the sake of that [meaning]," since this [rule] would not apply here, there would occasionally arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a feminine remainder even under the *ekaśeṣa* rule "of similar forms" (*sarūpāṇām*). This should be inferred in other cases as well; further details are to be seen in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

As for that which is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *samartha-sūtra*: "For what purpose is the mention of the word (*pada*) made? So that an operation depending on letters (*varṇa-āśraya*) might be understood as occurring merely upon immediate succession [of sounds], as in the examples: *tiṣṭhatu dadhi aśāna tvam śākena*, *tiṣṭhatu kumārī chatram hara devadatta*," and so forth—this refers to the mention of the word (*padagrahaṇa*) specifically regarding operations concerning letters (*varṇagrahaṇa*).

Because of the observation of exclusion (*vyāvartya*), the word *pada* here denotes that which conveys meaning. Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is: "A rule (vidhi) which has as its objective a meaningful aggregate (*arthavat-samudāya*) is dependent upon semantic competency (*samartha*). And thus, there is no fault in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of one of several identical words) or in forms such as *kvip* derived from nominal stems (*prātipadika*), because even there, a meaningful aggregate is the objective. For this very reason, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in rules such as "after *aṅguli*, [the suffix] *saṅ* [is added]" (Pāṇini 8.3.80) is purposeful; it should be understood that in those cases, the letter *s* itself is the objective. [Objection: That is not so; for even in the case of what ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) or a case-ending (*sup*), the state of forming a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) would result.

Nor should it be argued that for you as well, there is no risk of non-application of rules such as *nerviśaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.17] and *antarāntareṇa* [Pāṇini 2.3.4] because they are word-based rules (*padavidhi*) that would not apply in the absence of *ekārthībhāva* (unity of meaning); for the meaning of those rules is that a rule conditioned by a word applies only where *ekārthībhāva* exists. This is because the application occurs through semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), and that maxim operates only where a word is directly the locus of the condition (*uddeśyatā*). For this very reason, the syntactic relation between the subject and predicate in forms such as *pacati* is logically consistent.
Therefore, this is an illustration of the purpose of the Bhāṣya. And this has been indicated in that very Bhāṣya.

Nor should it be argued that, if the meaning were "one who relies on five cooks," the usage *apañcapācakaḥ* would result; for even in the case of simple kṛt-suffixes, the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted.

Furthermore, since a root expresses an action whose distinctions [of number, etc. have been set aside, the connection of number with its referent is difficult to establish; thus, such a usage does not occur. This is the direction of the argument.

And "being a compound" (*samāsatva*) consists simply in possessing the status of a compound word by virtue of a specific conventional relation (*saṃketa-viśeṣa*). As for the view that "being a compound" is the state of being a collection of nouns whose preceding members do not have case-endings (*vibhakti*) considered for the purpose of semantic comprehension—this is not problematic even in cases such as *dadhi madhuram asti* (the curd is sweet), because the elided case-ending is indeed mentally supplied (*anusandhāna*). For this very reason, the causal efficacy of the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case for the connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is logically consistent. However, in the case of *nīlotpala* (blue lotus) and the like, there is no such mental supply, because comprehension occurs even for one who does not recognize the elision. It is for this same reason that the superiority of the *karmadhāraya* over the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* is logically established.

If one were to accept the recollection of the elided sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, that [position] would indeed be inconsistent because it lacks *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication). That is not so; for there is the complexity (*gaurava*) of assuming the recollection of case-endings in countless instances, and because understanding occurs even in one who does not know the elision. Furthermore, it is accepted that the cause for the connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is simply the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word other than a word ending in a non-nominative case-ending.

Nor does the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the connection with *bhāvanā* arise even in cases such as "eat that curd" (*taddadhi bhuṅkṣva*), because the intention (*tātparya*) is for that [curd] to be connected only as an object (*karman*). Otherwise, for you as well, the fault would remain exactly as it was; for even when both case-endings are considered due to the lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) based on the force of rules such as "svamornapuṃsakāt" [Pāṇini 7.1.23], the fault cannot be avoided.

Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that regard, because for those who are proficient in grammar, the understanding from a sequence such as "the jar does not exist" (*naghaṭo'sti*) arises from that very sequence itself.

By this, it is refuted that [the definition] should be understood as having a non-different case-ending (*anasundhīyamāna-vibhaktikatva*) with respect to the *ānupūrvī* (sequential order) that is the cause of verbal cognition; for, in that case, there would be no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) here, since [in examples like] "ghaṭo na" (there is no jar), the cause of cognition is precisely the knowledge of the *ānupūrvī* "ghaṭo na," etc. Furthermore, the direction [of the argument] is that there would likewise be an over-extension in the aggregate "artham" in the verse "śruter ivārtham" (as if the meaning from the Veda).
Similarly, being a *tatpuruṣa* compound and so forth is simply the possession of the word "tatpuruṣa" and so on, by virtue of that [same] relation.

As for the claim that an *avyayībhāva* compound has the meaning of the first member as its primary referent, a *tatpuruṣa* has the meaning of the final member as its primary referent, a *bahuvrīhi* has the meaning of another [member] as its primary referent, and a *dvandva* has the meanings of both members as its primary referents—that is not correct.

In the case of *unmattagaṅgam* (the "Mad Gaṅgā"), which is an *avyayībhāva* compound where the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of its definition and over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of a *bahuvrīhi*. Similarly, in the case of *sūpapratīti*, an *avyayībhāva* where the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*) is predominant, there is non-pervasion of its definition and over-pervasion of the definition of a *tatpuruṣa*. In the case of *ardhapiplālī* and similar *tatpuruṣas*, there is non-pervasion of their definition and over-pervasion of the definition of an *avyayībhāva*. In the case of *dvitrāḥ* ("two or three"), a *bahuvrīhi* where the meanings of both members are predominant, there is non-pervasion of its definition and over-pervasion of the definition of a *dvandva*.

Furthermore, these definitions are impossible even under the theory of *jahatsvārthā* (where words abandon their own meanings), because they would result in meaninglessness. Even under the theory of *ajahatsvārthā* (where words do not abandon their own meanings), since words lack the capacity to produce separate individual cognitions, it is impossible to determine that "this much is the meaning of the preceding word" and "this much is the meaning of that word. Therefore, rather than attempting to justify those [definitions] by resorting to what is obtained through a retrospective understanding (*bhūtapūrvagati*), our stated definitions are indeed simpler; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Furthermore, another point to be noted here is this: in a *vṛtti* (compound), whenever there is no indicator of a specific number for the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), the number "undifferentiated unity" (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) is understood. And it is precisely as a number that this very number is designated by the term "undifferentiated unity. With this very intention, they say that the various specific numbers exist in an undivided state, or that "undifferentiated unity" is the general category of number (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*) from which specific distinctions have been discarded. [The example] "the lions of Bhartṛ" (*bhartuḥ harayaḥ*) is the remainder [of the discussion]. For instance: "Just as all medicinal juices, when their powers are deposited in honey..."
"They exist without division; they know that number to be of such a kind.

The phrase "possessing imparted powers" (*āhitaśaktayaḥ*) means those by whom the power consisting of opposition—which is based on the distinctions between various defects—has been surrendered. That is to say, their opposition has been set aside. For this very reason, "without division" (*avibhāgena*) means "without opposition" (*avirodhena*). "That" (*tām*) refers to the number of non-dual unity. "Of such a kind" (*tādṛśīm*) means similar to the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) residing in the mind.

In this view, there is the manifestation of number-generality (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*) alone as the category of number, and not of a specific number (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*). Although this may appear inconsistent—since a generality cannot exist unqualified by its particulars—it is nevertheless not inconsistent because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "the son of a barren woman" or "the head of Rāhu" are possible. As it has been said: "For a word produces cognition even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent."

However, in cases such as *indragopa* and others, although the plural number is present in words like *vārṣika* ("born in the rainy season"), the number is understood solely as "number" (*saṃkhyātva*), and not as "plurality" (*bahutvatva*) and so forth; for the plural suffix exists there in relation to a plurality [of individual instances] rather than a plurality [of the class]. For this very reason, the cognition of that which is born even during a single rainy season is consistent with it. And this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the *samartha*-sūtra.

Nor should it be argued that when there is a context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, the compound "released from the two small ones" (*stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ*) would be grammatically correct even with the non-elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending]; for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Bhāṣya* is that, due to the lack of specific prescription (*anabhidhāna*), no such compound occurs in that instance. The point is that the understanding arises in that manner solely from expressions such as "released from a little" (*stokānmuktaḥ*) when accompanied by the context. The singular number, however, is the default (*autsargika*).

Having this very point in mind, one might raise the following objection regarding such examples as *dantoṣṭhasya dantāḥ snigdhatarāḥ* ("the teeth of the lip-toothed person are glossier"): since there is no occurrence of the technical dual number [in *dantoṣṭha*], and because the compound is singular (*samāhāra*) while the subordinate members (*vartipadārtha*) are plural, the suffix *-tarap* would not apply due to the absence of a dual word as its *upapada*. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states: "In a compound (*vṛtti*), because distinction is abandoned and the number of unity characterized by non-distinction is adopted, the suffix is based on two referents (*artha*) characterized as 'teeth' and 'lips'. This refers to the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade*.

This is stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other commentaries on the sūtra [Pāṇini 5.3.57]. However, when even in that case a specific number is understood through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, the suffix *tarap* does not occur at all. In examples such as "Among the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees, the *plakṣas* are the longest," there is no *tarap*. Likewise, in examples such as "Among the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees, the *plakṣas* are the longest," there is no *tarap*, because by means of the plural number, only a specific number among the individual members is perceived.

If it is asked: "What is the determining factor for designating this [number] with the term 'the number one-ness of non-difference,' since it is possible to designate it even with terms such as 'non-dual two-ness' and so forth? [The answer is: By the sentence "One should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds," the sacrifice of *kapiñjala* birds qualified by a number subsumed under plurality (*bahutva*) is enjoined.

In this regard, when there is a doubt as to whether three or four and more [animals] are to be sacrificed, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that since the property of being pervaded by plurality (bahutva-vyāpyatva) is common to all numbers beginning with three, one should sacrifice exactly as many as are indicated. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that four and more are to be sacrificed; for it would involve the unnecessary complexity (gaurava) of assuming a restrictive interpretation—such as that the general prohibition "one shall not kill" applies only to instances other than those specifically mentioned—whereas the scriptural statement finds its purpose simply by referring to the number three, which is the first to present itself in the act of counting.

Furthermore, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), it has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that among many [numbers], only the number three is the meaning of the plural suffix. By that same logic, here too, it is only singularity (*ekatva*) as a number that serves as the basis for the function (*vṛtti*), and not duality (*dvitva*) and so forth; for the intent of the section is that singularity whose specific attributes are not perceived is "non-dual singularity" (*abheda-ekatva*), according to the etymological derivation. Understand this by the logic of the *Kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the partridge), since singularity is the first to be presented. And thus, they say that even for this purpose, the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is necessary.

Others, however, maintain that there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here of the number itself toward its own relatum as a possessor of number, because there is no evidence for such a thing and because no such cognition is experienced. Nor can such a postulation be made on the strength of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*); for knowledge produced by words is not the determining factor for a specific desire to know. Otherwise, the mere sight of a mango fruit would result in a desire to know its specific taste. Furthermore, since a substance is never found without a number, the knowledge of the latter is possible; and since the causal relationship between a specific knowledge and a specific desire must be observed in its particularity, it follows that the denotation must also be specific. Therefore, there is simply an absence of number.

The meaning of the term *abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā* (the number one of non-difference) is as follows: by the word *bheda* (difference), duality (*dvitva*) and so forth—which co-occur with it—are meant; and there is simply a non-perception (*apratīti*) of that [duality] along with its oneness. Thus, even in examples such as *varṣāsujaḥ*, there is indeed the manifestation of that [oneness]. However, when context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors are present, there certainly occurs a specific manifestation of it. In that case, there is indeed *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in that very form. This has been indicated in the *Padamañjarī* on the rule *pañcamyāstokādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.27], they say; and both views are clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *samartha* rule.

As for what the Mīmāṃsakas say: in the sūtra "A rule concerning words applies when there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*)," semantic competency means independence from others. By the term "rule concerning words" (*padavidhi*), a rule that effects a word is understood, such as [Pāṇini 2.3.18] "The agent and the instrument [take the third case-ending]," and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that a rule concerning words which is to be enjoined indicates its object through independence from others. For this very reason, from sentences such as "One should sacrifice with rice-grains" or "Or one should sacrifice with barley," the accomplishment of the sacrifice occurs through either the rice-grains or the barley independently of anything else.

Furthermore, only that which is of the same class (*sajātīya*) is understood [by the term *samartha*]. Therefore, expressions such as "he makes a jar with a stick and a wheel" (*daṇḍena cakreṇa ghaṭaṃ karoti*) are not ungrammatical. Moreover, by repeating the rule regarding semantic competency (*samartha-sūtra*), the meaning stated by you is also established. To this we reply: no; for there is no evidence (*māna*) for such a repetition.

In cases such as "the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*) or "he is cooking" (*pacati bhavati*), even though there is no indicator of the aforementioned capacity [of the verb], the understanding of the objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth as independent of other factors occurs through logic alone—since the qualifier has the result of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) or excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). This being possible even in instances like "with rice" (*vrīhibhiḥ*), there is no further purpose [for postulating a distinct function].

In examples such as *gārgya*, since the rule prescribing the suffix (*pratyaya-vidhi*) does not itself effect the status of being a word (*padatva*), your proposed paribhāṣā would fail to apply; consequently, there would be no cognition of [the meaning] "being the descendant of Garga" and so forth independently of other factors. If one were to resort to some manner of treating it as a "word-rule" (*pada-vidhi*) by any means, then since every rule in grammar would be such, the term "word-rule" (*padavidhi*) would become redundant, and furthermore, the expression "word-rule" would have to be taken as a metaphorical designation (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which is prescribed by it. Thus, everything is established as desired. Now, the understanding regarding the difficult compound words is set forth.

*Pūrvabhūtaḥ* means *bhūtapūrvaḥ*. Here, *pūrṇam* is an adverbial qualifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); the root *bhū* signifies an operation conducive to origination; and the word *pūrva* refers to that which exists in a prior time. Thus, the understanding is: "one who is the substratum of an operation conducive to origination that occurred in the past and has passed away.
In *apadiśam*, within the scope of this compound formation, the word *apa* indicates the middle; the meaning is "the middle between two directions" (*diśoḥ madhyam*).
In *barau adhihari*, here the preposition *adhi* indicates the locative force (*adhikaraṇaśakti*); the meaning is "Hari as the locus" (*harirūpādhikaraṇa*).

In the expression *upakṛṣṇam*, the prefix *upa* indicates proximity; thus, the meaning is "near Kṛṣṇa. In *duryavanaṃ*, the word *dur-* indicates the absence of prosperity (*ṛddhi*); the understanding is that there is a connection with the Yavanas characterized by the absence of prosperity. Prosperity refers to the possession of wealth and so forth. In *atinidram*—meaning "sleep does not apply"—the word *nidrā* indicates the absence of the action of being currently engaged in sleep performed by the agent of sleep; *ati-* is the indicator of this [absence]. Regarding usages such as *atinidram āsīt* ("he was beyond sleep"), they say that the term *atinidram* functions as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) within the scope of such conventional usage.
Others hold that the cognition is "sleep is characterized by the absence of connection," where the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) is reversed in the compound.
Regarding *iti-hari*: the word *hari* refers to its own form (*svarūpa*), and *iti* indicates manifestation (*prakāśa*); thus, the cognition is "the manifestation associated with the word *hari*.
The meaning of *anurūpam* is "that which possesses a connection whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is form"; here, the prefix *anu* indicates suitability (*yogyatā*).
In the expression *yathāśakti* ("according to one's ability"), the meaning indicated by the word *yathā* here is "not exceeding the objects denoted by the words uttered together.
In the case of *sa hariḥ devadattaḥ* ("He is like Hari, Devadatta"), the cognition is that there is a similarity residing in Devadatta, having Hari as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
In expressions such as *anujyeṣṭhaṃ praṇamati* ("He bows according to seniority"), the meaning is that he bows following the order of seniority.

Regarding the expression *sacakram*, the understanding is that it possesses a concomitance (*sāhitya*) coextensive with simultaneity (*ekakālikatva*) relative to the wheel (*cakra*); this should be understood because the rule for compound formation is prescribed in the sense of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*). In the present case as well, there is no fault, because simultaneity enters [the compound] as a subordinate attribute (*guṇatayā*). In the term *sakṣatram*, the word *kṣatra* has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning; thus, the understanding is "an attainment whose object is the status of a Kṣatriya" (*kṣatriyatva-viṣayā saṃpattiḥ*). The word *sa-* signifies "attainment" (*sampatti*). "Attainment" is a corresponding state of being (*anurūpa ātmabhāvaḥ*), which means, in other words, "possessing a suitable ground for one's own activity" (*yogyasvappravṛttinimittavattvam*).

Regarding the expression *satṛṇam atti* ("he eats with the grass"): here, the meaning of "together" (*saha*) is the state of being an object for a particular cognition (*buddhiviśeṣaviṣayatva*). The sense is "together with grass. For by this, it is understood that he eats every edible thing; for the understanding arises: "How could he abandon anything else if he were to eat even grass? The intended purport (*tātparya*) lies precisely in this [comprehensiveness], and not in the eating of grass itself. Some maintain that the cognition is simply that "he eats" (*atti*).

Regarding the expression *sāgni adhīte*—"he studies together with the *agni* [section]": here too, the expressed meaning is "together with the book (*grantha*) concerning the *agni*. Through study accompanied by that [section], the completion of the study of the entire book up to its end is understood. It is by this much alone that the word *saha* conveys the sense of "ending" (*anta*). Some, however, say that both "finality" (*antatva*) and "concomitance" (*sāhitya*) are conveyed by *saha*; thus, they claim the understanding is: "study having as its object [the text] together with the final *agni* section. Regarding *yāvacchlokam acyutapramāṇāḥ*—"those whose measure is the number of verses": what is conveyed by *yāvat* is the state of being delimited by a specific measure; [thus, the meaning is] "delimited by a number consisting of the measure of verses."
The understanding is that "praṇāmāḥ" (prostrations) is the meaning.

In expressions such as *akṣapari* ("around the dice"), the sense of the prefix *pari-* is "turning in the opposite direction. This opposition is in relation to victory (*jaya*). The dice (*akṣa*) are construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, the understanding is: "turning in the opposite direction with the dice as the instrument," which amounts to "defeat" (*parājaya*). In the phrase *anuvanam aśanir gataḥ* ("the thunderbolt went along the forest"), the word *vana* (forest) has the sense of "proximity" (*samīpa*), and its function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is indicated by the suffix. Thus, the understanding is: "the thunderbolt is the object of the action of going, which is characterized by being known [to have occurred] in a location proximate to the forest."

"Anugaṅga Vārāṇasī"—here, the extension [along] the Gaṅgā is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), and its being located therein is what is to be illuminated. The indicated (*lakṣya*) is the extension of Vārāṇasī, because Vārāṇasī itself is not made known by its own form. And thus, by the word "Gaṅgā," that which possesses the length of the Gaṅgā is indicated. It should be understood that the quality of being an indicator of length is due to similarity with length. Regarding "pāregaṅgā-pārāt," it is explained as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

Regarding "ddhimuni vyākaraṇasya"—the understanding is: "two sages who possess descent (*vaṃśyatva*) related to grammar. This state of descent is understood through the process of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*).

In the case of *dvimuni-vyākaraṇam*, the understanding is that "grammar is non-different from two sages," just as in the case of [the term] *vaiśya*. This is incorrect because of the intended expression of non-difference (*abheda*) between the knowledge and its possessor.

In *saptagaṅgam* and similar compounds, the understanding is "the collection (*samāhāra*) of the seven Gaṅgās. In *unmattagaṅgam* and similar cases, the understanding is "that which has the intoxicated Gaṅgā as its locus.
Thus ends the section on Avyayībhāva compounds.
Now, regarding the analysis of *tatpuruṣa* compounds:

in cases such as *kṛṣṇa-śritaḥ* ("resorted to by Kṛṣṇa"), the understanding arises in the manner of "the agent of the act of resorting whose object is Kṛṣṇa. Here, Kṛṣṇa and the like, obtained through the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) [of the compound], are construed with the subsequent member's meaning through a relation of "objecthood" (*karmatā*) and so forth. This should be inferred in other cases as well.

In the case of *svayaṃ-kṛtaḥ* ("self-made"), the understanding is "the object of the act of making whose agent is oneself. For this very reason, this [compound] has the power of the agent as its primary element in the sense of necessity (*nitya-samartha*).

The word *khaṭvārūḍha* is a purely conventional (*rūḍha*) term denoting one who acts without due reflection; therefore, this is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*), because that meaning is not understood from the analytical sentence (*vākya*).

Regarding *māsapramita*: the understanding is "one who effects a measurement with respect to a month. This is based on the rule: "The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action and denotes the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.71).

It is clear in the *Bhāṣya* that in examples such as *śaṅkulākhaṇḍa* ("a piece made by a wedge"), the application occurs only when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) mediated by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*), neither when there is direct mutual syntactic relation (*parasparānvaya*), nor when the connection is mediated by another action.

*dhānyenārthaḥ*, *dhānyārthaḥ*: because of the rule beginning with *prakṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.18), the third case is used. The word *artha* denotes wealth; the understanding is that it is wealth non-different from grain (*dhānya*). *māsapūrvaḥ*: "one who was previously [born] by means of a month. Here, the meaning of the word *pūrva* is that which originates at a time that is neither the time of the limit of origination nor the locus of its destruction. Its connection with "time," which is a part of that [meaning], occurs through identity with the month. *māṣonam*: "less by a māṣa. The meaning of *ūna* is "possessing an absence" (*abhāvavat*). In that context, the māṣa and so forth connect to the absence by way of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

*Vākkalahaḥ*—*kalaha* is an action preceded by anger; in this context, it is construed as being related to speech (*vāk*). *Ācāranipuṇaḥ*—the meaning is one who possesses skill caused by proper conduct (*ācāra*).

*Guḍamiśraḥ*—here, the meaning of the word *miśra* is "possessing a conjunction" (*saṃyogavān*); within that conjunction, which is a part of the whole, *guḍa* (molasses) is construed as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitayā*).

The term *ācāraślakṣṇa* is explained by one skilled in usage (*ācāranipuṇa*) as "smooth" (*ślakṣṇa*), meaning "bright" (*ujjvala*). Regarding the expression *kākapeyā nadī* ("the river drinkable by crows"): the meaning is that the river is the object of the drinking performed by crows. Through the state of having full water, there is praise; or, through the state of having little water, there is censure—this is what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

In the case of *dadhyodana* ("curd-rice"), the understanding here is that it is rice sprinkled with curd (*dadhyupasikta odana*). The act of sprinkling (*upaseka*) is obtained through the formation of a single semantic unit (*ekārthībhāva*).

*yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post) and *yūpadāru* (sacrificial post-wood): here, there is a compound with a word ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*) expressing "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*). This [type of compound] also occurs only when there is a relationship between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*). However, compounds such as *aśvaghāsa* (horse-food) are genitive-tatpuruṣas; this is explained in detail elsewhere. *sarveṣāṃ śvetataraḥ* (whiter than all) means *sarvaśvetaḥ* (all-white). The meaning is that, in comparison with the white color residing in other substances, this quality of whiteness is superior among all the cloths. Alternatively, the meaning is "the whitest among all. And there is no occurrence of the suffix *-tama* [instead of *-tara*], because they say that the suffix *-tara* is accepted even in the selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) from among many in certain cases.

In expressions such as *pūrvakāyaḥ* ("the front half of the body") and *ardhapippalī* ("half a long pepper"), the understanding proceeds according to the sequence: "the part preceding that which is related to the body," and so forth; here, the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) is predominant. However, when words such as *kāya* are used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote a part thereof, the understanding is: "the prior portion non-different from a part of the body."

*Māsajātaḥ* means "one month old," that is, one for whom a month has passed since birth (*māso jātasya*). Although in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) the month is the primary element, nevertheless, in the compound (*vṛtti*), as seen in examples such as *jāto māsajātaḥ* or *dṛśyatām*, it is understood that the person who was born (*jāta*) alone is the object of the act of seeing and so forth. To indicate this very point, some also employ the formulation "of whom [the month] is [the measure]" (*yasya saḥ*) in the analytical statement; furthermore, the reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified is achieved through the process of unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). In the analytical statement, the cognition is "the month which delimits the born," whereas in the compound, it is "the born person delimited by the month."

The state of being "determinable" (*paricchedyatva*) for one who is born (*jātasya*) is by virtue of being the locus for the production of a determination (*paricchedajananāśrayatvena*). When the question is asked, "How much time has passed for this person who is born? the answer "one month old" (*māsajāta*) should be understood as having an implied meaning (*ārtha*). Others, however, hold that the understanding arises from the analysis (*vigraha*) "the month subsequent to birth" (*jātottaramāsa*). In this case, the genitive case-meaning (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is the state of being subsequent (*uttarakālikatva*); and within the compound, the state of being subsequent to birth (*jātottaratva*) is understood by taking it to mean "subsequent to birth" (*jananottaratvam*). It is precisely to suggest this that the phrase "that which belongs to whom" (*yasya saḥ*) was stated. They say that because of the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), the formation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound would not otherwise apply; however, that point is questionable, since *bahuvrīhi* compounds are observed even in cases where there is no coreferentiality.

The understanding is that "one who has bathed first" (*parva-snātaḥ*) refers to one who is subsequently anointed (*paścād-anuliptaḥ*), meaning one who is the locus of anointing subsequent to bathing, which is understood through the principle of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning). Similarly, *pañcagavam* means "a collection of five cows," that is, a collective aggregate of five cows numbering five.

*Ghanaśyāmaḥ*—the understanding is either "one who is dark like a cloud" (*ghanasadṛśābhinnaḥ śyāmaḥ*) or "darkness non-different from a cloud" (*ghanābhinnaḥ śyāmaḥ*). In this compound, both in its analytical explanation (*vigraha*) and its formation (*vṛtti*), the first member is indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) of something similar to it, or is superimposed (*āropita*) upon it. It is precisely to suggest this that the particle *iva* is employed in the analytical explanation. For this very reason, in expressions such as *mṛgacapalā* ("fickle like a deer"), there occurs the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) because of the subsequent word being a coordinate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) compound ending. Furthermore, the similarity [of the first member] is with respect to qualities such as "darkness" (*śyāmatva*) which are present [in the referent]; the details of this are found elsewhere.

In *puruṣavyāghra* ("man-tiger"), the second member (*uttarapada*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote something similar to it, or it is superimposed (*āropita*). The resulting cognition has the meaning of the first member as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.56: *upamitaṃ vyaghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge* ("A word compared with 'tiger' and the like forms a compound when a common attribute is not employed"). In examples such as *prasanne dṛgabjene* ("in the gracious lotus-eyes"), there is no similarity based on an explicitly mentioned attribute; rather, it is based solely on an unmentioned one. Thus, since a common attribute is indeed present (albeit implicit), there is no fault.

In reality, this sūtra operates only when there is identity of gender and number, because of its inclusion under the governing rule for co-ordinate compounds (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *paravalliṅgam* (2.4.26)—"Which tatpuruṣa does it apply to? That which is a partitive compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) where the meaning of the first member is predominant"—as well as the rejection of the mention of *tatpuruṣa* by proposing the reading *dvandvaikadeśinoḥ* instead, is consistent with the Bhāṣya.

Otherwise, in cases such as *dṛgabjena* ("lotus-eye"), there would be an obvious inconsistency, because there would be no reason to abandon the primary gender of the preceding member (*dṛk*)—which is seen to follow the gender of the subsequent member—in favor of the latter's gender. However, in *dṛgabjam*, it is simply a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Furthermore, in expressions such as *dṛgabjena vīkṣate* ("he looks with the lotus-eye"), the connection with the act of seeing is entirely unimpeded, since the identity with the eye is perceived within the principal element [the eye]. For this very reason, modern theorists of poetics (*alaṅkārikas*) maintain that the figure of speech here is *pariṇāma* (transformation).

In cases such as *mukhacandra* ("moon-face") and the like, it is indeed a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). However, the conventional designation of it as a "metaphor" (*rūpaka*) is based on the fact that the non-difference having the moon as its counter-correlate is also perceived in the face, being cognized through the same cognitive act (*samānavittivedyatayā*), and this is accepted figuratively.

As for [compounds] such as *anyo rājāntaram* ("another king"), their taking the gender of the final member should be understood precisely because they belong to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* class. In that context, the word *antara* signifies "different"; it qualifies the meaning of the prior member by way of non-difference. They say that the state of being a counter-correlative of something residing in the cognition that is the substratum of the mode of the understanding produced by the prior member is obtained in the case of difference through the force of a specific linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

Others, however, maintain that even in the compound *upamitam*, the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*) remains predominant. Furthermore, the cognition [of meaning] in negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) has been explained in the *Nirṇaya of the Meaning of Nañ*. In cases such as *prācāryaḥ* (one who has departed from his teacher) and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has gone out from Kauśāmbī), the meanings of "departed," "gone out," and so forth appear in the compound by virtue of the force of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning).
Thus concludes the analysis of the *tatpuruṣa* compound. Now follows the analysis of the *bahuvrīhi* compound:

"That village to which water has come" is *prāptodako grāmaḥ*. In this case, the understanding derived from the compound (*vṛtti*) is that the village is the object of the arrival whose agent is the water. In the analytical statement (*vigraha*), however, it is "the water which is the agent of the arrival whose object is [the village]. The same should be inferred for examples such as *ūḍharatho 'naḍvān* ("an ox that has drawn a chariot") and so forth. The justification for this has already been stated above.

Those which are near to ten are "upadaśāḥ" (near-ten). Here, *upa* has the sense of proximity (*samīpa*). The word-meaning "ten" is construed with "proximity" by means of the relation of being the counter-positive of the state-of-being-ten that resides in itself (*svavṛttidaśatvapratiyogikatva*). The resulting cognition is: "those possessing proximity to ten. It should be understood that its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) arises only through such a relation, due to the force of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) and the authority of rules such as Pāṇini’s *saṃkhyayā'vyaya* [2.2.25].

For this very reason, nine or eleven are conveyed by this [compound], but those cows and other animals that are near ten trees and so forth are not conveyed. By this, the expressions *asannaviṃśāḥ* ("not far from twenty") and *adūratriṃśāḥ* ("not distant from thirty") are explained. Regarding *adhikacatvāriṃśāḥ*: here the meaning is "more than forty. Regarding *dvitrāḥ* ("two or three"): here the word *vā* indicates contradiction (*virodha*). And that contradiction appears as the state of not occurring simultaneously in a single substratum.

In some cases, however—such as in "one should sacrifice with rice (*vrīhibhiḥ*) or one should sacrifice with barley (*yavaiḥ*)"—even in the absence of the word *vā*, an option (*vikalpa*) is understood because, by virtue of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), the instrumental case-ending conveys an independent means of accomplishment, and because a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is impossible. This is just as conjunction is understood even without the word *ca*. Here too, multiple factors that are mutually independent are construed with the action; for after one factor has been construed with the action, the other is construed through repetition (*āvṛtti*). Thus, in this instance, the word *vā* indicates the difference in time (*bhinnakālikatva*) regarding the action qualified by the co-occurring factors (*kāraka*).

In some cases, however, even the absence of the meaning associated with a word co-occurring with *vā* is expressed by that particle. For example, in rules such as *dīrghāt padāntād vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.76), and in expressions like *sthāṇur vā navā*, the meaning of *vā* is indeed contradiction in the form of non-coexistence within a single locus (*ekādhikaraṇāvṛttitva*), which generates a doubt (*saṃśaya*). This is because one of the two alternatives is entirely sublated. Furthermore, the presentation of distinct alternatives arises precisely from the co-occurrence with the word *vā*; otherwise, if it were simply said *sthāṇur na*, the resulting cognition would be merely "it is different from a post."

In some cases, however, the meaning is "contradiction" (*virodha*), which consists of being simultaneous, having the same substratum, and not exceeding [the number] by one; as in the expression "beauty in a cloth or a jar," where there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the connection with the action, but not regarding the presentation from the word itself. Therefore, since many things are invariably presented by the word, it necessarily ends in the plural suffix; this is explained in detail elsewhere. *Dvidaśāḥ* means "ten repeated twice. Here, they say that the compound occurs through the inclusion of the sense of the suffix *-su-* (possessive), by virtue of the force of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning).

In expressions such as *dakṣiṇapūrvā* (southeast), the meaning is "the intermediate direction between the southern and eastern directions," and so on; this is due to the force of *ekārthībhāva* (syntactic integration). For it is the intermediate direction of the whole [compound] that is denotable.

"Having seized each other by the hair, this battle proceeded; [this is] *kāśākeśi*. In this compound, the suffix *-ktvā* should be understood as referring to an action such as "staying" (*sthiti*) that is supplied. Furthermore, the status of being the object (*karman*) of the seizing belongs, by virtue of proximity, only to the two persons qualified by their hair and so forth. The "reciprocity of action" (*karmavyatihāra*), consisting of the mutual seizing of others' hair and so on, is denoted by the entire compound, as are actions such as fighting.

And thus, the understanding is that there is an action whose agent is the person who remains after the act of seizing—characterized by having those [two] as its substratum and whose substrata are their mutual hair—performed by the person who was the agent of the seizing. As for the nature of this action, it is sometimes understood from the context to be in the form of battle, and sometimes from the co-occurrence of words denoting battle and the like. For example:
"Desirous of seeing the dance of the parasol-staffs of the kings, hand-to-hand, what need is there for war?"

In such cases as these, the examples "fame spread from ear to ear" (*karṇākarṇi prathitam ayaśaḥ*) and "touching the slope of her breasts under the pretext of hand-to-hand contact" (*hastāhastimiṣāt spṛśan kucataṭīm*) are explained. Regarding the first, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "having heard this great battle from ear to ear"; here, *prathitam* (spread) is an adverbial adjunct (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
By this, the view of Kaiyaṭa and others—that such a compound occurs only in the sense of a battle—is refuted; the details are found elsewhere.

The phrase "he went with his son" (*saputro gataḥ*) and so forth is explained by the analysis of the meaning of the *sub* suffixes through the understanding established in the discussion of the *saha* compound (*sahaputreṇa gataḥ*).
Thus concludes the investigation of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Now follows the investigation of the *dvandva* compound.

In cases such as *dhavakhadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees"), the understanding is that the dhava and khadira are conjoined (*sahitau*). In cases such as *pāṇipādam* ("hands and feet"), the understanding is a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of hands and feet.

In *upadaśam* ("near ten") and *dantoṣṭham* ("teeth and lips"), there is a collective aggregate of "near ten" and "teeth and lips. Regarding the aggregate, it should be understood that "ten" and "nearness" possess parts whose number possesses proximity relative to the number ten residing in itself. The term *upadaśam* expresses non-excess (*abhībhāva*).

However, there is no subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) for a *bahuvrīhi*, because, being invariably plural in form, it is unfit to be construed with [the singular term] "teeth-and-lips" (*dantoṣṭham*). In this same manner, [the principle] should be inferred elsewhere as well.
Thus ends the investigation of *dvandva*.
Thus ends the investigation of the expressive power (*śakti*) of compounds and so forth.
Now, the meaning of suffixes such as *kyac*, which have words ending in case-terminations (*subanta*) as their base (*prakṛti*), is examined.

In that regard, in the example "Devadatta desires a jar" (*ghaṭamicchatīti ghaṭiyati devadattaḥ*), the meaning of *kyac* is "desire," while there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the base word's referent, the jar, as being connected with the agent. For this very reason, one does not say "Devadatta considers himself a son" (*putrīyatyātmānaṃ devadattaḥ*). It is for this same reason that the Bhāṣya on the rule *supa ātmanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.8) is consistent, stating: "Because this [verbal root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *l*-suffix [denoting the object] does not occur here from [the base]."

And here, *kyac* alone is the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). According to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, its meaning is that *kyac* is applied to a word denoting the object of a desire related to the desirer, when there is a wish. Thus, the understanding is: "a desire whose agent is Devadatta and whose object is a jar related to himself. The status of being the object (*karmatva*), however, is obtained through a specific expressive power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*). The same applies to *kāmyac* as well.

Likewise, the suffix *kyac* is also applied by the rule *upamānādācāre* [Pāṇini 3.1.10]. The meaning of this rule is that *kyac* is added to an object denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) when the sense is "behaving like. Here, only that which is the standard of comparison as determined by the act of behaving (*carana*) is taken, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). An example is *viṣṇūyati dvijam* ("he behaves toward the twice-born like Viṣṇu"). In this case, the word *viṣṇu* signifies an act of behavior similar to that performed by Viṣṇu; the act of behaving is the meaning of the suffix *kyac*. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "an act of behaving directed toward the twice-born, having Devadatta as its agent, which is similar to an act of behavior performed by Viṣṇu."

In that context, by virtue of proximity, even the ritual practice of Viṣṇu has Devadatta and others as its agent, either because of the continued application of the term "of oneself" (ātmanaḥ) or due to proximity.

Furthermore, in this view, there would be no inconsistency even in the verse: "The heaven, adorned with the gods (suparvan), acts like Bhārata," because it is not established that the conduct of the inhabitants of heaven resembles the conduct of the Bhārata people. As for the phrase "adorned with the gods (suparvan)," one must state that through *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) there is only an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) [of the two meanings], and not an identification based on similarity (*sādṛśyādhyavasāya*); for just as the cognition of non-difference arises from being expressed by a single word, so too the cognition of similarity is possible through the common property of their verbal form.

In the expression "kṛṣṇāyate devadattaḥ" (Devadatta acts like Kṛṣṇa), the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs in the sense of "acting like Kṛṣṇa. Here too, the meaning of the base of the *kyaṅ* suffix is an action similar to the action performed by Kṛṣṇa; the meaning of *kyaṅ* itself is "action. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "an action performed by Devadatta that is similar to an action performed by Kṛṣṇa. It should be noted that the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between Viṣṇu and the twice-born (on one hand) and Kṛṣṇa and Devadatta (on the other) is understood through implication, but is not expressed directly by the words.

In this context, when items such as *putra* (son) and *kṛṣṇa* (Kṛṣṇa) undergo semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*) with the meaning of suffixes like *kyac*, they appear solely as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*), due to the very nature of the power of words (*śabdaśakti*). For this very reason, in a sentence such as "he composes a grammatical rule" (*vyākaraṇaṃ sūtraṃ karoti*), although grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is construed as a related entity (*sambandhitvena*), it functions as the object (*karmatva*) in expressions such as "he formulates grammar" (*vyākaraṇaṃ sūtrayati*); other such cases are to be inferred accordingly.
This concludes the investigation into the meaning of *kyac* and similar suffixes.
Now, the meaning of *taddhita* suffixes derived from nominal stems (*subanta*) is being defined.

In this context, the meaning of "offspring" and so forth—prescribed by rules such as *tasyāpatyam* [Pāṇini 4.1.92]—as well as the meaning of the genitive case and so on, is understood through the composite whole. Therefore, the meaning of words such as *aupagavaḥ* is "the offspring related to Upagu. It has been established here that because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted, there is no syntactic connection with qualifiers and the like.

In the examples of the rule *sāsya devatā* [Pāṇini 4.2.24], such as *āgneya* and others, the meaning of the suffix is that which is to be given (*deya*) as qualified by the deity. The meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is a qualifier of one part of the meaning of the suffix through the relation of identity (*abheda*). (Note: The qualification is to be understood either through the relation of the owned and the owner (*svasvāmibhāva*), or through the relation of being the object of an act of renunciation directed toward the deity.)

Alternatively, according to the commentary on the sūtras "devatā" [is derived] from the root *div*, meaning "to possess sovereignty," and "devāt tal," deityhood (*devatātva*) consists in being the locus of a fruit other than the results such as heaven produced by the renunciation of an oblation accompanied by a mantra, as well as being the object of praise by that mantra. This is stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: "He whose words [the mantra] are, is the seer (*ṛṣi*); that which is expressed by it is the deity. For this very reason, the two types of usage—such as "an Indra-mantra" and "an Indra-oblation"—are established.

The power (*śakti*) residing in the deity and that residing in the offering substance (*pradeya*) are indeed distinct; therefore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*ekadeśānvaya*). Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "that which is related to a deity non-different from Agni. Furthermore, the offering substance is the meaning of the suffix precisely as a relatum; the mention of "the offering substance" is also intended to include the mantra.

Nor should it be argued that the suffix’s denotative power (*śakti*) regarding the deity is redundant because the deity is already presented by words such as *aindra* (belonging to Indra); for [the deity] is not presented from those words in its capacity as a deity (*devatātvena*). The ancients maintain that words such as *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) merely provide the specific qualification of the substance to be offered, which is already understood as being related [to the deity]. [This refers to the Bhūṣaṇakāra.]

The Neo-grammarians (Navyas), however, maintain that in cases such as the dative case, since the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is already obtained by the base itself, the dative merely expresses its status as the "intended recipient" (*uddeśyatva*). Similarly, here too, both "divinity" (*devatātva*) and "that which is to be offered" (*pradeya*) are the meanings of the suffix. Therein, the divinity is construed with that which is to be offered through the relation of "defining" (*nirūpakatā*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "that which defines a divinity residing in Agni.
But if this is so—[then one might ask:
"Is it by the *taddhita* suffix, or by the dative case, or again by the wording of the mantra?"...
In that case, the conjunction with the deity is indeed weaker than each subsequent one.

If it is asked how the weakness of the Mīmāṃsaka position is established, it is as follows: they say that through the dative case (*caturthī*), the relationship with the status of a deity (*devatātva*) is obtained from the sentence (*vākya*), whereas in the case of a *taddhita* suffix, it is obtained through direct denotation (*śruti*) because of its occurrence within the same word; thus, that [relationship] depends on the relative strength and weakness of *śruti* and *vākya*. Others, however, maintain that for the deity to be presented [in the mind], one must admit that the base (*prakṛti*) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), while the suffix serves merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Consequently, the power (*śakti*) of the suffix resides only in that which is not obtainable by other means—namely, the substance to be offered (*pradeya*). Furthermore, in the grammatical rule (*sūtra*) as well, the term "deity" (*devatā*) is indeed a qualifier of the meaning of the base.

And this is a *nirūḍhalakṣaṇā* (conventional metaphorical indication), because only a metaphorical indication that has been delimited by usage from time immemorial is considered a *nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*. As for the relation, it is the *saṃsarga* (syntactic connection). [The sense is as follows: This is a *nirūḍhalakṣaṇā* because, according to the statement of Vardhamāna—"Metaphorical indication occurs when [the primary meaning] is known through a form other than its own capacity"—even though the deity in the form of Indra is the primary meaning (*śakya*) of the word "Indra," this [indication] is appropriate for the purpose of cognizing him as being non-different from the deity [Vaiśvānara]. Furthermore, a relation is simply a *saṃsarga* (connection).]

Furthermore, they say that even the substance (dravya) would not be impossible to grasp as the meaning of words such as *dadhi* (curd), because even when that [substance] is not explicitly heard, it is understood from the word *aindra* alone, and because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *aindra-dadhi* and so forth.

In that case, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) through the relation of being the specifier of the deityhood residing in the well-formed [word].
Similarly, in the rule *tadasyāṃ praharaṇam iti krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.2.57], there is a game characterized by weapons, or rather, the weapon and the game.

Or, the meaning may be "mere sport. Similarly, regarding the rule *so'sya nivāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.89), the meanings are "his residence" and "his connection," even though no suffix has been specifically prescribed for this rule. Here, the word *nivāsa* (residence) is a noun ending in a locative suffix (*adhikaraṇa*). By the prefix *ni-*, an excellence in the form of continuity (*nairantarya*) is conveyed regarding the dwelling. And that [excellence] is to be understood as being delimited by time, based on context and other factors. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses a connection with the locus of a residence that is non-different from the *sradhna* [a specific measure]. Furthermore, the residence must have as its agent a person who is connected with the referent of the suffix.
For this very reason, there is no such usage when the agent is one who performs the act only occasionally. This should be inferred for rules of this kind, such as *sāsmin paurṇamāsī* [Pāṇini 4.2.29].

By the rule *tena dīvyati* [Pāṇini 4.4.2] and others, suffixes are applied in cases such as *akṣair dīvyati* (he plays with dice) resulting in *ākṣikaḥ*. In that context, although action (*kriyā*) is predominant in the verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix (*dīvyati*), one must understand that in the derivative formation (*vṛtti*), there is a reversal of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified. This is because of the established doctrine that "nouns (*nāman*) have substance (*sattva*) as their primary meaning," and also due to the association with what precedes and follows. Thus, the understanding is: "one who is the agent of playing, having dice as the instrument. However, tense, person, and number are not intended to be expressed at all. The same should be inferred for other cases as well; likewise, it should be inferred for rules such as *tad adhīte tad veda* [Pāṇini 4.2.59].

The meaning of the rule *tena tulyaṃ kriyā cedvatiḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.115] is that when the object of comparison (*upameya*) is an action (*kriyā*), the suffix *vati* is applied after a word denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) ending in the third case, in the sense of "equal to that. Now, one might object: in such cases as *brāhmaṇavad adhīte* ("he studies like a Brāhmaṇa"), this would not apply; for there is no similarity having the Brāhmaṇa as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*) residing in the act of studying, because of their absolute difference.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the words "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth are used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) to refer to the study performed by them, and that qualities such as excellence are common [to both]; for this is weak, since [the figurative usage] finds its application even in non-figurative cases such as "walking is like standing" or "walking is just like standing. If this is said, we reply: No.

Because the third case ending conveys its meaning through syntactic connection (*anvaya*), and because that [agent] also possesses the nature of an action (*kriyārūpatā*) by virtue of being the locus of a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), there is no possibility for it to be the denoter of a primary action; therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), when "past" form (*bhūtarūpa*) is understood—as in examples such as *brāhmaṇavad adhīte* ("he studies like a Brāhmaṇa")—there is no fault. And thus, its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) consists precisely in its connection with an action.

In expressions such as "the face is beautiful like a lotus," the verb "is" (bhavati) must be supplied.
