Furthermore, by the word "lotus" (*aravinda*), the state of being a beautiful lotus is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "the state of being a beautiful face is similar to the state of being a beautiful lotus. It should be understood that subsequently, the similarity between the lotus and the face, characterized by the quality of beauty, is apprehended either through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) or by the mind.

For this very reason, the suffix *vati* does not occur in expressions such as *brāhmaṇena tulyā'sya gaur* ("this cow is equal to a Brāhmaṇa"). The suffix *vati* occurs by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116), which applies when there is an expansion (*vistāra*) of that substance, quality, and so forth. In that context, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the meaning of the suffix *vati*. The resulting cognition is: "In Pāṭaliputra, there is a rampart possessing a similarity whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the rampart of Mathurā. Since the rule *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.55) indicates that the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) must have the same case-ending, the locative case is used for the standard of comparison.

The wall (*prākāra*) is the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*), which is the object of a cognition of non-difference based on similarity. In reality, the understanding arises only through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of words such as "in Mathurā" or "the wall" within the sentence "as if in Mathurā. Furthermore, there exists a relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) between the two walls.

Thus, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in both instances precisely to denote the location as defined by the wall. However, it should be understood that in the compound (*vṛtti*), the words "Mathurā" and so forth possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to the wall and other features located therein, solely for the purpose of expressing the similarity between Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra.

Others, however, say: even in the analytical exposition (*vigraha*), words such as *mathurā* are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*), just as they are in the compound (*vṛtti*). The locative and genitive cases, moreover, denote the nominative sense due to this very indicator (*jñāpaka*). And this has been indicated in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the expression "worshipped according to rule" (*vidhivat pūjyate*), the understanding is that there is an act of worship having the ritual rule (*vidhi*) as its object and Devadatta as its agent. Because of the word *vidhi* itself acting as an indicator, it denotes the nominative sense. And this has been indicated in the *Bhāṣya*. They say this.

Regarding the expression "it is worshipped according to rule" (*vidhivat pūjyate*), the understanding is that there is an act of worship having "rule" (*vidhi*) as its object and Devadatta as its agent. By the word "rule," the aforementioned manner [of performance] and so forth are indicated; this is to be inferred accordingly. Now, the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is investigated:

On this point, some maintain that in expressions such as *ghaṭatvam* (pot-ness), the base (*prakṛti*) refers to the phonetic form of the word itself; the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, however, have the sense of "being a qualifier" (*prakāra*) in its respective form. Furthermore, by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), this [qualifier] is precisely that which serves as the locus of the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) determined by the objectivehood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the cognition produced by the base. Consequently, there is no fault even if "king-hood" (*rājatva*) and so forth function as qualifiers in compounds like *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man). The relation [between the base and the suffix], moreover, is the state of being a qualifier in the cognition produced [by the whole expression]. Thus, in cases such as *gotvam* (cow-ness), the meaning is: "cow-ness is the qualifier in the cognition produced by the word *go*. And that qualifier is necessarily the ground for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*).

Therefore, in the view of those who maintain that even the word itself appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is no abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) for the word in expressions such as *ghaṭatva* ("the state of being a jar"). Accordingly, the Bhāṣya states: "All words (*bhāvāḥ*) exist by means of their own referent; that is their referent. When denoting that [referent], the suffixes *tva* and *tal* occur. Here, "words" (*bhāvāḥ*) are so called because they "exist" (*bhavanti*)—that is, they function—as signifiers. They "exist" by means of that referent which is their own signified object.

Words function as denoters because words are employed for the purpose of conveying meaning. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here with the intention of expressing the word's status as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the production of the meaning. Since there is an obligatory connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the word "since" (*yasmāt*) is required [to complete the sense]. That basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), by virtue of which words are employed in common usage as instruments through their denoted meanings in order to convey themselves, is the meaning that serves as the basis for application. The implication is that, through the aforementioned relationship, this meaning connected to the word is the referent of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

The basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) [of words] is as follows: in the case of "jar" and so forth, it is the cognition of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like; in the case of words such as "white," it is the quality (*guṇa*); in the case of words such as "cook," it is the action (*kriyā*); in the case of words such as "king's man," it is the relationship (*sambandha*); and in the case of words such as "Ḍittha," it is the very form of the word itself (*śabdasvarūpa*). All this is to be understood in accordance with experience. And thus, the cognition occurs in such a manner as "the basis for the application of that particular word," and so on.

As for what they say—that "the word also appears in the verbal cognition (śābdabodha)," as established in the *Nāmārthanirṇaya*—and that it is a qualifier (*prakāra*) precisely through the relation of denotative power (*śakti*), and that although the word is one, its power is manifold, so there is no elimination of words with multiple meanings.

Or, let there be a single power; even so, there is no elimination of multiple meanings, as in the case of pronouns (*sarvanāman*). To explain: just as it is universally established that, in the case of pronouns, they function as specific presenters in accordance with experience; and just as in that context, the apprehension of the power (the *śaktigraha*) is simply that "this word is powerful with respect to those things possessing potness and so forth, which are presented by way of being objects of cognition, and which possess the status of being objects of cognition."

However, being the object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*) is merely a common factor (*anugamaka*) during the process of presentation; it is not the denotable meaning (*śakya*), and thus it does not appear in the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Rather, it is [the universal] such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth that appears. Likewise, in this case as well, when the word *akṣa* has its power grasped in the sense that "the word *akṣa* has the power to denote those things possessing the nature of a noose, a *vibhītaka* fruit, and so on, which are presented under the form of being objects of cognition," there is no polysemy (*nānārthatva*) despite the fact that the understanding occurs through various specific forms, because the understanding is merely by way of [the general property of] being an object of cognition.

In reality, since even multiple universals (*jāti*) and so forth serve as delimiters (*avacchedaka*) here, it is easily established that there is a plurality of meanings. Therefore, in all cases, it is the word itself that is denoted by the abstract suffix (*tva*), and not the universal or other such factors. All words function toward their objects by depending upon their own form (*svarūpa*) as the mode (*prakāra*) through their respective meanings; thus, that alone is the meaning of the abstract suffix—such is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*. That [position] is incorrect, because it contradicts experience.

Regarding the terms *nānātva* (diversity) and *yaugapadya* (simultaneity), here too the meaning of "non-simultaneity" (*asahabhāva*) and "simultaneity" (*yugapadbhāva*) refers to the mode of cognition produced by words such as "diverse" (*nānā*) and so forth. However, in the case of a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*), the word itself serves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); therefore, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to that very [word]. The status of being the ground for application consists in appearing as a qualifier of the denoted individual (*vyakti*)—which is the object of power (*śakya*)—by way of the objective state known as the "delimiting factor of the subject-locus" (*dharmitāvacchedakatā*) during the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*). How this status belongs to the word has been explained in the *Nāmārthavāda*.

In cases such as "Why [is there] *kutva*?", however, there is no fault, because the word *kutva*, which possesses a power (*śakti*) whose nature is the word *ku*, functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to those things understood by it. In compounds such as *aupagavaḥ* ("son of Upagu") and *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("king's man"), since the relation denoted by the genitive case is included within the compound formation (*vṛtti*), that very relation is the ground for the application of the term; thus, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied precisely to that. And this is according to the view that the compound is "denotative of its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā vṛtti*). At that time, the word *rājapuruṣa* is considered to have a primary power (*śakti*) with respect to a person who possesses a connection to a king, based on the apprehension of that power (*śaktigraha*).

Even under the view that a word does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthāvṛttipakṣa*), the word *rājapuruṣa* possesses a specific power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) with respect to a person who is related to a king; it is precisely this that constitutes the apprehension of specific power.

By the maxim of "distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not" (*prāptāprāptavivekanyāya*), this specific power ultimately resides in the relation alone; thus, there is no loss of the relation's status as the ground for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*). And it has been stated by Bhartṛhari: "The expression of a relation [occurs] through an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied after primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*). This point is indeed established by logic.

Nor is it the case that the agent (*kartṛ*) or the relation itself serves as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term, because of the misconception that agency and so forth are merely forms of the relationship between an action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*). This too is only a general rule; for in cases such as *dāmodaratva*, *kṛṣṇasarpatva*, "whiteness in a cloth," and "existence" (*sattā*), the resulting cognition is established by experience as having a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*) as its qualifier. As it has been said: "In other cases [the term is used] conventionally (*rūḍhi*); here, however, because the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is somehow unknown, it is well-known in a specific sense. (The meaning is that it is established as a specific object).

The meaning is that [the suffix] expresses the meaning of the suffix as conjoined with the meaning of the base (prakṛti), according to the maxim: "That which remains, even when it has a different form due to the elision of a suffix, being identical in form to the base, denotes the meaning of the elided [suffix]. Regarding the phrase *avyabhicaritasambandhinaḥ*: *avyabhicāri* means that which is not the counter-positive (*apratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in an individual (*vyakti*); *sambandhaḥ* refers to a relation consisting of inherence (*samavāya*). Thus, the meaning is: "from that which denotes something qualified by such a genus (*jāti*), etc."

Therefore, [the essence] is not destroyed by cooking or other such means, because it is the counter-positive of an absence residing in its own substratum. This is stated [by the author] as: "due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), non-differentiation of form (*abhinnarūpa*), and invariable relation (*avyabhicaritasambandha*). In this regard, in examples such as "Dāmodaratva" (the state of being Dāmodara), there is conventional usage; in "śuklatva" (whiteness), there is non-differentiation of form; and "sattā" (existence) is the third, based on common usage such as "the cloth is white. It should be understood that the relationship between "being" (*sat*) and "existence" (*sattā*) is never subject to deviation.

As for the Mīmāṃsakas’ position—that in cases such as *daṇḍī* ("the man with a staff"), the suffix *matup* denotes merely a substance qualified by the meaning of the base, since the relation is cognized only as a sentential meaning; and that this is likewise the case in *pācaka* ("the cook") and so on—and that there is no impossibility of grasping the denotative power (*śakti*) regarding infinite substances because it is possible by taking a single [substance] as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*); and that even the indicators, such as the staff, are not manifold because they are subsumed under a universal (*jāti*) residing in them.

Nor is that [universal] itself manifold in the form of "stickness" (*daṇḍatva*) and "crookedness" (*kuṇḍālatva*), because it is subsumed under the meaning of the base noun (*prakṛtyartha*). To this we say: no; for in cases such as *daṇḍitvam* ("the state of being a stick-bearer"), the cognition of a relation would not otherwise be possible.

Nor can it be postulated out of fear of the uselessness of the suffix *-tva*, since in cases like *ghaṭatvam* ("pot-ness") the requirement is satisfied by the very power (*śakti*) already established as the delimitor of the base's meaning.

The statement "from primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*)" is not an original injunction; rather, it is a statement by Haribhadra that restates a meaning established by logical necessity (*nyāyasiddha*). Nor should it be argued that a specific expressive power (*śakti*) is postulated there in accordance with experience; for, rather than postulating a separate power, it is more appropriate to explain the phenomenon by assuming that the suffixes *in* and others—which already possess an established power—merely have as their object the relation [of the denoted] to the property-bearer (*dharmin*).

They maintain that if this were the case, the cognition of "being a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍitva*) and so forth would be possible through the very power of the established basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

Others, however, maintain: the base (*prakṛti*) has only the referent as its primary meaning, since there is no evidence for secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). In reality, the mode of cognition produced by the base—namely, the universal such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which serves as the ground for application—is the meaning of the suffixes *tvā* and so on in their respective forms. In this regard, in the expression *ghaṭatvam*, the base-meaning is the individual qualified by the universal. And that [individual] is the qualifier through the relation of subsistence (*vṛttitva*) as determined by the state of being a locus (*ādhāratā*), due to the force of expectancy. Thus, the resulting cognition takes the form: "pot-ness residing in the pot," and so forth.

Thus, in expressions such as *ghaṭatvatvam* (the-ness of pot-ness), the meaning of the suffix *-tva* is precisely *ghaṭatvatva* (pot-ness-ness), which is the locus of the cognition produced by the word *ghaṭatva*.

Nor should it be argued that, due to complexity (*gaurava*), there is only secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) there and no primary denotative power (*śakti*); for there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*) to maintain that one should prefer primary denotative power rather than secondary indication in this case. Furthermore, since *ghaṭatvatva* and the like—consisting of specific properties that are non-empirical (*āvidyaka*)—are the delimiters of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *ghaṭatva*, there is no complexity.

In reality, the individual (vyakti) itself is the qualifier (prakāra) through relations such as self-residence (svavṛttitva), while the word-potency (śakti) remains unconditioned (niravacchinna). However, when qualities (guṇa) and the like are the denotable objects (vācya), the genus (jāti) residing therein serves as the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedikā). Nor does this result in polysemy (nānārthatā), for such a consequence is accepted. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "When a word is applied to a substance due to the presence of a certain quality, that quality is what is expressed [by the suffix], and the suffix -tva or -tal is used. Here, the word "quality" (guṇa) is an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for any property (dharma) in general.

When it is said, "due to the existence (*bhāva*) of which," [it follows that] because the word "father" is applied to the father due to the existence of the son, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) would apply to the son as "fatherhood. "Due to existence" means "due to being present. By the term "substance" (*dravya*), the object which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and has attained the state of being an entity (*sattvabhāvāpanna*) is expressed. Among those, for those [words] such as "color" (*rūpa*) and so forth which function solely as qualities (*guṇamātra*), the abstract suffix occurs in relation to the genus (*jāti*) residing in the quality. From words like "white" (*śukla*) when they refer to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), [the suffix occurs] in relation to the quality; from those referring solely to the quality, it occurs in relation to the genus itself.

Those words such as *aṇu* (minute) and so forth that denote a possessor of dimension (*parimāṇin*), from them the quality in the form of dimension [is denoted]; however, in cases such as *pācakaḥ* (cook), because there is a cognition of a qualifier consisting of an action, that very [action] is expressed as the qualificand by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following it. But in cases such as *ghaṭatvam* (pot-ness), it is the universal (*jāti*).

Nor does it follow that, because the universal (*jāti*) is one—being of the nature of the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*)—the cloth would also become a qualifier in the cognition "this is potness" through the relation of self-residence (*svavṛttitva*). This is because that very [universal] becomes the form of "potness" and so on only when differentiated by its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The denotative power (*śakti*) resides in words such as "cow," which denote the universal alone, with respect to "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) and the like, which are specific illusory properties (*avidyaka-dharma-viśeṣa*) residing therein.

Kaiyaṭa, however, says: "The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to words that denote a mere universal (*jāti*) to signify the word's own form (*śabdasvarūpa*). Since the word-form is superimposed upon the object, namely the universal, that which is the word 'cow' is itself the object; therefore, the word-form alone is the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and nothing else."

As for the claim that only "mere property" (*dharmamātra*)—and not each specific property (*tattadrūpeṇa*)—can be the denotable meaning (*śakya*) of the suffix *tva* and so forth, because otherwise there would be the fault of polysemy (*nānārthatā*): the cognition of "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) and so on in expressions such as *ghaṭatvam* arises from beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*). Nor is there a lack of evidence for "property-ness" (*dharmatva*) being the denotable meaning, since it is a rule that a power (*śakti*) must have a delimitor (*avacchedaka*). Otherwise, let there be no such delimitor. For this very reason, the experts (*tāntrikāḥ*) maintain that in the word *paṅkaja*, "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*) is the contextual condition of usage (*prayogopādhi*).

"It is said that whatever appears by necessity due to the force of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) during the application [of a word] is called the 'limiting adjunct' (*upādhi*) of that application. This is not so; for if it were thus, there would be no occurrence of the diversity of cognition seen in cases such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*). If it is argued that the manifestation of the particular occurs by the force of mental impressions, then since that [particular] is not the object of the [verbal] function (*vṛtti*), it could not possibly be the object of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

Nor should it be said that if the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) itself is what is denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), then there is no difference from the previous view; they say that the difference lies precisely in this: in the previous view the word is the qualifier (*prakāra*), whereas here it is the individual (*vyakti*).

However, some say: since a single power is possible through the commonality of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate multiple such powers; therefore, let those [genus and so on] be denotable as properties (*dharma*). Nevertheless, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is indeed the individual (*vyakti*). By accepting that the individual is the qualifier (*prakāra*) through the relation of "subsisting in its entirety" (*nikhilasvavṛttitva*), delimited by "not subsisting in anything other than itself" (*svetarāvṛttitvāvacchinna*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). In cases such as "existence" (*sattvam*), however, the relation is simply "inherence" (*samavetatva*). And the regulator here is merely the requirement for a complement (*ākāṅkṣāmātra*). Thus they speak.

Two parts of barley are the measure (*nimāna*) for this part of whey (*udaśvit*); thus, whey is two-barley-measured (*dviyava-udaśvit*). Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *saṃkhyāyā guṇasya nimāne mayaṭ* [Pāṇini 5.2.47]. The meaning of that rule is: the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the sense of the genitive case after a word expressing a number in the nominative case, provided that it denotes a "quality" (*guṇa*) which functions as a "measure" (*nimāna*, i.e., a price) for another "part" (*bhāga*). This suffix is employed only when both the measure (*nimāna*) and the thing measured (*nimeya*) consist of parts; this is clear from the commentary on the form.

Because the word *dvi* (two) is always dependent [on another term], the suffix occurs even when it is dependent on *yavānām* (of barley). The understanding is that the portion of curdled milk (*udaśvit*) obtained as a price consisting of two portions related to barley is what is meant. Although the suffix is applied to the portion of curdled milk, nevertheless, because that too is curdled milk (*udaśvit*), the expression *dviyavam udaśvit* (curdled milk worth two barley-measures) is used. Alternatively, it should be understood that by the very nature of linguistic usage, a suffix prescribed for a part denotes that which possesses the part.

Furthermore, this sūtra operates only when the number of the measuring instrument (*nimāna*) exceeds the number of the object to be measured (*nimeya*); the details are explained elsewhere. [Note: By this sūtra, possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) are prescribed after a word ending in the nominative case that has the sense of "existence" as its qualifier, provided it denotes a related entity (*sambandhin*) or a location (*adhikaraṇa*). Although the use of the form *asya* suggests that the prescription of possessive suffixes applies only to relations denoted by the genitive case, nevertheless, in accordance with the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) seen in examples such as "Caitra is cow-possessing" (*gomāṃścaitraḥ*), these suffixes denote the related entity itself.]

And thus, in cases such as *gomān* ("possessor of cows"), there arises a relational cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) such as "one who possesses the relation of ownership as characterized by the cow. In the rule *tadasyāstyasminniti matup* (Pāṇini 5.2.94), both [the words *asti* and *asmin*] are included for the sake of ensuring the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the suffix *matup* in a cognition characterized by those respective modes. The [word] *asti* ("exists") is not intended to convey person or number; for, since there is no reason to bypass the first [two] [categories], they are applied by their mention, which results in a restriction of the scope of the treatise (*śāstra-saṅkoca*).

Because there is a lack of evidence [for its existence]. Time, however, in the form of "presentness," is indeed intended; for this very reason, the suffix *matup* is not grammatically correct when cows are in the past or future. This is clear in the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, the meaning of the suffix *asti* (in *astimān*) is also a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Thus, from the word *gomān*, the understanding is: "one who possesses a connection with cows that are the locus of present existence. Regarding expressions such as *gomān āsīt* ("he was cow-possessing") or *bhavitā* ("he will be cow-possessing"), some hold that there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward that which was or will be the object of such usage. Another method is also clearly explained in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

However, regarding the suffixes such as *kalpa*, which are prescribed to express "partial non-completion" (*īṣadasamāpti*) and so forth, even the meaning of the suffix—namely partial non-completion—is itself a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Some also maintain that, due to the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of such a meaning by the base, while the suffix serves merely to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya-grāhaka*).

In the expression *paṭutaraḥ* ("more clever"), the suffix *tarap* occurs in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*), and this meaning of excellence, which is the referent of the suffix, functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Although there is no excellence in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the base-meaning itself, its excellence is nonetheless understood through the excellence of qualities and so forth that serve as the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the suffix *tarap*. In cases such as *gotaraḥ* ("a better cow"), although there is an absence of excellence even in the excellence of the birth (the species) which is the ground for the application, its excellence must nevertheless be understood through the excellence residing in activities such as carrying or milking, which are concomitant with that [birth].

And thus, when used in conjunction with suffixes such as *tarap*, it should be understood that there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the base word in the sense of being qualified by an excellence such as greater sharpness. In this context, *tarap* occurs when a word expressing two meanings serves as the governing term (*upapada*). For example, "Of these two, this one is sharper" (*anayor ayaṃ paṭutaraḥ*), or "Between us and Devadatta, Devadatta is more handsome" (*asmākaṃ devadattasya ca devadattato 'bhirūpataraḥ*).

In the case of "The teeth of Dantoṣṭha are smoother," there is no fault, because the constituent member of the compound signifies the two meanings—the teeth and the lips—by denoting the single number "one" through a secondary signification that has abandoned difference and accepted non-difference.

However, when the *upapada* (the word following the suffix) itself denotes plurality, the suffix *-tamap* alone is used; likewise, even when the *upapada* denotes plurality, the suffix *-tarap* is used when it expresses the counter-correlative of a division (*vibhāga-pratiyogin*), as in: "The Northerners are more learned than the Easterners" (*prācyebhyaḥ paṭutarā udīcyāḥ*). Similarly, for selection from among many (*bahūnāṃ madhye nirdhāraṇe*), the suffix *-tamap* is used: "Which one among you is a Kaṭha? (*katamo bhavatāṃ kaṭhaḥ*). For selection between two (*dvayornirdhāraṇe*), the suffix *-atarap* is used: "Of these two, which is a Vaiṣṇava? (*anayoḥ kataraḥ vaiṣṇavaḥ*). The reverse is also possible, according to the authority of the *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the term *kākatālīyam*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) as "just as a crow [meets] a palm fruit," the compound is formed with the word *iva* (as if) by the authority of the rule prescribing the suffix, namely Pāṇini 5.3.106, "And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a compound referring to that [same situation]. Because it is stated "referring to that," the form *tālakākam* does not occur.

As for what Haradatta stated—"This compound applies only to this specific case; therefore, there is no independence, no connection with another qualifier, and no analytical expansion (vigraha)"—that is not correct. It contradicts the Bhāṣya, which says: "Like a crow and a palm tree is *kākatāla*"; "like the event of the crow and the palm tree is *kākatālīya*. In that context, the first member (*pūrvapada*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote something resembling the arrival of the crow.

The final member [of the compound] is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its inherent nature as being distinct from other actions, resembling the falling of a palm fruit; and there is a coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between those two. The meaning of the compound is: "that which resembles the falling of a palm fruit is coreferential with that which resembles the coming of a crow."

By this, the objection that a compound is impossible due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*)—because there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meanings of the prior and subsequent members—is refuted. Consequently, in the sense of "like the *kākatāla*," the suffix *cha* is applied. Since it is established that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) connects as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) with the meaning of the suffix within this governing rule (*adhikāra*), the word *kākatāla* possesses a conventional metaphorical function (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) directed toward the death of the crow caused by the palm fruit. In that case, the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) connects with the meaning of the suffix as a counter-correlative, while the literal meaning (*śakyārtha*) connects through the relation of being the instigator (*prayojyatva*).

And thus, the understanding is that Devadatta’s death is similar to the death of a crow caused by a palm fruit—where the co-occurrence [of the events] is like the coming of a crow, and the causal agent [the falling fruit] is like the falling of a palm fruit; and this similarity is based on factors such as being brought about unexpectedly.

Although the suffix *vat* is prescribed for the sense of "like" (*iva*), and the sense of "like" is indeed similarity, nevertheless, in its application (*vṛtti*), the suffix should be understood as denoting that which possesses similarity, due to the inherent nature of word-potency (*śabdaśakti*). The same should be understood in other cases as well, such as in the word *aśvaka*.

In reality, the term *kākatāla* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the coincidence of the crow and the palmyra fruit (*kākatālasamāgama*). This very [coincidence] is construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) within the meaning of the suffix *-cha*. Through its co-occurrence with various words denoting the object of comparison (*upameya*), there arises the cognition—depending on the context—either of the death of the crow caused by that coincidence, or of the enjoyment [of the fruit] performed by the crow. It is with this very intention that the theorists of poetics (*ālaṅkārikāḥ*) maintain that in the simile involving the suffix *-cha*, there is an elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānalopa*).

The intention is that there is an absence of any indicator [of the object] by way of the specific form that delimits its status as a standard of comparison (*upamānatāvacchedaka*). They say that even in the former view, the designation "elision" (*lopa*) occurs because of the absence of any word denoting the standard of comparison alone.

Regarding the phrase "in the eastern region": *prāg* means "eastern," as in "to the east of the village are mango trees. Here, the word *prāc* signifies the eastern direction; and because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) whose primary force is the power of location (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), it is devoid of gender (*nirliṅga*).

Then, in the case of the word *khe* (in the sky), because it is by its very nature primarily that which is to be supported (*ādheya*) and thus lacks immutability (*avyayatva*), there is a connection with gender; yet this is not femininity and so forth, as that would result in an absolute contradiction with its base form (*prakṛti*), given the stated principle that suffixes with inherent meaning (*svārthika*) are identical to their base forms. Rather, it is only neuter gender, and only the singular number. And thus, the understanding is: "mango trees located in the eastern region beyond the village."

When words such as *prāc* (eastern) and others, which denote directions and so forth, function with respect to mango trees and the like through the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of their connection [to those regions], then the suffix *kha* is applied according to the rule "taddhiteṣv acām ādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.117). Since there is no evidence for abandoning the gender of the substantive presented by that suffix, one may even say "prācīnā āmrāḥ" (eastern mangoes); this is explained in detail elsewhere.

In the expression *pañcakṛtvo bhuṅkte* ("he eats five times"), the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is applied by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc* [Pāṇini 5.4.17]. Here, *abhyāvṛtti* (repetition) means birth (*janma*). In this context, the word *pañca* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote an origination qualified by the number five. Furthermore, its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is with the action alone, according to the natural force of the rule. By means of the verb, the act of eating—which consists of five occurrences of origination—is expressed as having its internal distinctions subsumed. And because the aggregate is not yet completed, it is regarded as being in the present tense.
And thus, the understanding is that the act of eating has rice and so forth as its object and arises with the number five.

In the case of "the rice is cooked five times" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ pacyate odanaḥ*), the understanding is that there is a softening (*viklitti*) produced by an action arising with the number five, which has a single portion of rice as its locus. Here, although the instances of softening are distinct, they are expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) precisely as having their distinctions subsumed; therefore, since the status of being the object (*karmatva*) belongs only to the aggregate (*samudāya*) which is their locus, there is oneness of the object.

However, when there is an intention to express a collection whose constituent parts are distinct, the form "pañcakṛtvaḥ pacyante odanāḥ" (rice is cooked five times) is indeed possible; for by its very nature, this [suffix] is grammatically correct when counting the occurrences of actions that have a single agent, a single type of object, and are of the same kind.

Expressions such as "pañcakṛtvo daṇḍī" (five times a staff-bearer) are correct by taking the verb "to be" (*bhavati*) as understood. Even in cases such as "pañcakṛtva utpadyate" (it arises five times), since the activity conducive to arising is the meaning of the verbal root, it is understood that the counting refers precisely to that arising; thus, there is no fault. By this, the objection that there is a fault here because arising lacks another arising is refuted.

However, one cannot say "pañcakṛtvaḥ pācakaḥ" (a cook five times), because the action, being a part of the meaning of the word [the agent], cannot be construed there [with the number]. For this very reason, one cannot say "pañcakṛtvaḥ pakvaḥ" (cooked five times) and so forth; for since the repetition can only belong to an action, the action is already obtained by that much alone, and furthermore, by the inclusion of the word "action" (kriyā) in the sūtra, only the action which has become the primary element (pradhānībhūta) is intended to be grasped. Moreover, due to the absence of any restrictive factor, the inclusion of the word "action" also indicates that the suffix *kṛtvasuc* occurs only where the action is of a purely "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) nature.

Therefore, the expression "fivefold cooking" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ pākaḥ*) is also not possible. As for [the forms] such as "twofold application" (*dvir prayogaḥ*), they are justified by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *dvirvacane'ci* [Pāṇini 1.1.59]. They say that all of this is clear in the *Bhāṣya*.

That which is not black becomes black; he makes it so, he blackens it (*kṛṣṇīkaroti*). Here, by the rule *kṛbhvastiyoge sampadyakarttari cviḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.50], the suffix *cvi* is applied. Regarding this, it is stated that "it should be expressed as 'the state of becoming what one was not'" (*abhūtatadbhāve iti vācyam*). Thus, there is a compound with the word *tad*, which ends in the instrumental case denoting the instrument (*karaṇa-tṛtīyā-anta*). There is also a compound with the word *abhūta*, ending in the genitive case denoting the agent (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhy-anta*). Furthermore, "not having been so" (*abhūtatva*) is to be understood here, by proximity, solely as being caused by the meaning of the word *tad* contained within the term *tadbhāva*.
And thus, it follows that "the becoming of that [entity] in a form in which it previously did not exist" is what is meant by *abhūtatadbhāva* (the becoming of what was not).

Furthermore, this suffix occurs only where the material cause itself (*prakṛti*), undergoing transformation into the state of an effect, is intended to be expressed as non-different from that effect; moreover, the suffix is applied only after a word denoting the effect. Consequently, in such cases as "that which was not black becomes black" (*akṛṣṇaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ sampadyate*) or "it becomes black" (*kṛṣṇībhavati*), the agency of the action of "becoming" belongs solely to the original material cause, the non-black entity, because that is precisely what is obtained through the force of the expression "in the case of the becoming of what was not."

Furthermore, since words such as *kṛṣṇi* are nipātas (particles), they function as indicators (*dyotaka*); thus, because their meaning is already encompassed by the verbal root *bhū* itself, it is impossible for them to possess agency or other such grammatical roles. For this very reason, there is a systematic arrangement of number and person in examples such as "the Brāhmaṇas become a group" (*saṃghībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ*) and "Devadatta becomes like you" (*tvadbhavati devadattaḥ*).

Thus, in expressions such as *kṛṣṇīkaroti* ("he makes black"), the status of being the object (*karmatva*) belongs to the material cause (*prakṛti*) alone. However, in other cases, there is no fixed rule regarding agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth for either the material cause or the product (*vikṛti*). This is because, in the *Paspaśā* section of the Bhāṣya, we see the product acting as the agent in the usage: *suvarṇapiṇḍaḥ khadirāṅgārasadṛśe kuṇḍale bhavataḥ* ("The gold lump becomes two earrings resembling acacia-charcoal"); and because in common worldly usage, we also see the material cause acting as the agent, as in: *eko vṛkṣaḥ pañca naukā bhavati* ("One tree becomes five boats"). And so, in such instances, agency is predicated of both the material cause and the product.
The designator takes on the number of the primary material, but not that of the modification.

Thus, the ancient traditional statement (*prācīnapravāda*) refers exclusively to the scope of the *cvī* suffix. To apply it elsewhere would be a mere error, as it contradicts the usage in the previously cited *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, a word ending in *cvī* possesses a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on similarity to its own primary meaning. For this very reason, because such a word is secondary (*gauṇa*), there is no occurrence of the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule "ānmahataḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.10] in examples such as *amahān mahān bhavati*; for there is no fault, since grammatical operations triggered by the connection with another word whose specific form has been introduced do not apply to words that are either secondary or metaphorically indicated.

Regarding the masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) in the expression *mahadbhūtā brahmaṇī*, it has been explained in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that this occurs either by resorting to some form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or through a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) based on the term *puṃvat*. However, in the case of *gomatībhūtā*, there is no masculine-like substitution precisely because of the usage in the *Mahābhāṣya*. This is clear from the *Mahābhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, and other works on the rules *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (P. 1.1.62), *ot* (P. 1.1.15), and *ānmahataḥ* (P. 6.3.46).

In expressions such as *brahmībhūta* ("become Brahman"), the suffix * cvi* is to be understood as an imposition (*āropa*) of causality preceded by an imposition of non-causality; for the rod (*daṇḍa*) is the cause [of punishment].

However, when neither the prior state nor the subsequent state is taken into account, there is no occurrence of * cvi*, as in "the threads become" (*tantavo bhavanti*) or "the cloth becomes" (*paṭo bhavati*). Enough of this elaboration.
Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*).
Thus has the *varṇasphoṭa* (the phoneme-sphoṭa) been defined.
Now, the *padasphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa) and *vākyasphoṭa* (sentence-sphoṭa) are being defined.

Since it has been established that substitutes (*ādeśa*) are expressive, in cases such as *ghaṭena*, there is a difference in substitutes due to differences in grammatical systems; furthermore, because the distinction between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is not perceived due to the influence of *saṃhitā*, meaning is not conveyed by each of those two individually. Therefore, the position of the *padasphoṭa* is that the expressive power resides in the word as a distinct entity, just as it does in a qualified whole.

For instance, in the case of *ghaṭena*, there would be no criterion for determining whether *ghaṭa* is the base (*prakṛti*) and *ena* the suffix (*pratyaya*), or whether *ghaṭe* is the base and *na* the suffix, and so forth; this would lead to the undesirable consequence of postulating an infinite number of delimiters for word-potencies (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, it would result in a lack of understanding for those who do not know these specific divisions. Moreover, since forms such as *vas* and *nas* are prescribed as indivisible wholes, their division into base and suffix is impossible to ascertain in every respect. Finally, even non-grammarians possess understanding through the mere conventional usage of the whole, despite their ignorance of each individual component.

Similarly, in cases such as *hare 'va* or *viṣṇo 've*, even though the individual words are clearly unknown according to the method previously stated, there is comprehension through the power (*śakti*) of the whole; thus, the whole alone possesses the power regarding the specific sentence-meaning—this is the *vākya-sphoṭa*. This has been discussed in the *Bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* "vṛddhir ādaic" [Pāṇini 1.1.1] and elsewhere, with the statement: "Sentences are seen to be either meaningful or meaningless. Now, an objection may be raised: since the sentence-meaning, which consists of a syntactic relation (*anvaya*), is something not previously known (*apūrva*), it is impossible to grasp the power [of the sentence] therein; furthermore, if one were to grasp the power with respect to that [sentence-meaning], its status as something "not previously known" would be lost.

However, one might argue that just as the initial determination of the expressive power (śakti) occurs through the mind based on the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), so too here, when word-meanings are presented by words, the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) occurs with respect to that presentation by means of the mind assisted by the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors. That is not correct; for since the words themselves are not clearly known, the presentation of word-meanings by means of those words is impossible, and because expectancy itself constitutes the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*), there is no apprehension of power beyond the apprehension of that [expectancy].

Furthermore, it is possible to grasp the word’s power (śakti) at that very moment with respect to the aspect of the syntactic relation (anvaya), which is presented as the object of the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (tātparya). And intention (tātparya) consists in being uttered by a speaker with the desire to communicate a specific meaning.

In cases such as "Bring the pot," when there is a cognition that the speaker did not utter the sentence with the intention of generating a cognition where the act of bringing is the qualificandum (viśeṣya) and the relation is "being determined" (nirūpitatva) with respect to the pot as the object (karmatva), or when there is a cognition that it was uttered with the intention of generating some other cognition, such a [desired] cognition does not arise. Therefore, rather than postulating those two cognitions as obstacles (pratibandhaka), it is simpler—and thus necessary—to hold that the cause [of the cognition] is simply the ascertainment of the previously mentioned intention (tātparya) as the qualifier.

[Objection: Since the object appears as a qualifier through its specific modes such as "modehood" (*prakāratā*) and "objecthood" (*viṣayatā*), the sentence-meaning would lose its "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) by virtue of being the object of the knowledge of intention (*tātparya*) in the very form in which it is understood from the sentence. [Reply: That is not so; for if that [sentence-meaning] were novel, then just as the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śakti*) regarding it would be impossible, so too would the determination of the intention regarding it be impossible. Furthermore, even in the apprehension of the expressive power, the object appears precisely through its specific modes such as modehood, and thus its novelty remains intact. Moreover, in the case of the speech of a parrot and the like, even when there is a determination of the absence of intention, the impossibility of its being a cause of verbal cognition [would follow if intention were a necessary condition].

Nor can the intention (*tātparya*) in that case belong to God, because since His existence is to be inferred solely from the results [of His actions], He would be difficult to know prior [to such inference]. For this very reason, there is understanding for the Mīmāṃsakas and others who are certain of God’s non-existence; otherwise, understanding from Vedic sentences would not occur for them.

Nor can the intention there belong to the teacher, because it is absent in the case of what is spoken by an ignorant teacher. However, the utility of Mīmāṃsā lies in the fact that the knowledge of parsimony (*lāghava*) and other principles produced by reasoning serves as a cause for the verbal cognition produced by the Veda, or for the ascertainment of its validity.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault [in our position] because the cognition produced by a sentence spoken by a competent speaker requires the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-dhī*) as its cause, whereas the speech of parrots and the like, as well as the Veda, lack such [an intention]. This is because "competence" (*vijñatva*) is not a fixed or determinable quality. Furthermore, this cannot be the cause of verbal cognition, as it contradicts the universal experience of all people: "From a single sentence, a verbal cognition arises regarding two possible meanings; however, due to context and other factors, we do not know which one [is intended]. For this very reason, when it is said, "Bring the *payaḥ*," it is consistent with the inquiry of one who does not know the context: "Is milk to be brought, or water?"

Nor should it be argued that there is no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) simply because there is no presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) therein; for such a consequence would apply even to the presentation of word-meanings generated by the sentence "milk, objecthood, bringing, and impulsion," which would lead to the undesirable result of the total abolition of verbal cognition, as this same consequence would apply everywhere. By this, the view that the cognition there is purely mental (*mānasa*), and that the accomplishment of questions and so forth occurs merely through the non-apprehension of the non-connection (*asaṃsargāgraha*) of the presented word-meanings, is also refuted. Furthermore, there is the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that "I am cognizing [this] verbally. Understand, however, that the utility of determining the speaker's intention (*tātparya-nirṇaya*) and so forth lies in the determination of validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*), which in turn leads to purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).

Nor does it follow that, because the sentence "There is *saindhava* in the house" has been determined to have non-horseness as its purport, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total elimination of the doubt as to whether or not there is salt in the house; for in that case, such doubt is not eliminated due to the presence of a doubt regarding the sentence's lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). In the absence of that [doubt regarding authority], however, the desired consequence indeed follows. Therefore, by the force of the observed result, one must simply postulate that the knowledge of the absence of that purport and the knowledge of another purport act as obstacles [to the arising of the relevant cognition].

If it is argued that, even if those [entities] exist, there is no experience of cognitions having those respective objects as their content—on the grounds that the postulation of additional entities (prāmāṇika-gaurava) is not a fault—we say: no; for the apprehension of that [relation] is possible through the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) regarding a qualified object already present, or through instruction (*upadeśa*), etc., as in the case of the meaning of "you" and so forth, or of the objective case (*karmatva*) and so forth in sentences such as "buy the cow. The same must be explained for the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) regarding the relation [of word-meaning]. It is with this very point in mind that it is said: "If it is argued that the relation is not apprehended by specifying the object, then that is the same for the word as well."

If it is argued that [the word] is now [defined] by its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), then let it be so even with respect to the meaning of that term. Thus say the Dīkṣitas in their work *Vaiyākaraṇamatōnmajjana*: "The *lakṣaṇa* is that by which something is characterized; it is either the mind or instruction. The particle *api* is displaced in order, meaning "even in the case of a sentence. This is the general direction [of the argument]. In this way, in cases such as "Bring the jar," the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) consisting of the relation (*saṃsarga*) itself is the denotation (*śakya*) of the whole [sentence], because of the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Even though the capacity (*śakti*) is first grasped for the sentence-meaning as a qualified entity, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), one postulates the capacity for individual word-meanings in the individual words; thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is established that the capacity of the sentence resides precisely in the relation.

Now, since the relation itself can be apprehended through the words alone by means of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*āsatti*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*), there is no evidence for postulating a separate expressive power (*śakti*) for the sentence, and such a postulation would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, expectancy consists in the cognition of specific co-occurrences (*samabhivyāhāra*); that is, for the understanding of "the bringing of a pot as the object" (*ghaṭa-karmaka-ānayanam*), the cognition of the specific sequence—namely, the word *ampada* (accusative suffix) following the word *ghaṭa*, then the verbal root, and then the finite verb—is the cause.

For this very reason, the understanding of one who possesses a contrary linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) from expressions such as "pot, objectness, bringing, effort," whereas the lack of understanding of one who possesses correct proficiency, is both logically accounted for.

By this, the following view is refuted: that "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*)—in the form of a word's preceding or succeeding another—in a given word, which generates a cognition of the connection of a certain meaning with another meaning that constitutes the intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya*); and that the knowledge of such [co-utterance] is the cause of such a cognition. For this would result in the collapse of the distinction between those who are proficient in language and those who are not.

If, in order to avoid this, it is argued that "expectancy" is simply the knowledge of the causality of a certain co-utterance toward a certain cognition, then let that very [knowledge] be the expectancy itself, as it is necessary.

As for the claim that the certainty of non-causality (*akāraṇatva-niścaya*) is the inhibitor, or that the certainty of not causing an experience of the connection (anvaya) with respect to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the scope of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-viṣayatā-avacchedaka*) as being conditioned by the absence of that word is the cause—here some say the qualified [certainty] is the cause. Since there is no deciding factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) between [the two alternatives]: whether it is the cause by virtue of being such a certainty, or by virtue of being a cognition of the speaker’s intention residing in the listener which has as its object that which is delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absence of the experience of the connection, the truth is that the certainty of the non-experience of the connection and the certainty of the intention are causes separately. That is not so; because from [sentences] such as "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), etc.,...

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognition arising for one who has grasped the individual word-potencies of "ghaṭa" and "pada," possesses knowledge of such a sequence, lacks the certainty that [the sentence] is not the cause [of the meaning], and is conversely educated; moreover, this would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

If it is argued that by this [explanation] even the final [view] is refuted, we say no; for then the relation between words and word-meanings (*padārtha*) would also fail to be established through *śakti* (intrinsic potency). There is no fault, because the cognition of the word "pot" and the cognition of its causal capacity are themselves the causes for a cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualifier and the "pot" as its substantive. Nor is there anything additional to be postulated by me, since the status of being the object of God’s will—namely, "this particular relation is to be understood from this sentence"—is already established for me as well.

Nor can it be argued that this [universal] is not a power (*śakti*), for there is no decisive evidence to the contrary. Nor should it be said that because the property of being a producer (*janakatva*) is constituted by multiple entities, it is more appropriate to regard an additional power itself as the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) rather than that [universal]; for this objection applies equally to me, and moreover, it involves the fault of theoretical complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating an additional category.

If, however, you accept that causality (*janakatva*) itself is an indivisible property (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) and assert that this alone is *śakti*, then the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*) is established; for you too must admit that the knowledge of the sentence’s power—consisting in its being the cause of the knowledge of the sentence as a whole—is the cause [of verbal comprehension], just as the knowledge of the word’s power—consisting in its being the cause of the knowledge of the word—is [the cause]. Nor should it be argued that if causality were *śakti*, the linguistic usage "the word is powerful" (*padaṃ śaktam*) would be untenable, because the word is not the cause of cognition, but rather the knowledge of it. For, just as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is the cause in inference, the word is also such [a cause] by way of its own knowledge.

And thus, it remains nothing more than a mere technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) for "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) as being simply the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*). For this very reason, the statement that "the meaning of a sentence is a relation" (*saṃsarga*) is consistent. Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the initial apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*). It is precisely for this reason that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other texts is consistent, as it serves to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to sentences. As Harivṛṣabha has said:
"If the meaning of a sentence were not denoted by words (*aśābda*), then the meaning of a word would also [not be so]."

However, some maintain that even in cases such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), there is only a single power (*śakti*) determined by the specific sentence-meaning, because for those who have acquired proficiency in the whole [sentence], comprehension arises from that alone; and because, through the first acquisition of linguistic competence dependent upon usage, one grasps a power determined by the specific [meaning] residing in the whole.

Nor should it be argued that this [theory] lacks scriptural authority because the power of the individual parts is determined through the method of inclusion and exclusion (*avāpodvāpa*); for it is only the [power] arising at a later time—when no contradiction has yet arisen—that is postulated as the true nature [of the power], and because this is likewise necessary in cases such as *hare 've*.

Nor is there a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the cognition [of meaning] despite the non-apprehension of the qualified power, because—as explained previously—the apprehension of the power [occurs] through the apprehension of the [general] power; for even if that [qualified power] is not apprehended as you claim, there is a deviation on your part as well, since cognition occurs merely through the apprehension of the qualified power. If it is argued that there is no fault because the very factor that apprehends the qualified power necessarily apprehends that [general power], then there is no fault for me either.

For instance, they say: since you yourself accept that the general causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is grasped through the cognition of the co-occurrence (*samabhihāra*) of specific words—given that the general apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) consists in the understanding that two qualified entities, namely a word characterized by a case-ending denoting a *kāraka* and a verbal root, denote an action qualified by a *kāraka*—and since you admit that the understanding of an action qualified by a specific word-meaning occurs subsequently by virtue of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), you necessarily accept that it is precisely the grasper of those respective causal relations that grasps the qualified potency. Thus they argue.

Others do not accept this, because even by the mere expression "the jar" (*ghaṭam*), one observes the cognition of the jar's status as an object (*karmatva*); since its expressive power (*śakti*) toward that [object] is thus necessary, and since the cognition can occur in that very way, there is no evidence for further postulating that the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) has that [object] as its domain. Furthermore, the power of the individual word (*pada-śakti*) must be accepted by you as well for the sake of cognizing an action qualified by a specific [object], and because those who are ignorant of [technical categories] such as being a *kāraka*, a case-ending (*vibhakti*), or a verbal root (*dhātu*) would be unable to grasp the power in that manner.

Therefore, for whomsoever there is the apprehension of a word’s expressive power (*śakti*) in a particular manner, for that person, comprehension arises from that very [apprehension] alone. Furthermore, by incorporating conditions such as "immediately following" (*avyavahitottaratva*), any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the causal relationship between the apprehension of power and comprehension is avoided.

The apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of a sentence is also indeterminate: for some it occurs specifically; for others who already know the status of the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth, it occurs in the general way previously described; and for others, it occurs in yet another manner. Furthermore, that [power] resides precisely in the meaning characterized by a relation of qualifier and qualified, wherein there is a relational objectivity (*sāṃsargikī viṣayatā*) determined by a particularity residing in each respective word-meaning and determined by a subject-objectness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in each respective word-meaning; thus, the linguistic unit (*samudāya*) is expressive of such an object.

By this, the following view is refuted: that when there is the presentation of word-meanings independently through their individual functions (*vṛtti*), there might occur a connection (*anvaya*) between the qualifier and the qualified by way of transposition.

In the theory that the power of words resides in the universal (*jātiśaktivāda*), it must be understood that even for a sentence, the object of its denotative power is precisely the property of relational function (*saṃsargavṛttidharma*).

As for the claim that the apprehension of the power of the individual words is the cause for apprehending the power of the qualified [sentence]—because the comprehension of the sentence-meaning does not arise when the power of each individual word is absent, yet it does arise even upon hearing a previously unknown sentence when that [word-power] is present—that is unsound; for the absence of that [sentence-comprehension] is accounted for simply by the absence of the apprehension of the sentence-power. When that [sentence-power] is present, [the comprehension] certainly arises.

For this very reason, they say that the fact established by experience—that even when there is comprehension of the collective meaning through the derivation of the whole (samudāyavyutpatti), there is an incapacity to analyze the division of words without the derivation from grammar—is consistent.

Nor is there any excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in accepting the expressive power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*), because it is based on authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*), and because for you as well, a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is nonetheless necessary. [Objection: Is it not the case that, in general, for any verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having "pot" as its qualifier, the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by either a meaningful suffix (*pratyaya*) or a particle (*nipāta*) following a word denoting the object "pot"? Similarly, for any verbal cognition having "objecthood" (*karmatva*) as its object through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), the cause is the presentation produced by the base (*prakṛti*) of the suffix denoting objecthood? Thus, the causal relationship exists in this general form alone.

Nor is there a deviation [in the logical rule] due to the cognition of someone with a reversed linguistic proficiency from the expression "ghaṭaḥ karmatvam," because the cause [of the cognition of the case-role] consists in being a cognition produced by a word following the word denoting the pot (ghaṭa), and being a cognition produced by a word preceding the word denoting the object-role (karmatva). Thus, there is no fault.

Nor should it be argued that—even given this—because one must include "the state of being a denoter of a jar" (defined as being endowed with the result of the cognition of a jar) in order to prevent such a cognition from arising from a sentence like "bring a jar made of cloth," which contains the word *paṭa* (cloth) as a defining characteristic; for, since there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), it would be impossible to grasp such a causal relationship. This is because, in that case, the cognition [of a jar] is prevented simply by the absence of the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the jar produced by a word-meaning function (*vṛtti*), so there is no harm even if one includes "essential fitness" (*svarūpayogyatva*). [Response: No; for...

[The opponent argues: "Pot-ness is the object" (*karmatvaṃ ghaṭaḥ*), because for those who have mastered the linguistic convention regarding such co-occurrence as 'the accusative case marker *am* [denotes] the pot,' there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in their understanding from that [word]; furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence of abolishing the distinction between those who have mastered the convention and those who have not.

Nor should it be said that there is no fault because even the knowledge of such a causal relation serves as the cause [of verbal cognition], for even a general knowledge of that [relation] exists [in such cases].

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the specific qualification of each respective linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) in a verbal cognition is related [to that proficiency] by way of both the relation of "having an occurrence immediately subsequent to itself" (*svāvyavahitottarotpattikatva*) and the relation of "co-occurrence in the same substratum" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for this would leave the problem of an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) as it stands, and because such a grasp of the cause-and-effect relation is impossible for one who does not know [the categories of] suffixhood (*pratyayatva*), particlehood (*nipātatva*), and so forth.

Now, let it be granted that in the case of a sentence, there is [the property of] being the object of an intention to convey that [meaning], because it conveys it; however, what is the proof for its being a *vṛtti* (linguistic relation)? If this is asked, you should understand that the absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamakābhāva*) and the parsimony of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāvalāghava*) are the proofs. To explain: [Objection: If a word were the generator of knowledge, then out of fear that all hearers would obtain comprehension from every single word, one must necessarily admit—based on positive and negative concomitance—that the cause of a verbal cognition regarding a particular object is the "presentation" (*upasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the *vṛtti*.

Furthermore, a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is not a cause for comprehension by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), like fire and other such things; for since that modification exists everywhere by its own nature, it would follow that everyone would have comprehension [of everything]. Therefore, it must be admitted that it is only when the modification is known (*jñātāyāḥ*) that it functions as a cause, because comprehension does not arise even upon hearing a particular word for a person who lacks the knowledge of the modification residing in that specific word.

Although it may be that understanding does not arise for everyone merely by hearing a word, one must nevertheless accept that, for a verbal cognition having a particular object as its content, the cause is the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (denotative function) as determined by that object. Thus, since the knowledge of the *vṛtti* as determined by "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) is the cause of a cognition having "cloth-ness" as its content, there is no cognition of a jar or other objects from the word "cloth," nor is there cognition from a word whose *vṛtti* is unknown; therefore, everything is well-established.

Nevertheless, if such a causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) were accepted, then even upon the cognition of a subsistence (vṛtti) relative to jaggery—which possesses attributes other than sweetness—there might arise a cognition having "sweetness" as its qualifier through that cognition of sweetness; thus, to prevent this, the fact of being qualified by the attribute serving as the qualifier (prakārībhūtadharmānirūpitatva) must also be admitted as a factor of the subsistence.

And thus, whatever is a cognition whose occurrence (*vṛtti*) has a particular property (*dharma*) as its qualifier, the resulting awareness (*bodha*) must have that very same property as its qualifier. Since, upon hearing the word "molasses" (*guḍa*), one observes only an awareness qualified by the property of being molasses (*guḍatva*), and not an awareness qualified by various properties such as sweetness (*madhuratva*)—even though those many properties do exist in the object—it follows that the *vṛtti* of the word "molasses" is restricted solely to the property of being molasses; therefore, there is no awareness qualified by sweetness and so forth. Keeping this intention in mind, he says: "qualified by that property" (*taddharmāvacchinna*), etc.

With respect to a verbal cognition delimited by the property of having that [object] as its content and delimited by that property, [the cause is] that which is delimited by that property and is related to that [object]. [Note: This is the underlying intention—logicians have established that both the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (semantic relation) and the knowledge of the word are independently causes for verbal cognition.]

However, if one were to accept the causality of each of those two separately, there would be great complexity in postulating two distinct cause-and-effect relationships; therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the Grammarians accept the causality of the qualified [cognition] as a whole. This very point is demonstrated by the phrase "qualified by its occurrence" (*vṛttiviśiṣṭa*): cognition qualified by its occurrence is the cause, and thus there is only a single cause-and-effect relationship.

In your view, however, for a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) that possesses a relational objectivity (*sāṃsargikaviṣayatā*) directed toward that [relation], there is an additional causal relation between the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣājñāna*) and its effect. Furthermore, there is another redundancy: in the causal relation between the knowledge of the word-meaning function (*vṛttijñāna*) and its effect, the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) and the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) must be specified individually. To prevent the cognition of a thing qualified by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) from arising from the word "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvapada*) when its expressive power (*śakti*) has been grasped through a reversal of the qualifier-qualificand relationship, the phrase "delimited by that property" (*taddharmāvacchinna*) is included.

The occurrence of that [word-meaning] and its qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) should be understood as existing in a cognition by way of two relations: (1) co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with an awakened latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is itself, and (2) having as its object its own substratum. Therefore, he states the result of the first relation constituting the qualification: "not for one who has not grasped the word-meaning" (*nāgṛhītavṛttikasya*). He states the result of the second: "nor for one who lacks knowledge of the word, etc. (*nāpi padādyajñānavataḥ*). In such cases, because there is no knowledge of the word in the word itself by way of being its object (*viṣayatā*), and because there is an absence of knowledge of the word in the self (*ātman*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

The term "word" (*pada*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*), since the cognition of meaning can occur even through the movement of limbs of the body and so forth. They say that there is no comprehension for one who has not grasped the word's function (*vṛtti*), nor for one who lacks knowledge of the word and its constituents.

By this it is shown that since there is no evidence for the existence of a single "objectness" (*viṣayatā*) common to the qualificand, the qualifier, and the relation, and since the triad of "qualificand-ness" (*viśeṣyatā*) and so forth is necessary to account for the linguistic usage of these three, it is possible to denote all three by the general term "objectness. Furthermore, regarding the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), there is greater parsimony (*lāghava*) in positing two [types of objectness] rather than three.

Now, although objecthood (*viṣayatā*) is not identical to the nature of the object itself—for from the cognition "the jar is the object" there does not arise the cognition "the jar possesses the nature of a jar," as it would if they were identical—and because otherwise cognitions of past or future objects would result in being objectless due to the absence of an object-natured objecthood, and because doubt as to whether something is an object or not would persist even when its jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth are determined, and because otherwise the distinction between the two specific cognitions "the jar and the ground" (a collective apprehension) and "the jar on the ground" (a qualified cognition) could not be established according to the principle of the relatum-ness (*anuyogitva*) of the conjunction between the jar and the ground; nevertheless, that [objecthood] consists solely in the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) and is not a distinct entity, for there is a lack of evidence [for its existence] and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

And thus, by way of its connection with various cognitions, "verbalness" (*śābdatva*) alone would be the delimiting property of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), which is cumbersome. Nor does it follow that if [verbal knowledge] were of the nature of cognition itself, there would be the unwanted consequence of an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I am a knower of the ground qualified by the jar," following a cognition like "the ground has a jar"; for this is because the objectivities (*viṣayatā*) residing in the jar, the ground, and so on, as determined by such cognitions, would result in being non-distinct [from one another]. Consequently, just as one has the after-cognition "I am a knower of the jar as the qualifier," one would likewise have the after-cognition "I am a knower of the ground as the qualifier."

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that a collective cognition such as "the pot and the cloth" is erroneous; for the objective state (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the cloth—which is of the nature of that cognition—is non-different from the objective state in that same form as it is determined by the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) of "pot-ness," and thus that [cognition] would be a determiner of an objective state residing in the cloth, which possesses the absence of that [pot-ness] as determined by the mode-ness of "pot-ness.

Moreover, just as a cognition, being connected with a pot and so forth by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), brings about the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of having the pot as its object, so too, because it is connected with time and so forth by its own nature, it would likewise bring about the linguistic usage of having those [time, etc. as its objects.

Furthermore, it must be said that in the cognition "the pot is the object," the understanding [of the relation] would be untenable because it is impossible for a single entity to possess both the state of being the qualified (nirūpyatva) and the state of being the qualifier (nirūpakatva). However, there is no such fault; for even though cognitions such as "the floor possesses a pot" are admitted to consist of a mode (prakāratā) residing in the pot and a qualificandness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the floor, this is due to the force of the result [of the cognition] and the force of experience, since [in the case of "the pot is the object"] it does not consist of a qualificandness residing in the pot and a mode residing in the floor.

Otherwise, even if you accept [the existence of] additional [entities], when asked why those cognitions do not possess the property of being the determiner of a qualificand-ness residing in that [pot, etc.]—which is itself determined by a qualifier-ness residing in the pot and so on—your only answer would be silence.

Likewise, although a collective cognition (samūhālambana) consists of a qualificand-ness residing in a pot as determined by a qualifier-ness residing in pot-ness, it does not have the nature of a false cognition (bhrama), because it does not consist of a cloth-residing qualificand-ness as determined by that [pot-ness], and because it is possible for that which determines [the cognition] as a cognition to be determined [in turn] as a qualificand-ness.

Nor should it be argued that, because that which has the nature of knowledge is not produced by [another] cognition and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the cognition "it was known prior to that"; for if knowledge exists, such a consequence is acceptable (*iṣṭāpatti*), and if it does not exist, the absence of cognition is explained simply by the absence of its own nature.
