This is rejected, however, because since individual instances of knowledge are not uniform (*ananugata*), the possibility of a uniform causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) remains as before; furthermore, this is refuted by the fact that a uniformity is possible through the acceptance of *viṣayatātva* (the universal of objecthood) as something over and above [individual instances].

They say that there is no harm even in accepting a distinct single objecthood (*viṣayatā*), because of the inclusive linguistic usage such as "object, object" and because it serves as the delimitor of the aforementioned effect-ness (*kāryatā*).

If it is argued that for one who hears the sentence "ākāśo'sti" (space exists), there would arise a verbal cognition having space as its object—even though the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the denotative function (*vṛtti*) of the word *ākāśa* has not been awakened—because space is remembered from that very word by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), we say: no. This is because the cause of a verbal cognition is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the denotative function itself, through either the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) or the relation of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). Thus, there is no fault. By the term "proximity" (*āsatti*), what is meant is precisely the mental presentation of the word-meaning produced by the word through its denotative function.

For this very reason, rice (*taṇḍula*) and the like, which are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), do not become objects of the verbal cognition produced by the sentence "he cooks" (*pacati*). However, the definition that "proximity (*āsatti*) is the non-interruption of words" is not tenable; for in the case of "The mountain, Devadatta has eaten, [is] possessed of fire" (*girir bhuktaṃ agnimān devadattena*), a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) would fail to arise due to the lack of such proximity. If it is argued that the syntactic connection arises from the "constructed sentence" (*yojanāvākya*) itself, we say no; for this would entail that the original sentence is non-expressive. It should be understood that the constructed sentence is useful as a factor that reveals the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), just like context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such factors.

Nor should it be argued that when one recalls both the sentence "Bring the jar" and the elephant by way of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), there would result a verbal cognition regarding the elephant-keeper just as there is regarding the jar—since the elephant-keeper would likewise be an object of the verbal cognition because the word-meaning presentation (*padārthopasthiti*) in the form of a collective apprehension is produced by the linguistic function (*vṛtti*). This objection is invalid, because the causal relationship between the knowledge of the word's power (*śaktijñāna*) and the word-meaning presentation remains intact when the requirement of having the same object (*samānaviṣayatva*) is applied.

As for the claim that—by way of being the object—the cognition produced by a *vṛtti* (linguistic function) with respect to the word itself is the cause [of the verbal cognition] through that very relation—that is not so; for it would result in a contradiction with the established doctrine of all the learned authorities (*tāntrika*) that the relation is manifested even when it is not itself presented [to consciousness].

Furthermore, the delimitor of the effect-ness of the knowledge of a sentence must be stated to be simply "the state of being a qualified cognition" (*viśiṣṭabuddhitva*), according to the reasoning previously mentioned. And thus, since the purpose would be fulfilled by the mere presentation [of the constituents], there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the elimination of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), as such a pair of cognitions is contrary to experience.

Thus, in cases such as *vasnasādi* ("purchase with money") and *hare'veti* ("O Hari, come"), there is initially only the presentation of word-meanings regarding the relational aspect (*saṃsargāṃśa*) through a specific power (*viviṣṭa-śakti*), due to the presence of the factors that awaken that power. Subsequently, when the awakening factors are present for that [relational] aspect as well, there arises the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-bodha*) having that as its object. For this very reason, the traditional maxim that "the sentence-meaning is unprecedented" (*apūrva*) is consistent. They say that "unprecedentedness" (*apūrvatva*) consists in not being the object of a memory produced by the words that generate the verbal comprehension at the moment immediately preceding that comprehension.

As for the argument beginning with "Furthermore," that is not correct; for the cognition of the meaning of a sentence lacks the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*), since even one who hears of heaven, hell, and so forth does not have the realization, "I am experiencing this. Therefore, verbalness (*śābdatva*) is simply a specific genus (*jāti*), postulated on the strength of experience, and is not subsumed under the nature of direct experience.

Furthermore, the very nature of being a distinct type of cognition (vijātīyajñāna) such as that of a sentence is the delimiting factor for the effecthood (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) of verbal cognition. Therefore, memory does not arise from it. Otherwise, since for you too there exists a relationship in the form of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) with the sentence, the suspicion that memory would be produced from it would be impossible to dispel. This [distinctive nature] alone is the delimiting factor for the effecthood of the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*).

Nor should it be argued that, because this [cognition] is of the nature of memory (*smṛti*), there would be comprehension of the sentence-meaning even for one whose latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has not been awakened regarding the knowledge of the cause of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*); for, in accordance with the observed result, we must assume that even in that case, an awakened latent impression is the cause. Furthermore, the presentation of the word-meanings is indeed nothing but memory.

And thus, from the word "jar" alone, there is only the recollection of the jar qualified by the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), not verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*); therefore, in that case, there is no requirement for an apprehension (*upasthiti*) produced by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*). Similarly, in cases such as "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), by virtue of the capacity of the assumed "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) within the compound, at the very time of the apprehension of the word-meanings, an awakening factor (*udbodhaka*) is necessarily assumed even with respect to the relational element; consequently, the apprehension of the word-meanings has the qualified object as its content.

It should be understood that the linguistic usage "I understand through verbal testimony" (*śābdyajñāna*) arises merely from its being produced by words, and is distinct from other types of memory; however, it should not be understood as being characterized by a specific universal (*jāti*) that serves as the delimitor of the causal efficacy (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the cognition of a sentence and the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*).

As for the argument that if the presentation of word-meanings were merely recollection (*smṛti*), it would entail the postulation of a foundational relation distinct from "being a reminder" (*smārakatā*); for the cognition of one related thing is a reminder of the other related thing, but that [cognition] itself is not the relation, since such is not observed in the case of elephant-drivers and the like. Furthermore, the relation between two word-meanings is simply their capacity to convey [each other], as it will be shown that there is no power (*śakti*) in addition to that. And in your own view, this cognition is clearly nothing other than the form of recollection arising from the word.

That is not so; for the delimitor of the causal capacity (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) of the cognition of a word is its being a cognition whose object is that meaning common to both [the remembered and the newly understood]. Thus, a relation consisting in the generation of a verbal cognition distinct from mere remembrance is already established. For when word-meanings are presented by words, it is by those very words—assisted by the sentence-potency (*vākyaśakti*)—that a verbal cognition is produced which has both the word-meanings and their mutual relations as its objects. This is the sequence; enough with further elaboration.

As for the Mīmāṃsakas’ claim that since the meaning is established through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, it is not proper to postulate a direct denotative power (*śakti*) for the sentence-meaning: this is not so. Nor is there any lack of novelty (*apūrvatva*), because a person who has never previously known the specific river named Haridrā, upon hearing the sentence "There are no cows in the Haridrā" and encountering the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "river," can at that very moment grasp the denotative power of the word "Haridrā" as referring to that specific river. Subsequently, just as the cognition of a bank arises through its connection [to the river] by means of the gender-indication (*liṅga*) of the word "river," so too, when the word-meanings are presented by the words, the sentence-meaning—which is presented from that very source through the assistance of the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors—can be grasped. Thus, the sentence-meaning is indeed apprehended.

Even though [the object] is thus presented, because it is not presented through the primary function (*vṛtti*), that cognition is not verbal; for there is an experience of a cognition qualified by the mode "verbal-ness," which implies that the apprehension of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs in the interim. And that [indication] is the presentation of [the secondary object] as being related to what is cognized by itself (*svabodhya*); for, according to the ancient system, indication consists precisely in the presentation of what is cognized by itself as being related to that which is cognized by itself.

Alternatively, its apprehension consists in [the understanding that] a sentence is that which makes known an object related to itself—just as the word *gaṅgā* makes known a current related to the bank. And "indicative function" (*lakṣakatva*) is precisely the state of making known an object related to itself. Furthermore, the "indicative function" (*lakṣaṇā*) is simply the relation with the object to be made known. And since "conveying an object not already apprehended" means the state of being a communicator [of meaning] unassisted by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, along with the presentation of the object of the word generated by the word, there is no loss of the Veda’s authority, which consists in its conveying an object not already apprehended.

That is not so; for such a pair of cognitions is never experienced, and because there is no apprehension of an inconsistency [in the primary sense], metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is untenable. Nor can it be argued that indication occurs because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) would otherwise be inexplicable, since that [intended meaning] is not a cause in all cases. Furthermore, given that one must necessarily assume a cognition of the intended meaning beforehand, it is more appropriate to assume a primary denotative power (*śakti*) itself.

In reality, however, it has been explained in detail in the *Ekārthībhāvavāda* that "metaphorical indication is simply a relation with the primary meaning (*śakyasambandha*), not a relation with the object to be understood (*bodhyasambandha*). Thus, according to that view, indication is impossible to maintain; this is the direction of the argument.

As for the claim that a sentence has no power (*śakti*) with respect to the sentence-meaning, but rather that only words have power with respect to the related meaning (*anvita*), since the cognition of that meaning is established by the words alone, there is no evidence for postulating power in the sentence as well.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for something to be the object of verbal cognition without being the object of a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), one must necessarily accept a function whose object is the sentence-meaning. And since this [function] is not distinct [from the word-powers], on account of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is postulated that the already established word-powers themselves have that [sentence-meaning] as their object. This is because, although words generally possess power with respect to what is related to another, there is no cognition of a generality that lacks a specific object.

The specific cognition of the relation (*anvaya*) determined by the particularities of each respective word-meaning is established solely through the general capacities of those words, by virtue of the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—which consists in the cause of a specific syntactic collocation (*samabhihāra*).

By this it is shown that if words themselves were the denoters of what is related to others (*itarānvitābhidhāyaka*), then for one who has grasped the capacity of a word such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) as being related to others, and who possesses the knowledge of the sequence [of words] in the utterance "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of a cognition of "the bringing having the jar as its object," even for one who has not grasped the aforementioned causal relationship [between the knowledge of the sequence and the cognition].

Furthermore, because there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the following four types of cognition would result in a general sense: "the pot is connected with something else," "the objecthood (*karmatva*) is connected with something else," "likewise, the bringing (*ānayana*) [is connected]," and "likewise, the action (*kṛti*) [is connected]"; thus, the cognition "this is the objecthood belonging to the pot" would not arise. Moreover, for one who has grasped the word-potency (*śakti*) as residing in the objecthood and so forth connected with something else—based on the statement "the pot, the objecthood, the bringing, the action"—such a cognition would likewise result; therefore, [the theory of] potency in the connected is refuted.

Furthermore, since even when only a single word is employed, there is invariably observed a desire to know the correlate of its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and since that desire is necessarily preceded by a general cognition of the relation (*anvaya-sāmānya*), and since such a cognition cannot arise from anything other than the word itself, it is the word alone that expresses the related meaning. Nor is this [meaning] something entirely new (*apūrva*); for although the specific sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), consisting of the particular relation with other word-meanings (*padārtha*), may not have been previously presented, it is easily available through the mode of a general property such as "being related," which was already present beforehand.

The claim that "the word-potency (śakti) resides in [the word] as related to another" is indeed incorrect; for since the other object-entity is obtainable from another word, it is useless to include that portion within the scope of the apprehension of potency. As for the cognition of the pot alone from the word "pot," they say this arises from an error regarding potency.

That is not so; because there is parsimony (lāghava) in taking the property of being a verbal cognition whose object is the pot (*ghaṭaviṣayaka-śābdatva*) as the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), rather than the property of being a verbal cognition whose objects are both the pot and its relation (*ghaṭānvayobhayaviṣayaka-śābdatva*).

Furthermore, even if you accept that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the syntactical connection (*anvaya*), you must also accept that co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) is the cause for the cognition of specific meanings. Moreover, to prevent the cognition of someone who has not grasped this causal relationship, you would have to accept that the *grasping* of that relationship is also a cause; thus, there is the fault of an excessive complexity (*viparīta-gaurava*). Furthermore, the expressive power of the sentence (*vākya-śakti*) is already established. Even the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding the meaning of a word or a sentence is justified because the rule [of their relation] was previously grasped, just as one desires to experience a particular flavor upon seeing a particular fruit.
If it is objected that, in that case, there should likewise be no fixed rule for the desire to know here, we reply: that is exactly what we intend to establish (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Furthermore, when there arises the desire, "May I have a cognition of the specific relation between these two," the cognition that this [desire] is a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatājñāna) regarding such a cognition serves as the cause. Since this [cause] is a cognition of a qualified qualifier (viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyabuddhi), just as there is a requirement for a cognition of the general property that delimits the qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakasāmānyadharmajñāna*), so too, due to the conformity with the cognition of such a specific [relation], and because of the causal relationship between the desire and the cognition based on their having the same object, the presentation of the specific [relation] is also necessary.

Nor should it be argued that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is terminated because the object is established even through its specific form (*viśeṣarūpa*), since the desire to know does not arise simply due to the absence of a cause when the object is known in its unknown form; for establishment (*siddhi*) in its own nature is not an obstacle, but rather knowledge characterized by the mode "it is established" (*siddhatvaprakāraka-jñāna*) is such an obstacle. For this very reason, when there is a desire such as "let there be knowledge of Caitra," even if that knowledge has not yet arisen, the cessation of the desire upon the cognition "knowledge of him has arisen"—due to the knowledge of its being established—is logically consistent.

If, however, it is argued that once the general relation (anvaya-sāmānya) is known, the specific relation (viśeṣānvaya) is inferred by means of it, then since the general relation can likewise be presented in that very same way, one has already proceeded on the basis of the capacity for relatedness (anvita-śakti).

Nor does the validity of verbal testimony (śabda) suffer annihilation by the possibility of establishing a relation through inference alone; for there is the experience that "it is not inferred, nor perceived directly, but rather understood from the word itself," and because the word possesses a distinct status as a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) in accordance with the requirement for the absence of a qualifier-qualified relationship sustained by the cognition of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā). Furthermore, there exists the universal "verbalness" (śābdatva), established by a unique experience which serves as the cause for the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya)—such as "I hear" or "I understand verbally"—and the causality of the cognition of expectancy and so forth toward that which is delimited by it.

There is no evidence for postulating that [the cognition] is an inference occurring within that [mental process], nor for postulating the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, especially since such a postulation would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, since inferential cognition does not arise even when the [inferential] proof (*siddhi*) is present—given that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) does arise—the inclusion of the qualification "being distinct from verbal cognition" within the defining condition (*pratibandhyatāvacchedaka*) for the obstruction of inference would entail further complexity.

Moreover, to prevent the simultaneous arising of an inference regarding fire and the like (which is not verbal) and another verbal cognition, one would have to posit that the causal complex for verbal and inferential cognition (*śābdānumiti-sāmagrī*) acts as an obstructor with respect to an inference characterized by being other than verbal (*śābdetara-anumititva*); this would result in excessive complexity.

For me, however, the principle is that [the cause of verbal cognition] is simply the presence of the verbal causal complex (*śābda-sāmagrī*) with respect to what is delimited by being an inference (*anumititva*); thus, the parsimony (*lāghava*) is quite evident. Furthermore, this is because inference is impossible [in this context]. Nor should it be argued that the following inference is easily available: "The cow possesses existence, because it is presented by a word which is the locus of expectancy and so forth conducive to a subsequent cognition of its own subject, like a jar. For, at a time when one perceives the absence of the cow's being presented by a word and so forth, there would be no occurrence of a subsequent cognition from such statements as "The cow exists."

The presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by a word (*pada*) is utilized for the cognition of the relation (*anvayabuddhi*) only as a real entity in its own right (*svarūpasatī*), not as something known (*jñātā*), because there is no evidence for such knowledge; furthermore, it would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a relation could be cognized even for that which is not presented by words, simply because one fails to perceive that it was not so presented. Nor should it be argued that the following inference holds: "The word 'cow' (*gauḥ*) is like the word 'is' (*asti*); it is an object of utterance preceded by the knowledge of the cow, because it is a word that requires another word [to complete its sense], whereas that which is not so [preceded by knowledge] is not so, like 'space' (*ākāśa*)"; for this is not the case during a state when one is certain of the absence of utterance preceded by knowledge regarding words such as 'cow'.

This is because it would result in the inconsistency of a cognition that is established by the universal experience of all people at the moment of its arising; furthermore, even under this view, a cognition possessing a primary objecthood (mukhyaviśeṣyatā) residing in a cow or similar entity remains unaccounted for. By this, the following is also refuted: the two views that either the recollection of the word’s expressive power (*śakti*) is the cause of cognition—since no cognition is observed in one who has studied but forgotten a scripture—or that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the awakened power is the cause. Even if one accepts that "power" (*śakti*) is simply causal capacity (*janakatā*), the authority of the Word (*śabda-prāmāṇya*) would be destroyed. This is because causal capacity is necessarily constituted by pervasion (*vyāpti*); since the knowledge of that specific [word-meaning] is invariably concomitant with the knowledge of pervasion, it would follow that its authority belongs solely to inference (*anumāna*). Thus, [the theory of] the authority of the Word is rejected.

Since the pervasion (vyāpti) defined by the property of being a generator (janakatā) exists between cause and effect, even if such a "cognized" term (*jñāyamāna*) leads to an inference of a cognition of its own effect, a cognition of the object possessing a distinct objective aspect (*viṣayatā*) is impossible. For the objective aspect in the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) is not the same as that in the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*). Even for those who maintain the theory of the threefold direct perception (*tripuṭī-pratyakṣa*), they assert that the form of the cognition is simply: "This is a jar; I know the jar."

If, however, the meaning of "the capacity resides in the related" (*anvite śaktiḥ*) is that the word-meaning itself as related to the meanings of other words is what is directly experienced (*anubhāvya*) by the word, and not the word-meaning in isolation—so it is said: the very capacity of words is their power to generate the experience of syntactic relation (*anvaya*), whereas the presentation of a single isolated word-meaning is of the nature of memory (*smṛti*).

This is because the fact that the cognition of one related member causes the recollection of its correlative is common to all cases, such as the elephant-driver and his elephant; furthermore, the primary relation consisting in the generation of the experience of syntactic relation remains present.

In that case, the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) is indeed established. To explain: that power does not reside in a single word, for otherwise the experience of a relational cognition would result even from the isolated word "jar" (*ghaṭa*). Furthermore, the cognition "a related jar" resulting from that [isolated word] is directly contradicted by experience. If, however, one accepts [the power] in the collection [of words], our own position is proven; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

As for the claim that it is the word-meanings (*padārtha*) or the recollection (*smṛti*) thereof that are the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), and not the knowledge of the words (*padajñāna*), because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*): namely, "with respect to verbal cognition, the presented word-meanings or their presentation are the cause, but the knowledge of the words is not, because even without it, verbal cognition arises; thus there is deviation. As it has been said: "For one who sees the white form and hears the sound of neighing, as well as the sound of the [horse's] hooves, there arises the cognition: 'A white horse is running.'"

That is not so; for otherwise, even the visual perception of a jar or the like, which arises without the aid of words, would result in being classified as verbal (śābda). If you argue that in that case there is no verbal character because of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)—"I see, I do not verbally cognize"—then the same applies to the present case as well. Since the aforementioned cognition is accounted for by inference alone, the claim that it is a verbal cognition (*śābdapratyaya*) remains unproven; such is the meaning of this section.

A person who perceives whiteness unqualified by being that of a horse or the like in that location, infers the presence of a horse from the sound of "hee" and movement from the sound of hooves, and—through the means of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)—knows the absence of any other object in that place capable of possessing such whiteness and so forth, forms the following conceptualization: the cognition [of the sentence] is assisted by the awareness that the whiteness and other qualities, which require connection with something else, would otherwise be inexplicable without mutual connection, and is further assisted by the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, resulting in the verbal comprehension of their mutual connection.

The cognition of "inexplicability" (*kāraṇi*) is as follows: whiteness, which is perceived in that location, is cognized as being unconnected with anything other than a horse; thus, it is inexplicable without its connection with a horse. In the same way, the cognition of inexplicability regarding the act of running should also be understood.

The intended meaning is as follows: the cognition of the object (*arthajñāna*) is the cause for verbal cognition (*śābda*) in general; however, its specific cause in particular cases may be the cognition of a word (*padajñāna*) and so forth. The delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) in that case is "being a verbal cognition subsequent to that" (*taduttaraśābdatva*). In other cases, it is the cognition of an inconsistency (*anupapattijñāna*). And the delimitor of the effect-ness in that case is likewise "being a verbal cognition subsequent to that. Thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). As it has been said: "For one who sees the white form and hears the sound of neighing, as well as the sound of the [horse's] hooves striking the ground, the cognition arises: 'A white horse is running.'"*1* *1 This verse is traditionally attributed to Kumārila Bhaṭṭa.*
That is not so; for [the cognition of a word] is accomplished by inference alone, and because there is no after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I am hearing [this].

Now, if it is argued that the cognition of words and sentences—which consist of a collection of phonemes—is impossible, whether on the theory of production (*utpatti-pakṣa*) or the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti-pakṣa*), since those two [phonemes] occur sequentially and thus do not exist simultaneously—[we reply: no; at the time of the perception of a subsequent phoneme, the possession of each preceding phoneme is apprehended in that subsequent phoneme through the relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*). Likewise, at the time of the perception of the phoneme following that, the possession of the previously presented qualified phonemes is apprehended in that subsequent phoneme.

Thus, at the time of the perception of each successive phoneme, the state of possessing that phoneme as qualified by the presence of each preceding one is apprehended; therefore, these two [the sequence and the phonemes] are easily apprehended. Consequently, there is a difference in cognition in cases such as *saros* and *rasaḥ*, or *nadī* and *dīnaja-rāja*.

As for the argument that—the cognition of a word, which has both real and unreal manifold objects, is produced by the causal complex of the perception of the final phoneme assisted by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by the experience of each individual phoneme, and being of the nature of both memory and perception, it involves the recollection of those very phonemes as they were presented in their sequential order; thus, there is no lack of distinction between the original sequence and its reversal—[that is rejected].

That is not so; for there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of experience and memory. Moreover, it is observed that even without remembering what was experienced on the previous day, one may remember what was experienced on the previous day.

Furthermore, they say: because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and the memory do not have the same object, and because the sequence is neither the object of the impression nor the object of the memory.

In this regard, the following should be understood: the threefold distinction of *sphoṭa* described here is not established according to a difference among disputants (*vādibheda*), but rather according to a difference among cognizers (*boddhṛbheda*). For some, comprehension arises from the apprehension of the respective powers of meaning for both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) individually; for others, from the apprehension of that [meaning] in a conventional word such as a *subanta*; and for others, from the apprehension of it in their aggregate. All three are necessary.
Any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the causal relationship [between word and meaning] is to be avoided by incorporating conditions such as "immediately subsequent" (*avyavahitottaratva*).

However, there is this distinction: for everyone, the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) regarding each specific combination occurs with respect to that particular aggregate. Furthermore, the truth is that even such an aggregate generates a cognition of a distinct type; it is not merely a recollector (*smāraka*).

It is with this very intention that it is stated under the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau* (Pāṇini 1.1.46): "Or rather, he teaches as much as he is able to teach in a general sense; first he teaches the base (*prakṛti*), then the verbal root (*dhātu*) beginning with *val* and followed by an *artha*, and thereafter the augment *ik*; through this, he understands a specific aggregate of other words."

The meaning is as follows: "By means of the form—namely, the instruction characterized by [the presence of] roots (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), augments (*āgama*), substitutes (*ādeśa*), and so forth, which are conceptualized by the intellect—the eternal word (*nityapada*) consisting of that aggregate is explained (*anvākhyāyate*).

Here, by the term "aggregate" (*samudāya*), a divisible entity (*sakhaṇḍa*) is indicated; and its divisibility consists in having parts such as roots, suffixes, and augments as taught by the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*).

Nor should it be argued that because phonemes (*varṇa*) differ according to the difference in their utterance, and because their respective sequences (*ānupūrvī*) differ, it is difficult to establish the apprehension of their expressive power (*śaktatāgraha*) due to the faults of infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for this is not the case when one accepts that phonemes and the like are unitary, all-pervading (*vibhu*), and eternal.

This is because, given that the base (*prakṛti*) and other elements possessing those parts serve as the designators of the aggregate form [of the word], there is an absence of both infinity and deviation; furthermore, just as cloth and the like do not differ in their spatial configuration even when located in different places, there is likewise no difference in the sequence constituted by them even when occurring at different times.

Just as a cloth is produced from the conjunction of threads, so too is a word produced from the conjunction of phonemes (*varṇa*); this is equally applicable. As for the objection that qualities (*guṇa*) cannot reside in other qualities, that is indeed unacceptable, because of common usage such as "of one form" (*ekarūpa*). Likewise, let there be a figurative usage here as well.

For this very reason, Pāṇini’s formulation of the great technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*), "conjunction is [the name for] consonants not separated by vowels" (*halo'nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ*), is consistent; moreover, according to the view that [phonemes] possess a single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*), their status as substances (*dravyatva*) is accepted.

Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the identity of the phonemes existing on the surface of the earth; for there is indeed proof in the form of the non-difference cognition known as *pratyabhijñā* (recognition), expressed as "this is that very same [phoneme]," which arises now after remaining unmanifest for a period of three hours. Nor can its object be the absence of difference whose counter-positive is delimited by the universal *gatva* (the property of being the sound *ga*), because a *gatva* distinct from the individual manifestation is not admitted.

If it is argued that the suffix *matup* would be untenable if [the universal] were non-different from the individual—since that suffix is not admitted in cases of identity, as one does not say "the pot possesses a pot"—we say no; for even when there is non-difference between a quality and its possessor, such usage is possible, as in the case of "the pot has color" (*rūpavān ghaṭaḥ*).

Or, let it be distinct; even so, there is no fault, because among distinct individuals such as pots, the absence of difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "pot-ness" exists. Furthermore, since the non-difference of the individual must necessarily be the object in that instance due to the occurrence of the cognition "this is that," and because recognition has the individual as its object, there is no sublation [of the claim].

Nor is the cognition "the letter *ga* has arisen" a sublater [of the theory of manifestation], because that [cognition] resides in the arising and so forth of the manifesting sound (*dhvani*). Since it can be accounted for as residing in the phoneme (*varṇa*) through a mediated relation (*paramparā-sambandha*), it lacks the power to invalidate [our position]. Furthermore, since we admit that [the cognition] resides in the phoneme through a mediated relation, it cannot be considered an error. What remains is the claim that it is an error regarding the aspect of the direct relation. But even that is equal to your own view that the cognition "this is that same [person]" is an error regarding the aspect of the non-difference of the individual (*vyakti*).

However, the assumption of my [position]—that there is the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of those infinite phonemes—is more parsimonious (*lāghava*). But for you, that would have to be the case, which is a great undesirable consequence (*mahadaniṣṭam*). By this, the argument that it is more parsimonious to assume the error of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) alone rather than assuming the error of both the cognitions of production and destruction, is refuted. Furthermore, the perception of "arising"—which consists in being existent while previously non-existent—is not experienced in the case of phonemes; therefore, the cognition and linguistic usage are "he utters the phoneme," and not "he produces it."

And "being uttered" consists in being characterized by a manifestation produced by the contact of the palate, lips, and so forth. Thus, when the non-difference between what was previously experienced and what is now being experienced is established,
then by the maxim, "Who shall destroy this which has remained stable for that long?",
its very permanence [is proven].

If it is argued that, in this case, there would be no such cognition as "this [sound] originates from a woman" or "this originates from a parrot," nor would there be an inference of the parrot and so forth upon hearing it;

furthermore, because of cognitions such as "this is that same *gurjarī* melody" or "this is that same lamp-flame," those too would have to be eternal—[we reply]: No. This is because the specific difference (*vaijātya*) experienced in the sounds (*dhvani*) that manifest the phonemes (*varṇa*), which serves as the delimiting factor for being produced by a woman, a parrot, and so on, exists in the phonemes themselves through a causal chain, and thus [the theory] remains unimpaired.

By this, the argument that there is a distinction [between phonemes] due to the superimposition of contradictory properties—such as nasality and non-nasality, acute and grave accents, shortness and length, and high and low pitch—is refuted.

That which was spoken by Rāma is now spoken by Kṛṣṇa; that very same high pitch (*tāra*) heard by me is now perceived as low (*manda*). Since there is no contradiction between its being high and its being low, and because it contradicts universal experience that the very same lotus which was read loudly by Viṣṇu relative to Devadatta is read softly by him relative to that same person—rather than this being a different verse—and because it would entail the consequence of it being a different verse, [the identity] in cases such as the *gurjarī* or the lamp is a delusion, since destruction is established through other means of knowledge.

Nor should it be argued that, given the eternity [of the phoneme], the property of being a direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) caused by the contact of air with the palate, lips, and so forth cannot be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the effect [the cognition of *ka*], whereas for me [the proponent of the theory of manifested sound] the property of being *katva* (the universal of *k*-ness) alone suffices, which is simpler; for this is not lighter than the postulation of infinite prior absences (*prāgabhāva*), destructions (*dhvaṃsa*), and so on, and because it has been established that even a cumbersome property can serve as a delimiting factor, and because *gatva* (the universal of *g*-ness) itself is the delimiting factor of the effect by virtue of being the objective content delimited by direct perceptibility.

If it is argued that, in this case, even a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth would be eternal, and that the conjunction of potsherds and the like would merely be its manifestor (*vyañjaka*), we say no. This is because the perception of [the jar’s] production cannot be considered an error regarding its direct relation [to reality] unless there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). In the case of phonemes (*varṇa*), such an error is impossible because both the apprehension of them as produced and the contrary apprehension [of them as unproduced] exist; furthermore, under the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), such an objection would lead to an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor should it be said that if the letter *ka* and others were perceived without a manifestor, there would necessarily arise doubt—just as with a jar situated in darkness—due to the absence of any defect (*doṣa*) [in our cognition]; for even for you, the doubt regarding their being produced and so forth would be equally unavoidable.

One might object: "In the case of non-phonemes (avarṇa), there is a lack of evidence for the existence of sound (dhvani), and its production is impossible due to the absence of [articulatory] effort (saṃskāra) and so forth. This must be answered: because the perception of sound is established by experience even when phonemes are not perceived. Furthermore, it is observed that in the case of phoneme articulation, when the tongue moves slightly away from its respective place of articulation, the phoneme is not perceived while the sound is perceived; thus, one must postulate that the impact of the tongue, the air, and the contact with the throat, etc., are the generators of that sound. Moreover, if one does not accept the production of sound in the case of phoneme articulation, it would lead to the unwarranted complexity (gaurava) of postulating a relationship of mutual obstruction and non-obstruction.

Nor should it be argued that, in the sense of "crosses by means of a jar" (*ghaṭena tarati*), the suffix *ṭhan*—which is characterized by two vowels (*dvyañ*)—would not apply; for this is established through the designation of "having two vowels" (*dvyañ*) based on the recurrence (*āvṛtti*) [of the vowel count]. This is because the prohibition regarding horses (*aśva*) and so forth indicates that even a secondary (*gauṇa*) application is included in that domain. For this very reason, in forms such as *kariṇā*, the acute accent of the case-ending prescribed by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.168] does not occur, since the designation of "having one vowel" (*ekāc*) has been set aside by the designation of "having two vowels" (*dvyañ*) resulting from the recurrence. Indeed, one who has three sons does not receive the designation of "having two sons."

Nor is there a confusion of grammatical operations (*anubandhasaṅkara*), because just as for a single person, Devadatta, the instructions regarding his being matted-haired or shaven-headed are regulated by the difference of location, so too is the application of markers such as *ṭit* and *kit* logically established by the difference of location. Nor does it follow that if [the phoneme] were one, there could be no perception of it in different locations; for since its substratum, space, is one, there is an absence of spatial differentiation itself. However, if one accepts that such differentiation is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), then there is no flaw, as such adventitious differentiation—caused by the limiting adjunct of conjunction with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*)—exists even in the case of a phoneme. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the sūtra "aiuṇ."

Nor is it impossible for there to be perception of a word (*pada*) due to the momentariness of its manifestation, because the same [objection] applies even if [the word] is produced (*janya*). Furthermore, such perception is possible because the ear, aided by preceding impressions (*saṃskāra*), perceives the subsequent letters as qualified by the previously manifested letters. Moreover, "immediately following" (*avyavahitottaratva*) means not being the object of a cognition that arises in a moment which is the locus of its own cognition uninterrupted by the production [of the preceding letter]. And thus, since the word is a single unit, there is no requirement for a unifying form (*anugamakākāra*), and consequently, there is no necessity for a delimiting property of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). That very [word-unit] itself, through identity (*tādātmya*), is the delimiting factor.

Even the cognition that [the word] makes its meaning known occurs only upon hearing the final phoneme as qualified by each preceding phoneme through an immediately preceding relation; thus, if there is a deficiency in the hearing of the phonemes, there is no comprehension. This is the general direction. Thus concludes the exposition of the *sakhaṇḍa* (composite) word- and sentence-sphoṭa.
Now begins the exposition of the *akhaṇḍa* (indivisible) word- and sentence-sphoṭa.

In the *Varṇamālā*, it is stated that because of the cognition "one word" or "one sentence," and because of the cognition "this very thing, bring the jar; this very thing [is the jar]" regarding a sentence, one must necessarily accept a word and a sentence that are distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), unitary, indivisible, devoid of divisions such as base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), and manifested by the phonemes. For it is not tenable that this cognition of unity has the phonemes as its object, since they are many. Nor is it the case that this [cognition] is like "one forest," because a forest, a heap, and so forth, are also entities distinct [from their constituent parts].

Furthermore, in that case (the compound), since the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—namely, being delimited by a single portion—is unitary, such a cognition as being accompanied by an adjunct is logically possible. However, in the present context, such an adjunct is impossible. Nor can it be the status of being the cause for the cognition of a single meaning; for if that were so, both the analytical expression (*vyāsa*) and the compound (*samāsa*) would result in being identical, and moreover, such a cause is impossible in the case of a sentence. As for the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *ādyantavat* (Pāṇini 1.1.21), which states that "a word is a collection of phonemes," etc., that is based on the view that the collection is something distinct [from its parts].

Furthermore, this being the case, since there is the experience of parts even within phonemes (*varṇa*), a phoneme as a whole distinct from those parts would not be established. For example, in the phoneme *ṛ*, there is the *repha* (the sound *r*); in *lṛ*, the *lṛkāra*; in *e* and *ai*, the *akāra* and *ikāra*; and in *o* and *au*, the *akāra* and *ukāra*. Even in long vowels and the like, there are short forms such as *a* and so forth. What need is there for more? Within the phoneme itself, the existence of parts is understood through rules such as "its beginning is acute" (*tasyādita udāttam*, Pāṇini 1.2.32). It is for this very reason that the two positions—whether the parts of a phoneme are included or excluded by the term "phoneme"—were explained in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *eoṅ*.

Furthermore, if this were the case, since the conventional usage "one cloth" could be accounted for by the collection of threads alone, it would follow that a distinct composite whole (*avayavin*) is not established even there. If you argue that the existence of a distinct composite whole is established in that case because of the usage "one," then the same applies to the present instance as well.

Nor should it be argued that there are no parts within phonemes (*varṇa*) at all, and that their manifestation is merely due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of a series of specific sounds (*dhvani*) produced by particular articulations which take on forms identical to those respective phonemes; for if the manifestation of phonemes in a word (*pada*) were explained in this very same way, it would result in the total abolition of phonemes. Furthermore, indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) consists precisely in the absence of constituent parts such as stems (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). Since, according to the aforementioned view regarding the divisible word-sphoṭa (*sakhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*), comprehension arises solely through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*), there is no evidence for the existence of [phonemes] therein. In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), however, this is established by the analogy of the "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavaya*).

In the *Paspaśā* section, within the passage beginning "Now, what is a word (*śabda*)?", the *Bhāṣya* states: "That which, when uttered, brings about the cognition of [an object] possessing a dewlap, a tail, a hump, hooves, and horns. By this singular number, this position is indicated. It is clearly stated by Kaiyaṭa at that very same place. As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "Just as parts do not exist in phonemes (*varṇa*), so phonemes do not exist in a word (*pada*).
There is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and a sentence (*vākya*)."

In this context, by the word *varṇa* (phoneme), one means the base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth; for in the expression *varṇasphoṭa*, that very meaning is intended because it is the subject under discussion, and because it is obtained in exactly that sense from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtras such as "the beginning and the end" (*ādyantau*) and "as if having a beginning and an end" (*ādyantavat*).

As for those who explain: "In a word, phonemes do not exist at all; the meaning is that just as parts are perceived in [the diphthongs] *ṛ* and so forth, yet do not exist, so it is here"—for them there is a contradiction with experience, because just as threads are established by experience in a cloth which is a whole (*avayavin*), so too are phonemes established by experience in a word. The meaning is that, due to the identity of the property of being partless (*akhaṇḍatva*), there is no absolute difference between a word and a sentence, or between a sentence and a word.

If it is argued that there is no evidence for the existence of phonemes (*varṇa*), and that since, according to the previously stated method, sounds (*dhvani*) are necessary in the case of phonemes, the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* can be accomplished by those sounds alone—making it cumbersome to posit phonemes as constituent parts between the sounds and the *sphoṭa*—then let those very [sounds] be the phonemes. For in the hearing of a distant clamor, the properties such as "g-ness" (*ghatva*) belonging to the sounds themselves are simply not manifested due to the defect of distance. For this very reason, it is said: "In common usage, sound (*śabda*) is that which has its object understood through the sound."

The commentary is consistent with this; for there, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It is with this very intention that it is stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "By the ignorant grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), the term ‘dhvani’ has been applied to that which manifests the manifested form of *sphoṭa*, which is the primary [element]. Here, the "primary *sphoṭa*" refers to the *sphoṭa* in the form of words, sentences, roots, and so forth; its status as primary is due to its being the conveyer of meaning.

And thus, when the relationship has been grasped, the cognition of meaning arises either from a collection of phonemes grasped in the aforementioned sequence, or from the *sphoṭa*—which is of the nature described above and whose relationship with the specific meaning has been grasped—by means of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Furthermore, in the case of synonyms, the expressive power (*śakti*) is indeed distinct; however, since this [additional] complexity is based on authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*), it does not constitute a fault.

By this [argument], what is being asked: does this *sphoṭa* convey meaning by its own nature, or only when it is cognized? Not the first, because it would follow that there would be comprehension of the meaning at all times. In the latter case, one must state that the perception "this is one word" and so forth is the grasper of it. In that regard, does this cognition apprehend the phonemes, or not? In the former case, let the denotative capacity belong to those very [phonemes] as delimited by their sequence, since that is necessary. In the latter case, there is simply a contradiction with experience.

Furthermore, [the opponent claims] that *sphoṭa* is manifested by phonemes (*varṇa*). In that case, is the sequence of phonemes that manifests the *sphoṭa* one whose relationship with the respective specific meanings has been grasped, or one whose relationship has not been grasped? Not the first, because upon hearing poetry and the like, even for one who has not grasped the relationship between those specific meanings, there would result the cognition of *sphoṭa* such as "this is one word" or "this is one sentence. Nor the second, because since the understanding [of meaning] occurs through those [phonemes] alone, the postulation of something additional [i.e., *sphoṭa*] would be redundant.
Moreover, the cognition of unity is merely adventitious (*aupādhikī*), based on the fact that they are the objects of a single cognitive act.

Nor should it be argued that its establishment is due to the cognition "this very word is that [same word]," for such a cognition is accounted for by similarity—just as when a nail or the like has perished and is produced again, one says "this is that same nail" or "these are those same hairs" or "this is that same tree. If you argue that a distinct entity such as a nail is contradicted by experience, then it is equally true that in cases such as the word *gaur*, a sphoṭa distinct from the letter *ga* and the visarga is also contradicted by experience.

Furthermore, regarding synonymous words, is there one *sphoṭa* or many? Not the first [option], because if there were one *sphoṭa* manifested by synonyms such as *kalaśa*, *ghaṭa*, and so on, then for a person who has already grasped its expressive power (*śakti*), the cognition of the meaning would result even upon hearing an unfamiliar word, since that same *sphoṭa*—whose power was previously grasped—would be manifested by that word as well.

Nor should it be argued that the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in the *sphoṭa* manifested by each respective synonym (*paryāya*) is the cause of the cognition of meaning upon hearing that synonym; for if this were the case, since the apprehension of power would necessarily occur for every synonym, it would be more logical to hold that the cause [of the cognition of meaning] is simply the apprehension of the power residing in those respective synonyms. For you, however, there is the complexity (*gaurava*) of having to postulate the apprehension of power as residing in the *sphoṭa* manifested by each respective synonym. Nor is the latter [position] tenable, because rather than postulating the power in those [synonyms] and in the infinite word-meanings, it is simpler to postulate the power in the phonemes (*varṇa*) which are already established.

Furthermore, they say that the objection is refuted as follows: Do the phonemes (*varṇa*) possess the capacity to manifest the sphoṭa individually or collectively? Not the first, because if the sphoṭa were perceived from each individual phoneme, it would follow that the meaning would be understood by that alone. Nor the second, because according to the maxim "from that which is the cause [of the effect]," the understanding of the meaning can be accounted for from those very phonemes; thus, the postulation of the sphoṭa would be rendered useless. Therefore, [the sphoṭa theory] is rejected.

Others, however, maintain that the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is apprehended by the sense of hearing. This is because there is no evidence for the postulation of infinite phonemes (*varṇa*) and sounds (*dhvani*); because it would be improper to adopt the "half-old-woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) principle—whereby the letter *a* is one while the letters *ka*, *kha*, and so on, are many; and because properties such as *katva* (the quality of being *ka*) reside solely in the conjunctions with the manifesting air-currents. It is more logical to hold that its manifestation as *ka*, etc., occurs through conjunctions with heterogeneous air-currents, whereas through other heterogeneous [conjunctions], it is manifested in the form of sound (*dhvani*) not occupied by those [specific qualities].

Furthermore, by means of the conjunctions of heterogeneous air-currents (*vijātīyavāyusaṃyoga*) that produce each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), there is the manifestation of that [phoneme] solely as a singular entity and so forth. However, through many such [conjunctions] arising in succession, there arises the cognition of meaning from what is manifested in the form of various words and sentences. It is precisely this [manifested entity], which serves as the conveyor of meaning in the form of words and so on, that is conventionally designated as *sphoṭa*. Nor is this improper, for it is the very single phoneme in the form of an indivisible word-meaning (*akhaṇḍapadārtha*)—manifested by specific, intended conjunctions of heterogeneous air-currents that produce those respective phonemes—that [is the sphoṭa].

This is because, in the view of others, just as there is a cognition of "highness" (*tāratva*) and so forth by taking into account the presence—through a causal chain—of a specific dissimilarity (*vaijātya*) residing in the conjunction with air (which is established in other systems as the delimiting factor for the production of various phonemes or the delimiting factor for their manifestation), so too in our own system, there is the possibility of a cognition [of phonemes] by way of "k-ness" (*katva*) and so forth.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* section of the *Bhāmatī*: "The qualities such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*), which reside in the air, are superimposed upon the phonemes (*varṇa*). Furthermore, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) expressed as "This is that same letter *ga*" or "This is that same word" must be understood as referring to a single phoneme manifested by the conjunctions of air (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) that serve as its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), appearing as if colored by the properties of the manifestor—just like the reflection of a face in a mirror.

In the same way, [the cognition] "one word" and so forth also [arise], because the referent of the word (padārtha) is a single entity. Even though this [word] is eternal, the cognition that "the letter *ka* has arisen" is indeed unimpaired, since the arising—which resides in the manifestor—is present therein through a causal series (*paramparayā*). However, regarding the aspect of the direct relation [between the word and its manifestation], there is error just as before. By this, it is explained that when sublation (*bādhagraha*) is apprehended, there is no apprehension of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth residing therein.

Furthermore, the argument that "because of the rule that whatever perceives the property (dharma) of something must also perceive that [substratum], it follows that air-conjunctions would also be perceived by the ear" is refuted; for even when a property is perceived through a direct connection, its substratum is not necessarily perceived through a mediated (paramparā) connection. By this, the objection beginning with "moreover" (*kiñca*) is also cast aside. Moreover, it is accepted by others that the tongue and other sense organs grasp only taste and their respective objects.

Nor can it be argued that the conjunction with a distinct air-current (*vilakṣaṇavāyusaṃyoga*) alone should be the denoter [of the phoneme], because the experience of "I hear" and so forth necessitates the existence of something additional that is perceptible by the auditory organ. Nor should it be said that this would result in the identity of the phonemes *ka* and *ha*, or that their difference would fail to be perceived; for they are distinct due to the specific differences residing in their manifestors (*vyañjaka*), just as there is a diversity in the manifested bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpasukha*) through the variety of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) produced by contact with objects according to the Advaita doctrine. Identity is indeed accepted with respect to the substratum (*viśeṣyāṃśa*). Furthermore, the perception of such identity need not be postulated, since there is no perception of a phoneme unconditioned by its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

By this, the following objections are refuted: (1) that there would arise the cognition "this very letter *ha* is now the letter *ga*," and (2) that there would not arise the cognition "this is *ha*, not *ga*.

Nor should it be argued that it is simply the distinct conjunctions with air that are perceived by the auditory organ, and that there is no need to postulate a single additional entity; for that [single entity] is indispensable in accordance with cognitions such as "this is one *ga*" and "this is one word."

For this very reason, Vācaspatimiśra, in his *Tattvabindu*, presented the view of the proponents of *sphoṭa* (sphoṭavādins) as follows: "Because there is no letter *ka* that is distinct from the letter *ga*. For this same reason, in the commentary on the *sūtra* "aiuṇ," regarding the [first] *a* in "asyacau" [Pāṇini 7.4.32], a doubt was raised that because it is different from the *a* situated in the phonetic inventory (*varṇasamāmnāya*), it lacks the status of being an *aṇ* vowel and thus cannot include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). To this, it was replied in the section beginning with "it is established because the *a*-sound is one": "If there were only one [phoneme], there would be no simultaneous perception of it in multiple locations; yet, one does perceive it."

Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "One does not even perceive the letter *a*, because sound is that which is perceived by the ear, apprehended by the intellect, manifested through effort, and manifested through effort as a region of space; furthermore, space is one. By the phrase "perceived by the ear," he establishes that sound has the region of space as its locus.

"Grasped by the intellect" (*buddhinirgrāhya*) means that which is grasped by the final cognition, assisted by a series of impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the manifestations (*abhivyakti*) generated by each preceding sound. "Application" (*prayoga*)—so called because one applies it—is the conjunction with air, or the impact on the throat, palate, and so forth, or the sound itself. Regarding this, Kaṇṭha states: "It is ignited, that is, manifested, by that. In this context, the compound is *buddhibhirnirgrāhyaḥ*. "To be grasped" (*nirgrāhya*) means to be grasped completely (*niśśeṣataḥ*); the meaning is that [it is grasped] both in its phonetic form and in its meaning. Others maintain that this very same meaning is clarified by the phrase "ignited by application" (*prayogeṇābhijvalita*).

As for the claim that the phrase "to be grasped by the intellect" (*buddhinirgrāhya*) means "an object of the intellect," that is not correct; for it would result in a redundancy with the expression "perceived by the ear.
Indeed, it is clear to those who know the nuances of words that this [phrase] naturally conveys that a single [sound] is manifested starting from the first sound up until the final sound.

Nor should one be deluded into thinking that this refers to a word distinct from what was established in the previously mentioned view; for that would contradict the opening statement, "one does not perceive even the letter *a*."

In this view as well, the process of grasping words and sentences is exactly like that of the *sakhaṇḍavākyasphoṭa*. The process of grasping the expressive power (*śakti*) and the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) also follows the method previously described. They further maintain that even this process is not fixed, as it varies according to the differences among individual cognizers.

If it is argued that, in this case, there would follow the consequence of the scripture being non-authoritative—since words and sentences are partless (akhaṇḍa) while the scripture is devoted to explaining [them] through bases (prakṛti) and suffixes (pratyaya)—we say no; for, just as in the Uttaramīmāṃsā the introduction of the five sheaths (pañcakośa) consisting of food, vital breath, mind, consciousness, and bliss serves to reveal the Brahman which is the support of all, so too the investigation into bases, suffixes, and so forth is not a fault, as it is a means for revealing the partless sphoṭa.

If it is argued that this treatise is not the means for knowing *sphoṭa*—just as the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) are not the means for knowing Brahman—because even common folk, such as a cowherd who has merely mastered the usage of the sentence "Bring the cow," acquire a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) there even without knowledge of the science, [we reply: no; for although that knowledge may be possible through other means, there is no fault in considering this [treatise] to have that [knowledge] as its fruit, since it produces a distinct kind of knowledge by first teaching bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), which, through its own prior application, results in the purification of speech. As Hari stated:
"It is the gateway to liberation and the medicine for the impurities of speech."

And thus, since the utility of the treatise (*śāstra*) lies precisely in the knowledge of heterogeneous elements (*vijātīyajñāna*), there is no fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) such as [the case of] grass and the like. Furthermore, the utility of the treatise should be understood as the comprehension of all words by means of a concise method (*laghunopāya*). Nor does the fact that the division into stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is conceptual imply that it is as non-existent as a hare's horn; for, like the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so forth, this too is characterized as being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadvilakṣaṇa*). In this way, the treatise is also a means [of knowledge] according to the maxim of the "line-drawn cow" (*rekhāgavaya*).

And thus, the meaning of "the *sphoṭa* with parts" (*sakhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*) is that a word conveys its meaning preceded by the knowledge of the division between base and suffix and their respective meanings. Similarly, in cases such as *hare'va*, comprehension occurs preceded by the knowledge of each individual word; this is the "sentence-*sphoṭa* with parts" (*sakhaṇḍavākyasphoṭa*). The conceptualization of bases, suffixes, and so forth, follows the maxim of the "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavaya*); the truth is that the indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) word-*sphoṭa* and sentence-*sphoṭa* convey the meaning of words and sentences without relying on the division into bases, suffixes, and the like. This concludes the exposition of the indivisible word and sentence *sphoṭas*. Now, the exposition of the genus *sphoṭa* (*jātisphoṭa*).

Thus, the five types of *vyakti-sphoṭa* have been described. However, according to the proponents of *jāti-sphoṭa*, phonemes (*varṇas*) are indeed infinite; for it cannot be said that their distinction arises from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), since there is no perception of them as being embraced by such adjuncts—just as in the case of the space within a jar or the space within a hut. Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as "this is that very same one" is based on similarity (*sājātya*).

Nor should it be argued that, while there is no problem of infinite regress or deviation (*ānantya-vyabhicāra*) regarding the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words and so forth, such a solution does not hold for *ānupūrvī* (word-order), because even that is infinite due to differences among persons and differences in time; for there is no such fault, since we accept that *ānupūrvī*, just like a universal (*jāti*), serves as the delimiting factor of expressibility (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) as well as the delimiting factor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

Because of the uniform cognition—such as "this is the word *ghaṭa*," "this is the word *ghaṭa*," "this is the base (*prakṛti*"), "this is the base"—it is necessary to postulate a specific genus residing in the word itself, just like the genus *ghaṭatva* (potness) residing in the object. This is because such a genus must necessarily enter into the scope of the delimitors of causality when the knowledge of the word *ghaṭa* and so forth is held to be the cause [of verbal understanding]. Furthermore, there is the disadvantage of complexity if the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) were taken as the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). As it has been said:
"Just as in the case of being the denotable (*śakyatva*), let the parsimony of a genus be observed in the case of being the expressive (*śaktatva*).
The phrase "in the case of being the denotable" and so forth means "in the case of its being the delimitor thereof."

Furthermore, if the causal status of both [the word and its meaning] were established solely through sequential order, then even "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth would result in being otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddhi*) by means of clay and the like qualified by specific conjunctions. Nor should it be argued that because a collection of successive phonemes cannot exist simultaneously, a universal (*jāti*) is difficult to establish there—according to the maxim that "if the word 'cow' (*go*) has not been produced, how could there be the property of being the word 'cow' (*gaśabdatva*)?"—for, according to the method previously stated, such [simultaneity] is possible when [the phonemes] are made the object of a single cognition.

Furthermore, for a specific universal (*jāti*), the phonemes (*varṇa*)—distinguished by a specific sequence—are the manifestors, just as a specific shape is the manifestor of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth. Therefore, in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, there is no lack of distinction in the cognition [of meaning].

If it is objected that since the universal exists in each individual phoneme, there would be the undesirable consequence of the meaning being understood from each one individually—the answer is no; because that universal resides collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) in the collection of phonemes manifested by multiple individuals, there is no flaw. As it has been said:
"The universal, which is manifested by many individuals, is known as *sphoṭa*."

Nor does it follow that the designation *sphoṭa* cannot apply to the genus (*jāti*), even though the genus is the delimiting factor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), because there is no evidence for the genus itself being the expressive power (*śakta*). This is because, just as expressive power resides in the delimitor of the denotable meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) by way of being its object (*viṣayatā*), the genus exists in the delimiting factor of expressive power by way of being its locus (*āśrayatā*); thus, its existence remains unimpaired. This is clear from the commentary on the sūtra "aiuṇ," as well as from the works of Bhartṛhari and Kaiyaṭa regarding the passage: "The nature of the phoneme *a* is variability."

Others, however, maintain that by the principle of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* and because it is necessary, the genus (*jāti*) alone possesses the expressive power (*śakti*). And this power of expression is either delimited by identity with that [genus] or is itself undelimited, since there is no requirement for a unifying form due to the unity of the genus. Furthermore, it is only when known that it expresses meaning, just like the individual (*vyakti*). By this, the view that the *sphoṭa* exists eternally and functions to produce the cognition of meaning is refuted. Moreover, the genus is a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) belonging to the realm of ignorance (*avidyaka*). In that regard, it is simply the existence of Brahman (*brahma-sattā*) as delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); as it has been said:
Existence itself, when differentiated in cows and other things by virtue of its connection [to them], is called "universal" (jāti); all words are established in that [existence].
"She is eternal; she is the Great Self (mahān ātmā); they call her the suffixes *tv*, *tal*, and so forth;
and they declare her to be the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as well as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

Thus, Brahman alone is the denoter; however, the technical grammatical analysis (*śāstrīyaprakriyā*) regarding the manifestation of universals (*jāti*) is exactly as before, for the purpose of conveying understanding—and in this way, everything desired is established.
Thus concludes the exposition of the *jātisphoṭa*.
Having studied the ocean of Patañjali’s commentary from Sughīndra Haridīkṣita, and the system of Nyāya from Rāmarāma and Vādirakṣodhnarāma—[I have composed this work]. (1)
May Śiva, together with Umā, be pleased by Nāgeśa, the grammarian, who has expressed the doctrine of the sage Sphoṭāyana after refining it. (2)
Scholars should not think that this man lacks practice in logic;
for even stones have crossed the ocean through the power of Rāma. (3)
Having properly produced the son Śabdenduśekhara and the daughter Majjaṣā from my own thought, I have offered them to Śiva and Śivā. 4.
Thus ends the *Sphoṭavāda*, titled *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā*, composed by Nāgeśabhaṭṭa, son of Śivabhaṭṭa, whose surname was Upādhyāya.
May the illustrious Lord Śiva, together with Ambā, be pleased with me by virtue of this *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā* which has been composed by me.
May it be auspicious!
